en: The Sages arose during the era of the Zhou dynasty; though their chronological order differs, when it comes to transforming humanity through the Way of Great Centrality and Ultimate Rectitude, they are no different.
Amidst the shifting of times and the alternation of laws, Venerable Yifeng’s mind dwells in *dhyāna* while his spirit roams through historical records.
He has extracted the essentials and annotated the events to aid in contemplation, like a mirror.

At present, those who harbor a spirit of admiration and longing may find inspiration herein. On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, in the year Wuzi of the Zhizhi era (1316) during the reign of Empress Xuanzong,
this was respectfully inscribed by Xue Tianyou, styled Andao, serving as the Administrative Assistant of Funing Prefecture in Fuzhou, holding the rank of Chengshilang.

I have heard that the vastness of the blue sea cannot be fathomed for its depth or shallowness without the black dragon; likewise, the profound subtlety of the Buddha-dharma cannot be investigated to its very source without one of wisdom.
Yet, at the beginning when the Three Powers were first established by the brush, the world was called the "Great Chaos.

Humanity dwelt in caves and lived in the wilds, unable to distinguish between the honorable and the lowly; even so, the ears and eyes of these people remained as if coated with the obscurity of their limited experience.
Thus it was. Since Fuxi drew the eight trigrams, written records first came into being. When Shennong fashioned the plow and the hoe, agriculture and sowing were first established.
When the Yellow Emperor created the fundamental musical scales, the sounds of music first became manifest. When Yao and Shun donned the ceremonial robes, the system of ritual was first clarified.
It was through these various sages that the principles of heaven and earth were opened up and the social order of living beings was established, so as to enable future generations...
The authors of these works have something to uphold and follow, and from them emerges the way by which the hundred kings maintained order amidst the transformations of the world.
As for the era of the Zhou dynasty of the Ji clan, thirty-seven sovereigns reigned in succession;
during this interval, the sages of the Three Teachings appeared one after another—namely, the Buddha, Laozi, and Confucius—as is clearly evident in the historical records. From the first...
In the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao’s reign, the Jia-yin year, on the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha manifested in Kapilavastu in Western India.
He was born into the royal palace with Kṣatriya Gautama as his clan name and Prince Siddhārtha as his personal name.
Upon attaining enlightenment, he took Śākya as his lineage name and was titled Muni, which translates as "Silent One. This refers to the three [aspects of his life].
His karma was free from worldly clamor. His golden body measured one zhang and six chi, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics;
thus he was titled "Buddha. "Buddha" carries the meaning of "awakened," signifying that through the propagation of the Dharma, he awakened himself and awakened others.

He remained in the world for seventy-nine years, reaching the third year of the reign of King Ding (the twenty-first sovereign), the *ding-si* year, three hundred and forty [years] after [the Buddha's passing].
Five years later, Laozi was born in the village of Quren in Lixiang, Kuxian, within the state of Chu. His surname was Li; his given name was Er, and his courtesy name was Boyang.
He was posthumously titled Dan. Some say he was four chi and six cun tall, with thick eyebrows and white hair;
thus he was called "Laozi. "Zi" is a general term for a man. This was during the twenty-first year of King Ling, the twenty-fourth sovereign.
In the year Gengxu, when Laozi was fifty-four years of age, Confucius was born in the village of Zou in Changping, Lu.
His ancestors had prayed at Mount Nichu for his birth; because the crown of his head was flat and protruding, he was named Qiu and styled Zhongni.
His surname was Kong. His stature was nine chi and six cun. "Fuzi" (Master) is simply a title used for a great man.
He passed away at the age of seventy-three, which was the forty-first year of King Gong, the *Renxu* year.
The scriptures of Laozi speak of nurturing one's nature to preserve longevity; the books of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius instruct people to cultivate ritual and music;
and the teaching of Śākyamuni is able to bestow compassion and gather in sentient beings, serving as a field of merit for all living creatures and a dam for the river of craving.
Within the myriad things, humans alone are most spiritually gifted; within the three realms, the Buddha alone is most supreme.

The Dharma was propagated in Western India, and its teachings have flowed to the Eastern Land of Thunder (China). His true body and śarīra relics have been revered and honored through successive generations; his jade-bound volumes and golden texts are recited by every person.
This is a great support...

The nation was transformed, and sentient beings were extensively benefited. I have briefly compiled this text and recorded it hereafter to clarify the compassionate grace bestowed by the Buddhas and Patriarchs and to manifest the reverent devotion of kings and ministers.
It is titled *The Record of Buddhist Resources as a Mirror for Successive Dynasties*.

The Annals of the Emperors:
The Three August Ones;
Taohao (the Great Dawn).

He took sacrificial animals to fill his kitchen. He was styled Bao Xi; in later generations, the pronunciation was erroneously changed to Fuxi. His first title was Huangxiongshi. He belonged to the Feng clan. Ruling over the world through the virtue of Wood, he made Chen his capital for one hundred and ten years. He established the Dragon as the basis for official titles, drew the Eight Trigrams, and created writing and seals to replace the use of knotted cords.

Yandi Shennong was of the Jiang clan. He succeeded Taihao and ruled the world with the virtue of Fire. His capital was Luli, and he reigned for one hundred and forty years. He designated officials based on the element Fire and taught the people the arts of plowing and sowing. He tasted the various herbs.

The Yellow Emperor, Lord of Xiong, was of the Gong-sun clan and named Xuanyuan. He succeeded Yan Di and ruled the world with the virtue of Earth for one hundred and ten years. A celestial omen of clouds appeared, so he recorded his offices by means of clouds. He established his capital at the foot of Zhuolu. He charged Da-nao to observe the moon and first created the sexagenary cycle (Jiazi), devised the calendar and mathematics, and fashioned the pitch-pipes and musical scales. He charged Cangjie to create written characters; he fashioned robes and garments, constructed boats and carts, and erected houses with ridgepoles to benefit the myriad people. He made bows and arrows to awe the world. He did not dwell in a fixed location.

The Five Emperors include Shao Hao of Jintian, the son of the Yellow Emperor, named Zhi. He succeeded the Yellow Emperor and ruled the world with the virtue of Metal. His capital was Qufu, where he reigned for eighty-four years; he appointed officials based on the names of birds.

Zhuanxu of the Gaoyang clan was the grandson of the Yellow Emperor. His surname was Ji. He succeeded Shao Hao and ruled the world with the virtue of Water. His capital was Diqiu. He occupied the throne for seventy-eight years and established offices based on human affairs.

Di Ku, of the Gaoxin clan, was the great-grandson of the Yellow Emperor. He succeeded Zhuanxu and ruled the world with the virtue of Wood. His capital was at Bo, and he occupied the throne for seventy-five years.

Emperor Yao of the Taodang clan was the son of Emperor Ku. His surname was Yiqi. He succeeded Ku and ruled the world with the virtue of Fire. His capital was Xianyang. He occupied the throne for seventy years. He abandoned his son Danzhu and elevated Shun, passing the mandate to the worthy rather than to kin. He ascended the throne in the year Jiachen; this was reckoned from that Jiazi cycle.

Emperor Shun of the Yushu clan was the sixth-generation descendant of Zhuanxu. Ji received the abdication from Yao and ruled the world as the sovereign of the Earth Virtue (*tùdé*). He established his capital at Púbǎn. On the Jiǎwǔ day, he was enfeoffed; he served as regent for twenty years. On the Rénwǔ day, he ascended to the true throne for fifty years. He abandoned his son Shāngjūn and transmitted the mandate to the House of Xià.
The Three Dynasties,
beginning with the Xia from the year Wuxu and ending with Jiyou, comprised seventeen sovereigns for a total of four hundred and thirty years.

Yu: surnamed Si, the son of Gun. Shun conferred the throne upon him. He ruled the world with the virtue of Fire and established his capital at Han. He occupied the throne for fifteen years. Under Jie, Tang deposed him, and the world passed to the Shang dynasty.
The Shang dynasty lasted from Gengxu to Wuyin, comprising thirty sovereigns for a total of six hundred and twenty-seven years.

Cheng Tang, surnamed Zi and named Lü, was the thirteenth-generation descendant of Qi. He ruled the world with the virtue of Water and established his capital at Bo. He reigned for thirteen years; having deposed Jie, the feudal lords enthroned him as Son of Heaven. Under Zhou, King Wu launched a campaign against him, and the world submitted to the Zhou.
The Zhou dynasty began at Jǐmǎo and ended at Yǐshì, spanning thirty-seven sovereigns over eight hundred and sixty-seven years.

King Wén was of the Jī clan; his name was Chāng. During the Zhou period, he served as the Western Hegemon (Xībó) and possessed two-thirds of all under heaven. His son, Fǎ, known as King Wǔ, campaigned against the Shāng, deposed Zhòu, and ruled the world by the virtue of Wood. He occupied the throne for seven years and established the first month of the year as the month of Zǐ (the eleventh lunar month). This continued until the thirteenth ruler, King Píng Yíjiù, who moved the capital to Luóyáng, thereby establishing Eastern Zhou. It reached its end with King Nǎn, when both the Eastern and Western Zhou territories were annexed by the Qín.
The emperors of successive dynasties mostly originated from the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi). Yu of Xia descended from Zhuanxu; Tang of Shang descended from Xie;
and the Zhou dynasty descended from Qi (all of whom were sons of Di Ku). The ancestor of Qin was Boyi (who was also a son of Zhuanxu).
The House of Liu of Han inherited the mandate of Yao (whose great-grandson was the Yellow Emperor). The House of Cao of Wei was the lineage of Cao Shuzhendo. From...
The Sima clan of Zhou and Jin originated from Zhongli; they were also descendants of Zhuanxu. The Liu clan of Song was descended from Jiao, the Prince Yuan of Chu of the Han dynasty;
they were also lineages of Yao. The Xiao clan of Qi and Liang originated from Xiao of the Spring and Autumn period;
Xiao was of the Zi surname and was a descendant of Shang. The Chen clan were descendants of Shun. The Yang clan of Sui originated from Zhuanxu. The Li clan of Tang...

The Shi (Shi) clan descended from Gao Yao, the son of Zhuanxu. Gao Yao served as the Grand Minister of Justice (later his descendants fled; because they survived by eating plums [li], they changed their surname to Li). The Zhu (Zhu) clan of Liang originated from the state of Zou during the Spring and Autumn period.
Zou was of the Ji lineage and a successor state of Zhou. The Guo (Guo) clan of Zhou descended from Guo Shu of Zhou; both were descendants of Emperor Ku.

The Zhao (Zhao) clan of Song originated with Bo Yi, the son of Zhuanxu. His descendant, Zhao Zaofu, was enfeoffed at Cheng during the time of King Mu of Zhou. His descendants took this as their surname. The Zhao clan of Jin were all his descendants. During the time of the First Emperor of Qin, his descendants dispersed to the four quarters.
The Han dynasty had Zhao Guangzhi, who resided there. The Great Yuan (Mahāyāna) school belongs to the Kṣatriya caste.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that at the beginning of the formation of the Bhadrakalpa, before the sun and moon existed, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended to be born here.
They all possessed bodily radiance and could travel through the air with ease. There was no distinction between male and female, noble and humble, or kin and stranger. They subsisted on...
The taste of the earth’s essence naturally appeared. Because they consumed this substance, their bodily radiance faded and their supernormal powers perished, and the mind of craving first sprouted.
Subsequently, the flavors of earth-cakes, earth-skins, and earth-fat appeared; by consuming these, all manner of evils converged, and the forms of male and female first emerged.
The earth produced non-glutinous rice that grew back by evening after being harvested in the morning; it was also free of husks and chaff.

At that time, the greed of the people increased, and everyone began to take up large stores in advance. Consequently, the rice ceased to grow. Thereupon, they began to demarcate fields and learn the business of tilling and sowing.

From this point on, wickedness and theft flourished, and there was no one to provide decisive judgment. Among them was a man whose physical appearance was exceptionally noble and majestic, one whom the world held in high esteem and trust. The multitude deliberated...
He was established as the sovereign of the people and titled Mahāsammatarāja, which means "Great King of Universal Equality.
Each person pledged to pay taxes and provide provisions; this was the beginning of land rent. Therefore, he was designated as a Kṣatriya, which means "Lord of the Fields."
When the fields and lands were first divided, disputes and litigations arose among them.
To preside over these matters, the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* states that at the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, there was a great Cakravartin King. A council was convened and established;

it was called the "Great Assembly for the Adjudication of Land" (*Mahāsaṃnipāta-bhūmi-vinirṇaya*) and also known as the Kṣatriya Kings. This king had an eldest son named Satya (True). His descendants...
The lineage was transmitted through twenty-seven generations, each having one thousand sons, totaling twenty-seven thousand, all of whom were universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).
Reaching the time of King Mahāmeru, the descendants continued in succession until the eighteenth generation of King Matsya.

The descendants then succeeded one another for seventeen generations, totaling one hundred seventy-three thousand two hundred and eighty-four, all of whom were minor universal monarchs. King Matsya had a son.

(He was named) *Jen* (True). From the minor kings (*kṣudraka-rāja*) down to the Great *Mao-cao* (Grass-Straw) King, there were thirty-one generations totaling one hundred and eight, all of whom were minor kings.
The *Mao-cao* King was also named *Śākyamuni* and belonged to the *Gautama* clan. In his old age, he abdicated the throne and left home to become a monk.
Having been struck by a hunter’s arrow, he passed away; his blood then dripped into the earth, from which two sugarcane sprouts subsequently grew.
From within one stalk he was transformed into a man, and from within another stalk he was transformed into a woman.

Honored and supported by the masses, he eventually succeeded to the royal throne and was known as King Ikṣvāku. This king had two queens who bore five sons; the eldest was named Āyuḥ, followed by Ulkāmukha and others.
The fourth son possessed great benevolence and virtue, yet because the senior queen slandered him to his father, he was compelled to leave the household life.
At that time, the king’s sons, mothers, retinue, and the multitude of his subjects followed him to establish a kingdom at the foot of the Snowy Mountains.

The kingdom was named Kapilavastu, and the king was also known as King Śuddhodana. Far and near, all were humbled by his majesty; before long, it had become a great realm where both the interior and exterior lands enjoyed abundant harvests.
The father-king, knowing this, sighed with remembrance and said: "Because my son is the Able One (Śākyamuni) of the Śākya clan, he is thus called the Śākya family.
The king had a son named Gopāla; another son was Gokula; and another son was Siṃhahanu. Siṃhahanu had four sons: Amṛtodana, Śuddhodana, Droṇodana, and Śuklodana.
From the assembly of the multitude, they established [the lineage] as a Great Wheel-Turning King. Counting through the generations, two thousand years have passed.
Five hundred [generations] from King Trivardhana, one arrives at King Śuddhodana.
According to the *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra*, starting from King Kṣatriya-rāja—also known as King Mahāsamata—and passing through King Saṃgha, twenty thousand kings followed until King Tṛṇa.
From King Tṛṇa, forty-one thousand two hundred and three [generations] passed.
Sixteen kings [passed] until the Gautama clan. There was a son named King Ikṣvāku.
After seventy-two thousand two hundred twenty-two kings, one arrives at King Śuddhodana. In total, there were one million two hundred seven thousand three hundred sixty-one kings.
Regarding these two translated scriptures, there are five differences in the Indian manuscripts. The World-Honored One has already, throughout incalculable kalpas, [attained... incalculable...

He attained Buddhahood in this world. At times he manifested as the bodies of Brahmā Kings, Śakra Devendra, Great Cakravartin Kings, Lesser Cakravartin Kings, or minor kings such as those of scattered territories.
Furthermore, at the abodes of countless Buddhas, he left the household life to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva and cultivate the path of a bodhisattva.
It is also said that upon encountering the Tathāgata Upadeśaketu, he first resolved his mind on Bodhi and surpassed Maitreya by more than forty kalpas. Or...

It is said that upon meeting Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he first received his prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). From Dīpaṃkara Buddha down to Kāśyapa, each was guided by the hand of a Buddha and each received a prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Reaching the stage of the Bodhisattva Roca, he ascended to Tuṣita Heaven;
subsequently descending to Kapilavastu, he renounced the precious throne of a golden wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), left the household life, attained the Way, and preached the Dharma.

He ruled the world for seventy-nine years. From the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) until the exhaustion of the Dharma, he delivered immeasurable sentient beings;
thus, the Dharma was not exhausted.
The *Mahābrahmādeva-rāja-prcchā-buddha-vinodana-saṃśaya-sūtra* states: "The Great Brahmā King went to the assembly at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and with..."

The monk Suvarṇavarṇa offered *sāla* flowers to the Buddha and requested that the World-Honored One preach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. When the World-Honored One ascended the seat, he held up a flower and showed it to the assembly, his blue-lotus eyes blinking.
A million beings, including gods and humans, were all utterly at a loss; only the *dhūta* practitioner Suvarṇavarṇa broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, the reality-mark which is markless."
This subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate does not rely on words and letters; it is a separate transmission outside the teachings, entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.

Regarding the incident of the flower, the world generally did not know its origin, until Lord Wang Jinggong, while on duty at night in the Han Garden, happened to discover this scripture (The Bequeathed Instructions of the Chan Forest) within a secret repository.

According to the *Dharmatara-piṭaka-śāstra*, the Buddha entrusted the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, charging him to protect and uphold it so that it would not be disparaged or defiled by celestial Māras, nāgas, ghosts, those with false views, kings, or ministers.
Having received this charge, he convened the council and compiled the Tripiṭaka.
He disseminated [the teachings] among humans, devas, and yakṣas, and entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda.
In this manner, it was transmitted in succession down to Siṃha, totaling twenty-five persons, all of whom were ṣaḍabhijña (sixfold-knowledge) sages of Jambudvīpa.

Mahākāśyapa caused them to remain within the rocky caves on the western peak of Gṛdhrakūṭa, seated in the samādhi of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) for five hundred and sixty billion and seventy million years. Then, Maitreya Buddha...
He was born into the world, transmitted the *Mahāsāṃghātī* robe entrusted by the Buddha Śākyamuni,
and subsequently entered *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, according to various sūtras and vinayas, the Buddha commanded the Great Arhat Piṇḍola to not pass into extinction,
so that he might transmit the Buddha-dharma throughout the three continents, benefiting sentient beings and enabling them to transcend birth and death.
The bhikṣu Huìyǒu, abbot of Fúchéng Kāiyuán Zhuāngyán Chán Monastery, has provided a supporting donation of one hundred strings of cash.
There are four castes in India: first, the kṣatriya, meaning the lineage of kings who have renounced the world;
this is the lineage of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Second, the brāhmaṇa; in the language of Qin, this means "external intention," referring to those who practice...
The *Zhìdào* (Volition for the Way) caste has its own distinct scriptures, which have been transmitted from generation to generation;
they practice either as householders or renunciants and engage in asceticism, yet they mostly rely on their own arts and look down upon others with self-conceit.
Third is the *Píshè* (or *Fúshè*), the merchant caste. Fourth is the *Shǒuduō* (or *Dáluó*), the agricultural caste.
The lineage of the Buddha Śākyamuni Tathāgata consists of the ten bodies: the Unattached, the Great Vow, Karmic Retribution, Sustaining, Nirvana, Pure Dharma, and True Mind.
Samādhi; the nature of the Path; the bases of psychic power; the ten powers (namely:

knowledge of what is possible and impossible; knowledge of karma; samādhi; knowledge of the faculties; knowledge of inclinations; knowledge of dispositions; knowledge of the path leading to all destinations; recollection of past lives; the divine eye; and the knowledge of the outflow-free).

The three types of clear knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*: [knowledge of] birth and death, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of realization); the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ abhijñāḥ*: the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, the power of psychic travel, and the exhaustion of outflows).

The Eighteen Unshared Dharmas: 1. No error in physical action; 2. No harsh or abrupt voice; 3. No loss of mindfulness; 4. No lack of concentration; 5. No perception of diversity; 6. No lack of equanimity toward the unknown;

7. No regression from desire; 8. No regression from diligence; 9. No regression from right mindfulness; 10. No diminution of wisdom; 11. No diminution of liberation; 12. No diminution of knowledge and vision;
13. All physical actions follow wisdom; 14. All verbal actions follow wisdom; 15. [All mental actions follow wisdom]; 16. No unconsidered indifference; 17. No loss of zeal; 18. No loss of energy.
5. All mental karma proceeds in accordance with wisdom; 16. Knowledge of the past without attachment or obstruction; 17. Knowledge of the present without attachment or obstruction; 18.
Knowledge of the future without attachment or obstruction.
The transformation of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms and the condensation of the four wisdoms into the three bodies:

the sixth consciousness, characterized by conceptual thought and mental imagery, becomes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna), which is the Complete Enjoyment Body (saṃbhoga-kāya).

The seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*) is the consciousness that transmits the habituation of bliss; it is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*). There are a thousand, ten thousand, and a billion transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The Sixth Patriarch Chan Master’s Verse on the Nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom: “The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure and clear; The Wisdom of Equality is a mind free from affliction.”
The wisdom of wondrous observation sees that there is no effort; The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done is identical to the great mirror-like wisdom.
In the transformation of the eighth, seventh, sixth, and fifth consciousnesses, It is merely a change of name with no real nature.
If one does not allow names to linger where transformation occurs, Then amidst the profuse arising of phenomena, one forever abides in the *nāga*-samādhi.
The Tathāgata (who is without falsehood), the Arhat (the excellent field of merit), the Samyaksaṃbuddha (who knows the dharma-realm), the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna (endowed with the three insights),
the Sugata (who does not return), the Lokavid (knower of the world— there being no "two worlds," namely the world of the physical realm and the world of sentient beings),

the Anuttara-puruṣadamyasārathi (the supreme charioteer who can subdue the evil of the body and mind of sentient beings), the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām (the teacher of gods and humans, able to act as eyes for sentient beings), and the Buddha (who knows the aggregates of wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, and neither-wholesome-nor-unwholesome dharmas).
The World-Honored One, a mass of wholesome dharmas, for whom there is no second Buddha throughout the two worlds;
his ten titles are perfectly luminous, his myriad practices are fully perfected, and he is venerated by devas and nāgas as the Unsurpassed Honored One.
The Three Pitakas of the Dharma: the Sūtra (compiled as sūtras by Ānanda and the assembly), the Vinaya (compiled as the Vinaya by Upāli),
and the Abhidharma (compiled as śāstras by the great Bodhisattvas [of the Mahāyāna]).
The Five Periods (*pañca-kāla*: Vaipulya, Avataṃsaka, Prajñāpāramitā, Saddharmapuṇḍarīka, and Mahāparinirvāṇa).

The twelvefold scriptures of the Deer Park (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*; Sanskrit: *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, *upadeśa*; translated into Chinese as:

*xièjīng* [Sūtra], *chóngshòu* [Repetitive Verse], *shòujì* [Prophecy], *shuōsòng* [Recited Teaching], *yīnyuán* [Causes and Conditions], *zìshuō* [Spontaneous Utterance], *běnshì* [Past Events], *běnxìng* [Original Nature], *pìyù* [Parable], *fāngguǎng* [Extensive Teachings], *wèicéngyǒu* [Unprecedented Events], and *lùn* [Treatise]).

The ritual transformation consists of the four teachings (Sudden, Gradual, Secret, and Indeterminate); the Dharma transformation consists of the four teachings (Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect).

The Ten Faiths (faith; resolve and mindfulness; diligence; wisdom derived from hearing; right concentration; non-retrogression; protection of the Dharma; dedication; observance of precepts; and making vows).

The Ten Abodes (the arousal of the mind; the stage of cultivation; the stage of practice; the stage of noble birth; the stage of fulfillment; the stage of right mind; the stage of non-retrogression; the stage of the youthful prince; and the stage of consecration).

The Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*): [1] Joyful (*pramuditā*), [2] Beneficial (*vimalā*), [3] Unopposed (*arciṣmatī*), [4] Undisturbed (*sudurjayā*), [5] Unconfused (*abhimukhī*), [6] Well-manifested (*dūraṅgamā*), [7] Unattached (*acalā*), [8] Difficult-to-attain Good Dharma (*sādhumatī*), and [9] Reality (*dharmameghā*).

The Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*): protecting living beings; being free from the marks of birth; being indestructible; being equal to all Buddhas; reaching all places; inexhaustible merit; entering into all equality; conforming to sentient beings; the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*); being without attachment or bondage;
and the immeasurability of the realm of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmadhātu*).
The ten stages (Joyful, Stainless, Luminous, Radiant Wisdom, Difficult to Conquer, Manifest, Far-Going, Immovable, Excellent Wisdom, and Cloud of Dharma).
The ten pāramitās (generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, great vows, great power, and great knowledge).
The Four Immeasurables: Great Loving-kindness (universal salvation), Great Compassion (extracting from suffering), Great Joy (fearlessness), and Great Equanimity (non-action).

The Four Means of Integration: Generosity (enticement through benefit), Affectionate Speech (extraction through wisdom), Beneficial Conduct (self-mastery), and Shared Purpose (harmonizing with others).

The Four Virtues: Eternal (the body is like suchness, unchanging in its lifespan); Blissful (the essence is eternally quiescent and unconditioned); Self (excellent observation without obstruction); Pure (dwelling in the world like a lotus).

The Four Noble Truths: Suffering (mistaking nirvana for samsara), Accumulation (mistaking bodhi for afflictions), Cessation (transforming samsara into nirvana), and Path (transforming afflictions into bodhi).
Proclaiming the Dharma with a single voice, universally responding to the capacities of all beings, ultimately pure, he is named the Honored One Who is Free from Desire.

The Sangha consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharmas*): the four foundations of mindfulness (contemplating the body as impure, contemplating feelings as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as non-self); the four bases of psychic power...

The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)—[desire, effort, mind, and investigation]; the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*)—[to abandon evil that has already arisen, to prevent evil that has not yet arisen from arising, to produce good that has not yet arisen, and to increase good that has already arisen];

the five faculties (*indriya*)—[the faculties of faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom]; the five powers (*bala*)—[the powers of faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom]; and the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)—[mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, effort, joy, pliancy,]...

The Factors of Concentration (samādhi): the factor of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga). The Eightfold Noble Path: right view (free from delusion); right intention (free from perversity); right speech (free from falsehood); right action (free from misconduct);
right livelihood (subsisting on alms); right effort (free from negligence); right mindfulness (free from duality); right concentration (free from distraction).
The Three Virtues (Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Eloquence); the Three Doors of Liberation (Emptiness, Signlessness, and Wishlessness);

the Four Great Vows (to deliver sentient beings, to sever afflictions, to seek the True Dharma, and to attain the Buddha-way); the Four Unimpeded Eloquences (mastery of phenomena, mastery of self, mastery of language, and unimpeded delight in preaching);

the Four Samādhis (constant sitting, half-walking and half-sitting, constant walking, and neither walking nor sitting); and the Four Wholesome Dharmas (associating with virtuous friends, hearing the True Dharma, contemplating its meaning, and practicing according to the teaching).

The pure livelihood regarding robes: (1) obtaining a robe anywhere that merely covers the body is sufficient; (2) collecting discarded refuse [or branches] or wearing only a simple shirt; (3) in lands of great cold, possessing the hundred requisites [for a kalpa].
Pure Life-Sustaining Food: 1. Always begging for food oneself; 2. Pure food from within the Sangha; 3. Food sent by a donor. The Five Contemplations: 1.

Calculating the amount of labor expended and measuring the distance it was brought; 2. Reflecting upon one’s own virtue—its completeness or deficiency—to determine whether one is worthy of this offering; 3. Guarding the mind to remain free from faults, taking the elimination of greed and other afflictions as the primary principle;
4. Regarding the food as wholesome medicine intended to treat the withered body; 5. Accepting this food in order to accomplish the work of the Path.
The three virtues (purity, softness, and accordance with the Dharma). The six tastes (salty, bland, sour, pungent, sweet, and bitter).

There are ten benefits of gruel (nourishing the complexion, increasing strength, prolonging life, providing comfort, accomplishing tasks, dispelling wind-disorders, clarifying speech, digesting undigested food, alleviating hunger, and relieving thirst).

The Eight Great Fields of Merit (widening roads, providing public wells, constructing bridges, leveling dangerous narrow passages, being filial to one's parents, making offerings to the Triple Gem, attending to the sick, relieving the poor and suffering, and establishing unrestricted assemblies).

The Four Graces: the Buddha as Teacher (who transforms and instructs through the Dharma), the King (who provides external protection such as land and water), one’s Parents (whose labor and toil provide nurture), and Faithful Benefactors (who provide the four requisites of support).

The six points of harmony (harmony in body by dwelling together; harmony in speech by being free from dispute; harmony in mind by being free from opposition; harmony in precepts by following them together; harmony in views by sharing the same understanding; and harmony in material gains by distributing them equally).
The Three Trainings: Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom (the three untainted trainings; they accomplish all-knowledge and give birth to eighty-four thousand pure and wondrous gateways).
The Three Poisons: greed, anger, and delusion (the Buddha said: "Among the poisons of the world, none surpasses the three poisons; they comprise the eighty-four thousand afflictions and delusions").

The Ten Categories of Monastic Activities: Translation, Exegesis of Meaning, Practice of Meditation, Clarification of the Vinaya, Protection of the Dharma, Spiritual Resonance, Renunciation of the Body, Recitation, Cultivation of Merit, and Miscellaneous Categories.

The Sangha possesses six treasures: 1. Meditative Concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*): [Through sudden awakening to one’s own mind, they transcend the mundane and enter the holy. 2. Exposition of the Vinaya: [Possessing precepts, concentration, and wisdom, they have great eloquence. 3. Noble Superiority: [With both practice and realization in tandem, they do not enter the worldly stream.

4. Literary Composition: [Their见闻 (what they see and hear) is profound and substantial; they study the ancients to verify the present. 5. Royal Affairs: [Wisdom, benevolence, discernment of results, compassion, and majesty are practiced in unison.
6. Constant Monastic Life: [Through diligent effort and achievement, they nurture the embryo of holiness.]

The Bhikṣuṇīs observe the Eight Rules of Respect: 1. A bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for a hundred years must pay homage at the feet of a newly ordained bhikṣu. 2. A bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu. 3. A bhikṣuṇī must not expose the faults of a bhikṣu. 4.

When a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must seek confession from the bhikṣu-saṃgha. 5. A śikṣamāṇā bhikṣuṇī must receive full ordination from the bhikṣu-saṃgha. 6. Every half-month, a bhikṣuṇī must attend upon the bhikṣu-saṃgha to receive instruction and admonition. 7. A bhikṣuṇī must reside near the bhikṣu-saṃgha to practice and cultivate the Path. 8.
At the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (varṣā), a bhikṣuṇī must perform the pravāraṇā ceremony according to the bhikṣu-saṃgha.

Detached from the mundane and distinct from the secular, with a shaven head and square-cut robes, he has entered the state of sagehood and transcended the ordinary, becoming the most honored among the multitude. The Three Realms of Existence (*tridhātu*): 1.

The Realm of Desire (*kāmadhātu*), which comprises the four continents, the four evil destinies, and the six heavens of the desire realm; 2. The Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*), which comprises the eighteen heavens of the form realm and the four dhyānas; 3.

The Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), comprising the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). [There are no non-deva realms here.]

The nine successive attainments (the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the sphere of the cessation of perception and feeling).

The twenty-five states of existence (consisting of: the four continents and the four evil realms; the six heavens of the desire realm together with the Brahma heaven; the four dhyānas and the four formless realms; and the five non-percipient beings and the two *naivasamjñānāsamjñāyatana*s).

The Sevenfold Method of Repentance (Constantly recollecting the Buddha’s kindness; giving rise to great shame and remorse; deeply fearing the retribution of karma; extensively generating wholesome thoughts; contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses; feeling weary of and detaching from the defilement of desire; regarding enemies and kin with equanimity).

The Six Recollections: Recollection of the Buddha: The compassionate guide; take refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One. Recollection of the Dharma: The Mother of the Buddhas of the three times; practice in accordance with the teachings. Recollection of the Sangha: The field of merit for humans and devas;

they should be honored with offerings. Recollection of Generosity: Bestow gifts universally upon all sentient beings to bring forth merit and wisdom. Recollection of Precepts: Purify body and mind to extinguish all evils. Recollection of the Deva Realm: Longevity, peace, happiness, sovereignty, and diligence.
The Three Aggregates (the precept of benefiting sentient beings, the precept of restraining oneself, and the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas);

the Five Precepts (not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not lying, and not drinking intoxicants). The five benefits of receiving the precepts: First: All Buddhas will take pity on one and protect one. Second:

On the day of death, one will possess right view and rejoice. Third: One will always dwell in superior states, with bodhisattvas as companions. Fourth: The aggregate of meritorious virtues and the precepts will all be fully accomplished. Fifth: In this life and in future lives, one’s merit and wisdom will be fulfilled.

The three realms. Regarding the five signs of decline in the heavens (the flowers on the head wither; sweat [and odor] appears under the armpits; the radiance of the body no longer manifests; the robes become stained with dust and grime; and one takes no pleasure in one's own station).

The four marks of human existence: birth (the uncertainty of longevity) constitutes arising; aging (the decline of physical strength and complexion) constitutes abiding; illness (the disharmony of the four great elements) constitutes decay; and death (consciousness following karma) constitutes emptiness.

The five aggregates: form (the emptiness of form), sensation (separation from contact), perception (forgetting what has been noted), mental formations (cessation and arising), and consciousness (stillness and movement).

The eighteen realms: consciousness (the eye seeing forms, the ear hearing sounds, the nose smelling fragrances, the tongue tasting flavors, the body feeling tangibles, and the mind cognizing phenomena; through the six internal faculties, the six intermediate consciousnesses, and the six external objects, the eighteen realms are formed).
The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination: Ignorance, Volitional Formations, Consciousness, Name-and-Form, the Six Sense Bases, Contact, Feeling, Craving, Grasping, Becoming, Birth.
Old age and death.

The three delusions (ignorance, views and thoughts, and the dust-like afflictions). The three obstructions (afflictions, karma, and retribution). The ten entanglements (shamelessness, lack of remorse, envy, jealousy, doubt and regret, restlessness, resentment, and hostility).
[The five hindrances: stinginess, sleep, torpor, concealment, and [restlessness].

The ten proclivities (anuśaya)—[namely: the view of a self-identity, extreme views, attachment to precepts and rituals, attachment to views, false views, greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt—these proclivities, when combined across the three realms, constitute eighty-eight proclivities.

The six kinds of false views (annihilationism, eternalism, spontaneity, asceticism, following perversities, and distorted causes not based on principle) give rise to ninety-six types of heterodox false views when combined.

The Six Heretical Teachers: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa (who propounds non-arising and non-ceasing, calculating the "neither-nor" as the single gate); Maskari Gośālīputra (who propounds emptiness and spontaneity, denying cause and effect);

Saṃjayin Vairaṭīputra (who propounds that after eighty thousand kalpas one transcends the path and need not practice); Ajita Keśakambalin (who propounds the practice of asceticism, such as plucking out the hair and other such methods);

Kakuda Kātyāyana (who propounds the doctrine of "both-and," which is confused and indeterminate); Nirgrantha Jñātiputra (who propounds the determinism of karma, maintaining that when a person dies, they are reborn as another person).

The seven emotions: joy, anger, sorrow, fear, attachment, aversion, and desire.

The eight winds: gain (delight in wealth), loss (sorrow and illness), defamation (slander and abuse), praise (admiration and laudation), renown (extolling virtue), insignificance (mockery and ridicule), suffering (oppression and affliction), and pleasure (indulgence and negligence).
The eight sufferings (birth, aging, illness, death, separation from the beloved, association with the hated, failure to obtain what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates).

The five kinds of wrong livelihood: first, falsely manifesting extraordinary feats for the sake of gain and honor; second, speaking of one’s own merits for the sake of gain and honor; third, divining good and bad fortune for the sake of gain and honor;

fourth, raising one’s voice and displaying an air of authority to inspire fear in others for the sake of gain and honor; fifth, proclaiming one’s own virtues to move the hearts of people for the sake of gain and honor.

The three great calamities: the great flood (submerging the world up to the first dhyāna heaven), the great fire (incendiating the earth up to the second dhyāna heaven), and the great wind (sweeping away Mount Sumeru up to the third dhyāna heaven).
The Three Minor Calamities (weapons, pestilence, and famine; they share the same *kalpa* but differ in their nature).
The Ten Non-virtuous Actions (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, harsh speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views). [The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:

"The retribution for the ten non-virtuous actions is the cause for the highest hells, the middle cause for hungry ghosts, and the lower cause for animals. To refrain from them constitutes the ten virtuous paths: the lower grade leads to rebirth as a human or deva; the middle grade to the Two Vehicles; and the upper grade to the Bodhisattva and Buddha Vehicles."
The Eight Difficulties: 1. The realm of hell (due to greed); 2. The realm of hungry ghosts (due to anger); 3. The realm of animals (due to ignorance); 4.

Birth in Uttarakuru (due to dullness and stupidity); 5. Being born before a Buddha appears (due to pride and envy); 6. Being born after a Buddha has passed away (due to indolence); 7. Being deaf, blind, or mute (due to slandering the Dharma); 8.
Worldly cleverness and eloquence (due to being an icchantika).
The four reliances (relying on rag-robes, relying on discarded medicine, relying on alms-food, and relying on dwelling at the foot of a tree).
Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat as the ultimate.
Birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, not obtaining what one seeks, and meeting with the hated—these are the eight sufferings.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these are the five aggregates.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four immeasurable minds,
and the ultimate severance of greed, hatred, and delusion—
(these four fruits of practice rely upon this culmination to realize the fruit).
The fruit of the pratyekabuddha consists of the twelve links of dependent origination; the fruit of the bodhisattva consists of the six pāramitās;
and for the mahāsattva, these are augmented by the four pāramitās of skillful means, aspiration, power, and wisdom.
The Rhapsody on Śākyamuni, composed by Wang Bo of Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty in accordance with imperial decree:
To begin with, "Buddha" means "Awakened. Through spiritual transformation, he cultivated himself for six years and attained the Way; he presides over the three realms as their Teacher.
Even Śakra and Brahmā pay him reverence; how could Laozi and Confucius not follow him? As of old...
Descending from Tuṣita Heaven, he was born in Central India. When his spirit descended, the great earth shook; as he manifested his traces, the various devas provided protection.
Nine dragons spat forth water that filled his body, while flowers fell in profusion. As he lifted his feet, auspicious clouds of the seven jewels gathered, and lotuses sprang up with every step.
Thus, with the jade carriage manifesting its auspiciousness and the golden wheel inaugurating his destiny, his grace moistened the nine realms. He walked...
The Dragon Countenance was greatly pleased by the three harmonies; what need was there to fear for the Phoenix Virtue of the Spring Encampment?

One now knows that the numinous mind of consecration shall cause the royal lineage to flourish, inevitably becoming the transformative sovereign of the myriad species and the central pivot of the empire.

How could one not know that the capacity of the sea is boundless and the sentiment of Heaven is infinitely vast? He grew weary of the colors of pearls and jade from the six palaces and loathed the presence of a thousand consorts.
Amidst the resonance of strings and flutes, deep within the Snowy Mountains, they completely cast aside their conditioned bodies and minds.
When the ocean moon is full, they suddenly awaken to the thought of unconditioned Dharma. Therein, the demonic armies tremble and the entire Dharma-realm is struck with awe.

They perceive the rising sun of Jambudvīpa and behold the blooming of the *utpala* flower. The Tamer of the Ten Directions all arrive, their perfect radiance sovereign and free, as they traverse the six realms of existence.
Sentient beings were all filled with joy as the golden body was revealed in its distinct clarity.

When all phenomena returned to emptiness and the twin śāla trees announced his passing, he expounded the teachings of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and demonstrated the secret instructions of *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Within the Hall of Universal Radiance, he convened the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka* of the Ten Stages;
on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he bestowed the prophetic predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) for the Three Vehicles. Thus we know that spiritual awakening is inexhaustible and that the divine principle...

It was not heard that within a mustard seed lies a trichiliocosm, nor that the fibers of a lotus root conceal a hundred thousand troops. His eyes were as long and wide as blue lotuses born from the waters of meditative concentration;
his *ūrṇā* mark was as distinct as the bright moon piercing through the clouds of delusion.

Yet, while the capacities of all beings failed to perceive his spiritual traces, for ten thousand generations only his holy remains have been left behind. Alas, the Final Dharma of Śākyamuni is about to end!

During the first five hundred years of the one thousand-year period of the True Dharma, liberation will be the primary teaching, while meditative concentration will be practiced as a secondary cultivation.

In the five hundred years following [the first five hundred], meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) shall be the primary teaching, while extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) shall be practiced as a secondary discipline.

During the first five hundred years of the one-thousand-year period of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), extensive learning shall be the primary teaching, while merit (*puṇya*) shall be practiced as a secondary discipline.
In the final five hundred years, merit and virtue will be the primary practice, while contention will be practiced as a secondary discipline.
In the ten thousand years of the Dharma-ending age, contention will be the primary practice, while indolence will be practiced as a secondary discipline.
From the time the Tathāgata Śākyamuni entered nirvāṇa until the second year of the Zhiyuan era of the Great Yuan dynasty,
the year Bingzi, a total of two thousand two hundred and eighty-five years have elapsed (from this point forward,
the number of years shall increase accordingly).
The Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra says: "This day has passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly. Like a fish in shallow water, what joy can there be in this?

Now, regarding the accounts of the Tathāgata’s birth in the kingdom of Shendu (India), it occurred during the period of the Ji and Zhou dynasties here in Zhendan (China).

As the years have gradually receded into the distance and human generations have diverged, attempting to point to specific dates leads easily to confusion regarding their chronological order. Therefore, I have now compiled a sequence of sexagenary cycles (*jiǎzǐ*) to connect the past and present, and have appended the reigns of the emperors to provide a framework for the eras.
In this way, the succession of abdication and the rise of hegemonic rulers may be as clear as a mirror before one's eyes. — From the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian).

The transformations of the court and the marketplace are as clear within a mirror or the palm of one’s hand. Thereafter, when examining the sovereigns and kings, their grace extends to all, and they provide comfort according to the times.

As the Buddha-dharma spreads its transformation, it responds to capacities and saves sentient beings; the Buddhist scriptures and the teachings of Confucius are in accord in principle, like a hidden resonance. It may truly be said that the spiritual power descended from the Five Indias.
This was a manifestation of auspiciousness reaching the eight directions. The mother of Ji Chang dreamed of a great man; through this inspiration, she conceived and gave birth to him.

Chang had the face of a dragon and the eyebrows of a tiger; he stood one zhang tall and had four nipples upon his chest. His state bordered the Western Rong tribes, yet his governance extended eastward to the sea.

The Master said: "How magnificent was the virtue of King Wen! He transformed others without moving. When his son Fa, King Wu, went forth to punish Zhou and moved the capital to Haojing, he encountered a man suffering from heat on the road;
he descended from his carriage to fan him. Thus, he humbled himself despite possessing a ten-thousand-chariot state, cherishing the myriad people."
Therefore, Master Sun Qingzi said: "When King Wu was born, the whole world sang; when he died, the four seas wept.

According to the *Lü Chunqiu*, on the night of the *xinmao* day in the fourth month of summer in the seventh year of Duke Zhuang’s reign, the fixed stars did not appear, and at midnight stars fell like rain.
Examining this, it corresponds to the time of the Tathāgata’s birth.
The *Biography of King Aśoka* states: One hundred and sixty years after the Parinirvāṇa, there was a king of Jambudvīpa named Aśoka.
He emerged from East India and ruled from the city of Pāṭaliputra. Having collected the relics, he erected eighty-four thousand precious stūpas, scattering them throughout Jambudvīpa.

He also greatly desired to extend them across all of India; what is recorded in the tradition can be summarized as follows: [the relics reached] the capital cities of China, the Yangtze and Han rivers...
To the left and right, throughout the regions of Guanzhong and Longshan, east and west, they were found everywhere.
At that time, it was the twenty-sixth year of the reign of King Jing of Zhou, the year Dingwei. A total of four locations were visited. Then, King Zhaoxiang of Qin ascended the throne;

after fifty-two years, he extinguished the state of Zhou and assumed the title of Qin. He changed the capital of Haojing to Xianyang and established his court there. This continued until the fourth ruler, the First Emperor.
In the twenty-sixth year [of the First Emperor], the six states were swept away. In the twenty-seventh year, the nine provinces were abolished and the empire was divided into thirty-six commanderies.
In the thirty-fourth year, all existing classics and records were completely incinerated;

only medical prescriptions and pharmacological arts were exempt from the flames, while everything else was reduced to ashes. It was for this reason that the sacred traces of the holy teachings and King Aśoka [were preserved].
Stūpas for the śarīras were constructed, but their biographies have been lost to oblivion, leaving no one to know their lineage.

Furthermore, during the time of the First Emperor, there were eighteen worthy śramaṇas, including Śrīvara and others, who brought sūtras to convert the people. The First Emperor would not follow them; he subsequently burned Śrīvara and the others.
At night, a Vajra deity, sixteen feet tall in stature, came and broke open the prison to release them. The First Emperor was struck with terror.
He bowed his head in apology. The four rulers together reigned for forty-nine years before being executed by the King of Chu. Subsequently, the Han dynasty extinguished them.
From the first year of King Wu of Zhou, the Jīmǎ year, until the year of defeat by the Second Emperor of Qin, the Jiǎwǔ year, there were nine hundred and thirty-three years and forty-two rulers.
Among these, from the establishment of the Zhou up to the sixteenth king, there were four hundred and fifty-three years. As for the Buddha—

Prior to its publication, it was known by name but not formally recorded. Beginning from the time Tathāgata Śākyamuni appeared in the world during the reign of King Zhao, until the beginning of the Han dynasty, when the chronology was finally established, there were twenty-six sovereigns over a period of four hundred and eighty-one years;
these are collectively summarized as the "Record of the Zhou and Qin Dynasties."
It is merely to clarify that the Buddha Vehicle should be taught to reach the Eastern Lands;
[this is like] the Zhou dynasty’s Wen (civilization), Wu (military might), Cheng (recitation), Kang (instruction), and Zhao (exemplary conduct).
In the twenty-third year of King Zhao’s reign, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the year Gui-chou, Lady Māyā dreamed that a white elephant, riding upon a solar disc, entered her womb;
upon waking, she knew of herself that her body had become heavy.
Jia-yin (24th year), the eighth day of the fourth month: there was an auspicious omen of a white rainbow piercing the sun.
On this day, Lady Māyā was strolling within the Lumbinī Garden beneath an Aśoka tree when the Prince was born from her right side.
He emitted a great radiance, and auspicious vapors filled the sky. Nine dragons spouted water to bathe his golden body; immediately thereafter, he walked seven paces.
He strode forth, his eyes gazing in the four directions; pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, he let out a lion’s roar: "In all that is above and below heaven, I alone am supreme.
King Zhao beheld the sun and moon appearing as double wheels (*cakra*), with various colors manifesting together. Struck by such an extraordinary marvel, he questioned his great ministers:
"What numinous anomaly is this? What auspicious omen has appeared? At that time, the Grand Astrologer Suyou performed a divination and reported: "The *I Ching* says..."
The Hexagram Qian (Heaven). It is the position presided over by Metal; its location is in the West. "The flying dragon is in the heavens" refers to the station of a sovereign.
This is a Great Sage. The King asked, "What will become of this land? He replied, "This Sage will not come to this land in person.
However, one thousand years after his passing, the teachings will surely flow to this country. The King then commanded the relevant authorities.
Beside the southern suburban altar in Luoyang, a stele was erected to record this for future generations (the *Fǎwángjì* in the *Zōushū* records it differently).
When the Prince was fifteen years old, he took Yaśodharā as his consort; at nineteen, he desired to leave the household.
At night, a celestial being addressed the Prince, saying, "The time for your renunciation has arrived. At midnight, he leaped over the city wall and went to Mount Dandaka.
He practiced in the middle [stage] at the abode of Udraka Rāmaputra, where he studied the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
After six years, on the eighth day of the twelfth month, at the time when the morning star appeared, he attained Buddhahood and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
At thirty, he preached the Dharma in the Deer Park, delivering Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya and others. He remained in the world for seventy-nine years, preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years.
King Mu’s name was Man. He reigned for fifty-three years. A brilliant radiance shone upon the level lands.
At that time, the Buddha was in the Western Regions, preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings. The King did not recognize this as a manifestation of the Buddha’s auspicious signs;
he merely said there was trouble within his realm and consequently ordered the National Preceptor to inspect the troops and horses to defend the western frontier.
Ren-shen (the 52nd year of King Mu’s reign), on the fifteenth night of the second month, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, heaven and earth shook violently, and twelve white rainbows pierced the sun, passing through it from south to north.
The King was greatly alarmed and summoned his ministers to ask, "What calamitous anomaly is this? The Grand Astrologer Hu Yi-duo replied, "There is no cause for concern within our kingdom."
This was when the Sage of the West entered parinirvāṇa. The King was greatly delighted and proclaimed to his ministers: "The Sage of the West has already passed away;

henceforth, I shall have no more worries. According to the *Record of the Western Regions*, the Buddha was born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, attained the Way in the kingdom of Magadha, preached the Dharma in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, and entered parinirvāṇa in the kingdom of Kuśinagara.
On the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the third year of the Yuanyuan era of Emperor Dingwang, Laozi was born beneath a plum tree in Qurenli, Laixiang, Kuxian, within the state of Chu.
He took the surname Li, his given name was Er, his courtesy name was Boyang, and his posthumous title was Nian.
According to the Dunhuang Shilu, in the nineteenth year of King Huan of Zhou, he visited the Xianyu Hall and engaged in a formal debate with his ministers concerning the present.
The Emperor asked, "What kind of man was Lao Dan’s father? Sui Suo, the Grand Governor of Tianshui, replied, "Dan’s father was surnamed Han, named Qian, with the courtesy name Yuanbei.
He was a native of Laixiang in Hao and died in Huaili. His mother was refined and intelligent."
Nan was born after being in the womb for eighty-one years. With bushy eyebrows and white hair, he became known as Laozi.
In the fourth year of the reign of King Yi of the Jian period, he served as the Recorder Under the Pillar. Later, he served as the Keeper of the Archives.

In the first year of the reign of King Wang of the Jing period, at the age of eighty-five, he entered the Hangu Pass to the west with Yin Xi, the Magistrate of San Pass, and did not return. At that time...
Three hundred and forty-five years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa (according to the Chronological Table),
in the twenty-eighth year of King Ling Xie’s reign, the *gengxu* year (one source says *gengzi*), Confucius was born in Zou County of Lu.
This was the twenty-second year of Duke Xiang. Because his ancestors had prayed at Mount Nichu, he was named Qiu; he was styled Zhongni.
In the fourteenth year of Duke Ai of Lu, he reached the end of his writing upon capturing the *qilin*. He passed away in the forty-first year, the *Renxu* year, at the age of seventy.
13. Qiu was originally surnamed Shiliang He; his mother was of the Yan clan. Later, he styled himself Kongzi (the Master Confucius).
When Kongzi departed from Zhou, Laozi saw him off and said: "I have heard that those of wealth and status see one off with gold, while the benevolent see one off with words.
Although I am not wealthy or noble, I have stolen the title of the benevolent; let me therefore see you off with words."
The Master said: "Generally, those of this age who are intelligent, deeply perceptive, yet come close to death, are those who love to criticize others.
Those who are erudite, eloquent, and grand, yet bring peril upon themselves, are those who love to expose the faults of others. Confucius reverently upholds these words."
According to the "Verses on the Emergence of the Three Teachings" in the *Śākyamuni-pu*: Śākyamuni was born in Kapilavastu during the reign of the fourth Zhou emperor, King Zhao (Jia-yin year).
It was the fifty-second year of King Mu (Ren-shen year). The Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa at the age of seventy-nine.

Two thousand years after the Buddha’s extinction, the teaching spread during the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty. Four hundred twenty-two years after the Buddha’s birth, Laozi [appeared].
Just as the era of the King of Stability was about to arise, four hundred and seventy-seven years after the Buddha’s birth, the Sage Confucius was born during the reign of King Ling.
To repay the toil of worldly existence, let this infant understand: though the tripod was divided into three legs, it returns to oneness.
From King Wen of Zhou downward, down to King Nan, there were thirty-seven sovereigns. Calculating the total duration from beginning to end, it was eight hundred and sixty-seven years.
It is said that the sages of the Three Teachings appeared in succession during this period.

That sages arose in succession during the Zhou dynasty, and that the Great Teaching flourished, was surely due to certain causes. The Buddha relied upon kings and ministers as external protectors, and the state relied upon [the Buddha].
Śākyamuni and Laozi perform their ascetic refinements; though their schools divide into three distinct branches, the Way originates from the same source and flows together.
As firm as the tripod’s three legs, it is difficult to lack even one; may they endure as long as heaven and earth, forever in harmonious peace.
Zhuangzi, Chapter Four: Zhongni of Zheng. The Grand Chancellor Pi of Shang asked Confucius, saying, "Qiu, are you a sage?

He replied, "As for being a sage, how would I dare claim that? However, I am merely one who has studied extensively and possesses broad knowledge. The Grand Chancellor said, "Were the Three Sovereigns sages?
He replied, "The Three Sovereigns were skilled at employing wisdom and valor; as for being sages, I do not know them. The Grand Chancellor asked, "Were the Five Emperors sages? He replied, "..."

[The Grand Historian] asked, "As for the Five Emperors, who were skilled at employing benevolence and righteousness—do you consider them sages? He replied, "I do not know them to be sages. [The Grand Historian] asked, "As for the Three Kings, were they sages?

He replied, "The Three Kings were skilled at employing the circumstances of their times—I do not know them to be sages. The Grand Historian asked, "Who then is a sage? He replied, "In the West there is a Great Sage.
He does not govern, yet there is no disorder; he does not speak, yet people trust him; he does not transform others, yet things proceed of themselves. Vast and expansive..."
It is impossible to name [the ultimate source].
From Bingwu to Jiawu, the Qin dynasty lasted for six rulers over forty-nine years, with its capital at Xianyang.
The rulers were Xiaowen (Zhu Yuan) and Zhuangxiang (Fan Yuan).
King Zhaoxiang. Le Yuanji succeeded to his hereditary rank and served as a protector of the House of Zhou. He deposed King Nan as a commoner and transported the Nine Tripods of Zhou to Qin.
Emperor Shihuang changed his surname back to Zhao; in the year Yimao, he ascended the throne and first assumed the title of "Emperor."
He considered his achievements to surpass those of the Three Sovereigns and his virtue to encompass that of the Five Emperors. He reigned for thirty-seven years.
In the twenty-sixth year, he annexed the six states, unifying all under heaven. He changed the calendar and established the month of Jiaihai as the beginning of the year.
In the twenty-seventh year, he divided the empire into thirty-six commanderies, standardizing the written script and the carriage ruts. He renamed the River "De" (Virtue), and the people said:
The Common People.
Guiwei (the 29th year of the reign). A śramaṇa from Śrāvastī named Śilabhadra, accompanied by eighteen worthy men, brought Buddhist scriptures to the capital.
The relevant authorities submitted a detailed report; however, the First Emperor did not recognize Buddhism and deemed it a demonic deception, issuing an edict [to suppress it].
He ordered that Śāriputra and the others be imprisoned, instructing them to produce only the sound of Brahma while recollecting the Buddha and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
At that time, a brilliant light illuminated Xianyang, and auspicious vapors swirled within the prison. There were eight divine beings.
He emerged from the earth, his body sixteen feet tall, wearing a phoenix helmet and lustrous armor. Grasping a vajra, he shattered the hells;
the shackles and fetters were all destroyed, and the hell-wardens fell to the ground in terror. Lìfáng and the others were simultaneously liberated.

The Left and Right Secretaries prepared a memorial for the Emperor. The Emperor was greatly shocked; he bowed in apology and repented his error. He issued an edict to carefully escort Śrībhara and the others back to India with the scriptures and teachings.
Wuzi (5th year): The thirty-fourth year. Li Si memorialized the Emperor to burn all the classical texts and bury the Confucian scholars alive.
(In the thirty-seventh year, Ximao, the Emperor went on a tour of the coast and passed away.)
The Second Emperor, Hu Hai, ascended the throne on the day of Renchen. After three years, Zhao Gao and Li Si installed the Prince Ying as emperor;
[Ying] killed Zhao Gao and reigned for forty-six days. When the Duke of Pei arrived at Baxiang, King [Xiang Yu] came out in a plain carriage to surrender, and the empire was brought under the Han.
Liu Bang of the Han dynasty, styled Jiku, was a native of Feng in Pei Commandery. His mother, Wenxi, while at the Great Marsh, dreamed of union with a divine being;
moved by this, she gave birth to Jiku. He had a dragon-like countenance, a prominent forehead, and broad, generous bearing. He possessed a fine beard and mustache, and on his left thigh...
On his body, there were seventy-two black moles. Taking advantage of the violent Qin dynasty, he spread his hidden wings; having swallowed the powerful Chu, he finally rose up like a cloud.
Throughout his career, he engaged in a total of seventy-two battles before the world was pacified—this was the fulfillment of the significance of those black moles.
The auspicious omen lies herein. Having distantly inherited the legacy of the Zhou, it was consequently called Han. Xianyang was renamed Chang’an, and the capital was established there.

From the time of the opening of heaven and earth through the Three Sovereigns, Five Emperors, Xia, Yin, Zhou, and Qin, down to the reigns of Emperors Wen and Jing, the years were designated by the names of emperors and kings alone, with no separate titles established.
It was during the era of Emperor Wu that the practice of designating specific titles for the years was first instituted, known as "Jianyuan" (Establishing the Epoch). Epoch.
In the second year of the Shou era, Huo Qubing campaigned against the Xiongnu. Passing Mount Juyan, he captured the King of Xiutu and seized his golden figures, regarding them as great deities;
these were placed in the palace and worshipped with incense offerings. This was the first time Buddhist images arrived [in China].
In the third year, the Kunming Pool was excavated, and at its bottom, there was entirely ash and black soil. Emperor Wu asked Dongfang Shuo about this matter.
Shuo reported: "This is not within my knowledge; you may inquire of the foreign Hu practitioners of the Western Regions.

Later, when Zhang Qian returned from his mission to Daxia, the *Hanshu* first recorded the existence of the kingdom of Shendu (India). Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Ping, Grand Master Liu Xiang declared:

I have searched back through the *Lieshan tu* (Illustrated Biographies of Transcendents) originally compiled by the Grand Historian. From the Six Dynasties down to the present, there are over seven hundred individuals.
Having examined their veracity, I have definitively identified one hundred and forty-six persons. Of these, seventy-four already appear in Buddhist scriptures.
Inferring from this, it is clear that they were included in the scriptures available during the Han period, as well as in the two ancient records and the twelve [biographies] recorded by Dao’an.

The *Xianzhe deng jing* (Sūtra on the Worthies and Others) follows this pattern for the remainder; it contains only seventy-two individuals and is titled the *Lie xian zhuan* (Biographies of Transcendents).

This was likely because those of broad learning perceived the grand principles [of the tradition], yet knowing that during the Zhou period the Buddhist scriptures had circulated for a long time, their minds and perceptions were not yet harmonized with them, and thus those who returned to faith were rare.
Although Qin burned and eliminated them, they reappeared upon the rise of Han. Thus, Liu Xiang was able to examine the collected books in the imperial archives and compiled them anew.

Verifying what he had previously sought, he recorded it as authentic. Wang Mang’s courtesy name was Jujun; he was a native of Yuancheng.

Wang Mang enthroned Ying, the great-grandson of Emperor Xuandi, and styled him the "Child" (Ruzi). Wang Mang held the position of Chancellor for three years while acting as regent (*jishè*), and for fifteen years after assuming the true imperial title;
this totals eighteen years, though in reality it lasted only seventeen. Wang Mang was a seventh-generation descendant of Emperor Jing of the Liu clan.
Xuanzi was killed by the Duke of Sheng. He styled himself Gengshi and changed the era name to Xuanshi. Two years later, he was killed by the Red Eyebrows.
Liu Xiu, styled Wenshu, was a ninth-generation descendant of the High Ancestor and a scion of Prince Ding of Changsha.
He resided in the Baihui Township of Nanyang; his father served as the Magistrate of Jiyang. Xiu was born within the commandery amidst an auspicious sign of crimson light. This was the year—
A stalk of fine grain bore nine ears, hence he was named Xiù (The Outstanding). He had a prominent nose, a "sun-angle" mark on his forehead, a large mouth, long eyebrows, and a square face;
his hair and beard were beautiful. By nature he was kind and benevolent. Rising from Nanyang, he swept away the Chìméi rebels and thereby stabilized the empire;
this was the Emperor Gāowǔ of the Later Han. He moved the capital to Luoyang and styled the era Jiān-wǔ. Having heard the accounts of former generations concerning Gāowǔ...
He was born in Nanyang. In Nanyang, there were no men of low station; he had always considered such [accounts of foreign lands] to be empty fabrications.

Now, seeing the accounts in the scriptures that Śākyamuni appeared in India and that India abounds in sages, he finally verified their truth. This occurred during the reign of Emperor Ming, in the third year of the Yongping era.

Suddenly, he was moved by a divine dream; upon waking, he was filled with joy. He commanded his messenger to travel westward, so that Mi might settle his mind and direct his aspirations toward the realm of blessings.

During a moment of leisure, he asked his younger brother, Prince Dongping, while the latter was living at home: "What is the greatest pleasure for one dwelling in the household? Dongping was noble and distinguished.
His waistband was ten spans in circumference. He immediately replied, "To do good is the greatest joy. The Emperor remarked, "These words are truly grand;

they are more than sufficient to match the girth of the King's waist and belly. Later, when the envoy returned, the Emperor issued an edict to proclaim and translate [the scriptures]. It was from this point that the transmission originated.
The stream continues to the present day; the ocean of Dharma is inexhaustible, and the profound river never runs dry.

From the former and latter Han dynasties through to the Xin dynasty, there were twenty-six sovereigns in total for a duration of four hundred and twenty-five years. This records the imperial eras of the Eastern and Western Capitals (from the Kaihuang Sanbao Ji).
The Western Han High Ancestor: from the establishment of the state in the year Yiwei until the year Yichou, there were twelve sovereigns for a total of two hundred and ten years.

Emperor Wu succeeded [to the throne]. On the day Xin-chou, the first year of Jianyuan (the sixth year), the practice of using era names (nianhao) began from this point.
On the day Ding-wei, the era was changed to Guang (the sixth year). On the day Gui-chou, the era was changed to Shuo (the sixth year).
Jiwei (179 BCE). The first year of the Yuanshou era; the second year. According to the records of Emperor Wu’s reign, Wei Qing and Huo Qubing campaigned against the Xiongnu.
The Xiongnu King Kunye surrendered, and they captured his "Golden Man" deity. They enshrined it in the Gandian Palace. Their worship consisted solely of burning incense and prostrating;
the Emperor permitted them to follow their own customs in making offerings to it—this was the Buddha image. (From Changli’s “Parting with Master Ling”).
Poetic Commentary: In the eighth year of the Yuanshou era, which was the year Yichou, the reign title was changed to Yuanding.
In the third year of the Yuanding era, the Kunming Pond was excavated to an extreme depth; only ashes and black matter were seen, with no further soil or stone remaining.
The entire court could not explain the cause and questioned Dongfang Shuo about it. Shuo said, "This is not something I know."
"Later, there will be a Central Asian barbarian monk who comes to China; you may question him.

During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna from the kingdom of India entered Luoyang. Those who remembered the words of Shuo questioned them accordingly. Dharmaratna said:
When the great kalpa of heaven and earth is about to end, there occurs the kalpa-fire conflagration; these ashes and soot are the remnants of that conflagration.
In the year Jǐchǒu, Emperor Chéng ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jiānshǐ. In the year Xīnchǒu, it was changed to Hóngjiā.

In its second year, Liu Xiáng, Grand Master for Imperial Entertainments, compiled the *Shénxiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Transcendents). In his preface, he states: "I have examined all works among the hundred schools and cross-referenced them, thereby obtaining [the following]..."
There were one hundred and forty-six immortals; seventy-four of them appear in the Buddhist scriptures.

One can know that the Buddha’s teachings have circulated for a long time since the Zhou dynasty; although they were suppressed during the Qin, they re-emerged upon the rise of the Han.
Thus, prior to the Former Han, tracing back to the Zhou, there were both Buddhas and scriptures. Their arrival was ancient.
Why did Fan Ye claim that they first entered China during the reign of Emperor Ming? (Note from the *Mingzhao* commentary on the poem "Sending Off Master Ling" by Li Bai).

The Xin Shi (New Chamber) dynasty began its reign as "Cai" (Interim) in the year Yichou and ascended to the true throne in Dingmao. This lasted until Gengchen, for fifteen years, totaling eighteen reigns under Wang Mang.

The Eastern Han dynasty rose in arms.

the capital was at Luoyang.
Emperor Shizu Guangwu (Liu Xiu) was the ninth-generation descendant of Gaozu. In the third year of Gengshi, he changed the era name to Jianwu.
He reigned for thirty-one years.
*Xinhai*, the twenty-seventh year of Jianwu: this was one thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Wu-wu: Emperor Ming ascended the throne and changed the era name to Yongping. On the eighth day of the fourth month of the third year, the Geng-shen year, the Emperor dreamed of a golden man.
He questioned his high ministers as to who could interpret the dream. The Left Chancellor, Han Xian, memorialized, saying:
"I beg Your Majesty to recount it. Yesterday I dreamed of a golden man, sixteen feet tall, with a halo encircling his neck and a script inscribed upon his chest."
The *svastika* symbol; a topknot of coiled hair upon his head; and light radiating from his brow—it was said that this was Śākyamuni Buddha.

He was born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in the Western Regions, and since his parinirvāṇa, a thousand years have now passed. It is said that he possesses a Great Teaching which he entrusted to me to retrieve.

Among you officials, who is capable of knowing its details? At that time, the Chamberlain for Ceremonial Affairs, Fu Yi, memorialized, saying: "Your servant has observed that during the Zhou dynasty..."

The *Shuyiji* (Record of Extraordinary Events) states: On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the fixed stars did not appear, and an extraordinary light shone everywhere.
The Grand Astrologer Suyou performed a divination and reported: "A Great Sage has been born in the Western Regions; this is the manifestation of the Buddha.
One thousand years hence, his teachings and influence shall circulate throughout this land. King Zhao then ordered [a shrine] to be established at the southern suburb of Luoyang.

Beside the altar, a stele was erected as a record for future generations. "The dream Your Majesty had—was it perhaps a manifestation of the Buddha-spirit? When the Emperor heard this report, he was greatly pleased.
