He then summoned twenty-eight men, including Wang Dao of the National Academy (Guozijian), Qin Yuan of the Hanlin Academy, and General Cai Yin, and dispatched them with imperial credentials and edicts to travel far to the Western Regions to seek out the sacred scriptures. Upon arriving in the south...
In the kingdom of India, [the Emperor] sought out the two monks Kāśyapa Mātaṅga and Zhu Falan.

They brought with them Sanskrit manuscripts of the sutras and a painted image of Śākyamuni on white *kāśika* cotton cloth, which they carried on white horses. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the tenth year of Yongping, the year Dingmao, they arrived in Luoyang and presented themselves for an audience.
The Emperor was greatly delighted and bestowed upon them a reward of ten thousand pieces of gold. He then issued an imperial edict to the two monks, Mātaṅga and Falan.
He was accommodated at the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si). There, he translated the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* and a true image of Śākyamuni, which were enshrined in the main hall.
The Emperor maintained his recitation and offerings without fail. Having traveled from afar, the White Horse grew emaciated with exhaustion and died;
by imperial decree, it was buried west of the city of Luoyang, and a monastery was established there, officially named "White Horse" (*Baima*). This was the first [monastery] in China.
At the very beginning of the construction of temples, when the Dharma flowed into the Eastern Land, it was Lord Ying of Chu alone who first took pleasure in and served it.

He presented yellow silk and white fine silk, approaching the Provincial Governor and saying: "As one entrusted with the status of a vassal ruler, my transgressions and evils have accumulated. [I now] rejoice greatly..."
"Your kindness is great. We have sent this silk and cloth to atone for our transgressions. The State Chancellor reported this to the Emperor, who issued an edict in reply, saying:
"The Prince of Chu recites the subtle words of Huang-Lao and honors the benevolent temples of the Buddha. Having purified himself for three months, he has made a vow with the divine.

What cause for suspicion or doubt could there be that he would incur regret or error? Let him return the ransom to assist in providing the abundant offerings for the *upāsakas* and *śramaṇas* during their fast."
This was the beginning of the *Seng* (Monks).

In the year *Xinwei*, the fourteenth year of the Yongping era, the Daoist master of the Five Peaks, Chu Shixin, and others submitted a memorial, which was presented to the Throne by the Secretariat and the Chancellery.
Upon reading the memorial, the Emperor ordered Song Xiang, an attendant of the Palace Gate, to lead them into an audience, saying: "I have heard from afar..."
I have sought the holy teachings. Spoken by the Buddha in the West, their purport is subtle and profound; they provide guidance for nourishing life and perpetually augment merit and benefit.
Why, then, do you intend to call them "barbarian deities" and command me to eliminate them? Your minds waver between proceeding and retreating.

According to my own intent, the Buddha-dharma shall not be eliminated and the Way of the Daoists shall not be extinguished. On the fifteenth day of the first month, let them compete before the Baima Monastery.
To determine their relative superiority and inferiority, and to establish their definitive strengths and weaknesses, the Emperor ordered the construction of three altars:

two hundred and seventy scrolls of Confucian texts and historical records were placed on the central altar; three hundred and sixty scrolls of Daoist texts and esoteric arts were placed on the eastern altar;

and Buddhist scriptures along with an image of Śākyamuni were placed on the western altar. On the fifteenth day, the Emperor led his hundred officials and various ministers to arrive before the temple.

The Daoist first displayed his magical arts, summoning wind and drawing down rain, and commanding spirits and deities to cease their activities. The two monks, Dharmaratna and Buddhabhadra, sat in the *paryaṅka* posture.

By imperial decree, the Attendant-in-Ordinary Song Xiang was sent to interrogate the two monks. The two monks submitted this memorial: "In our Buddhist tradition, we practice the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*).
These illusory arts are not performed by us. Before the presence of the Emperor, [we must distinguish ourselves from such practitioners]."

To verify the true from the false: there is nothing more impartial on this earth than fire. We pray that Your Majesty will take these scriptures of the Three Teachings, pile them together in one place, and test them with fire.
Those that do not turn to ash shall be deemed true; those that burn to ash shall be deemed false.

Upon hearing these words, the Emperor issued an order to take the texts from the heap, stack firewood above and below them, and announce to Heaven before setting them ablaze. The two monks offered their prayers.
After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, the Buddha-dharma was entrusted to kings, ministers, and my disciples.

Having brought the scriptures from afar to this eastern land, they have falsely propounded heterodox views and slandered the True Vehicle. Today, let the fire distinguish between the true and the false. I pray that you will grant your secret protection:

if it remains entirely unharmed, may the Dharma flourish in this land to teach and transform sentient beings; if it turns to ash along with the flames, then [the Dharma shall not remain] in this land.
"Sentient beings have not heard the Buddha-dharma. Having finished speaking, the flames soared to the heavens, and both the Confucian and Daoist scriptures were reduced to ashes.
From within the fire, a golden lotus pedestal appeared, supporting a Buddhist scripture and an image that radiated light with solemn dignity.

At that time, the Emperor and his ministers, witnessing this extraordinary marvel, were struck with awe and alarm. They sighed, saying: "The pack of wolves and foxes is vast, while the phoenix is rare and the common birds are many."
The two monks took the sutras and presented them to Emperor Dian, who then spoke this verse: "The fox is not of the lion’s kind; A lamp is not as bright as the sun and moon.
A pond lacks the waves of the great ocean; A mound is not as towering as a mountain peak. Yet within this very Buddha-world, The seeds of goodness have begun to sprout."

He manifested the Dharma of my True Suchness (tathatā) and saved sentient beings everywhere. The Emperor increased his veneration and respect, enshrining a statue of Śākyamuni and scriptures at Xianjie Ling and Qingliang Terrace for offerings.
The Emperor permitted Yangcheng Hou Liu Jun and others to leave the household life, and further allowed the women of Luoyang, such as Ap'an and others, to leave the household life.
He issued an edict for the two monks, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, to shave their heads on their behalf.
[Emperor Ming] had his hair shaved and ordered the relevant authorities to construct ten temples: seven for housing monks and three for housing nuns.
This was the beginning of the establishment of monks and nuns in China (from the *Shiwu ji yuan*).
The Tang Emperor Taizong inscribed this poem at Baima Monastery: "The path is desolate, overgrown with long green moss; Each time I ascend these steps, I linger in reflection.
It is in vain that the Blue Ox is said to have departed through the Pass of Han; The White Horse personally brought the Dharma from India. To settle right and wrong, one relies on a fierce flame;
To distinguish the true from the false, one builds a high platform. Even the spring breeze understands the sense of disorder, And blows it all away."
According to the *Fanyi mingyi* (Explanations of Terms in Translation) by Daoxuan,

the *Han Fajing zhuan* (Biographies of the Transmission of the Dharma in the Han) records that the thirtieth day of the twelfth month in the Western Regions corresponds to the full moon of the first month in this region,
which is called the Month of Great Miracles (*mahāprātihārya-māsa*). Emperor Ming of the Han ordered lamps to be lit to symbolize the great illumination of the Buddha-dharma.
Bingzi: Emperor Zhang ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jianchu. In Jiashen, he changed it again to Yuanhe.

In the first year, there were auspicious omens of divine sparrows, phoenixes, white deer, and white crows. Wang Jing, the Inspector of Xuzhou, presented the "Eulogy on the Golden Man" (Jinren song) to praise Emperor Guangwu for his achievement in bringing the Buddha [to China] (*Hanshu*).
Dinghai: Emperor Huan ascended the throne. He changed the era name to Jianhe. On Guisi, he changed it again to Yongxing.
In the first year, he cast a golden stupa and an image of Laozi for worship within the palace, covering them with a canopy of a hundred jewels; the Emperor served them with the utmost reverence.

Wu-xu: The year nine of the Yanxi era was changed [to Yongping]. Pei Kai submitted a memorial, saying: "Now, Buddhist stupas and shrines for the Yellow Emperor and Laozi have been established within the palace.
These teachings favor life and loathe killing, and advocate reducing desire and abandoning extravagance. Yet today, Your Majesty does not abandon your cravings and lusts."
To carry out executions and warfare beyond the bounds of reason violates the Way; how could such acts possibly secure divine blessing?

Now, as for the Buddha (Futu), he does not stay beneath a *sāla* tree for more than three nights, for he does not wish to engender long-term attachments. This is the height of spiritual refinement. When a celestial deity presented him with a beautiful woman, the Buddha said:
"This is merely a leather bag filled with blood," he said, and thus he did not even look at her; such was his constancy in guarding the One, and only thereby could he achieve the Way.
Now, Your Majesty’s wanton women and beautiful concubines possess the utmost splendor in the world, and their sweet delicacies and fine drinks exhaust all the flavors of the realm.

"How can you wish to be like the Buddha or Laozi? He submitted this memorial to inquire about the circumstances. The Minister of Revenue, following the imperial decree, reported that Cai Xie had slandered the Emperor and committed acts of deception.
Thus, Cai Xie’s crime was adjudicated (as recorded in the *Book of Han* and the *Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government*).
Wu-shen: Emperor Ling ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jianning. In the third year, the śramaṇa An Shigao arrived at the capital and translated ninety-five sections of sūtras.
First he produced one fascicle of the *Jueyi* (Deciding the Meaning), followed by the various monastic prohibitions and precepts (*bhikṣu-śīla*).
Xin-hai, the fourth year. An Shigao arrived at Mount Lu. There was a temple at Qiuting that was extremely efficacious.
At one time, more than thirty boats had come to request special blessings. The deity suddenly descended and spoke, saying: "There is a śramaṇa among the boats; you may invite him to come."
The guest invited Hui-gao to come. The deity descended again and spoke, saying: "In the past, I and you both left the household life to study the Way.

I was fond of giving but prone to much anger; now I am a temple deity, yet my lifespan will end this very morning. I fear that hereafter I shall fall into hell. I have a thousand rolls of silk and various household goods;
you may use these to establish the Dharma and construct a stupa for me, so that I may be reborn in a good realm. Hui-gao...
Manifesting his form, the spirit appeared as a giant python. Weeping with tears like rain, it gathered up the silk goods and departed.

Upon arriving at [Yuzhang, he built the pagoda of Dajian Temple; this was the beginning of temple pagodas in the Jianghuai region], according to the *Zhenjing lu*, the spirit soon passed away. It was reported that he had been reborn in a good realm.
Later, someone saw a dead python in a marsh west of the mountain, its head and tail spanning several li. This occurred in Xunyang.
The county is Da’mao Village.
At the beginning of Emperor Ming’s reign, he heard that there was a deity in the Western Regions named Buddha. Consequently, he dispatched envoys to India to seek his Way.
They returned with scriptures and śramaṇas. These scriptures generally take emptiness as their fundamental principle and value compassion.
Out of compassion, they do not kill. For when such a person dies, their spirit is not extinguished; it follows them as they receive another form.
Whatever good or evil one performs while alive all has its retribution. Therefore, what is prized is the cultivation of the spirit until one attains Buddhahood.
Using grand and magnificent words, they exhort and lead the secular world. Those who are refined in this Way are called śramaṇas. From [the time of] Yong...
Since the time of Emperor Ping, the methods [of Buddhism] first began to be transmitted in China; its images were depicted, and even kings, dukes, and nobles all venerated them.
Although there were subjects and citizens who practiced these methods, the Son of Heaven did not favor them.

It was not until the time of Emperor Huan that he took a profound interest in them, frequently performing prayers and sacrifices himself. Consequently, these methods gradually flourished; thus, when Pei Kai submitted his memorial, it resulted in...
What deficiency could there be in the crime of slandering the Sovereign? During the Jianning era of Emperor Ling’s reign, An Shigao arrived;

he translated the *Jueyi lü* (Decisions on the Vinaya), and for the first time, monks were subject to formal prohibitions. At that time, the deity of Qingtong Temple knew that his life was nearing its end and that he was destined to fall into the evil realms.

I humbly request Your Highness’s favor. Although the silks and treasures I offer are but material things, by entrusting them to the construction of the stupa, I may expiate my transgressions and be reborn in a virtuous realm.
How manifest is the efficacy of the Buddha-dharma!

The *Shishi Shiwu Jiyuan* (Origins of the Affairs of the Śākya Clan) records that the beginning of the establishment of altars for the reception of precepts—the fundamental source of the Great Precepts (*mahāśīla*)—dates back to the third year of the Huangchu era of the Cao Wei dynasty, the Renyin year.

By that time, [the teachings] had already reached Xuchang; however, due to many domestic disturbances within the state, they remained dormant for over thirty years until the reign of Emperor Fei, also known as Gao-gui.

When the Prince [Liu Ying] ascended the throne, he changed the era name to Zhengyuan. In the first year of that cycle, Jiaxu (594 CE), the Indian Vinaya Master Dharmakāla submitted a memorial proposing the commencement of the rite of receiving the precepts.

Counting backward from this to the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han dynasty (62 CE), the year Dingmao—the year the Buddha-dharma first arrived in China—it was one hundred and seventy-eight years later.
During this entire period, those who had left the household life had received only the Three Refuges precept.
In the Western Heaven’s Jeta Grove, the Bhikṣu Lohitya requested the Buddha to establish an altar for the purpose of conferring the precepts upon bhikṣus.
The Tathāgata established a single altar in the southeast of the outer enclosure of the grove; this was the beginning.

In this land, in the seventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty (the Gengwu year), the Indian monk Guṇavarman (known as Gongde Kai during the Liang dynasty) arrived at the bamboo grove in front of Nanlin Temple in Yangzhou.
Within the garden, an altar was erected, called the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) Altar; this marked the beginning of the conferral of precepts. The *Sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of the Sangha) states:

"The reason for the precept altar is that it originally arose from the teachings of the Hīnayāna, corresponding to the monastic disciplinary laws (*vinaya*) of the monks, with every detail according to the rules.

If even a slight good deed deviates [from the rules], one will not receive the precepts. As for those presiding at the altar committing offenses, the present Fangdeng Dharma is precisely for this purpose. According to the *Dafangdeng*...

Regarding the Vehicle of Teaching (*yāna-vinaya*): it does not depend on the impairment of the faculties or differences in conditions; rather, simply by generating the great resolve and receiving [the precepts], one immediately attains the precepts.
This may be called vast, equal, and all-pervasive; therefore, it is termed the Vaipulya Mahāyāna.
It is also named "Amṛta" (Nectar). Amṛta is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*. Since the precepts are the initial gateway to human *nirvāṇa*, they are designated by the name of their fruit.
The *Jietan tujing* (Diagram Sutra of the Precept Platform) states:

"Now, those who wish to receive the precepts must first be exhorted and instructed by a person of wisdom to give rise to a mind of compassionate protection toward all phenomena. Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:

'By universally giving rise to a benevolent intention toward all sentient beings and attaining a mind free from harm, one receives the precepts. When approaching the assembly of the Sangha, one should perform the ritual."
Regarding the matter: to simply say that one who has aroused the superior grade of mind (śīla) obtains the superior grade of precepts is something the śrāmaṇeras have never heard before;
they do not know what constitutes the superior grade of mind. This is like thunder ringing out from the sky above a wondrous peak while the sweet rain fails to fall upon the golden earth.
The "superior grade of mind" refers precisely to the arising of a heart of compassionate protection toward all objects of the ten thousand realms. — Upāsaka...

The *Saijie jing* (Sīla-saṃvara-sūtra) states: "There are two fruits of the precepts: first, the bliss of the heavens; second, the bliss of bodhi. The wise seek the bliss of bodhi and do not seek the bliss of the heavens.

The *Zhengfalianchu jing* (Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra) states: "If one upholds the precepts while keeping the bliss of the heavens in mind, such a person defiles purity, like water mixed with poison.
This is because the bliss of the heavens is impermanent; when their lifespan ends, they will inevitably fall back and must undergo great suffering."
Suffering. Therefore, one should seek the bliss of nirvāṇa. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: first, the mind that is weary of the conditioned;
second, the mind that seeks to proceed toward bodhi; third, the mind of compassion for sentient beings. A verse from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says:
"The person of wisdom who can guard the precepts shall obtain three kinds of happiness: reputation and gain in this life, and upon death, rebirth in the heavens."
Regarding the bestowal of purple robes and monastic titles, the *Sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of the Sangha) states:

During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian of the Tang dynasty, nine monks including Falang and others, having completed the re-translation of the *Dayun jing* (Mahāmegha-sūtra), were all granted titles, purple robes, and silver tortoise-shaped insignia.

At the beginning of the Taiping Xingguo era, permission was granted for monks from all quarters to enter the palace precincts to request these honors and undergo an examination in the Three Studies; the Kaifeng Prefecture was ordered to appoint monks to verify their mastery of the Sūtras and Vinaya.

Regarding the doctrinal debates (*lunyi*): having fully mastered all ten topics, he was granted purple robes and a monastic title and appointed as a "Hand-Table Monk" (*shou biao seng*), because he presented his memorial with his own hand.

Subsequently, upon the petition of the Office of Merit (*gongde si*), it was stated that since the world is now a single family, there is no longer a need for hand-written memorials to seek selection.

By imperial decree, from this time forward, whenever it was the Emperor’s birthday, from the princes, chief ministers, and regional commanders down to the prefects, all were permitted to submit petitions recommending monks they knew for purple robes (*zīyī*).
However, only those recommended by the two monastic offices (*liàngjiē sēngyín suǒ*) were allowed to enter the palace.

On that day, their disciples would receive official documents for the four items of the purple robe; this was known as the "Bestowal of Purple before the Curtain" (*liánqián cìzǐ*), which was considered the highest honor.
However, this robe was obtained through the grace of the state; it was by no means easy to receive. Only when one’s physical appearance and character are fully perfected may one be granted it.
(The *Dongguan zouji* records that during the Dazhong era, the monk Xiu Hui of Daguangsi Temple was able to compose poetry for imperial occasions, his talent being clear and outstanding.
One day he requested from the Emperor that he be granted a purple robe. Xuánzōng said: "I [do not...]")
"You are being stingy. I have observed that your features are deficient; therefore, I shall not grant it. When the gift was finally bestowed, he returned to the monastery and passed away.
Recently, there have been several similar instances. It can be said that on the path to the human and celestial realms, merit must come first.

Emperor Dezong summoned Dharma Master Duānfǔ to the inner palace to debate with representatives of Confucianism and Daoism. He was granted a purple cassock and ordered to attend upon the Crown Prince.
The Eastern Court [Emperor] Shunzong esteemed him as if he were a brother, while Emperor Xianzong treated him like a guest or friend.

He presided over the ritual protocols of the inner palace and recorded the affairs of the monks of the two streets (the eastern and western monastic districts). During the Kaicheng era of Emperor Wenzong, he was established as the Left and Right Street Monk-Recorders (Zuoyou Jielu);

this was the beginning of that office. During the Qianning era of Emperor Zhaozong, the title of "Head Seat" (Shouzuo) was changed to "Vice Monk-Recorder" (Fusenglü), with Juehui being the first to hold it.

Furthermore, regarding the establishment of *daochang* (Dharma assemblies) for the Emperor’s birthday, the *Sengshilüe* (Brief History of the Sangha) by the *Senglü* (Registrar of Monks) Zanning states:

In the second year of Shiguang of Emperor Taowu of the Wei dynasty, *daochang* were established to offer prayers for longevity. In the fourth year of Shenjia, they were established throughout Jiazhou. This was on the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday.
It is said that this was merely the temporary establishment of a *dharmapūjā* assembly during the reign of Emperor Yunsheng.
During the Shiguang era, this marked the beginning of the Emperor’s own veneration for merit; during the Shenjia era, it marked the beginning of his ministers’ offerings.

What is practiced in the present day all originated during the Tang dynasty under Emperor Daizong, who first recited the *Ratnatriparivarta Sūtra*. This was likely initiated by Yuan Zai and Wang Jin. (From the *Wudai huiyao*).

In the second year of the Guangming era of Emperor Zhou, an imperial edict was issued to the officials and ministers stating that on the occasion of the Buddha’s birthday (the Holy Festival), they were to visit the monasteries and establish dharma assemblies there;
this has remained a long-standing tradition to this day.
A Mirror for Buddhist Aid through Successive Dynasties, Volume One;
A Mirror for Buddhist Aid through Successive Dynasties, Volume Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xizhong of Yifeng, Min.
Beginning with the Three Augusts, Heaven had but one sovereign; ending with the two Han dynasties, Earth had no second minister.

From the Wei and Jin periods down to the Great Sui, the imperial capitals during this interval were as numerous as bristles on a hedgehog; there were twenty-two states where capitals stood like crows perching or cranes standing.
Among these, the eight states of Wu, the Three Qin, Liang, Wei, Qi, and Chen, though each claimed to preserve its own name, [were but fragments].
They were all translators of Buddhist scriptures who enabled the Three Jewels to endure; thus, the four modes of birth were sustained by their grace.
Consequently, those who devoted themselves to goodness received blessings, which is why the records of the world have been handed down in succession.

Yet, regarding those who seized the opportunity to become hegemonous rulers—there were fourteen such states—since they did not propagate the holy teachings, we know nothing of their ancestral practices. Now...

Based on their respective *Shi* (Poetry) and *Shu* (Documents), I have roughly indicated their dates and eras, so that one may understand the origins and developments of their strengths and weaknesses.
Wen Di of Wei, Cao Pi, son of Cao Cao, received the abdication of the Han in the first year of Huangchu, the gengzi year. He established his capital at Luoyang.
Shu Xianzhu Liu Bei, [reigned] from the xin-chou year; he established his capital at Yi. The two rulers [of Shu] held power for forty-three years before returning to Wei. Wu...
Sun Quan [established his capital] at Jiankang in the year Renyin. Under four successive rulers, the dynasty lasted fifty-nine years before returning to the Jin.

The Wei dynasty, under five successive rulers, lasted forty-five years before the abdication was received by the Jin. In the fifth year of Xianning of Emperor Wu of Jin, the year Jihai, the entire universe once again shared a unified system of laws and culture.
Twenty-three years later, in the first year of Yongning of Emperor Hui of Jin, the year Xinyou, the various provinces and territories—
Rulers along the various banks vied with one another to establish their capitals. In the first year of Dà'ān, the *rénxū* year, Zhāng Guǐ rose in Liángzhōu; this was Former Liáng.
Seven rulers reigned for sixty-two years before it fell to Fú Jiān of Former Qín. In the first year of Yǒngxīng, the *jiǎzǐ* year, Lǚ Yuān rose in Píngyáng; this was Former Zhào.
Four rulers reigned for twenty-six years before it fell to Shí Lè of Later Zhào. It was the same [year] as...
In the first year of the Daxing era, Li Xiong rose in Shu; this was the Later Shu. It had four rulers and lasted forty-four years before being destroyed by the Jin Emperor Mu.
In the third year of the Daxing era of the Eastern Jin Emperor Yuan (the Gengchen year), Shi Le rose at Xiangguo and later moved his capital to Ye;
this was the Later Zhao. Including Min, it had four rulers and lasted thirty-five years before being absorbed into Former Yan. —Eastern Jin—
In the *yīmǎo* year, the eleventh year of the Yǒnghé era of Emperor Mù, Tányǔ Wǎng founded Huanglong; later, he moved the capital to Yè, establishing what was known as Former Yan.
This dynasty lasted for nine years under two rulers before being absorbed by Former Qin. In the *bǐngxū* year, the eleventh year of the Tàiyuán era of Emperor Xiàowǔ of the Jìn dynasty—
Murong Chui rose from Zhongshan and returned to assume the title of Yan; this was Later Yan. He moved the capital to Huanglong.
Five rulers reigned for twenty-six years before it fell to Feng Ba of Northern Yan. This lasted until the twelfth year, the Dinghai year (347 AD), when Lü Guang rose in Liang.
This was the Later Liang dynasty. It had four rulers and lasted for sixteen years before being absorbed into the Later Qin under Yao Xing.
In the first year of Long’an of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the year Dingyou (397 CE), Tufan Wugu rose in Xiping; this was called the Southern Liang.
It had three rulers and lasted for eighteen years before being absorbed into the Western Qin under Qifu Chipan. In the second year, Wuxu (398 CE), Murong De rose in Guang.
Gu was the ruler of Nan-yen (Southern Yan). Two rulers reigned for thirteen years before it was destroyed by Jin.

In the fourth year, the gengzi year, Li Gu rose in Dunhuang; this became Xi-liang (Western Liang). Three rulers reigned for twenty-two years until the sixth year, the gengxu year, when it fell to the Northern Wei under Emperor Taizu.
During this period, Feng Ba rose and extinguished Hou-yen (Later Yan), establishing his capital at Changli; this became Bei-yen (Northern Yan).

The two rulers reigned for twenty-eight years. This period also spans from the reign of Emperor Taizu of Northern Wei up to the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of Song, the *ji-mao* year.
It was in the fifth year of the Dayan era of Northern Wei that Emperor Taizu launched a western expedition and subsequently extinguished the Northern Liang.

From this point on, various states were successively annexed until they were almost entirely eliminated; only Northern Wei remained until the first year of the Longchang era of Emperor Ming of Qi, the *jia-zi* year.
Xushen (the Dog year). This was the eleventh year of Taihe of the Northern Wei. Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital south to Luoyang.
○ The sixth year of Datong of Emperor Wu of Liang, the Jia-yin year, was the third year of Yongxi of the Southern Wei.
Emperor Wu first established his base in Chang’an, relying on Zhou Taizu Yuwen Helü of the Later Qin and Qi Taizu Gao Guan; he then separately established the Prince of Qinghe.
Zi Yuan succeeded to the throne as King. He resided in the northern capital at Ye; it was for this reason that the realm later divided into Eastern and Western Wei.
In the fourth year of Chengsheng of Emperor Xiaoyuan of the Liang dynasty, the year Yihai, the capital was at Jiangling, where he was extinguished by Western Wei.

From then on, the imperial mandate of the South returned to the North. That year was the second year following the establishment of Wei. Xiao Yan’s grandson Chao was granted the title and established by Wei.

It succeeded the foundation of the Liang dynasty and was thus called the Later Liang. Having become a vassal state, it was a shadow kingdom. When the Zhou received the abdication of the Wei, they maintained its existence;
it remained with its capital at Jiangling for thirty-three years under five rulers before yielding to the Sui.

Regarding the governance of the Sui dynasty: Yang Jian was a native of Huayin in Hongnong. His father, Yang Zhong, served Emperor Wen of the Zhou dynasty as Grand Tutor (Taifu) and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Sui.

Jian inherited the title and served Emperor Wu; during the reign of Emperor Jing, he became Chancellor of the State (Xiangguo) and was enfeoffed as a Prince. He subsequently usurped the mandate, establishing his capital at Chang’an.

Having been a kinsman of the imperial harem through his marriage to the daughter of Emperor Xuan of Zhou, he had long held significant power. By nature, he was grave and dignified, and possessed a broad...
Possessing majestic presence, he was able to extend his sincere heart to treat his former ministers, allowing each to display their talents.

Thus, the conquest of the Southern Dynasties—a kingdom that had endured for three hundred years—was as easy as turning over one's palm, bringing the world under a single unification during the Kaihuang and Renshou eras.

The Way of the King was serenely proclaimed; under his rule, the world was unified as if by the tallying of chariots and books. His transformative influence brought great merit, yet the people lacked words to praise his virtue.

How could one have expected that Emperor Yang would betray the legacy of such wealth and strength, seeking instead to indulge his insatiable desires? Before long, bandits rose up like bristling quills.
Consequently, the rebellion at Jiangdu occurred. When Li Yuan’s army conquered Chang’an, he established the Gongyang Emperor;
though he wished not to abdicate, how could he have avoided it?
The Sui dynasty possessed the realm. It passed through three sovereigns for a total of thirty-nine years.

From the *gengzi* year of the Wei dynasty to the *wuyin* year of the Sui, there were forty-seven sovereigns spanning three hundred and ninety-eight years across seven dynasties and five capitals; such is what is recorded in the *Shilu*.
The Three Kingdoms:
Wei (High Ancestor Emperor Wen), Cao Pi. Son of Cao Cao. He received the abdication of the Han dynasty and established his capital at Luoyang.
He ascended the throne on the day of Gengzi (changing the era name to Huangchu). [Five rulers; forty-five years.]
Shu: The First Sovereign, Liu Bei. A descendant of Prince Jing of Zhongshan. He established his capital at Yi (Chengdu).
He ascended the throne in the year Xinchou (establishing the Zhangwu era; the second ruler; forty-three years).
Wu: Sun Quan, the son of [Sun] Wu. Initially based at Wuchang, later at Jianye. Ascended the throne on a *renyin* day (establishing the Huangwu era).
[He was succeeded by] four rulers for fifty-nine years.

Dingwei (the 10th day of the 4th month). In the first year of the Dàhé era of Emperor Ming of the Lièzǔ (Later Zhao), a eunuch of the capital felt ashamed of his status as a castrated remnant and petitioned to enter the mountains to practice the Way.
An imperial edict granted him permission. He then took the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with him and recited it day and night, performing prostrations and repentance without ceasing.

Before the summer retreat was even half-finished—six months having passed—his hair and beard grew back, and he attained the physical marks of a man. He reported this situation to the throne, and the Emperor read the report.
He was greatly astonished and held it in high esteem. Thereupon, he came to revere the *Avataṃsaka* and placed deep faith in the Buddha-dharma (*Gantong lu*).
Wushen (120 CE): In the fifth year of the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty, Cao Zhi, Prince of Chen-si, styled Zijian, was profoundly skilled in calligraphy and the arts.
He did not favor the teachings of Huang-Lao; he read only Buddhist scriptures, always lingering over them with admiration and appreciation, regarding them as the pinnacle of the ultimate Way.
He once composed the "Discourse on Distinguishing the Way" (*Bian dao lun*) to express his views (as recorded in the *Hongming ji*).
Xinyou (the 4th year of the Chiku era): In the fourth year of the Chiku era, the śramaṇa Senghui from the kingdom of Kangju first arrived in Jinling.
He constructed a thatched hut and established an image to perform the Way. When the people of the state first saw a śramaṇa, they were struck with wonder and astonishment.

The officials reported this to the Ruler of Wu, who summoned him to question him. Senghui extensively explained the causes of the Tathāgata’s transformation and how his traces had already transcended a thousand years; his spiritual...

As for the bone relics, their divine manifestations are boundless. King Aśoka erected eighty-four thousand stupas, and the founding of this temple’s stupa serves as a manifestation of his transformative power.
Huiquan said, "If we obtain the relics, I shall have a stupa built; if there is no such proof, the state shall impose its regular punishments.
He then requested a period of seven days and addressed his disciples, saying, "The rise or fall of the Great Dharma depends upon this single undertaking."
One should apply oneself with earnest supplication and together establish a purified chamber. Place a copper flask upon a stand and burn incense.

If no signs appear by the appointed time, extend the period for twenty-one days. At the fifth watch, suddenly a sharp metallic sound was heard from within the flask; looking inside, one indeed obtained śarīra relics, which emerged in a variegated array of five colors.
At dawn, they were presented [to the King], who and his ministers were greatly delighted and exclaimed in amazement, "What a rare and auspicious omen!"
Hui also said, "The majestic spiritual power of the Śāri-kapāla is such that nothing can destroy it. The Ruler of Wu sent a strongman to strike it with a hammer;

though both the anvil and the hammer were shattered, its radiance remained as before. Thereupon, a stupa was built at Fotuo-li and a monastery was established, which was granted the name Jianchu Monastery.
This is how Bao Ning recorded its origins and its arrival here. As for the stupa, it is the Tianxi [Stupa], which was built by the Emperor of Jin.
He crossed the river and further adorned [the structure] with gold and turquoise. This is the origin of the construction of pagodas in China (*Fanyi mingyi*).

When Kan Ze was serving as Counselor to the Heir Apparent under the Wu state, the Ruler of Wu asked Ze: "In what year did the Buddha enter China? For what reason has he not yet reached this region? Ze replied:
"In the Yongping era, the Buddha-dharma first arrived. Calculating from that time until the fourth year of the Chihu era, it is seven..."

It has been more than a hundred years since then. In the fourteenth year of the Yongping era, the Daoist practitioners Chu Shanxin and others requested to compete in the Dharma with the Western monks;
Shanxin died from the consequences of his arrogance and delusions. Since no one in China had left the household life, there was no one to propagate [the teachings].

Furthermore, they suffered through times of turmoil; thus, it was only after many years that [the texts] finally reached their own country. The Ruler of Wu said: "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi may be compared with those of the Buddha."
Zé asked, "How so? He replied, "The teachings of the two masters, Confucius and Laozi, establish their applications by taking Heaven as the model;

they dare not disobey Heaven. The Buddha’s exposition of the teachings has Heaven follow its ordinances; [the Buddha] dares not disobey the Buddha. By this one may see the difference in their relative excellence. (Zong Bing, *Mingfo lun*) Jiaxu:
In the first year of the Wufeng era of the Wu dynasty, Zhi Qian arrived here. He translated eighty-eight sections of scriptures and was widely learned.

He was deeply versed in the classics and scriptures, earning him the contemporary sobriquet of "The Satchel of Wisdom. The Ruler of Wu held his talent in high esteem and appointed him as a *boshi* (Court Scholar), but he firmly declined.
He served as a tutor to the Crown Prince, providing great benefit to the education of the heir apparent (*Shijiao lu*).
Yihai (the second day of the tenth month): The Tripiṭaka Master Dharmadeva from India (translated as Fǎzàng in Chinese) arrived at Luò carrying the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The Anxi śramaṇa Tandi also arrived; he too was well-versed in the study of the Vinaya. Together they produced one fascicle of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

In the early years of Jiaping, Dharmakāla from the Western Regions (translated as Fǎshí in Chinese) arrived at Xù and Luò. He saw that the bhikṣus within the Wei territory had their hair specifically cut short, yet... [the text ends].
There was a Vinaya master who subsequently transmitted it to Tandi. Together they translated the *Caturvargika-karman* and the *Sāṃghāṭī-śīlacitta-tu*.
In the Jiaping era, he invited Dharmatrāta and others to establish the *karman* and precept rituals, employing ten monks to perform Buddhist rites on his behalf;
this was the beginning of the formal ordination of the great monks in the Central Kingdom.
Yiyou (the second year of the sexagenary cycle): The first year of the Ganlu era of Wu. Sun Hao systematically destroyed all spirit shrines, and his persecution extended even to Buddhist temples.

He dispatched an envoy to interrogate the monk Senghui, who refuted the envoy’s arguments. Sun Hao then summoned Senghui and questioned him regarding the Buddha’s teachings on good and evil karmic retribution. Senghui replied:
When an enlightened ruler governs the world with benevolence and virtue, vermilion phoenixes soar and auspicious grain sprouts. As there is a response for good, so it is for evil.

The *I Ching* proclaims that accumulated goodness brings surplus blessings; the *Odes* praise seeking fortune without turning back from righteousness. Hao said: "Since the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are already clear on this..."

"What use is Buddhism? [Sun] Hui replied: "The Duke of Zhou and Confucius did not wish to speak of things in depth; they merely recorded their outward traces. The Buddha does not stop at shallow words;
therefore, he reveals the essentials. All are for the sake of goodness. The Sage only fears that goodness is not sufficient; why does Your Majesty consider it a source of suspicion?
Sun Hao had no reply and consequently ceased [his objections]. On another day, while the imperial guards were tending the garden, they found a...
Sun Hao had a golden statue placed in his latrine to serve as a source of amusement. Shortly thereafter, he contracted a swelling disease, with excruciating pain in his private parts.

A divination stated that this was due to offending a great deity. Sun Hao offered prayers at various shrines without success. A palace woman who served the Buddha said, "Why not seek blessings from the Buddha and perform repentance?
Sun Hao replied, "If the Buddha is such a spirit as this, is he not a mere monster? The woman said, "It is the majestic power of the Buddha."
The various devas provided protection. Hào suddenly realized and said, "It was because of my arrogance toward the image that I brought this upon myself.

He then welcomed the image, bathed it with fragrant water, and enshrined it within the inner court for offerings. He further invited Huì to preach the Dharma and perform repentance. Huì expounded for him the profound essentials of the teaching.

He then received the five precepts. He hoped that [the Emperor’s] illness would soon be cured; for this reason, he took Senghui as his teacher and lavishly adorned the stupas and monasteries (*Fayuan zhulin*).
During the forty-four years of the Three Kingdoms' tripartite division, only the Ruler of Wu reigned for approximately sixty years.

At that time, Dharma Master Hui crossed the Yangtze River, and the Ruler summoned him to question him. Hui extensively recounted the traces of the Tathāgata’s transformations and subsequently prayed for śarīra relics, which appeared within a bronze bottle.

When the Ruler of Wu saw this, he was struck with wonder and joy, saying, "This is a most extraordinary matter; I hold it in deep reverence. He then erected a stupa, constructed a monastery, and ordained monks.
From that time on, the Buddha-dharma flourished in the region south of the Yangtze.
The Western Jin was founded by Sima Yan, the son of Emperor Zhao, who received the abdication from the Wei dynasty.
From the year Bingxu to Dingchou, four emperors reigned for a total of fifty-three years, with the capital at Luoyang.
Emperor Wu, the World-Ancestor, ascended the throne in the twelfth month of the year Yiyou and changed the era name to Taishi.

Possessing a majestic countenance with dragon-like features, this sovereign of great brilliance initiated a new epoch and extensively promoted Buddhist affairs, widely constructing monasteries as recorded in the regional gazetteers.

In the second year [of the reign of Emperor Hui], Zhu Fahu (translated here as Dharmarakṣa), a native of Dunhuang, first traveled to the Western Regions and brought back a vast collection of Sanskrit scriptures to return to the Eastern Land.
He arrived in Chang’an in this year; regarding the transmission of Buddhist teachings to this land, Dharmarakṣa’s contribution was particularly distinguished.
He was, in fact, the first among the śramaṇas of this land to seek out the scriptures.
Gengxu: Emperor Hui changed the era name to Yongxi. The following year, he changed it again to Kang.
In the sixth year, the Indian physician Jīvaka first arrived in Jiaoguang, manifesting various supernatural wonders. He traveled east to Luoyang and, upon seeing the palace halls, remarked:
"The palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven resemble these; the craftsmen who built this palace came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and once it was completed, they returned to the heavens. There...
The fifteen hundred construction tools should be placed beneath the roof tiles. Originally these were made by celestial artisans through the power of the Way;

yet to have them produced by the labor of birth and death—is this not toil and hardship? Later, in the first year of the Dà'ān era (the *rénxū* year), Jīvaka, knowing that Luoyang was about to fall into chaos, took his leave to return home.
A monk requested a word from him as a testament, and Jīvaka ordered the assembly to gather.
Having entered meditative concentration, he ascended the seat and said: "Guard your speech, restrain your body and mind; be careful not to commit any evil. Practice all forms of goodness;

in this way, one attains deliverance from the world. Having finished speaking, he remained silent. Thereupon, several hundred people each invited him for the midday meal, and Fo-yu consented to go to them all.

On the following day, there was a Fo-yu at each of the five hundred households. Only after they had exchanged greetings did they realize that he had manifested multiple bodies to attend their invitations.

Thus they parted. That evening, merchants gathered at Liusha. In the second year of the Dà'ān era, the śramaṇa Lǐ Xiàolóng, who possessed eloquence and discernment, lectured on the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra* (Fàngguāng bōrě).
All people revered and admired him; Ruan Zhan and Yu Kai especially held him in high esteem.
When someone mocked him for his Hu-style clothing, Long said: "Viewed through the Way, I truly see no difference between inner substance and outward dress. He—

This means: "I am humiliated; I have cast aside that glory. Thus, the nobility of the mindless becomes ever more noble, and the peace of the mindless becomes ever more peaceful. (From the *Jin Seng Shi*).

During the Jianxing era of Emperor Min, there was a man named Li Heng, originally of humble origins. He encountered a monk who said to him, "Your fortune is about to arrive, yet calamity will follow later.

If you can maintain your poverty and not yield to it, your misfortune will diminish and prosperity will arrive. It would be well if you were to wear the purple and gold [robes of office] only until you have served three commanderies, at which point you should stop.
Li Heng replied, "I may as well enjoy wealth and honor; what concern is that for future troubles? Thus, he became a monk of the Jin dynasty.

At night, he saw a figure filling his entire bed; he would constantly startle and call out for his family members to look at it. It would also transform into a bird and perch upon the ridgepole of the beam.
At dawn, it would resume its form and depart. He always followed it outside until it suddenly vanished. Because of this, he came to believe in the Buddha and no longer followed the man's advice.

He served as the Grand Administrator (Dàshǒu) of the three commanderies of Xichāng, Jiāngxiá, and Lújiāng. During the Dàxīng era, he was executed during the rebellion of Qián Fèng (as recorded in the Gǎnyìng Lù).
On the jiǎxū day, the second year of Jiànxīng, a sun fell to the earth; three days later, another appeared in the west and moved toward the east.
Buddhataraṃgu was a man from the country of the Zhushis, the son of the Bashi family. He studied the Way in his youth and attained profound mastery of esoteric arts.

In the fourth year of the Yongjia era, he arrived in Luoyang, claiming to be over one hundred years old. He constantly practiced the cultivation of vital energy (*qi*) for self-nourishment and was able to abstain from food for many days at a time.
He was skilled at reciting divine mantras and could command ghosts and spirits. There was an opening on the side of his abdomen which he plugged with cotton wool.

At night, he would pull out the wool, and light would emerge from the opening, illuminating the entire room. He would frequently go to the side of a stream, draw out his five viscera and six bowels through the opening to wash them, and then reinsert them into his abdomen.
Taking oil mixed with vermilion, he would smear it upon his palms; then, all matters beyond a thousand li would become clear.

He could see things as clearly as if they were before his face; at times, by listening to the sound of a bell, he would know whether an event would be auspicious or ominous, and there was nothing that did not prove true.
When he wished to establish a Buddhist monastery, he encountered the incursions of Liu Yao, who drove the imperial court from the capital;

thus his ambition was not realized. He then withdrew into the marshes and fields to observe the changes of the age. In that year, Shi Le was stationing troops at Gepei and was intent solely on slaughter. Fajing desired to convert him. Le—

There was a general named Guo Heilüe who had long been devoted to the Buddha-dharma. When Fotudeng saw him, he invited him to receive the five precepts and treat him with the etiquette due to a disciple.
When Heilüe went out to battle alongside Shi Le, Fotudeng predicted the outcome of every engagement. Because Heilüe possessed such extraordinary insight, Shi Le questioned him, saying:
There was a master named Fotucheng, whom Shi Le called "Heaven’s Gift. Shi Le summoned him for an audience and asked, "How miraculous is the Buddha-dharma?

Cheng knew that Shi Le did not yet understand the profound principles, so he requested to burn incense. He took a bowl, filled it with water, and recited mantras over it; in a short while, blue lotus flowers sprang up within it.

Its radiance dazzled the eyes. Because of this, Shi Le revered it with divine awe. (In the twelfth month of the fourth year, the *bingzi* year, Liu Yao captured Chang’an. The Emperor surrendered, and Yao took control of the Central Plains.)
The Eastern Jin was ruled by Sima Rui, the great-grandson of Emperor Xuan.
From the year Dingchou to Jiwu, there were eleven sovereigns for a total of one hundred and thirty-three years; the capital was established at Jiankang.
Dingchou: Emperor Yuan ascended the throne. He changed the era name to Jianwu and established the Longxing and Waguan monasteries, convening an assembly of a thousand monks (from the *Book of Jin*).
Bingxu: Emperor Cheng ascended the throne and changed the era name to Xianhe. In the second year, Su Jun incited a rebellion, and the Emperor fled to Shitou.
The palace city was entirely reduced to ashes; only Danning Hall remained, where a Buddha image painted by the hand of Emperor Ming upon the wall stood firm and undamaged.
At that time, people marveled at it and regarded it as a divine marvel.
Wuzi (17th day of the 5th month): The third year. The eleventh year of the Guangchu era of Former Zhao.
The Chancellor Liu Yao led his army and ascended the throne at Chibi. Later Zhao’s Shi Le intended to go to Gaohou to attack Yao, but hesitated and could not decide.
He therefore consulted Fotudeng, who said: "The sound of the bells on the top of the stupa says: 'Xiūzhī tìlìgāng pǔgǔ qútùdāng.'"
"Ke" is the word for "to speak. "Xiuzhi" means "army. "Tiligang" means "to go out. "Puguo" refers to Liu Yao’s position as a Hu chieftain.
This signifies that the army has gone out and captured Yao. Fotudeng said to Shi Le, "If the Great General goes out, you will certainly seize Liu Yao."

Shi Le was greatly delighted. He then left his son Shi Hong behind with Fotudeng to govern Xiangguo, while he personally led his cavalry directly toward Luoyang, executing anyone who dared to remonstrate.
Upon reaching Lingchang Ferry, as soon as the two armies engaged, Yao’s forces were utterly defeated; his horses sank into the water.
Shi Kan captured him alive and sent him to Shi Le. At that time, Fotudeng had smeared his palms with oil and held them up for the boy to see.
The youth said, "Among the cavalry is one man who is fair-complexioned and has his elbows bound with red silk cord. He informed Hong [Daoxuan] accordingly;
this was Liu Yao. At that time, more than fifty thousand heads were beheaded, and their corpses were cast into the Jin Valley Garden (*Jingu-yuan*).
The *Book of Jin* states that he was subsequently destroyed by Later Zhao.
Gengyin (the 1st day of the 10th month), the fifth year of Xianhe: Shi Le then usurped the title of Heavenly King of Zhao and acted as Emperor. He changed the era name to Jianping.
After Shi Le ascended the throne, his devotion to Fotudeng became even more earnest; he would consult with him before carrying out any matter.

He addressed Fotudeng as "Great Monk" (Dashi). Thereupon, Fotudeng admonished him, saying: "When a king’s virtue and transformation permeate the universe, then the four auspicious creatures manifest their omens."
Government was corrupt and the Way was in decline. Comets and planetary aberrations manifested portents, appearing constantly and clearly; auspicious and calamitous signs followed in their wake.

This is a constant omen throughout antiquity and the present, a clear admonition from Heaven to humanity. Shi Le was greatly pleased; of those who were to have been executed, eight or nine out of ten were instead granted reprieve.
Consequently, both within and without the realm, all took refuge in the Buddha. Later, Shi Le became enraged and intended to harm [the monks].

The śramaṇas having departed, Fo Tucheng then fled to the residence of Heilüe and said to his disciples, "If the general’s messenger arrives and asks for me, report that you do not know where I have gone.
When the man arrived and could not find Tucheng, he returned to report this to Shi Le.
Le said, "I harbored evil intentions toward a holy man, and the holy man has abandoned me and left. He did not sleep all night, longing to see Tucheng.
Fotucheng knew that Shi Le had repented his intentions. He visited him the following morning. Shi Le asked, "What were you doing last night? Fotucheng replied, "Your Majesty harbored an angry mind;
therefore, I intentionally avoided you yesterday. Since Your Majesty has now changed your mind, I have ventured to come. Shi Le laughed heartily.
The source of the moat water for the city of Xiangguo was located five li west of the city wall. Suddenly, it ran dry. Shi Le requested that Fotudeng bring forth water.

When Fotudeng arrived at the source, the ground had long since cracked like a tortoise shell. Fotudeng burned incense and recited mantras over it for three days; the water then began to flow slightly, and a small dragon emerged following it.
In a short while, the water came in great volume until the ditches and moats were all filled. At that time, the Xianbei leader Duan Bo was attacking Shi Le, and his host...

The army was very large. [Feng] Fei was afraid and questioned Fotudeng. Fotudeng said, "Yesterday, the bells on the temple tower rang, saying: 'At the time of the morning meal tomorrow, you shall encounter the troops of Duan Bo.
Fotudeng gazed toward the city from the waves of the army; seeing neither front nor rear, [Fei] turned pale with fear. As the army marched, the earth tilted. How could Bo possibly be captured?"

He sent someone else to inquire of Fo Tucheng about the situation of Bo. Tucheng said, "I have already captured Bo. A hidden force from the north of the city went out and encountered Bo, capturing him.
Tucheng urged Shi Le to pardon Bo and send him back to his own country; Le followed this advice, and in the end, Bo proved useful to him.
Prince Zhongshan Liu Yue led troops to attack Shi Le. Shi Le dispatched Tiger Division infantry to resist him. A great battle was fought west of Luoyang, and Yue took refuge at Baoshan.
At Shiliangwu, a tiger erected a palisade to guard it. Fo-teng and his disciples traveled from Guansi to Zhongsi;
upon entering the gate, he sighed, saying, "Liu Yue is pitiable. When Fazuo asked for the reason, Fo-teng said, "Last night at the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.), Yue was already captured.
It turned out exactly as he had said. (The above is from the *Sengshi* and the *Book of Jin*).
Shi Cong was about to rebel. In that year, Fotudeng warned Shi Le, saying, "This year there are insects within the onions;
eating them will surely harm people. You should order the common people not to eat onions. He issued a proclamation throughout the realm, cautioning everyone not to eat onions.
When the eighth month arrived, Shi Cong indeed fled. Shi Le held Fotudeng in even greater esteem.
Shi Hu had a son named Bin, whom Shi Le doted upon. He suddenly died a violent death; two days had already passed.
Shi Le said, "I have heard that when the Prince of Guo died, Bian Que was able to restore him to life. The Great Monk is a divine man of this land; you must go to inform him at once."
"It will surely bring about blessings. Fo Tucheng took a willow branch and recited a mantra over him; in a short while, he was able to rise, and after a brief interval, he had recovered.

Consequently, Shi Le kept most of his sons at Buddhist temples to be raised there. Whenever the eighth day of the fourth month arrived, Shi Le would personally visit the temple to make vows for his children.
In the fourth month of the fourth year of the Jianping era, the sky was calm and windless, yet a single bell on a pagoda rang out by itself.
Fotudeng said to the assembly, "The sound of the bell says that there will be a great national mourning before the end of this year.

In the seventh month of that year, Shi Le died; his son Shi Hong succeeded him to the throne. After a short time, Shi Hu deposed Hong and made him the Prince of Haiyang, then established himself as emperor.

He moved the capital to Ye and adopted the era name Jianwu. Devoting himself wholeheartedly to Fotudeng, he treated him with even greater honor than he had shown to Shi Le, and subsequently issued an edict stating: "The Monk is the State..."

This is a great treasure. Yet, honors and titles have not been conferred upon him, nor has he received a high stipend. Since such honor and emolument are no small matter, by what means shall his virtue be distinguished?
From this point forward, it is fitting that he wear brocade and silk, and ride in an ornate palanquin. On the days of court assemblies, the Upādhyāya shall ascend the hall.

The Attendants and those below them all assisted in lifting the palanquin; the Crown Prince and the various Dukes supported him from both sides as he ascended. The presiding official announced, "The Great Master!

and the entire assembly rose to manifest their reverence for his virtue. Furthermore, an edict was issued to the Minister of Works, Li Nong, to inquire after him personally morning and evening, while the Crown Prince and the various Dukes were to pay him a visit once every five days to demonstrate my own respect.
Thereupon, the people of the realm spoke among themselves, none of whom gave rise to ill will.
"Master, you know where Cheng is; no one dares to spit, sneeze, or relieve themselves in his direction.
Shi Sui is wild with drink and intends to plot rebellion. He said to his attendants: 'The Master possesses supernatural powers; he might reveal my scheme.'"
"Those who come tomorrow must first be cleared away. On the day of the full moon, Fo Tucheng was about to enter the palace for an audience with Emperor Hu.
He said to the monk Hui, "Last night a celestial deity called out to me, saying: 'If you enter tomorrow, do not pass by anyone. If I happen to pass by, you must stop me.
Whenever Tucheng enters, he invariably passes by Sui; knowing that Tucheng was entering, Sui waited for him with great hardship. Then Tucheng ascended toward the south.
At the platform, the monk Hui led the hem of his robe [to signal him]. Fo Tucheng said, "The matter cannot be stopped. Before he was even seated comfortably, he rose;
Sui insisted on keeping him but could not. Consequently, the plot went awry. Returning to the temple, he sighed and said, "The Crown Prince intends to incite a rebellion;

its form is about to take shape. To speak of it is difficult to say; to endure it is difficult to bear. He then used the occasion to gently admonish Shi Hu, but Hu ultimately did not understand. Shortly thereafter, the affair broke out.

Only then did he realize the truth of Fotudeng’s words. When the Jin army emerged from the Huai and Si rivers and besieged the northern walls of the city, all three directions were in urgent distress and the people were thrown into a state of peril and agitation.
Fu Jian (Hu) said in despair, "I have served the Buddha and made offerings to the monks, yet I am still beset by foreign invaders;

the Buddha has no divine power! The next morning, Fotudeng entered the palace, and when Fu Jian questioned him about these events, Fotudeng took the opportunity to advise him, saying, "Your Majesty has committed a transgression."
After passing away, he became a great caravan leader and presided over a monastery in Jibin (Kashmir). He once hosted a great assembly in which there were sixty arhats;

I, with this humble body of mine, was also present at that gathering. At that time, a man who had attained the Way said to me: "The master’s life is coming to an end, and you shall next take the form of a rooster.
Later, you will rule the land of Jin, and as the current king, you shall be a sovereign—is this not indeed a blessing? As for the military incursions on the borders, the state..."

"This is merely the constant way of things. Why do you harbor resentment and slander the Triple Gem, giving rise to such deluded thoughts in the night? The tiger then attained faith and enlightenment; it knelt and apologized.
The tiger asked Fotudeng, "The Buddha-dharma forbids killing. Yet I am the sovereign of the realm; were it not for killing, there would be no means to bring stern clarity to the world."

How much less could one obtain merit by violating the precepts and taking life? Fotucheng said: "When emperors serve the Buddha, they should always maintain physical reverence and mental compliance to manifest the Three Jewels;
they must not be tyrannical, nor harm the innocent. As for those who are wicked, ignorant, and reckless—"

One is not subject to transformation by external forces. If there is one who has committed a crime, one cannot but kill them; one cannot but punish them. One should only kill those who deserve to be killed and punish those who deserve to be punished.
If one commits violent and cruel slaughter against the innocent, even if one exhausts their wealth to serve the Dharma, it will not dispel the resulting calamity and retribution.
I pray that Your Majesty will give rise to compassion and extend it widely to all beings; then the Buddha-dharma will flourish forever, and your blessings and reign will endure for a long time.
Although I, Hu, am unable to follow this entirely, the benefit it would bring would not be small. (The preceding is from his original biography.)

At that time, there was a prolonged drought from the first month until the sixth month. Fahu sent his crown prince to the mouth of the Fu River west of Linzhang to pray for rain, but after a long time it did not fall.
He requested that Fotudeng go in person; immediately two white dragons descended at the shrine.

On that day, a great rain fell over an area of several thousand *li*. That year’s harvest was bountiful. The Rong and Mo peoples, who previously had no knowledge of the Dharma, heard [of these events].

His spiritual manifestations were so clear that all paid him remote respects and were transformed by him without a word being spoken. At Linzhang, Shi Hu was restoring an old stupa when it lacked a dew-receptacle (śīlabhājana).
Fotudeng said, "Within the city of Linzi, there is an ancient stupa of King Aśoka;
within the earth lies a dew-receptacle and a Buddha image. You may excavate them. Following these words, they indeed obtained them.
Fo Tucheng sat with Shi Hu in the central hall. Whenever Hu wished to launch an expedition against Yan, Cheng said, "The destiny of the state of Yan has not yet ended;

it will be difficult to conquer them. Hu suffered repeated defeats, only then believing in Cheng’s warnings. At that time, many among the people were devoted to Buddhism, all of whom built temples and pagodas.
Because the true and the false were practiced together, many transgressions arose. Hu issued an edict and questioned the Secretariat, saying: "The Buddha is titled 'World-Honored One' (Shizun)."
Regarding those whom the state honors: as for the commoners of the villages and neighborhoods who hold no official rank, are they permitted to serve the Buddha?

Furthermore, śramaṇas should all be lofty, pure, and diligent before they may practice; yet now the number of śramaṇas is vast, and some are even criminals or evaders of labor—many are not the right people.
It should be carefully deliberated to distinguish the true from the false. [This was submitted by] Wang Du, Court Historian of the Secretariat.
He addressed the Emperor, saying: "Now, when a sovereign performs sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and offers worship to the myriad deities, these matters are recorded in the sacrificial canons;

such rites include seasonal offerings and ancestral feasts. Buddhism originated in the Western Regions and is the deity of a foreign land. Its merits have not been bestowed upon the people, and it is not something that the Son of Heaven or the people of China ought to serve or revere.
In the past, when Emperor Ming of Han was moved by a dream, the Way was first transmitted; however, he permitted only Westerners to establish monasteries."
The capital shall be used to serve its deity. None of the Han people are permitted to leave the household life. Wei inherited the regulations of Han and likewise maintained the former precedents.
Now that Great Zhao has received the Mandate, it generally follows these established statutes. The systems for the Chinese and the barbarians differ; humans and spirits have distinct categories.

What is external is not the same as what is internal, and the rituals for offerings and sacrifices are different. The sacrificial rites of the frontier regions and the Central States should not be intermingled. The state may therefore prohibit the Zhao people [from practicing such rites].

He prohibited the burning of incense and performing prostrations in all monasteries, treating them as objects of veneration for ancestral sacrifices. This prohibition applied equally to the high officials and ministers down to the common serfs.

Anyone who violated this was to be punished with the same penalty as those guilty of illicit sacrifices. As for those among the people of Zhao who had become *śramaṇas*, they were ordered to return to the dress of the four classes of commoners.
The false Palace Secretary Zhongshu Ling Zhupobo was likewise stripped of his status, as reported in the decree issued by Shi Hu.
The *Shu* (Book) records: The deliberation stated that the Buddha is a deity of foreign lands, one whom the Son of Heaven and the various peoples of China ought not to worship.
I was born in the borderlands, yet by the grace of destiny, I have ascended the throne over the Central Kingdoms. Regarding sacrifices and offerings, I should follow my own ancestral customs;
for the Buddha is a deity of the barbarians, and it is precisely he whom I ought to revere. Now, regulations originate from those above and serve as a model for all ages forever. If...

"Affairs are numerous and there is no leisure for play; why should we be bound by the precedents of former generations? As for the various tribes of the Yi and Zhao peoples, those who abandon licentious sacrifices and delight in serving the Buddha shall be permitted to do so.
Thereupon, those who were negligent regarding the precepts took this as an opportunity to become even more unrestrained.
In Wei County, there was a man whose clan and surname were unknown. He constantly wore a hempen tunic and begged in the marketplace; people called him "Hemp-Tunic. His speech was extraordinary.
Whenever he obtained rice or grain, he would scatter it upon the main road, saying, "This is for feeding the celestial horses.
Ji Ba, the Governor of Zhaoxing, arrested and sent him to Shi Hu. Previously, Fo Tucheng had said to Hu: "Two hundred li to the east of the capital, on such-and-such a month..."

One day, [the tiger] sent an extraordinary person, saying, "Do not kill him. When the appointed time arrived, he indeed came. The tiger conversed with him, and there were no words at all that differed from the truth;
he spoke only of how His Majesty should establish a single pillar beneath the palace. The tiger did not understand this, so he ordered the man to be sent to see Fotudeng.

He said, "We met long ago during the Guanghe era, and suddenly today we have come together again," and so forth. They discussed these matters throughout the entire day, yet no one was able to understand them, as recorded in the *Lun* (Discourse).
Regarding events spanning several hundred years, he was sent by post back to his home county; his gait was as swift as flying (as recorded in the *Book of Jin* [Pǔ Jìnshū] and his own biography).
In the twelfth year of the Jiānwǔ era, the Grand Astrologer reported: "A star of an immortal has appeared; there shall be a man of lofty virtue entering our borders."
In the eleventh month, the Imperial Protector of Qinzhou submitted a memorial reporting that Shan Daokai had arrived. Initially, he stayed at the Falin Shrine west of the city;
later, he moved to the Taide Monastery in Linzhang. Shi Hu provided him with very generous support. Fotudeng said, "This practitioner observes the rise and fall of the state;
if he departs, a great calamity will arrive. In the first year of Shihuo’s Daining era, Daokai and his disciples—

He crossed the Yangtze southward to Xuchang. By this time, Hu’s nephew had already passed away during the chaos. Daokai was a native of Dunhuang who entered the monastic order in his youth. He abstained from grain, subsisting instead on pine and cypress.
Later, he swallowed several small stones and became immune to both cold and heat. Subsequently, he entered Mount Luofu, where he died at over one hundred years of age.
Daokai’s disciple Daojin was well-versed in both Buddhist and secular learning; he was highly esteemed by Hu, who would speak of him whenever mentioning recluses.
The Emperor said to Jin: "There is one Yang Ke, who is a subject of mine. Though I have summoned him for over ten years, he has not obeyed the royal decree.
Thus, when I sent an official to inspect him, he lay there in utter arrogance. Although I lack virtue, I rule over the myriad states;

wherever the imperial carriage inquires after all, heaven boils and earth surges. While I may not be able to compel wood or stone to kneel, how can this common man remain so long in such haughtiness?"
In ancient times, when Taigong went to Qi, he first executed the King of Hua. Was Taigong not a man of sage wisdom? How could his actions have been erroneous?
Regarding their advancement or withdrawal from office: in the past, Shun showed favor to Puyi, Yu visited Bocheng, Wei honored Ganmu, and Han [honored] Zhou Dang.

Guan Ning did not respond to the Cao clan, and Huangfu [Ji] did not submit during the Jin dynasty. Two sages and four rulers alike esteemed their integrity, intending thereby to stir others to emulation.
"Encourage competition through greed and establish a stern, pure wind. I pray that Your Majesty will follow the virtue of Shun and Yu, rather than imitating the punishments of Duke Tai.
Since every action of a ruler must be recorded, how can you allow the annals of Zhao to lack a record of those who have hidden from office? Tiger was pleased by these words.
He immediately sent Daokē back to his residence and provided ten households to support him. When Sengjin returned and informed Fotudeng, Fotudeng smiled and said, "Your words were correct;
however, Daokē’s fate was already determined. Later, when the troops in Qinzhou rose in rebellion, the disciples carried Daokē westward on an ox.
The army captured and killed him. Fotudeng ascended with Shi Hu to the central hall. Suddenly he cried out, "Change! Change! and [the atmosphere] became dark and ominous.
A fire broke out in the prefecture. [The Master] took wine and sprinkled it upon the flames. After a long while, he laughed and said, "The rescue has been accomplished.
In the seventh month of the fourteenth year of Jianwu, Shi Xuan and Shi Tao plotted to harm one another; at that time, Xuan arrived at the monastery.
He was sitting together with Fotudeng when a single bell on the stupa rang out alone. Fotudeng asked Daoxuan, "Do you understand the sound of the bell?

The bell says, "The old barbarian is being saved. Daoxuan changed color and said, "What kind of words are these? Fotudeng replied mockingly, "The old barbarian practices the Way; he cannot dwell in the mountains in silence.
Clad in fine robes upon double-layered cushions—is this not indeed 'being saved' (luodu)?"
Shi Tao arrived later. Fo Tucheng gazed at him intently for a long time. Frightened, Tao asked why. Tucheng said, "I was merely observing you because I found your blood to be foul-smelling.
In the eighth month, Tucheng had ten of his disciples perform a purification ritual in a separate room. He then briefly entered the eastern gate.
When Emperor Hu and Empress Du visited him to inquire after his health, Tucheng said, "There is a thief beneath your ribs; he will leave within ten days of his own accord."
"To the west of the Buddha-hall and to the east of this hall, blood shall flow. Be careful not to go east. Empress Du said, "Is the Master senile? Where are there any bandits?
Fo Tucheng changed his words and said, "All that is perceived by the six sense-faculties are bandits. It is only natural for an old man to be senile;
I merely require that the young remain clear-headed. He then spoke in parables and no longer expressed himself with direct clarity. Two days later...
Xuan sent men to kill Tao within a Buddhist temple, intending to commit a great treason while Hu was still in mourning for his father.
Hu was spared from death because he had previously received a warning from Fotudeng. When Xuan’s crime was exposed and he was arrested, Fotudeng remonstrated with the Emperor, saying:
"Since he is Your Majesty's own son, why inflict such a heavy calamity? If Your Majesty can restrain your wrath and show him compassion, there will still be sixty years remaining."
"In another year, if you do not execute him, he will become a comet to sweep down upon the palace at Ye. Hu did not follow this advice;
instead, he pierced Shi Le’s jaw with an iron chain, dragged him up onto a pile of firewood, and burned him alive. He then arrested over thirty thousand of his officials and subordinates.
All were torn apart at the yokes and dismembered, and their bodies were cast into the Zhang River. Daorong then commanded his disciples to cease the retreat in the separate chamber.
More than a month later, a demonic horse appeared; its mane and tail were all scorched, as it entered through the Zhongyang Gate and exited through the Xianyang Gate.
He headed east toward the Eastern Palace, but was not permitted to enter. He fled toward the northeast and suddenly vanished.
Upon hearing this, Fo Tucheng sighed and said, "A calamity is about to befall us. In the eleventh month, Shi Hu held a great banquet for his ministers in the Great Martial Antechamber.
Tucheng chanted: "O Hall! Thorns shall grow in a forest, soon to ruin people's robes. Hu ordered that the stones beneath the hall be removed to examine them.
Thorns grew there. ○ Tancheng returned to the temple in deep regret that he would not be able to complete the magnificent adornments.
Speaking to himself, he asked, "Could I have three more years? He answered himself, "No, no. Again he asked, "Two years? One year? A hundred days? A month?
To each he replied, "No. Thereafter he said nothing more. Returning to his quarters, he told his disciple Fazuo, "In the year Wushen, there will be calamity and chaos."
The signs began to sprout. In the year Jǐyǒu (1009), the Shí clan was destined for extinction. I have taken advantage of this period before the chaos breaks out to first follow the Way.

He immediately sent a messenger to take leave of Shihū, saying: "The principles of nature must undergo change; one’s own life cannot be preserved. This poor monk’s body is like a fleeting illusion, and the time for its transformation has arrived.
Having received your exceptionally great kindness, I have ventured to inform you. Shihū said sorrowfully: "I have not heard that the Master..."
Feeling ill, he suddenly announced that his end had come. He immediately left the palace for the temple to offer words of consolation.

Fo Tucheng said to Shi Hu: "To emerge from life and enter death is the constant way of the Dao. Longevity and brevity are determined by destiny and cannot be extended. Now, the Way values the completion of practice, and virtue prizes lack of indolence.
If one's conduct is free from frivolity, one exists even in death. To violate these principles and yet obtain longevity is not what I desire."

Now, as for those whose intentions have reached their end: although the state’s mind dwells upon the principles of the Buddha and it honors the Dharma without parsimony—founding monasteries and temples that are exalted, magnificent, and worthy of praise for their virtue—it ought to enjoy auspicious blessings;
yet its administration of government is violent and its punishments are licentious, cruel, and excessive.
This openly contravenes the sacred scriptures and secretly defies the precepts of the Dharma. Failing to reform oneself through self-restraint, one will ultimately find no blessings or protection.

If you were to subdue the mind and transform your thoughts, bestowing kindness upon the common people, then the state’s mandate would be prolonged, and both the clergy and the laity would rejoice and rely upon you; when your life finally comes to its end, you would have no regrets in your final moments.
Tiger was moved by profound grief, knowing that his departure was certain. He immediately commissioned the construction of a tomb for him at Zimo Road to the west of Ye. By the tenth [day]...
On the eighth day of the second month, he passed away at Yegong Temple. The officials and commoners followed him in mourning to the state funeral and interred him there;
he was one hundred and seventeen years of age. This was the year Wushen, the fourth year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Jin dynasty.
Later, a śramaṇa came from Yongzhou claiming that he had seen Fotudeng enter the Guanzhong region from the west. When Shi Jilong opened the tomb, he saw only a—
The stone contained no corpse. Shi Le (Ji Long) loathed this, saying, "The stone is I myself; he has buried me and departed. I shall surely die. Thereupon he fell ill.
Shortly thereafter, Liang Du incited a rebellion. The following year, Shi Le died, leaving his adopted grandson Ran Min in charge.

There was great chaos following the usurpation and slaughter. Min (Míng) was the childhood name of Jí (Jí). Táng Chéng had previously said that "Jí's sons will form a forest" referred to this very person.
