Later, when Tǔmù Jūn made Yè his capital, [Min] resided within the palace of Shí Hǔ. He frequently saw Shí Hǔ in his dreams biting his arm, leading him to believe that Shí Hǔ was manifesting as a malevolent spirit.
He then sought out Shí Hǔ’s corpse at the Dōngmíng Hall and found it; the corpse was stiff and undecayed. Jūn stepped upon it and cursed, saying: [The text ends here.]
"A dead barbarian dares to fear a living Son of Heaven? You have completed this palace only to be schemed against by your own son; how much more so for me!
He threw it into the Zhang River, but the corpse leaned against a pillar and would not move. The Qin general Wang Meng collected the remains and buried them.

This was the omen of the "Hemp-Robed One" and the "Single-Pillar Palace. Later, when Fu Jian campaigned against Ye, Shi Jun’s son, Shi Wei, served as Jian’s great general. [He was captured] by Guo Shenhua...
[The Master] said: "This is indeed the verification of my previous dream of the tiger. Tian Rong’s *Record of Zhao* states: "Before his death, Fotudeng prepared his own tomb.
Since Fotudeng already knew that the tomb would surely be opened and the corpse would not be within it, why would he have pre-emptively made this [tomb], fearing execution by Rong?
Zhi Dun of Daolin was in the capital when he heard that Fotudeng was traveling with the various Shi clan members. He then remarked: "Master Fotudeng must have..."
Ji Long was a seagull. Sengcheng was eight chi tall; his demeanor was dignified and elegant. His exegesis was profound and subtle, and his spiritual manifestations were manifold.
He himself recounted his life’s origins: he was ninety thousand li from Ye when he left home to enter the Way.

He had been a renunciant for nineteen thousand years, abstaining from food after midday and never transgressing the precepts. Free from seeking and desire, he always had several hundred disciples receiving instruction from him.
His disciples, both former and later, numbered nearly one hundred. Throughout the provinces and commanderies he visited, he established eight hundred and ninety-three Buddhist temples;
the flourishing of his propagation of the Dharma was unsurpassed by any before him. Furthermore, his compassion permeated all living beings as he rescued those in peril and suffering.
When the two Shi rulers were tyrannical and violent, harming others through unrighteous means, had it not been for [Fotudeng] being of the same era as Cheng, who could have spoken of such things?
Yet the common people received great benefit, using it daily without even realizing it. Later, the Shi clan of Later Zhao ruled the state for six sovereigns over a total of thirty-three years.

Jichou (47th year of the sexagenary cycle): In the seventh month of the fourth year of the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng of the Jin dynasty, Gao Kui, the Governor of Danyang, obtained a golden image from the waters of Zhanghou Bridge.

In the third month of the following year, Zhang Xi, a native of Linhai, found a golden-copper lotus pedestal in the sea and used it to support the feet of Gao Kui’s image; they fit together perfectly. That evening, a light shone upward toward the heavens.

The Brahma-music was played with a chilling resonance; it ceased after two nights. This occurred during the seven dynasties of Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Chen, Sui, and Tang (as recorded in the *Tongji* regarding the manifestation of auspicious light within the palace).

Gengzi: The sixth year of the Xiankang era. Emperor Cheng was still a child; Yu Bing of the Zhongshu Secretariat assisted in governance. He submitted a memorial proposing that śramaṇas should pay full homage to the sovereign.

On behalf of the Emperor, he issued an edict ordering śramaṇas to show respect. The Director of the Imperial Secretariat, He Chong, and others deliberated and submitted a report. Chong and his colleagues stated:
"Emperor Wu, the World-Honored Ancestor, established the new dynasty during a time of great brilliance. Emperor Ming, the Venerable Ancestor, was sagacious and possessed profound insight."
"Is it that at such a time, śramaṇas cannot easily bend their knees? I wish that by not altering the methods of cultivating goodness, the wills of all under heaven may be harmonized.
I, Yu, believe it is appropriate to follow the late Emperor’s principle of acting for the sake of the world through righteousness.

Let the officials in charge of ritual and the *boshi* (doctors of state) deliberate upon the Imperial Decree and issue a rebuttal. [The Emperor] granted this petition. The initial decree stated: "Now, the myriad regions have diverse customs..."

The Way of the Gods is difficult to discern; it has existed since time immemorial. One who possesses comprehensive insight and universal understanding should truly have no cause for fear (and so forth).
Moreover, these individuals are all subjects of the Jin dynasty. In terms of their talent and wisdom, they are merely ordinary people.

Yet, because the Way they profess is difficult to distinguish, they have donned foreign attire to overstep the bounds of propriety, flaunting the arrogant customs of a foreign land and presenting their physical forms directly before the Son of Heaven.

"Furthermore, this is something I cannot accept. You gentlemen are all men of national caliber; in speech, you ought to fathom the profound and subtle, and in discussing governance, you ought to value the national statutes.
If it were otherwise, what could I possibly report [to the Emperor]? (The Director of the Imperial Secretariat submitted this memorial a second time.
"Although we, Chong and the others, are indeed ignorant and obscured, failing to comprehend your far-reaching intent, from the Han through the Wei to the Jin, we have heard no dissenting opinions."
The statutes governing the distinction between the honorable and the humble must never, even for a moment, be violated. Now, the śramaṇas are singularly devoted to their observance of the precepts;

if we were to command them to perform prostrations, we would ultimately destroy their dharma. This would surely cause those accustomed to cultivating goodness to fall into grief and fear. In my heart, I find this deeply unsettling.

Whenever I see them burning incense and offering prayers, they invariably place the State first, desiring that blessings and protection descend upon it; their sincerity is boundless, as they revere and honor [the sovereign].
This is in accordance with what arises naturally. How could we dare to treat our physical bodies with such disregard as to neglect the rites of reverence?
The simplicity of these ceremonies is intended solely to maintain focused adherence to the Dharma; therefore, when the former sages governed the world, they followed this practice without alteration.

The heavenly net is vast and wide—loose yet nothing escapes it. We, your subjects, have repeatedly considered that not requiring prostrations would not constitute a violation of the Law. Thus, we act according to this principle.

Benefit them and bestow kindness upon them, so that even the worthy will not dare to withhold their sincerity. Thus, above, there will be the sovereign’s grace like the sky covering and the earth supporting;
below, there will be those who cultivate goodness and maintain the One. I have briefly set forth these concerns; I pray you will examine them with care.
At that time, Yu Bing’s proposal was shelved and was never implemented (*Hongming ji*).
Bingwu (the year 346 CE): The second year of Emperor Mu’s Yonghe era. He Chong, courtesy name Cidao, a native of Lujiang, was the Director of the Imperial Secretariat.

He was fond of the Buddhist scriptures and devoted himself to the restoration and construction of Buddhist temples and the support of śramaṇas. He expended hundreds of thousands and wasted millions of coins for the sake of the masses, yet he never hesitated.
At that time, Ruan Yu teased him, saying, "Your aspirations are as vast as the universe, and your courage surpasses all who have come before. He Chong asked him the reason for this.
He said, "I have sought to govern a commandery of several thousand households, yet I have not yet attained what you seek—to become a Buddha—is that not truly great?
May your descendants for generations propagate and clarify the Buddha-dharma. Later, he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works (Sikong) (*Book of Jin*).
The sixth year. Fu Jian occupied Chang’an. In the second month of this year, a golden image appeared in Jingzhou.
Sima Huanwen went to welcome it, but it would not move. At that time, Xi Jun of Jiangling had donated his residence to become a monastery and appointed Tan-yi to preside over it.
Tan-yi led a multitude to go and welcome the image; it moved with a light, soaring grace and returned to be reverently enshrined. Its miraculous manifestations were manifold.
Shi Zhidun, styled Daolin, entered the monastic order in his prime. He specialized in the study of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

At that time, renowned worthies such as Wang Xizhi, Xie An, Yin Hao, Xi Chao, He Chong, and Xu Xun became his friends beyond the mundane world (*fangwai*). Upon entering the capital to lecture on the Dharma, he won the admiration and submission of both the court and the commonalty.
At that time, Xi Chao wrote to his relatives and friends, saying: "Master Dun has attained the Way of the Divine Principle; he is profoundly transcendent and peerless."
Awakened. For several hundred years, it was as if the Great Dharma of the Shaoxing era had not been sustained by even a single person.

In the first year of the Dahe period, he submitted a memorial to take his leave and return to the mountains. An imperial edict provided him with provisions and sent high officials to see him off at a farewell banquet.

He withdrew to the Shan Mountains, where he established a monastery in Wozhuo; later, he moved to Shicheng Mountain and founded Qiguang Monastery. There he lived on wild fruits and drank sparingly, setting his mind upon the unborn (*anupapatti*).

Later, he went out to Mount Yin and lectured on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, with Xu Xun serving as the *dougǎng* (the assistant lecturer). Xu Xun raised challenging questions on the meaning of the text several times, and those who listened were filled with admiration and submission.
(Du Fu wrote: "In vain do I feel honored to be among the likes of Xu Xun, debating and instructing on the words of Zhi Dun; there is indeed profound significance in this.")

Ren-shen: The first year of Emperor Xiaowu’s Kangning era. Huan Wen, styled Yuanzi, was appointed Grand Marshal (Da Sima) with the title of Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shizhong), overseeing all military affairs both within and without the court, and was invested with the golden battle-axe.
Possessing great martial prowess, he harbored ambitions of exclusive territorial expansion and usurpation.

In his later years, he served the Buddha with great diligence. At that time, there was a nun who came from a distant region to visit him; Wen treated her with such warmth and respect that he never grew weary of it. Whenever she bathed in a separate room, she would invariably occupy it for hours. Suspecting something, Wen secretly peered inside.

The nun had stripped naked and used a knife to cut open her own abdomen, followed by severing both her feet. When she finished bathing and emerged, Wen asked whether she had met with good fortune or misfortune. Knowing that Wen had been watching, the nun replied: "I have already attained the fruit of Arhatship. Wen was filled with remorse and immediately went to the temple to repent. He then shaved his head and became a monk. Later, he traveled to the capital where he encountered the Dharma Master Senglang. Senglang said to him, "The Master of the Law has already attained the Way. Wen then returned to his former residence, where he lived out his life in seclusion. He passed away at the age of eighty-seven. It is said that when he died, his body was warm and his face remained as if alive.

His remains were enshrined in a stupa at the side of Mount Xue. During the Kaiyuan era, an imperial decree was issued to rename the mountain Mount Guoqing. It is located approximately twenty li southeast of the city. This is the account of the Venerable Master Huiwen. (Note: *Arhatship* is the Sanskrit term *arhattva*, representing the fourth and highest stage of sainthood in the Theravada and Mahayana traditions.)
"If Your Excellency were to become the Son of Heaven, you too would surely be like me. At that time, Sima Wen was plotting to inquire about the tripod [of state authority];

hearing these words, he felt despondent and desisted. The nun then took her leave, and it was not known where she went. Later, Wen passed away without having been granted the nine emoluments of regency (according to the *Book of Jin* and the *Gantong lu*).
Shi Dao’an was the son of the Wei family; he was a native of Fuliu in Changshan. Having lost his parents early, he was raised by his maternal uncle, the Kong family.

He was raised [by his parents]. At the age of seven, he began to study; upon reading a text a second time, he could recite it from memory. His neighbors marveled at this extraordinary talent. At twelve, he left home to become a monk.

His physical appearance was quite unattractive, so his teacher put him to work in the fields for three years. He labored diligently without ever showing a trace of resentment. Later, he requested permission from his teacher to seek out scriptures.

Whatever sutra he was taught in the morning, he returned with by the evening; when he sought further scriptures, his teacher would hold up the texts to test him. The teacher was greatly astonished and came to revere him.
He was ordained with full precepts and allowed to travel freely for study. Upon arriving at Ye, he met Fotudeng, who beheld him and sighed in admiration. They conversed all day long;

when the crowd saw that his physical appearance did not match his reputation, they looked down on him and wondered at him. Fotudeng said, "This man possesses far-reaching insight; he is not one of your kind."
For this reason, Dao’an took Faching as his teacher. During An’s lectures, difficult questions arose like sharp blades;

An blunted their keenness and resolved the entanglements, possessing such surplus energy that people of the time had a saying: "The lacquer-colored monk startles his neighbors. Having spent a long time in lecture halls, his soaring eloquence and piercing analysis were such that no one dared look up at him.
At that time, Lu Xin, the Governor of Wuyi, heard of his reputation and sent a śramaṇa to invite him to open [the teachings].

He lectured on the teachings, and both monastics and laypeople admired him with great devotion; his followers numbered in the tens of thousands. He constantly proclaimed the Dharma and transformed others.

When Prince Pengcheng succeeded to the throne, he dispatched an envoy to invite him to enter the Huayuan Garden, where extensive offerings were made for him. Later, together with over four hundred disciples, including Huiyuan, he crossed the river.
General-in-Chief of the West, Huan Langzi, was stationed at Jiangling and invited him to go to the western commandery of Zhu Xu; subsequently, he was again requested to return.
Xiangyang. Fu Jian sent a golden image, embroidered Buddha banners and streamers, and jeweled pendants. These were arranged at the lecture hall, and all who saw them were moved to solemn reverence.
Xi Zuochi was an extraordinary and talented man from Xiangyang. He went to visit Dao’an; once seated, he announced himself, saying, "Xi Zuochi of the Four Seas.
Dao’an replied, "Shi Dao’an who fills the heavens. Contemporaries considered this a famous exchange. Xi Zuochi [then] visited Xie...
An Shu wrote: "Coming here to see Shi Dao'an, I find him truly superior and extraordinary. With several hundred disciples, they lecture in unison without weariness.
He possesses no miraculous transformations or arts to deceive the ears of ordinary people, nor does he have any imposing majesty or great power to rectify the irregularities of the local officials.
Yet his disciples are solemn and reverent toward one another, creating an atmosphere of vast harmony."
This assembly is truly something I have never seen before. These individuals have refined their principles and rectified their inner natures;

they are extensively learned and have read nearly all the various texts of both the inner and outer traditions. They are proficient in the arts of Yin and Yang and mathematics, and they handle the profound principles of the Buddhist scriptures with ease.
Their compositions on doctrine seem to harmonize the Dharma and the Way. It is my regret that I did not encounter you on the same day.
He also frequently remarked that he hoped to obtain one opportunity for a formal discourse.

Fu Jian said to his Chief Secretary Quan Yi, "I have taken Xiangyang with an army of one hundred thousand, yet I have gained but one man and a half. Quan Yi asked, "Who are they? Jian replied, "Master An is one man; Zao Chi is half a man.
He then issued an edict that among the scholars, both within and without the court, all those with doubts should take Master An as their teacher. Initially, during the Wei dynasty...
The Śramaṇas of the Jin dynasty took their teacher’s name as their clan name. Dao’an, out of reverence for Śākyamuni, instead adopted “Śākya” as his family name.

Later, the *Ekottarika Āgama* indeed stated that when the four rivers enter the sea, they no longer retain their individual river names; likewise, those of the four castes who become Śramaṇas all come to be called members of the Śākya lineage.
This subsequently became the established rule. In the seventh year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, the Qin King Fu Jian intended to take the region south of the Yangtze River.
In the east, [Fu] Jian could not sleep day after day. Although his ministers offered earnest remonstrances, he ultimately could not be turned back.

The multitude regarded Dao’an as one of firm faith and reverence, and so they petitioned him, saying: "The Sovereign is about to undertake military operations in the southeast; how can you, Sir, not speak a word on behalf of the common people?

It happened that Jian was departing for the Eastern Garden when he ordered Dao’an to ascend the palanquin to travel with him. The Vice President of the Secretariat, Quan Yi, remonstrated, saying: "Your servant..."

He heard that the Emperor was traveling in his ceremonial carriage, accompanied by the Chief Attendant. Dao’an, having renounced his physical form as a layman, wondered if he could join the procession.
Yao Xian said abruptly, “Master An’s virtue and Way are worthy of the highest honor. I would not exchange the empire for anything else; the splendor of a carriage does not truly match his merit.
He immediately ordered the Vice Director of the Secretariat to assist Dao’an onto the carriage. Looking at Dao’an, he said, “I intend to travel south with you to Wu.”
"Yue, you would array the six armies to conduct a tour of inspection, crossing Mount Kuaiji to gaze upon the vast blue sea—is this not a source of great pleasure? An replied:
"Your Majesty responds to Heaven and governs the world; you possess the wealth of the eight provinces and occupy the Central Kingdom to command the four seas.
You ought to settle your spirit in a glory equal to that of Yao and Shun. Yet now you wish to lead a host of one million men to seek out that land of the lowest grade (the 'xia-xia' fields)."
"Furthermore, the land in the southeast is low-lying and its climate is pestilential. In ancient times, Shun and Yu traveled there and did not return;

the First Emperor of Qin went there and did not come back. Why should you trouble the Great Chariot with such a journey? Fu Jian said, "Heaven gave birth to the masses of people and established rulers to govern and shepherd them.
How could I be afraid of toil? Why should that one region alone not receive my grace? If it must be as you say, then it is..."
"The ancient emperors all refrained from military expeditions. An said, "If the imperial carriage must indeed move, you may first proceed to Luoyang.

Rest there to consolidate your power and store up your sharpness, then issue proclamations to the south of the Yangtze. With the six armies gathered behind you, they will surely prostrate themselves and submit as subjects."
It is not necessary to personally involve oneself. (The *Tongjian* does not record this).
Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, hearing of his reputation and admiring his virtue, dispatched an envoy to establish contact. The Emperor issued an edict stating:

"Master Dao’an possesses a penetrating understanding of the Way and a brilliant, refined character. Abiding in the Path to instruct the common people, his illustrious achievements are doubly manifest. He shall not only provide guidance for the present age, but..."
He may wash away the taints of future lives. His stipend shall be equal to that of a prince or high official. Provisions shall be provided from wherever they are available.
○ On the twenty-seventh day of the first month of the twenty-first year of the Jianyuan era of the Qin dynasty, there was a strange monk who stayed overnight in the lecture hall.

The *vīnāyaka* (chant master) saw him at night entering and exiting through a crack in the window. He informed Dao’an, who questioned him about his place of rebirth. The monk answered by means of a hand-gesture.
To the northwest, clouds parted, revealing the vision of the Tuṣita Heaven’s wondrous and supreme realm; this was seen by the entire assembly.

On the eighth day of the second month of that year, he addressed the crowd, saying, "I am about to depart. Having finished his midday meal, he passed away. This was in the tenth year of the Dàyuán era of the Jìn dynasty, the year of Yǐyǒu (485 CE).
(According to his biography, there was flesh on his left arm that could be raised or lowered at will; people of the time called him "Hand-Seal Bodhisattva.")

Xinwei (the 10th day of the tenth month). In the first year of Emperor Jianwen’s Xian’an era, a comet appeared. An edict was issued for Zhu Fakuang to perform rites to avert its influence. Fakuang memorialized:
“Your Majesty should diligently cultivate virtuous governance to block this celestial reprimand. This humble monk shall, of course, exert his utmost efforts.

Thereupon, the Emperor daily engaged in fasting and repentance with his disciples; in a short while, the calamity vanished. Xu Xun, courtesy name Yuandu, purified his mind through the study of Buddhism. He was a public figure... [text ends].
The Emperor admired his character and held his integrity in high esteem; he also summoned him for an audience and had him stay overnight.

Unconsciously, the Emperor drew his seat closer and said, "Yuan-du’s pure discourse and subtle principles are truly not easily matched. In the seventh month of the following year, the Emperor passed away (Biography).
Guiyou (the 10th year of the sexagenary cycle): Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty ascended the throne and changed the era name to Ningkang;

it was the twelfth year of Jianyuan of the Qin. The eminent monk Shiye was a native of Shu. His predictions regarding future events were frequently verified. He did not eat the five grains and could travel five hundred li in a single day.

He was able to subjugate dragons through incantations to bring down rain. In that year, he arrived in Chang’an. Whenever the state of Qin encountered drought, the Emperor summoned the Master to pray for rain.
The Master recited mantras and caused a dragon to enter his alms bowl. Yao Xian ordered the ministers and officials to observe this; the dragon then ascended into the sky and rain fell.

The king, ministers, scholars, and commoners all revered him. From then on, Qin no longer suffered from the distress of scorching droughts. In the twelfth month of the Gengchen year, he passed away without illness.
After seven days, Fu Jian, marveling at this anomaly, opened the coffin to look inside; only the shroud remained.
The following year there was a great drought, and Jian said, "If Master She were alive, would he allow me to burn with anxiety over the clouds and the Milky Way?
Zhao Zheng of Qingshui, style name Wenyue, became the Court Historian (Zuozhuan Lang) of Qin at the age of eighteen. He subsequently served as Gate Attendant (Huangmen) and Governor of Wuwei.
In the final years of Fu Jian’s reign, he was infatuated with the Xianbei and became negligent in his governance. Consequently, [Tao] Kan admonished him through song, saying:
"I have heard of the Mengjin River, Which bends in a single curve for a thousand li. This water was originally clear; Who has stirred it to make it turbid?

Fu Jian moved with emotion and said, "It is I. Kan then sang again: "In the northern garden there is a jujube tree, Whose spreading leaves cast a heavy shade. Though its exterior is thick with thorns,"
Internally, he possessed a sincere heart. He laughed heartily and said, "Could this not be Zhao Wenye? His quick-witted humor was always of this kind.
Later, due to the persecution of the Buddha-dharma in Guanzhong, he wished to leave the household life. Yao Jian, pitying his talent, did not grant permission.
Only after Yao Jian’s death was he able to fulfill his aspiration; he changed his name to Daozheng. A verse says: "Why was the Buddha born so late? [Nirvana...]"

"How premature was the passing of [Dharmatrāta]! I take refuge in Śākyamuni. Now I come to entrust myself to the Great Way; later I shall withdraw to Mount Shangyu and devote myself exclusively to the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Dharmmanandi (translated as "Dharma-Joy" in Chinese; also known as Dughuqinren) traveled far across the shifting sands, carrying his treasures as he entered the East.
Fu Jian received him with courtesy and had him transmit the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and other major scriptures; this was due to the power of his literary achievements.

Xi Hui, the Governor of Yongzhou under the Jin dynasty, admired his character and lifestyle and urged him to travel together. However, by the time they reached Luoyang, [Sengzhao] was already over sixty years of age.
(The Former Qin had six rulers for a total of forty-four years; according to the *Monastic Biographies* and the *Book of Northern Qi*).
Bingxu: The eleventh year of Taiyuan of Emperor Xiaowu of Jin; the first year of Jianchu of Yao Chang of Later Qin;
the first year of Dengguo of Emperor Daowu of Northern Wei.
Kumārajīva, translated here as "Child-Longevity," was a native of India whose family had served as prime ministers for generations.

His father, Kumārayāna, resigned from his ministerial post to enter the monastic life and traveled east across the Pamir Mountains. Upon hearing that he had renounced worldly glory, the King of Kucha welcomed him outside the city to appoint him as State Preceptor.
The king had a younger sister, twenty years of age, who was exceptionally talented and perceptive; she bore a red mole on her body, which was said to signify the birth of wisdom.
Her son was sought in marriage by various states, but he would not accept them. When he saw Guṇabhadra, his heart desired to take him as his wife, so she forced him to wed her.

Subsequently, she conceived Guṇavarman; while he was in the womb, her mother’s wisdom and understanding became twice as great as usual. After Guṇavarman was born, his mother delighted in leaving the household life.

Her husband did not grant permission, yet later she gave birth to a son named Puṣyadeva. Later, while out on an excursion, he saw dry bones strewn about and vowed not to eat until he had shaved off his hair;
having done so, he received the precepts, practiced meditation, and attained the first fruit of the path when he was seven years old. Kumārajīva was seven years old at that time.

They both left the household life together and received the scriptures from their teacher; Kumārajīva mastered their meanings on his own. At the age of nine, he accompanied his mother to Kaśmīra, where a non-Buddhist master of treatises challenged him.
Kumārajīva seized the opportunity to defeat him, leaving the opponent ashamed and submissive. The King’s respect and offerings increased accordingly;
he assigned five senior monks and ten śrāmaṇeras from the monastery where [Kumārajīva] resided to attend upon him. When he reached the age of twenty, his mother took him back to Kucha.

He then traveled to the country of the Yuezhi. There was an arhat on the northern mountains who, upon seeing him, marveled at him and said to his mother, "This śrāmaṇera, though only thirty-five years of age, has not broken a single precept;
he will greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma and deliver countless people, no different from Upagupta.
In Kucha, the king fashioned a golden lion throne, spread it with brocade rugs from Daqin, and [the Master] ascended it to preach the Dharma.

The various kingdoms of the Western Regions were all in awe of his divine brilliance. Whenever he gave a lecture, the king would kneel long at the side of the seat and command Kumārajīva to step upon it to ascend.
At that time, Fu Jian had usurped the title of ruler in Guanzhong. The King of the Frontier Tribe of the foreign lands and the younger brother of the King of Kucha came to court.
When Jian received them in audience, the two kings said to him, "The Western Regions produce many rare and precious things; we request—"

Having pacified the regions through military force, he sought their internal submission. In the first month of the thirteenth year of Jian’s Jianyuan era, the year of Dingchou, the Grand Astrologer reported:
"A star has appeared in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands; there shall be a man of great virtue and wisdom who enters to assist the Middle Kingdom. Fajian said:
"I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in the Western Regions and the śramaṇa Dao’an in Xiangyang; could it not be one of these two?

In the ninth month of the eighteenth year, Fu Jian dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry Lü Guang, the General of Jiangling Jiang Fei, and others, leading an army of seventy thousand to campaign westward against various kingdoms.
As they were about to depart, Jian hosted a farewell banquet for Lü Guang at the Jianzhang Palace and addressed him, saying:
He said: "The sovereign and the emperor respond to Heaven in their governance, taking the paternal love of all living beings as their fundamental principle.

How could they covet territory and wage war against it? It is solely for the sake of those who cherish the Way. I have heard that in the Western Regions there is Kumārajīva, who profoundly understands the characteristics of the Dharma and is well-versed in the principles of Yin and Yang;
he is the preeminent master for later students. I long for him greatly. A man of wisdom and virtue is the treasure of a state."
A great treasure. When he had conquered Kucha, he dispatched an express messenger to send Kumārajīva. Before the vanguard of the army had arrived, Kumārajīva said to the King of Kucha, Chūnbai:
"The destiny of your kingdom is declining; you shall soon face a formidable enemy. A person from beneath the sun will come from the east."

"You ought to respectfully submit to him. Do not oppose his advance. Śrīpuruṣa did not follow this advice and went to war; consequently, Kumārajīva defeated his kingdom and established Śrīpuruṣa’s younger brother, Zhèn, as the ruler.
After Kumārajīva had captured Śrīpuruṣa, seeing that he was still young, he forcibly gave him a Kucha woman as a wife.

Śrīpuruṣa refused and would not accept her. Thereupon, [Kumārajīva] forced him to drink strong liquor and confined them both in a sealed room. Being thus coerced, Śrīpuruṣa eventually violated her. When Kumārajīva returned, he...
They stationed their army midway on the mountain slope. Kumārajīva said, "It is not possible to remain here; you will surely meet with disaster. You should move the army to the top of the ridge.
Fǎguāng did not accept this advice. That night, a great rain fell, and the water rose several zhang deep. Thousands died. Only then did Fǎguāng begin to regard him with wonder.
"Shi [Shirui] said, 'This is a place of misfortune and death; it is not fitting to linger here. If you return east, there will surely be a blessed land where you may dwell.

Faguan followed his advice. Upon reaching Liang, he heard that Fu Jian had been killed by Yao Chang. Faguan ordered his three armies to don white mourning garments and held a great wailing ceremony south of the city.
Thereupon, he assumed a private title and designated the year as Dà'ān. Zhang Zi, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, possessed refined and elegant literary talent. Faguan...
He held him in high esteem. When Sengzi fell ill, a foreign physician named Rakṣa arrived and claimed he could cure Sengzi’s ailment.
Kumārajīva was delighted and bestowed upon him very generous rewards. However, Kumārajīva told Sengzi that the physician would not be able to help, and suggested they test his skill.

He then had a cord made of five-colored silk, tied it into knots, burned it to ash, and threw the powder into the water. If the ashes were to form a cord again, the illness could not be cured. After a short while, [the ashes] floated up.
A cord was produced from it. Shortly thereafter, his father Zī passed away, and Guang also died. His son Shào succeeded him on the throne.
After several days, Zuǎn murdered Shào and established himself as ruler, styling his era Xuānníng. In the second year, a pig gave birth to a single body with three heads.

A dragon emerged from a well in the Línxiāng enclosure and coiled itself before the palace hall; by dawn, it had vanished. Zuǎn took this as an auspicious omen and renamed the Great Hall Lóngxiáng (Dragon Soaring).
Suddenly, a black dragon ascended the gate of the Jiugong (Nine Palaces) at Dangyang, which was subsequently renamed Chongxingmen (Gate of Prosperous Favor).

Kumārajīva submitted a memorial, saying: "These are all manifestations of a hidden dragon venturing forth; the omen of the boar demon signals an anomaly. The dragon belongs to the Yin category and its appearances are subject to fixed times.
That it is seen now portends calamity; there must surely be a rebellion of subordinates plotting against their superiors. You should discipline yourself and cultivate virtue to respond to Heaven."
Huigui admonished him, but Zuan would not accept his advice. Later, everything occurred exactly as he had foretold. Master Kumārajīva resided in Liangzhou for many years;

since Lü Guang and his son did not propagate the Dharma, he retained his profound understanding without being able to spread its transformative teachings. Although Fu Jian was deeply devoted to him, he ultimately never met him in person.

What a pity it is that it has already come to this! (From the *Book of Jin* and his biography. Later Qin’s Yao Chang usurped authority over Guanzhong and, admiring Shi Hu’s character, sent envoys with sincere invitations.
Because the various Lü brothers feared that Shi’s extensive strategic wisdom might be used for Yao’s own schemes, they refused permission for him to enter the east.

When Yao Chang died and his son Yao Xing succeeded to the throne, he later dispatched messengers to respectfully invite him. In the third month of the third year of Hongshi of the Former Qin, there were trees growing together in a "conjoined-fruit" (*lianli*) manner.

A branch grew in the courtyard of the ancestral temple; in the Xiaoyao Garden, leeks transformed into *chǎi* (a fragrant herb), which was regarded as an auspicious omen signifying that a wise man was about to enter.
In the fifth month, Emperor Xing dispatched Shuode, Duke of Longxi, to the west to replace Lü Long. Lü Long submitted his surrender, welcoming Kumārajīva into Guanzhong.
On the twentieth day of the twelfth month, he arrived in Chang’an. Emperor Xing treated him with the etiquette due to a National Teacher (*guoshi*), conversing with him tirelessly.

Since the Great Dharma was first transmitted to the East, the number of sūtras and śāstras has gradually increased; however, those translated by Zhi Qian and Dharmarakṣa were characterized by archaic phrasing and interpretive approximations (*geyi*).
Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei, who had little devotion to the Triple Gem, suddenly became keenly intent on lecturing and compiling scriptures.

He invited [the masters] to enter Ximing Monastery and the Xiaoyao Garden to translate various sūtras. The Emperor commissioned the śramaṇas Sengqie, Sengqian, Faqin, Daoliu, Daoheng, Daobiao, Sengrui, and Sengzhao, among others.

More than eight hundred people were permitted to receive Kumārajīva’s instructions and were further ordered to translate the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Kumārajīva held the Sanskrit manuscript, while Yao Xing held the previous Chinese version.

He compared and collated these with one another; their meanings were all perfectly coherent. The hearts of the multitude were satisfied and submissive, and there was none who did not rejoice and praise him.

Because he considered the Buddha-way to be profound and subtle, and that its practice is virtuous, he believed it to be the excellent ford for escaping suffering and the grand standard for governing the world.

He then composed the *Tongsanshi lun* (Treatise on the Three Times) to exhort and demonstrate the law of cause and effect. From princes and dukes downward, all praised his character and requested [him] at Chang...
At Andasi Temple, he lectured on new sutras and continued to produce over three hundred scrolls of various chapters on the essentials of Chan, precept manuals, vinaya, and treatises.

Furthermore, he elucidated the divine source and brought forth its profound subtleties; his fame resounded throughout the four quarters, and scholars of principle inevitably gathered there. His magnificent legacy was enduring and vast, and even today it remains an object of reverence.
As for the monk Dao-sheng of Longguang Temple, his wisdom and understanding reached the subtlest depths, and his literary compositions were profound and structured.

Externally, he constantly feared his words might be erroneous; thus, upon entering the Pass, he requested a definitive resolution. Huìyuǎn of Lúshān had mastered the various scriptures, yet there were points of doubt that could not be resolved.

Consequently, he sealed the questions and consulted Kumārajīva. Huìruì, whose talent and insight were brilliant, regularly accompanied Kumārajīva to transcribe the texts and also composed treatises for him.

They deliberated upon the similarities and differences between Western literary forms and those of China. In the customs of the country of India, literary elegance is highly esteemed; they compose their works according to the principles of *gōngshāng* (melodic pitch).
Regarding rhyme, it is best when it enters the strings [of musical instruments]. Whenever one has an audience with a king, there must be praise for his virtue;

as for the ritual of seeing a Buddha, the singing of hymns is held in high esteem. The gāthās in the sūtras all follow this model. However, by transposing the Sanskrit into the Qin (Chinese) language, its elegant refinement is lost.

Kumārajīva was deeply fond of the Mahāyāna and was committed to its propagation. He often sighed, saying: "If I were to take up the pen and compose a Mahāyāna Abhidharma, it would not be comparable to that of Kātyāyanīputra.
Yet, here in the land of Qin, those with profound understanding are few; my wings are clipped here—what more could I possibly discuss?
He composed only two fascicles of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Real-Character Treatise) for Yao Xing, as well as his commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Yao Xing...
They revered him as if he were a deity. He frequently preached the sutras at Caotang Monastery, attended by over a thousand people, including Emperor Xiaowen, court officials, and eminent śramaṇas.
As they gazed upon him with solemn countenances, Kumārajīva suddenly descended from his high seat and said, "Two small boys have climbed onto my shoulders."
This was indeed an obstacle of desire. Yao Xing said to Kumārajīva, "The Great Master’s brilliance and transcendent realization are peerless in the world;
how can you allow him to have so few descendants? He then summoned ten palace women and compelled them to consort with him. From one union, two sons were born.
Thereafter, he no longer resided in the monks' quarters but established a separate residence for himself, where provisions were provided in abundance. Whenever he gave lectures, he would always...
He first spoke for himself, saying, "It is like a lotus flower growing from foul mud; one should simply take the lotus and not the mud.
Many of the monks wished to emulate him. Kumārajīva then filled his bowl with needles and said to them, "If you can emulate this by eating these, then you may maintain a household.
He then took seven mouthfuls of the needles and ate them without any difference from ordinary food. The monks were ashamed and submitted to him in reverence.
Thereupon he ceased [speaking]. Kumārajīva composed a verse and presented it to Fǎhé, saying: "The mountain of mind nurtures brilliant virtue; Its fragrance flows for ten thousand *yojanas*.
Like a grieving crane upon a solitary paulownia tree, Its clear sound penetrates the nine heavens. Kumārajīva felt that his physical elements were failing to recover.
He then recited a divine mantra three times from his own mouth and had his foreign disciples chant it. As his condition grew increasingly critical, he took leave of the assembly.
He said: "We have met through the Dharma, yet we have not fully realized our original aspiration. As we look toward future lives, our deep sorrow remains such that it can barely be expressed.

Believing myself to be ignorant and dull-witted, I have mistakenly served as a translator. May all the sutras and śāstras I have produced circulate widely in future generations and be propagated by all together.
Now, before this assembly, I make a sincere and truthful vow: if what I have transmitted is without error, may [the fire] burn..."
After his body was cremated, the tongue remained unimpaired.

On the twentieth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of Hongshi of the pseudo-Qin dynasty—this being the year Jiyou, the fifth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Jin—he passed away while seated in Chang’an.
He was cremated according to foreign rites in the Xiaoyao Garden; only the tongue remained undamaged. The Dharma Master’s other name was Kumārajīva.
“Jiapo” (Jīvaka) is a name established according to foreign custom; it is generally derived from the names of one’s parents. Since his mother’s name was Jīva, he took both [names] together.

As for the Master’s character, his spirit and intellect were clear and penetrating, and his dignified bearing rose above the crowd. In responding to circumstances and grasping the essence of things, few could equal him.

By nature sincere, benevolent, and kind, he made universal compassion his core principle. He humbled himself to guide others well, never growing weary throughout the day. Regarding all the places he visited...

The state honored him with the utmost propriety. His translated writings were elegant and refined; his fame spread throughout both the Chinese and the barbarian realms, serving as a mirror for ten thousand generations—he alone was such a person (Beishi, original biography).
Buddhayaśas arrived in Guzang. He had previously been in the Western Regions for some time and had studied together with Kumārajīva.

Hearing that he was propagating the Dharma in the Qin state and that Kumārajīva had received palace women from the Qin court, he sighed and said: "Kumārajīva is like a fine brocade; how can one make him prickly and thorny?"

When Kumārajīva heard that Guṇavarman had arrived, he urged the Qin ruler to revere him. Once he had arrived, a separate vihāra was specially constructed for his residence, and royal provisions were provided for him;
yet Guṇavarman accepted nothing at all. When it was time for alms, he would eat only a single meal.

He was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā* treatises and had red whiskers, so he was popularly known as "Red-Whiskered Vibhāṣā. [Also mentioned is] Vimalākṣa (translated into Chinese as Wugouyan, "Undefiled Eyes").

Upon reaching the Qin dynasty, he extensively propagated the Vinaya in the region east of the Pass. It was due to his efforts that the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva and the Vinaya-piṭaka were widely disseminated.
His own composition, the eleven-fascicle *Neijing qingzhong* (Internal Prohibitions: Light and Heavy), circulated throughout the world.
His eyes were blue, and he was thus known at the time as the "Blue-Eyed Vinaya Master" (*Sengzhuan*).

Master Xuán asked the deity Veda: "As for the scriptures translated by Dharma Master Kumārajīva during his single period of propagation, why is it that their reception and practice remain so flourishing even to this day?
The deity replied: "That man was brilliant and possessed a profound understanding of the Mahāyāna.

As for those who followed him, they were all destined to become treasures of their respective eras—men who would surpass all who came before and leave none behind, such that even those who look up to them cannot reach their heights. Therefore...

Regarding his translations, he prioritized spiritual realization, thereby capturing the intent entrusted to him by the Buddha. Furthermore, when asked about the common discourse among the laity regarding the violation of monastic precepts, Tian said:
"There is no need to evaluate this; it is not a matter for those who are merely idle.

Master Kumārajīva was one whose rank was equal to that of the Three Sages (Tri-vidyādhara), and through whom transformation was spread. Nevertheless, in his translation of the scriptures, he exercised editorial revision."

There are many omissions; [the work] was produced accordingly. Thus, one entire volume of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* has been abbreviated by nine-tenths. Other sutras and śāstras may be understood by this same principle.

Since the translation of the sutras, he has recited them with utmost sincerity without interruption or neglect. His spiritual resonance has invited divine responses that have remained ever-fresh through successive generations.
Judging by this, it is clear that he profoundly grasped the Sage’s intent. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī bestowed his instructions, commanding him to edit and finalize [the texts]. Especially...

To differ from the common standard—how can one be censured for staying in a separate room? To suddenly forget the profound teachings is truly not worthy of even a single word from a śramaṇa (from the *Sanzao Gantong Lu*).

In the eleventh year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, the Sovereign, since Master Kumārajīva’s entry into the capital, had revered and placed his faith in the Triple Gem and extensively propagated the Great Transformation.

He established assemblies and held vegetarian feasts, such that half of every ten households abandoned worldly life. As monks and nuns from near and far gathered in great numbers, there were occasionally lapses or transgressions.
Daoxing said, "Ordinary practitioners and student-monks have not yet attained the stage of *duḥkhakṣānti* (endurance of suffering); how could they be without faults? If one commits a fault..."
"The transgressions of [Hui-]Zheng have become too numerous. It is appropriate to appoint a Monastic Head (Sengzhu) to establish a clear and great reputation.

Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "Now that the Great Dharma has moved eastward, it flourishes more than ever. Since the number of monks and nuns is vast, there must be a governing authority to proclaim far-reaching regulations and rescue the declining traditions.
Master Sengquan has possessed superior learning since his youth, and his virtue has blossomed in his later years. He shall serve as the Monastic Head of the realm."

Dharma Master Sengqian cultivated both meditation and wisdom, and was appointed as the *yuezong* (director of the assembly). Fashu and Huibin jointly served as the *senglü* (monastic registrar). They were provided with carriages, attendants, and laborers;
their stipends were equal to those of the *shizhong* (Palace Attendant), and they were granted the privilege of riding in the imperial carriage when transmitting edicts.

To each of them, including Sengqian, generous provisions were granted. Their administration was pure and frugal, perfectly suited to the needs of the times. The five groups of monastics were strictly disciplined, and the six periods of daily practice were never neglected. Such was the role of the *Sengzheng* (Director of Monks).
"Xing (Rising) is the beginning of 'Sheng' (Prospering). (From the *Beishi* and his own biography).

The Ruler of Qin, perceiving that the two Dharma Masters Daoheng and Daobiao possessed spirits and countenances of remarkable brilliance and the capacity for statecraft, issued an edict to Yao Xian, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, ordering him to earnestly urge Daoheng and Daobiao to renounce the monastic life and assist in the promotion of the royal enterprise. He further issued a decree:
The Emperor said: "Your pure and resolute conduct, O Ministers, is truly praiseworthy. However, if one is to preside over the four seas, effective governance urgently requires talent.

I hereby issue an imperial decree to Xianling, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to strip you of your monastic robes so that you may assist in extraordinary ways and contribute to the current age.

If your hearts remain fixed on the flavor of the Way, what does it matter whether one is clad in black or white? I hope you will understand this mandate and not decline on account of maintaining your vows. — [From] the records of Hengbiao and others.
I reply: On the twenty-eighth day of last month, an imperial edict was issued to strip Heng, Biao, and the others of their Dharma robes.

Receiving this command, we were overcome with grief and our five emotions lost their composure. Heng and the others are of dull and inferior character; our immersion in the Dharma has not been profound.

Beneath these black robes, we have vowed to devote our lives to practicing the Buddha-dharma, being unacquainted with worldly affairs. To pointlessly abandon our extraordinary vocation would ultimately yield no merit.
The merit of this difference lies in the fact that in the past, Emperor Guangwu was still able to grant Yan Guang his heart’s desire, and Emperor Wen of Wei tolerated Guan Ning’s integrity;

thus, they bent the lofty will of the Sovereign to accommodate the humble resolve of a commoner. How much more so for Your Majesty, who governs all things through the Way and simultaneously propagates the Three Jewels!
We pray that you will examine the sentiments of the common people and bestow upon them the principle of vast and open governance. Furthermore, he sent a letter to...

The two Dharma Masters Shi and Li said: "We have been separated for several dozen days and have constantly harbored thoughts of you. It has gradually grown warmer, and we hope your physical condition is now at ease."

The petty barbarian has launched a distant incursion; there is no further disposition to be made, and I am left only in a state of confusion. Lately, as all affairs have become pressing, there was a need for talent to manage them.
Recently, an imperial edict was issued to Heng and Biao, ordering the two of them to cast off their robes of Arhatship and follow the liberated course of a Mahāsattva.
"However, the Way is omnipresent. We pray that the Dharma Masters will assist us by providing metaphors for this. Kumārajīva and his colleagues replied:
"We have heard that the Supreme One nourishes the people through the Way, and things naturally attain their proper state. To govern the world, one must rely on virtue;

therefore, the enlightened rulers of antiquity understood the difficulty of governing those who act contrary to their nature, and realized the many advantages of allowing things to follow their own course. Thus, Yao banished Xu You..."
Because of Mount Ji, Boyi declined the throne and cast aside his staff at the state of Wei; because of Mount Zhongnan, the High Ancestor released the Four Elders;
and because of the Han Peak, Bo Shudu declined the carriage with dragon-veined wheels. This was because they sought to accord with the nature of the worthy, thereby attaining true worthiness.

Now, Hengbiao and his companions possess no virtue of universal penetration, yet their lot lies in maintaining their integrity. Having studied the profound transformation since youth, they have submitted themselves to the Buddhist Way. As for their exposition...
He has collated the wondrous scriptures and researched their profound subtleties; this is sufficient to enlighten the young and ignorant and to assist in the merit of transformation.

We pray that Your Majesty will grant him the grace of his past deeds and allow him to pursue his future aspirations. Throughout the entire region, people rescued him when he was on the verge of death and narrowly escaped [persecution].
He then sighed and said: "The ancients had a saying: 'That which increases my wealth diminishes my spirit; that which gives me fame kills my person.'"
Thereupon, he withdrew his shadow into the crags and gullies. He passed away in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty at the age of seventy-two.

Heng was a native of Lantian. At the age of nine, while playing on the road, Zhang Zhong saw him and said, "If this boy remains in the secular world, he will surely achieve merit in assisting the administration.
He lived in seclusion, bringing great luster to the Buddha-dharma (as recorded in the *Monastic Biographies* and the *Beishi*).
Since Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty had set his heart upon the Buddha-vehicle, from the high officials down to the commoners, there was none who did not revere and follow him.
Over five thousand śramaṇas arrived from afar; he erected a *stūpa* in Yonggui Li and established a Prajñā Terrace within the palace.

Those engaged in meditation and lecturing were always numbering in the thousands, and among the prefectures and commanderies, nine out of ten households worshipped the Buddha. (From the three rulers until Hong)

In the thirty-third year [of the reign], Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty served the Dharma with a refined mind; his aspirations and thoughts were in mystical resonance with the truth. The King of the Kingdom of Siṃhala, admiring his devotion to the Way, [sent an envoy].
He dispatched the śramaṇa Tanmo Zui to deliver a jade statue four chi and two cun tall, thereby expressing his sincere devotion.

During the Ningkang era, a pagoda was constructed at Tanchi Temple and a bronze statue was cast. When the statue rose up on its own, its light pierced the heavens and illuminated the mountain valleys (from the *Gantong lu*).
In the fourteenth year of the Dàyuán era, the Emperor venerated Buddhism, exhausting his resources and incurring immense expenses.

Those close to him—monks and nuns who were like maternal uncles and aunts—along with those in his immediate entourage, vied for power and manipulated affairs of state. They colluded and made improper requests, and bribery was practiced openly.
Official rewards were bestowed indiscriminately, and the judicial system fell into chaos. Lù Nà, the Grand Chancellor, sighed upon beholding the palace gates, saying: "Alas!"
The family home was dilapidated. The child wished to strike down the earthen wall. ○ Xu Rong, General Commanding the Left Guard, submitted a memorial, saying:

"Your servant has heard that the Buddha is a mysterious and transcendent deity from a distant land who takes the Five Precepts as his teaching: to abstain from alcohol and to refrain from sexual misconduct."
As for those who serve them now, they are arrogant and ignorant, addicted to wine and sensual beauty. It is further said that monks and nuns gather in crowds, relying on their clerical robes;
they cannot even observe the coarse precepts of the fivefold discipline, let alone the refined and subtle ones. Yet these common folk compete to honor and serve them.
Moreover, they prey upon the common people, seizing their wealth as a form of "charity," which is not in accord with the true Way of giving.
The memorial was submitted but not granted (*according to the *Book of Jin* and the *Comprehensive Mirror*).
Shi Huiyuan was of the Jia clan; he was a native of Loufan in Yanmen. At thirteen, he followed his maternal uncle, the Liangfu family, to study in Xuchang and Luoyang.
He comprehensively mastered the Six Classics and was particularly proficient in the works of Zhuangzi and Laozi. At twenty-one, he heard that the śramaṇa Dao’an had established a monastery at...
He traveled to Mount Taihang and Mount Heng, where he paid his respects to all he encountered, regarding them as his true teachers.

When Dao’an lectured on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, [Huiyuan] listened with such realization that he sighed, "The nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism are nothing more than chaff and husks. Huiyuan, along with several dozen disciples, headed south toward Mount Luofu; upon reaching Xunyang, he beheld the azure and magnificent beauty of Mount Lu, which was sufficient [to settle him there].

Later, when Xunyang suffered a severe drought, Huiyuan went to the side of a pond and recited the *Nāgarāja Sūtra*. Suddenly, a giant serpent ascended into the sky, and in a short while, a great rain fell.
The entire region was filled with joy, and consequently, it was named Longsi (Dragon Temple). At that time, Huiyong resided at Xilin; he and Huiyuan were fellow disciples.
As Huiyuan’s followers grew numerous, the Regional Inspector Huan Yi established a vihāra on the eastern side of the mountain.

During the study of the sūtras and śāstras, thunder and lightning broke out one night. At dawn, fine timber was found piled up in abundance. When Huan Yi witnessed this event, [he was deeply impressed].

Startled by his divine and extraordinary nature, [the Emperor] submitted a memorial to establish a monastery, naming it Donglin (East Forest). In the eleventh year of the Dàyuán era of the Jin dynasty, the monastery was completed. The caves exhausted the mountain’s beauty;
a separate Chan grove was established there, where clear springs flowed and trees grew in dense profusion. All who came to pay their respects felt their spirits become pure and their breaths solemn.

Yīn Zhòngkān visited Huiyuǎn, and they together went to the northern stream. There they recited the *Yì* (Book of Changes) while contemplating its principles, remaining untiring even as the shadows shifted. Yīn sighed in admiration.
[The Emperor] said: "Your consciousness is profoundly clear; it is truly difficult to find one who can deliver you. The Imperial Preceptor Wang’s posthumous title record states:
"At the age of forty, his decline was like that of one who has reached sixty. The Master replied: "The ancients did not prize a foot-long jade disc, but valued an inch of shadow [of time].

Hui-ling: "I have long since grasped this principle. When Lu Xun first occupied Jiangzhou, he entered the mountains to visit Huiyuan.

To maintain such close ties with him—will you not be suspected? Huiyuan replied, 'In our Buddha-dharma, the mind takes nothing and rejects nothing.'"
"Is this not something that would be observed by those who possess discernment? This is not worth fearing.

When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty pursued Lu Xun and established his headquarters at Sangwei, his attendants remarked, "Master Huiyuan has long been the sovereign of Mount Lu and was on very close terms with Lu Xun. Emperor Wu said, "Master Huiyuan is a man beyond the mundane world;

This was Huiyuan. He was renowned for his clear vision. When Huan Xuan went to campaign against Yin Zhongkan, his army passed by Mount Lu.

Huan Xuan requested that Huiyuan come out to the Tiger Brook, but Huiyuan cited illness as an excuse. Huan Xuan entered the mountain himself, and his attendants said to him, "Huiyuan treats Yin Zhongkan with such courtesy."

"I hope the General will not pay him respect. He replied, "How could such a thing be possible? Zhongkan was originally nothing but a dead man. Yet, upon seeing Huiyuan, he unconsciously paid his respects.
Daoyuan asked Huiyuan, "The precepts state that one must not damage or injure the body; why then do you shave your hair? Huiyuan replied, "To establish oneself and practice the Way.
Daoyuan praised this as excellent. Later, relying on the prestige of his martial prowess, Xun sent a letter urging him to enter government service, but Huiyuan declined.

This truly accords with the fundamental intent of the mind. For if the Jing River is allowed its natural division, then clarity and turbidity will each follow their own course;

Thereafter, those who adorn themselves with hypocrisy will be cut off from the path of feigned communication, while those who cherish the truth will no longer suffer the reproach of violating worldly norms. Consequently, he extensively elaborated upon the profound regulations, and Xuán followed his lead (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and the *Book of Northern Qi*).

When Huiyuan was stationed at Gushu, he wished to require [the monks] to pay full reverence. He wrote to Huiyuan, saying: "If śramaṇas do not pay homage to the King, this is because their inner sentiments are not yet resolved, and from the perspective of principle, it is something I have not yet understood.
This is a momentous matter for the age; one must not allow its fundamental substance to be inconsistent. He further addressed the Eight Seats (*bāzuò*).
I write this letter now to present to you. You may describe therein those matters for which I have not yet expressed my respect; these are precisely the points upon which I shall act.
I hope you will consider them with thorough detail, for there must surely be a way to resolve my doubts. Yuan replied in his letter, saying: "What, indeed, is a śramaṇa?

The Way of "simultaneous forgetting" proceeds together with all under heaven, enabling those who aspire to the heights to draw from its lingering influence and those who sip the flowing stream to taste its residual essence.

"Those outside [the realm] ought not to pay homage to the King. Although Daoyuan stubbornly clung to his former resolve and felt ashamed to immediately follow [the foreign custom], he observed the purport of Zhu Fawen’s words and hesitated, unable to decide.

[The Emperor’s decree: "That which cannot be fathomed, one honors out of a sense of devotion to the sovereign, and thus gives rise to reverence. Now that the matter rests with me, you should embody humble radiance;
