The essence of the ultimate does not admit of duality. Fifth, it is said that when the body perishes, the spirit is not extinguished. The preface states:

Formerly, during the Xiankang era, General Yu [Hui] questioned why the śramaṇas should offer salutations to those of ten-thousand chariots (the sovereign). Later, during the Yuanxing era, Grand Marshal Huan [Xuan] likewise held this same view.

At that time, there were many eminent scholars and worthies among the court officials who responded; although their words did not yet lead to enlightenment, each of them possessed their own [arguments].
Alas! Those who merely exhaust themselves in destroying [the Dharma] leave its underlying principles buried within their emotions.

Consequently, the robes of the unsurpassed Way are ruined by worldly vulgarity, and the sincere aspiration for realization is thwarted by human affairs. How tragic! This is the origin of mutual ruin and a period of misfortune lasting a thousand years.
Deeply fearing that the Great Dharma is about to sink into oblivion, and moved by the fact that past events have been forgotten, I have therefore composed these five chapters.
I have investigated and set forth its meaning. Is this not like the morning dew awaiting the deep abyss?

It is intended to extend that which is boundless, and it is my hope that future gentlemen who honor the teachings may examine it in detail (as the five chapters contain much text, they are not recorded here).

When Huan Xuan fled westward, Emperor An of the Jin dynasty returned from Jiangling to the capital. He Fuyuan was urged by the Protector of the State, He Wuji, to go out to welcome him; however, Fuyuan cited illness as an excuse.
The Emperor sent an envoy to inquire after his health, to which Fuyuan sent a letter in reply: "Huiyuan bows.

It is mild and warm in the first month of spring, and I trust Your Majesty’s meals are suitable to the season. This humble monk has long been afflicted by a serious illness, and with advancing years, it has grown even more severe. I have humbly received your compassionate decree."

Your gracious letter bestowing consolation has reached me; my feelings of gratitude and trepidation are indeed as profound as a hundred thousand eons. It is a great fortune to have encountered this auspicious occasion, yet my body cannot move of its own accord.
These sentiments and this lamentation are truly beyond description. The Imperial Response: I am deeply moved by your words. I know that your ailment has not improved.
My feelings are most earnest. Departing from Jiangling last month, I encountered many hardships on the road; my spirits were sluggish and my condition was as it usually is.

I originally hoped to meet you by chance along the way, but since the Dharma Master has been cultivating your essence in the mountain forests and your ailment remains unhealed, there is no further possibility of such a meeting.
This increases my profound lamentation and regret (as recorded in the *Benzhuan* and the *Book of Jin*).
King Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty admired his virtuous influence and marveled at his talent and insight.

He sent letters and gifts, ordering Yao Song to present him with a jeweled image as well as a finely embroidered image of various transformations from the kingdom of Kucha, thereby extending his sincere devotion.
Eighteen eminent men of the Jin dynasty followed this master to receive the Way. The Master said to Liu Chengzhi, Zong Bing, Lei Cizong, and others:
"Gentlemen, having cast aside the world and forsaken worldly glory, if you have the heart to journey to the Pure Land, you should establish a vegetarian feast and take vows before Amitāyus Buddha.
With one mind, make this aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land. He then instructed Liu Yimin to compose a text, which read:
"In the year of Sheti (Jupiter), on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in autumn, the Dharma Master Huiyuan—whose pure resonance reached into the profound and mysterious—[like] frost..."
Huaiwei then invited his fellow practitioners— those gentlemen of pure faith who had stilled their minds— to assemble, numbering one hundred and twenty-three,
at the Vihāra of Prajñā Terrace on the southern slope of Mount Lu before an image of Amitābha, where they led the assembly with incense and flowers.
With reverence, I present this offering and make this vow. Now, as the principle of conditioned transformation is clarified, the transmission through the three periods of time becomes manifest.
As the patterns of shifting responses coincide, the retribution for good and evil is certain.

Inferring from those who have vanished in the blink of an eye, one realizes that the arrival of impermanence is urgent; examining how the three types of retribution press one another, one knows the perilous nature of existence.
This is why those of like mind have been vigilant at dusk and diligent through the night, looking upward with thoughts of a far-reaching salvation.
For the spirit can be reached through resonance, but cannot be sought through outward traces. If there is a substance to one's resonance, then the path to the unseen realm is but a few inches away;
yet if one seeks it without a guiding principle, it remains as vast and distant as the crossing of the Yellow River. Now, fortunately, without prior consultation...

All hearts were turned toward the western realm. Upon reading the text, faith and clarity arose from the depths of their spiritual natures. Thus, the signs of this karmic response manifested even in dreams; the joy was a hundredfold greater than that felt at the birth of a son.

Thereupon, the cloud-patterned charts revealed their brilliance, and the shadows aligned with divine creation. This merit arises from the realization of principle; it is not a matter of human contrivance.
This is truly the case that Heaven has revealed its sincerity, and that the dark workings of destiny have gathered in harmony. How could one not cultivate the mind and hold this in high esteem?

How can one not let their thoughts layer upon one another to concentrate their reflections? Yet, as their achievements vary and their merits differ, though we pray together at dawn, our returns may be separated by evening.
Thus, it would surely be improper for me to neglect the affection due to my teachers and friends. For this reason, I am filled with solemnity and issue this summons;
we shall straighten our robes in the Dharma Hall, bestow our single-mindedness equally, and settle our hearts in profound stillness. We vow here to be of one mind, all together.

Wandering through remote frontiers, there are those whose extraordinary emergence is beyond compare; they first ascend to the divine realm, no longer seeking solitary excellence upon the cloud-capped peaks, but forgetting themselves to preserve all things within the deep valleys.
Those who have advanced before and those who ascend after should strive to contemplate the way of collective advancement.

Furthermore, by wondrously observing the celestial patterns and opening the mind to pure illumination, consciousness awakens to novelty and the physical form is transformed through refinement, taking root amidst the lotus flowers of the center.
Flowing along, I shelter beneath the jade branches to prolong my reflections; my cloud-garments drift to the eight extremities of space.

Floating upon fragrant breezes for the rest of my years, my body forgets comfort yet remains ever serene; transcending worldly pleasures, I find joy within myself. Facing the three miserable realms, I offer a distant farewell; looking with pride upon the celestial palaces, I bid them a long adieu.
I summon the myriad spirits to follow in my footsteps, pointing to the Great Rest as my destination. Having investigated this, is it not so?
How vast! Xie Lingyun, relying on his own high talent, was haughty and disdainful toward others. Upon seeing the Master, he was struck with solemn reverence and submitted his heart;
he requested to join the community, but the Master declined him, citing his impure mind. The two ponds, East and West, were excavated by Mr. Xie himself;
as for the red and white lotuses, the community was named after the white lotus. Táo Qián lived at Cháisāng, which was near Mount Lú.

It was said that if one were permitted to drink, they would immediately join the community. The Master granted him permission, and he entered the mountains. After a long time, [Huiyuan] knit his brows and departed.

Whenever the Master saw guests off, he took the Tiger Brook as his boundary. One day, when Yuanming and Lu Xiujing entered the mountains, the Master accompanied them for some distance and conversed with them.
Unaware that they had crossed the stream, they looked at one another and laughed heartily. To this day, people paint them as the "Three Laughs of Mount Lu.
Huiyuan had a disciple named Huiyao, who was learned in the Sūtras and Vinaya and particularly gifted in ingenious contrivances. At that time, the assembly of worthies was gathered together;
since there were no water clocks (leke) in the mountains, he fashioned a twelve-petaled lotus from a spring, which rotated with the current to determine the ten [hours].
At both times, the shadow of the sun-dial showed no discrepancy. Thus, the text of his vow states: "There is a record of a lotus flower [appearing] in the middle of the stream.
He also constructed a wooden kite that flew for several hundred paces. On the sixth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, the Master...

He gathered the assembly for the entrustment of his final instructions and took his leave to depart for eternity. He was eighty-three years of age. For seven days, both monastics and laypeople paid their respects.
Ruan Bao of Xunyang erected a stupa to the west of the mountain; Xie Lingyun composed the inscription for the stele to commemorate his enduring virtue.
Zong Bing of Nanyang subsequently erected a monument at the temple gate (*Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
The Master’s deportment was upright and refined; his discernment was brilliant and transcendent. His character was vast and noble, and his virtuous conduct was as pure as ice and frost.
Among the veteran scholars and eminent men, as well as kings, dukes, and great officials, there were none who did not bow their knees upon seeing him from afar, admiring his profound depth.

He resided on Mount Lu for thirty years, never venturing beyond the mountains nor entering the secular world. He was skilled in composing literary works, whose phrasing and tone were elegant and refined. At his table...

His discourse was refined and concise in meaning. The treatises, prefaces, inscriptions, eulogies, poems, and letters he composed fill ten volumes and comprise over fifty pieces, which are held in high esteem by the world.
In the thirteenth year of the Yuexing era of Emperor An, Helian Bobo occupied Xia and proclaimed himself the Great Xia.

He invaded Chang’an and plundered the territories of the two Qin states. He abolished the five punishments and declared that those who speak of the Buddha are already Buddhas among men and deserve the ritual homage due to monks.
Consequently, he had images of the Buddha painted upon people’s backs and ordered the śramaṇas to prostrate before these images, asserting that this constituted paying homage to him. Later...
He was struck dead by a thunderbolt from heaven. After his burial, the corpse was once again struck by lightning and cast out, with the characters "Wúdào" (Unprincipled) inscribed upon it.

Soon thereafter, he was swallowed up by the Northern Dai; this may well serve as a laughingstock for all under heaven. ○ Bobo esteemed his own virtue as supreme, yet he was ignorant of the Way of the Sages.
He claimed that "Bo" meant "Buddha," saying, "I am the Buddha among men; I deserve the prostrations of monks. Why indeed?
He placed a statue of Chen at the rear of his seat and ordered the śramaṇas to assemble for morning audiences to pay him homage.

Thus, he harbored both fear and affection toward them. In the year Yichou, he was struck dead by a thunderbolt from heaven. After his burial, a subsequent thunder shook the earth and brought forth his corpse, with the inscription: "A ruler without the Way.

Soon thereafter, he was swallowed up by the Northern Dynasties, becoming a laughingstock for all under heaven. As the Book of Documents says: "When Heaven sends down calamities, it is still possible to rectify the situation."
"One who has committed their own misdeeds cannot be punished for them. How profoundly true these words are! (From the *Beishi*).
The monk Tanhuo could walk as swiftly as the wind. His pronouncements regarding people’s births and deaths, or their nobility and lowliness, were remarkably accurate.

Carrying a single *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), he would have others kneel before it and say, "This is the Eye of Prajñā; by honoring it, one may attain the Way. On other occasions, he would hide his staff and then weep aloud.
After several sounds, he closed his eyes for a moment, then rose and took it up; its spiritual wonder was beyond measure (according to the *Jingshu*).
On the day of Bingshen, the first year of Huangshi of Emperor Taizu of Wei, he issued an edict stating: "The rise of the Buddha-dharma has been far-reaching for a long time.
Its merit in providing salvation extends secretly even to those who have passed away. The divine traces and the bequeathed Dharma can truly be relied upon. He then commanded the relevant authorities.
In the capital, he sent his disciples to maintain proper decorum and repair the monasteries, providing a place of refuge for those with faith.
By imperial decree, the śramaṇa Faguo of Zhaojun was summoned to serve as the Sanghe-tong (Supreme Patriarch). (*Weishu*)
Shi Daosheng, whose secular surname was Wei, was a native of Julu. Encountering Zhu Fatai, he changed his status from a layman to a monk to study under him.
He traveled to Chang’an to assist Master Kumārajīva in translating the scriptures. Empress Dowager Churu of the Jin dynasty’s Gongsi era founded Qingyuan Temple and invited him to serve as its abbot.
In the summer months, thunder shook the Buddha hall at Qingyuan Monastery, and a dragon ascended into the sky, leaving its radiance upon the western wall.

Consequently, the monastery was renamed Longguang (Dragon Radiance). Contemporaries sighed, saying, "Since the dragon has already departed, Master Sheng must surely go as well. Shortly thereafter, he set out for Mount Lu.
At first, he traveled to Mount Huqiu in Wu. Arranging stones as his disciples, he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

When he reached the section on the Icchantikas (*icchantika-pada*) concerning the presence of Buddha-nature, he asked, "Does what I have explained accord with the Buddha’s own mind? Thereupon, the stubborn rocks nodded their heads. Within ten days, several hundred students had gathered.

(He had previously taught that even those who are icchantikas can all attain Buddhahood; the assembly did not yet believe him. Later, when the full version of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* arrived in the capital, it was indeed so.)

It is stated that icchantikas all possess Buddha-nature; this accords with what was previously taught. Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty held him in profound reverence. On the day the assembly was convened, he...
The Emperor personally joined the assembly at the banquet and began to serve the food. The assembly suspected it was already late in the day, but the Emperor said, "It is only just noon.
Huisheng said, "The bright sun adorns the heavens; if Heaven says it is just noon, how can it not be noon? He took up his chopsticks and began to eat, and the entire assembly followed his example.

All were moved to sighs of admiration and submission. His pivotal responses were always perfectly balanced. In the eleventh month of the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, as he was concluding his lecture series at Mount Lu, his fly-whisk suddenly fell from his hand.
He sat upright with a composed countenance, leaning on his armrest as if entering a state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Both monastics and laypeople were struck with awe (from his *Benzhuan*).
Shi Daorong was a native of Linlü in Jijun. He entered the monastic order at the age of twelve. Five years later, hearing that Master Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he went there to seek instruction.
When Kumārajīva saw him, he remarked to Yao Xing, "Yesterday’s Master Rong is once again a remarkable person of great intelligence.

Upon this, Yao Xing invited him for an audience and praised him highly. An imperial decree was issued for him to enter the Xiaoyao Garden to participate in the verification and detailed translation of the scriptures. Kumārajīva then commanded Daorong to lecture on the new translations.
When Dharmarakṣa heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he sighed and said, "The rise of the Buddha-dharma is due to such a person as [Kumārajīva].
I am a Brahmin from the Kingdom of Siṃhala, clever, eloquent, and widely learned; I was the preeminent teacher of the non-Buddhists in that foreign land.

Hearing that Kumārajīva was propagating the Buddha-dharma extensively in Guanzhong, I said to my disciples: 'It would be better to let the influence of the Śākya clan spread alone in China, rather than for us..."
His correct teaching did not spread to the eastern lands. He subsequently traveled on camel, carrying his scriptures, and arrived in Chang’an.

The Sun’s majesty covers all living beings, and it has bequeathed its writings as a model for the world. Thus, among the four great things within the realm, the King occupies one.

From my youth, though I was of humble station, I have unworthily received the grace of the state, allowing me to dwell in leisure within the academy of learning under the tutelage of Master Kumārajīva for over ten years.

The Southern and Northern Dynasties period of the Song dynasty: from Gengshen to Jiwu, eight rulers reigned for sixty years, with the capital at Jiankang.
During the fifth year of Emperor Mingyuan’s reign as Taizu of the Wei dynasty, they possessed all of Hebei.
The High Ancestor Emperor Wu received the abdication from the Jin dynasty and ascended the throne. He changed the era name to Yongchu, in the sixth month of the year Gengshen.

he summoned Dharmakṣema and recruited twenty-five men to travel to the Western Regions to seek scriptures; and he issued an edict to Sengjin.

He was appointed as the Preceptor of the Monks for the Empire. A troupe of musicians for the Dharma, twenty personal attendants, and a monthly stipend of thirty thousand strings of cash were granted to him, along with carriages and laborers.

Furthermore, that which is cultivated by a sovereign differs from that of a commoner. If a commoner cannot overcome themselves and practice rigorous austerity, how can they be of use?
A sovereign takes the four seas as their home and the myriad people as their children. When they utter a single virtuous word, then the scholars and the commoners..."
All will be joyful. When one good policy is spread, ministers will be harmonious; punishments will not take life prematurely, and labor will not exhaust strength.

Thus, wind and rain will arrive in their proper seasons, and the hundred grains will flourish. To observe the fast with such results—how great the fast is! To refrain from killing with such results—how great that abstinence is!
The benefits are also many. Why settle for gathering enough food for half a day or saving the life of a single bird before claiming to provide vast salvation?
The Emperor struck his desk and sighed, saying, "The laity are deluded regarding the ultimate principle, while the monks are mired in superficial teachings.

As you say, Master, one may truly discuss the boundary between heaven and humanity. The Emperor honored him as his teacher and ordered him to reside at Qiyuan Temple, providing him with abundant and generous support. He then lectured...

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika*) chapter, Emperor [Wu] personally led the high officials to assemble daily at his seat. The grandeur of this Dharma assembly was unprecedented in history.
The King of Śrīvijaya dispatched an envoy with a memorial stating: "The Great Lord of the Song State, Auspicious Son of Heaven."
He transformed beings and perfected wisdom, bringing peace and security to all sentient beings. Although I am far away, I too am moistened by his spiritual influence (*Tongji*).
The divine monk Beidu first appeared in Jizhou; his supernatural powers were preeminent. At times he would strike the ice to bathe;

at times he would wear wooden clogs while climbing mountains; at times he would walk barefoot into the marketplace. He carried only a single reed basket, which ten men could not lift. Or he was seen...

The four children were none other than the Four Heavenly Kings. They had been worshipped by the Li family of Guangling for quite some time. Suddenly, they demanded a *kāṣāya* (monastic robe). Although Li prepared one, it had not yet arrived;

[the children] said, "We shall go out for a moment," and though the night passed, they did not return. When they were sought the following day, they were found beneath the northern cliff, lying dead upon the ground with a tattered *kāṣāya* spread out before them.
Lotus flowers grew from both their heads and their feet. The people of the district buried them together.
A few days later, someone arriving from the north reported that he had seen Du carrying a reed basket on his back, traveling toward Pengcheng.

Thereupon, they opened the coffin together and found nothing but flower-patterned sandals. Huang Xin of Pengcheng was a profound devotee of the Buddha-dharma; upon seeing Beidu, he prostrated himself and invited him to his home.
His family was extremely poor and could offer nothing but wheat porridge, yet Beidu partook of it with silent satisfaction. He remained there for only half a day.
Fadu suddenly said to Huixin, "You may seek thirty-six bundles of reeds. Huixin prepared them and arranged them in the courtyard; Fadu sealed them tightly.
He then told Huixin to open them, and they were found to be filled with coins and silk. Huixin accepted them and dedicated them all toward meritorious deeds.
After one year, Fadu took his leave to travel east to Wu. Seeing a fisherman, he begged him for some fish; when the man would not give any, Fadu threw two small stones into the water.

While he was in the midst of this, two oxen suddenly began to fight, and their nets were torn apart; the oxen then vanished. [The Master] manifested his body in various forms to provide for the offerings of the faithful, wandering and dwelling without a fixed location.
Zhu Lingshi of Wu Commandery was sent as an envoy to Liaodong. Having lost his way, he drifted at sea for over a month until he reached an island where both provisions and water were exhausted.
Entering the island to seek a spring, he beheld a temple with majestic and beautiful halls and buildings. A monk asked him where he had come from.

[The monk] followed him and related the details of his journey in full. He provided food and water and asked whether he would stay or depart. Sengshi said, "This is a dwelling for sages; it is not a place where an ordinary person may reside.
The monk said, "I wish to go wherever my heart desires. Sengshi took his leave. The monk said, "My home is more than two hundred thousand li away."
Shi was startled and asked, "By what means can I reach him? The monk said, "I shall send him; do not worry. Shi asked again, "Do you know the recluse Beidu? The monk replied, "I know him.
He then pointed to a bowl-bag on the wall and said, "This is his property. He has committed a slight transgression and must undergo punishment among men.
He took the bowl-bag and gave it to Shi, along with a letter written on it in characters that could not be recognized. [He said,] "You may take this letter."
He gave him his alms bowl and instructed the śrāmaṇera to carry the rock, not by the usual path, but directly to the place where the boat was moored.

The śrāmaṇera placed a bamboo branch at the prow of the boat and said, "Just close your eyes. The rock did as he was told; hearing only the sound of the wind, in the space of a few breaths, they arrived.
When Da Yangdu reached the great bridge, he happened upon Beidu riding across the bridge railing, shouting, "Horse! Horse! A stone arrived; the letter flew up of its own accord into Beidu’s hand.
Startled, Beidu asked, "How did you obtain this letter from the Immortal of Penglai? Is he calling me to return?
Beidu related the circumstances in detail and gave him his bowl, saying, "I have not seen this for over forty years. He tossed it upward, and it entered the clouds, descending [from there].
He returned and received him. At that time, Chen Shi of the Southern Region had served Sengdu with the utmost devotion; on this day, he did not return until late in the evening.
Sengdu had propagated his teachings for over forty years, yet later there were several instances where people saw him as before (in one version: *Lingqi Gantong Lu*).

Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu established a religious society (*shè*). The two men Tao Yuanming and Xie Lingyun did not join the society; Tao was fond of wine, while Xie’s mind was distracted by worldly concerns.

Tao Yuanming died at the age of sixty-three in the *dingmao* year of the Song dynasty. He composed the *Soushen lu* (Records of Searching for the Divine), which contains many accounts of the miraculous efficacy of the Buddha.
There was a man named Meng Yi who served the Buddha with diligent devotion, yet he was constantly held in low esteem by Xie, who said to Yi:

He said, "To be born in heaven must be before Lingyun; to achieve Buddhahood must be after Lingyun. Zhiyi took these words to heart. Later, he declined his appointment as Interior Minister of Linchuan.
He passed away while traveling from Guangzhou at the age of forty-nine, in the year *guimao*, the tenth year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty.
At the time of his death, he composed a poem which says: "Solitary are the cypresses after the frost, Fragrant are the mushrooms embracing the wind. Meeting by chance, in the end..."
The time having arrived, Xiuju did not feel resentment; rather, he lamented that his noble lord’s aspirations could not be extinguished upon the mountain crags.
Sending his mind before the Perfectly Awakened One, he has long since endured this pain (from the *Hongming ji*).
Yihai (the 12th day of the 10th month). In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen, Xiao Mo, the Governor of Danyang, submitted a memorial stating:

"The Buddha-dharma has been spread throughout the Middle Kingdom for many generations. Statues, stupas, and monasteries exist in thousands at various locations. Lately, however, people's devotion has become superficial;
they do not regard sincere piety as the ultimate goal, but instead prize ostentatious competition. [They expend] timber, bamboo, and copper..."

The expenditure of colored silks and other materials is boundless; it does not concern the spirits or deities, yet it burdens human affairs. Since no prevention has been established, this practice continues unabated.
From now on, those who wish to cast bronze statues or construct stupas and temples must submit a formal petition for reporting;
only then may they proceed. [Otherwise, it shall not be permitted. The Emperor asked the Palace Attendant He Shangzhi and the Minister of Personnel Yang Yuanbao: "I have..."
In my leisure time, I have been reading the scriptures; yet, regarding the matters of cause and effect, I remain obscure and have not yet fully investigated them.

Since you gentlemen are all eminent scholars who are generally faithful and respectful, and since Fan Tai and Xie Lingyun both stated that the regulations of the Six Classics are fundamentally intended to save the world, and that if one seeks the wondrous Way, one must take the Buddha as one's guide—I have recently seen Yan Yanzhi’s *Analysis of the Discourse on Nature* and Zong Bing’s *Refutation of the Black-and-White Discourse*.

This teaching brilliantly elucidates the principles of human nature and destiny. If all the people throughout the realm were to be imbued with this transformation, then I would sit and achieve Great Peace.
Yesterday, when Xiao Mo requested the establishment of regulations, I immediately showed them to you and entrusted you with the task of revising them.

There must be a way to restrain and suppress frivolity and excess without harming the promotion of the grand [teachings]; this is precisely what should be recorded. Shangzhi replied: "The common folk..."
However, there have been those who lacked reverence and faith. As for myself, being of mediocre and humble capacity, I am indeed possessed of foolish diligence;

yet the eminent figures of former dynasties did not fail to respond to Your Majesty’s enlightened edict. Since the crossing of the Yangtze River, there have been Wang Dao, Zhou Yi, Yu Liang, Wang Meng, Xie An, and Xi Chao.

Wang Xi, Wang Gong, Xie Shang, Zhang Kui, Guo Wen, Sun Chuo, and others—some were the crowning ornaments of high ministers, some were the paragon models of human relations, some directed their sentiments toward the interface between heaven and humanity, and some left their traces among the clouds and mists—all of them took refuge [in the Buddha].

Huiyuan said: "The transformation wrought by Śākyamuni is such that there is nothing it cannot encompass; for attaining the Way, it is truly the source of the teaching, and for saving the world," [it is the means].
This is also a matter of vital importance. Contemplate these words closely; they accord with the ultimate truth. Why is this?

In a village of a hundred households, if ten people observe the five precepts, those ten will become pure and prudent. In a hamlet of a thousand houses, if a hundred people cultivate the ten wholesome deeds, those hundred will live in harmony.
If this moral influence is propagated throughout the world until there are billions of registered households, there will then be one million benevolent people. Indeed!
If one can practice a single good deed, then one evil is removed; if one evil is removed, then one form of punishment is stilled.

When one punishment is stilled within the family, ten thousand punishments are stilled throughout the state. This is precisely what the "Bright Edict" refers to when it speaks of "sitting and teaching Great Peace.

Thus, when Fotudeng arrived in Zhao, the two Shi rulers diminished their violence; when the spirit-tower emitted light, Fu Jian abandoned his pretensions. It is evident that the Way of the Spirits assists in transformation.

It is worthy of consideration. I do not say that Emperor Mu’s request to establish regulations is entirely wrong; however, it is regrettable that it harms both the clergy and the laity, as its primary aim lies in the unrestrained conduct of monks and nuns.
Yet, since it is difficult to distinguish between the sincere and the hypocritical, determining what to eliminate and what to retain is not easy.

As for the construction of temples and monuments, although they appear to be wasteful expenditures, they serve to cultivate merit and repay kindness, and thus cannot be abruptly discontinued. Having recently deliberated upon this matter, I have found no secure course for either advancement or retreat. This day...
I have received Your Majesty’s gracious edict in person and am truly filled with joy and gratitude. Yuanyou Bao said: "This discourse concerns the study of Heaven and Man;
it is not something that a humble and ignorant subject such as I should be permitted to hear.

I fear deeply that the discussions on the arts of strengthening the military by Qin and Chu, or the exhaustive strategies for annexation by Sun Wu and Wu Qi, would find no place for the Way of Yao and Shun—let alone the teachings of Buddhism. The Emperor was pleased and said to Shang...
The Emperor said, "That you, Huiqing, exist within the Buddhist school is like Qilu existing within the school of Confucius.

From that time on, the Emperor’s esteem for profound transformation increased, and Xiao Mo’s proposal was consequently shelved. When Yan Yanzhi composed the *Lishi lun* (Treatise on the Separation of Consciousness), he commanded Huaiyan to debate it;
the Emperor often remarked, "You gentlemen do not fall short of Zhi Dun and Xu Xun."
In the thirteenth year of the Yuanjia era, on the day of Shangsi, the Emperor went to Qu-shui. The high officials and ministers all assembled; the Emperor commanded them to compose poems.
The śramaṇa Huiguan completed his composition first and presented it. The Emperor was greatly pleased and showed it to the hundred officials, all of whom were impressed by his talent.

Previously, Huiguan, together with Huiyan, Xie Lingyun, and others, had carefully edited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, making considerable additions and deletions to its wording. [He then] dreamed of a divine being...

He rebuked him, saying, "How dare you, with your ordinary sentiments, recklessly defile the sacred scriptures? Guān was terrified and desisted. The Emperor once asked Huìguān, "Which of the teachings on sudden enlightenment is most refined?
Guān replied that it was Dàoyóu, a disciple of Master Shēng. An imperial decree was issued to summon him into the palace, where eminent scholars were assembled in great numbers.
Dàoyóu expounded the teachings in a systematic and orderly manner; his exposition of the Dharma and its principles was brilliant and radiant, and those who heard him were enlightened.
Whenever there were those who raised challenges or objections, Sengyou would invariably refute them and resolve the matter. The Emperor praised his excellence (according to the *Monastic History*).
In the fourteenth year, the monk Sengliao wished to cast a sixteen-foot golden image.

Hearing that the temple of Wu Zixu in Xiangzhou possessed many copper vessels, Sengliao informed the Regional Inspector Zhang Shao, requesting one hundred strong men and ten large ships. Zhang Shao said:
The temple was already renowned for its spiritual efficacy; those who violated its sanctity were certain to die, and moreover, it was guarded by barbarians—how could [the boat] possibly reach it?

Liang said, "If there is indeed merit, then let it be shared with you, my patron. If there is any transgression, I shall bear the consequences myself. Shao immediately provided men and a boat. After three days, they arrived at the temple.
Before the temple stood two cauldrons, each with a capacity of over a hundred hu, within which dwelt a giant serpent several... [chi] long.
It was over ten *zhang* long and blocked the path. Huilang then took up his *xi* staff and recited mantras over it; the snake immediately vanished.

A moment later, a man appeared holding a ceremonial tablet (*hu*) and said, "I have heard that the Master’s spiritual practice is extraordinary and that your undertaking for the accumulation of merit is significant. I shall now accompany you with joy.
Thereupon, he had people transport the temple's bronze, taking one-tenth of it until the boat was full. The return voyage was exceptionally swift. The various tribes...
[He] replied, "It is too late; [the monk] has already passed away. When the statue was completed upon his return to the capital, only the flaming halo (jvālā-prabhā) was not yet complete.
Emperor Wen had a circular halo made of gold leaf for it and enshrined it at Pengcheng Temple. During the Dashi era, Emperor Ming moved the statue to Xianggong Temple (according to the *Sengzhuan*).

Shi Lingche initially studied under Dharma Master Huiyuan. He was well-versed in the sutras and śāstras, and his poetry and prose were renowned. He asked Master Huiyuan, "The monastic discipline prohibits pipes and strings;

the precepts forbid song and dance. Is it permissible to compose poems and verses? Huiyuan replied, "When one encounters objects and gives rise to thoughts, they disturb the emotions and obstruct the Way;
such things are not worth pursuing. Thereupon, Lingche abandoned his brush and inkstone and devoted himself to expounding the Great Dharma (according to the *Monastic Biographies*).
Gengchen: The first year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of the Wei dynasty; the seventeenth year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty (19 years after its commencement).
The Western Regions presented a fire-washing robe (*huoban bu jiashā*). Emperor Wen personally wore it at that time.
Jia-shen (548): The twenty-first year of the Song; the fifth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of Emperor Wu of Wei.

The third sovereign, Emperor Shizu Wudi Tao, was the eldest son of Emperor Yuan. He was the foremost martial ruler in the history of the suppression and abolition of the monastic order and its teachings.

The Wei Emperor issued an edict: "From the princes and dukes down to the common people, anyone who privately maintains śramaṇas or shamans and diviners within their households shall be ordered to send them away."
They went to the government offices. When they did not emerge by the fifteenth day of the second month, the śramaṇas, wu, and xi (the latter being the female counterpart to the male *wu*;
pronounced *hu* in the rhyme) were executed, and the master of the house was punished with the death penalty at his gate.
In the seventh year of the Zhenjun era, Emperor Taizu of Wei and Cui Hao both placed great trust in and revered Kou Qianzhi, receiving his teachings.
Hao had long been disinclined toward the Buddha-dharma and also addressed the Emperor, saying: "The Buddha-dharma is empty and extravagant; it is a source of waste and harm to the world.
It should be prohibited and eliminated. When the Emperor went to Chang'an to suppress Gaowu, he entered a Buddhist monastery, where the śramaṇas were drinking...
The officials entered his room and found a great quantity of weapons. They reported this to the Emperor, who said in anger, "These are not things used by śramaṇas;
he must have been in league with Gai Wu to plot a rebellion. He ordered the authorities to arrest and execute all the śramaṇas in the monastery and to inventory their property.
Among it was found a large amount of brewing equipment, as well as goods deposited there by provincial governors, commandants, and wealthy men.

The number reached ten thousand. He further constructed subterranean chambers to hide his women. Fu Hao said, "I order the execution of all śramaṇas throughout the empire and the destruction of all scriptures and images.
The Emperor followed his advice. Kou Qianzhi and Fu Hao argued strenuously against this, but Fu Hao would not listen.

First, he executed all the śramaṇas in Chang’an and burned their scriptures and images; he then issued an edict to the Retained Court (Liutai) to decree that the laws of Chang’an be applied uniformly throughout the four quarters.
The Imperial Edict states: "The decadent rulers of the Later Han dynasty believed in and were moved by heterodox and false doctrines, thereby subverting the eternal laws of Heaven.

From antiquity until now, within the Nine Provinces, there has never been such boastful and grandiose talk that disregards human nature. In these degenerate ages, there are none who are not dazzled by it."
Consequently, the King’s teachings were not implemented, and rites and righteousness fell into utter ruin. Within the nine provinces, all was reduced to desolate ruins.

I, the Emperor, succeeding to the heavenly mandate, desire to eliminate the false and establish the true, restoring the governance of Fuxi and Nongci. All else shall be swept away and its traces obliterated.
From this day forward, whoever dares to serve the spirits of the Hu barbarians, or to fashion images of clay or bronze— [They shall be punished.]
[The palace] gates were executed. Only with a man of extraordinary character can one perform extraordinary deeds;
who other than I could abolish these deceptive artifacts of successive dynasties? The authorities are hereby commanded to proclaim to all military governors, regional inspectors, and commandants:
"All Buddhist statues and foreign scriptures shall be smashed and burned. Monks, regardless of age, shall all be buried alive in mass graves. The Crown Prince—

Huang Su was fond of Buddhism; although he repeatedly remonstrated [against the persecution], his advice was not followed. He therefore delayed the proclamation of the imperial edict so that those far and near might hear of it and each could devise a plan.
Many śramaṇas fled into hiding and thus escaped, while they collected and preserved the scriptures and images. This applied even to those stūpas and temples located within the borders of Wei.
Not a single person remained. Among the ruined clay images of the Buddha, two jade seals were found (according to the *Wei Shu* and the *Tongjian*).
At the beginning of the suppression of the Dharma by the Wei, Kou Qianzhi contended with [Deng] Hao, but Hao would not comply. Kou said, "Your life span shall now be shortened."
Their family line was extinguished. In the eleventh year, Hao carved the national history he had compiled at the suburban altar; it recorded the affairs of the Wei dynasty’s predecessors in detail.
The court and the commonalty then reported this to the Emperor, claiming that it publicly exposed the state's evils.

The Emperor grew enraged and issued an edict to execute the five clans of Cui Hao, along with one hundred and thirty-eight of his subordinates, clerks, and scribes. Hao was confined within a cage and sent to the city.
He was executed south of the city. Several dozen guardsmen were ordered to urinate on Hao’s mouth; passersby likewise urinated upon his corpse.
Initially, when scriptures and images were discarded on the road, Hao would invariably urinate upon them. How swift was the retribution! (Tongjian)
The śramaṇa Tanshi was originally a disciple of Kumārajīva. Toward the end of the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin, many people in the Three Commanderies followed him as their teacher.
When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty destroyed the Qin, he left his son Yizhen to garrison Chang’an. Later, He Lianchui Gou of the Xia state pursued and defeated him;
both monastics and laypeople were slaughtered in the pits, yet Tanshi was unhurt when facing the blades. He Lianchui Gou was greatly incensed and summoned Tanshi before him, taking [the sword]...
He drew his sword and struck him himself, yet still could not harm him. Frightened, he apologized for his offense, and Baishou was finally spared from that cruel torment;

this was due to Baishi’s power. In the fourth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, when Emperor Taizu of Wei subdued Helian Chang, Baishi retired to the mountains to practice dhyāna for over fifty years, never once lying down to sleep.
This continued until the first year of the Zhengping era of the Wei, the *xinmao* year.
Thus it was known that the Great Dharma was about to flourish. Coinciding with the New Year’s assembly of the Wei court, he struck his mendicant’s staff and arrived at the palace gate.

An official informed Emperor Taizu of Northern Wei, who said, "Execute him immediately! When the blade fell, he was not wounded. The official reported this again as [the monk] approached the palace steps.

Enraged, the Emperor drew his girdle-sword and struck him himself, yet he could not wound him; the sword left only a slight mark like a thread. At that time, tigers were being kept in cages in the northern garden.
Emperor Wu ordered Dao-shi to feed them first; the tigers all crouched in fear, not daring to blink. His attendants requested that he be tested by a Daoist priest;

the tigers immediately roared fiercely, and Emperor Wu was greatly alarmed. He invited Dao-shi up to the palace hall, where he prostrated twice, repenting and apologizing, and granted him permission to resume his instruction.
His feet became as white as his face, and he was thus known at the time as the "White-footed Śramaṇa" (as recorded in the *Beishan lu* and noted in the commentaries to Su Shi’s poetry).
Renchen (592): Following the destruction of Buddhism by Emperor Wu of Wei, from the beginning of the Zhengping era, the Emperor suffered from a severe illness for two years;

sores broke out over his entire body, with pus and blood flowing together. Consequently, the prohibitions against Buddhism gradually relaxed, and there were those among the common people who privately venerated the Buddha.
In this year, he was assassinated by Zong Ai, the Palace Attendant.

Emperor Wencheng Di (r. 452–465) of the Wei dynasty was named Shun; he was the son of the Crown Prince Huang. On the *renchen* day of the tenth month, he ascended the throne and changed the reign title to Xing’an.

When the various ministers requested the restoration of Buddhist teachings, he issued an edict stating: "Now, those who act as sovereigns must reverently serve the enlightened spirits and manifest the Way of Benevolence.
As for those whose kindness is manifest among the people and who provide benefit to all classes of beings, even though they belong to the past..."

In antiquity, their heroic deeds were still recorded in historical accounts; thus, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* praised the rites of clarifying the divine, and the ritual canons preserved the lineages of those who bestowed merit.

How much more so for Śākyamuni Tathāgata, whose merit rescued the great trichiliocosm and whose grace flowed through all realms of dust. Those who investigate the cycle of birth and death sigh in admiration of his profound insight;
those who examine the meanings of the scriptures value his wondrous gateway. He assisted the prohibitions and laws of royal governance and augmented benevolence and wisdom.

This is the nature of goodness. It repels all heterodoxies and expounds the Right Enlightenment; therefore, from previous dynasties down to the present, there has been none who has not held it in high esteem.
It is likewise that which our national house has always venerated.

Since Emperor Taizu Wudi opened up the remote frontiers and his virtuous bounty spread afar, śramaṇas and daoshi of pure sincerity and virtuous conduct—such as those like Tan-shi—have reached every distant place. Its influence...

Meanings resonate with one another, often occurring as frequently as a forest. Now, within the depths of mountains and seas, strange creatures abound; likewise, among those of wicked and licentious character, there are opportunities for feigned pretenses.
Within lecture halls and monasteries, there are even found gangs of the violent. For this reason, the previous dynasties, taking advantage of these flaws and blemishes, [took action].

Those who committed crimes were executed, and the officials failed to grasp the essential intent, resulting in the total prohibition [of Buddhist practice]. Emperor Jingmu also felt profound regret for this;

however, as the military and state affairs were many and pressing, he had no leisure to restore it. I, your servant, having inherited the great legacy and presiding over the myriad states, reflect upon the will of my predecessors and desire to promote this Way.
I now decree that in all prefectures and counties, at every place where people dwell together, one Buddhist temple (buddhastūpa) shall be permitted to be established.

In these districts, if there are those who delight in the Dharma and wish to become śramaṇas, whose character and conduct are naturally sincere and whom their fellow villagers recognize as exemplary, they are permitted to leave the household life.
This is sufficient to transform the wicked into the good and to propagate the holy teachings. Thereupon, [he went] toward the aforementioned Buddhist monastery.
The world followed this wind, and all generally undertook the restoration [of monasteries] (as recorded in the Wei History and the Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government).
Shi Suxian was of royal lineage from Jibin; encountering the cessation of the teaching, he temporarily relied on medical arts to maintain the Way.

The Wei ruler personally shaved the heads of Suxian and four others, and decreed that Suxian be appointed as the Sanghasthavira. He further commanded the relevant authorities to [establish him] at the Five-Story [Pagoda].
At the Great Monastery, for the five emperors beginning with the Founder (Taizu), five statues of Śākyamuni were cast, each sixteen feet in height,
using two hundred and fifty thousand *jin* of gold (*Wei shi Tongjian*).
Guṇabhadra was invited by Prince Yixuan of Qiao to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As he had not yet mastered the Chinese language, he prayed to Avalokiteśvara;

in a dream, a deity changed his head for him, whereupon he suddenly became proficient and could expound the fundamental tenets of the Mahāyāna. Before this, Prince Yixuan had secretly plotted treason, but Guṇabhadra remonstrated with him, which he refused to follow.
When the army was defeated at Liangshan, Emperor Xiaowu issued an order to the troops that anyone who captured Guṇabhadra should be sent back by express courier.

Soon he found him. He was sent to Jinling for an audience with the Emperor, who questioned him in detail. By imperial decree, he was to reside in the rear hall, where he was provided with clothing and offerings.
One day the Emperor asked, "Do you still think of Prince Qiao? He replied, "The ancients did not forget a single meal.
Your Majesty fed me for ten years; how could I dare forget it so soon? I intend to ask Your Majesty to perform rites for his posthumous merit on his behalf. The Emperor—

He was moved to grief and changed his expression. When Zhongxing Temple was completed, an imperial decree ordered him to serve as its abbot. During an imperial banquet at the Eastern Palace where high officials were all assembled, the Emperor summoned Guṇabhadra;
his responses were prompt and his eloquence was sharp, leaving the Emperor greatly delighted (as recorded in the *Benzhuan*).
Shi Baoliang was twelve years old when he paid his respects to Dao Ming of Qingzhou to become his teacher.

Later, while traveling to the capital, Yuan Can of the Zhongshu Secretariat beheld him and marveled at his extraordinary nature. He sent a letter to Baoliang’s teacher, stating in brief: "Recently I have seen Master Liang; he is no ordinary man."

Every day I hear what I have never heard before, and I am unaware that the year is drawing to a close. Yet, when pearls are produced in Hepu, the people of Wei take them to illuminate their carriages;
when jade is found in Handan, the Lord of Qin requests it to adorn his state. The treasures of the world cannot be monopolized by oneself alone.
One should share in this with him. From this point on, Hui-liang’s reputation grew even more prominent (as recorded in his biography).

In the year Dingyou, Emperor Xiaowu changed the reign title to Daming. In the following year, he issued an edict for the Dharma Master Tanzong to perform a rite of repentance. The Emperor then remarked:
"What crime have I committed that you should trouble yourself to perform this repentance for me? Zong replied, "Shun said, 'It is my fault; you are my counselor.
Yu said, 'If the myriad regions have sin, it lies with me alone. Your Majesty treads the Way with humble reflection; how could you alone be an exception? The Emperor was greatly pleased (*Tongji*).

Shi Sengdao. When Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty campaigned westward against Chang’an, he had long been aware of Sengdao’s reputation and sought an audience with him, saying, "I have looked toward you for a long time;
why have you remained so long among these alien customs? Sengdao replied, "Your Excellency has swept clean the nine realms and brought forth your imperial carriage to the Yellow and Luo Rivers."

"Would it not be well for us to meet at this time? When Emperor Wu of Song was returning eastward, he left his son, the Duke of Guiyang, Yizhen, to govern Guanzhong, saying, "I hope you, Master, will look upon him with care from time to time.
Later, when the Duke was pursued by the northern barbarians, Sengdao said, "Lord Liu has entrusted his son to me;
I, a poor monk, shall die escorting him. The barbarian leader was struck with awe by his spiritual bearing and consequently withdrew. Emperor Gaozu was deeply moved by this and, because of it—

He caused his sons and nephews to serve him as their teachers. When Emperor Xiaowu ascended the throne, he dispatched an envoy to welcome and escort him; Sengdao responded to the imperial decree with alacrity and took up residence at Zhongxing Temple.
The Emperor went in person to receive him, and moved by the circumstances and reminiscing of the past, he was overcome with grief.

The Emperor also choked with emotion for a long while. He then issued an edict for Sengdao to open a lecture series at Waguan Temple, where the Emperor and the high officials all assembled. Sengdao said to the Emperor: "Hufa..."

In propagating the Dharma, none precedes the sovereign. If Your Majesty could exercise the four immeasurable minds, commiserating with those in peril and exhorting them toward goodness, then even sand, soil, tiles, and rubble would become the celestial palaces of the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Ren-yin (the year of the Ren-yin cycle): The sixth year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty. In the ninth month, the Right Counselor submitted a memorial, stating:
"The branches of Confucianism and Legalism diverge, and the schools of Name and Mo are divided; yet when it comes to honoring one's kin and respecting one's superiors, their principles do not differ.

Only the teaching of the Buddha, originating from afar at the Dragon Mound [India], has inverted the classics and distorted the transmissions, clinging to literal texts while obscuring the Way. As this has spread extensively in recent times, Your Servant has heard that the Buddha..."
One should cultivate oneself through humility and take loyalty and obedience as one's path. One must not treat bhikṣus lightly, but must bow whenever encountering them.

The Great Being Maudgalyāyana would pay homage to anyone he met who was senior to him; how could he stoop his knee before the four classes of disciples yet omit the rites for his own parents, or prostrate his forehead before the elderly while maintaining an upright posture toward those of ten-thousand-chariots?
We, your ministers, have deliberated and concluded that when śramaṇas are received in audience, all should manifest the utmost reverence.

Regarding the deportment of ritual reverence, the court ceremonies were orderly. Although the Emperor believed in the Dharma, he was particularly prone to arrogance. When [the memorial] was submitted, the Emperor issued an edict granting his request.
○ The śramaṇa Yanzong said: "The *Biography of Emperor Xiaowu* states that during the second or third year after his accession to the throne, the Emperor finally gave rein to his desires.
His refusal of remonstrance was sufficient to ruin his virtue and leave the world in disappointment, despite possessing extraordinary talent."

He was intelligent and disciplined himself with a degree of ritual propriety. Had he reflected upon the frugality of Emperor Wu or the magnanimity of Emperor Taizu, even the Han emperors Jing and Wen would be insufficient to mention by comparison.
From the sixth year of the Daming era to the first year of the Jinghe era, a total of four years passed;
though he was commanded to prostrate before the sovereign, the monk ultimately did not do so. Was this not a violation of the natural order that compelled the imperial decree?
[The *Monk Biographies*] says this was merely a hollow fabrication.
The year *Guimao*, the seventh year [of the reign], there was a great drought throughout the realm. The Emperor requested Guṇabhadra to pray for rain. Guṇabhadra burned incense and offered prayers;
he ceased eating and drinking, silently reciting mantras. At the hour of *bù* (the fifth watch) the following day, the wind shook and the clouds gathered, continuing—
It rained daily. An imperial edict was issued to grant him audience and offer consolation, and the bestowal of robes and offerings continued without end, beyond all reckoning.

In the following year, an edict restored the status of śramaṇas to their former position and exempted them from the requirement to pay homage to the sovereign (according to his biography and the *Tongjian*).
Originally, thirty *li* northwest of Heng’an, on the northern face of Mount Wuzhou, Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty carved into a stone cliff to establish Lingyan Monastery.
The larger niches were over twenty *zhang* high and could accommodate three thousand people; these, along with those for various holy monks, extended for thirty *li*.

At the eastern end of the monastic complex, there was a temple that regularly provided sustenance for one thousand people. Although Emperor Taiwu destroyed [the Buddhist establishments], these niches remained.
[He] did not dare to damage [the statue] (Weishu).

Anamoditi (whose name means "Precious Intention") from India arrived at the capital. He could constantly turn over several hundred small statues and immediately know whether they portended good or bad fortune.
He was skilled in divine incantations; by applying incense to his palms, he could see the past deeds of people. Emperor Shizu bestowed upon him a bronze spittoon.
Suddenly, someone discarded it. [Hui]di took a single mat, rolled it up empty, and recited the incantation over it several times. After a night had passed, the jar was found inside the mat;
both monastics and laypeople were struck with wonder (from his *Benzhuan*).
Shi Hui-liang was renowned for his eloquence at the lecture hall. Yan Yanzhi sighed in admiration, saying: "Hui'an and Sengtai have spat forth pearls and jade before us;

Sengbin and Hui-liang now vibrate with golden tones behind them. These pure discourses and subtle threads, which were nearly extinguished, are now flourishing once more. Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued appointing Liang and Bin [to official positions].
Successively serving as Dharma Kings (according to the *Monastic History*):
In the third year of the Dashi era, the year Dingwei, the monk Zhilin was commanded by Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty to lecture at the monasteries in the capital.

He elucidated the meaning of the Two Truths, identifying three different schools of thought. At that time, Zhou Yong also composed the *Treatise on the Three Schools*, which accorded with Zhilin’s views.
Fu Lin then sent a letter to Zhou Yong, stating that no one else was capable of grasping this doctrine;

he expressed his hope that Yong would clarify and widely propagate this meaning so that the principles of the Three Schools might be transmitted to the present day. Zhou Yong, styled Bo Lun, was successively promoted to the rank of Zhishizhong (Attendant of the Palace).
When Emperor Ming was cruel and tyrannical, Yong did not dare to offer open remonstrance; instead, he would recite from the sutras on the causes and conditions of sin and merit.

This matter somewhat discouraged the Emperor, who established a separate vihāra on the western side of Mount Zhong. There, he would retire during his days off from official duties; for the rest of the year, he maintained a vegetarian diet.
Although he had a wife and children, they lived far away in mountain lodgings. When the Chancellor Wang Jian asked him, "What do you eat in the mountains?
he replied, "Red rice and white mustard greens; green chives and purple dock. Xiao Zixian jokingly asked, "Regarding your vegetable diet, what..."

The flavors are most excellent: namely, the early leeks of early spring and the late cabbages of late autumn. Such is their character. During their peak season, one might hang up one’s official cap and dwell in the mountains. Alas!

Those who occupy their positions in the imperial gardens as mere figureheads, seeking only light food and fine clothing for their mouths and bodies, racing about in the field of fetters and reins—how do they compare to this?
(From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
The Great Being Baozhi came and went beneath the mountains and rivers of Mount Xuan. His hair hung down and he walked barefoot;
he wore a brocade robe and his face was square and as clear as a mirror. Both his hands and feet had bird-claws.

Formerly, when a daughter of the Zhu family from Dongyang in Jiankang was fetching water, she heard the sound of a child crying in an eagle’s nest in a tree. She took the child and raised him; at the age of seven, he followed Zhong.

The mountain monk Tanjian left the household life to devote himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna and contemplation. In the first year of the Taishi era (the Yi-si year), during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty, he entered the capital to manifest his spiritual traces.
Sometimes he would seek wine and food; at other times, he would go without food for several days without showing any sign of hunger.

Once, he encountered a fisherman seeking food and followed him to share some fish. Upon eating it, the fisherman immediately conceived a frivolous thought; Tanjian then spat it back into the water, whereupon it all turned into [gold].

Living fish. Today, there are "returning fish" (*huíyú*) in the Yangtze River; those who are ill may eat them without harm. He would sometimes compose lines of poetry that were initially unintelligible, yet later all came to be verified.
He constantly carried a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), upon which he hung scissors, a ruler, and a whisk.
Carrying these as he walked, he thereby provided a prophecy regarding the future emergence of the Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties.

The destiny of the Jin dynasty having come to an end, Emperor Wu ascended the throne during the rise of the Song. His profound anxieties gradually subsided, yet the course of state affairs remained obstructed.

For two years, his path was blocked; through four battles, he endured military toil. A hundred concerns were unfolded within his breast, and ten thousand matters of governance were consolidated within his bosom.

Yet he never grew weary of the practice of *dāna*, constantly maintaining a mind dedicated to protecting the Dharma. With his own hand he transcribed the precept scriptures, and with his mouth he recited the Sanskrit texts, making offerings to the Buddha.
He summoned the worthy; moved by the spirit of Mount Song, it presented him with jade discs. The Great Illumination was humbled and submitted.

Although Emperor Xiaowu was deluded by treacherous ministers and the mists and clouds briefly darkened the sky, how could this harm the sun and moon? Thus, the work of translation and exposition flourished here.
Song: Wumwu (the third year of Shengming), the fourth month; Emperor Shun abdicated the throne to the Prince of Qi, Xiao Daocheng.
Northern and Southern Dynasties: Qi. Surname Xiao, name Daocheng. Capital: Jiankang. From Jiwu to Xinwei.
[End. Seven rulers for twenty-four years. He abdicated the throne to the Liang dynasty.
○ In the third year of Chengming of Emperor Xiaowen of the Wei, the year Jiwu (459), the Taizu Gaodi received the abdication from Emperor Shun of the Song in the fourth month and ascended the throne.
He changed the reign title to Jianyuan (Six Posters).
At Songwang Temple in Pengcheng, there was a gilded image eighteen feet tall. Whenever military conflict arose within the surrounding borders, the image would invariably perspire.

In that year, the image suddenly broke into a sweat. During winter, the Wei invaders raided the Huai region; at that time, the officials of Runzhou were forcibly compelling the śramaṇas to assist in their battles and defenses.

The Wei army falsely accused them of aiding the rebellion and ordered their execution. Just as the sentence of death was about to be carried out, the image sweated profusely until it flowed upon the ground. [The Wei] Governor of Xuzhou, Liang...
The King honored the Dharma and sent several attendants to wipe [the image] with silk. As they wiped it, [the moisture] would not cease to emerge.

The attendants then prostrated themselves and said, "We monks vow to protect ourselves; you must certainly not inflict punishment upon us. If our sincere devotion moves [the divine power], the moisture shall stop as soon as we wipe it. Having finished speaking, they wiped it themselves, and it became dry at their touch.
Furthermore, they prepared a memorial to inform Empress Dowager Feng, but she issued a decree that it was not permitted. A subsequent imperial edict was issued, and all were seen [to comply].
Pardon (from the *Tongjian* and *Gantong lu*).
On the *Renxu* day, in the first month of the fourth year, Emperor Gao visited Zhuangyan Temple to listen to Dharma Master Xingyuan lecture on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.

The high officials and ministers were all assembled; however, as the Emperor’s seat was somewhat distant, he could not hear the sound of the Dharma. Zhang Xu of the Secretariat urged Xingyuan [to speak more loudly].
He moved his seat closer to the Emperor, but the Emperor would not allow it from afar; after a short while, the Emperor himself moved his seat to draw near him.
The Emperor founded the Zhuhu and Zhenguan monasteries, cast golden images, transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra*, and constantly recited the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he universally sent offerings of *bowl-and-palanquin* (alms-bowls) to all the monasteries. He said every time: "If I were to rule the world for ten years, I would cause gold and..."
The price of the soil was the same. It is a pity that his life was not long; he occupied the throne for four years and reached the age of fifty-six.
He passed away in the third month of this year (according to the local gazetteer).

In the fourth month, on the fifteenth day, when Emperor Wudi, the World Ancestor, had ascended the throne, the Crown Prince assembled the Mahāyāna monks at Xuānpǔ for the ninety-day summer retreat (*an-jū*).
He lectured on the Dharma until the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the lectures concluded. Thereupon, he relinquished his person, including his carriage, crown, and ceremonial robes;

from his neck-tie down, there were ninety-nine items in total. By the power of this merit, he prayed that it might universally reach those in the realms of the unseen and the seen who are submerged in suffering.
As for Hai (Haiming), he attained realization of the principle as circumstances arose (*Nanshi*).

On the eighth day of the second month of the geng-wei year, when the reign title was changed to Yongming, Prince Jingling of the Qi dynasty established a lecture hall at Fayun Vihāra in the Upper Residence and extensively assembled the monastic community to expound the Dharma for six nights (*Hongming ji*). [Recorded under] Zhongxing Temple.
Sengzhong was well-versed in the Three Treatises and possessed great eloquence. When the Wei envoy Li Daogu came to court, Sengzhong was summoned to serve as his host and engage him in conversation.
It was past noon, yet Sengzhong had not eaten. Li asked, "Why do you not eat? He replied, "It is the bequeathed instruction of the Buddha:
one must not eat after midday. Li remarked, "Are you not then a śrāvaka? Sengzhong said, "If there are those who should be delivered by means of the śrāvaka vehicle, then [I appear as such]."
He manifested as a śrāvaka to preach the Dharma for them; this was during the reign of Emperor Ming (as recorded in his original biography).
The second year of the Jiǎzǐ cycle. Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince Wenxuan of Jingling, Ziliang, were both deeply versed in Buddhist principles.

You, however, serve as General of the Household Protectorate and concurrently as Minister of Education and Commander of the Garrison Troops. You have a profound devotion to the teachings of Śākyamuni;

you frequently invite renowned monks to lecture on and discuss the Buddha-dharma. The grandeur of both the monastic and lay assemblies has never been seen in the region south of the Yangtze River since the river was first crossed. At times, you personally distribute food and serve water for the multitude.
The world generally considered this a lapse. The Chancellor (Xiao Zixian) modeled himself after Fan Zhen and vigorously advocated that there were no Buddhas.

Xiao Ziliang said, "If you do not believe in cause and effect, how can there be the distinctions between the wealthy and noble versus the poor and lowly? Fan Zhen replied, "Human life is like the blossoms of a tree that open together and then scatter with the wind.
Some brush against the curtains and hangings, falling upon cushions and mats; others pass through fences and walls, landing in the midst of filth and latrines."
"One who falls from the mats and cushions is Your Highness; one who falls into the latrine is this humble official.

There is no difference between the noble and the lowly in their paths, yet where, ultimately, does cause and effect reside? Ziliang remained silent and did not answer (as recorded in the *Tongjian* and the *Nanshi*).
In this year, Zheng Mao of Jin’an’s mother fell ill. He invited monks to perform rites and used a bronze pitcher to hold water with which he offered lotus flowers before the Buddha.
His son, Mao, prostrated himself and recited a prayer, saying: "I pray that my mother’s illness may be pacified and overcome; I pray that all Buddhas shall cause these flowers not to wither.
After seven days, the flowers were even fresher than before; upon examining them, they were seen to have roots and filaments. (From the *Qi Shi*).

In the third year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, an imperial edict appointed the śramaṇas Faxian and Yuanchang as joint *saṃgha*-leaders (*saṃghanāyaka*), assigning them respectively to the northern and southern banks [of the Yangtze].
Subsequently, an edict was issued regarding the śramaṇas and śramaṇīs of the Three Wu regions: Faxian’s observance of the Vinaya was pure and refined, and his virtue served as a model for all beings;
Yuanchang maintained the purity of the monastic prohibitions and served as the Preceptor of Precepts (*śīlācārya*) to Crown Prince Wenhui (Sengshi).
The monk Zhong of Zhongxing Temple met the Emperor at the Qianhe Hall and addressed him as "poor man of the Way" (*pindao*). The Emperor then asked the Minister Wang Jian:
"When śramaṇas from the northern regions converse with the King, what title do they use? Do they take their seats in the formal hall? Jian replied:

"At the beginning of the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇas of various kingdoms all used the title 'poor man of the Way' and were permitted to sit in the assembly. During the middle period, Yu Bing and Huan Xuan wished to..."
The monastic community and the nuns paid their respects with full deference, while the court and the commonalty were in a state of confusion. Consequently, all such matters were suspended.

From the Song dynasty until the present, many have participated in these assemblies while addressing themselves as "this poor monk" (*pindao*). The Emperor said, "If even the two masters Xiàn and Chàng, whose spiritual accomplishments are such as these, still address themselves by name, how much more so for others?
To bow down in prostration would be excessive; to address oneself by name is without fault. From this time forth, monks addressed emperors by name. From...
Xianchang was the first [to witness this].
At the eastern city wall of Jingzhou, a Heavenly Bodhisattva appeared and produced brocade; men and women took it, and it was no different from the brocade of the human realm.
It ceased after a month (according to the *Sengshi*).
Dingmao (5th year), first month: Jiaozhou presented a pearl two cun high, within which was contained a Buddha image complete with pedestal and throne, its eyebrows and eyes all fully formed.
○ Sixth month: Dongyang presented a six-eyed tortoise (*Sanbao ji*).
In the seventh year, the Emperor, believing that the Great Being Master Bao was deluding the masses, had him arrested and imprisoned in Jiankang.

On that day, people saw the Great Being wandering through the market streets, yet upon inspection, he remained in the prison. That evening, he said to his guards, "Outside the gate there are two carriages of food."
"A golden bowl filled with rice—take it. Subsequently, Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince Jingling sent offerings to Jiankang and ordered Lü Wenxian to report the matter.
The Emperor expressed regret and apologized; he welcomed [the monk] into the inner palace. Shortly thereafter, the Emperor held a banquet for the ladies of the harem.
The Great Being (Mahāsattva) briefly went out, yet was later seen walking in the Xianyang Hall. The Emperor, startled, dispatched an official to inquire;

the official reported that Zhigong had been in the palace for a long time. The Emperor’s reverence for him increased further. Eleven years later, while Bao Gong was in the Hualin Garden, he suddenly put on three-layered cloth caps.
In the seventh month, the Emperor passed away, followed by Crown Prince Wenhui and the Prince of Yuzhang.

The kings passed away one after another; only then did it become known that this was the prophecy. When Wang Zhongxiong asked Master Bao where he would reach in his official career, the Master did not answer.

Instead, he untied the left cord from the end of his staff and gave it to him. Later, Zhongxiong indeed attained the rank of Left Vice-Minister of the Department of State Affairs (*Shangshu Zuocheng*).
When Xu Ling was a child, his father took him to visit the Master. The Master rubbed the boy’s head and said, "This is a stone qilin from the heavens. Later, he became prominent.
In this world, Xu Ling’s courtesy name was Xiaomu. His mother was Lady Zang; she dreamed that five-colored clouds transformed into a phoenix which alighted upon her left shoulder before he was born.
Prince Xiao Ziliang of Jingling established the *Jingzhu jingxing famen* (The Dharma-gate of Pure Abiding and Pure Conduct). As for "pure abiding," it refers to the *poṣadha*.

This translates the name [of the scripture]. It means to purify body, speech, and mind, and to abide according to the precepts. As for the "Dharma-gate of Purifying Conduct," because all karmas are purified, one transforms and acts within the world;
because one thoroughly understands all dharma-gates, there are distinctions among their characteristics and natures (the text consists of two fascicles).
Shi Tanchao resided at Lingyuan Mountain in Qiantang. After he had remained in meditative concentration for several days, a man suddenly appeared and paid his respects, saying:

"Your disciple lives seven *li* away. Because people from Fuyang have cleared the forested foothills and excavated the base of the mountain, they have encroached upon and destroyed the dragon’s abode.

The dragons were all enraged and swore that it would not rain for three hundred days. Now that one hundred days have already passed, the fields and ponds are parched and dry; we wish to entreat you to employ your virtue and wisdom."

He proceeded forward. He was certain to be able to bring moisture and prosperity to the common people, and his merit would have a rightful destination. Chao excused himself, and the spirit then departed.
Chao traveled south for five days until he reached Mount Chiting, where he offered prayers for the dragons. When night fell, the dragons manifested as human beings.
They came to pay their respects to Hui-chao. Chao preached the Dharma for them, whereupon they requested the Three Refuges and the Precepts. They declared themselves to be dragons.
Chao then requested that they send down rain, but they looked at one another and remained silent. That night, they appeared in a dream and said: "Originally, we made this vow out of anger;

since you, Master, have now guided us toward goodness, we dare not disobey your command. At the hour of *bū* (the late afternoon) tomorrow, it shall rain. When the appointed time arrived, the rain fell in abundance, and the harvest was gathered that year (from the *Benzhuan*).
Jiaxu: In the first month of Qi, Emperor Yulin was deposed; the era name was changed to Longchang. In the seventh month, he was assassinated.
Emperor Haoling Zhaowen ascended the throne; the era name was changed to Yanxing. In the tenth month, Gaozong Emperor Ming ascended the throne.
During the eighteenth year of Chengming of the Northern Wei, the capital was moved to Luoyang. In the twentieth year, the imperial clan name was changed to Yuan.
Emperor Ming ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jianwu. The Emperor applied his mind to the sacred scriptures, protected the Dharma, and propagated the teachings.

He observed the six fast days, cultivated the ten wholesome deeds, recited such sutras as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*, transcribed various sections of the canon, and fashioned a golden image worth a thousand pieces of gold.
It is a pity that his lifespan was not long; he reigned for five years and passed away in the seventh month of the year Wuyin (318 CE). (From the *Biàn zhèng*).
Dingchou: The Buddha of India first arrived at Heng’an in the Northern Terrace of Wei. Emperor Xiaowen provided him with special provisions and support.

Later, following the Emperor’s southward migration and the establishment of the capital at Yiluo, he again established a pure courtyard for him to reside in; however, his aspirations were set upon Mount Song.
By imperial decree, a monastery was established for him on Mount Shaoshi; this is the present-day Shaolin Monastery.

He ordained his disciples Huiguang and Sengchou, both of whom were deeply devoted to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). A benevolent deity constantly followed them like a shadow to protect them.
When Sengchou passed away, the deity painted its own image upon the wall (as recorded in his original biography).
Ji-mao: Emperor Gaozu Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty reigned for twenty-nine years. At Ye, he constructed An-yang Monastery;
his hands never left his books, and in his leisure time, he would lecture on them himself. The ladies of the six palaces all observed the six fasts (liu-zhai).

Those among them who were diligent in their recitation of the scriptures were permitted to leave the household life. His offerings and support to the various monks were always exceptionally generous. [The year] Chengming 23.
In the fourth month of this year, [Emperor] Bianzheng passed away. In the fourth month of this same year, Sejong (Xuanwu Di) Ke ascended the throne.

He issued an edict stating: "Since the laity and the clergy differ, their laws and regulations also differ. Thus, while Buddhism is manifested through explicit prohibitions and admonitions, each has its own appropriate application.
As for monks who commit crimes such as homicide and above, they shall be judged according to secular law codes. All other offenses shall be entirely entrusted to the [Buddhist] authorities."
Xuán judged this according to the internal monastic regulations (as recorded in the *Weishu*).
In the seventh month of the year Jǐmǎo, Emperor Wěngyuán of the Qi dynasty ascended the throne and changed the era name to Yongyuán.
