In the following year, at Waguan Monastery, he dismantled a jade statue and used the resulting fragments to fashion hairpins and bracelets for his favorites, providing them with magnificent ornaments. This was the manner in which Wěngyuán destroyed the jade statue.
Thus it was. Initially, his two arms were severed. When he died, the sword-bearer Huang Taiping injured his knee with the blade;
he fell to the ground and was killed. How swift was the retribution! (From the *History of Qi*).
In the second year of the Yongyuan era, Emperor Donghun summoned the various princes to the palace; each harbored feelings of unease.
Prince Baling issued an edict to Xiao Zhou, instructing him and his younger brother, the Marquis of Yongxin, Zhao Ying, to both become śramaṇas and flee to the west of the Yangtze River.

Prince Liang, Xiao Yan, held the imperial seal of authority and appointed Xiao Yingzhou as Commander-in-Chief, ordering them to each contribute their private money and grain, and to borrow from wealthy families to raise funds.
To assist with military expenses: A monk at Changsha Temple had long been wealthy; he had cast gold into the shape of dragons and buried several thousand *liang* of it in the ground.
Yingzhou took it to provide for the costs of the army (*Tongjian*).
Renwu, the third month of the second year of Zhongxing. Emperor He abdicated the throne to the Prince of Liang.
The Taizu of Qi received the abdication from Song and ascended the throne. Since his accession, he has revered the Triple Gem and extensively saved all living beings.

Opening his heart with benevolence and bestowing transformation through frugality, he has throughout successive reigns transcribed scriptures, fashioned images, practiced almsgiving, and observed the fasts, universally praying for the welfare of both the unseen and the visible worlds.
Attaining realization of the principle as it arises. Alas! Rare indeed in this world (from the *Lidai Fabao Ji*).
Volume Three of the *Lidai Shishi Zajian*.
Volume Four of the *Lidai Shishi Zajian*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xīzhòng of Yǐfēng, Fúmián.
The Liáng dynasty of the Southern and Northern Dynasties. Surname Xiāo, name Yǎn. Capital: Jiànkāng. From the year Rénwǔ to Dīngchōu. Four sovereigns. Fifty-six years.

In the year [of the reign], he abdicated the throne to the Eastern Wei. From the Yuan clan down to Emperor Xiaowu, they were divided into eastern and western courts (as recorded in the third year of the Jingming era).
On the *renwu* day of the fourth month, Emperor Wu ascended the throne by receiving the abdication; at that time he was thirty-seven years old, and he changed the era name to Tianjian.
Once the Emperor had ascended the throne, he resolved to share with all living beings the realization of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and together attain Omniscience (*sarvajñā*).

Wearing his robes as he presided over the court, he extensively propagated the scriptural teachings, widely inviting those learned in antiquity, and searching far and wide for lost texts. He fanned the pure winds of virtue, benefiting both the Dharma and the secular world.
When the kingdom of India heard that the Emperor was propagating the Dharma, they presented a coral Buddha image to express their profound reverence (from the *Tongji*).
The Emperor issued an edict appointing Shi Huichao as the Great Sangzheng (Chief Administrator of the Monks). Huichao was over eight chi tall, with a waist girth of ten spans.

He cultivated the virtue of the precepts within and maintained pure deportment without; all his fellow monastics followed his established instructions. An imperial carriage drawn by sheep was provided for his transmissions of edicts, as he possessed feet sturdy enough for swift travel.
Regarding his clothing and other provisions, from the time the teachings first reached this land, the regulations of the five schools have all taken him as their model. Once—
During an interval between lectures, a powerful benevolent deity suddenly spoke, saying, "You should assemble those with similar affinities and come together to partake of a meal.

On the day they arrived for the lecture, the seats were suddenly filled; their appearances were extraordinary and strange, such that no one could recognize them. It was only when the session concluded and the assembly dispersed that [the truth became clear].
The manifestations of his spiritual responses were extraordinary in this manner (as recorded in his biography).
The Emperor summoned the Great Being Baozhi to the palace and treated him with great honor and favor. Consequently, he issued an edict stating:

"Master Zhi’s physical traces are constrained by the mundane world, yet his spirit wanders in profound stillness. Fire and water cannot burn or submerge him; snakes and tigers cannot harm or intimidate him. As for his speech..."
Regarding Buddhist principles, they pertain to those above the level of the Śrāvakas; regarding the discourse on hidden realms, there are those such as the reclusive immortals who are most exalted.
How can one constrain them with the ordinary sentiments of worldly men? From this day forward, you may propagate the teachings as you please; do not impose further prohibitions.
Consequently, the Duke frequently entered and exited the inner palace.
Guiwei (the 10th day of the tenth month): An imperial decree was issued for the Dharma Master Yunguang of Fayun Temple to enter and exit the various halls to preach the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Heaven rained down flowers, and the Emperor paid him reverent homage, believing that he had attained sainthood.

One night at the Hanguang Hall, while burning his commentaries, he invited both Master Zhigong and Master Yunguang to attend a vegetarian feast on the day of practice; however, only Zhigong arrived, while Yunguang did not know of it. The Emperor held him in high esteem.
Recorded in the *Monastic History* (*Sengshi*).
One day, the Emperor summoned Master Zhi to the private audience hall. Suddenly, Zhi knit his brows, craned his neck, and sighed deeply. The Emperor questioned him in wonderment.
Zhi replied, "An enemy has been born. The Emperor could not fathom this; it was because that year Hou Jing was born among the Xianbei in Huai.
Shuo-zhen was the reincarnation of Emperor Donghun. At the beginning of the Southern Qi dynasty, Emperor Gao’s consort, Lady Xi, had three daughters.
When the Emperor served as the Governor of Yongzhou, the Consort passed away. She was by nature cruel and jealous;

having transformed into a giant serpent, she entered the inner palace and appeared in the Emperor's dreams, seeking merit and virtue to rescue her from suffering. The Emperor consulted the Tripitaka and composed the *Cibei* (Compassion) [Sutra].
Through the ritual of repentance (*chánfǎ*), he invited monks to prostrate before the Buddha and repent for his transgressions. He was immediately transformed into a celestial being (*deva*).

From mid-air, he thanked the Emperor for his merit, stating that he had already attained rebirth in heaven. Thereafter, the Emperor did not again consider appointing a consort for the remainder of his life (from the *Nanshi*).
Jia-shen (the third year), the eighth day of the fourth month. The Emperor led more than twenty thousand monastics and laypeople to ascend the Chongyun Hall.

He renounced the Way and took refuge in the Buddha, personally composing a prayer of aspiration which stated in brief: "I, the disciple Xiao Yan, Emperor of the Liang State, prostrate myself and pay homage to the Triple Gem of the Buddhas, Dharma, and Sangha of the ten directions.
I have humbly observed that the sutras state: 'One who gives rise to the bodhicitta is [equivalent to...']"
The Buddha-mind cannot be compared to any other mundane virtues; it is able to exit the gate of suffering within the triple world and enter the supreme path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Your disciple was formerly lost in ignorance and delusion, indulging in the practices of Laozi. For generations, our lineage has inherited this corrupt teaching.
Now, casting aside these old habits, I take refuge in the Perfect Enlightenment. I pray that in future lives, my children shall leave the household life as novices and widely [propagate the Dharma].

To transform sentient beings so that they may together attain Buddhahood—how could one prefer to remain long submerged in the paths of suffering within the True Dharma rather than delighting in following the teachings of Laozi to temporarily gain rebirth in heaven?
One must enter the causes of the Mahāyāna to forever leave behind false views. (Byan Zheng) On the eleventh day, an imperial edict was issued to the Secretariat:
"The Great Sūtras state that there are ninety-six kinds of paths; only the path of the Buddha is the one true path."
This is the True Path; all others are heterodox paths. I, the Emperor, have renounced heterodoxy to serve the Tathāgata.

If you high officials are able to enter into this vow, each of you should give rise to the bodhicitta. Although Laozi and Confucius were disciples of the Tathāgata acting as skillful means for conversion, they were merely teachers of worldly goodness;
they could not transform the mundane into the sacred. [May] the high officials, the various ministers, the marquises, and the kings [embrace this].
My kinsmen, you should turn away from the false and return to the true; abandon the heterodox and enter the orthodox. The sūtras and śāstras state:

"If one’s mind is heavy toward non-Buddhist paths and light toward the Buddha-dharma, this constitutes wrong view. If the mind is equal toward both, it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). If the mind directed toward serving the Buddha is strong..."

Laozi’s “weakness of heart” is precisely what constitutes pure faith (*qingxin*). "Pure" means that both the inner and outer are cleansed; "faith" means believing in what is correct and not deviating into the heterodox.

Therefore, one is called a disciple of the Buddha who possesses pure faith. All other forms of goodness are merely heterodox views and cannot be termed "correct faith. May Your Excellency quickly carry this out.
On the fourteenth day, the high officials presented a memorial to respectfully receive the imperial decree. The Emperor—

The imperial edict replied: "To be able to turn back from delusion and enter the correct path may be called having planted roots of goodness in a former life; you should apply yourself with even greater vigor.
On the seventeenth day of the third month of the following year, the Palace Attendant Xiao Lun submitted a memorial, which stated in brief:

"Your servant has heard that the Tathāgata descended the cloud of compassion and let fall the rain of ambrosia. It coincides with the occasion when Your Majesty, a Bodhisattva-Emperor, governs all things and transforms the people through the Dharma."

As he expounded the Way and transmitted the scriptures, his virtuous voice filled the ears of all. Your servant has now awakened from delusion and roughly understands where one should turn for refuge.
Having received the Bodhisattva Great Precepts, I shall restrain my body and mind; I renounce the heterodox winds of Laozi and enter the true teachings of the Dharma-stream.

I prostrate myself, entreating that Your Majesty’s compassionate grace may graciously grant this request. From this point on, all officials abandoned heterodoxy and returned to the orthodox path. (From the *Bian zheng lun*) ○ This.
In the [first] year of the reign, the Emperor established Guangzhai Monastery at his own palace residence and cast a gilded bronze image eighteen *zhang* in height.

As the artisans were about to place it in the furnace, they suspected that the copper was insufficient and wished to petition the Emperor for more. Suddenly, a messenger arrived leading fifteen carts of copper, stating that he had come by imperial decree to deliver it to the monastery.

They immediately proceeded with the melting and casting; it was completed in a single pour. However, they perceived it to be exceptionally tall and large; upon measurement, it was found to be twenty-two *chi*.
He submitted a report on these circumstances to the throne. The imperial edict stated: "At first, no copper was sent; this is truly a marvelous manifestation of spiritual resonance.
Consequently, it was engraved upon the lotus pedestal as an inscription of its miraculous nature (*Gantong lu*).
Biyou (the fourth year). Initially, the Emperor dreamed that a divine monk told him: "The six realms and four modes of birth are undergoing great suffering and affliction;

why do you not perform a great *zhāi* (fasting ritual) to rescue and deliver them? The Emperor questioned various śramaṇas, but only Master Zhìgōng urged the Emperor to seek out the scriptures, saying that there would surely be a causal connection.
Thereupon, he took the Tripitaka and personally examined it, composing the ritual texts over the course of three years.

It was thus completed. Thereupon, he held up the text, set out incense and candles, and addressed the Buddha: "If the principles of this text accord with the sentiments of both the sages and the common people, I pray that upon my prostration and rising, the incense and lamps may shine of their own accord.
If the ritual procedures are not yet detailed, may the lamps remain dark as before. Having finished speaking, he prostrated himself once on the ground;
as he first rose, the incense and candles all blazed brightly. He then summoned Master Zhigong and asked him: "In what place would it be suitable to establish this assembly? Gong—
It was said: "At Ze Xin Temple in Runzhou, a single peak rises from the heart of the river; the waters stretch for a thousand li, while the moon reflects in the deep pool.

Clouds and sky hang four-square above, and the realm extends through both the hidden and the manifest, a place fit for the assembly of spirits. By imperial decree, on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, the rites were performed at Ze Xin Temple according to the prescribed ritual.
The Emperor personally attended the site, and by imperial command, Vinaya Master You proclaimed the texts, so that the benefits reached all.
"You-ming" refers to Jinshan Temple (from the Jinshan Temple Stele and the Weijiang Ji). Shuzhou Qianshan is most extraordinary, and its foothills are particularly magnificent.
Master Zhigong and the Immortal of the White Crane both desired this location; they therefore petitioned Emperor Wu.
The Emperor, considering that both men possessed supernatural powers, ordered each to mark the site with an object, and whoever obtained it was to reside there. The Immortal said: "I..."

He used the place where the crane had perched as his marker. Master Zhi said, "I shall use the place where my monk’s staff (*zhuxi*) was planted as my marker. Shortly thereafter, the crane flew off first;

as it was about to land at the foot of the mountain, the sound of the staff flying through the air was suddenly heard from above. Startled, the crane stopped and went elsewhere, and the staff consequently planted itself at the base of the hill.
The Master then built a dwelling there. However, the Daoist was displeased, for he could not bear to go back on his previous word.
(*Shiwen Leiji*) Bingxu, the fifth year, winter.
The rain-sacrifices were performed exhaustively, yet the rain did not fall. Master Zhigong requested that the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* be expounded to pray for rain.
The Emperor immediately commanded Dharma Master Fayun to lecture on the *Śrīmālā* at Huaguang Hall. When the lecture was finished, that night—
During a great snowfall, Master Zhigong required a basin of water; he placed a blade upon it, and suddenly a heavy rain fell, providing enough for all places, high and low (Nan shi).

On the *wuzi* day of the seventh year, an imperial edict was issued for the court painter Zhang Sengyou to paint a portrait of the Venerable Bao. The Master then slit open his forehead, and [the image] emerged.
The image of the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara was sometimes compassionate and sometimes majestic; even Zengyou was ultimately unable to capture its likeness.
On another day, while he and the Emperor were gazing out over the river, they saw something moving upstream. The Master used his staff to guide it ashore;
it was a piece of purple sandalwood, from which he immediately carved the image of the Bodhisattva, whose divine spirit appeared as if alive (*Gantong lu*).
In this year, the first year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xuanwu of the Wei dynasty,
the Censor-in-Chief Yang Gu submitted a memorial stating that the current priority of state affairs should be to cease discussions on empty metaphysics and profound abstractions,
and to eliminate the useless expenditures of the *śramaṇa* community in order to alleviate the suffering of cold and hunger (*Tongjian*).
Jichou (491): At the Qiancheng Hall, Emperor Xuanwu of the Wei dynasty lectured on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra for various monks and court officials.
At that time, the Wei ruler was exclusively devoted to Buddhism and neglected the classical scriptures.

Pei Yanjun, the Secretariat Director, submitted a memorial stating that although Emperor Guangwu of the Han and Emperor Wu of the Wei were amidst the turmoil of war, they never ceased their studies; so too did the late Emperor.
When a general leads an army, his hands do not let go of the scroll; this is truly because learning provides manifold benefit that cannot be set aside for even a moment.

When Your Majesty ascends the Dharma-seat to personally expound the Great Enlightenment, all who listen find their mental obstructions cleared away. However, the Five Classics are the models for governing the world and the priority for managing affairs.
I humbly pray that you will peruse both the scriptures and the classics, and maintain both the teachings of Confucius and Śākyamuni; thus, internally—
Externally, everything was identical; thus, both the ultimate and conventional truths were fully elucidated. At that time, Buddhism flourished in Luoyang.
Apart from the Chinese śramaṇas, more than three thousand people arrived from the Western Regions and established the Yongming Temple, where they resided in over a thousand rooms.
From far and near, all received the wind [of his influence], and there were none who did not revere the Buddha (Tongjian).
Gengyin, the ninth year: The Emperor, as Taizu Wendi, established the Great Aijing Monastery at Zhujian on Mount Zhong;
for the Empress Dowager, he founded the Great Zhidu Monastery. The Emperor visited the Aijing Monastery and established the Unobstructed Assembly (Wu’ai Hui).

He filled his bowl with water and floated the śarīra relics therein; the smallest one remained hidden and did not emerge. When the Emperor prostrated himself, it emitted light from within the bowl that reached up to heaven.
It circled for a long time, and the entire nation marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence (from the *Gantong lu*).
Xinmao, the tenth year. In the first year of the Tianjian era, the Emperor dreamed that a sandalwood image was entering the realm.
He consequently ordered Hao Qian and seventy-nine others—eighty people in total—to travel to India to invite the Buddha image carved by King Udayana.

The king then had a replica carved from purple sandalwood and entrusted it to Hao Qian and his party to bring back. On the fifth day of the fourth month of this year, they arrived at the capital of Yangdu.

The Emperor and his hundred officials traveled forty li on foot to welcome him back to the Taiji Hall. There, he established a purification ritual (*zhāi*) to deliver sentient beings, issued a general amnesty, and prohibited killing.
From then on, he maintained a vegetarian diet and abstained from desire (from the *Gantong lu*).
Gui-si (the year of Gui-si): The second year of the Yuanchang era of the Wei dynasty. Ratnamati from the Western Regions translated the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* in twenty-four fascicles.

Emperor Xuanwu invited him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Suddenly, while at the high seat, he saw a celestial deity arrive and say, "The Lord of Devas requests that you lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
He, along with the *dougang*, the *weina*, and four others—five people in total—passed away simultaneously from their seats.
Those who saw and heard of it sighed that such a thing had never existed before (*Gantong lu*).

In the year Bingshen, the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era, the stone Buddha image at Yinyue Temple in Yuezhou was originally intended for construction by the monk Shi Senghu at a height of ten *zhang*.
During the Jianwu period of the Qi dynasty, he had barely finished carving the facial features when he passed away. Subsequently, the monk Sengshu took up his work.

The work was nearly complete but remained unfinished until the sixth year of the Tianjian era. Lu Xian of Wu Commandery dreamed of a monk who said that Prince Jian’an was suffering from an illness that had not yet healed;
if he could successfully complete the stone Buddha of Shan County, the Prince would surely recover. Although Xian gradually forgot this for a year, the monk appeared again in a dream to urge him on.
Xian then informed Prince Jian’an, who donated gold and entrusted the matter to the monk Sengyou, charging him exclusively with the task of completing the image.
The work was completed over twelve years; it was only this spring that it was finished. The pedestal was five *zhang* high, while the body of the image was ten *zhang*.
Once the image was completed, the King’s illness was cured (*Sengshi*).
This was the first year of the Xiping era of Emperor Suzong of the Wei dynasty. Emperor Shizong had been constructing Yaoguang Temple, but it was not yet finished.
Empress Dowager Hu then built Shiku Temple and also constructed Yongning Temple beside the palace; the craftsmanship of Yongning was particularly magnificent.
It contained a true-gold image eighteen feet high and ten images of medium height, as well as two jade images. Furthermore, a nine-story *stūpa* was erected.
The diagram [shows] it is over ninety *zhang* in height. When the foundation was excavated down to the Yellow Springs, thirty-two golden images were obtained.
The Empress Dowager considered this an auspicious omen and a sign of the true Dharma. Their ornamentation and craftsmanship were extraordinary and reached the pinnacle of worldly splendor.

Above stood a stūpa-pole (*śikhara*) another ten *zhang* high; at its summit was a precious vase with a capacity of twenty-five *hu*, supported by an eleven-tiered dew-receiving basin (*amṛta-dhāra*).
All were fashioned from gold. During the long nights, the sound of bells and chimes could be heard for ten *li*. The main hall was like the Taiji Hall, and the three gates were like the Duan Gate.
There were a thousand pillars of monastic quarters, adorned with pearls, jade, and brocade that dazzled the eyes and startled the mind. Such was the entry of the Buddha-dharma into China.

The magnificence of these pagodas and temples throughout China is such that all say it has never been seen even in Jambudvīpa. When they were first completed, Emperor Ming and the Empress Dowager ascended them together to look out;
the affairs within the palace appeared as clear as if held in the palm of one's hand. Consequently, they prohibited people from ascending them.

Li Chong, the Governor of Yangzhou, submitted a memorial stating that although the High Ancestor had resided in the capital for nearly thirty years, the Hall of Bright Virtue (Ming-tang) had not yet been constructed, which constituted a great disorder.
It lies in ruins; its city walls, palaces, and government offices are crumbling. This is not the way to honor the ancestral legacy and provide a model for the myriad states.

Although the National University currently bears the title of "academic office," it lacks the substance of instruction. How is this different from the "rabbit's floss" or "swallow's wheat," or the "southern winnowing basket" and "northern dipper"?
These things cannot flourish together; there must be a choice between them. It is appropriate to abolish the extravagant and wasteful works of the Imperial Workshop (Shangfang).

This was composed [as a memorial]. It proposes to reduce the labor for the timber and earthworks of Yongning Temple, decrease the manpower required for the materials and tiles of Yaoguang Temple, and distribute the toil of carving and chiseling among other tasks.

Furthermore, during the three intervals between the farming seasons when there is no urgent work, these several measures shall be carried out so that the state’s appearance may be solemn and magnificent, and rites and transformation may flourish.
Would this not be a most auspicious thing? Although the Empress Dowager responded with gracious edicts, she ultimately...
They did not follow his words (*Tongjian*). Emperor Hu of the Wei dynasty was fond of Buddhism; many people ceased their household duties to become *śramaṇas*.
Li Zhan, a friend of the Prince of Gaoyang, submitted a memorial stating: "Among the three thousand offenses, none is greater than filial impiety.

Regarding filial impiety, nothing is more serious than severing one's lineage. How can one lightly indulge sentiments that run counter to ritual propriety, merely to give free rein to an inclination toward the Dharma?"

To personally neglect one's aged parents, abandon the family to sever their sustenance, and violate the rites of the present world in pursuit of benefits in the future—Confucius said, "If you do not know life, how can you know death?
How could there be anyone who abandons such magnificent governance to follow the teachings of ghosts?
Furthermore, the southern regions are currently not at peace, and various public services remain burdensome. In the hearts of the common people, there is indeed much desire to evade service;

if we were to permit this again, I fear they would abandon filial piety and compassion, and every household would become a community of śramaṇas. — [Submitted by] the Metropolitan Superintendent (Dūtong) Sengxian and others.
Fen Zhang referred to it as "Teaching of the Ghosts" (*guǐjiào*), considering it a slander against the Buddha. He wept and appealed to the Empress Dowager, who rebuked him. Zhang said:

"Regarding the celestial deities, terrestrial spirits, and human ghosts, the *Analects* states: 'In the realm of clarity there are rites and music; in the realm of mystery there are ghosts and spirits.

Thus, that which is manifest is called the 'Grand Hall' (*tángtáng*); that which is mysterious is called the 'Teaching of the Ghosts. The Buddha originally arose from among humans; to name him a 'ghost' is foolish."

This means it was not a slander. Although the Empress Dowager knew that Zang’s words were justified, she found it difficult to go against the wishes of Xian and the others, and thus fined Zang one *jin* of gold (*Tongjian*).
*Dingyou* (the sixteenth year). For all the construction of temples, the Emperor ordered Xiao Ziyun to write the characters for the nameplates in *feibai* (flying silk) script.
People of the time referred to these temples as "Xiao Temples" (*Guoshi bu*). ○ Dharma Master Sengyou had extensively propagated the Vinaya since the beginning of the Qi dynasty.

Emperor Wu of Liang treated him with profound courtesy and respect; whenever there were doubts regarding monastic affairs, they were all resolved through consultation with him. When he grew old, an imperial edict was issued...

The Emperor took his carriage into the inner palace to receive the precepts for the six palaces. Over ten thousand people, including princes, dukes, nobles, and commoners—both monastics and laypeople—attended as disciples.
The Master’s works include the *Sanzang ji*, the *Fayuan ji*, the *Shijie ji*, the *Shijia pu*, and the *Hongming ji*, all of which circulate in the world.
Jihai (the year 519), the eighteenth year of the Tianjian era: the monk Jiaoran of Kuaiji compiled the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* in fourteen fascicles.
It begins from the Yongping era of the Han dynasty and concludes with this year, covering a total of one hundred and fifty-odd years and the lives of one hundred and fifty-seven individuals.
More than two hundred people were listed as witnesses (in the *Dazang*).
On the eighth day of the fourth month of this year, the Emperor lectured at the Dengjue Hall and received the Bodhisattva precepts from Dharma Master Huiyue.

The Emperor humbled himself by setting aside the dignity of his ten-thousand-chariots station and extended the reverence due to those in the Threefold Assembly. For a time, he set aside his dragon-robe (*qǔnfú*) and respectfully donned the field-garment (*tiányī*).

He proclaimed the rites of purification and prostrated himself with sincere solemnity. Furthermore, he established a Great Unrestricted Assembly (*wūzhā dàhuì*), attended by over one hundred thousand people from the court and the countryside, both clergy and laity;

the incense, flowers, and musical performances reached their peak at this time. From then on, when Master Yue was summoned for an audience, a separate lacquered couch was provided for him. The Emperor—

First, he performed prostrations, and only then took his seat; from the Crown Prince downward, all paid him their respects with full ritual decorum. Thereupon, he issued a general amnesty for the empire. The Imperial Edict stated:
"The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says that those who occupy the position of sovereign should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

Thus we know that although one is noble as the Son of Heaven and possesses the wealth of the four seas, one ought to cultivate the body, the precepts, and the mind to propagate the Way of Governance. It is my reflection..."
If one does not receive the Bodhisattva precepts, how can one give rise to a heart of compassion and practice impartial conduct?
Therefore, I have no doubt that you should uphold the True Dharma, so that the myriad beings of the world may together partake in blessings and prosperity.
All crimes throughout the realm, whether light or heavy, shall be universally pardoned and removed.
In the year of Gengzi, the first year of the Putong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, and the first year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Xiaoming,
the Suzong of Wei. On the twenty-first day of the ninth month of this year, the Great Master Bodhidharma, the twenty-eighth patriarch of India, [arrived].

Upon arriving at the South Sea, Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, submitted a memorial to report his arrival. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree to welcome him.

On the first day of the eleventh month, he arrived in Jinling. The Emperor asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting.
What merit and virtue do these deeds possess? The Master replied, "There is no merit or virtue whatsoever. The Emperor asked, "Why is that?"
“It possesses no merit. The Master said, “This is merely a minor fruit of humans and devas; it is a cause of outflows (āsrava). Like a shadow following a form, though it exists, it is not real.
The Emperor asked, “What, then, is true merit? The Master said, “Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and tranquil.
Such merit as this is not sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked again, “What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?”
The Master said, “Vast and empty—there is no sage. The Emperor asked, “Who is it that faces me? The Master replied, “I do not know. The Emperor did not grasp the profound meaning;

the Master, knowing his opportunity was not in accord, departed from Liang on the nineteenth day. He broke off a reed to ferry across the river and, on the twenty-third day, headed north toward the borders of Wei.
Eventually arriving at Luoyi, he stayed at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, sitting facing a wall all day long.
No one could fathom him. After the Master had departed, Emperor Wu asked Master Zhi about him. The Master said, "Your Majesty, do you recognize this person? The Emperor replied, "I do not.
The Master said, "This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who transmits the Buddha’s Mind-Seal. The Emperor felt remorse.
He immediately dispatched people to pursue him. Master Zhigong said, "Do not speak merely of sending messengers;
even if the entire nation were to go, he would still not return" (Monastic History).
Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty. In this year, he added ceremonial court robes and issued a general amnesty. He commanded the two sects of Buddhism and Daoism to ascend the dais.
Upon the conclusion of the fast, Palace Attendant Liu Teng proclaimed the imperial decree, requesting that the various Dharma masters engage in debate with the Daoist practitioners.
At that time, the śramaṇa Tanwuwei of Rongjue Monastery in the capital of Luoyang debated against the Daoist Jiang Bin. The Emperor said, "The Buddha and Laozi are the same..."

At that time, Jiang Bin said, "Laozi entered the West to convert the barbarians and become a Buddha; this is recorded in the *Laozi Kaitian Jing* (The Scripture of Laozi Opening Heaven), which clearly shows they were contemporaries.
Daoshui asked, "Under which Zhou king was Laozi born, and in what year did he enter the West?

Bin replied, "He was born on the night of the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the third year of King Ding of Zhou. In the fourth year of King Jian, he served as the Archivist. In the first year of King Jing..."
At eighty-five years of age, seeing the virtue of the Zhou dynasty being executed by slicing, he departed westward with Yin Xi, the Magistrate of San Guan.
It is most clearly stated that the Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of Zhou;
he entered *parinirvāṇa* at night on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu. Three hundred and forty-five years later, it first reached the time of King Ding.
"Three years later, Laozi was born. By the first year of King Jing’s reign, a total of four hundred and thirty years had elapsed since that time, at which point he fled westward with Yin Xi.
This represents a vast discrepancy in the dates; is it not erroneous? Bin said: 'If it were as you say...'"

From which records do these accounts derive? Huiguan said: "The *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies from the Book of Zhou) and the *Han Fa Ben Neizhuan* (Inner Biography on the Origin of the Dharma in the Han) both contain explicit evidence.
Daobin asked: "Confucius was a sage who established the laws; he ought to have been clearly aware of the Buddha. Yet there is no mention of him at all in the records—why is this? Huiguan replied:

"Confucius was fully equipped with the Three Collections (*Sanbei*). The words of the Buddha appear within the *Zhongbei* (the *Analects*). Your reverence’s understanding is like looking through a tube; you have not seen it."

"How could such vast and profound [teachings] reach us on their own? Yuan Yi, the Director of the Secretariat, proclaimed an imperial decree stating that the Daoist Jiang Bin’s discourse lacked a fundamental principle and that he should be dismissed from his seat.

Furthermore, as it was debated who had spoken the *Kaitian jing* (Scripture of Opening Heaven), Wei Shou and others, the Attendants of the Secretariat, went to the observatory to retrieve the scripture.
After Xiao Zong, the Grand Tutor, Li Shi, and one hundred and seventy others had finished reading it, they submitted a formal indictment.

The memorialist submitted: "Laozi composed only the *Wenzi* (Five Thousand Words); there are no other recorded teachings. Your servants have deliberated and find that Jiang Bin’s literary compositions are perverse and erroneous;
his crime merits the deluding of the masses. The Emperor imposed the ultimate punishment upon Bin. Bodhiruci memorialized for his release, and he was instead banished to Mayi (*Weishi*).
As for the Dharma Master Tanwuwei: he was of the Dong clan of Wuan. His spiritual intuition was profoundly penetrating, and his learning was preeminent.
Cheng Yu was a preeminent general for the Triple Gem and served as a golden fortress for the Semblance Dharma. His discourses were purposeful and profound;

his reputation surpassed that of the Wei Shu. High officials and eminent scholars descended from their steps to pay him respect. That the Buddha-dharma was revived was solely due to his diligent efforts.

The Wei ruler was fond of roaming through gardens and parks and did not personally attend court audiences. He excessively venerated the Buddha-dharma, leaving most matters concerning the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples to the relevant officials.
Zhang Puhui submitted a memorial offering earnest admonition, arguing that [the Emperor] was planting the karmic seeds of unreflective ignorance and inflicting immense expense upon the common people.
By reducing stipends and curtailing manpower, he provided for monks who were of no practical use, while lavishly adorning spirit halls to seek blessings from afar.
Those who have not yet received their retribution—the officials at the break of dawn—bow their heads outside; the assembly of profound stillness roams within.

When ritual errors offend the timing of the age, the spirits of men and gods are not harmonious. I, in my ignorance, believe that by cultivating causes morning and evening, one seeks the blessings of kalpas.
It is not equal to winning the hearts of the myriad nations to serve one’s parents, thereby bringing peace and harmony to the world so that calamities do not arise.
I humbly pray that you will be prudent and careful in your dignified demeanor to serve as a model for the myriad states;

that you will reverently offer devotion at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, personally perform the rites of the first and fifteenth days of the month, conduct the ritual offerings at the National University (Chengjun), and exert yourself in the thousand-acre fields [of agriculture]. Furthermore, I pray that you will proportionately eliminate the non-essential buildings of the Buddhist monasteries.
[Emperor] Huar restored the long-abolished ranks of the hundred officials. Those already established he sought to simplify and expedite; those not yet established were never to be created again.
Thus, filial piety and fraternal duty can communicate with the divine spirits, and virtuous instruction can illuminate the four seas.
By practicing frugality and loving the people, both the secular and the monastic orders shall rely upon this (from the *Tongjian*).
Xin-chou (501 AD): During the early years of the Xiping era, Empress Dowager Hu of the Wei dynasty dispatched Song Yun and the bhikṣu Hui-sheng to the Western Regions to seek Buddhist scriptures.
After one year, they reached the kingdom of Qianluo; that winter they returned, arriving back in Luoyang in the second month of the following year.
They had obtained one hundred and seventy collections of Buddhist scriptures. The Empress Dowager ordered that a five-story pagoda be constructed on every major road.
Various kings and high officials each established monasteries in Luoyang, which were all exceptionally lofty, magnificent, and imposing.

The Empress Dowager frequently organized vegetarian assemblies and bestowed wealth and goods upon the monks, numbering in the tens of thousands. Her distribution of rewards to her attendants was without restraint, and the expenditures were beyond measure (as recorded in the *Beishi* and the *Tongjian*).

Gui-mao (the year 503 CE): At the beginning of the Jingming era of the Wei dynasty, Emperor Shizong ordered the eunuch Bai Zheng to carve two Buddha niches at Longmen Mountain for Empress Wenzhao, the consort of the High Ancestor.
Each was one hundred feet high. During the Yongping era, Liu Teng further carved one niche for Emperor Shizu.
From that time until now, twenty-four years have passed; in total, more than one hundred eighty-two thousand [cubic feet] of material were used.
The work was underway but not yet completed; what else could be done? (Tongjian) ○ Sima Cheng, Prince of Rencheng and Minister of Works, memorialized:

"In the past, when the High Ancestor moved the capital, he decreed that within the city walls only one monastery for monks and one for nuns were permitted; all others were to be established outside the city."
This was because the paths of the clergy and the laity diverge, as the former dwell in tranquility beyond the dust of the world.

In the third year of the Zhengshi era, the *Sāṃghārāma-ādhipati* Huishen first violated the previous prohibitions; he personally rolled up the imperial edicts and did not implement them, while private audiences with him became increasingly numerous.

Within the capital city, monasteries exceeded five hundred in number, usurping and seizing one-third of the civilian residences. Slaughterhouses and places of trade and filth were situated in close proximity, intermingling with them. In the past...
In the north of Dai, there was the plot of Fa-xiu; in Jizhou, there occurred the upheaval involving the Mahayana. The regulations established during the Taihe and Jingming eras were not mere schemes;

they were intended to ensure that the monastic and the lay followed distinct paths, thereby preventing small evils from becoming great and stopping gradual corruption before it could manifest. In the past, when the Tathāgata expounded the teachings, he mostly relied upon mountains and forests;
yet today these monks are so attached to cities and towns that they are surely being seduced by profit and desire, unable to [cultivate themselves].
This is the dregs of the Śākya clan and the "rats in the granary" of the Dharma King; they are not tolerated by internal precepts and are collectively discarded by the national histories.
Your servant suggests that those monasteries within the capital city which are not yet completed and can be moved should all be relocated outside the city walls.
Those with fewer than fifty monks should be merged, the small following the large; the same principle should apply to the provinces. The imperial edict followed this recommendation. However—
In the end, he was unable to carry this out. When the Wei dynasty possessed the empire, by this time Buddhist scriptures had been circulated and were making great progress within China (*Tongjian*).
He Yin initially indulged in rich flavors; Zhou Yong sent him a letter urging him to adopt a vegetarian diet, saying: "Of all great transformations, none is greater than..."
Transmigrating through birth and death: among the things most weighty in life, none exceeds one's very life and nature (*jīva*).

Life and nature are of the utmost urgency to that [other world], whereas the flavors of this world may be deferred. This would be acceptable if the principle of the three periods of existence were false;

however, if this principle is indeed true, and the taking of form does not cease—one going and one returning, with birth and death as constant occurrences—then even the most heart-wrenching sorrows must naturally [be endured].

Furthermore, although a gentleman may not personally tread upon the category of things with the flavor of blood, as for the wild goose at dawn or the carp at night, how could he fail to exercise caution regarding the butcher’s gate?
Once wealth and possessions have passed through the hands of a thief, they are still rejected by the upright;

once life and limb are opened to the golden blade, how could one ever again endure it with a compassionate heart? Though the *zouyu* (a mythical beast) may be hungry, it does not eat that which has died of its own accord.

Even the grasses there do not eat [meat]. Upon hearing of such a reputation, how could one not feel deeply ashamed? You, sir, have long possessed this virtue; I have merely offered these few words to provide further inspiration.

From this point on, Zhiyin completely abstained from the taste of blood. He frequently encountered extraordinary monks and received from them the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Great Ornament Treatise), a work that had never before existed in the world.
Later, he entered Mount Huqiu to lecture on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. At the time of his death, he dreamed...
He saw more than sixty celestial maidens standing in a row before the hall; he saw them even upon waking.
He immediately bathed, dressed in ceremonial robes, and passed away shortly thereafter (Old History).
Biyi (Year 6 of the Putong era; Year 1 of the Xiaochang era of the Northern Wei). An envoy from the Western Regions returned, having obtained the Buddha’s nail-clippings and hair.
The hair was a deep azure-black color; when extended with an object, it would lengthen according to the size of that object, and when released, it would curl back into a spiral.

When Emperor Ming of the Northern Wei heard that Bodhidharma’s virtue and Way were solitary and lofty, the assembly of both monastics and laypeople turned toward him in droves, and his fame shook the land.

In the capital city, the Emperor thrice extended his summons, yet the Master did not emerge from the mountains. The Emperor held him in high esteem and subsequently bestowed upon him two monastic robes (*mantra-kāṣāya*) and various gold and silver vessels.
The Master declined them each time, returning them three times in succession; nevertheless, the Emperor ultimately conferred them upon him (*Zhengzong Ji*).
In the first year of the Xiaochang era of the Northern Wei, Empress Dowager Hu and the Wei Sovereign resided in separate palaces. Facing the Emperor, the Empress Dowager said:
The ministers said, "Now that you have severed the bond between mother and son and do not permit our coming and going, what further use have we for you?
We shall instead leave the household life at Songju Monastery. Thereupon, they intended to shave their own hair. The Emperor and the ministers prostrated themselves, weeping with tears.
After he had earnestly and repeatedly entreated him, [the Emperor] finally desisted (*Tongjian*).
On the day Dingwei, the first year of Datong, Emperor Wu established Tongtai Temple during the first year of Putong; after seven years of winter and summer, it was completed in that same year.
Furthermore, he heard that there was a gate named Datong facing it, adopting this as a correspondence based on the reversal of its name.
Morning and evening he visited the temple, entering and exiting through this gate (*Tongjian*).
In the *Jiyou* year, the era name was changed to Zhongdàtōng. It was the second year of the Yǒng'ān era of Wèi Xiàozhuāng.
Empress Dowager Hú summoned all the ladies of the inner court of Emperor Sùzōng and ordered them to become nuns; the Empress Dowager herself also shaved her head (*Tongjian*).
In the ninth month of this year, on the day of Guisi, the Emperor visited Tongtai Temple and established a fourfold *amogha* (unrestricted) great assembly.

He cast off his imperial robes and donned dharma robes, practicing pure conduct and performing a great renunciation; he used his former palace as a dwelling, employing plain beds and earthenware vessels.

Riding in a small carriage, with private attendants holding his armor and banner, he ascended the Dharma seat in the lecture hall and expounded the title of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly.
On the day of Gui-mao, the ministers offered one hundred million coins to pray to the Triple Gem, requesting that they redeem the Emperor Bodhisattva;
the monastic community gave their silent consent. On the day of Ji-si, the various officials went to the eastern gate of the monastery and presented a memorial requesting his return to the palace.
(Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government).
In the year of Jiyou (689), the Great Master Bodhidharma sat in silence for nine years. Suddenly, he said to his disciples: "I have gazed toward the southeast."
You possess the spirit of the Mahāyāna and have come to this land. Having transmitted the Dharma and found its recipient, the time has arrived for you to return to the West.

The World-Honored One’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was handed down to me through successive transmission; I now entrust it to you. More than two hundred years after my passing, the robe shall no longer be transmitted, yet the Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra.
There will be more than ten million who secretly correspond with and intimately accord with it; you must propagate and transform them, and do not slight those who have not yet awakened.
He attained enlightenment. With a single thought he turned his faculties back toward the source, and thus he was identical with that which is originally possessed.

He then went to Qiansheng Temple on Mount Yumen, where on the fifth day of the tenth month, he sat upright and passed away. His worldly age was one hundred and fifty. His disciples enshrined his entire body and buried it at Dinglin Temple on Mount Xiong’er.
Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty sent the envoy Song Yun on a mission to the Western Regions; they encountered the Master on the Pamir Mountains (Congling) while returning.
Carrying a single sandal in his hand, he walked on alone with graceful ease. Yun asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven.
He then said to Yun, "Your master has already grown weary of this world; return home at once. Upon hearing these words, Yun’s heart was filled with anxiety, and he hurried back to the capital.
When Emperor Xiaozhuang ascended the throne, he submitted a full report on the matter. An imperial decree was issued to open the tomb; it contained only an empty coffin and a single shoe.

The entire court was struck with wonder and admiration. By imperial command, the shoe was taken to the Shaolin Temple for veneration. (The *Chuanteng* records that he died in the nineteenth year of Taihe, which is an error. The Wei dynasty’s Mingdi changed the era to Taihe in the Dingwei year, lasting only six years.

The Eastern Jin’s Feidi changed the era to Taihe from Bingyin to Gengwu, lasting only five years. How could there have been a nineteenth year of Taihe under the Wei? [This is confirmed by] the *Tongji*.)* [Emperor Wu of] Liang.
When the Emperor heard of the Master’s manifest transformations, he personally composed an inscription carved upon Mount Zhong. Its conclusion reads: "Alas! To see and yet not see;
to encounter and yet not encounter. Whether now or in the past, I regret and lament this. Although I am but a single ordinary man, I am moved by the Master’s legacy for posterity.
During the reign of Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty, he was posthumously titled Great Master Yuanjue (Shi Tongjian).
Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty, Tong, mastered the Five Classics at the age of five. At twelve, he adjudicated legal cases within the Inner Ministry.

By nature, he was fond of Buddhism and devoted his mind to the Buddhist scriptures (*nèidiǎn*). He personally lectured upon them; indeed, he had read through almost all the sections of the Śāstras and Sūtras.
He compiled liturgical manuals for religious rites and established doctrines such as the Three Truths (*sandi*). For twenty years after leaving the palace, he did not keep musical instruments.
Joy. Only the Dharma is joy. In the third year of the Zhongdàtōng era, the *xiǎnh* year, he passed away in the fourth month.
The whole world wept for him as if they had lost their own parents (according to the *Lìáng Shǐ*).
Gui-chou (the 10th day of the tenth lunar month), the twenty-sixth day of the second month of the fifth year.
The Emperor visited Tongtai Temple to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and establish an Unrestricted Great Assembly (*wu zhe da hui*).

From the Crown Prince and the princes and nobles down to the various officials—numbering six hundred and ninety-eight persons—and one thousand monks specializing in doctrinal studies, they listened with one mind during the day and further refined the ritual protocols at night.
The remaining monks, nuns, Daoists, female Daoist adepts, and lay devotees—these five groups—as well as foreign envoys, numbered thirty-one thousand nine hundred and sixty-four persons.
Furthermore, there were tens of thousands more from the Imperial Guard on night duty.
At the beginning of the Tianjian era, Master Zhigong personally presented a fly-whisk fan and an iron staff to Emperor Wu; yet the Emperor still did not understand [the significance].
His intention was such that, after more than thirty years had passed, he finally struck his staff and ascended the hall to hold a fan and deliver a lecture;

this indeed possessed a profound, hidden resonance with the past. Regarding this lecture, the Crown Prince requested it, but initially permitted it for only seven days. The monks, who looked up to him with deep reverence, could not bear to stop;
they extended the period by another fourteen days to seek further instruction, continuing until the end of twenty-one days. On the morning of the conclusion of the lectures, precisely—
Suddenly, the Great Image in the Hall emitted a brilliant light, and the Bodhisattvas on its left and right likewise continued to radiate light.

The Emperor personally paid reverent homage while the entire assembly gazed upon it. The Emperor bestowed as offerings one million nine hundred and sixty thousand *zhí* in coin, silver, silk, and other goods.

The Crown Prince offered a precious case for the scriptures as a gift, along with the contributions of the six palaces, totaling more than six million *zhí*. At that time, the court officials arrived...
The common people all rejoiced accordingly. The sum was one million one hundred fourteen thousand coins.
Jia-yin: The sixth year of the Zhongdàtōng era of the Liáng dynasty. [This period] from Jia-yin to Bing-shen was ruled by three sovereigns for thirty-two years:
the Western Wèi Emperor Xiǎowǔ (r. Yǒngxī 3–5), and the Eastern Wèi Emperor Xiàojìng Shànjiàn (who moved the capital to Yè in the first year of Tiānping; from Jia-yin to Gēng-wu, seventeen years).
In this year, the stupa of Yongning Temple in Wei was struck by a disaster. Those who witnessed it all wept, and the sound of their lamentation shook the city gates and palaces.

In the second year of the Xiaochang era, a great wind arose and blew down the roof and the precious vase of that pagoda; they fell into the earth more than ten *zhang* deep. An order was issued to rebuild them anew. By the time [the work] reached...
In the second month, it was struck by a celestial thunderbolt and reduced to ashes.

After more than three months had passed, in the fifth month of that year, people arrived from Donglai Commandery and saw the stupa in the midst of the sea, its radiance solemn and majestic; those who witnessed it together were numerous. Suddenly, clouds arose.
His whereabouts were lost (from the *Gantong lu*). In this year, Master Fu Daoshi sent his disciple [Ming]wang to the imperial palace to present a letter;
an edict was issued for him to proceed to the capital during the intercalary twelfth month. Upon hearing of the Master’s spiritual wonders, the Emperor had all the gates pre-locked.
The Great Being already knew this; he had prepared a pair of large wooden mallets beforehand. He first struck one door, and all the gates opened.

He entered directly into the Zhengyan Hall, where he prostrated himself and did not follow the usual path, ascending the precious throne presented by the Western Kingdom. The Emperor questioned the Great Being.
"Whom do you serve as a teacher? He replied, "I follow from nowhere; I have no teacher to serve, and I serve nothing.

After the meal was finished, he returned to Zhongshan Dinglin Temple, where an imperial decree ordered that he be provided with sustenance. Later, in the third month of the Jiwu year, the Great Being entered the capital once more.
Emperor Wu held discussions on the ultimate truth at Shouguang Hall. Fu said, "It is quiescent yet not extinguished. The Emperor then requested [further instruction].
When he was lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Great Being struck his desk once and rose. The Emperor did not understand this;

when he requested the lecture again, the Great Being then asked for a clapper, ascended the seat, and sang forty-nine verses of praise before departing (from the *Biographies of the Three Masters Who Reached the Capital*).
Dingsi (the third year of the Datong era of the Eastern Wei). Sun Jingde of Dingzhou served Avalokiteśvara with great devotion.

He was falsely implicated by bandits and consequently confessed to the crime. The next day, he was to be executed. During the night, he dreamed of a monk who instructed him to recite the *Jiuku Guanyin Jing* (Sutra of Avalokiteśvara Who Relieves Suffering) one thousand times to escape his suffering.
Jingde had only recited half when the officials seized and bound him, leading him toward the marketplace. As they marched in the morning, he continued to recite it throughout the day.
When he was brought to execution and struck with an axe, the blade broke into three pieces without harming his skin or flesh. This happened three times, and each time the blade broke as before.
The executioners questioned him about this, and the matter was reported to the Chancellor, Gao Huan. Huan submitted a memorial on his behalf requesting that he be spared from death.
When Sengqiong returned home, there were three scars from the blades upon his head; this is what is now known as the *Gao-wang Guanyin Jing* (Sutra of Avalokiteśvara of King Gao). (*Qi Shu*)
Li Yin of Shangyu County in Yue dug into the earth and discovered a Buddha-tooth image measuring two inches square, with twelve figures on one side and fifteen figures on the other;
its exquisite carving was peerless, and within it were six authentic śarīras. He presented this report to the Emperor.

He did not take this to heart. When the year Wumu arrived, Yuan Yin was imprisoned in Dongye for his transgressions. At that time, śarīra relics descended into the inner palace, their radiance manifesting brilliantly;
it was truly for this reason that Great Compassion came to the rescue from suffering. An imperial edict was subsequently issued regarding these true-form śarīras.

He has appeared again in the world; both the hidden and the manifest turn their hearts toward him. In accordance with the times, he spreads virtue, truly harmonizing with both humanity and the spirits.

It is fitting that he should rely on the power of the Buddha to propagate this broad magnanimity. All crimes throughout the empire, whether light or heavy, shall be universally pardoned and remitted. (From the *Hongming ji*)
The *xīnyǒu* (Gengyou) year, the twelfth day of the third month: At the Chongyun Hall in Hualin Garden, the Emperor lectured on the *Golden-letter Prajñā-samprajanya Sūtra*.

The Crown Prince, princes and dukes, members of the imperial clan and maternal relatives, high officials and ministers, foreign envoys from various regions, and a thousand monks specializing in the study of doctrine—all those in the assembly listened with solemn countenances. The lectures continued for twenty-three days in total. From...

From the opening of the lectures until their conclusion, offerings were established and distributed universally. The civil and military guards of the capital were all bestowed with generous gifts (according to the *Liang shi*).
The Emperor frequently composed the *Jingye fu* (Rhapsody on Pure Deeds); its preface states: "I do not eat fish or meat, nor do I share [the same meals] with my consorts and attendants."

He remained there for over forty years. Since he no longer consumed living beings, he was free from the obstacle of killing; since he no longer indulged in the inner life, he was free from the obstacle of lustful evil.
Having removed these two obstacles, his mental consciousness became somewhat clear, and he composed the "Rhapsody on Pure Karma" (*Jingye Fu*). Its brief summary states:
Contemplate the innate nature of human life: it harbors a wondrous vital energy (*qi*) that is inherently pure and still.

Yet, it is stirred by external objects, and the mind of desire clings to them, thereby creating afflictions. Transgressions constantly arise from external dust; these burdens must stem from the realms before one.
Clutching a greedy heart without weariness, one lets internal thoughts run wild at will. The ears linger among the sounds of strings and flutes; the eyes shift among the five colors.

Fragrances waft upward; they strike the nose and give rise to consciousness. The tongue experiences flavors, sweetening the mouth as one chews and eats. The body experiences touch, finding therein self-comfort and delight.
With slender waists, delicate hands, supple bones, and full flesh, their bodies are fragrant and pure; when touched, they feel like fat.
With a deranged mind, deluded and harboring inverted perceptions, one deceives oneself. Thus, the six sense objects alike obstruct the path of goodness;

they eclipse the purple with their violet hue, and like grass bending before the wind, one is born moved by them and grows old together with them. Following after ignorance, everything is nothing but affliction.
By this, the external objects of the eyes are purified and the internal dust of the mind is cleansed. One follows virtue and dwells as a neighbor to the Way.
Seeing that pure karma is lovely, one takes non-killing as its cause; distancing oneself from desire and evil, one cultivates oneself.

Thus, there is no obstruction to the spirit, afflictions and entanglements are already removed, and hindrances are likewise purified. It is like water long settled, or like a mirror newly polished, reflecting outwardly.

There are many such accounts. Within, one perceives the various maladies; once the adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*) have been removed, one returns to one’s own nature. The mind becomes as clear as water and the will as pure as snow.
When fetters are severed, sorrow and fear likewise perish. One then grows ever more distant from the bonds of affection and attains eternal parting from the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
(As recorded in the *Hongming ji*.)

Jiazi: In the tenth year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, the Great Being (Bao Gong) manifested his traces. For over forty years, his fame spread throughout the world, and the Emperor revered him as his teacher.

One day, the Emperor asked, "How long will my realm and the altars of state endure? The Master pointed to his own throat and then to his neck; this was a prophecy concerning Hou Jing. The Emperor asked again, "Who shall succeed me? The Master replied:

*The one who follows after me is he who possesses the mark of the dragon.* *He shall ascend to the throne in the year of the Dragon.* *When the Dragon’s head is severed, the realm will fall into ruin.* (Note: This refers to Emperor Wu of Liang, whose name contained the character for "dragon" [龍], and the subsequent reigns of Emperor Jianwen and Emperor Yuan, following the rebellion of Hou Jing.)
"Dust arises within the lake" (Master Chen Ba was in Huzhou). Later, he again inquired about the fate of the state's altars.
The Master said, "When my humble tower collapses, Your Majesty’s altars of state will perish along with it."
Bingyin (the year 548), the first year of the Zhongdatong era. As the Master was about to manifest his passing into *nirvāṇa*, the Emperor went outside.

The Master entered the inner palace, lit a single candle, and placed it in the rear chamber. A palace attendant reported this to the Emperor. When the Emperor returned and saw that the Master had departed, he said, "The Teacher will not remain with us anymore;
has he entrusted me with his final affairs? He returned to the mountain and entered *parinirvāṇa* on the sixth day of the twelfth month. His age was...
93. By imperial decree, a wooden pagoda was constructed on Mount Zhong. Wang Jun of Dulonggang composed an inscription commemorating these meritorious deeds, and both projects were completed.

Suddenly, the Emperor wondered whether the wooden pagoda could endure for long; he subsequently demolished it and commissioned a stone pagoda instead, intending to ensure its immortality in accordance with a prophetic omen.
Hardly had the dismantling of the old pagoda been finished when the troops of Hou Jing arrived. Master Zhi passed away.
Later, in the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era of Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty, he descended and appeared in a city market.
Emperor Taizong issued an edict, and to avoid the imperial taboo name, he was referred to as "Master Bao" (Bao Gong).

In the sixth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era of Emperor Zhenzong, he was posthumously titled "Great Master Baoguo Daolin Zhenjue" (one source states he passed away in the Jia-wu year of the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era; this is recorded in the *Nan shi* and the *Shiwu jihui*). Yang Wenyong’s *Tanyuan* records the śramaṇa.
The copper plaque of Master Bao contains a prophecy concerning future events, stating: "There shall be a True Man in Jizhou; with mouth open and bow drawn, he stands on the left side.
For ten thousand myriad years, his descendants shall flourish. The Southern Dynasties ruler of Jiangnan named his son Hongji (弘冀).
The various sons of the rulers of Wuyue all bore names beginning with the character Hong (弘), anticipating that these would fulfill the prophecy. Furthermore, regarding Song Xuanzu’s...
[Emperor] Huì remarked, "This is precisely it.
When the pagoda of Tongtai Temple was destroyed by fire, the Emperor said, "This is the work of Māra. We should extensively perform Buddhist rites. The assembled ministers praised this as excellent.

He issued an edict stating: "When the Way is lofty, demonic forces flourish; when one practices goodness, obstacles arise. We must exhaust our resources to build this wooden structure, making it twice as grand as before.
Thereupon, he constructed a twelve-story pagoda (*Tongjian*).

Jisi (16 June 549), the fourth month of the third year of the Daqing era. The rebel Hou Jing breached the Tai City. As the Emperor sought to punish him without ceasing, he became enraged and fell ill;

yet his observance of the fast did not diminish, nor did his recitation of the Buddha’s name stop. In the fifth month, his condition grew critical. He refused food when served, and after a long while, he asked for honey.
Before it could arrive, he passed away at the Jingju Hall. He was eighty-six years old. —From the *Beishi* (History of the Northern Dynasties) — Taizong, Vol. 3, Biography of Emperor Wu of Liang.
Emperor Wen of the Liang dynasty, Xiao Gang, ascended the throne.

Although the Emperor’s affairs were as numerous as those of billions, he never let go of his scrolls. He was observant and took pleasure in hearing lawsuits, possessing a clarity that seemed to penetrate the divine.
He personally practiced frugality and lived simply with coarse food. Outwardly, he abolished the ritual of the threefold hunt; inwardly, he eschewed banquets of ten *zhong* of grain. From himself...
He did not prioritize extensive sacrifices, nor was music permitted during various religious rites. This was because the Way relies on people to propagate it;

in principle, there is no empty bestowal of teachings, and in practice, success depends on personal devotion. Thus, the people’s faith reached its peak. After the Emperor himself received the precepts, he completely renounced all flavors and tastes.
They ate but one meal per day, consisting merely of vegetable soup and coarse rice. When business was particularly heavy, they would pass the time after midday by merely sipping water.

None of the attendants in the inner palace wore fine silks or brocades. The expenses for the kitchen staff alone amounted to ten thousand pieces of gold annually, while the expenditures for the掖庭 (Yètíng) were reduced by more than four hundred and ten million pieces of gold per year.
Consequently, the private chambers and inner halls were abandoned, as were the beds and bedding used for sleep.
He wore plain white cloth for his robes and a *guan* mat with straw sandals. Even within his dark room of ramie curtains, he maintained his formal attire;
during the hot months, he never bared his shoulders. His private quarters were much like those of a śramaṇa: there were no attendants nearby and no playthings;

on his left and right were only rolls of sutras, and facing him were only a water jar, a mendicant’s staff, and an incense burner. He would taste the morning air while sitting at court until the sun reached his liver before he would finally rest.
At night he sought the Dharma-treasure, and at dawn he rose without sleep. His benefit was directed solely toward others, while his self-restraint was directed solely toward himself.

This was truly his constant practice in daily life, serving as a veritable record of the inner palace. Since antiquity, no sovereign has been able to emulate this. Consequently, as this one individual trod the Way, the four quarters were transformed by it;
throughout the land, all observed the six fast days, and the myriad people all received the eight precepts. Each time [he] abstained...
Regarding these grave offenses, he did not hesitate for a moment throughout the day. He provided exegesis and composed literary works, bestowing both material wealth and the Dharma.
Within the palace, the Buddha images all emitted radiance; it rained heavily at night, yet dawned clear and bright by morning. Heaven and earth shook, and a wondrous fragrance filled the realm.

The entire nation turned in reverence, all hoping to attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death. The grandeur of these Dharma services was unprecedented since antiquity. Myriad manifestations of spiritual wonders are detailed as follows:
Lu Yun’s preface says: "It is merely a matter of hearing. On the Discourse of the Recluse: Some claim that the Liang dynasty perished because of Buddhism.

Is this not perhaps a failure to reflect? Let us compare it with Emperor Wu of Han. Among the sovereigns of the two Han dynasties and the Southern and Northern dynasties, none enjoyed their thrones for as long as the two Emperors Wu—the Wu of Han and the Wu of Liang.

Both were alike in their grand promotion of schools and academies and their cultivation of human talent. The Han Emperor studied the arts of immortality; the Liang Emperor studied Buddhism. What difference does it make?

The object of their preference was likewise the same. Yet, during the fifty-four years of Emperor Wu of Han’s reign, he held no one more in honor than the fangshi (immortal-seekers), neglected the myriad affairs of state, exhausted his troops, and indulged in militarism;
though his treasuries were depleted and the people’s hearts turned away from him, why did he not perish?

It was because the Han never abandoned its military forces. Toward the end of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor gradually distanced himself from his generals and aides and discarded armor and weapons; this was where [the two cases diverged].

This is because they were defeated by their own prior [errors]. Master Sōng’s *Guǎngyuánjiào* states: "The teaching must not be adhered to dogmatically; the Way must not be pursued through deception. To go too far and to fall short—these are equally harmful.
Now, in affairs there is what is appropriate, and in principles there is what is ultimate. One should follow what is appropriate and treat it as such."
This is how the teaching of the sages is realized: by reaching the ultimate, one attains it. This is how the Way of the sages is realized.
For Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty to reverse this proclamation and instead prioritize mere ritual instruction—is this not mired in pedantry?
The two rulers of the Wei and Zhou dynasties were mired in their devotion and yet presumed to understand the Way; was this not delusional?

This was the Buddhist disciples’ reckless pursuit of the times, and the rulers’ miring themselves in the Buddha was likewise so. By this, one may verify that the Liang dynasty’s miring in the teachings was not entirely without fault.
Indeed, there is a Middle Way in the study of Buddhism itself. Although the Liang dynasty erred by miring itself in the Way, it did not meet its downfall because of this alone. Its...

The fault lies in the laxity of military preparedness and the neglect of the worthy. In essence, the rise and fall of dynasties are determined by fixed destiny; they cannot be prolonged through mere expediency.
Since antiquity, instances of sovereigns and ministers, fathers and sons, being usurped, murdered, or slain by madmen and bandits have been beyond counting.
Now, you specifically cite the rebellion of Hou Jing to slander the Buddha—why is this? [It is no different than] Gonggong’s assault upon Fuxi or Chiyou’s [attack upon the Yellow Emperor].

Under the Yellow Emperor, Yi hastened his end; under Xia and Chu, King Zhao did not return; it was extended to Zhou with the assassination of King You; under Qin, Xiang Yu and Wang Chong-sheng rose up; under Wei, Jia Chong and Cheng Ji brought about its fall;
under Jin, Liu Yao and Shi Le did the same; under the Yuan Wei, Er Zhu Rongzhi caused its ruin; and under the Tang, An Lushan, Zhu Ci, and Huang Chao wrought havoc.

In what dynasty has there not been a Hou Jing? Furthermore, regarding the morning... (Note: The final phrase "旦以" (dàn yǐ) appears to be an incomplete fragment or a transition to another topic, as the provided text ends abruptly.)
A son’s killing of his father is like the wildness of a shadow; what hesitation could there be in doing it?
Although Jing fell into Taicheng, he did not commit regicide against Emperor Wu; how can he be subject to reproach for that?
Gengwu: The first year of the Dàbǎo era of Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty; the sixteenth year of the Dàtǒng era of Emperor Wendi of Western Wei.
Gao Yang, the Emperor Wen of Northern Qi, succeeded the Eastern Wei by means of abdication and ascended the throne at Jinyang (from Gengwu to Dingyou, five rulers).

In the eighteenth year [of his reign], Emperor Wen of the Jianwen era entrusted his heart to the wondrous Dharma and extensively surveyed the profound scriptures. He compiled the *Fají* (Collection of the Dharma) in two hundred fascicles and the *Fǎbǎoliánbì* (Linked Jades of the Dharma Treasure) in over four hundred pieces.
He drew blood to transcribe ten sets of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and constructed Zijing and Baoen Monasteries. Thus it was done.
His natural disposition was lofty and brilliant, yet his character was weak and yielding; in the end, he was controlled by Hou Jing and could not establish himself independently.
This, too, was brought about by the workings of time and destiny. (Byan Zheng) The Emperor ascended the Chongyun Hall. Hou Jing and the Emperor prostrated before the Buddha and made a vow, saying:
"From this day forward, between sovereign and subject, there shall be no mutual suspicion or duplicity. I, your servant, shall certainly not betray Your Majesty, nor shall Your Majesty fail me."
Fu Chen. Northern Qi.
Emperor Wenxuan Gao Yang, the Xianzu of the dynasty, received the abdication of Emperor Xiaojing of Eastern Wei in the fifth month of this year and ascended the throne.

He changed the era name to Tianbao. The Emperor had cultivated Buddhist wisdom from an early age, and his sagely intelligence was rarely fathomable. Having attained the great mandate, he promoted [the faith].
He promoted the Buddhist faith. The following year, an imperial edict stated: "I look up with reverence to the Compassionate and Enlightened One, who brought peace and stability to the four seas.

In wishing to repay His virtue, I rely upon the Perfectly Awakened One. All species of predatory birds that take life should be released into the mountains and forests for the sake of the Empress Dowager."
A jeweled stūpa was erected, and the Office of Falconers was abolished to establish Bode Temple (Baode Si).
From the beginning of time until this Xinwei year, there have been a total of two hundred eighty-three generations spanning seven hundred sixty-two thousand four hundred fifteen years.
This is the period from the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One until the present year.
One thousand five hundred years later, in the year *wenshen* (792), Emperor Yi of the Later Liang, who was formerly the Prince of Xiangdong, changed the era name to the first year of Chengsheng.
In the third month, he decisively defeated the army of Hou Jing; Jing fled and was subsequently killed by Hou Tian. In the eleventh month, Yi ascended the throne.
He was located in Jiangling. He was Emperor Shizu Yuan (Emperor Yuan of the Liu Song dynasty). The Emperor possessed a versatile nature and attained subtle, profound insight.
He founded the two monasteries of Tianju and Tiangong. Whenever he lectured on the Lotus Sūtra, he would expound upon the Chengbao lun (Treatise on the Accomplishment of Jewels) by Bian Zheng.
During the Northern Qi dynasty, in this year, an imperial edict summoned Master Sengchou to the capital. The Emperor personally led the imperial procession out of the city to welcome him.
Sengchou was over seventy years of age, and his spiritual bearing was serene and expansive. The Emperor supported him as he entered the inner palace, where he expounded the True Principle for him;

the Emperor prostrated himself to receive the path of dhyāna. From then on, he increasingly sought instruction, his devotion becoming profound and earnest. Consequently, he received the Bodhisattva precepts and thereupon [ceased...]

He prohibited alcohol and meat, released hawks and falcons, and abolished official hunting and fishing, thereby transforming the realm into a land of benevolence. He further banned slaughter throughout the empire;

thus, in the third month of that year, he earnestly exhorted the people to observe the fasts and precepts. Officials were required to abstain from vegetables grown for private consumption, and all pungent roots and spices were eliminated.

He remained in seclusion within the imperial palace for over forty days before taking leave to return to the mountains. By imperial decree, he was established at Yunmen Monastery in the city of Ye to reside there.
One day, the Emperor traveled in his carriage to pay a visit to Huida. Huida sat upon his meditation seat and did not rise to welcome him.

Someone slandered him to the Emperor, who intended to enter the monastery to investigate this lack of respect. Huida learned of this and went out to wait for the Emperor twenty *li* away. When the Emperor arrived, he asked why Huida had come so far to meet him.
Huida replied, "I feared that my body might be impure and defile the *saṃghārāma*; therefore, I waited here. The Emperor felt ashamed and repented.
Having said this, he personally carried Sengchou’s body to the monastery. Sengchou would not accept it.
The Emperor said, “A disciple carrying his master about the world is not enough to atone for my transgressions. He then asked the Master, “What did you do in your previous life?
