He replied, “I was once a rākṣasa king; that is why I still have a fondness for killing even now. He then recited a mantra over water in a basin and had the Emperor look at his own reflection in it; it was indeed as described.
The Emperor was greatly startled. From that time forward, he practiced *dhyāna* and cultivated the Way with even greater intensity than before.

He further issued an edict to all provinces to establish separate meditation halls (*zenji*), ordering those who had attained mastery in concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to go there and provide instruction. The state treasury was divided into three parts; one portion was to be used for the needs of the state.

One [statue] was for his own personal use, and one was offered to the Triple Gem. From that time on, he thoroughly renounced worldly attachments and turned toward the Dharma with a devotion unparalleled since antiquity.
He extensively constructed temples and stupas until monks and nuns filled every province; thus did the Buddha-Dharma flow eastward and flourish here (from the *Sengshi*).
Jiaxu: During the Datong era of the Northern Wei, an imperial edict was issued to Master Sengshi, stating: "Your eyes are beautiful with double pupils, resembling those of Yu Shun;
your back is prominent and hunched, much like that of Duke Zhou. Your virtuous character is pure and sublime, and your capacity for conduct is difficult to emulate.

You may be designated as a 'Sacred Tripitaka Master' so that your words may serve as a treasure for the world... (and so forth). At this time, because the Master’s talent was profound and his virtue great, he was again requested [to serve as...].

The Tripitaka Master of the State [resided] there; from this time on, he transformed and edified those in the capital, and his influence grew ever more flourishing over the long years (according to the *Sengshi*).
Initially, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty had commissioned two golden statues and constructed the Chongyun Hall, where he performed rites for some fifty years.

By this time, the region south of the Yangtze River was not yet settled, and various factions vied for power based on their respective interests. Consequently, Wang Sengbian dispatched Du Kan to take charge of the protection of the palace gates.

Kāṅ was by nature obstinate and fierce; he wished to destroy the two statues to make them into ingots. He first ordered several men to ascend the Sanxiu Pavilion and have them chisel the crowns of the Buddhas' heads.
As soon as the hammers and chisels were raised, the two statues turned their heads simultaneously, and the arms of all those sent could no longer be lifted.
He lost his speech and became like one intoxicated; Du Kan experienced the same. He continued to see Vajrapāṇis vying with one another to strike him;
his entire body was severely burned and blistered, and he died with his skin pierced through to the bone (from the *Gantong lu*).
Emperor Wenxuan of the Northern Qi greatly promoted the Buddha-dharma.

During the Tianbao era, the Daoist Lu Xiujing, perceiving that Emperor Wu of the Liang had opened his reign with good fortune, issued an imperial edict in the third year of the Tianjian era to abandon Daoism and honor Buddhism.

Lu Xiujing and his disciples defected to the Qi state, exhausting their gold and jade to bestow upon various nobles and officials, hoping to entrust them with their aspirations so as to revive the Daoist teachings. The Emperor then issued an edict summoning him.
The śramaṇas competed in magical arts with the Daoist practitioners. The Daoists cast spells upon the śramaṇas’ robes and alms bowls, causing them to spin;

they cast spells upon the rafters of the various directions, making them shift from horizontal to vertical. The śramaṇas remained silent, unable to offer a counter-response. Nobles and commoners, both men and women alike, regarded the Daoist disciples as superior.
The Daoist practitioner, Jing, then spoke loftily in self-conceit, proclaiming: "Supernatural powers are employed as expedient means to suppress the arrogant and humble the haughty. The śramaṇas...
[The opponent] manifested one [form]; I shall manifest two. Now I will briefly display a minor artifice; let us both withdraw from the debate, and the matter may then be seen for itself.
The Emperor commanded Master Shangtong to compete with Jing. Shang said, "Mundane arts and minor skills are a disgrace even to secular scholars, let alone to those who have transcended the world.
Nevertheless, since Heaven has ordained that we oppose one another, how can I remain silent? Let the monk from the lowest seat in the assembly face him. At that time—
Shi Tanyan was seated at the end of the row. Intoxicated from drinking wine, he was supported by attendants as he ascended to the high seat;
standing there, he laughed and said to Li Zong, "Just now you boasted of your magical arts. 'One and two'—this truly has its profound significance.
He then stood upon the seat with one leg raised and said, "I have already manifested one; you should manifest two. Neither could respond with a word. Tanyan then recited a spell.

"As for those garments and articles that flew up, it was merely to test your skill. He then commanded that the robes and bowl of Master Chou be brought forth and incanted over them, yet they remained entirely motionless.
The Emperor ordered ten men to lift them, but they were as immovable as before. Thereupon, he placed the robes upon the rafters of the hall.
The matter remained unresolved and without proof; the Daoist masters looked at one another with shame, yet they still claimed victory through verbal sophistry.

They then said, "In our own tradition, we designate the Buddhist school as 'Inner' (Nèi), which is small; we designate the Daoist school as 'Outer' (Wài), which is great. Xuǎnying immediately replied:

The Prince sat within; he settled the minor commoners and remained silent with his attendants, their mouths sealed and speechless. As Wenxuan took his seat, he personally examined their merits and faults.

His followers sought his compassion for their deliverance, and all abandoned heterodoxy to return to the orthodox path. He issued an edict ordering them to shave their heads and don the monastic robes.
As for those who claim to be "Immortals" (Shenxian), they were all made to ascend the Three-Jade Terrace and commanded to cast themselves down to fly away;

yet their corpses were all found abandoned on the ground, and their deceptions were thus exposed. Thereupon, an edict was issued, stating: "The Dharma-gate is non-dual, and the True Doctrine resides in Oneness.

To seek it via the correct path, tranquility and detachment are the foundation. The *Jijiu* and Daoists are false pretenders in this world whom the common people have not yet awakened to. Thus, there arose [only] reverence...
As for the veneration [of spirits]: yeast and malt are their flavors; where, then, is purity and emptiness? The *gāthā* and *bhūmi* are sweet, yet compassion is forever severed.

Above, it differs from benevolent shrines; below, it deviates from sacrificial rites. It is fitting that all such practices be prohibited and no longer observed. A decree is hereby issued to be known by those far and near:

those among the Daoists who wish to take refuge [in the Buddhist path] shall all be entrusted to the Great Master of the Supreme Mystery (Zhaoxuan Dastong Shangfa Shi), who shall grant them permission to leave the household life.

The details are as found in his separate biography. At that time, the realm of Qi was single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha; there were no dualistic concerns in the state. This continued until the Sui dynasty.

As for Master Xuán, he was a leader of the highest caliber. If one evaluates a person by their bone-structure, he was like a thousand-li steed whose hooves would have matched those of a legendary horse in another age.

To judge a man solely by his outward appearance is an error since antiquity; thus, one might merely distinguish between black and yellow robes, but how could such a person ever withstand [the challenges of the times]?
Bingzi (the year 656), the seventh year of the Tianbao era. Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty was at Jinyang.
He dispatched a man on a white dromedary to my temple to take away the scripture cases. When the messenger asked which temple it was, the Emperor said, "Simply let the dromedary lead the way;

you will know the location of the temple yourself. At evening, they departed the city. The dromedary traveled with great speed and suddenly seemed to fall asleep; in an instant, they arrived at a mountain named...
It was dark and silent. At the midpoint of the mountain was a temple. A group of śrāmaṇeras said, "Gao Yang has arrived on a camel," and they led him into the temple.

There he saw an elderly monk. After bowing, Gao Yang asked, "How is it that Gao Yang has become the Son of Heaven? The monk replied, "He is sagely and wise. Gao Yang asked, "For what purpose have you come?
The monk replied, "I was ordered to fetch a scripture case. The monk said, "While Yang is at the temple, he is too lazy to read the scriptures; order him to travel north to Dongdu."
"This is his room; you may take the casket and give it to him. He then mounted a camel and returned. It was as if he had been in a dream, and suddenly he arrived at Jinyang.
He returned with the casket to report his success. Not long after, the Emperor traveled to Guokou Well Temple, where there was a foolish man who had practiced self-immolation.
He did not understand the speech. Suddenly he said to the Emperor, "I shall go on ahead; you may follow later" (*Gantong lu*).
Bingzi year, the first year of the Taiping era of Emperor Jing of the Liang dynasty. The Western Wei Gongdi abdicated the throne to Yuwen Jue.
This was the Northern Zhou Emperor Xiaomin. He ascended the throne on the twelfth month.
Dingchou: In the ninth month of the second year of the Taiping era of the Liang, the Emperor Jing abdicated the throne to the High Ancestor of the Chen dynasty.

The Treatise says: Observing the rise of the Liang dynasty, there was something that distinguished it from the Wei and Jin; observing the governance of the Liang, there was something by which the present age was established.
In the histories of the Song and Qi, its civil virtue was praised with these words: "It possesses this martial achievement.

Beginning with the campaigns of Tang and Wu, it ultimately completes the legacy of Yao and Shun. This is the factual record. How could the Liang have any cause for shame? Emperor Wu received the Mandate.
Thereafter, for several decades, its rites, music, and cultural institutions were preeminent among the Southern Dynasties.
This governance of the Liang stood alone, surpassing that of the five preceding Southern courts and the eight successive dynasties of both the North and South. Song Jingwen’s *New History* states:

"The Liang, the Xiao clan, rose in Jiangzuo and truly possessed merit toward the people; they ultimately committed no great evil and perished only because their power grew faint. Their remaining blessings—"

As for his descendants, eight branches emerged during the rise of the Tang dynasty, yet no one among them is heard to have served as a prime minister. [The historian] Liang was demoted because of his devotion to Buddhism;
this was something Wen Zhongzi understood. Thus, he recorded in the *Zhongshuo*: "The state of Liang perished because its observance of fasting and ritual purity was corrupted;
it was not the fault of Śākyamuni. This was likely because he lamented that the court historians did not understand why Liang fell, instead contending over superficial details.
Thus, the blame is cast upon the Buddha. Emperor Wu failed to seek out worthy talent, instead promoting the mediocre and base.

As his years grew advanced, he devoted himself to ritual sacrifices and became mired in worldly attachments to Buddhism; consequently, there were no remonstrating ministers at court. One knows one’s son best as no one does the father;

yet, while three pests were being exterminated together, he alone preserved his heir to maintain the correct virtue. Had he not inflicted immediate execution, he would have allowed the dark summons of a rebellious fledgling to draw near within the span of a few inches.
The jade steps [of the imperial court] were overgrown with lush weeds. Thus, Hou Jing was able to raise his banner in defiance of the rightful order.
This was because he knew that Liang possessed famous generals whom they neglected to employ; the soldiers were ignorant of warfare, and so there was an opportunity for him to exploit.
Who were these famous generals? Wang Shen-nian, Yang Kan, Wang Seng-bian, Hou Tian, Xu Shi-pu, and Lu Fa-huo. Such was the talent of these several men in Liang.
He was unable to employ them. Du Sengming, Zhou Wenyu, Hou Sengdu, Mai Tiezhang, and others all possessed the talent of generals;
yet the Liang court did not utilize them, instead providing resources to the usurping ministers. Xiangdong lacked the way of commanding generals, and thus Hou Jing remained unhanged.
Yet the Chen family inquired about the tripods; the house of Liang collapsed swiftly. This was the source of its calamity.

Those who argue that benevolence, righteousness, ritual, music, precepts, and wisdom were the misfortunes that caused the fall of Liang are mistaken. Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music—these were the means by which Yao, Shun, and the Three Dynasties achieved great order;
we have never heard of them causing great chaos at the outset. That which led to disorder was what followed [them].

It was merely that the succession lost its virtue. As for the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, Emperor Ming of the Han sought out their practitioners and transmitted the teachings to the world for two hundred years.
During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Taizong greatly promoted them; this did not hinder his governance during the Zhenguan era, yet the tradition lasted for three hundred years.
The Taizu and Taizong emperors of the Song dynasty also greatly promoted Buddhism, and its transmission lasted for over three hundred years. For these reasons, [the tradition continued].
If this is clarified, it will be evident that the Buddha does not act as a parasite upon the royal transformation [of the state], but rather provides resources for its governance.
Indeed, those who claim that the Buddha brought about the ruin of the Liang dynasty likely do not present a correct argument (as seen in the "Treatise on the Hidden Son of the Liang House").
A Mirror for Buddhist Aid Through Successive Dynasties, Volume Four.
A Mirror for Buddhist Aid Through Successive Dynasties, Volume Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xizhong of Yifeng in Min.
Southern and Northern Dynasties:
Southern Chen (The Chen clan [Baxian]. Received the abdication from the Liang. Capital: Jiankang. From Dingchou to Jiyou. Five rulers. Thirty-three years).
Later Liang (Xiao Zhao; capital at Jiangling; three rulers; thirty-eight years).
Northern Qi (the Gao clan; Gao Yang succeeded to the abdication of Eastern Wei; capital at Ye; from the year of Gengwu to Dingyou; five rulers; twenty-eight years).

The Zhou [posthumous name: Wenjue]. Having received the abdication from the Western Wei, it was headquartered in Chang’an. From the year Bingzi to the end of Xinchou, there were five rulers for twenty-five years.
Emperor Gaozu Wudi of Chen received the abdication from the Liang; he ascended the throne in the ninth month and changed the era name to Yongding.

The Emperor, having received the precious mandate to rule as sovereign, rose with the Huichang era to govern and shepherd the people. He stood nine chi tall, with a beard three chi long, reaching past his hands when hanging down.
Xie Xuanming was lofty and unrestrained in spirit; he quelled many hardships and restored the old administration of the Liang dynasty. He held the followers of Śākyamuni in high esteem.
Of the seven hundred or so temples that had existed in Jinling since ancient times, most had been burned and destroyed by Hou Jing; once the Emperor ascended the throne, he restored them all.

The translation of scriptures and the preaching of the Way continued without interruption from the previous dynasty. On the sixth day of the intercalary month, the Buddha’s tooth relic was brought forth from the residence of Du Mu, and a great assembly was convened.
The Emperor went out before the palace gate and prostrated himself. In the following year, during the Great Assembly, he made offerings to the monks and bestowed alms;

he released captive creatures and pardoned criminals, widely proclaimed the ten wholesome deeds, and guided the four classes of the people. He transcribed scriptures, ordained monks, cast images, and constructed temples—all of which were magnificent and served as adornments for the state.

This influence reached all spirits. In the fifth month, he visited Zangyan Temple and performed the ritual of "giving away his body. The ministers submitted a memorial requesting that he return to the palace.
In the year Jǐmǎo, the Emperor passed away (according to Biàn Zhènglùn).

Emperor Xiàomǐn of the Northern Zhou dynasty received the abdication from Western Wei in the twelfth month of Bǐngzǐ. The Emperor was sagacious and refined, possessing penetrating insight and broad erudition;
Heaven had bestowed upon him divine martial prowess. The people brought their lawsuits to him, and he sat holding the "Golden Mirror," exalting like the "Jade Balance."

He established the supreme standard and greatly propagated the transformation through the Buddha’s image; he widely opened the gate of compassion. The men of renown and virtue within the realm all admired his righteousness and returned to his benevolence.
Alas, Heaven did not grant him a long life. He passed away in the ninth month of the year Dingchou.
Dingchou (1st year), the ninth month: Emperor Sejong, the filial and enlightened Emperor Yù, ascended the throne.

The Emperor reverently served the Three Vehicles and drew close to his nine branches of kin, even down to his own progeny and the pillars of state. From the high officials to the common functionaries, all five ranks and ten classes recognized the path of taking refuge;
through external observation and internal awakening, they ascended together through the gate of liberation. In the year Wuyin, he constructed a *lú* (monastery) for the sake of the late Emperor.
The *kāṣāya* robes were woven into the form of one statue, together with two bodhisattvas, reaching a height of twenty-six feet.

There were also sixteen sandalwood statues of the same size, each accompanied by two bodhisattvas, as well as figures such as Vajrapāṇi and lions; they were so exquisitely crafted that they surpassed the natural world and were as wondrous as divine creation. (Bian Zheng)
Ji-mao: Emperor Gaozu of the Chen dynasty was about to prepare for his funeral and had constructed a carriage for the warm and cool [procession].

Emperor Wen wished to take the pearl ornaments from the Buddha-canopy in the Chongyun Hall of Emperor Wu of Liang to adorn the funeral rites. When the laborers were sufficient in number, suddenly clouds gathered and coalesced;
a great rain poured down in torrents, while thunder shook and lightning flashed. Smoke spread across the surface of the hall, and flames blazed amidst the clouds. Suddenly—
When the shadow of the Chongyun Hall was observed, the two statues made of gold and silver, the eight classes of divine kings, and their curtained seats all rose up simultaneously.
Enveloped by smoke and fire, they suddenly vanished into the distance. Spectators filled the nation. After the weather cleared, when they looked back, only the foundations remained.
On that day, people saw the hall and its images flying through the air over the sea (*Gantong lu*).
Gengchen (the 17th day of the 8th month): Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty, named Yong, ascended the throne. He was styled Wendi.
He commissioned a sixteen-foot statue of Śākyamuni Buddha, along with statues of Bodhisattvas, holy monks, and Vajrapāṇi lions. He further had two hundred and twenty jeweled pagodas constructed.
Furthermore, he established the Ningguo, Huichang, and Yongning Monasteries in the capital to cultivate merit for the deceased. (Bian Zheng)
Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty once said to Chan Master Chou during a leisure moment, "I wish to witness the spiritual wonders of the Buddha.
Chou replied, "This is not appropriate for a śramaṇa. The Emperor insisted, so Chou cast his *kāṣāya* robe upon the ground. The Emperor ordered ten men to lift it, but it would not move.
Chou then commanded a novice monk to retrieve it, and he did so without any difficulty. Thereupon, the Emperor’s faith became profound, and he bestowed many rewards and honors upon him.

He was treated with great generosity. Every New Year, the Emperor would ask Master Chou about the auspiciousness or misfortune of the coming year. In the tenth year of the Tianbao era, the Master said, "This year will not be good.
The Emperor was displeased. He asked again, "How about [the future]? The Master replied, "I, this poor monk, shall also not remain long.
That summer, the Master passed away; by winter, the Emperor had died (according to his biography).

Xinsi (the year 561 CE): In the first year of the Baoding era of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty, a thunderstorm struck a cliff on Mount Yugu in Liangzhou, causing a stone image eighteen feet high to emerge, though it was headless.
At the beginning of the Zhou dynasty, a light emanated from a gully east of the city; upon inspection, it was the head of the image.
When the head was brought and placed upon the body of the statue, they fit together perfectly. This miraculous event occurred approximately forty years after the image’s initial emergence.
The image had square feet. In that year, it was established as Ruixiang Temple. When Jian-de was about to abolish the Dharma, the head of the image fell off of its own accord.

The Emperor ordered it to be restored; by the following morning, it was as it had been before. Consequently, there arose a prophecy concerning the abolition of the Dharma and the destruction of the state. Although the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Dharma, it did not reach this image.
Its spiritual wonders were manifold (as recorded in the *Gantong lu*).

Renwu: Emperor Wucheng of the Qi dynasty was deeply devoted to the Buddha-vehicle. He initiated the construction of temples and stupas, discarding his precious imperial robes and contributing his personal wealth as alms.

He recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* several times every month. On his tiered terraces and detached pavilions, he established monasteries, filling them with jade, pearls, and gems as ritual offerings.
Within these, he constructed altars and invited the Dharma Master Shang to bestow upon him the precepts of taking refuge.

The Dharma Master prostrated himself with his hair touching the ground; having joined him in salutation, he ascended the seat. Once the reception was complete, he commanded the eight high-ranking ministers, as well as the empress, consorts, and their kinsmen, to all receive the precepts of taking refuge.
He then founded Baode Temple and appointed the Dharma Master Shang to preside over it. As for the Dharma Master Shang:
The mountain of his precepts was lofty and steep; the ocean of his wisdom was profound and deep. His virtue served as a model for others, and his majesty could inspire awe in all beings.
Although he held the high office of National Preceptor under the Great Sovereign, he wore coarse cloth garments and never rode in a sedan chair. Consequently, the world esteemed him all the more.

Thus, during the Wei and Qi dynasties, he served successively as the Metropolitan Superintendent (Tongdu) for a period when the monastic community comprised nearly two million monks and nuns, and he maintained the supreme administrative order of over forty thousand.

In the year during the reign of Emperor Wenxuan, the Buddhist scriptures flourished greatly. [Sengshang] bore the responsibility of unifying and harmonizing them, propagating them both within and without the court, earning the trust of both the monastic and lay communities (from the *Sengshi*).

Jichou (493): In the fourth year of the Tianhe era of the Northern Zhou dynasty, in the third month, Emperor Wu summoned renowned Confucian scholars, monks, Daoists, and the high officials to the main hall.

The Emperor ascended the throne and personally deliberated upon the relative merits of the Three Teachings. By the beginning of the fourth month, he issued an edict to extensively summon both monastics and laypeople to state their arguments with full candor.
He further commanded the Grand Master Zhen Luan to examine the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism and determine which preceded the other.

Regarding the subsequent [discussion on] the shallow and the deep: Sengluan’s *Xiaodao lun* (Treatise on Ridiculing the Dao) in three fascicles (contained in the Tripitaka). In the fifth month, he again assembled his ministers to examine Sengluan’s treatise.

Gengzi, the second month of the second year of the Daxiang era. An imperial edict stated: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and sublime; it has been revered by all throughout antiquity.

"Understand my intention," [said the Emperor] (Beishi). In the fourth month, he issued another edict, stating: "The principles of the teachings are profound and subtle; their spiritual wonders are vast and great.

Although the rituals for broad propagation have been extensively opened up and the procedures for cultivation made accessible, those who revere and serve [the Dharma] should not all shave their heads.

It is appropriate that they model themselves after the dignified appearance of a Bodhisattva and temporarily wear crowns and sashes. Let the relevant authorities draft a formal protocol. Thereupon, Senglin and others composed an elegant manual based on ancient precedents.
One hundred and twenty śramaṇas of renowned virtue entered Zhuhusi and continued to reside there as its abbots (same source). In the fifth month, Emperor Tianyuan passed away.

During his reign, the Emperor had commissioned four niches for statues totaling over ten thousand figures, transcribed three thousand copies of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, and maintained the practice of the six fasts and eight precepts with unceasing recitation and contemplation (Bian Zhenglun).
Emperor Jing was still a child when Yang Jian governed the administration; he was subsequently enfeoffed as the Duke of Sui and greatly propagated Buddhism.

In the sixth month, the monk Fazang descended from the mountain and engaged the Duke of Sui in a debate on the *Sambhāṣa-sūtra* (Sanbao jing) for one night. He was immediately granted tonsure and bestowed with dharma robes and other items before returning to the mountain.
Regarding the two teachings of Śākya and the Way, those among the former śramaṇas and Daoists who were diligent and resolute were selected to enter the Buddhist path.
In the seventh month, Fazang was summoned down from the mountain to further discuss the propagation of the teachings.

On the fifteenth day, he was ordered to conduct an inspection and ordain one hundred and twenty monks; each was granted monastic robes and sent back to their respective residences (from the *Tongjian*).

The Dharma Master Zhixuan was the son of the Xu family of Chengdu. He entered the monastic order in his youth and traveled to the capital to pursue studies, where he gained renown throughout the regions of Jing and Luo.

During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, he was summoned for an audience; his eloquence in debate surpassed that of his peers, and his voice was clear and resonant. Later, he returned to his hometown.
During the auspicious era of the Great Sui, Zhou Xuanming, the Regional Inspector of Shu, entered the court for an examination. Emperor Wen of the Sui asked him, "Where is Dharma Master Zhixuan?"
"Huìyá. Xuānmíng did not know how to respond. Emperor Wén said, "He is a renowned monk of this entire kingdom, yet you do not even recognize him;
how can you claim to be conducting an inspection? Xuānmíng bowed his head in apology. Upon returning, he went first to the monastery to pay his respects.
The Master resided at Fúshèng and later entered Sānxué Mountain, where he spontaneously composed a poem, saying: "Rugged peaks meet with layered mists, The steep crags rise halfway up."

O Celestial One! The precipitous cliffs, having lowered, rise once more; the perilous peaks, severed, join again. Slanting stones overlook the cascading ravines; swirling currents pour forth from the winding springs. The wild flowers’ crimson hue betrays the frost upon the grass;
the arrival of spring is heralded by the birds themselves. The trees are like brocade, woven without a loom; the monkeys' cries need no borrowed strings.

Leaves so dense that the wind finds it hard to pass; branches so sparse that shadows easily pierce through. Clutching my books, I lean beside the secluded pond; leaning on my staff, I wander among the fragrant blooms.
Tian Youxin wandered his mind beyond the clear Milky Way and fixed his thoughts at the edge of the white clouds. Renown was not his wish; he stilled his intentions and remained serene.
Worn out by the clamor of the world, he eventually retired into seclusion. He passed away with a joyful smile at the age of one hundred and two.

the first year of Dading was changed). From the Northern Dynasties— the Yuan Wei, Eastern and Western Wei, Northern Qi, and Later Zhou— these five states together comprised one hundred and sixty [years].

During the eras of Yao and Shun, the dynastic chronologies were transmitted together. Someone asked: "The Liang dynasty arose when Wu Pi overthrew the cruel and violent, successfully establishing an imperial enterprise and reigning as sovereign for over fifty years;

Entering upon this practice, you served as a bridge for the Ten-Thousand-Chariot Sovereign to cultivate the virtues of a commoner; yet your cultivation remained untainted even as the threat of ruin approached.
Was it that the bridge was not sufficient? Why did the merit of your humility fail to take effect? The Master replied:

"The Buddhist teaching is the ferry and bridge to transcend the world, the track for severing the dust of defilement. When it is applied within the square inch of the heart, one transcends the realm of non-existence."

This is the manifestation [of the Way]. Once the accumulation of defilements is exhausted and攀緣 (pān-yuán, the grasping of external objects) has ceased, one subsequently enters the gate of liberation.
As for the methods for transforming the world, there are generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
these constitute the six *pāramitās*. How are they any different from benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and sincerity? It is simply because of what is cultivated.
The cause is the factor, and the retribution is the fruit. When people cultivate these six practices, they are mostly incomplete;
if even one is deficient, the fruit likewise perishes accordingly. This is why Zongming was ugly in appearance yet wise in mind;
Zhao Tai was eminent in talent yet humble in station; Yan Bao was wealthy yet lacked literary refinement; and Yuan Xian was poor yet possessed the Way. Their differences were as follows:
This gap is vast and profound; prosperity and ruin, gain and loss, all necessarily depend upon it.

Taxes were lightened and punishments mitigated; corvée labor was reduced and levies diminished. All who possessed teeth and wore hair rejoiced in the Great Peace.

When Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty suppressed the teachings, the nun went into hiding within the imperial household; she passed away shortly thereafter.
It so happened that the Emperor himself subsequently entered from the east of the mountains to become the Son of Heaven and greatly promoted the Buddha-dharma, exactly as the nun had foretold.

The blockade suddenly opened. The Emperor loathed this omen and consequently sold himself as a slave to a Buddhist temple to suppress it.
In that year, the kingdom was destroyed by the Sui. From the founding of the Sui until this point, the empire had been unified.

An envoy was dispatched to summon Jñānagupta, who arrived and was ordered by imperial decree to translate ancient Sanskrit texts at the Office of the Interior (Neishisheng), where he was appointed exclusively to oversee the translation work (according to the *Sui Shu*).

Xue Jun, whose courtesy name was Daize, was appointed at the beginning of the Kaihuang era as Vice Minister of the Department of Waterways in the Ministry of Personnel. He was subsequently transferred to Vice Minister of the Department of Merit.
When he was a child, he was playing with several other children of his clan on the banks of the Run River when he saw a yellow snake that had horns and feet.

He summoned his children to look together, but none saw anything at all. Believing it to be an ill omen, he returned home deeply distressed. When his mother questioned him about it, Xu Jun told her the truth.
At that time, a monk came to the house seeking a meal; the mother informed him of what had occurred. The monk said, "This is an auspicious sign for this child;
he will early on become famous throughout the world. However, his lifespan will not exceed six or seven years. Having finished speaking, the monk vanished. Later...
Entering the court, he held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem. He passed away at the age of forty-two; thus, the words of the "Four Sevens" were verified.
In the tenth year, the *gengxu* year, the Emperor visited Jinyang and issued an imperial decree for Dharma Master Qian to accompany the imperial entourage.

Upon arriving in the Bingzhou region, the Emperor again issued an edict ordering the monk to perform rites within the palace hall. At night, he summoned Qian to enter the inner quarters and shared a couch with the Emperor. The Emperor said, "Brother..."

When the Prince traveled to this place, he encountered a monk who had been privately ordained during the Dàyu era and wished to ordain him. Huìqiān said, "In the past, when Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu dynasty suppressed the Dharma, the assembly of monks went into hiding.
Now that Your Majesty presides over the Great Mandate, you have further expounded the Gate of the Dharma; there are none who do not sing its praises.

This man came here seeking refuge in Your Majesty’s sacred virtue. Although he has repeatedly received permission for ordination, his arrival was earlier than others, which resulted in this discrepancy."

[The Emperor] agreed. Furthermore, as heaven and earth cover and sustain all, there are none who are not the subjects of the King. Since the Most Honored One draws in people from all quarters, how could the blessing stop with Gao Meng alone?
After the Emperor had reflected for a short while, he finally granted his consent. He then issued an edict stating:

"From the fourth month of the tenth year onwards, all monks and nuns who have been privately ordained shall be permitted to remain in the monastic order. Consequently, throughout the land, tens of thousands received ordination.

This was due to the efforts of Sengquan, who gathered ten thousand people. Shortly thereafter, an imperial edict was issued establishing Shengguang Temple in the capital for the Fourth Prince, Xiao Shu, the Prince of Shu.
By imperial decree, Sengquan and his disciples were invited to reside within the temple and receive the Prince’s offerings, while the Grand Ministers and high officials [also attended].
In the intervals between state affairs, [the officials] all took up their scrolls to receive his instructions (as recorded in the *Sengshi*).
That year there was a drought, and an imperial decree ordered Dharma Master Tanyan to pray for rain. When the rain did not fall, the Emperor asked him the reason.

He replied: "Your Majesty and your ministers, though you have mastered the principles of governance, still fall short in the profound transformation of the Way. That the rain is desired yet does not fall is due to this."
This was the first and second [instance]. The Emperor perceived his intention and commanded the relevant authorities to select an auspicious day to establish the ritual in the main hall.

He then ordered that [the monk] be invited to receive the eight precepts. After the ministers had received them in succession, the scorching heat was like a conflagration, yet a great rain poured down profusely. The Emperor was greatly pleased.

From then on, whenever he entered the court, he would invariably personally serve the imperial meals to him. In this year, an edict was issued for Chan Master Zhishun of Mount Zhanhuang. The edict stated:
"The Emperor respectfully inquires after the health of Chan Master Zhishun of Mount Zhanghong in Zhaozhou.

We hope that your physical well-being remains clear and excellent as you guide the common people so that they may achieve realization early. We are deeply pleased. We, the Emperor, shall extensively protect the True Dharma from long ago..."

Do not be indolent at night. I have now dispatched the Grand Master of the Palace (Kaifu) Lu Yuanshou to personally convey my intentions and to deliver incense offerings, as detailed in the separate document (from the *Monastic Biographies*).

Xin Hai, the eleventh year. The Imperial Edict stated: "The Tathāgata established his teachings with the principle of equality at their core; the Bodhisattva’s application of mind is fundamentally without distinction.
Thus, he is able to serve as a bridge for all categories of beings and to deliver the multitudes of living things. I, the Emperor, occupy the position of the sovereign of men."
To cause the Three Jewels to flourish and to contemplate the ultimate truth forever;

to propagate and expound the Mahāyāna so that all dharmas are suddenly revealed as being without self or other—how much more so regarding meritorious deeds, which may involve both the public and the private. From this day forward, for all acts of constructing merit throughout the realm under heaven:

They were integrated into the construction of the monument. According to his wishes, no discrimination was made; thus all dharma-gates may together return to non-duality, and the worlds of the ten directions shall all reach Bodhi.

(The Kaihuang Record of the Three Jewels) As for the Dharma Master Tan Yan, when he approached the end of his life, he submitted a memorial to the Emperor to take leave, entrusting him with external protection.
The Emperor was deeply grieved. On the day of the funeral, the hundred officials wore white mourning garments to escort him, while the Grand Secretary [Shi]...

Dowei’s *Text for Sacrifice* states briefly: "In the past, when the Way fell into ruin and the profound guiding principles lost their fastenings, he dwelt his mind in the remote and vast, remaining firm and unshakable.
High positions and generous emoluments could not turn his thoughts; stern authority and severe laws were insufficient to intimidate his heart."
The Sage Emperor initiated his auspicious reign, and the Semblance Dharma was restored once more. Among the monastic community, he stood out as one who truly pleased the Imperial Will.

He humbled the gravity of the imperial throne to reaffirm the principle of the teacher-disciple relationship. Through him, the Triple Gem was propagated and protected; through him, the Two Truths were proclaimed and spread.
Truly, he was sufficient to follow in the footsteps of Fotudeng and Kumārajīva, surpassing even Dao’an and Huiyuan (from the *Monastic History*).
Gui-chou, the eighth day of the twelfth month of the twelfth year. Emperor Yang Jian of the Sui Dynasty, a disciple of the Buddha, respectfully addresses the Triple Gem of the ten directions.
Looking up with reverence, I reflect that the Tathāgata, through his great compassion, propagated the Way to deliver all living beings;
he severed the source of evil and opened the path of benevolence and goodness. From the court to the common people, all rely upon him. Since the Zhou dynasty’s violation of the constant order...

The sacred traces were treated with contempt; temples and stupas fell into ruin; and scriptures and images perished. Consequently, the ignorant had no means to guide those in delusion, and the wise had no way to seek out the numinous and holy.
Your disciple, having formerly relied upon the causal conditions of the Triple Gem, now enjoys this prosperous era and serves as parent to the people.

Desiring to rescue the common folk, I intend to once again manifest the venerable forms and re-establish the divine transformations. Where foundations have crumbled and traces been destroyed, [I shall restore them].

Regarding the adornment of the Dharma, the discarded images and lost scriptures were all restored through carving and transcription. Although my sincere devotion was earnest and thorough, I still feared it might not have been exhaustive;
thus, I sought them out again with renewed diligence until they could now be brought to light. Yet, for many years they had lain buried, defiled in improper places.
Such matters were the fault of your disciples. Now, before the Triple Gem, I repent with a resolute heart. At the time when the Zhou dynasty was extinguished—

Whether public or private, superior or inferior, those who have defaced images, destroyed scriptures, treated the Sangha with contempt, or demolished monasteries—may all such grave offenses be confessed.
I reverently offer one hundred and twenty thousand rolls of silk for all ruined and discarded scriptures and images; the Empress likewise offers the same amount as previously stated.

From the princes and dukes downward, even unto the common people, they further reverently offered one million coins, praying that the Triple Gem would bear witness and accept the repentance of their disciples.

At that time, the generals of the palace, the officials of the provinces and ministries, the subordinates and clerks of the prefectures and counties, the monks and nuns of various temples, and the long-established virtuous elders of the capital city all exhorted and led one another to provide vegetarian feasts on two successive days to celebrate the consecration of the scriptures and images. One hundred and ten...
Ten thousand people gathered.
When the Tiantai Master Zhiyi returned to Mount Lu, Prince Jin again invited him out of the mountains. There he composed the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.

Coincidentally, Empress Xiao fell ill; the Prince sent a letter requesting his aid. The Master established a seven-day vegetarian retreat and performed the *Guangming* Repentance. Suddenly, a bird appeared...
It flew into the altar and died after writhing about; a moment later, it flew away. The Master knew that the Consort would recover, and indeed she was cured the following day.
The King was greatly delighted. On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of the Ding-si year, he passed away while sitting upright at Shicheng Temple.
He composed seven sheets of writing to bid farewell to the Prince of Jin and entrusted him with the Great Dharma. The monk Guanding received these final instructions.

He wrote a letter to the Prince of Jin. The Prince dispatched his attendant, Wang Hong, to the mountain to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks and to establish Guoqing Temple (according to the *Benzhuan*).
Ding-si, the seventeenth year: Fei Changfang, a native of Chengdu, a scholar-translator of scriptures who had originally been a monk under the Zhou dynasty...

Having abandoned his religious life to return to secular status, he resumed the practice of a layman upon the rise of the Sui dynasty. He participated in the translation process, serving as a scribe and receiving the oral explanations of the terminology and meanings.
On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month of this year, he submitted the fifteen fascicles of the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through Successive Dynasties) which he had composed.

This work comprehensively records the scriptures translated throughout successive dynasties, along with the names and biographical details of the monastics and laypersons who served as translators. An imperial edict was subsequently issued for its circulation.
Regarding its inclusion in the canon:
On the day of Wumu, the Emperor wrote a letter to the śramaṇa Huìzé of Shānglín Monastery and others, saying: "I, the Emperor, have received the Mandate of Heaven to rule over the world.
I nurture the common people and hold the Triple Gem in supreme honor. I have caused the teachings to flourish once more, so that those in the four modes of birth may receive blessings. Ten...
May all sentient beings together ascend to benevolent longevity. You all, for the sake of the myriad living beings, propagate the holy teachings;
your sincere devotion and ascetic practices deeply console my heart. Since the benefits are manifold, do not decline the labor. (From the *Benzhuan*).

Xin-you (the 10th year of the sexagenary cycle), the first year of the Renshou era. When the Emperor was formerly in the state of a hidden dragon, he encountered a foreign monk who presented him with a packet of śarīra relics, saying:
"In the future, you, Dānapati, shall become the compassionate father of all under heaven. These are the remains of the Great Awakened One;

I have therefore left them for you to offer worship. After the Emperor ascended the throne, he once took the śarīra together with the Dharma Master Tanqian, each placing them in his palm to count them.
Whether few or many, they could ultimately not determine the exact number. Sengqian said, "The Dharma-body of all Buddhas transcends numerical measure;
it cannot be grasped or fathomed through worldly means. The Emperor then began to store them in a casket made of the seven precious gems.
When the realm attained great peace, the Emperor recalled this matter and consequently erected śarīra stupas in thirty prefectures, including Qiqi, Yong, Tai, Hua, E, and Heng.

In the sixth month, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "I look up with reverence to the Perfectly Awakened One’s great kindness and great compassion, which rescues and protects all sentient beings and serves as a bridge for the myriad classes of creatures.

I take refuge in the Triple Gem and have restored the holy teachings. It is my thought that I may share with the people of the four seas in cultivating meritorious deeds, forever establishing wholesome causes so that we may together ascend to the wondrous fruit.
It is fitting, therefore, to invite thirty śramaṇas who understand the characteristics of the Dharma and are capable of proclaiming and guiding it."

Each [official] shall take two attendants and one subordinate official, carrying one hundred and twenty *jin* of frankincense (*kūnyoku-kō*), to escort the *śarīra* along designated routes to thirty provinces to erect stupas.

In each province, three hundred and sixty monks shall perform ritual circumambulations (*gyōdō*) for seven days on behalf of me and all officials, both internal and external, as well as the common people.
They may accept offerings from individuals, limited to a maximum of ten *mon*. The money thus donated shall be used...

To provide for the construction of the stupa, separate the monks and nuns from the laity, and universally offer a vegetarian feast for the śarīra relics, limited to the hour of noon on the fifteenth day of the tenth month.

At that time, the stone casket shall be lowered together. From the Regional Commander and Prefectural Governor downward, all regular duties shall be suspended for seven days, except for matters of military emergency.
He was exclusively occupied with supervising the performance of the rites, striving to exhaust his utmost sincerity and reverence.
On the thirteenth day of this month, the Emperor personally took a casket made of the seven precious gems containing thirty *śarīra* relics and brought them forth from the inner palace.

He placed them upon the imperial table and, together with various *śramaṇas*, burned incense and prostrated, vowing that as a disciple he would always uphold the Triple Gem through the True Dharma and deliver all sentient beings. Thereupon, he took up a golden pitcher.
There were thirty lapis lazuli vases, each containing a golden vase, within which the śarīra was placed. The various śramaṇas each received the śarīra and proceeded forth.
Upon first entering the city, the regional governor, the military commissioner, and all the officials lined the road, leading the procession on foot.
The fourfold assembly, with dignified and solemn deportment, all came together with banners, canopies, platforms, and palanquins, accompanied by various kinds of music, to offer worship.

They surrounded him, chanting praises. Facing the fourfold assembly, the śramaṇa made this proclamation: "The Most Honored One, through the great compassion of a bodhisattva, took pity on sentient beings;
for this reason, he has distributed his relics to erect stūpas, so that the entire world may participate together."
This was a virtuous cause. He then requested a text for repentance, which read: "The Bodhisattva Precept Disciple, the Great Sui Emperor [Name], respectfully declares:
As a disciple of the Triple Gem, by the power of the Triple Gem, I have become the sovereign and father of all living beings. I now distribute the śarīra relics and erect stupas;
I pray that you will repent on behalf of all sentient beings for their manifold transgressions. When the great assembly heard this, they relinquished and offered wealth, goods, and clothing.

Beyond all calculation, they all made a vow: "From this day forward, we shall cultivate goodness and sever evil. Even those who were butchers, hunters, or cruel oppressors personally turned their thoughts toward the good.
When the śarīra was about to be placed within the casket, the śramaṇa Gao held the precious vase and paraded it before the great assembly.
All beheld a brilliant light together and wailed in mournful longing, the sound of their cries shaking the earth. At every place where it was enshrined, it was likewise...
It was all thus. On the fifteenth day of the tenth month at the hour of the horse (noon), the Emperor stood holding a jade scepter in the southwest of the Daxing Palace.
He invited the Buddha image and three hundred and sixty śramaṇas. With banners, canopies, incense, flowers, hymns, and music, [the image] came from Daxingshan Monastery to reside in the hall.
After burning incense and prostrating, he descended to the eastern corridor and personally led [the procession].
The officials of the civil and military ranks fasted and observed the precepts. When the enshrinement of the śarīra in the stūpa was completed, the Emperor said, "The Buddha-dharma has been restored;
there must surely be a spiritual response. Subsequently, reports were submitted from various locations, all of which recorded auspicious responses (*Hongming ji*).
In the tenth month, the Emperor and the Empress, whenever they ate, obtained śarīra from beneath their teeth. They placed one in a golden bowl where it floated upon the water and emerged.
He presented them to the officials. In a brief moment, two more grains suddenly appeared; in total, nineteen grains were obtained, many of which emitted brilliant light.

The King, dukes, and the hundred officials, perceiving that the manifestations of the śarīras were manifold, submitted a memorial to offer their congratulations. Furthermore, the Emperor issued an edict, saying: "I look up with reverence to the Truth."

To awaken all sentient beings under the universal canopy—this is why I, the Emperor, with a sincere heart, dedicate my merits and contemplate the exaltation of this supreme enterprise, so that it may extend throughout the realm, that all together may cultivate the causes of goodness.
Thus, I have distributed the śarīra relics and constructed divine stupas.

That the Great Sage has shown compassion and repeatedly manifested radiant signs, and that the śarīra has descended as a spiritual presence within the palace, is truly a great fortune for all living beings, extending these auspicious blessings far and wide.
I, the Emperor, together with the princes and dukes, as well as all the common people, ought to redouble our efforts to cause the Three Jewels to flourish.
There are currently still more than fifty relics of the True Body remaining; the relevant authorities should distribute them throughout the realm according to the previous protocol.

In this way, may those in the three evil paths and the six realms of existence alike be freed from their entanglements, and may all sentient beings, according to their natures, ascend together to the wondrous fruit of enlightenment. — Dated [Year], Goryeo.
The envoys from the three kingdoms of Baekje and Silla were about to return; each requested a śarīra to erect a stūpa for veneration in their own country.

The Emperor granted all these requests (both accounts are in the *Suíshū*). On the second day of the twelfth month, an imperial edict was issued to send the śarīra to Daxingshan Temple in the capital to erect a stūpa.
Ten million monastics and laypeople escorted it with reverence to the temple, where a Great Unobstructed Assembly was held.
Thereupon, they performed rites of repentance (as above).

In the second year, on the *renxu* day of the first month, the Emperor again distributed the śarīra relics to fifty-three prefectures, including Qin, Shan, Heng, Hang, and others, establishing spirit-stupas (*lingta*) in each.
He commanded all officials from the regional commanders (*zongduan*) and provincial governors (*cishi*) down to the county magistrates (*xianwei*) to suspend their regular duties [to attend].

For seven days, he invited the monks and offered them money, following the same procedure as before. It was scheduled that on the eighth day of the fourth month at noon, the stone caskets would be lowered together.

In each prefecture, there were auspicious responses: in Shan Prefecture, light was emitted four times, and within it were seen flowering trees, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth—not merely a single occurrence.
In the fifth month, within the capital city of Yongzhou, the heavens rained silver flowers. Six.

In the [blank] month, the envoys from various provinces who had escorted the śarīra relics returned to the palace. After they had been granted audience and comforted, on the ninth day, the Emperor departed for Cishi Monastery to hold a vegetarian feast in celebration of the auspicious omen.
Again, silver flowers rained down. At Shengguang Monastery, light was emitted daily; those who came to pay their respects filled the roads, and all conceived the aspiration for the Way.
Those who were carving images also saw light being emitted. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, at Yanxing [Monastery] in the capital...
At the temple, a sixteen-foot gilded bronze image was cast; heavenly silver flowers rained down. ○ Dharma Master Yuǎnwǎn completed the casting of a sixteen-foot image;
flowers rained down like mica, and celestial music filled the sky, ceasing only at dawn the following morning (the above is from the *Hongming ji*).
○ In the eighth month, Empress Wénxiàn passed away; music spontaneously resounded in the air. Thereupon, she questioned Śīlananda, who said: "The Empress has been reborn..."
In the Pure Land of Amitābha, the various devas come to welcome [the deceased]. Wang Shao, Court Gentleman for the Promotion of Literature, submitted a memorial stating:

"The Buddhist scriptures say that when a person is destined to be born in heaven or in the highest grade of the highest birth in the Land of Immeasurable Life (Amitāyus), the devas and the Buddha emit a great radiance and come to welcome them with fragrant flowers and musical instruments.
We humbly reflect that the late Empress Dowager possessed sagely virtue and benevolence..."
Compassion brings forth blessings, goodness, and auspicious signs that accord with various secret records, all of which state that she was the Bodhisattva Miaoshan.

On the twenty-second day of the eighth month, within the Renshou Palace, golden and silver flowers rained down once more. On the following day, behind the main hall, there was a divine light at night.
Furthermore, on the following day, various kinds of music spontaneously resounded from the north of the palace, filling the void.
On the twenty-fourth day at the fifth watch, she suddenly passed away as if falling asleep. These events all accorded with what was described in the scriptures.
On the day of her ascension to heaven, there were sounds of bells within the garden striking more than two hundred times during the night; this was a manifest sign of her rebirth in heaven.
The Emperor heard of this; he was both moved by sorrow and joy (*Sui Shu Tongjian*).
Jiazi, the fourth year of Renshou: The Emperor issued another edict, saying: "I reverently receive the initial mandate of Heaven and nourish the common people."
In accordance with the sacred scriptures, we shall restore the wholesome Dharma. For the Tathāgata’s great compassion universally covers all classes of beings;

moved by this, we have beheld the śarīra, which serves to guide and enlighten all living creatures. Having fashioned [the stūpas], they were distributed far and near, and in each place, spirit-inspiring towers were erected.

Yet, among the various provinces, there are still those where they have not reached. We now request that the Venerable Ones escort the śarīra to each of these provinces and, as before, construct stūpas. It is fitting that—
To share this meritorious karma with all living beings, he commanded the Vinaya Master Fazun and others to carry the śarīra relics to more than thirty prefectures, including Bo and Jiang.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, they simultaneously enshrined them in stupas, each accompanied by auspicious omens. In the seventh month, the Emperor passed away.

He had occupied the throne for twenty-four years; throughout his reign, he directed his mind and heart toward nothing but the promotion of the foundations of merit, issuing edicts to spread [the Dharma].
He spoke thus: "I must surely harbor a wholesome intent to guide others. He transcribed forty-six collections of the sutras and repaired old scriptures.

He fashioned more than sixty million images of the Buddha in gold, copper, and sandalwood; he restored countless ancient images; and the number of embroidered and painted icons, as well as five-colored silk and pearl banners, was beyond reckoning.
He erected more than five thousand temples and pagodas. To examine this period in detail, the four seas were tranquil and waveless.
The Nine Provinces were free from dust. Twenty-four monastics and laypeople served as translators, producing nearly five hundred fascicles of sutras and śāstras.

Through this, the compassionate transformation of the Triple Gem flourished greatly; the benevolent wind of humanity spread throughout the myriad nations, and its influence was once again proclaimed. Thus, the Buddhist monasteries rose up in majestic grandeur.
The city walls and moats were variegated and intricate; banners and canopies soared aloft, adorning the realm. The Dharma halls and Buddha temples were equal to celestial palaces;
the land of Zhendan and Shenzhou was restored to its likeness as a Pure Land. Sramanas thronged together, cultivating the six perfections to perfume their hearts;
lay believers gathered in great numbers, practicing the ten wholesome deeds as their conduct. Thus, those with plump bellies and yellow teeth vied with one another to purchase the Jetavana Garden.

From the *Jiāngxiǎng* and the *Qīngjīn*, the lands of King Ajātaśatru were ultimately gathered; it was here that the Buddhist stūpas first emerged, and precious monasteries soon spread out like stars across the heavens.
That the empire was unified as one was something unprecedented in antiquity. Alas, how magnificent! In this year, Crown Prince Guang ascended the throne.
Yichou: Emperor Yang ascended the throne and changed the era name to Daye. When the Emperor presided over court, he was grave and dignified in his speech;

the wording of the edicts he issued was worthy of admiration. Yet, he remained attached to sensory pleasures. During his stays in the two capitals and on his imperial tours, he took monks and Daoists with him to serve as an inner chapel (*nèidàochǎng*).
He commissioned a seated image of Śākyamuni made of gilded copper, and furthermore, at Longshan, he had a seated image of Amitābha made, [standing] several... feet high.
It measured one hundred and thirty chi. He also constructed seven monasteries and established an *amogha* (unrestricted) assembly to secure posthumous merit for Emperor Wen.
In the tenth month, he conquered Silla and Lin’i, obtaining five hundred and sixty bundles of Sanskrit texts, all of which had been transcribed by the *kūṇala* people upon palm leaves (*pattraka*).
These were subsequently entrusted to the Institute for the Translation of Buddhist Scriptures (*Shijingguan*). (From the *Tongjian*)
Bingyin (the third year of the reign), the second year [of the era]. The kingdom of Wa (Japan) lies three thousand *li* by water and land to the southeast of Baekje and Silla.
Situated amidst the great ocean, its people dwell among mountains and islands. Its king, Tōri-Sibeoku, dispatched an envoy to present tribute. The envoy said:

"We have heard that in the lands west of the sea, the Bodhisattva Son of Heaven has caused the Buddha-dharma to flourish once more; therefore, we have sent this mission to pay our respects and to bring with us śramaṇas."
He taught ten people, who came to study under him. The letter from his country read:

"The Son of Heaven from the land where the sun rises sends this letter to the Son of Heaven from the land where the sun sets, inquiring after your well-being (and so forth). When the Emperor saw it, he was greatly pleased (*Sui Shu*).
Dingmao (Year of the Rabbit), the twenty-eighth day of the first month of the third year. The Emperor, disciple of the Buddha under the Bodhisattva precepts, respectfully addresses the Triple Gem.

Within the realm, he has established a supreme condition: monks shall be invited from each prefecture to perform the ritual practice for seven days, and one thousand persons shall be ordained into the monastic life.
By this merit, may it universally purify the defilements of all sentient beings, so that they may together attain [liberation].

*Bodhi* (from the *Hongming ji*). When the Emperor had established his capital in the Eastern Metropolis, he further established a Translation Hall within the Shanglin Garden to invite Dharmagupta to translate scriptures as offerings to the Wenhuang Emperor.
Subsequently, he constructed two monasteries and a pagoda in Chang’an, where he corrected six hundred and twelve scriptural collections and separately established ten monasteries (*Sui shu*).
In the fourth month of the third year of the Daye era, the Emperor went on a northern tour to Heng’an. Seeing bleached bones strewn across the wilds, he questioned his attendants.
His attendants replied, "This was the site where Han Hong formerly fought against the barbarians. The Emperor was moved with compassion and sorrow;
he collected the remains for burial and commanded five groups of śramaṇas to perform Buddhist offerings on their behalf (from the *Sui Shu*).

Wuchen (4th year). Emperor Ping issued an edict ordering the Daoist master Yang Hong to lead various Daoists and renowned Confucian scholars to enter Zhizang Temple to inaugurate a dharma assembly for the exposition of principles.
He commanded Dharma Master Huìjìng to debate the principles with the Daoist Yú Yǒngtōng.
Huìjìng questioned the Daoist, saying: "Laozi said: 'There was something formless yet complete, born before heaven and earth. I do not know its name; I give it the designation...'"
He said, "It is the Way. Furthermore, is it mixed because the substance of the Way is one? Or is it mixed because its substances are different?
If it is mixed because the substance is one, then at the very moment of being mixed, it has already become one; thus, this oneness would not have arisen from the Way.

If it is mixed because the substances are different, then even before they were mixed, they had already become two; thus, these two would not have originated as one. The Daoist was bewildered and did not know what to say.
[The Emperor] faced [the monks] in silence and desisted (according to the *Sengshi*).

In the fifth year, the Jisi year, at the beginning of the Daye era, the Emperor issued an edict stating that whenever monks or Daoists had petitions to present, they must first pay their respects and then proceed with their formal address.
This edict was ultimately not implemented by the monks. Shi Yanzong could not bear this situation.

He then composed the *Futian lun* (Treatise on the Field of Merit) to oppose [the Emperor]. It consists of seven sections (the text is found in the *Hongming ji*). Later, when the Emperor had an audience with the various śramaṇas, none of them paid him homage.

That year, at the Southern Suburban Sacrifice (*nanjiao*), the ceremonial regalia were displayed in full splendor. When the two religious orders appeared before the court, the Emperor issued an edict saying, "The regulations have long been in effect;
why do you followers of the Way not prostrate? Upon hearing these commands, they bowed repeatedly without ceasing, while the monks and nuns remained solemnly composed.
The śramaṇa Mingzhan of Xingshan Temple replied to the Emperor: "The monks rely upon the Buddha’s precepts; it is not fitting for them to prostrate before the laity.

The Emperor said, "During the time of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, why did the monks perform bows? Mingzhan replied, "Emperor Wu was tyrannical and violent; had they not bowed, he would have met with severe punishment."
"Your Majesty possesses the Way; I do not prostrate, nor do I fear public execution. When the Emperor questioned him, he replied with his monastic name and then dispersed.

How could there have been a Buddha during the time of King Zhao, and yet Daoism be sought as late as the time of King Jing? Xuanyan said: 'In the *Lingbao jing*, there is the Great... "
The Dao was born before Heaven and Earth. It broods within the vast void and shines brilliantly above the Jade Purity (Yùqīng). This is the teacher of the Buddha. Cheng said:
"Before the Five Emperors, we had not heard of the Way of the Celestial Honored One (Tiānzūn). Only at the end of the Three Kings did the name Lǎodàn first appear.
From the time of Emperor Jǐng of the Hàn dynasty onwards, the study of the Dao flourished. Exhausting the present and investigating the past, who exactly is this 'Dao'?"
According to the *Zhouyi*: "One Yin and one Yang are called the Way (*dào*). This refers to the Way of principle and number (*lǐshù*). How could such a thing give birth to a Buddha?

How could there be one who wears a star-crown on his head, a saffron robe upon his body, with white hair hanging down from his temples, holding a cypress-wood tablet in his hand, bearing the title "Celestial Honored One" (*Tiānzūn*), dwelling atop the Daluo Heaven, uniquely named the Great Way (*Dàdào*), and ruling within the Jade Capital (*Yùjīng*)—a being unknown even to the mountains and seas?
"Examine this closely. It is not recorded in the Classics or Histories; the 'Great Lo' (Mahāmeru) is but a fiction, and the 'Jade Capital' (Yujing) is originally a baseless talk.
This is an egregious error. Having finished speaking, he descended from his seat. (From the Old Histories and the Biographies of Eminent Monks.)
Bingxu, the ninth year. The Grand Astrologer Fu Yi submitted a memorial requesting the abolition of Buddhism, stating: "The Buddha is in the Western Regions;

his words are strange and his land remote. I fear that the Han translations of barbarian books are fabrications, which cause people to become disloyal and unfilial, shaving their heads to bow before neither sovereign nor parents, wandering about and living off others' charity, changing their dress to evade labor and taxes, and propagating these demonic scriptures. He further described...

Depraved teachings falsely open the gates to the three miserable realms and erroneously claim the existence of the six paths of rebirth. They intimidate the ignorant masses and deceive the common folk;
among all the common people, those with true discernment are rare. Failing to examine the fundamental source, they believe in such frauds and thereby pursue their past transgressions.
They vainly schemed for future blessings, giving a single coin in the hope of a ten-thousandfold reward; they observed a fast for a single day, hoping for a hundred years' worth of provisions.
Thus, the ignorant and deluded falsely sought merit, showing no dread of legal statutes and lightly violating the penal codes.

There are those who commit heinous crimes and fall into the net of punishment; only then do they worship the Buddha within the prison and recite Buddhist scriptures day and night without weariness, seeking to evade their guilt.
Furthermore, birth and death, longevity and premature demise, depend upon natural law, while rewards and punishments, majesty and fortune, are governed by the sovereign.
Yet, these people claim that poverty, wealth, nobility, and meanness are all summoned by one's own merits and deeds—this is merely the deception of foreign monks.
All claim that it is by virtue of the Buddha that they have usurped the authority of the sovereign and appropriated the power of the Creator;

that such subversion of governance is truly lamentable. According to the Book of Documents: "Only the ruler may exercise favor; only the ruler may exercise awe; only the ruler may enjoy the jade-food.
If a minister exercises favor, exercises awe, or enjoys jade-food, it will bring ruin to his house and misfortune to his state. People followed this principle with great partiality.

[This] is a digression. From the time of Fuxi and Shennong down to the Han and Wei dynasties, there was no Buddhist Dharma. When rulers were enlightened and ministers were loyal, the reigns were long and enduring.
It was under Emperor Ming of the Han that the "barbarian deity" was first established based on a false dream; subsequently, śramaṇas from the Western Regions began to transmit their teachings.
From the Western Jin dynasty onwards, the state maintained strict regulations that prohibited Chinese people from arbitrarily shaving their heads.

When the Hu and Shi tribes successively brought disorder to China, their rulers were mediocre and their ministers sycophantic; their governance was tyrannical and their reigns short-lived—all of which resulted in calamities caused by Buddhism.
The Liang Emperor Wu and the Qi and Yan dynasties serve as sufficient mirrors [for this truth]. In the past, a single woman, Bao Si, deluded King You with her charms.

If this can lead even to the ruin of a state, how much more so for the tens of thousands of monks and nuns throughout the empire who, by cutting and embroidering silks and fabrics to dress clay figures, act as malevolent spirits to delude the myriad people?
I request that the current monks and nuns be required to marry; they would then form over one hundred thousand households.
By producing sons and daughters, raising them for ten years, and instructing them for a dozen, the benefit [to the state] would be natural and spontaneous.

The state will then be able to maintain sufficient military strength; the people of the four seas will be spared from being devoured like silkworms, and the populace will know where authority and fortune reside.

Thus, the winds of demonic delusion will naturally be transformed, and the cultivation of simple sincerity will flourish once more. Furthermore, throughout antiquity and the present, those who offer loyal remonstrance rarely escape calamity.
I have privately observed that during the Qi dynasty, Zhangqiu Zituo submitted a memorial stating that the assembly of monks and nuns causes the state to waste its resources.
The temples and pagodas were extravagant, wasting gold and silk in vain. Monks colluded with the Chancellor to slander [the Emperor] before the court;
nuns relied upon the Empress and high officials to spread calumnies and slanders. Consequently, my son Tuo was ultimately imprisoned and executed in the marketplace.
When Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty conquered Qi, he decreed that his tomb be sealed. Though I am not gifted, I have humbly followed his example in this matter. — Daoist Li.

Zhongqing submitted the "Discourse on Ten Differences and Nine Delusions," and Liu Jinxi submitted the "Discourse on Manifesting the Correct. Both disparaged the sacred teachings and deluded the Emperor’s mind.

Zhuan Yi submitted seven memorials in succession, requesting the abolition of the Śākya school. The High Ancestor entrusted the matter to the various officials for detailed deliberation, all of whom stated:
"The Buddha-dharma has flourished since successive reigns; it promotes goodness and restrains evil, providing secret assistance to the state. In principle, there is no [reason to abolish it]."

The proposal was rejected; only Zhang Daoyuan, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stables, commended Li Yi’s memorial as being reasonable. The Chancellor Xiao Yu rebuked Li Yi in court, saying:
"The Buddha is a sage. For Li Yi to propose such a theory—where there is no law for one who treats sages with such disregard—I request that he be subjected to severe punishment."

Yi said: "Ritual is rooted in serving one's parents and loyalty in honoring one's superior; this is how the principles of loyalty and filiality become manifest, and how the conduct of a minister and a son is perfected.
Yet the Buddha left the city to enter the homeless life, fleeing from his father, and as a mere commoner, he opposed the Son of Heaven."

To succeed to the throne while acting in opposition to one’s own kin—Sengyu was not born from the "empty mulberry tree" (a myth of miraculous birth), yet he follows a teaching that disregards the father.

I, your servant, have heard it said: "He who is not filial has no kin. This refers precisely to Sengyu. Sengyu joined his palms and said: "The establishment of hell is precisely for people such as this.
The Emperor distributed Yi’s memorial to all the monks. At that time, Shi Minggai composed the *Juepo* (A Decisive Refutation).

Fu Yi slandered the Buddha and reviled the Sangha in eight articles. Shi Falin further composed the *Ten Similes* and the *Nine Admonitions* to refute the errors of Li Zhongqing’s *Ten Differences and Nine Delusions*.
Li Shizheng, the Director of Rites at the Gate, wrote the *Treatise on Inner Virtue* in three chapters, all of which set forth the benefits of the Buddha’s transformation.
At that time, while Fu Yi’s arguments remained unresolved, various monks composed treatises, which were combined with those of Li [Shizheng].

The Eunuchs’ Discourse on Inner Virtue was presented together [with other memorials] at court. By this means, the Emperor attained enlightenment. [The Eunuchs] Yi and others praised the Way (Daoism) and slandered the Buddha (Buddhism) in order to curry favor with their private high officials.
Having no other recourse, the Emperor consequently purged those who were excessive in both teachings, and these measures were put into practice.

On the *xinsi* day of the fifth month, an edict was issued, stating: "When Śākyamuni expounded his teachings, purity was paramount; he remained far removed from worldly dust and defilement. To eliminate...

To eliminate craving and desire, he extensively proclaimed sublime deeds, cultivated and planted roots of goodness, enlightened the ignorant and deluded, and served as a bridge for all classes of beings.
For this reason, he expounded the scriptural teachings, disciplined his disciples, tamed body and mind, and abandoned all defiled attachments.
Since the Great Awakened One passed away, the Dharma has spread; yet in these degenerate times, it has gradually declined and become corrupted. Thus, there have arisen those who are base and lowly...
These companions set themselves up as high and noble. Idle and indolent people, merely seeking to evade corvée labor and taxes, falsely undergo tonsure and take refuge in the name of "leaving home.
Their cravings for desire are insatiable and their pursuits never cease; in practice they are no different from common householders, and in appearance they are equal to ordinary citizens.

Advancing, they violate the texts of the precepts; retreating, they lack the instruction of the ritual canons. They constantly fall into the net of the law and bring heavy punishment upon themselves, defiling and disgracing [the Sangha].
Suchness. This impairs the sublime Dharma, much like weeds defile a fine crop, or as floating silt muddies clear water.
Furthermore, the grounds of a *saṃghārāma* are originally termed "Pure Abodes. In recent times, many temples have been established;

people do not seek out secluded and spacious sites, but instead flock only to places of clamor and confusion. This merely fosters frivolous and superficial minds, thereby failing to honor [the sacred].

Regarding the meaning of this reverence: Furthermore, the teachings bequeathed by Laozi fundamentally value emptiness and stillness (*śūnyatā*). To nurture the will through non-action (*wuwei*) and cast aside worldly attachments is the way of the Mysterious Gate (*xuanmen*).

To let the body run about in worldly affairs is especially contrary to this fundamental principle. Having received the mandate to rule the realm, I have sought to cause the Buddhist teachings to flourish;
my resolve is to bring benefit, and my intent lies in their protection. I wish to distinguish between the true gem and the common stone, so that the fragrance [of the Dharma] may spread.

There must be a distinction between the worthy and the unworthy. To ensure the wondrous Way endures forever and the field of merit remains eternally firm, one must rectify the root and clarify the source; thus, a thorough purge is appropriate.

All monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and female adepts who are diligent in their cultivation and practice, and who observe the precepts and regulations, shall be required to reside in major monasteries and observatories, where they will be provided with food and clothing so that they lack for nothing.
Those who are unable to be diligent, who possess no virtuous conduct, and who are merely common...

Those who were vulgar, coarse, and impure were all ordered to renounce the monastic life and return to their native villages. Only three temples were retained in the capital, and one temple each was retained in the various provinces;
all others were abolished (the above is found in the *Tang Ce* and the *Tongjian*).
The preface to Li Shizheng’s *Discourse on Inner Virtue* states briefly: "As for the Tamer Possessing the Ten Powers, who steers the Dharma-boat across the sea of suffering;
