and the Three Vehicles, who draw people upward to level the path within the burning house—their breadth in exhorting goodness and advancing virtue surpasses that of the Six Classics, and their depth in restraining evil and preventing calamity has no peer among the Nine Schools.
Yet, as for their exhaustive exploration of the spirit and knowledge of transformation, their words..."
It is vast and awe-inspiring; it dispels delusions and severs worldly attachments. Its path is pure and remote, difficult to tread upon.

Among the officials and commoners of both China and the barbarian lands, and among the scholars and literati of court and countryside, most find their peace in established fame and rarely savor this Way. Unless one applies oneself with refined diligence to examine what is true and what is false, [one cannot grasp it].
Contemplating deeply, one observes suffering and emptiness. One must establish a root of faith as steadfast as a rock and cast off the canopy of doubt that feels as if one were perishing.

Some may claim that the Three Kings lived long ages without the Buddha, while the two Shi rulers suffered tyranny despite having monks; thus, they argue that transformation depends on serving the Buddha, whereas the benefit of the state lies in abolishing the Sangha.
Such views merely cling to partial perspectives and fail to perceive the universal principle. One must extensively examine the rise and fall of dynasties to reach a comprehensive understanding.
This is sufficient to clarify and dispel falsehoods. Why is this so? He who brought Qin to ruin was Hu Hai; at that time there were no Buddhists, yet the realm collapsed like crumbling earth.

He who caused the Han to flourish was Emperor Ming; in his reign there were monks, yet the state was well-governed. When the Zhou dynasty abolished Buddhist temples, Heaven deprived them of its protection and their longevity did not endure.

During the Sui dynasty, when the teachings of Śākyamuni were propagated, the edicts of the Kaihuang era faced no perils. Thus, prosperity and decline depend on the administration of government, while order and chaos reside with the various officials.
To cast blame upon the Buddha and the Sangha is truly not a comprehensive argument. Furthermore, the Buddha solely propagates goodness and does not encourage evil among his subjects.
Since the precepts are fundamentally for the prevention of wrongdoing, how could they harm the governance of the family or the state?

If every person were to maintain goodness and every household were to uphold the precepts, how could punishments be widely applied, and from what cause could calamity and disorder arise? Though a qíjì horse is magnificent, it cannot travel far without being ridden.
Medicines and tonics may be abundant, yet how can they cure an illness if one does not take them? Fu Jian’s loss of his army was not due to Dao’an’s lack of wisdom;

Shi Le’s rise in tyranny was not because the Buddha is unkind. It is simply that disorder and violence arise when one opposes [the Dharma], whereas there has never been a case where following it led to cruelty.
Viewed from this perspective, the truth is sufficiently clear. Yet faith arises with hearing, and doubt is resolved through understanding.
[The text] has been extinguished. For the most part, it has been slighted and disparaged rather than revered; this is entirely due to the fact that its discussion has not yet been fully investigated.

If one were to explore its mysteries and seek out its hidden depths, one would surely find it to be profoundly deep and worthy of sincere reverence. Consequently, he composed three treatises on the subject.
Bingxu: On the day of Dingyi in the sixth month of the ninth year of Wude, Venus passed through the heavens.
Four days later, on the day of Gengshen, Prince of Qin, Li Shimin, assassinated Crown Prince Jiancheng and Prince of Qi, Yuanji. A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire;
the previous purge was suspended, and monks, nuns, and Daoist priests were all permitted to follow their former customs.
On the day of Guihai, the Prince of Qin was established as the Crown Prince. Having been abolished for two months, the teaching was now revived once more.
The Emperor said to Fu Yi, "The teaching of the Buddha is profound and subtle, worthy of being taken as a model. Why is it that you alone have not realized its principles?

Fu Yi replied, "The Buddha was merely a clever and cunning man from among the Hu; he deceived and dazzled the people of his own land. Those who are heterodox and perverse in the Middle Kingdom have simply appropriated the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi."
Xuantan used words of demonic illusion as a pretext to deceive the ignorant masses; this was of no benefit to the people and harmful to the state.
The subject was not unaware of this, but merely despised such learning. The Emperor loathed his words and would not associate with him for the rest of his life.
On the *jiazi* day of the eighth month, the High Ancestor abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince and assumed the title of Taishanghuang (Retired Sovereign).

At the beginning of the Imperial founding, the course of the state was still precarious. Xue Ju pointed his forces directly at Youzhou and Qizhou, while Wang Shichong massed his armored troops in the region of the Yellow and Luo Rivers.
Other subordinate commanders were scattered like swarms of bees or bristling hedgehogs. The state maintained its fundamental principles, resolutely determined to eliminate these threats.

Nevertheless, our reverence for Buddhism remained profoundly sincere; yet, regarding Fu Yi’s memorials denouncing and defiling the teachings of Śākyamuni, this was the prevailing orthodox view of the time.
The ministers all despised his doctrine; only the inner court official Zhang Daoyuan praised it as being reasonable.

Jinglin and Senggai, the two Dharma Masters, exerted their efforts to refute his heterodox views. Together with the eunuch Li Gong’s *Neide lun* (Treatise on Inner Virtue), they presented these works to the court.

Only then did the enlightened and virtuous [rulers] realize that the slanders and praises directed at Yi and the others had arisen from private collusion. The Chancellor Xiao Yu rebuked him in court, saying: "Buddha..."
He was a sage. Yi’s proposal—that there are no laws for those who are not sages—is indeed a most profound statement.

Nevertheless, although the High Ancestor (Emperor Wu) held deep reverence for the Buddha-vehicle, he lacked resolute decisiveness. In his final years, he acceded to Fu Yi’s request to purge the spurious and the corrupt;

yet his true intent lay in protecting and upholding [the faith], and throughout his life he promoted the excellence of our Way. It was only that, in certain instances, he fell short in relation to the Great Teaching. Once the edict was issued...
A month passed, and upon the outbreak of the Xuanba Incident, when Taizong ascended the position of Crown Prince, the decree was immediately suspended. What harm was there in that at first?
Alas, there is truly a profound reason for both the will of Heaven and human affairs.

Dinghai: Emperor Taizong changed the era name to Zhenguan. In the spring of this year, he ordered the monks and nuns of the capital to perform ritual services for seven days at their respective temples;
the necessary provisions for the vegetarian offerings were to be supplied by the relevant authorities. On the day of the concluding feast, they were all to assemble at Daxingshan Temple (Tongjian).

In the third month of the second year, the Emperor, reflecting upon his past, considered that during the initial pacification of the empire, he had executed and suppressed many who were in hiding or obstructed, making it difficult to atone for these deeds.
He then issued an edict, stating: "Since I first established the cause of righteousness at the end of the Sui dynasty, my resolve has been to rescue those drowning in calamity.

Whether campaigning northward or striking eastward, wherever I turned, I brought lands to submission. The total number of those wounded or slain is beyond reckoning; those whom I personally executed or eliminated approach one thousand. I consider this with great earnestness..."
The holy teaching of the Tathāgata deeply prizes benevolence and compassion; among the precepts, the prohibition against killing is paramount.

Therefore, I have commanded the relevant authorities to establish a vegetarian feast at all temples within the capital for seven days and nights, wherein they shall practice the Way and perform rites of repentance with utmost sincerity, offering all their clothing.

They were employed together with the *shanshe* (abandoned) [rites], hoping that the hardships of the three miserable realms might thereby be liberated and the sufferings of ten thousand kalpas might be extensively relieved through them (*Tang Shi*).
When the Emperor rose up with Gaozu, a deity appeared who called himself Vaiśravaṇa Deva King, vowing to exert his power to quell the chaos.

He possessed the head of a pig and the trunk of an elephant; therefore, wherever he turned, he achieved success. Upon his accession to the throne, he issued an edict that all government offices throughout the empire should offer sacrifices to him.

In the ninth month, he issued another edict stating: "The Buddhas and the Way establish their teachings with compassion and benevolence as their priority. Their profound transformation permeates secretly, and their nurturing influence flourishes."
At the outset, I, the Emperor, have personally received the Great Treasure and have governed the common people with affection. My heart of compassion has extended to all things.
Therefore, I have sought divine favor from afar and invoked the secret assistance of the luminous spirits, hoping that the nine merits would be orderly and the five blessings would manifest.

Recently, however, the severe frost fell early and the autumn harvests did not ripen. Reflecting quietly upon my own meager virtue, I am filled with shame and trepidation. Now, as the hundred grains flourish once more...
As the myriad treasures are about to be completed, there is still fear that wind and rain may disrupt the timing, leaving the nurtured offspring with no place to dwell.
Daring to rely upon Your wisdom and Your external compassion for manifold blessings, it is fitting that You bestow Your protection upon the billions of beings throughout the vast heavens.

During the first month of every year, monks, nuns, Daoists, and others should recite scriptures and perform rites for seven days and seven nights at the temples and monasteries in the capital and in all provinces throughout the empire.
The seventh month. All cases follow this precedent (*Bian zheng lun*).
Paramārtha (also known as Paramārtha) was in the capital for two months. The Emperor [reflected that] all conditioned existence is not true happiness.
All things and the self are empty; when one reflects upon the essential truth, nothing surpasses the Buddhist scriptures.

Thereupon, an edict was issued to the relevant authorities to search for men of eminent virtue who were well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and fully proficient in the ten fields of learning. Nineteen such individuals were selected to inaugurate the work of translation at Daxingshan Monastery.
Śramaṇa Xuānmó and others served as translators of the vernacular, while the Vinaya Master Jñānagupta acted as the certified translator, with Fǎlín and Huìmíng serving as assistants.

Deng was the scribe; Hui-cheng and others received the imperial decree to certify the meaning. Furthermore, by imperial command, the Vice President Fang Yuan-ling, the Palace Attendant Du Zheng-lun, and the Minister Li Xiao and others participated to assist in the collation and determination.
Xiao Jing, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness and Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, [also participated].
The General Overseer was notified, and the relevant authorities provided for his needs; thus, the four requisites were abundantly supplied (*Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*).

In the third year, the year Jichou (629 CE), the Dharma Master Xuanzang felt constant regret that although the scriptures already disseminated were treasured within his heart, they remained insufficient.
He resolved that he must seek out and behold them in their entirety. That winter, he went to the palace to submit a memorial, but an imperial decree forbade it, so he immediately fled in secret.
Departing from Wonju through the Yumgwang Gate, he arrived at Insungsa Temple (formerly known as Yeongnamsa).

There he saw a pine tree in the courtyard and stroked its branch with his hand, saying, "I am now departing to seek the Buddha-dharma; you may grow long toward the west. When I return, you shall turn eastward.

The branch indeed pointed westward for a distance of several *zhang*. Some ten years later, the branch suddenly turned eastward. His disciples went out to welcome him, and he had indeed returned. This is why—
Sū Dongpo’s poem says: "I ask the courtyard pines: do they still point west? I know not when the aged Xuanzang will return.
(From *Shihua*) On the day of Guichou, the intercalary twelfth month, an imperial decree was issued, stating: "When the Sui dynasty lost its governance, the nine provinces were in turmoil.

I personally led the vanguard army to inflict this manifest punishment. Among them were those who were like 'Jie's dogs' caught in Tang's net; though they bit their whiskers in righteous indignation, they ultimately fell into my grasp."

Each has followed what they were entrusted with, and all are truly praiseworthy. Yet, I fear deeply that beneath the nine springs of the underworld they may still sink into cauldrons and pans, and amidst the eight difficulties they may forever be entangled in ice and fire.
With a sorrowful heart, I have not ceased to think of this whether waking or sleeping. Therefore, I establish fields of merit to rescue their wandering spirits.
At the sites where armies clashed since the establishment of the Righteous Cause, for the sake of the righteous warriors and the fallen enemies—

For each person who has sacrificed their life on the battlefield, a temple shall be established to invite eminent companions. It is hoped that where the Dharma-drum resounds, the blazing fires may be transformed into blue lotuses;
and where the pure *brahman*-chant is heard, the ocean of suffering may be changed into sweet nectar. Let the relevant authorities determine and designate the locations.
Temples were established concurrently, and a detailed report of these matters was submitted to convey the Emperor’s sentiments of compassion (Old History).
On the day of Guisi, in the seventh year, Prajñāvarman translated the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* in fifteen fascicles. Fali composed its preface, stating:
"This treatise was composed by the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. It [explains] that [all things] are like illusions..."

When one’s mind reflects upon things that do not truly exist and realizes that objects are not [substantial] objects, then the nature of every object is empty. When one knows that the mind is no-mind, then the essence of every moment of mind is quiescent.
Thus, one exhausts the principle of non-arising and investigates the school of the true mark (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*). So it is said (from the *Bian zheng lun*).

Jiawu, the eighth year. Because the Daoists Liu and Li and others had all composed vulgar writings to slander and defame the True Dharma, Fali composed the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct) in twelve chapters.
It exhaustively investigated the sources of the teachings of Śākyamuni and Laozi, and reached the ultimate limits of their refined principles.
Chen Ziliang, a scholar of the Eastern Palace, annotated it and composed a preface, saying: [The character "ming" (明) appears frequently]. (11)
The Imperial Edict states: "The three vehicles share a common path, with salvation as their primary aim. The eightfold noble path relies upon refuge, with compassion as its sovereign principle.
It flows like an ocean of wisdom to nourish all living beings; it clears away the forest of afflictions to serve as a bridge for all things.

These matters accord with the accumulation of goodness, and their principles harmonize with supreme benevolence. I, the Emperor, dwell as a Cakravartin King, reverently receiving the precious mandate. The regulations of the Great Sage leave no hidden corner unilluminated."

I have examined the teachings of the Ultimate Virtue; there is nothing far-reaching that it does not contemplate. My desire is to enable all people to escape the entanglements of worldly existence and to bring every family to benevolence and longevity.
However, due to recent wars and turmoil, the ranks of the monastic community have diminished. The flowered terraces and jeweled stupas have no one to look out from their doors;

the blue-lotus-hued robes and azure hair are weathered by wind and drenched by rain. Reflecting upon this decay and ruin, I am truly filled with sorrow. Therefore, in all the prefectures throughout the empire where temples are located:

It is appropriate to ordain monks and nuns, with a limit of thirty per instance. Depending on whether a province is large or small, the number ordained at each location shall be determined by the relevant authorities.
Efforts must be made to select those whose virtue and practice are refined and brilliant.

As for those who previously reduced their numbers, returned to lay life, or were privately ordained as laypeople (*baiyi*), if their conduct and practice are praiseworthy, they shall also be included within the quota, and so forth (Old History).
The Dharma Master Yuǎn Wǎn sent a letter to the Crown Prince, earnestly urging him to follow four essential points: first, practicing compassion; second, reducing the slaughter of living beings;

third, nurturing life in accordance with the natural flow of vital energy (*qi*); and fourth, observing the fasts. The Crown Prince replied, stating that he would deeply engrave these four principles in his heart.
In the twelfth month, he submitted a final memorial to the Sage Emperor concerning the rewards and punishments of a sovereign and the Three Jewels.

He was not being overbearing. He felt deep compassion for the śramaṇas who had violated the law, noting that they should not be subject to the same legal statutes as the common people. He requested that they be handed over to their respective jurisdictions so they might be governed according to the monastic discipline (*vinaya*).

He also submitted one scroll each of the *An-yang lun* (Treatise on Peaceful Nourishment) and the *Tian-de lun* (Treatise on Heavenly Virtue). The Emperor graciously accepted his request and issued an edict expressing his sorrow and sympathy.

The Crown Prince was dispatched to attend the funeral rites, and the high officials offered their condolences. At the time of the cremation, the followers were as vast as clouds and the seven assemblies filled the mountains.
A stupa was subsequently erected at the site of the cremation, for which Li Boyao composed an inscription (as recorded in his biography).

Jihai, the thirteenth year. Initially, Yu Shinan, the Minister of the Interior, passed away. During this year, the Emperor dreamed that Shinan presented him with candid advice, just as in his lifetime.

Consequently, he issued an edict stating: "The late Minister of the Court of Rites, Duke Wen-yi Yu Shinan, was pure and complete in his virtuous conduct and devoted his will to loyal service and benefit.
He has suddenly followed the transformation of all things, and time has swiftly passed. Last night..."
In a dream, I suddenly beheld this man, who further presented forth candid words as if it were a day from my own lifetime. Recalling his enduring virtues, I am truly moved by grief and lamentation.

It is fitting that he be aided by merit for his afterlife; out of my sentiment of cherishing the old, you may immediately go to his home to provide a vegetarian feast for five hundred monks and commission one statue of him (*Jiushi*).
In this winter, Huangjin Qin Shiying, relying on his arts, sought honor at the imperial court.

2. [The Emperor] privately learned that the monk Falin had composed the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct), which slandered the imperial lineage; his crime was deemed equivalent to treason (*ningshang*).

The Emperor became incensed and ordered an investigation to locate Falin’s person for interrogation according to the law. Falin then presented himself before the public court, facing the legal process with a disregard for his own life.

The Emperor issued an edict to question him, saying: "In the ancestral alliances of the Zhou dynasty, those of different surnames were ranked last. To honor one's ancestors and value kinship is truly a practice derived from antiquity. Why is this so?"
They pursue his shortcomings and waver like a rat between two ends, extensively citing words of superficial resemblance and fully setting forth disrespectful metaphors.
To thus insult my ancestors and vilify my forebears for the sake of seeking fame—their crimes cannot be pardoned.

Lin replied: "King Wen was a great sage and the Duke of Zhou were great worthies; they honored the distant past and were careful in their funeral rites. The vastness of Heaven matches that of the ancients. Regarding partisan bias: [text continues].

One should act according to principle rather than show partiality toward kin. Though a kinsman may have committed a crime, they must be punished; though a stranger may have performed a service, they must be rewarded.

The August Heaven shows no favoritism; it assists only those who possess virtue. Laozi’s Way and Virtue were bestowed upon the common people, and his humble radiance manifested throughout the four seas.
He once said, "The one I call my Teacher is named Buddha. 'Buddha' means one who awakens all people. This Ancient Sovereign of Gandhāra has long since ascended and departed to the West.
I have investigated the ancient teachings; their origins and conclusions can be traced. Now, Liu and Li have slandered the Master of Laozi.
Therefore, I have composed the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct) in eight fascicles, briefly addressing over sixty points raised by the Daoists and citing historical records.

This is truly not intended to defame the state, as I have submitted this formal petition for imperial review. The Imperial Edict states: "Regarding the *Bianzheng lun* you have authored, specifically the chapter 'The Reciprocal Retribution of Faith and Slander'..."

The Emperor said, "There is one who contemplates Avalokiteśvara; even when facing the blade, he is not harmed. Grant him a seven-day reprieve so that he may contemplate for himself. When his execution is due, we shall see whether he can remain unhurt.
When the term of the reprieve had expired, Senglin suddenly experienced a vision of a valiant being. An imperial messenger arrived to inquire, saying, "The period of the amnesty has ended.
Is there efficacy in your contemplation? Senglin took up his brush and replied: "At the end of the Sui dynasty, virtue was lost and the four seas were in turmoil."
Since the August Sovereigns have conducted punitive expeditions to bring clarity to both sea and land, this has been due to the power of Avalokiteśvara and the causal support of Śrīkūṭa.

Their virtues are comparable and their traces linked; their Way is equal to that of the Supreme Sages. They rescue those facing untimely death within the imperial court and spare those subjected to cruel punishments in the capital markets.
Since seven days ago, I, Lin, have not called upon Avalokiteśvara, but have thought only of Your Majesty. [I submit this] by imperial command to the Secretariat Drafter.
Wei Chong asked Daolin: "There is an imperial decree ordering you to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara; for what reason do you not recite it, but instead say only 'I think only of Your Majesty'?

Daolin replied: "I humbly receive that the holy discernment of Avalokiteśvara manifests forms within the six realms of existence; from the heavens above to the earth below, he serves as a teacher and model for all."

However, the Great Tang now illuminates the four seas; the nine tribes submit to their duties, and throughout the eight directions, the law is clear. With a sage ruler and worthy ministers, there is no injustice or excess.
Now that Your Majesty nurtures all beings like a parent—according to the scriptures, you are none other than Avalokiteśvara—since our spiritual resonance thus accords, I think only of Your Majesty.
Furthermore, the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Discerning the Correct) composed by Lin is comparable to the classics and histories.
Lun: "A single word may be at variance; yet my life rests upon the axe and the halberd. If Your Majesty follows what is right and what is loyal, then Lin will not lose so much as a hair.
If the punishment is excessive and falls upon the innocent, then Lin shall suffer the pain of seeing a prostrate corpse.
He reported these matters in full, and consequently, no charge was brought against him (as recorded in the *Jiu Tang Shu* and the *Sengshi*).
Gengzi, the fourteenth year. An imperial edict was issued, stating: "The images of the Buddha and the Way are matters of supreme reverence and solemnity.
Artisan households frequently cast and forge them, and those who wish to make offerings compete to purchase and redeem them. They judge their craftsmanship and skill, and estimate their weight;
yet the buyers do not consider cause and effect, seeking only to acquire them at a low price, while the sellers originally hope for profit, caring only for the value."
His transgressions were particularly grave, and his roots of merit were entirely exhausted; he had violated the scriptures and teachings, thereby contravening the prohibitions of the unseen world.
From this day forward, artisans shall not be permitted to pre-fabricate Buddha images for sale.

As for those images already completed, each shall be distributed to temples and monasteries, and their value shall be reimbursed from the public funds. (Old History) ○ Xiao Yu, the State Chancellor, was the son of Emperor Ming of the Liang dynasty.

Since the reign of Emperor Wu, his family had successively served the Buddha and maintained a life of pure cultivation. Xiao Yu and his grandson Xiao Mian were particularly rigorous and austere in their practice.

When Emperor Taizong ascended the throne, Xiao Yu entered the相位 (prime ministerial position) several times; he frequently requested to be ordained as a monk, but this was eventually halted because it was deemed impossible.

Throughout his service to two dynasties, he held the position of prime minister five times. He passed away at the age of seventy-four. The *History of Tang* praises him, saying: "The Liang dynasty arose from the Xiao clan."

In the region east of the Yangtze River, [the Sima clan] truly possessed merit for the people; yet they perished because their final transgressions were minor and their power declined. Thus, the remaining blessings extended to their descendants:
from Sima Yu down to Sima Gou, there were eight generations of prime ministers whose fame and virtue followed one another in succession, sharing the rise and fall of the Tang dynasty.
The prosperity of this noble family has never had a precedent in antiquity (Original Record).
In the fifteenth year, the first month of the fifth lunar month, the Emperor visited Hongfu Temple. He summoned five virtuous monks, including Daode Dao-yi, and granted them seats.
He instructed them on the founding of the temple, stating that it was intended exclusively for the veneration of Empress Dowager Mu. As he spoke these words, his tears fell and he hesitated.
Xuán composed a preface himself and bestowed two hundred rolls of silk upon him, styling himself "the Emperor, Disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts.
After the dedication was completed, Xuán said to Yì and the others, "Recently, because Laozi is my ancestral progenitor, I have placed his name and rank at the forefront;
you all must feel resentment over this. Yì replied, "Your Majesty honors your ancestors and establishes the formal precedents; we, Yì and the others, are deeply grateful for this favor."
Having received the imperial grace, I am at peace and leisurely practicing the Way. When the imperial edict was issued, everyone rejoiced; how could anyone dare harbor resentment? The Emperor said:
"I have long known the relative scales of the Buddhist and Daoist paths. As for the relative status of Śākyamuni and Laozi, those of broad learning discern this for themselves.

How can one be deemed superior simply because they were in power for a time? I prioritize honoring my ancestors and valuing the people, for these are the fundamental roots of all living beings; therefore, I have placed them first."

Laozi [established] the order of distinguishing between the near and the distant; it was not that he set his heart upon Buddhism. Since the founding of our state, we have never established Daoist monasteries;
all merit has been dedicated to the monasteries of the monks. Even when in the past we took up arms and faced the enemy on the battlefield, [we did so for the sake of the state].

"Furthermore, I have never from the beginning indulged in the excessive use of power or engaged in indiscriminate killing. Now, Buddhist temples have been established at every site of former battlefields;
even my old residence in Taiyuan has been dedicated to the service of the Buddha. Such is the intent of my heart, which you ministers have likely not yet understood.

When Li Yi and the others rose abruptly to offer their thanks, the Emperor said, "Sit for a moment. This is my own intention; if it were not recounted, people would not know. The season is now turning..."
"It is hot. The temple buildings are not yet complete. The items now offered may be used to construct a separate hall, allowing the assembly of monks ample space to practice the Way.
(As stated at length in the *Hongming ji*, much of the text has not been recorded here.)
In the fifth month of the sixteenth year, the Emperor offered prayers for the posthumous merit of Empress Taimu. He personally drafted a prayer text and sent it to Hongfu Monastery, stating:
"That which the sagely and wise esteem is filial piety; that which the benevolent love is their parents. In my youth, I was burdened by the grace of being nurtured;
in my maturity, I have received the instruction of being raised within the clan. How could I ever forget the longing expressed in the 'Liao'e' poem? My debt of gratitude is boundless."

This is the ultimate limit of human feeling. The vast heavens cannot be repaid. In the past, Zilu lamented that his salary of a thousand *zhong* could not provide for his parents; Yu Qiu sighed that his two parents were no longer waiting.
As these thoughts arise, my longing is eternal and my grief is profound. Desiring to repay their kindness, I find no means; I can only rely upon the aid of the unseen realm.
I respectfully offer two hundred rolls of silk to the Compassionate Sage. If my utmost sincerity moves you, I hope that past transgressions may be extinguished;
for good deeds have their causes, I pray that I may attain the blessings of future karmic conditions (as before).
At Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, there was Chan Master Fenggan, whose origins were unknown. He had previously established a hermitage in the northwest corner behind the Tripitaka Library.
While wandering along a pine-lined path, he encountered a young boy, about ten years of age, who claimed to have no family and no surname.
The Master brought him back to the temple and assigned him to the storehouse office, naming him Shidi (The Finder). Later, there was also a gentleman from Han... [text continues]
Yanlai arrived; he was styled Hanshanzi. The three men met and conversed with great joy, such that it was impossible to discern whether they were sages or ordinary people.
Later, when Lü Qiu Yin was departing to serve as the governor of Taizhou, he suddenly suffered from a severe headache en route. Fenggan went out for a stroll and encountered him by chance.
The Master took pure water and sprinkled it over him; in a short while, they were all dispelled. Because of this, Lüqiu increased his prostrations and reverence, asking where they had come from.
[The Master] replied, "From Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. Lüqiu asked, "Are there any sages there? He replied, "Hanshan is Mañjuśrī and Shide is Samantabhadra.
One sees them but does not recognize them; one recognizes them but does not see them. Three days after Lüqiu arrived at his post, he went personally to the temple to visit them.
The Ruins of Fenggan. When Lü Qiu went to visit the two Great Beings, the monk led him to the kitchen. Upon seeing him, Lü Qiu prostrated;
the two men rose and ran away, laughing and saying, "Fenggan was too talkative! You do not even recognize Amitābha—why would you bow to us? They immediately departed for the Cold Rock.
The following day, Lü Qiu personally delivered robes and medicine. When the two saw him arrive, they cried out, "Thief! Thief! and retreated into a cave in the rock.

"I inform you all: each of you must exert yourselves, and the cave will close of its own accord. Hanshan and Shide composed poems, which they scattered throughout the mountains, forests, villages, and on rocks and walls;

these were all words intended to admonish the world. Lüqiu collected them extensively to form a compendium, and he wrote a preface, verses of praise, and a biography that have been transmitted to the world (as recorded in the *Hongming ji*).
Gui-chou (Kǐchǒu), the fourteenth year of the reign [of the Tang], the fourth day of the eighth month.

At Hongchi Valley in Songchang, Yuanzhou, five stones suddenly appeared, all of which were blue in substance with white characters forming inscriptions that read: "The August Emperor emerges from the sea with many sons;
The Nǐ Yuán Wáng shall rule for eighty years. The Heavenly Son of Peace, Lǐ Shìmíng, shall rule for a thousand years. Written by Crown Prince Lǐ Zhì. The people of Yanshan rejoice."
O Great Sovereign! Your benevolence surpasses that of a thousand ages.

From the five, six, and seven kings, to the seven Buddhas and eight Bodhisattvas, as well as the sons of Heaven of the Buddha-fields of the higher fruits, down to those who perform good deeds—Yuanzhou submitted a memorial to the court regarding these matters. The various officials deliberated and established [the rites], which were clearly and brilliantly set forth.
On the *xinmao* day of the eleventh month, there was a sacrifice at the Southern Suburb. An imperial edict dispatched an envoy with jade and silk to proceed to that valley.
Regarding the Sacrifice (from the *History of the Tang*).
The commentary states: The inscription on the auspicious stone emerged spontaneously, manifesting the permanence of the divine mandate.

Although the old histories listed it in the Basic Annals (*Benji*), Ouyang Wenchong deleted it and included it in the "Treatise on the Five Elements" (*Wuxingzhi*), asserting that Empress Wu Zetian claimed to be Maitreya and that Zhongzong...

He was titled King Fuguang (Buddha-Light). This is precisely the manifestation of a Buddha or Bodhisattva. Now, throughout the Tang dynasty’s rule over the world for twenty successive reigns, only Emperor Wuzong’s correct faith was meager;
all others were individuals who had attained the stage of the Buddha-dharma.

Therefore, the Seven Buddhas, the Eight Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas of the highest fruition acted as rulers of the world, manifesting according to the needs of the occasion and sporting within the cycle of birth and death. How could this be otherwise?
"Is it not merely that when one ceases [from worldly affairs], one becomes a patriarch among the heavens?
(From *Fojiao Tonglun* by Zu Xi of Shu). Jiachen, the eighteenth year. Emperor Taizong Wen enacted the *Yijiao Jing*. His imperial decree stated:

"The Dharma, after the Nirvana of the Tathāgata, because of the decadence and frivolity of the Final Dharma Age, was entrusted to kings and great ministers to protect and uphold the Buddha-Dharma. However...
When monks and nuns leave the household life, their observance of the precepts must be complete. If they indulge their passions and become negligent, they will encounter afflictions at every turn.

By involving themselves in worldly affairs, they constantly contravene the sūtras and the vinaya. Thus, they lose the profound and subtle intent of the Tathāgata and fail in their duty as subjects who have received the mandate from the King.
The *Śāsanānuśāsanī Sūtra* was spoken by the Buddha on the verge of his parinirvāṇa; it is extremely detailed and essential for instructing his disciples. At the end...

Neither the laity nor the clergy held [this teaching] in high esteem. As the Great Way was about to become obscured and subtle words were on the verge of being lost, I constantly cherished the holy teachings and resolved to propagate and expound them.
I secretly instructed the relevant authorities to dispatch more than ten scribes to transcribe many copies of the scriptures, endeavoring to ensure their full implementation.
The necessary paper, brushes, ink, and other supplies shall be provided by the relevant authorities.
One copy each shall be distributed to those of the fifth rank or above in the capital, as well as to the Prefectural Governors of the various provinces.

If the conduct or practice of monks or nuns differs from the scriptural texts, the authorities should encourage and exhort them so that they must surely comply with and follow [the teachings]. (Cited from *Wenguancilin*, Volume 693).

Yisi (19th year), first month: The Dharma Master Xuanzang returned from the Western Regions after a journey of seventeen years, having traveled through more than one hundred countries and brought back scriptures and images to the capital.
The Palace Guard, Fang Yuanling, lodged him at Hongfu Monastery and reported the matter by official memorial.
On Renchen day, Xuanzang proceeded to the Eastern Capital; on Jihai day of the second month, he had an audience with the Emperor at Yiluan Hall.
"Your Majesty," he said, "when the Master departed, why did he not inform you? He replied, "When I was about to leave, I submitted three memorials.

Because my sincere aspirations were humble and shallow, I did not receive your gracious permission. Unable to bear the gravity of this matter, I have proceeded privately; I am guilty of the offense of acting without authorization."

I am deeply ashamed and fearful. The Emperor said, “The Master’s renunciation of secular life sets you apart from the common world. That you could risk your life to seek the Dharma for the benefit of all living beings is something I greatly admire.
You need not feel ashamed at all. I only marvel that you were able to reach this place, considering the vast distance of mountains and rivers and the differing customs of the lands.
The Emperor then asked about the realm of India: “Is the climate there harmonious, and what are its natural products and customs like?”
"Secular sites, the ancient traces of the Eight Kings, and the remains of the Seven Buddhas—all of these should be recorded.

As for those things not transmitted by the *Shanhai jing* or *Shanhai shi*, and which Ban Gu and Sima Qian were unable to include, since Xuanzang has personally traveled to those lands, he remembers them all without omission.

His responses to questions are systematic and well-ordered. The Emperor was greatly pleased and said, "Of the more than one hundred kingdoms you have traversed, you may select and extract the most prominent mountains [to record]."
Regarding the customs of the River regions, it would not be a fine thing to compile a record of the Western Regions to bequeath to future generations?

As Xuanzang was about to conclude his service upon receiving the imperial decree, the Emperor said to his attendants: "In the past, Fu Jian praised Dao’an as a 'divine vessel,' and the entire nation held him in reverence.
I observe that the Master’s speech is refined and elegant, and his character and integrity are pure and lofty; he does not merely live up to the ancients, but truly surpasses them by far."
"It is so," said Minister of Education Changsun Wuji. "Truly, as Your Majesty’s enlightened decree states:

although Dao’an was of lofty conduct and vast learning, his merit in propagating the Dharma certainly does not equal that of the Dharma Master, who has personally reached the sacred realm, investigated the myriad mysteries, and thoroughly explored the ultimate depths of the sublime essence.

At that time, the imperial carriage was about to set out on a punitive expedition against Goguryeo; upon hearing of the Dharma Master’s scheduled return, the Emperor briefly summoned him for an audience.
During their discussion, they were unaware that evening had fallen. The Emperor said, "Our hurried conversation has not exhausted what I wish to express.
I wish to travel east with the Dharma Master to inspect the regions and observe the customs. Would it be possible to have further discussions during the intervals between our official duties?

Xuanzang replied, "I have returned from afar and am moreover afflicted by illness; I am unable to accompany Your Majesty on this journey. The Emperor said, "The Master was previously able to travel alone to remote frontiers; why then [is it now impossible]?"
"To travel [this far] is merely like taking a single step; what excuse could there be for declining? He replied, "When Your Majesty marches eastward, the six armies shall provide protection.
To subdue the rebels and execute the treacherous, there will surely be the merit of Muye and the victory of Kunyang.

As for Xuanzang, I can offer no assistance and shall only bear the burden of the expenses for the journey. Furthermore, when weapons clash in battle, the Buddha’s precepts prohibit śramaṇas from observing such scenes. Only Your Majesty—"
The Emperor showed compassion and consideration, commending his proposal and halting [the previous plan].

Consequently, he presented the six hundred and fifty-seven Sanskrit versions of sūtras and śāstras obtained from the Western Regions, requesting that they be translated for the sake of the state at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song.

The Emperor said, "Recently, for the sake of Empress Dowager Mu, I established Hongfu Monastery; as it is both spacious and serene, you may conduct the translations there. I shall provide everything required."

Fang Yuanling was the Chancellor. Xuanzang consequently requested an official to oversee the gate in order to prevent any breach of security. The Emperor said, "The Master may indeed be said to have devised a plan for self-preservation;
I shall grant this. Fang Yuanling was specifically charged with supervision, and all necessary provisions were supplied entirely from the imperial treasury (*Tang History*).
Wu-shen (the 22nd year, the sixth month). The Emperor was at the Yu-hua Palace. He summoned Dharma Master Xuanzang to the Yu-hua Hall.

Because the Emperor regarded the Master’s virtue and achievements as profound and vast, he wished to have him renounce the monastic life so that they might together manage the affairs of state. The Master replied:
Xuanzang humbly submits this: Your Majesty’s strategic mastery over the eight cardinal directions weaves together the cosmos; you exalt and propagate the legacy of peace and prosperity.

This is bestowed by Heaven and requires no human artifice—this is the first point. You honor the Confucian tradition and esteem virtue; you lighten taxes and mitigate punishments throughout the nine provinces and the four seas.
All have thus attained peace and security. This is secondly that the Sage’s mind, regarding both self and others, does not rely on others.

Deep benevolence reaches afar, and the four barbarian tribes present tribute. This is thirdly that the majesty of Heaven moves them, without reliance on others. The Xianyun have become a source of affliction.

No emperors were able to subdue them. Yet, when Your Majesty ascended the throne, you subdued them with a single campaign; their nests were overturned and their lairs destroyed. Thus we know that where there is the Way, success is attained;

it does not depend on others. This is the fourth point. Goryeo was a minor vassal state; Emperor Yang returned with his army defeated, whereas Your Majesty led troops and marshaled forces to capture tens of thousands of prisoners.
Thus we know that victory depends on the sovereign; it does not depend on others. This is the fifth point. These are the auspicious signs of universal harmony.

All who arrive do so by virtue of their merit; they do not depend on others. This is the sixth point. Even if Your Majesty further required talent, there are currently many such as Yi Yin and Lü Shang.

As for the humble and mediocre Xuanzang, how could he be worthy of inclusion? As for observing the precepts within the monastic community and propagating the bequeathed Dharma, this is my sincere wish.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty’s compassionate grace will allow it to continue without being revoked. The Emperor said: "Since you, Master, desire to propagate..."
He propagated the wondrous Way and did not obstinately oppose the Emperor’s lofty aspirations. The Emperor then asked, "What sutra have you recently translated?
He replied, "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. The Emperor asked, "What doctrines does it clarify? He answered, "It clarifies the meaning of Maitreya’s seventeen stages (*bhūmi*).

The Emperor had the treatise brought into the palace; it consisted of one hundred fascicles. Upon reading its words and meanings, which were vast and profound, the Emperor said to his attendants, "I observe that the Dharma Master’s new [work]..."

The treatise states: "It is like gazing at the heavens or looking out over the sea; one can never reach the limit of their height or depth. When compared to the Confucian and Daoist traditions and the nine schools of thought, they are like small marshes and rivulets facing the vast ocean.
Consequently, the Emperor issued an edict to the relevant authorities to select scribes from the Imperial Library to transcribe nine newly translated scriptures and treatises each.

These were to be bestowed upon the governors-general of the nine circuits so that they might be circulated and disseminated, with the hope that throughout the entire realm, all people would receive the Dharma previously unheard."

The Minister of Education, Changsun Wuji, and the Director of the Secretariat, Chu Suiliang, memorialized: "The Buddhist teachings are profound and mysterious, beyond the comprehension of gods or men.

Your Majesty’s supreme Way is brilliantly manifest as you have established the Three Jewels. You dispatched the Dharma Master to traverse perilous lands to seek the scriptures, which he has now brought back to the realm for translation.
These are like the initial preaching of Amra, as if the golden mouth of the Buddha had newly opened its discourse; all this is due to Your Majesty’s sagacity."

This is what has been moved by [the Emperor’s] virtue. We, your humble and ignorant ministers, have had the fortune to witness and hear this; the waves of the sea of suffering now have a vessel upon which to rely.

Moreover, since imperial compassion is vast and far-reaching, it has caused this to be spread throughout the Nine Provinces, so that all the teeming masses may partake together of the wondrous Dharma.
For us, it is a joy encountered after billions of kalpas; we cannot contain our profound gratitude. (From the *History of the Tang*)

The Emperor completed the *Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka of the Great Tang*. He proceeded to the Qingfu Hall, summoned Dharma Master Xuanzang, and had him ascend the hall to be granted a seat.
He then commanded the Grand Scholar of the Hanlin Academy, Shang Guan Yi, to proclaim it before the assembled ministers. The text read as follows:

"The Two Polarities possess form, manifesting their covering and supporting to harbor all living beings; the Four Seasons possess no shape, secretly operating through cold and heat to transform all things. Therefore..."

To peer into heaven and examine the earth, even those of mediocre intelligence and folly can recognize their beginnings. To clarify the yin and penetrate the yang, even the most sagacious and wise rarely exhaust their calculations.
Yet, although heaven and earth encompass yin and yang, they are easily known because they possess manifest forms;
whereas yin and yang reside within heaven and earth yet are difficult to fathom because they are formless. Thus we know that when forms are manifest, they can be verified—even by the foolish.

It does not manifest; its form is hidden and cannot be seen, such that even those with wisdom remain bewildered. How much more so for the Buddha-way, which is profound and empty, riding upon the obscure and controlling the silent.
It broadly delivers the myriad species and presides over the ten directions. Its majestic spirit is supreme without peer, and its divine power is unsurpassed from below.
Passing through ten thousand kalpas without growing old, it brings forth a hundred blessings that endure forever. The wondrous Way is concentrated and profound;
though one follows it, its limits remain unknown. The flow of the Dharma is deep and tranquil; though one draws from it, its source cannot be measured.

Thus we know that for the ignorant and foolish masses, the petty and vulgar, to cast themselves into its essential purport and yet remain free of doubt—how could this not be so? Nevertheless, the rise of this Great Teaching is founded upon...
From the Western Land, [the Dharma] crossed the Han court like a radiant dream; it illuminated the Eastern Realm with its flowing compassion.

In the past, during the time when forms and traces were divided, transformation was achieved even before words could be dispatched. In the age when the eternal is ever-present, the people looked up to virtue and came to know the Way.

When the shadow of his presence faded and he returned to the truth, and his physical form transcended the world, his golden countenance was shrouded in color, no longer reflecting the light of the three thousand worlds;
yet the magnificent image opened its diagram, revealing the thirty-two marks at the tip of the void. Thus, his subtle words spread widely, rescuing all sentient beings from the three miserable paths;

his bequeathed instructions were proclaimed afar, guiding the multitudes of living things toward the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Nevertheless, the True Teaching is difficult to look up to, and none are able—
The ultimate goal is one, yet its various interpretations are easy to follow; herein, the heterodox and the orthodox become confused.
Thus, regarding the discourses on emptiness and existence, people judge right and wrong according to their customs, and the Great and Small Vehicles rise and fall according to the times.

There was the Dharma Master Xuanzang, a leader of the Dharma-gate. In his youth, he possessed integrity and acuity, and early on he awakened to the mind of the three kinds of emptiness. As he grew, he accorded with...

His demeanor was such that he first embraced the practice of the fourfold patience (*catvāri kṣāntīni*). The pines, waters, winds, and moonlight were insufficient to compare with his purity and brilliance;
how could the celestial dew or bright pearls equal his luminous serenity? Thus, his wisdom penetrated all things without entanglement, and his spirit fathomed the unmanifest.

Transcending the six sensory passions, he stood far beyond them; stretching back through a thousand ages, there was no one to rival him. Concentrating his mind within the realm of inner realization, he grieved for the decline of the True Dharma.

Dwelling his thoughts upon the profound gateway, he lamented the errors and corruptions of the deep texts. Desiring to categorize the sections and analyze the principles, he sought to broaden the learning of those who came before;
he aimed to cut away the false and continue the true, opening the way for future students. Therefore, with a heart uplifted toward the Pure Land, he traveled to the Western Regions.

Setting out on a perilous journey, he advanced alone, staff in hand. In the mornings, accumulated snow flew as he lost his footing along the path; in the evenings, startling sands rose up from the void.

I journeyed through the heavens of delusion; across ten thousand *li* of mountains and rivers, I pushed through mist and fog to advance my shadow; through a hundred cycles of cold and heat, I trod upon frost and rain to follow my path.

Truly, I held the goal as weighty and the toil as light, seeking the profound with the desire to reach it. I traveled throughout the Western lands for seventeen years, exhausting every Buddhist kingdom to inquire after the True Teaching.
At the Twin Trees and the Eight Waters, I tasted the flavor of the Dharma and partook of its wind; at the Deer Park and Vulture Peak, I beheld the wonders.

How extraordinary! Having received the ultimate words from the former sages and inherited the true teachings from the supreme worthies, he has explored the mysteries of the profound gate and applied himself with diligence to the abstruse practices.
The Way of the One Vehicle and the Five Vinayas gallops across the field of his mind; the texts of the Eight Baskets and Three Canons surge like waves within the ocean of his speech.
From the various countries he has visited, he has compiled a total of six hundred and five essential expositions from the Tripiṭaka.

Seventeen schools were translated and disseminated throughout China, proclaiming the holy enterprise. They drew the clouds of compassion from the western extremity and poured down the rain of Dharma upon the eastern borders.
Where the sacred teachings had been deficient, they were restored to completeness; where the common people had fallen into transgression, they were returned to merit.

The parching flames of the house on fire were moistened, as all together were pulled from the path of delusion; the murky waves of the waters of craving were clarified, as all together reached the further shore. Thus we know that evil causes arise from karma.

It falls; skillfully using conditions, it ascends. The point of ascending and falling depends solely on what the person relies upon. It is like the cassia tree growing on a high peak, where only the dew can cause its blossoms to glisten;

or the lotus emerging from green waves, where flying dust cannot soil its leaves. This is not because the nature of the lotus is inherently pure or the substance of the cassia is fundamentally upright;
rather, it is truly because that which they are attached to is high, such that even minute things cannot burden them. What they rely upon is lofty, and thus they remain untainted.
If one relies on purity, then turbid influences cannot defile them. Now, even grasses and trees, which lack consciousness, still draw upon goodness to achieve goodness;

how much more so for those of human nature who possess awareness—should they not rely on auspiciousness to achieve auspiciousness? It is my hope that this sutra shall spread its influence far and wide.
May it endure as long as the sun and moon, so that this merit may spread afar; may it be as eternal and vast as heaven and earth.

Thereupon, the Emperor personally inscribed these words with his own brush and appended them to the beginning of the new scripture. The Dharma Master submitted a memorial to express his gratitude, to which the Emperor replied by imperial decree:

"My talent falls short of the excellence of a jade vessel, and my speech is ashamed of its lack of erudition. As for the Buddhist scriptures, I am particularly unacquainted with them. Yet yesterday, I composed this preface."

I am deeply ashamed of my own meager and clumsy abilities. To defile golden tablets with my filthy brushwork and to set a mere pebble against a grove of pearls is an offense. Having suddenly received your letter, I have mistakenly been granted such praise;

yet as I examine my own person and reflect upon my thoughts, my embarrassment grows ever greater. My virtues are insufficient to be praised, and your thanks are but a weary labor bestowed upon me in vain.
An imperial edict was issued for the Crown Prince to compose the Postscript to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*. Its summary states:

"It is heard that the most profound and refined mysteries of the Yellow Emperor (Xīhuáng) were exhausted in the patterns on tortoise shells; the subtle and abstruse insights of Emperor Xuān (Xuánhòu) reached their limit in bird-script characters.

Examining the 'Cinnabar Books' to seek out hidden truths, one remains utterly ignorant of the source of actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Investigating the records and cross-referencing them to study the subtle workings of phenomena (*jī*) is not the way of eternal bliss. Thus it continues.

Moreover, your deeds illuminate the annals and chronicles; you spread the fragrant breeze throughout the eight extremities of the earth. Your virtue permeates all living beings, stirring the waves of Yao for ten thousand generations.

We humbly observe that while Your Majesty turns the wheel of Dharma with easeful hands, your transformation gradually reaches the Kukkutārāma; while you sit in the Hall of Victory with the imperial crown upon your brow, your spirit communes with Vulture Peak.
To encompass the titles of the Tamer of Men (Śāstṛ) is beyond what can be fathomed by mere literary thought; to reach the pinnacle of Prajñā through your imperial edicts is truly unsurpassed.
It is said: How could the diagrams and trigrams of the *Xici* ever approximate this? Yet the teachings have spread even beyond the vast ocean, and all transmit the sounds of the Eight Liberations;
the instruction has permeated the entire world, and all tread the path of the Four Dhyānas.

Thus, it has caused the three thousand worlds to be entirely filled with living beings worthy of being enfeoffed, and the ten billion Mount Sumerus to enter within its borders as its capital. When compared to former kings, how could they possibly be considered of the same era?
It has been said: "The *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* is the essential tenet of the Great Enlightened One’s doctrinal tradition (and so forth).
When the Dharma Master Xuanzang had completed his work of translation, I, in the leisure time between my inquiries after his well-being, clarified my mind upon the jewel of the Sublime Dharma.
I respectfully recorded the Imperial decree to offer a modest expression of praise, and have ordered the relevant officials to append this to the end of the volume."

In the eighth month, [the Emperor] bestowed upon him a robe of variegated brocade worth a hundred pieces of gold, along with a precious razor. Xuanzang submitted a memorial of thanks, which stated in brief:
"The garment of patience has colors that blend with the flowing clouds; the blade of wisdom is sharper than jade-cutting steel.
I shall respectfully wear it to subdue the demons of affliction, and gird it on to sever the net of worldly toil... (and so forth).
After the Emperor returned from his campaign against Liaodong, his physical strength no longer matched that of former times, and he harbored anxieties regarding his life.

Upon meeting the Dharma Master, he turned his mind toward the Great Teaching and gradually recovered his health. He then asked: "If I wish to plant seeds for the benefit of the Dharma-gate, what should take precedence?

Xuanzang replied: "Sentient beings lie dormant in delusion; without wisdom, they cannot be awakened. To cause the sprouts of wisdom to grow, the Dharma serves as their nourishment. Therefore, [the propagation of the Dharma should come first]."
"The Dharma requires people; therefore, the ordination of monks is of the utmost importance.

The Emperor was pleased. In the ninth month, he issued an edict stating: "At the end of the Sui dynasty, governance was lost and the empire fell into fragmentation. I, the Emperor, was personally tasked with quelling the chaos and have myself encountered the front lines of battle.
I have frequently braved wind and dew, sleeping upon horseback. Lately, I have been afflicted by illness and have taken medicine, yet it has not yet healed. For several days..."
Upon his arrival, [the Emperor’s] condition was finally restored. Could this not have been brought about by the power of merit and goodness?
One thousand people were ordained at each of the monasteries in the capital and throughout the various provinces of the empire (the above is from the *Shì tōngjiàn*).
Jiyou (the year of the Earth-Sheep): In the fourth month of the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, the Emperor visited Cuiwei Palace. Dharma Master Xuanzang accompanied the imperial entourage.
Whenever they discussed profound and abstruse matters, the Emperor would invariably roll up his sleeves and say, "It is my regret that I met the Dharma Master so late;
I have not yet fully realized the intent of propagating the Dharma. In the fifth month, the Emperor passed away at the age of fifty-three. The Crown Prince ascended the throne.

Since the Emperor ascended the throne, he has reverently served the Gate of Compassion and extensively promoted the welfare of beings. He has opened the sun of the Four Immeasurables, which shines everywhere like the clouds of Yao;
he has raised the wind of the Six Perfections, which flows across all lands like the rains of Shun. His intent is to forever empty the prisons and eternally quell the smoke of war.
The wriggling multitudes of living beings alike turn toward benevolence and longevity; the vast realm of the earth together reveres True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Since the Emperor’s heart has been moved and the power of the Sage provides secret support, though there was drought for one year and locusts for two, from the third year onward, peace was established as a matter of course.
The eight directions turned to benevolence; letters were cultivated and arms were laid low. Thus, the true teachings of Vulture Peak have spread their radiance upon this land, and the Great Pond...
The auspicious stone: its inscriptions manifested spontaneously, manifesting the glory of the enlightened sovereign who nurtures the common people;
it illuminates the great mandate, clearly transmitted for eternity.
On the first month of the gengxu year, the High Ancestor changed the reign title to Yonghui. At this time, the Dharma Master Xuanzang took his leave to return to the Great Ci'en Monastery.

The temple’s petition for the translation of scriptures was granted. In the following year, as the construction of the Great Stūpa was nearing completion, [the Master] respectfully submitted the Sanskrit sūtras and śāstras he had obtained for safekeeping, reporting this to the throne.
An imperial edict issued by Li Yifu, Secretary of the Chancellery, stated: "Regarding the stūpa you wish to construct, it has now been approved.
The deceased garments and belongings of the seven palaces, including those from the Imperial Palace, the Eastern Palace, and the Yeting, shall be provided to assist you, Master, in its execution."
This Dharma Master was granted the architectural systems of the Western Regions; before long, it was completed, reaching a height of two hundred *chi*.
In the *renzi* year, the Emperor visited Ganye Monastery for the incense offering on the anniversary of [Empress Wu’s] death and saw the nun Wu.
The following year, Wu was summoned into the palace; she was none other than Empress Zetian (Tongjian).
Jiayin (5th year). By special imperial edict, the śrāmaṇera Kuiji was ordained as a bhikṣu and entered the Great Ci'en Monastery to participate in the correct translation of the scriptures.
Kuiji was the younger nephew of Wei Qi Jingde. Initially, Master Xuanzang had sought out Kuiji’s father.
He sought ordination as a monk. Kuiji said, "If you permit me to consume meat, I shall comply. Xuanzang, admiring his brilliance, granted him permission.
Since entering the monastery, he would read a passage once and memorize it; he also grasped its meaning instantly. He became proficient in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.

Having participated in the translation of scriptures, he received the core tenets of Yogācāra-Vijñaptimātra from Xuanzang and composed approximately one hundred treatises, earning him the contemporary title of "The Hundred-Treatise Master" (Bǎiběnlùn).

The Master was by nature extravagant; whenever he went out, he invariably prepared three carriages, for which reason he was also called the "Master of the Three Carriages" (as recorded in his *Benzhuan*).
In the first month of the first year of the Xianqing era, the Bingchen year, on the Bingyin day, Crown Prince Hong was established as the Heir Apparent.

On that same day, five thousand monks were provided with a vegetarian feast at Ci'en Monastery. Master Xuanzang consequently requested officials to oversee the translation of the scriptures, to supervise them, and to carefully edit them. And...

Regarding the stele for Ci’en Monastery, Minister Xue Yuanchao submitted its draft text, which was approved by imperial decree. On the *renshen* day of this month, during the court assembly, Cui Dunli of the Secretariat proclaimed the edict, stating:
"The Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Great Ci’en Monastery has newly translated various sutras and śāstras."

The phrasing and meaning must be refined. It is appropriate that Yu Zhining, Left Vice President of the Chancellery; Lai Ji, Xu Jingzong, and Xue Yuanchao, Secretaries of the Department of State Affairs;

and Li Yifu and Du Zhenglun be commissioned to review and polish the text from time to time. At the conclusion of the court session, dispatch Wang Junde, an Official of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, to inform the Dharma Master.
The Dharma Master requested assistance from friends for the translation of the scriptures, which has already been arranged. His compassion...

"Regarding the inscription for the Ensi Temple, I hope to compose it myself; I do not know what the Master’s intention is. Xuanzang received this decree and immediately led the assembly to the palace, where they submitted a memorial to request [the Emperor's composition].
Before long, Gaozong personally composed the inscription and presented it to the high officials and ministers. The text, in brief, stated:

"His Way illuminates the dust-like kalpas, and his transformation permeates all living beings. He bestows blessings upon the multitude of sinful creatures and revives those whose decline was imminent."

In this era, the Dharma-rain flows like silken threads, purifying the fire-houses of the world to extinguish their flames; the wheel of wisdom rises like the sun, illuminating the deep darkness and returning all to daylight.

I, the Emperor, have examined the annals of the past with great care and scrutinized the principles of the Way. Is there any teaching that bestows blessings upon eternal kalpas other than the Śākya doctrine?

When Empress Dowager Wen-de passed away—the celestial essence eclipsed the moon and the cords of the earth’s axis snapped—I harbored a profound desire to restore and propagate [the faith], and thus established the Zhaoling Monastery.

[The Emperor] said: "With my heart of devotion fixed upon the Eightfold Path and my will reverently set upon the Twin Śāla Trees, I hope to extend great blessings and provide spiritual support through the afterlife.
I respectfully carve this enduring stone to commemorate the True Realm. On the gengshen day of the third month, the various officials presented a memorial praising the sacred composition.
A separate edict was issued to Xu Jingzong, the Minister of the Court of Ceremonies, to deliver the inscription of the stele for the Master of Dharma Xuanzang to review. On the jiazi day, Xuanzang...

Leading his disciples to the Imperial Palace, he presented a memorial of thanks, which stated in brief: "Your Majesty, having first felt sorrow for the bridal mirror, immediately established a *caitya*;
soon thereafter you erected a triumphant banner and promulgated the laws of literature. Thus, the vestiges of Jetavana have been entrusted to your precious thoughts and rendered ever more sublime;

the lingering fragrance of the Pomegranate Garden has been lent the grace of your jade-like compositions and made imperishable. I, Xuanzang, believe that these writings ought to be transcribed by Your Majesty’s own sacred hand. He thus requested this a second time.

In the beginning of the fourth month, it was permitted for Dharma Master Xuanzang to prepare ceremonial banners, carriages, and Indian ritual implements. He knocked at the gate of Fanglin Monastery to welcome the imperial stele.

By imperial decree, the nine divisions of music of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Taichang*), along with various acrobatic performances, and the princes, dukes, and high officials were sent to escort it.

The Emperor presided over the Anfu Gate tower to observe Xuanzang’s procession; as he led the way according to Indian ritual protocols, his retinue was most magnificent, and the Emperor gazed upon them from afar.
In the eleventh month, during the month when the Empress Dowager was in labor, she ordered Master Xuanzang to enter the palace to pray for blessings.

When the labor was eased, a divine light filled the palace, shining from the courtyard up to the heavens. Consequently, he was named Prince Foguang (who was later Emperor Zhongzong). Previously, the Emperor had once said to Xuanzang: "If..."

A son was born; he was immediately granted permission to leave the household life. At this time, Xuanzang submitted a memorial requesting that Prince Fuguang be permitted to become a monk so as to ensure the flourishing of the Triple Gem.
The Emperor issued an edict granting his consent (as recorded in the aforementioned *Tongjian*).

Sima Qiaoqing served as a Judicial Rectifier at the Court of Judicial Review. When his mother passed away, he was overcome with grief; he drew blood to transcribe one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
As soon as he finished, three stalks of *zhicao* (mushroom) suddenly grew upon his mourning hut, each one foot eight inches long, with green stems and crimson caps.
Though he plucked them, they grew back again (*Ganying Zhuan*).
Wu-wu: The fourth month of the third year. The Emperor summoned monks and Daoists to enter the palace to debate the principles of doctrine.

Dharma Master Huìyǐn established the principle of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), while Dharma Master Shéntài established the principle of the nine knowledges of abandonment (*navābhisamaya-jñāna*). The Daoist practitioners Lǐ Róng, Huáng Shòu, and others did not understand these names or meanings and were utterly bewildered.

Although they engaged in back-and-forth exchanges, they were left stranded and without recourse. Consequently, the Emperor issued an edict ordering the Daoists to establish their own doctrinal positions.
Li Rong established the doctrine that the Dao gives birth to the myriad things. The Dharma Master Huili questioned him on this, asking whether the Dao possesses consciousness or lacks consciousness.

Li Rong said, "Man models himself after the Earth; the Earth models itself after Heaven; Heaven models itself after the Dao. Since it is the model for both Heaven and Earth, how could it be said to lack consciousness?
Huili said, "If it necessarily possesses consciousness, then it ought to produce only that which is good. For what reason..."
Evil is likewise produced. Since good and evil lead to ascent and descent, and these arise in a chaotic and intermingled fashion, they must be devoid of consciousness.

According to the Buddha’s teaching, which exhausts all principles and fully realizes their nature, the myriad things are karma; sentient beings experience different results due to the power of their karma.
You, my friend, do not understand this and recklessly claim that they are produced by the Dao; yet the Dao truly does not produce them. How pitiable! Rong was speechless.
Feeling abashed, he descended from his seat. Next, the Daoist Huang Shou ascended the seat and established the names and meanings of Laozi.

The Dharma Master Huiyin addressed the Emperor, saying, "Shou does not know the taboos regarding names; how can he publicly discuss the imperial ancestor’s name before Your Majesty? Shou was also overcome with shame and ceased speaking.
Thereupon, Huili addressed the Emperor, extensively proclaiming the various principles of the causal conditions. The Emperor was pleased and adjourned the assembly shortly thereafter.
The Emperor selected the Palace Attendant Wang Junde and instructed him, saying, "Why do you Daoists not study Buddhist scriptures?
Thereupon, Sengrong and the others were ashamed and shrank back, their spirits stifled. (From the *Lunheng*) In the sixth month, the construction of Ximing Monastery was completed.

On the thirteenth day, the Emperor brought forth embroidered images and long banners, escorting them to the monastery for enshrinement. Shortly thereafter, an imperial edict was issued summoning seven monks and Daoists to enter the palace.
The Emperor visited the Bai Fu Hall. An inner court official led the monk eastward while [the Emperor] proceeded westward, and they both ascended the hall together.

The Emperor said, "The two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism both converge upon the same goodness. Thus, the empty principle of the Brahma realm is directed toward non-action (wuwei), while the profound mysteries of the Dark Gate (Daoism)..."

The Master’s virtue stands in contrast to those lacking it; as a teacher, he has studied to illuminate both past and present, and his achievements have brought glory to both the empty and the existent.
We may together discuss the principles of names and reality to mutually enlighten one another. Furthermore, seats were provided for each, and an imperial decree was issued stating:

"The Dharma Master may ascend the seat alone to open the discourse. At that time, the Daoist Zhang Huixuan submitted a memorial, saying: "In the ancestral alliances of the Zhou dynasty, those of different surnames were ranked last. If we establish our principles today according to the Way..."
"A scholar must necessarily take precedence. Furthermore, the customs of the barbarians and the Chinese differ, and the positions of host and guest are distinct.

I request that the Daoist masters be seated first. The Emperor remained silent for a long time. Huilì then submitted a memorial, saying: "Our Buddha’s virtue is loftier than all other sages; his Way surpasses that of humans and devas.
He is the sole Honored One of the trichiliocosm and the compassionate father of ten billion four-continent worlds. He leads the deluded and rescues..."
Sunk [in error]. Only the Buddha alone [is the master]. This land has not yet emerged from the Sahā world; it is the domain of Śākyamuni.

How can Huiyuan presume to speak indiscriminately of host and guest, or recklessly determine the distinction between China and the barbarians? Your Majesty, having humbled the dignity of the Ten-Thousand-Wagons Throne to grace this Jambudvīpa, has received the Buddha’s entrustment to manifest and propagate the holy transformation.
As the Book says: "The August Heaven shows no partiality; it assists only those who possess virtue. Hui...
The original heterodox doctrines cannot be relied upon as a basis. The imperial decree stated, "Excellent; you may submit further [arguments] in succession, with the monks taking precedence.

At that time, Dharma Master Huiyin ascended the seat and established the principle of *abhaya* (fearlessness). Seven Daoist practitioners each presented their arguments and challenges, which would be impossible to describe in full.
Next, the Daoist Li Rong expounded upon the doctrine of the "six caverns," comparing them to the Buddha’s six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*). Hui Li then rose to the debating platform and said:
"Now, does 'penetration' (*tong*) not mean being unobstructed and pervasive regarding all things? He replied, "It is so.

The challenger asked, "If one is to be unobstructed regarding all things, I do not yet know whether the Lord Lao attained such penetration. He replied, "The Lord Lao is a supreme sage; how could he not have attained penetration?
The Dharma Master said, "If the Lord Lao was unobstructed and penetrating regarding all things, why did he say, 'The great affliction of the world is...'"?
"If I had no body, what would I have to worry about? Based on this, even the Old Lord (Laozi) was still hindered by the body;
how could he have attained penetration into the myriad things? Rong Wudui then said, "During my time in Shu, I heard of your reputation long ago.

Since both you and I are renunciants who have left the household life, do not trouble yourself with disputes over right and wrong. Li Daoliang said, "Your words, sir, are like seeking a mother-in-law."
When meeting outside, one may exchange pleasantries regarding the weather; however, at this assembly, it is necessary to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

You say that we are both renunciants, yet when examining our outward forms and scrutinizing our affairs, how can we be the same? Your hair and beard are unshorn, and you have not yet discarded your trousers.
Holding peach-wood talismans in their hands and hanging red pouches from their waists, they patrol doorways to exorcise ghosts and traverse alleys to stroke children’s heads.
This is fundamentally no different from licentious sacrifices and heterodox sorcerers; how could it be considered the same as our pure and empty disciples of the Śākya?

Rong said in anger, "If you consider shaving the hair to be virtuous, why do you not pluck out your eyebrows? Both are likewise hair. Hui-li replied, "Both are likewise hair, yet plucking the hair [of the brows] is also..."
"When you pluck your eyebrows, since you have already shaved your hair, why not shave your beard as well? Sengrong was unable to respond, and the Emperor laughed heartily.

He issued an edict stating, "Excellent," and commanded that they each return to their respective monasteries and observatories. Thus, it was through the power established by these men that their meritorious achievements were guided forward and the discourse on the Way was brought to glory.
The Emperor repeatedly told Xuanzang, "Master Falang of Youzhou is truly excellent.

Within seven days, he issued an imperial decree to Wei Qingjian, the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, to appoint him as the Director of Monastic Affairs (Du Weina) of Ximing Monastery (as previously cited in the *Shi daolun heng*).

Jiwei (4th year). Due to a severe drought, Zu Shi, the Prefectural Governor of Fuzhou, led the officials and the common people with incense and flowers to travel twenty li on foot to Dongsan to welcome the processional image.
His devotion was so sincere that three men could support it as it moved with a light, ethereal grace.
