Upon returning to the state temple, rain fell in sufficient measure. (The stone image had originally been in Tanzhou; having been lost, its path of travel was sought, and two tracks were revealed, each three chi long. *Note: The term "xiang" (跡) refers to the footprints or traces left by the image.*
(To Zhulin, five hundred *li* away).
On the Gengshen day of the eighth month of the fifth year, an imperial edict summoned the monk Jingtai and the Daoist Li Rong to the palace in Luoyang.
The Emperor asked about the origins of the *Laozi huahu jing* (Scripture on Laozi Converting the Barbarians). Sengtai submitted a memorial stating:

"According to the *Jin dai zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and Pei Ziyang’s *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), both state that the Daoist Wang Fu engaged in debate with the śramaṇa Bozu. Being repeatedly defeated by Bozu, Wang Fu took the 'Western Regions' chapter from the *Hanshu* (Book of Han) and fabricated the *Huahu jing*.
Furthermore, this is corroborated by the *Shoushen ji* (Records of the Search for the Divine) and the *Youming lu* (Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds)."

...and so forth. It was also said that this was the fault of Wang Fu’s fabrication of falsehoods. He then engaged in several rounds of debate with Li Rong; Rong repeatedly found himself at a loss for words.
Rong further remarked, "The Great Way and Lord Lao are what Your Majesty honors. Why have you come from the Western barbarians to disturb the Eastern Land?
Tai replied, "When the Tathāgata appeared, he was the Heavenly One in that place. Now that our Emperor governs the realm, this land is [the center]."
The grounds were correct. The Buddha-dharma has its entrustment, which is committed to sovereigns and kings; when there is resonance, there is surely communication—why discuss "this" or "that"?

Later, he was repeatedly summoned for difficult inquiries, and only dispersed when the night grew deep. The next day, the Emperor ordered the attendant Wang Junde to interrogate Li Rong regarding the absence of his doctrinal arguments.
Because of this, Li Rong lost his composure, and the Emperor ordered him to return to Zizhou. As for the Daoists' reputation, it pointed only toward [him].

When Daorong lost his words during their debate, his entire school was shorn of its luster. At that time, Fayai was already renowned for his eloquence; furthermore, he won praise for his poetic compositions.
The Emperor then issued an edict to the relevant authorities, decreeing that Jing’ai Temple should be Fa’ai’s residence.
After Fa’ai entered the temple, he frequently ascended the halls of honor (as recorded in the *Lunheng*).
Xin-you (the 1st year of Longshuo). During the Xianqing era, the Emperor founded Ximing Monastery;
by this time, he ordered Dharma Master Lingrun to select a person to preside over it. A monk from Puguang Monastery in the capital named Mingjie was of keen intelligence;

in lute-playing, poetry, chess, and painting, there was no one at that time who could rival him. However, he was addicted to wine and dissolute in his habits. Several of his colleagues came together to visit Lingrun.
They jointly presented Mingjie for recommendation. Run said, "Gentlemen, you ought to seek the study of precepts, concentration, and wisdom to increase your field of merit.
Why do you instead propose a lute player, a chess master, a wine connoisseur, and a painter to fulfill such a great trust? The gentlemen withdrew in shame, and Mingjie was left feeling resentful.

Shortly thereafter, an imperial summons was issued for those of the four categories of talent, regardless of whether they were monastics or laypeople. Fayuan, understanding the decree, presented himself for selection; having successfully passed the written examination, he ascended the rankings and could not contain his joy.
Not long after, he fell ill and saw dozens of people carrying fierce torches coming to meet him. Fayuan was greatly terrified.
Before he had finished speaking, he passed away; this was in the eighth month of that year. Later, he appeared in a dream to the monk Huizheng, saying:

"Mingjie failed to follow the Inner Teachings in the past, and now he undergoes great suffering. I beg you for a single meal. Upon waking, Huizheng prepared food. That night, Mingjie appeared again in a dream to thank him.
In the autumn of the second year, he again appeared in a dream to a painter, saying: "Because I was addicted to non-Buddhist (outer) books..."

"I am currently in great suffering. Please transcribe two or three fascicles of scripture for me," he said, and further composed a poem to bid him farewell. The painter then transcribed the scriptures for him.
Later, in a dream, [the deceased] came to express his gratitude (from the *Zizheng lu*).

Renxu (the second year). An edict was issued regarding the ritual of prostrating before sovereigns and parents. The decree stated: "The principle of loyalty and filiality is paramount among the three cardinal relationships.

The way of love and reverence is the foremost of all human conduct. Now, although the two traditions of Buddhism and Daoism transcend the ordinary realm in their underlying principles, their traces of respect and filial piety accord with the fountainhead of Confucianism.
Consequently, in the presence of the Most Venerable [the Emperor], the practice of kneeling and prostrating shall not be observed."

Ritual has followed its natural course for a long time, continuing until the present day. During the Song dynasty, this custom was briefly altered, but upon its restoration, the former tradition was once again honored.
I, the Emperor, have received the heavenly mandate to propagate filial piety and draw upon the earthly principle of righteousness to proclaim ritual propriety.

Since Xuanzang’s teachings of the Name and Instruction have reached both the sacred and the secular, the foundation of Laixiang has been able to fulfill its celestial design, and the transformation along the banks of the Yellow River is entrusted to the King. [Thus] it is concluded.

The source of these regulations truly lies herein. Now, you desire that Daoist priests and priestesses, as well as Buddhist monks and nuns, prostrate themselves before the Emperor, the Empress, and the Crown Prince, as well as their own parents.

There is concern that this may conflict with their customary practices; it is therefore appropriate to entrust the matter to the relevant authorities to draft a ceremonial protocol for your consideration.
The monks Wei and Xiu of Dazhuangyan Monastery submitted a memorial stating: We have humbly received Your Majesty’s enlightened decree ordering monks to perform prostrations and kneeling.

Toward one’s sovereign and father, it is right by principle to follow their commands; there is no reason to resist their decrees. However, both Confucianism and Buddhism clarify the teachings and present texts of upright admonition;

both promote transformation and expansion, and both offer the counsel of the common people. We monks, bearing the profound grace of the state, have been permitted to observe the rites of those beyond the secular world.
Dwelling in peace throughout the land, we are able to propagate our aspiration for transcendence. Therefore, since ancient times, emperors and kings—
They have uniformly observed its measurements and reverently honored its rites for transforming local customs, thereby preserving the traces of its transcendent etiquette.

Consequently, the scriptures and teachings have spread widely, increasing gradually with each successive generation. From the Han dynasty until the end of the Sui, whenever a royal destiny first arose, there were none who did not revere these sacred traces and establish monuments to the remaining sites;
thus, it became possible for Indian monks to come and pay their respects in an unbroken succession. If one were to return and prostrate here now—
"Regarding Your Majesty’s father: [the matter] diverges from the various scriptures (and so forth). Although it is called a mere rumor, it will ultimately entangle public discourse.
Moreover, when Xia Bo was ordered to prostrate himself, he incurred the wrath of Heaven; when Emperor Taowei of Wei carried out his execution, he unleashed the retribution of pestilence.

I fear that once these imperial edicts are issued, they will be promulgated throughout the ten thousand realms, inevitably causing the entire world to take notice and spread the reputation that Your Majesty has promoted the practice of losing propriety. I humbly beseech Your Majesty..."

The Three Jewels have been revived and the four classes of beings gathered under compassion. Having personally received the intent of this entrustment, we strive to fulfill the expectations placed upon us as students.
Within, the monks follow the orthodox teachings and firmly maintain the refusal of prostrations; without, they comply with the Imperial decree and adopt the respectful rites of Confucianism.

Looking up and down at these conflicting requirements, our shame and trepidation are truly profound. If we do not set forth our circumstances, it would be a violation of our duty as subjects and children.

Metaphorically speaking, [this would] perhaps obscure the Buddha’s transformation [of the world], causing one to fall into the crime of deceiving the sovereign. We humbly pray that Your Imperial Majesty’s compassion will deign to grant its consideration.

Liu Xiangdao, Duke of Kaiguo and Grand Master of the Court of State Ceremonial, and others, in their deliberations, have privately considered that in the ordering of the court, solemn reverence is paramount;
in the kindness shown to the living, filial care through countenance and nourishment is of primary importance. As for Śākyamuni and Laozi...
Regarding these two teachings, we now reverse them entirely: [the monastics] offer their salutations to emperors and kings, yet they receive reverence from their own parents.
This generous tolerance has existed from antiquity until the present day. To investigate its profound cause, it is likely due to this:

shaving the head differs from wearing the ceremonial cap (*guānmǐn*), and the *kāṣāya* robe does not conform to the requirements of official dress (*zhāngfú*). Those who have left the household life respectfully renounce secular etiquette; how could they be constrained by court protocol?

Consequently, the eight delusions and four ignorances cause one to revolve within the six destinies, while the ten entanglements and five hindrances cause one to sink beneath the three miserable paths.

Furthermore, with Vulture Peak standing solemnly to the west and the Elephant-Drawn Carriage driving toward the east, the Dharma King of the Wisdom Sun surveys from on high, transcending the four great elements;
the Tamer of the Central Heaven dwells in supreme dignity, surpassing the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Encompassing the Iron Ring Mountains, he stretches and contracts aeons as numerous as grains of sand.
As for his essence, it is neither born nor extinguished; as for his marks, there is neither going nor coming. Through the foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts...
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitute his practice; the four immeasurable states—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—guide his mind.

The power of his skillful means is inconceivable, and the capacities of those he perfectly responds to are manifold. When merging with the great void as his measure, how could it ever be exhausted by calculation?
When entering the minute realm of a single speck of dust, it cannot be described in words. That which is beyond attainment and beyond praise—its...
Is this not solely due to the Great Awakened One? In past kalpas, I planted the seeds of causality and was humbly granted the Buddha’s prophecy.

When the Golden Mountain [Śākyamuni] bestowed his decree, the verses of the *Mahāmegha* (Great Cloud) Sūtra first manifested; when the Jade Screen [the imperial throne] revealed auspicious signs, the text of the *Ratnavarṣa* (Precious Rain) Sūtra subsequently reached me.

Furthermore, through the accumulated blessings of my past virtues, these have descended upon my humble person. Thus, the earth has been leveled and the heavens perfected; the rivers have become clear and the seas tranquil. Extraordinary constancy and peerless auspicious omens arrive daily.

Furthermore, the sacred texts inscribed upon moon-stones and conch-shell tablets have arrived in abundance both seasonally and annually. From beyond the seas and across the deserts, the rites of presenting precious treasures have been fully observed;
through perilous journeys and deep crossings, the words translated through successive layers of interpretation have been exhausted.
As for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is the secret treasury of all Buddhas and the ocean of the Tathāgata’s nature. Those who look upon it cannot discern its ultimate meaning.

Returning [to this source], those who draw from it find its limits difficult to fathom. Those with or without further training (śaikṣa/aśaikṣa) have long since abandoned the desire to peer into its depths;
how could those of the Two Vehicles or Three Vehicles hope to hear or receive its teachings? The traces of its adornment by the most supreme knowledge (sarvajñā-jñāna) are already magnificent;

thus the causes for the vows and practices of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī are fulfilled. Within a single phrase, the boundlessness of the Dharma-realm is encompassed; within a single hair-tip, [all things] are placed.
The Buddha-lands are not narrow; in the kingdom of Magadha, the conditions for the initial emergence of this wondrous assembly arose.

In the Hall of Universal Radiance, the principle of nirvana was thus expounded. Reflecting deeply upon these profound meanings, their translation dates back to the Jin dynasty. Six dynasties have passed and nearly four hundred years have elapsed.
Yet, of this entire body of scriptures, we have obtained only some thirty thousand words—having merely opened half the jewel, we have not yet beheld the whole.
Precious One. Your Majesty has heard that the Sanskrit original was previously located in the kingdom of Khotan; an envoy was dispatched to welcome it, and only recently has it arrived here.
Having beheld its hundreds of thousands of wondrous verses, I have now opened its one hundred thousand authentic texts.

In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, the year of Yiwu (the Wood-Sheep year), during the month of Guxi, on the day Wushen of the new moon, on the fourteenth day, Xinyou, at the Great... [text continues].
At Biankong Monastery, [the Master] personally oversaw the editorial revisions and reverently translated this sutra. Consequently, the nectar of the Dharma began to flow;

it was as if he had previously dreamed that on the evening of the Gengshen day, a heavy rain drenched and nourished the earth. Later, at the time of the Renxu year, the gateway to the True Mark (Shixiang) was opened, perfectly corresponding to the translation of the Single Flavor (Yiwei).
This occurred on the eighth day of the intercalary tenth month of the second year of the Shengli era, the cyclical year Jihai.
On the day Jichou (the twenty-second), the task of transcription was completed. The waves of the ocean of nature have been augmented, and the boundaries of the Dharma-realm have been expanded.
The sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna now universally covers the infinite; the true exposition of the Vaipulya scriptures reaches far across all conscious beings.

Who would have thought that in this final five-hundred-year period, one would suddenly receive the words from the Golden Mouth, and that within the realm of the ordinary world, the secrets of the pearl casket would suddenly be unveiled? What is more...

I hope to propagate [the Dharma] throughout the sands of the world-systems and spread it across all realms of dust, so that the two luminaries may hang forever in the sky and its light be eternally distributed throughout the ten directions.
Having once beheld these precious verses, joy overflows my spiritual mind; having repeatedly contemplated their profound essence, delight fills my body and spirit.
Although there is neither speaking nor showing, as the principle accords with the gate of non-duality, yet by means of words one reveals words, thereby finally elucidating the Great Trichiliocosm.

I have ventured to submit this humble composition and hereby provide its preface: By Imperial Decree, the śrāmaṇera Kang Fazang was commissioned to expound the essential principles of the newly translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Taiyuan Temple.
Just as he was about to introduce the title of the scripture, a white light emerged from his mouth, forming a canopy that suspended in the air.

The multitude marveled at this extraordinary occurrence. Thereupon, an edict was issued commanding ten eminent virtuous monks (*da-de*) of the capital to confer the full ordination (*pūrṇa-saṃvara*) upon Fazang.
He was conferred the title "Worthy Chief" (Xianshou). By imperial decree, he was invited to enter Dabiankong Monastery to participate in the translation of scriptures.

In the first year of the Chang'an era, he was summoned to preach the newly translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital. Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," he caused the earth to tremble.

That same day, he was summoned for an audience at Changseng Hall, where the Emperor questioned him regarding the meaning of the ten layers of Indra’s net and the six characteristics; he then expounded upon them.

There was a thread [of understanding]. Furthermore, when he pointed to the golden lion at the corner of the hall to clarify the principle of encompassing the inexhaustible, Empress Wu attained sudden and complete realization.
Consequently, she compiled these words and titled them the *Jinshizi Zhang* (The Chapter on the Golden Lion). — [End of] Initial Section by Venerable Huian.
Dushun transmitted the essential tenets of the Huayan school. Fazang served Yan and fully inherited his teachings. After Yan passed away, Fazang preached the Dharma while wearing a turban and cap;

by imperial decree of Empress Wu, he was granted the tonsure and received full ordination. Upon Fazang’s death, National Teacher Chengguan of Qingliang transmitted his teachings, and scholars took him as their model.
This tradition is designated as the "School of Sudden Perfect Interfusion and Endowment of Virtue," and he is revered as its patriarch.
The Imperial Preceptor issued an edict to the Sixth Patriarch Master, saying: "Your Reverence has attained harmony with the Way through non-action; your virtue outshines the former sages.

You have entered the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna and manifested the true principle of formlessness. Consequently, your fame has resounded throughout the ten directions and your reputation has spread across the four seas."
The myriad affairs of state cause no distress; the eight consciousnesses are all at peace. Your merit transcends the gateway of liberation, and your mind has realized the shore of Bodhi.

As I, the Emperor, occupy the highest station, I am burdened by the anxieties of governance. In vain I wear my crown with sincere devotion, while I long for the flavor of the *amṛta* (clarified butter).
Regretting that I cannot hasten to accompany you in your lower rank to listen to your voice from the side, I yearn to seek the source of deliverance and follow in your lofty footsteps.
At the summit of Mount Wufeng, you, our Master, have extensively propagated the Dharma within, providing great salvation for all sentient beings.
You have laid out oars and rudders amidst the sea of suffering and rescued those drowning on the banks of the river of craving.

Now, I dispatch Wu Cuying, Secretary of the Central Secretariat, specifically to present one set of crystal bowls, one monastic robe, two rolls of white felt, five cakes of fragrant tea, and three strings of coins.
One hundred *guan*. The aforementioned items are offered as a modest act of veneration to express my sincere devotion.

Furthermore, I entrust the Prefect of Shaoyang Commandery with the charge of conveying my greetings and inquiries after his well-being, and to show compassion for the mountain gate so that heterodox sects may not cause disturbance within the Buddhist precincts.
The First Year of Wansui Tongtian. Imperial Decree (Southern Huaya Stone Inscription).

Wu-xu: The first year of the Shengli era. Empress Wu wished to construct a great statue, employing several million laborers and ordering every monk and nun throughout the realm to contribute one coin daily to assist in the work.
Di Renjie submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying:
"Your servant has heard that in governing, one must prioritize human affairs. Your Majesty, while the myriad creatures are lost in delusion, drowning in ruin, and without refuge..."

It is intended that the teachings of the Image Age be practiced concurrently so that people may perceive the forms and give rise to wholesome thoughts. It is not for the sake of stupas and temples that one must insist on such extravagant luxury;

how could it be required that monks and nuns all depend on alms from donors? If even those who have attained some degree of spiritual excellence must practice renunciation, how much more so should others?

The current monasteries exceed the scale of imperial palaces in their construction, exhausting themselves in extreme opulence and display. Their murals are executed with the utmost craftsmanship, and their precious storage cabinets are depleted by decorative ornamentation, while lapis lazuli and jade are exhausted in their adornment.
To build such magnificent halls and pavilions, the laborers cannot be ghosts; they must surely be the common people. Materials do not come from heaven; they must emerge from the earth.
If this causes harm to the common folk, how can one seek a time for their survival? To use resources without measure, the subjects pay tribute as if they could never suffice.

Though it cuts deeply into their flesh, they do not refuse the lashes of the whip. A wandering monk offers a single sermon, falsely proclaiming blessings and calamities, and they shave their beards...
They strip off their robes, yet still feel ashamed of their meager resources. Some even cause estrangement between close kin, treating them as mere strangers;

they take wives for themselves while claiming there is no distinction between self and other—all under the pretext of the Buddha-dharma, leading the people astray. Monasteries (*bǎofáng*) spring up along every street and lane, and monastic halls (*jīngshè*) are established even within the marketplaces.
The funds provided for conversion and inducement are more urgent than official tax demands; the requirements for religious rites are stricter than imperial decrees.
The most fertile lands and excellent estates were seized in double measure; water-mills and manors were likewise obtained in no small number.

Those who had evaded corvée labor and avoided punishment flocked together into the Buddhist order; among these nameless monks, there were tens of thousands, yet after a thorough search throughout the capital, several thousand had already been identified.

Moreover, if even a single husbandman does not plow, society still suffers the resulting hardship; yet those who live on others' sustenance are numerous, and they further plunder the wealth of others.

I have long been troubled by this, and my grief is truly profound. In the past, when we were south of the Yangtze River, the semblance-dharma flourished greatly; Emperor Wu of Liang and Emperor Jianwen gave away their possessions without limit.

Now that the waves boil across the three Huai Rivers (the *Tángshū* records "two Huai," but here we follow the *Tōngjiàn*) and smoke rises from the five Ling Mountains, pagodas line the streets yet fail to save us from the calamity of ruin;
monks in black robes cover the roads, yet where are the armies to support the sovereign?

In recent years, the dust of war has repeatedly disturbed the land, floods and droughts have been irregular, and corvée labor has become increasingly heavy. Households were first emptied of their assets, and the wounds of suffering have not yet healed. This...
At that time, labor was mobilized; the people’s strength could not endure it. I humbly submit that the merit of Your Majesty’s reign is immeasurable.
Why must you insist on constructing a Great Image, taking it as a pretext for such toil and expense? Although monastic funds were collected, they did not cover even one hundredth of the cost.

Since the sacred countenance is vast, it cannot remain exposed; yet even with a hundred layers of roofing, there is still concern that it will not be fully covered. Furthermore, the remaining corridors and galleries cannot be entirely without shelter. Moreover—
[The Emperor] said: "Without depleting the state's wealth and without harming the common people—serving the sovereign in this manner, how can one be called a loyal minister?
I, your servant, have now reflected upon this and consulted the collective opinions of the assembly; all agree that the Tathāgata established his teachings with compassion as the primary principle.

To provide relief to all classes of beings must be his fundamental intent. How could he wish to exhaust the people for the sake of maintaining empty formalities? At present, there are affairs on the frontiers."

Peace has not yet been established. It would be appropriate to relax the corvée labor of the regional garrisons and reduce expenditures on non-essential matters. Even if one were to employ laborers by hiring them out, they would all pursue their own profit;
having lost the proper time for the fields, they will naturally abandon their primary occupation. If no crops are planted now, there will surely be famine next year.

With such labor service already consuming their resources, it will be difficult to provide for themselves; moreover, without official assistance, it is impossible to achieve success. If official funds are expended, they will again be exhausted by the people.
Power. When there is a calamity in one corner [of the realm], how shall it be rescued? (The *Tang Ce* and *Tongjian* do not record this.
Xinchou, the first month of the first year of Chang’an: because ancient Buddha footprints appeared at Chengzhou, the Great Footprint was made at Banya.
In the fourth month, the Empress Dowager again exhorted the monks and nuns throughout the world to construct a Great Image at Baima Pass, ordering that it be completed in the spring.

The Palace Secretary (Gong Shangshu) Wu Youning was in charge of supervision, and the expenditure reached hundreds of millions. Li Jiao, the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Tianguan Shilang), submitted a memorial stating:

"The registered households throughout the empire are largely poor and weak. Of the funds currently available for the construction of images, there are one hundred and seventy thousand strings of cash (*mǐn*).
If these were distributed as alms, giving one thousand coins to each person, it would provide relief to more than seventeen million households, thereby alleviating the hardships of hunger and cold."
This will alleviate the hardships of labor, accord with the compassionate hearts of all Buddhas, and receive the benevolent care of the Sage Ruler.

Both humans and spirits will rejoice, and the merit shall be inexhaustible. This serves as a cause for future conditions; how could it compare to the retribution of the present? [The Emperor] was moved by these words.
Zhang Tinggui, Censor-in-Chief, submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant has heard that 'Buddha' (Fo) takes awakening and knowledge as its meaning. Because...
It is accomplished through the mind; it cannot be attained through various deluded views, nor can it be sought through external adornments. As the Sūtra says:
"If one sees me by form, or seeks me by sound, this person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.

This clarifies that the fruit of True Suchness (Tathatā) is not to be sought externally. Your Majesty has taken refuge with a sincere heart and given rise to great vows. [The text continues with the word] *zhuang* (adorned).
The stupas and temples, with their expansive and venerable forms, have long been widespread throughout the world. This is because there are those who practice giving while dwelling upon signs;
this is not the most supreme, foremost, or rare Dharma. Why is this so? As the Sūtra says:
"If a person were to fill the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and use them for giving, or even give away their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River..."
The merit thereof is exceedingly great. If a person, from within this sutra, receives, upholds, or even recites a single four-line verse for others, their merit shall surpass that of the former.
As the Buddha has said: "Your Majesty has exhausted the wealth of the four seas and the strength of ten thousand men;
you have felled every tree upon the mountains to construct stupas and monasteries, and melted down the finest gold to fashion sacred images. The labor involved is indeed immense."
The expenses are indeed great, yet the resulting merit and conditions for fortune do not exceed those found in the traces of a ruined chamber.
Furthermore, the merit that a Bodhisattva creates should not be grasped with attachment; for conditioned phenomena are not worthy of high esteem.

Moreover, this construction involves extensive labor with earth and wood: sometimes it requires the excavation and leveling of vast areas, the building of steep stairways and courtyards, or the filling of rivers and ravines to facilitate passage.

Furthermore, in the process of felling timber and pressing earth, insects and ants are crushed by the millions. How could this not contradict the Buddha’s prescribed ritual for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), which out of compassion for all wriggling creatures forbids the taking of life?
Moreover, it is improper to employ spirits; to do so would only exhaust human labor. When calculating the craftsmen involved, most are impoverished and destitute;
driven from morning until night, their sinews are strained and their bones are worn out, subsisting on mere mats and gourds, cooking their meals at dawn.
Rice for the stars [offered during famines] is provided due to hunger and thirst, yet poverty and deprivation still abound. Districts and counties impose taxes with the urgency of a shooting star;
some plot to evade them, while others sell their property to fulfill the demands. The sound of resentment fills the roads, and the harmony of the breath of Heaven has not yet been restored.

How could this be the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching on "rejoicing" (anumodana), which pities the ignorant and deluded and would never bear to seize their livelihood? Furthermore, as the frontier regions have not yet found peace, the military—

Provisions for travelers have been exhausted; the empire is depleted and the people within its borders are weary and distressed. We humbly beseech Your Majesty to rectify this through the weight of your grace.
This is the practice of a Bodhisattva: to act for the benefit of all sentient beings.

One should give in this manner, for then one’s merit and virtue would be as vast as the emptiness of the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—beyond all measure. Why need one labor [over lesser matters]?

To dwell upon appearances is to wither the karma of sentient beings and to exalt urgentless tasks. From the perspective of current statecraft, the priority should be the defense of the borders, the replenishment of the treasuries, and the nurturing of the people’s strength.
Yet, from the perspective of the Buddhist teachings, one ought to rescue those in suffering and distress, extinguish all marks of appearance, and exalt non-action (*wuwei*).
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will examine this humble servant’s folly and act according to the intent of the Buddha, striving instead for the principles of reason.
This is the highest principle: not to reject words because of the person who spoke them. How fortunate, how fortunate!

Empress Wu summoned Liu Tinggui and bestowed upon him gold and silk, while comforting and encouraging him (as recorded in the *History of Tang* and the *Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government*). ○ Li Jiao, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, again submitted a memorial, the gist of which stated:
The Great Chongfu Temple involves such vast expenditures that I fear it will incur the resentment of the Three Spirits and invite slander throughout the four seas.
Currently, there are nearly hundreds of thousands of monks who have been privately ordained. The state’s fiscal planning and military defense both rely upon the registered population;

if all able-bodied men now leave the household life and all soldiers enter the monastic order, how can the requirements for military expeditions and tax revenues be met? I pray that you will investigate and conduct a comprehensive census to ensure that the wicked and the crafty are not exempted.

[He] obtained [the position] but remained hidden (*Tongjian*). ○ Su Huan, courtesy name Changrong, was appointed as the Grand Commander (Dadu du) of Fuzhou. At that time, ten provincial inspectors were dispatched to conduct a census of the population throughout the empire.
Su Huan said, “The number of monks and nuns is excessive and intermingled with the laity. I request that all temples be registered and that the permanent quota of monastics be fixed;
when vacancies occur, they shall be filled. Empress Wu approved of this proposal (*Tongjian*).
In the second year of the Yibsi era, in the first month, the high ministers requested that the Empress Dowager transfer the throne to the Crown Prince and move her residence to Shangyang Palace.
The Emperor led the hundred officials to bestow upon the Empress Dowager the honorary title of Empress Dowager Zetian Dasheng Huangdi.

In this same month, Zhongzong ascended the throne and changed the reign era name to Shenglong. In the fourth month, he issued an edict of courtesy, summoning the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi to the capital.

The Imperial Edict stated: "I have invited the two masters, Huian and Xuanzhuo, to provide for them with offerings within the palace. In my leisure from the myriad affairs of state, I have frequently investigated the One Vehicle.
Both masters have declined, suggesting that I should consult Master Neng of the South, who received the robe and dharma of the Great Master Bodhidharma in secret.
I have now dispatched the Palace Attendant Xue Jian to ride with this edict to respectfully invite you. I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and proceed quickly to the capital."

The Patriarch declined the invitation on behalf of his master, expressing his wish to spend his final years among the forested foothills. Xue Jian said, "The Chan masters of the capital all desire to realize the Way;

they ought to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). I do not know what kind of Dharma you, Master, teach. The Patriarch replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting?
Xue Jian said, "When I return to court, the Sovereign will surely question me. I pray that you, Master, will point out the essentials of the mind so that I may [report them]."
[Zhao] said, "One attains entry into the Way. The Patriarch said, "The Way has neither light nor darkness. [Zhao] said, "Light is a metaphor for wisdom; darkness illustrates affliction (*kleśa*).
If one does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter affliction... The Patriarch said, "This is the capacity of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
[Zhao] asked, "What is the insight of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*)? The Patriarch said, "Luminosity and ignorance—these two natures are non-dual. This nature of non-duality is precisely..."

The true nature (*dharmatā*). As for this true nature: it does not diminish among ordinary beings, nor does it increase among sages. It remains undisturbed while dwelling amidst afflictions, and it is not quiescent while abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

Its essential character is suchness (*tathatā*); this is what is called the Way (*mārga*). Jiǎn asked: "The Master speaks of the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished; how does this differ from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)? The Patriarch said:
"The non-Buddhists seek to extinguish birth by means of cessation, using birth to manifest cessation. Yet even their cessation is not [true] cessation."
"Extinction. To speak of birth as non-birth, I say that it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning and is likewise without extinction now. This is why it differs from the heterodox paths.
If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not engage in any deliberation regarding good or evil;

naturally, you will enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally abiding, with its wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Jianli took his leave and returned to the capital, where he presented the words of the Patriarch to the Emperor.

The Emperor praised him with admiration for a long time. Shortly thereafter, he dispatched an envoy to bestow upon him a *kāṣāya*, a water flask, an alms bowl, and other requisites, expressing the Emperor’s profound devotion and aspiration.

(From the *History of the Tang Dynasty*) In the eighth month, an examination of the scriptures was held for novice monks throughout the empire. Those who could explain the meanings without impediment were ordained as monks.
(From the *History of the Tang Dynasty*) While the Emperor was at the Luoyang Palace, he summoned the Dharma Master Huìyǐn to debate the principles of doctrine with the Daoist Huáng Yí. Yí...
His argument fell into error. Furthermore, he ordered the Dharma Master Jingtai to debate with the Daoist Li Rong at the Hebi Palace, where all the officials were assembled;
Rong’s argument also fell into error. An edict was issued to establish Qinghua Palace as a monastery in honor of the late Emperor (Tongjian).
Dingwei, the first year of Jinglong (707 CE). The monk Huifan was granted the rank of Silver Light Qu Lu Da Fu and the title of Duke of Shayong County.
The other nine monks were all promoted to the fifth rank and granted the titles of Marquis or Count of a commandery or county. Huifan had constructed a Great Image.
He established Shengshan Monastery on Changle Slope; at the Eastern Capital, he presided over Zhongtian and Ximing Monasteries as well.

Both the Sovereign and Empress Wei held him in high esteem. At that time, his influence overwhelmed both the inner court and the outer world, such that no one dared to even glance at or mention him (as recorded in the same source).
Wu-shen (the 25th day of the seventh month of the second year). Lü Yuantai submitted a memorial, stating: "The construction of Buddhist temples expands monthly and proliferates yearly;

the labor of the people and the expenditure of wealth are without end. In the past, Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu established their virtue and left behind their fame solely through frugality, restraint, benevolence, and righteousness.
From the Jin and Song dynasties onward, stupas have been vied with one another in their construction, yet calamities and chaos have followed one after another."
This is because people’s cherished pursuits have lost their proper direction, and they vie with one another in extravagance;

this is due to the fact that the people can no longer endure their lot. I humbly pray that you would redirect the funds used for construction toward the expenses of the frontier defenses, so that the beacon fires may cease forever and all living beings may enjoy abundance.
What could more perfectly embody the Tathāgata’s compassionate and impartial mind than this? (The *Tongjian* records that this memorial was submitted but not accepted. —Xin Tifu.
He remonstrated against the construction of Buddhist temples, submitting a memorial that stated: "Now, great monasteries are being built and private residences are expanded.

Trees are felled from the empty mountains, yet they are insufficient to provide for the beams and rafters; earth is transported to fill the roads, yet it is insufficient to provide for the walls and foundations.

To boast of antiquity and dazzle the present, you have exceeded all precedents and violated all regulations. The hundred officials hold their tongues, and the four seas are grieving at heart. Now, the teaching of Śākyamuni takes purity as its foundation."
Taking compassion as the primary principle, one constantly embodies the Way to rescue all beings; one does not act out of profit or desire to harm others.

Thus, one always removes what is superfluous from oneself to preserve others, rather than seeking glory for the body through virtuous instruction. To excavate mountains and dig into the earth during the months of the three seasons is to take life.
To exhaust the treasuries and empty the granaries is to harm people. To construct vast halls and long corridors is to glorify the body; yet in so doing, one takes life.
Lacking compassion, harming others without aiding sentient beings, and seeking personal glory without purity—how could this be the heart of a Great Deity or a Great Sage?

It is considered contrary to the intent of the Buddha and opposed to the hearts of men. From the time the Elephant King descended in the west and Buddhism was transmitted to the east, the Green Mule did not enter as it had before;
only with the White Horse did it proceed after the Han. Through the passing of wind and rain, across a thousand emperors and a hundred kings.

The more lavish the adornments, the more empty the state becomes; the more weighty the preservation [of these things], the greater the calamity. One chariot overturning follows the tracks of another, yet the path is never changed.
The ministers of Jin incurred disaster by flattery toward the Buddha; the Emperor of Liang constructed calamity by "giving away his body.

If the construction of temples were necessarily the correct principle, and if providing for the people were insufficient to govern the realm, then all dynasties prior to Yin and Zhou would have been dark and chaotic, and the Han dynasty...
From the Wei dynasty onwards, all have been sagely and enlightened. From the Yin and Zhou dynasties onwards, their reigns were not long; from the Han and Wei dynasties onwards, they were not short.
Your servant has heard that the Xia served as the Son of Heaven for over twenty generations before the Yin succeeded them;

the Yin served as the Son of Heaven for over twenty generations before the Zhou succeeded them; and the Zhou served as the Son of Heaven for over thirty generations before the Qin and Han succeeded them. From... [text continues]
The dynasties following the Han may be known through history. Why is this? It is because those who possess the Way endure long, while those who lack the Way are short-lived.
How could the longevity of their reign depend upon exhausting gold and jade to construct stupas and temples? I have heard it said in the scriptures:
"If a Bodhisattva’s mind dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness; they see nothing. Furthermore, it says: "All..."

Conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning. Your servant believes that by reducing the expenses of carving and ornamentation to provide relief for the poor, one possesses the virtue of the Tathāgata;
and by ceasing the suffering caused by boring and excavating to preserve the lives of insects, one fulfills the compassion of the Buddha.
This possesses the principles of the reigns of Yao and Shun. Yet Your Majesty treats what is urgent as non-urgent and treats what is non-urgent as urgent;

you draw near to the future while distancing yourself from the present; you lose the real and hope for the void; you value the deeds of commoners while slighting the achievements of the Son of Heaven.
I feel deep pain over this. Nowadays, those who pay bribes and rely on their influence all obtain ordination as śrāmaṇeras, evading [the law].
To employ those who are deceitful and fraudulent as *śrāmaṇeras*—and to leave those who have not yet been ordained to consist only of the poor and the virtuous—how can this serve as a model?

How can it be used to mobilize labor? [I believe that] leaving the household life and abandoning worldly俗 (vulgarities), distancing oneself from factions, and supporting a wife and children are not acts devoid of self-interest.
This leads people to disparage the Way; it does not broaden the Way in order to attract people. I prostrate myself.

Behold the current palaces, observatories, terraces, and pavilions; from the capital to Luoyang, even without further embellishment, they are already feared to be excessively luxurious and magnificent.
Your Majesty still desires to fill in moats and ditches and reduce the size of the parks and gardens in order to relieve the poor who have no means of livelihood.
Yet today, the monasteries throughout the realm are beyond counting; one single monastery is equivalent to one palace of Your Majesty, and its grand adornments exceed those of the imperial halls.
This has already been squandered to excess. If one-tenth of the world’s wealth were divided, the Buddhists would possess seven-eighths of it. What would Your Majesty have left?
What would the common people have to eat? Even if one were to use the Yin and Yang as charcoal and the myriad things as copper [to smelt it], [it would not suffice].

If even those officials who do not eat their rations and those scholars who do not wear the robes provided by the state find themselves insufficiently supplied, how much more so for those who depend on Heaven for birth and Earth for nourishment, obtaining sustenance only after the movement of the wind and the moistening of the rain?
Your servant has heard that if a state lacks a nine-year reserve, it is no longer a state.

I humbly beseech Your Majesty to calculate the granaries and measure the treasuries, taking into account the provisions for the hundred officials and the expenditures for the hundred affairs; I fear [the reserves may be insufficient].
If they do not suffice for a single year, how much less could they sustain a nine-year reserve?

Should the winds and dust of war once again disturb the realm, or if frost and hail strike repeatedly, novice monks cannot don armor to fight, nor can temples and pagodas ward off famine. I am deeply pained by this and submit this memorial.
The proposal (from the Tang strategists) was not accepted.
Wei Sili, considering that the reason for the state’s decline lay in the construction of temples and monasteries, submitted a memorial to remonstrate, saying:

"I consider that the number of temples and monasteries constructed has become exceedingly great; all strive for vastness and compete to honor grandeur and beauty. On a large scale, the expenses amount to one or two [units of currency]..."

One hundred thousand [pieces of wood]. Even for a small pagoda, some thirty or fifty thousand are used. Calculating roughly the total expenditure of wealth and resources, it amounts to over ten million.
The transport of timber and stone keeps men and oxen without rest; it consumes human labor and harms agricultural pursuits.

Since the matter is not urgent, many people murmur in resentment. As the Book says: "If one does not create the useless to the detriment of the useful, success will be achieved. Do not value rare objects and debase..."

"When resources are employed, people will have sufficiency. How true these words are; they are no empty talk. As for observing the profound and subtle principle, it ultimately returns to emptiness and stillness.
If one does not cultivate the mind through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), all phenomena will involve the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Such things as the labor of carving tiles and wood merely exhaust human effort; they only result in a mutual competition for grandeur and splendor—how could they serve to subdue the body and mind?

Furthermore, whenever construction work is undertaken, it inevitably requires excavation and digging. The species of hibernating insects are truly numerous; each month, those killed and injured number in the tens of thousands.
If this continues year after year, the resulting harm is evident. Since the sages take compassion as their core principle, how could there be any reason to carry out such an activity?
The truth that this is not the case is as clear as the sun before one’s eyes. It is only because the laypeople and the monastics have not yet understood this principle [that they remain ignorant].

You worry that the treasuries are empty and exhausted, yet you do not consider the sage’s diligent toil. You claim that by extensively planting fields of merit, it will suffice to augment the practice of the Dharma teachings.

However, should floods or droughts bring disaster and people fall into starvation, or if barbarians and autumn pests cause obstruction and military forces require provisions—then even if Your Majesty possesses monks as numerous as clouds and monasteries that cover the sun, how could they possibly contribute even a ten-thousandth part toward aiding the root?
How bitter it was in the beginning! Since it has already come into conflict with the Way and the Dharma, it has caused extreme harm to living beings.
Your Majesty, how could you not have contemplated this deeply? (Tang Strategy)
In the gengxu year, Emperor Ruizong changed the era name to Jingyun.
At that time, the Great Being Sengqie of Sizhou first traveled from the kingdom of Shule to Xiliang, and subsequently manifested his transformative teachings in Luoyang.
In the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, he registered his name at Longxing Temple in Chu Prefecture and discussed the construction of a Buddha hall.

The Master said, "I shall contribute five hundred strings of cash. He then went to the riverbank and saw several boats approaching. He boarded the rearmost boat and rebuked them, saying, "To have no heart for saving sentient beings is already foolish;
why then do you plunder others and further inflict injury? If you do not relinquish [your loot], I shall [cast you out]. Sa... [text fragment]
He was certain to meet with punishment. The boatman then abandoned him along with Wu-bo Guàn; they pleaded for his protection, but soon he was captured by the authorities of Yangzi County.

He then called to mind the Great Being (Mahāsattva) on the riverbank, and the Master suddenly appeared amidst the clouds, consoling him, saying: "I know that you have focused your thoughts single-mindedly;

there is no need for further anxiety. He sighed over Yuan’s case, commuted his sentence to banishment throughout the realm, truly causing embers to flare up once more and life to spring from rotten bones.
[The Emperor] was moved to tears. In the first year of the Jinglong era of Emperor Zhongzong, an imperial edict summoned the Master to enter the palace, where he was lodged at Jianfu Temple.

The Emperor treated him with the etiquette of a disciple; the Three Dukes inquired after the Dharma, and the hundred officials turned their hearts toward him. During a severe drought, the Master was requested to go to the inner palace to pray for rain.
The Master said, "There is no need for anything else; I require only the Imperial flask. As the Master poured it out, sweet rain fell in torrents. The officials...
The people bowed with joy. The Emperor was greatly pleased in his heart and ordained three men—Huiyan, Huian, and Muxia—as his attendants.
He personally inscribed the nameplate for their residence, calling it Puguangwang Temple (Puguangwang Monastery).
In the first year of the Jingyun era (the gengxu year), on the third day of the third month, Emperor睿宗 (Reizong) manifested signs of illness;

his countenance remained as if alive. An imperial decree was issued to construct a pagoda at Jianfu Temple using fragrant clay. Suddenly, a foul odor filled the city. The Emperor prayed, saying, "I permit you to return to your own place;

I pray that you turn back this auspicious fragrance. Immediately, a wondrous incense-like scent wafted forth, leaving the entire capital in awe of the marvel. His whole body was then escorted back to Sizhou, where a pagoda was erected.
Later, the Emperor asked Wan Hui, "What kind of person is Śāṅgha? Hui replied, "He is but an emanation of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.
The Great Being Śāṅgha is a Bodhisattva who responds to the world; at times he sits peacefully in a deep chamber, and at times he travels great distances shaking his mendicant’s staff.
He cast his water-purifying flask into the room of Lord Pei, and Lord Xin’s ailment was instantly cured. He sprinkled water into the mouth of the stone lion, and it was completely [restored].
He cured his mother’s toothache; by giving her a fan, he ensured that wind and waves could cause no harm. By compassionately offering fruit to a child, Lady Zhao’s illness was spontaneously healed.
Because he did not give a bronze gong, the bronze gong of the Pei family vanished. Because he did not give a fine horse, the district magistrate fell from his horse and died.
When he left Shanyang, both monastics and laypeople followed him with longing; when he reached Huaiyin, his boat was [crowded].
I prostrate myself. There was no place where they did not halt their sails to present offerings or stop their oars to burn incense.

His worldly lifespan was eighty-three years; he fulfilled his transformative conditions in twenty-seven locations. For the first thirty years, he remained in his native land; for the subsequent fifty-three years, he transformed beings in this region.
His divine traces were manifold, but as the texts are voluminous, I have not recorded them all here. (General Discussion) Wanhui was styled Guo; he was the son of the Zhang family of Min County.

He was born in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era. When he was eight or nine years old, his elder brother was stationed at Anxi. His mother missed him deeply as they were separated by more than ten thousand *li*.
The Master would carry letters back and forth, departing in the morning and returning by evening; consequently, he was given this name. Emperor Gaozong subsequently ordained him as a *śrāmaṇera*.

In the fourth year of the Chuixiong era (the Wuzi year), Empress Wu invited him into the palace, bestowed upon him a brocade robe, and ordered palace women to attend to him. [This occurred during the reign of] Emperor Zhongzong.
In the second year of the Shenlong era, he was granted the title of Dharma-Cloud Duke (Fayun Gong). When Emperor Xuanzong was still a prince, he once visited [the Master] in private;

upon his departure, the Emperor patted him on the back and said, "May you take care of yourself, for you shall become a Son of Heaven presiding over fifty years of peace. When Ruizong was the Prince of Xiang, whenever he was about to depart [for his post], [he would consult the Master].

Upon his return, he invariably informed the people of the marketplace, saying, "The Son of Heaven is coming. A short while later, Prince Xiang arrived. His supernatural manifestations were many and of this kind.

In the tenth month of the second year of the Jingyun era of Emperor Ruizong, an imperial edict summoned him to the palace, where he was lodged in the Jixian Academy and served with the finest attendants.
In the twelfth month, he suddenly requested water from the River Wei. His attendants could not obtain it; he then said, "Dig the ground in front of the hall."

He immediately attained [realization]. Upon returning and finishing his drink of water, he passed away in a state of profound stillness. He was posthumously granted the title of Minister (Situ) and the rank of Duke (Guogong), and his portrait was enshrined in the Jixian Academy (as recorded in the Tonglun).

Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song was a native of Yique and a son of the Li clan. He left home to become a monk at a young age and received full ordination in the second year of the Yongchun era of the Tang dynasty.
He was registered at Xianju Monastery and studied the *vinaya* without ever flagging. Later, he visited National Teacher Huian, who certified his realization through the True Dharma;
he attained sudden enlightenment into the profound essence. Thereupon, he chose a secluded dwelling in Pangwu on the mountain. One day, a strange man appeared, wearing a tall cap and trousers...
He was dressed in pleated robes and was accompanied by several dozen attendants. Walking with light and leisurely steps, he announced his arrival for an audience.

When the Master beheld his appearance, it was extraordinary and unlike any other; he then addressed him, saying, "Welcome, O benevolent one. For what purpose have you come? He replied, "Do you perhaps know me?
The Master said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view all with a single eye. How could I make such distinctions? He said, "I am a mountain deity."
"You can cause birth and death in others; how could you, Master, look upon me as one who dies? The Master said: "I am fundamentally unborn; how can you cause me to die?
I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you. Can you destroy space or yourself?"
"If you can destroy emptiness and destroy me, then I shall neither be born nor perish. Since you are not yet capable of even this, how could you possibly bring about my birth and death?
The spirit bowed his head and said, "I am also as intelligent and upright as any other spirit."
"How could I have known that you, Master, possess such vast wisdom and eloquence? I pray that you will bestow upon me the true precepts so that I may cross over the world.
The Master said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you have already returned to the precepts. Why is this? Because there is no precept outside of the precepts;

what further precept could there be? The Spirit said, "This is indeed the principle. Previously, I heard it and was utterly bewildered. I sought only for the Master’s precepts, for I am now your disciple."

The Master prepared a seat for him, held up the incense burner, and straightened the table, saying: "I shall confer upon you the five precepts. If you can receive and uphold them, you should say 'I can';
if you cannot, you should say 'no. Be reverent and carefully receive my instruction. The Master said, "Can you refrain from sexual misconduct?
He replied, "But I am married. The Master said, "That is not what I mean. I mean that you must have no lustful desire. He replied, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from stealing?"
[The officer] said, "How could I lack for anything? How could there be any theft? The Master said, "I do not mean this.

I mean that you bestow blessings upon the licentious while failing to provide for the virtuous. [The officer] said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from killing? [The officer] said, "I truly hold the authority over it;
how could I say I do not kill? The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that there are errors, mistakes, confusions, and mix-ups. [The officer] said, "I can."
[The student] said, “I can. The Master asked, “Can you refrain from falsehood? He replied, “I am upright; how could I be capable of falsehood? The Master said, “That is not what I mean.
I mean that your actions before and after do not accord with the Will of Heaven. He replied, “I can. The Master said, “Will you not be ruined by alcohol? He replied, “I can.
The Master said, “As for the above, these constitute the Buddha’s precepts. He further said, “One upholds them with a deliberate mind, yet...”

Do not harbor attachment through the mind. To take the mind as an object while having no thought of the body—if one can act thus, then one is born before heaven and earth without being a vital essence;
one dies after heaven and earth without being subject to aging; and throughout the day one undergoes transformations without being moved.

One reaches ultimate stillness and silence, yet does not rest therein. To awaken to this means that though one marries, it is not for the sake of a wife; though one feasts, it is not for the sake of taking;
though one holds office, it is not for the sake of power; though one acts, it is not for the sake of habit; and though one drinks, it is not for the sake of intoxication.

If one can be without mind regarding the myriad things, then even if one is ensnared by desire, it does not constitute lust; even if one enjoys blessings or incurs calamity through sexual conduct, it does not constitute theft. Thus, there is no confusion between excess and error, nor between suspicion and entanglement.

Not killing is not for the sake of [external] restraint. Not violating the heavenly laws before or after is not for the sake of non-falsehood. Not being muddled, chaotic, or inverted is not for the sake of intoxication.
This is called "no-mind. Where there is no mind, there is no precept; where there is no precept, there is no mind.

There is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is neither you nor me. Without you, who would there be to observe the precepts? The Spirit said, "My spiritual powers are second only to the Buddha's. The Master said, "Your spiritual powers..."

In ten propositions, there are five things one can do and five things one cannot do. For a Buddha, however, there are seven things he can do and three things he cannot do. The spirit was struck with awe and withdrew from his seat, kneeling on his right knee and saying, "May I hear these? The Master said, "Can you cause the Supreme Deity to turn eastward while making the Seven Luminaries move westward?

He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you seize the Earth-Spirit, melt the Five Sacred Peaks, and congeal the Four Seas? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "If you cannot do these things, how can you claim to possess supernatural powers? The spirit was terrified and prostrated himself, saying, "I am truly a fool. I beg for instruction. The Master said, "The mind is originally empty; it is only because of deluded thoughts that it gives rise to various phenomena. If you can simply abandon all thoughts, then the myriad dharmas will naturally vanish. This is called 'the power of non-action. As for the seven things a Buddha can do: first, he can manifest the three realms within a single pore; second, he can cause the great earth to tremble in six ways; third, he can transform the four elements into gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; fourth, he can extend his life to the end of a kalpa; fifth, he can enter nirvana at will;

sixth, he can manifest the body of a Buddha in all places; and seventh, he can preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings. As for the three things he cannot do: first, he cannot change his original vow; second, he cannot alter the nature of reality; and third, he cannot act contrary to the laws of karma. The spirit bowed deeply and departed. The Master then said to the assembly, "This is what is meant by the power of the Tathāgata."
[The disciple] said, "I cannot. The Master said, "This constitutes the five things that cannot be done.

The Buddha can empty all phenomena and perfect the wisdom of all dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma. The Buddha can know the inherent nature of all sentient beings and exhaustively understand the events of kalpas past."

Yet there are those who cannot be transformed or guided due to a lack of conditions; the Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings—these are the three things that cannot be done.
Determined karma is neither fixed nor eternal; even for those lacking the conditions [to meet the Buddha], it is said they have but one period [of life].

The realm of sentient beings fundamentally has no increase or decrease. Furthermore, not a single person can be the master of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Conditioned phenomena have no master; this is what is meant.
There is no dharma; there is no dharma and no master. This is called "no-mind. As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*);
he is simply able to penetrate all dharmas through no-mind. The deity said: "I am truly shallow and ignorant; I have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
"The precepts bestowed by my teacher, I shall faithfully practice. Now I wish to repay his compassionate virtue by manifesting what I am capable of.
The Master said, "I contemplate the body as having no substance; I contemplate all phenomena as impermanent. Being but a lump of flesh, what further desire could I have?

The Spirit said, "My teacher must surely command me to perform a worldly task, so that I may display my slight divine power for those who have already resolved their minds, those who have newly resolved their minds, and those who have not yet resolved their minds..."
"One who possesses faith must be one of the five classes of faithful people. They witness my divine traces and know that there is Buddha and there is the Divine;
they know there is capability and incapability, and there is that which is spontaneous and that which is not spontaneous. The Master said, "Non-action is it! Non-action is it! The Divine said:

"The Buddha also commands the spirits to protect the Dharma. How could you, Master, dare to disobey and rebel against the Buddha? I pray that you will grant me your instruction as you please. Reluctantly, the Master said:
"The area around Dongnamsa Temple is overgrown and lacks trees; only those on the northern ridge exist, yet they do not form a protective screen behind the temple.
Can you move the trees from the northern ridge to the eastern peak? The spirit replied: "I have received your command. However, it is now the dead of night..."

"There will surely be commotion within this interval; I pray that you, Master, do not be startled. Thereupon, he paid his respects and departed. The Master saw him off at the gate and continued to watch him.

He beheld the ceremonial guards stretching out in long procession like those of a sovereign, amidst swirling mists and rosy clouds, while banners and streamers, and tinkling pendants, vanished into the air.
That very evening, there was indeed a violent wind, thundering peals, rushing clouds, and flashing lightning, [shaking] the rafters.
The sky was turbulent and the birds of the night chirped in clamor. The Master said to the assembly, "Do not fear, do not fear; the spirit has entered into harmony with me.
At dawn the next day, when it was clear and bright, the pine trees on the northern cliff had all moved to the eastern ridge, standing there in dense, orderly rows.

The Master said to his disciples, "After my passing, do not let outsiders know of this, lest it become a subject for idle talk and people will regard me as a sorcerer. This was during the Kaiyuan era.
In the fourth year, the year of Bingchen, he instructed his disciples, saying, "When I first resided at this temple, I lived on the eastern ridge. After my passing, you must place my remains there.
Having spoken these words, he appeared as if casting off his skin. He was seventy-three years of age. His disciples erected a stupa for him (as recorded in the *Sengzhuan*).
*Shishi Zajian* (Mirror for Buddhist Worthies), Compiled through Successive Dynasties, Volume Six.
Postscript by Great Councilor Lord Zhen of Xishan. Regarding Yang Wen Gong Dainian’s transcription of the *Yijiao jing* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching), it states:
"This is the final instruction given by Gautama to his disciples. Scholars rarely recite or study it; this is because a certain faction within the Chan school [often]..."
They believed that the Buddha could be attained without relying on written words; consequently, they disregarded the scriptures and teachings, seeking instead what they called "Chan.
While their approach was indeed lofty, it led to instances where body and mind became inverted, reaching points that could not withstand scrutiny.
On the contrary, those who recite the sutras and uphold the Vinaya follow established rules and regulations so closely that they do not fall into great error. This scripture [ends] with this point.
With the mind upright, intention is paramount. It is said that upholding the precepts is the foundation of wisdom.
The treatise compares the regulation of the mind to tending cattle or driving horses, ensuring they do not run wild. One must eliminate anger, cease delusion, and quell desire with few cravings.

Proceeding from seclusion to diligence, and from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to the cultivation of wisdom, there are distinct stages and gradations; it is not as some practitioners of meditation claim.
To leap directly into the stage of a Tathāgata—this is what students find troublesome about its teaching; they feel that Chan is more expedient than it.
Our former sages taught that taking foundational study as the basis allows one to subsequently attain higher realization.

To seek Buddhahood without relying on the observance of precepts and yet desire to reach concentration and wisdom is like a Confucianist who abandons the practice of the Six Classics and rushes toward the Great [Learning].
It is accomplished. To speak of the subtlety of the Way of Heaven while merely attending to ritual greetings and responding to commands—how could such a thing be possible?
Master Wen devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures; this sutra is the very brushwork of his own hand. Is this not the true foundation for studying the Buddha?

In True Master’s colophon, he clearly elucidates that upholding the precepts is the beginning of the myriad practices, and that the deity of Mount Emei was no ordinary being; even he remained reverent.

He earnestly requested the precepts from Master Guī, saying: "I am truly shallow and ignorant; I have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If you, Master, confer upon me the dharma of the precepts, I shall faithfully practice them.
Ah! The Spirit of Mount E’ (Mt. Odae) claimed his own supernatural powers were second only to the Buddha’s. Was this because he wished to uphold the precepts and cultivate wisdom?
How much more so for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is full of self-conceit (*māna*)! As a Confucianist once said: "Our discussions do not even reach those of the *Bān*..."
If the *Heart Sūtra* were but a single fascicle, it would truly not be a false statement.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Xizhong of Yifeng in Min,
this concludes the seventh fascicle of the *Zhishi Jian* (Mirror for Buddhist Aid) through Successive Dynasties.

In the year of Gui-chou, Emperor Zhongxuan (Minghuang) of the Tang dynasty ascended the throne and changed the era name to Kaiyuan. In the first year, he decreed that every military prefecture and commandery throughout the empire must establish a Kaiyuan Temple as a site for prayers for the longevity of the Sovereign.
Monks who lacked virtuous conduct were dismissed from the monastic order and returned to lay life. In the capital city...
Afternoon: Monks and Daoists were not permitted to go out into the streets.
Jiayin (2nd year). Yao Chong, courtesy name Yuanzhi, submitted a memorial stating: "The Buddha is not to be sought outside; he is sought within the mind.
Fotudeng was most virtuous, yet he could not save all of Zhao. Kumārajīva possessed many arts, yet he could not prevent the fall [of the Later Qin]."
In the Qin dynasty, He Chong, Fu Jian, and Fu Rong all met with ruin and extinction. In the Qi, Emperor Xuan and Emperor Wu of Liang could not escape calamity and disaster.

However, if one gives rise to compassion and acts for the benefit of others, such that the common people are at peace and happy, this is itself the Buddha-body. Why then should you recklessly abolish [the Sangha] and allow wicked men to destroy the True Dharma?
The Emperor followed his advice and ordered the relevant authorities to purge the monks and nuns throughout the realm, returning those who were fraudulent or deluded to lay life.
There were more than twelve thousand such individuals. An edict was issued stating that from this day forward, no new temples or monasteries shall be constructed anywhere.

As for existing temples that are dilapidated and require repair, those responsible must submit a formal petition to the relevant authorities for inspection; only after this may repairs be authorized (from the *History of the Tang*).
The Emperor issued an inquiry to Shen Guang, the Dharma Master and Director of the Left Street Monastery, saying:

"What benevolent virtues does the Buddha possess toward sentient beings, such that one might abandon sovereign, parents, wife, and children to serve him as a teacher? If what you say is reasonable, I shall establish [the Buddhist teachings];
if it is unreasonable, I shall abolish them. The Director of the Monastery replied: "The Buddha’s benevolence toward sentient beings exceeds that of heaven and earth; his clarity surpasses..."

"The sun and moon possess the weight of virtue surpassing that of parents; their righteousness exceeds that of sovereign and subject. The Emperor said, "Heaven, earth, the sun, and the moon possess the power of transformation and creation;
parents and sovereigns and subjects possess the virtue of generation and completion. Why do you say that the Buddha surpasses all of these? Guang replied:
Heaven can cover, but cannot support; earth can support, but cannot cover. The sun is bright during the day but does not illuminate the night;
the moon is clear at night but is not bright during the day. A mother can nourish, but cannot give birth; a father can give birth, but cannot nourish.
When a ruler possesses the Way, his ministers are loyal; when a ruler lacks the Way, his ministers are sycophantic. By this logic, their virtue is incomplete.
The Buddha’s grace toward sentient beings is not like this: in terms of sheltering, it universally covers the four modes of birth;

in terms of support, it sustains all six realms of existence. In terms of illumination, it shines throughout the ten directions; in terms of brilliance, its radiance pervades the three worlds. In terms of compassion, it uplifts...

He pulls [beings] from the sea of suffering. When discussing compassion, he delivers those in the dark realms; when discussing the holy, he is the King among all Sages; when discussing the divine, he is sovereign over the six paths of existence.
Thus, he universally saves both the living and the dead, and leads away both the noble and the humble. We pray only that Your Majesty will turn your heart toward reverent faith.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said: "The Buddha's grace is such as this; were it not for you, Master, it could not be proclaimed. I vow to turn my heart, life after life."
Respectfully following the *Old History*:

In the third year of the Yimao (1095) cycle, the Emperor dispatched Zhang Qia, Director of the Court of Ceremonies, to Mount Dangyang with an imperial edict to summon Chan Master Xingyi to the palace.
By imperial decree, he was installed in the Guangtai Hall. The Emperor frequently consulted him on matters concerning the peace of the nation.

Regarding the essentials of governing the people, some claimed that a single practice was superior to mere recitation. One day, the Emperor ordered the palace registers to be brought out and showed them to him.
After Xing had finished reading them, he commanded an attendant to hold the document while he recited it back to the Emperor; not a single character was mistaken.
The Emperor was struck with wonder and, looking at his attendants, said, "This is truly a sage. From then on, he summoned Xing frequently to consult him on the essentials of the Buddha-mind. Xing...

The Master was dignified and composed in his exhortations and enlightenments; the Emperor’s favor toward him grew daily more profound. The whole world followed the Emperor as he sought instruction from him, and thus he was called the "Teacher of the Son of Heaven" (Jiushi).
The Grand Historian submitted a memorial stating that the Linde Calendar had gradually become inaccurate and that solar eclipses frequently failed to coincide with predictions.

In the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict was issued for the Master to create a new calendar. In compliance with the decree, he calculated the figures and established the methods to respond to the requirements, composing the *Kaiyuan Dayan Calendar*.

On the tenth month of the gui-hai year, the Master completed the construction of the Yellow Path Instrument (*huangdao yi*); the Emperor himself composed an inscription for it, and by imperial order, it was installed in the Wucheng Hall.
This was displayed for the officials to see. Its design was modeled after the form of the round heavens, fully depicting the constellations and the degrees of the celestial equator.

Water was poured to drive the wheel, causing it to rotate automatically; in one day and night, the movement of the heavens completed one full circuit. Two wheels were attached externally to represent the sun and moon, allowing them to move in their orbits:
every time the heavens completed one circuit to the east, the sun moved one degree to the west, and the moon moved ten [degrees].

Three times [a day]. A wooden chest was used as a level base, causing the *yi* (time-measuring device) to be half-submerged beneath the ground. This provided a standard for the dark and bright phases of the moon, as well as the new and full moons.
Two wooden posts were erected upon the level base; on one, a drum was placed in front to mark the *ke* (hour), which it would strike automatically when a *ke* arrived.
On the other, a bell was placed in front to mark the *chen* (double-hour), which it would toll automatically when a *chen* arrived. Both were fitted with rudimentary wheels.
The axes were interlaced and held each other fast; this was called a divine achievement. Xing Hepu said to Yin Qin, the Grand Astrologer:

"Master Yi Xing—is he not a sage? When Luoxia Hong of the Han dynasty created the Tai-chu calendar, he recorded that eight hundred years hence, it would be off by one day, and that a sage would surely appear to rectify it. This year, the predicted period has now fully elapsed."
Master Xi performed the *Dayan* (Great Divination) to rectify the errors of various schools of numerology; thus, the words of Luo Xiahong were not false. Yin also agreed with this.
There was a village woman who had long provided offerings to the Master, but her son happened to commit a crime and was about to be executed.
The woman wept bitterly, begging for his life. The Master took pity on her and ordered his disciples to catch living creatures; they obtained seven chickens and pigs. The Master said: "Hide them..."
One of them was in a jar. After he performed a Brahmanic incantation for seven days, the Big Dipper completely vanished from the sky, and the imperial court was thrown into a state of alarm.
