The Grand Astrologer memorialized, saying, "A portent is about to occur; we pray that you perform rites to avert it. The Emperor questioned the Master, who replied, "There is nothing else to this; it is merely a demonic spirit."
"Anger destroys all goodness; compassion subdues all demons. If one grants a general amnesty to the empire, then malevolent spirits can do no harm. The Emperor agreed with this.
He issued a great amnesty for the empire, and by this means the old woman’s son was spared. The Master said, "With the release of each pig, a star would appear;
after seven days, the Dipper returned to its former state. His secret arts were mostly of this kind. (From the *Jiu Tang Shu*)
In the *dingmao* year, the Emperor summoned the Master into the inner palace and asked: "How long will the national destiny endure? Will there be any obstacles? The Master replied:

"In twenty years, Your Majesty’s carriage shall travel ten thousand *li*; thereafter, the state shall ultimately be auspicious. The Emperor asked in astonishment for the reason, but the Master did not answer and withdrew.
He then presented a small golden casket, sealing it and saying: "Open this when you have traveled ten thousand *li*. One day, the Emperor went secretly...

He opened it to look; inside was a small amount of *angui* (angelica). When the rebellion of An Lushan broke out and the imperial court fled to Chengdu, he reached Wanli Bridge and suddenly realized that the medicine was indeed *angui*.
"Ending in good fortune" (*zhongji*) likely refers to Emperor Zhaozong’s initial investiture as Prince Ji; the destiny of the Tang dynasty perished during Zhaozong’s reign.
In the eleventh month of that year, the Master submitted a memorial to decline [the invitation] and return home; he bathed, sat upright, and—
He passed away at the age of forty-five. The Emperor mourned him with profound grief, suspending court for three days and keeping his coffin in the shrine for twenty-one days.

His countenance remained as if alive. The Emperor personally composed an inscription, which was engraved upon stone. Fifty thousand coins from the Imperial Treasury were disbursed to construct a stupa at the site of the Bronze Man.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dahui. In the sixteenth year, the year Wuchen, an imperial edict was issued to Zhang Yue and others to compile [the records].
Next, regarding the application of the Dayan Calendar: in the third month, the Emperor traveled to the Warm Springs. On the way, he passed by the site of the Master’s stupa.

The Emperor halted his carriage there and lingered, ordering an official of the palace to visit the stupa and inform the Master of his intention to go on a pleasure tour, and he bestowed fifty bolts of silk as a gift.
He ordered that pine and cypress trees be planted before the stupa. Such was his devotion as a member of the Buddha’s holy family (Tang History).
Master Xingxiang, surnamed Zhang, was the grandson of Duke Gongjin of Tan. Having become a monk, he lived in seclusion on Mount Song.

At first, he thoroughly investigated the meaning of the *Tai-xuan jing* and mastered the calculations of the *Tai-yan*. Hearing that there was a monk on Mount Tiantai whose mastery of the *Yan* was quite extraordinary, he went there to seek him out.

Upon arriving before the temple, he did not dare enter; instead, he secretly peered through a gap in the door. He saw the monk laying out his calculations in the courtyard and exclaiming in an emphatic voice:
"There shall be a disciple who comes to seek my *Yan* calculations. When the water in front of the gate flows to the west, then I shall teach him."
Yixing entered abruptly to seek instruction. The monk looked out at the mountain stream outside; suddenly, it reversed its course and flowed westward.
Thereupon, [the monk] exhausted his skills to teach him (*Shi Wuku*). Later, he entered Mount Song and attended upon Chan Master Pujì, where he profoundly investigated the fundamental tenets.
In the second month of the year *Xin-hai*, the second year of Jingyun during the reign of Emperor Ruizong, he issued an imperial decree excusing him on grounds of illness and withdrew into seclusion.
At Mount Dangyang in Jingzhou, he studied the Vinaya under Master Huiwu. Whenever he read a scripture or text once, he never forgot it for the rest of his life.
In the fourth month of the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Xuanzong reign, he was summoned once more by imperial decree; he subsequently compiled the Kaiyuan Da Yan Calendar.

Jisi, the seventeenth year [of the Kaiyuan era]. Zhang Yue, Duke of Yan, was a preeminent minister of the Tang dynasty. His prose was refined and powerful, and he was particularly adept at the Buddhist scriptures.
He composed a preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, which states: "The myriad practices arise from the mind; the mind is the master of man."
The three vehicles converge into one; this oneness is the essence of the Dharma. To know that the mind is unattainable is true realization.
That there is nothing that does not penetrate is profound penetration (and so forth). Furthermore, the eulogy for the Dharma-pool, the Dharma-courtyard, and the Dharma-hall states:

"This Buddha is the mark of emptiness; this Dharma is subtle light. Concentration and wisdom are inseparable; this is the meaning of the harmony of the Saṃgha. Sentient beings are empty, and phenomena likewise [are empty]."
Emptiness. The two kinds of emptiness must also be empty. Abiding in the jewel of the threefold emptiness is called the triple refuge.
If seeing does not stain, and knowing does not grasp consciousness, this is called true seeing; it is also called the knowledge of liberation.
The Buddha’s contemplation is free from arising and ceasing; all phenomena are thus (from the *Benlu*).
In the eighteenth year, the Emperor presided over the Huá'èlóu Hall and summoned eminent masters of the two teachings to debate.

Dharma Master Dàoyīn engaged in dialectical exchange with the Daoist Yǐn Qián for more than forty rounds. Qián’s arguments were defeated, and by imperial decree, the records of the discussion were compiled and included in the Tripiṭaka.
The title is *Kaiyuan Fodao lunheng*.
In the twenty-seventh year, the Jīmǎ (Yǐmǎo) year, the śramaṇa Fǎxiù dreamed that a strange monk exhorted him to provide five hundred monastic robes (*kāṣāya*).
He entered Zhongnan Mountain to offer it to the monks of Huixiang Monastery and proceeded to build it. Upon reaching the mountain, he searched everywhere but found no monastery named Huixiang.
Suddenly he encountered a monk who said, "I will lead you in. Daoshou followed him into the mountains until they reached a place of profound seclusion.
Seeing only clouds shrouding the rocky caverns, he drilled wood for fire and burned incense before them in worship. Suddenly, the clouds parted to reveal a lofty vermilion gate halfway up the cliff.
Xu entered it and saw that the monks there were all extraordinary and magnificent. He took off his *kāṣāya* robe and distributed it throughout the monastery.
A monk from the temple led Xu into an empty room and said, "This was the former residence of the Tang Emperor."

Furthermore, he had previously been fond of music and song; for this reason, he was reborn as a ruler of men. He would soon return again, whereupon [the deity] bestowed upon him a jade flute and a single cassock, entrusting him with these, saying:
"Take these back and present them to the Son of Heaven of Tang. Daoshou returned to the imperial court and submitted the cassock and jade flute sent by the deity.
When the Emperor examined them, he took the jade flute and played it; the melody was exactly as if he had been playing it before.
(General Discussion).
The Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra traveled to the Western Regions to extensively seek out masters and broaden his learning.

In the Kingdom of Siṃhala, he received from the Ācārya Samantabhadra the rites for the Vajra Consecration and the construction of the maṇḍala for the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha). His King...
A herd of wild elephants was fleeing in haste; not empty-handed, they suddenly halted on the road and sat down. When the elephants arrived, they knelt and prostrated themselves.

From this, the entire nation came to revere him with divine awe. The *Sengshi lüe* (Brief History of the Sangha) states: In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, the year of Rénwǔ, five Western Tibetan kingdoms launched an invasion of Ānxī.
On the eleventh day of the second month, he requested military assistance to repel the invaders; an army was dispatched ten thousand *li* away, but it would not arrive for several months.
A close minister then memorialized that, on the following morning, the Emperor summoned the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to enter the palace for recitation.

As Emperor Xuanzong held the incense burner, Amoghavajra chanted the *Benevolent Kings’ State-Protecting Dhāraṇī*. When he had completed only fourteen recitations, the Emperor suddenly beheld more than five hundred divine beings clad in armor.
Carrying a halberd, he stood before the hall. The Emperor asked Amoghavajra, who replied, "This is Vaisravana Deva’s second son, Dujan.
He has responded to Your Majesty’s sincere devotion to go and rescue Anxi. In the fourth month of that year, Anxi submitted a report:
"On the eleventh day of the second month, after the hour of the snake (si-shi), thirty li to the northeast of the city, the sky was shrouded in dark clouds and mist. There appeared a deity..."
He was over ten feet tall, clad in golden armor and leading his troops with majestic and formidable prowess. At the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), drums and horns resounded loudly;
the earth shook and the mountains trembled. After two days, the barbarian raiders fled in disarray, folding up their armor and departing. In an instant, atop the city tower—

The Heavenly King Guangming (King of Radiance) manifested his form. [The Emperor] respectfully commissioned a portrait of him and submitted it with a memorial. Upon reading it, the Emperor was greatly pleased.

Consequently, he issued an edict to all the provincial governors and prefectures throughout the various circuits, ordering that a shrine for the Heavenly King be established in the western corner of each city’s wall, as well as in all military camps throughout the realm, and that Buddhist temples be built alongside them, both bearing the title "Heavenly King" (Tianwang). (From the *History of the Tang*)
Yiyou (17th day of the third month), the fourth year: The Emperor summoned the Daoist Ruyun to an audience at the Dading Hall.

The Emperor inquired about the essentials of the Way, but Gao Lishi, who was a devotee of Buddhism, spoke disparagingly of the Daoist. Consequently, Ruyun took his leave and returned to Maoshan, where he composed writings in which he severely censured the followers of Śākyamuni.
Critics censured him for his inconsistency. At that time, Chen Shaoyou, the Inspector-General of Zhexi, detested what Li Yun had done;

he consequently commissioned the Dharma Master Shen’ung to compose a treatise to refute him. Shen’ung wrote the *Fanmi lun* (Treatise on Overturning Delusion) to correct Yun’s errors, and Yun’s treatise was subsequently discarded.
When the Palace Secretary Dou Shao saw Shen’ung’s treatise, he sighed and said: “Shen’ung may truly be called a *maṇi* jewel beyond the mundane dust.”

[He was] the Master of Central Siṃhala (Old History). ○ An imperial edict was issued for the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra to enter the palace and establish a maṇḍala to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for the Emperor.

He was granted the title of State Preceptor Zhizang. At that time, the court sorcerer Luosiyuan had gained favor; an order was given to have him compete with Amoghavajra to test their relative merits.
On another day, they met in the private hall (*biandian*). Luosiyuan held a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) and directed it toward [the Emperor], engaging in debate. Next, Amoghavajra...
He then took the *cintāmaṇi* and threw it to the ground, commanding Puṇyodana to lift it. Although Puṇyodana possessed great strength, he was unable to move it.

When the Emperor attempted to take it up himself, Amoghavajra smiled and said, "Third Prince, that is merely the shadow of the *cintāmaṇi*. He then raised the *cintāmaṇi* in his hand and showed it to him.
Siyuan was filled with admiration and withdrew. Whenever Amoghavajra performed prayers, he would invariably set up a brocade seat and hold a wooden deity in his hand.

As he recited mantras and cast the deity, it would stand upright upon the seat. The fourfold assembly would look on from all sides, and they would inevitably see the deity’s eyes and lips twitching and moving.
"Though the power of creation may be wrested away, that which one prays for remains. (Shì Tōngjiàn) The *Táng Huìyào* states:
"In the fifth month of the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era, an edict was issued ordering that all monks and nuns throughout the realm be granted certificates by the Cíbù Ministry;
thus, the practice of granting certificates to monks and nuns began with Emperor Mínghuáng. (*Shìwù Jǐyuán*)
Wuzi (the seventh year). Gao Lishi, who served as Director of the Office of Palace Attendants and was promoted to General of the Flying Cavalry, had enjoyed imperial favor for many years;

consequently, both those within and outside the court stood in awe of him. He established Bao-shou Monastery in the Western Capital, and on the day the bell was completed, Lishi held a vegetarian feast to celebrate.
The entire court assembled, and for every single stroke of the bell, he donated one hundred strings of cash. There were many who delighted in making such offerings.
It lasted for twenty strikes of the pestle; the fewest cases did not fall short of ten strikes (Tang History).
On the day of Gengyin, the ninth year, a giant serpent appeared at Mount Mang in Luoyang. It was over a hundred *zhang* long, and anyone who encountered its breath would die immediately.
An imperial edict was issued for Amoghavajra to recite mantras over it. Amoghavajra looked on in alarm and said, "This will turn Luoyang into a vast lake."
...and after being incanted for three days, it died (Old History, Annals of the Five Elements). Yiwu:

The fourteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era. Lǐ Línfú, wishing to block the frontier armies from entering the capital, requested that all ministers be appointed from among the Hu people, thereby bringing about the calamity of Lù Shān.
Lù Shān memorialized requesting thirty-two non-Chinese generals to replace [the Chinese commanders].
The Han general Wei Jiansu remonstrated [against the Emperor’s decision], but his advice was not followed. In the eleventh month, An Lushan captured the capital (Old History).
When Emperor Minghuang fled to Shu and reached Chengdu Prefecture, he passed by Wanli Bridge. He asked those around him for the name of the bridge, and they replied that it was "Ten-thousand-li.

[The Emperor recalled that] in the past, when Zhuge Liang sent an envoy to Wu, he said at this very spot, "A journey of ten thousand li begins from here. The Emperor then sighed, saying, "At the end of the Kaiyuan era, Master Yixing..."
The Emperor said to him, "In twenty years, there will be a national crisis; you shall travel far beyond ten thousand *li*. This is it.
Consequently, he halted his imperial progress at Chengdu Prefecture (*Fangyu Shenglan*).
In the first month of the fifteenth year, An Lushan usurped the throne and established the state of Yan. In the sixth month, An Lushan breached the Tongguan Pass and reached the capital.
In the seventh month, the Crown Prince ascended the throne at Lingwu, honoring the Emperor as the Retired Sovereign (Taishang Huang).
When the Emperor fled to Shu, there was a local official who had rebelled alongside An Lushan; he had previously served as the Governor of Lang and possessed a painted portrait.
As he was passing by on the road, Emperor Minghuang saw him and grew enraged; he then ordered his attendants to draw their swords and sever the head of the statue.
That man was in Shaanxi, yet the head suddenly fell to the ground. In the fifteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era, the year of Bǐshēn, Sùzōng changed the era name to the first year of Zhìdé.
In the seventh month of the Bingshen year, Suzong ascended the throne at Lingwu Terrace. Within ten days, the troops from the various provinces arrived;

he then appointed Fang Guan as Chancellor and concurrently as Supreme Commander. At that time, the invasions were still raging. Some suggested that it would be appropriate to rely upon divine blessings;
the Emperor accepted this advice and led more than a hundred śramaṇas into the mobile palace to establish a *dharmāśālā*, where they recited hymns morning and evening. One night, the Emperor...
In a dream, he saw a śramaṇa with a golden body reciting the name of the Tathāgata Ratnottama.

He asked those around him, and someone replied that there was a monk named Wulou in Helangu Valley who constantly recited this Buddha’s name and possessed many miraculous powers. Thereupon, he summoned Wulou.
He firmly declined and did not go. Soon thereafter, the Emperor issued an edict for Guo Ziyi to convey his instructions. Wulou then appeared at the imperial encampment (xingzai).
The Emperor was delighted and said, "He is truly the monk I saw in my dream. Meanwhile, the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra also appeared at the imperial palace (xinggong).
The Emperor retained both of them and entrusted them with the performance of prayers and exorcisms (tonglun).
Dingyou (1782): In the second year, An Lushan was assassinated by his son, Qingxu, and established himself as ruler.
In the ninth month, the Crown Prince, Guangping Wang Li Su, recaptured the capital. Qingxu fled to Shan. In the tenth month, the Emperor returned to the capital.
In the twelfth month, the Retired Emperor arrived from Xishu.
Master Zhigong recorded prophecies of future events; he once painted a deer carrying a saddle as it ran through the mountains. He also said:
"A two-horned woman in green robes turns her back on Mount Taihang and hastens toward the Sovereign; in the month of 'One-Stop,' she shall surely perish.

Later, when Lü Shan’s rebellion broke out, it was revealed that the "two horns" were the character for *lù* (deer), which is a homophone for *lù* (Lü); the "woman" was the character for *Ān* (An); and "Mount Taihang" was... [text truncated].
The name of the mountain is Mount Zhizhi; "zhí" refers to the first month, the first lunar month. Indeed, in the first month, [the Tang dynasty] met its downfall (from the *Táng cè yíshǐ*).

In this year, Chengguan received ordination and full precepts, vowing to encourage himself with ten matters. Initially, he studied under Chan Master Zhong of Niutou and Chan Master Qin of Jing Mountain.
Later, at the residence of Chan Master Xun, he was transmitted the essential doctrine of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (from the *Shìwù jìyuán*).

The *Shihuozhi* (Annals of Food and Commodities) states: When Suzong reached Fengxiang Prefecture, the following year Zheng Shuqing deliberated that, as the state’s expenditures were insufficient, the various circuits might be permitted to call for the payment of money from the populace in exchange for issuing blank-name certificates (*kongming duedie*) to ordain monks and Daoists.
Thus, the blank-name ordination certificate originated with Suzong (*Shiwujiyuan*).

Wu-xu, the first year of the Qianduan era. The Emperor established an inner *dharma-śālā* within the palace precincts, where the recitation of scriptures and the chanting of *bhāṣya* were conducted with great solemnity.
Zhang Gao remonstrated, saying: "A sovereign should cultivate virtue to quell disorder and bring peace to the people; I have never heard that feeding monks can bring about the Great Peace.

[The Emperor] issued an edict to establish temples on each of the Five Sacred Peaks, appointing venerable elders of the Śākya school to reside therein, and permitted them to announce their appointments.

One who could recite five hundred sheets of scripture was ordained as a monk by Yi. Alternatively, one could pay one hundred strings of cash to request a certificate for tonsure and ordination, and would also be granted the status of a scholar who has mastered the classics (*mingjing chushen*).
More than ten thousand monks were ordained through such payments; this practice of making offerings for ordination began from this time (Tongjian).
Jihai (679), the third month of the second year. An edict was issued to all provinces throughout the realm, ordering each to establish a pond for the release of living beings (*fangsheng chi*).
In the tenth month, Yan Zhenqing, the Regional Inspector of Shengzhou, composed the "Inscription on the Emperor’s Pond for the Release of Living Beings" of the Tang Dynasty. Its preface states:
"Our Sovereign has taken the entire world as his pond, so that all within the realm may receive his blessings. He relies upon the empowerment of *dhāraṇī*..."
Exhausting the power to cross the ford of birth and death across the ocean of afflictions—when measured against the ancients, how could there have been even a semblance of such a thing? (etc.

On the first day of the ninth month of the first year of Shangyuan, the Gengzi year, during the Festival of the Stabilization of Heaven and Earth, the Emperor established a *dōjō* at the Three Palaces, taking the palace women as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the northern gate guards as Vajra Devas. He summoned his ministers...
Prostrations and Circumambulations (from the *Tongjian*). *Xinchou* (the second year).
An imperial edict was issued to Chan Master Huizhong of Nanyang. The edict stated in brief: "I have heard that the Supreme Vehicle of the Tamer has long been at peace within the Central Lands.
The Great Hero’s entrustment truly rests upon my person. I contemplate how to join with Dao’an in widely proclaiming [the Dharma]."

This esoteric scripture extensively promotes the flow of merit and grace throughout the great trichiliocosm. It transmits the mysterious pearl of the formless and extracts the poisonous arrows of delusion.
Since this auspicious condition exists, do not consider it a labor. You have come to the capital with your staff; it is not far now.
Having long purified your mind through fasting, quickly fulfill my wishes. The spring is warm; I hope you are well. I send these instructions and shall say no more. Thus [it was said].

He proceeded to the capital. Initially, he was stationed at Qianfu Temple. The Emperor frequently summoned him into the inner palace to inquire about the Way. One day, the Emperor posed ten questions to the Master. The first asked:
"After realizing one's nature, should one still practice giving to cultivate merit? The Master replied: "To give without attachment to signs accords with realizing one's nature.
The second asked: "What kind of practice should one perform to accord with this Way? The Master said: "To cultivate without seeking achievement accords with it."
Regarding this path, the third question was: "If there should arise the difficulty of illness, how shall one practice to withstand it? The Master said: "Realize that karma is fundamentally empty;
thus, you will attain immovability. The fourth question was: "At the time of death, how can one attain mastery? The Master said: "Exert yourself and have confidence in the Way."
Fifth, [the student asked]: "When afflictions arise, how should one bring them to rest? The Master said: "The fundamental mind is profoundly still;
afflictions return to its wondrous function. Sixth, [the student asked]: "After seeing one's nature, should one continue to practice Buddha-recitation and seek rebirth in the Pure Land?

The Master said: "Nature is itself the Buddha; birth is itself the Pure Land. Seventh, [the student asked]: "Once these aggregates are cast off, where will one be born? The Master said: "There is no casting off, and there is no [rebirth]."
"Regarding birth at will: eighth, it is said that at the time of death, a flower pedestal and a jeweled seat will come to welcome one.
May one go? The Master said, "Do not grasp at appearances. "Ninth, how does one attain supernatural powers and become a Buddha?

The Master said, "Realizing one's nature is like a poor man finding treasure, or a subject gaining a king. "Tenth, is it sufficient to cultivate samādhi based solely on this original nature to become a Buddha? The Master said:
One will certainly attain Buddhahood; yet for the Buddha, there is neither form nor attainment—this is true attainment. These ten pairs have extensive explanations [as follows].
The Emperor, because of this, concentrated his mind upon the profound principle (*wǔdēng*). The Emperor asked, "What Dharma did you receive at Caoxi?
The Master said, "Does Your Majesty see a single cloud in the sky? The Emperor said, "I see it. The Master said, "Nail it down."
It was suspended there.
In the fourth month of the first year of Baoying (the Renyin year), the nun Zhenru of Longxing Temple in Chu Prefecture had a vision as if someone were leading her up to heaven.
There she beheld the Heavenly Emperor, who bestowed upon her thirteen treasures and said to Zhenru: "In the Middle Kingdom, there is..."
Disaster. It is appropriate to suppress it with the second treasure. Cui Shen, the Regional Inspector of Chu Prefecture, submitted a memorial to present these to the court:
first, the Mysterious Broad Celestial Token; second, the Jade Cock; third, the Grain Disc; fourth, the Return of the Queen Mother;
fifth, the Azure-Colored Treasure; sixth, the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel; seventh, the Red Maṇi; eighth, the Langqian Pearl; ninth, the Jade Pendant; tenth, the Jade Seal; eleventh, the Mulberry Tree.
12. The Thunder Axe. 13. [Name lost]. When the Emperor examined them, he was greatly pleased and named them the "State-Stabilizing Treasures.

Since the Emperor had received these offerings from Chu Prefecture—the very state to which the Crown Prince had been enfeoffed—and had further heard that the Central Plains ought to be secured by the second treasure, he subsequently issued an edict for the Crown Prince to assume the affairs of government, granted a general amnesty, and changed the era name. In the fourth month of this year, the Emperor...

[Emperor Dezong] was not yet prepared [to ascend the throne]. Empress Wei personally wrote out sutras with her own blood as an expression of her sincerity. The various officials held vegetarian feasts for the monks at the monasteries.
On the fifth month, the Retired Emperor passed away. The Emperor was so overcome with grief that he fell ill; fourteen days later, he passed away. The Crown Prince ascended the throne;
this was Daizong (Old History: *Jiu Tang Shu*).
Guimao: Emperor Daizong. He changed the era name to Guangde. In the eleventh month, the Tibetans captured the capital, and the imperial court fled to Shan.
The Tibetans installed Prince Chenghong of Guangwu as emperor. Guo Ziyi led his troops, and upon their arrival, the Tibetans withdrew.
In the twelfth month, the court returned to the capital. While the Emperor was at Huayin, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva appeared on Mount Wutai; the Emperor received him with secrecy.

He addressed the Emperor and requested to return to the capital. By imperial decree, the Mañjuśrī Hall was renovated; copper tiles were cast and coated with gold, at an expense of hundreds of millions (Tongjian).
Jiachen (Year 2). An imperial edict was issued for the Inner Dao-chamber (Nei-daochang), ordering three hundred monks to be selected;

they were to serve in shifts of one hundred men each, riding horses when entering or leaving the palace, and lecture on the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. In this year, National Teacher Zhong was welcomed to reside at Guangzhai Temple (*Tongjian*).
Zhang Gao, whose courtesy name was Congzhou, served concurrently as Chief Counselor of the Secretariat and the Chancellery and at that time recruited śramaṇas to serve within the Inner Dao-chamber.

Chang Hao remonstrated, saying, "The fortune of the Son of Heaven lies primarily in nourishing the people. One may employ a single volume of scripture to promote moral transformation, but I have never heard that the mere practice of Buddhist dharma brings about great peace.
I pray that Your Majesty will take 'non-action' as your guiding principle and not disturb your sagely deliberations with the Lesser Vehicle.
The Emperor followed his advice (from the *Jiu Tang Shu*).
Yisi (October 10, 765), the ninth month of the first year of the Yongtai era. Pugu Huaien arrived with troops from the Uyghurs and the Tibetans.
At the Zisheng and Ximing Monasteries, one hundred high seats were established to lecture on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.

Two carriages of scriptures were sent out from the palace, accompanied by human figures dressed as bodhisattvas and spirits, led by music and ceremonial processions. The officials welcomed them at the [monasteries].
Outside the Gate of Radiant Harmony (Guangshunmen), he followed [the Emperor] to the temple.

When the Tibetans reached Bīn Prefecture, the Emperor ordered the Chancellor and various high officials to the Ximing Temple to offer incense, hold a vegetarian feast, and perform music. Upon hearing this, the Tibetans withdrew.

He abolished the hundred high-seated lecture assemblies and, for ten months, collected resources from the people to provide offerings for the stūpa. Yuan Zai, Du Hongjian, and Wang Jin—these three were [the officials involved].
Both [Li] Xiang and [Wang] Jing were devoted to the Buddha, Jing being particularly so. Together with [Liu] Hongjian, they constructed temples without end.

The Emperor once asked them whether the words of the Buddha regarding retribution and cause-and-effect were real or not. Jing and the others memorialized, saying: "The longevity and prosperity of our dynasty’s mandate are due to no small measure of accumulated merit and karma;
how else could such a thing be brought about? Since this merit and karma are already established, even if there should be minor calamities from time to time, they cannot cause harm. This is why..."

An Lushan and Shi Siming (in the eleventh month of the first year of Baoying, Shi Chaoyi killed Siming and established himself as leader) saw their poison spread and their influence flourish, yet both met with the calamity of their own sons.

Pu Guohuai’en raised troops to commit internal rebellion, yet died of illness upon leaving his gate. The Uyghurs and Tibetans launched a massive invasion deep into our territory, yet they withdrew without a fight.
These events were all beyond the reach of human power; how can one say there is no retribution? Thus it was said.

Because of this, he believed deeply in the Buddha. Consequently, within the palace, the chanting of Buddhist hymns (*braṃ-pai*) and the offering of incense during fasting rituals never slackened for even a moment.

High and low officials, both inside and outside the court, followed this influence and transformed themselves, revering the Buddha. Yin Jing (styled Xiaqing) was the younger brother of Wang Wei; both were renowned for their fame.
Jing served as the Commissioner of the Henan Vice-Commander-in-Chief. He revered the Buddha and abstained from meat and blood; in his later years, he was especially observant in these matters.
During the final years of Emperor Daizong’s reign, he held Buddhism in high esteem and would frequently engage in relaxed discussions with its practitioners.

He established an inner chapel within the palace, where he regularly invited over a hundred śramaṇas and provided them with sumptuous and abundant offerings. When an invasion occurred, he ordered the monks to preach the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) to ward off the calamity;
once the invaders had departed, he bestowed lavish rewards upon them. The foreign monk Amoghavajra was appointed to the rank of Minister (Qingjian) and enfeoffed as a Duke of the State.
Moving freely between the imperial gates, his influence overwhelmed the powerful and noble. Fertile lands and excellent profits throughout the capital region were mostly transferred to monasteries.
He constructed Jinguesi on Mount Wutai, casting copper for the roof tiles and coating them with gold; the expenditure reached hundreds of millions.

By imperial decree, he was granted official documents from the Zhongshu Secretariat, ordering dozens of monks from Mount Wutai to disperse to the four quarters to seek profit and manage the enterprise.
(Above, all from the *Tongjian*). Bingwu:
The first year of Dali. On the full moon of the seventh month, Renwu, the Almsgiving Assembly for the Hungry Ghosts (*Ullambana*) was held within the imperial palace.

Adorned with silver and pearls, seven ancestral seats were established for the High Ancestor and the two Emperors. Banners, ritual whisks, and ceremonial canopies bore the imperial titles inscribed upon them.

The remains were escorted from the Imperial Ancestral Temple into the Inner Sanctuary amidst the sounding of *nāga-bhāṇḍa* and *chui* music, and the beating of drums; banners and streamers reached toward the heavens.

On this day, the hundred officials stood in formation at the Gate of Light and Compliance (*Guangshunmen*), bowing in welcome as they escorted the procession. From then on, this was performed annually for the Emperor. [Gui] year.
In the two chambers of the Tai Miao (Ancestral Temple), living *lingzhi* mushrooms grew. The Emperor composed a poem to celebrate this, and all his officials followed suit (*Tang Shu*).

On the day Dingwei, in the second year, Yu Cha’en memorialized that the granted estate should be established as Changjing Monastery to provide merit for the posthumous blessings of Empress Dowager Zhangjing.
The construction was so magnificent and lavish that even all the timber from the marketplace was insufficient; he further memorialized for the destruction of the Qujiang Park and...
The Huaqing Palace was provided as a residence for her. The expenses amounted to ten thousand billion. Gao Ying, a jinshi of Weizhou, submitted a memorial, the gist of which stated:
"The sacred virtue of the late Empress Dowager did not seek to enhance the glory of the state by means of a single temple; she sought instead a long-term plan for peace and stability."

"The people are the foundation. To abandon human beings for the sake of temples—what merit could there be in that? Furthermore, it has been said: 'It may be tolerable to have no temples, but it is not tolerable to have no people.
Moreover, Your Majesty should model yourself after Xia Yu by keeping your palaces humble, yet you instead exalt pagodas and shrines."
"Are you following the example of Emperor Liang Wu? Furthermore, he submitted a memorial, stating in brief: "The enlightened kings of antiquity accumulated goodness to bring about fortune;

they did not expend wealth to seek calamity. They cultivated virtue to dispel disaster; they did not exhaust the people to avert misfortune. Yet now, construction projects are hurried and cease neither by day nor night.
Those whose strength cannot keep pace are immediately subjected to flogging and caning. The sounds of grief and pain fill [the land]."
"Roads. To hope for blessings through this, Your Majesty fears not so. He further said: "Your Majesty turns back toward the correct Way yet seeks omens within external objects;
you follow the erroneous calculations of those around you, thereby harming the great principles of the August Kings.

I deeply regret this on Your Majesty’s behalf. All these matters were suppressed and no reply was given (*Tongjian*). ○ Gao Ying again submitted a memorial, saying: "Your Majesty is profoundly filial."
Their kindness is equal to Heaven’s; it is boundless. One’s filial longing is such that nothing can surpass it. To exhaust one’s strength in pursuing filial piety is truly beneficial;
yet to neglect one’s duties and exhaust the people is inevitably harmful. Abandoning one’s kin to dwell in a monastery—what merit could there be in that?

Formerly, when Lord Zhuang of Lu renovated the pillars of Duke Huan’s temple and carved its rafters, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* recorded this as a violation of propriety. [Likewise, the conduct of] Emperors Xiaohui and Xiaowu...
Emperor Jing, Xiaowen, and Xuan decreed that the various commanderies, kingdoms, and feudal lords establish ancestral temples for the High Ancestor’s civil and military virtues.
Upon reaching Emperor Yuan, he consulted with the *boshi* (scholars of ritual) and, drawing upon ancient rites, abolished them. Now, even temples were not established in violation of the rites;

how much less so those which are not places where the ancestral protection resides or where the spiritual essence dwells? To exhaust the strength of ten thousand people in pursuit of all-encompassing retribution—what purpose does this serve?

That this is impossible is also clear. Why? Because our military campaigns against the barbarians have not yet been pacified, the occupied territories have not yet been recovered, weapons of war have not yet been laid down, and the exhausted people have not yet been comforted.
The imperial granaries lack a year’s supply, and the Ministry of Agriculture suffers from the弊 (disadvantages) of state-monopolized brewing.
How can we, at such a time, mobilize the labor force for public works? Furthermore, he did not receive a reply (from the Emperor). (*Tang Shu*)
Wu-shen (17th day of the 8th month), the third year of the Dali era. An imperial edict was issued for the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to establish a *maṇḍala* at Xingshan Monastery.
The Emperor commanded his close attendants, high ministers, and various generals to all receive the *abhiṣeka*. The Emperor personally conferred an official title upon Amoghavajra:

*Tetjin Honglu Qing* (Special Advance, Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial). He summoned National Teacher Zhong to the inner palace and introduced the man from Taibai Mountain to him. The Emperor said:
"This man seems to have some insight; I ask you, Master, to test him. Zhong said, "What abilities do you possess?

The mountain man replied, "I respectfully claim to know mountains, know lands, know characters, and am skilled at calculation. The Master asked, "Is the mountain where you dwell a male mountain or a female mountain?
The mountain man was utterly bewildered and could not answer. The Master pointed to the floor of the hall and asked, "What kind of ground is this? He replied:
"I shall allow my disciple to calculate it, and then I will know. The Master drew a single stroke on the ground and said, "This is the character 'Shen' (甚).

You say it is the character 'Yi' (一, one). The Master said, 'A single stroke upon the earth is the character 'Wang' (王, king); why do you call it the character 'Yi'? The Master spoke again, 'What is three times seven?
He replied, 'The National Teacher is teasing his disciple. Three times seven is surely twenty-one. The Master said, 'But it is actually the character for "mountain" (山). "
"Human calculation," the Master said, "is that seven times three equals ten. Why do you say twenty-one? The Master asked again, "What other abilities do you possess?
He replied, "Even if I possessed such abilities, I would not dare to speak of them to the National Teacher. The Master said, "Even if you possessed such abilities, they would still not be sufficient.
The Master then said to the Emperor, "To ask about the mountain while not knowing the mountain; to ask about the earth while not knowing the earth; to ask—"
He could not recognize characters when asked about them, nor did he understand arithmetic when questioned on calculation. "Your Majesty, from where have you obtained this muddled fellow?
the Emperor said to the mountain man, "I possess a kingdom and a throne, yet these are not what I consider treasures; you, Master, are a treasure of the nation.
The mountain man replied, "Your Majesty truly recognizes a treasure. (From the *Monk Biographies*)

An imperial edict was issued to Chan Master Daqin of Mount Jing: The Edict states: "I have heard that in the region south of the Yangtze River there is a Chan practitioner who has long cultivated the Way, whose virtuous nature is as pure as ice and frost, and whose ascetic conduct dwells among the forests and wilds.
With an empty mind, I gaze toward him with longing; my yearning is constant and deep. Where there is resonance, there must be communication."
The nation also celebrates this great joy. We pray that the Venerable Master will descend from afar to the Central Kingdom, so that we may fully turn toward you in devotion.

May you not fail your power of aspiration, manifesting forms in response to sentient beings. Now, I dispatch the Inner Attendant Huang Feng to proclaim this decree, specifically to come and welcome you by imperial edict.

Please quickly fulfill our hearts' desires. The spring is warm; does the Master remain in good health? I send this message with no further words, along with an imperial decree. It shall now be provided by this prefecture. Upon its arrival—
The prefectures and counties opened a quiet court to accommodate the officials, forbidding them from visiting so as not to exhaust the master’s mental and physical strength;

as for disciples, they were not permitted in large numbers, though he allowed a few to attend upon him. When the Master arrived at the palace, the Emperor personally paid him homage and offered his greetings, speaking with ease:
"I have heard," the Emperor said, "that the divine dragon offered its pool to Mount Jingshan. Were it not for the Master’s virtue and wisdom, such a thing could not have occurred.
When the Master entered the Baifu Hall (Hall of Hundred Blessings) and was granted an audience within the inner palace, he rose upon seeing the Emperor approach. The Emperor asked, "Why do you rise?

The Master replied, "How can Your Majesty perceive this poor monk within the four modes of deportment? After the audience concluded, the Emperor bestowed upon him the title Guo Yi Dajue Chan (National First Great Enlightenment Chan Master).
The Master [Chen] was honored with the posthumous title Senglü; Zanning composed the "Biography of Master Qin," which runs to no fewer than a thousand words.
Even for a single cock that crowed at dawn, one would record its name even upon its death; why then is this [Master Chen] not accorded such treatment? (Linjian Lu). Li Zao’s *Guoshi Bu* states:
Lord Cui Zhao asked Chan Master Qin of Mount Jing, "May I, your disciple, leave the household life?
Qin replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. Lord Zhao sighed in admiration of these words.
While the Master was residing at Mount Jing, he sat alone beneath a stone screen on the northern peak. A layman in white robes came before him and prostrated, saying:

The disciple was a man from Jinzi Mountain. Having heard that the Buddha-dharma was facing persecution in Chang’an, he wished to become a śrāmaṇera under the Master to go and rescue it, for the Master’s conduct was lofty and pure. The Master asked, "What power do you possess?
He replied, "I recite the *Koṭi-avalokiteśvara-mantra*; its efficacy is peerless. The Master said, "There is a stone screen behind me; can you shatter it?"
He replied, "It may be done. After a short while, he struck it with a shout. The stone screen split into three pieces; this is the present-day He Shi Yan (Drinking Stone Cliff).
The Master, recognizing its divine and extraordinary nature, immediately shaved his head, provided him with robes and a bowl, and changed his name to Chonghui (according to the *Sengzhuan*).

Gengxu (the 5th year). Amoghavajra manifested illness and submitted a memorial to take his leave. The Emperor dispatched an inner attendant to inquire after his health and conferred upon him the rank of Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si and the title of Duke of Xiao.
Amoghavajra declined these honors four or five times, but the Emperor would not permit it.

On the day of Guiwei in the sixth month, he passed away while lying peacefully. The Emperor suspended court for three days. On the day of his cremation, an imperial decree was issued to bring the ritual prayer and ancestral offerings.

His sagely words were profound and penetrating, and his ritual conduct surpassed all others. He was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works (Sikong) and bestowed the honorific title of the Tripitaka Master Dapian Zheng Guangzhi.
In the ninth month of the following year, an imperial edict ordered that a stupa for Amoghavajra’s relics be erected at his former residence temple.
Yan Ying, the Censor-in-Chief, composed the "Stele Recording His Virtues."
Gui-chou: Du Hongjian. Having celebrated the merits of Emperor Suzong, he served as the Military Governor of the Southern Capital and subsequently assisted in the administration of government.

He resigned from his ministerial post on account of illness and passed away three days later. At the time of his death, he bathed and solemnly donned his court robes over a saṃghāṭī; he shaved his beard and hair before departing this life.
His final testament was that he be interred according to the rites of a śramaṇa, with a stūpa erected for his burial (Old History).

Jiayin (the year of the *jiayin* cycle), the ninth year of the Dali era. The Daoist Shi Hua gained favor through his arts and requested that a blade-ladder be erected to compete with the śramaṇas in a contest of supernatural powers.
An imperial decree was issued for monks from the two monastic districts (*liàngjiē*) to be selected, and a date was set to determine victory or defeat.

The śramaṇa Chonghui regularly recited the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* and submitted a memorial requesting to subdue him. The Emperor led the hundred officials to witness the event. Shi Hua ascended the blade-ladder.

The Emperor then commanded Huì to tread upon blades and ascend; he went back and forth without injury. Taking advantage of this success, the Emperor ordered that firewood be piled in the courtyard and a great flame ignited.
Huì entered the mass of fire and called out for Huā to enter as well. Huā, overcome with shame and perspiration, did not dare to look him directly in the face. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
He was granted the title of "Protector of the Nation" (Huguo) and the purple robe (zijī).
In the tenth year, the year Yimao (795), National Teacher Zhong took his leave of Emperor Daizong. The Emperor said, "After the Master’s passing, what shall your disciples use to commemorate you?
Zhong replied, "Inform the donor to have a 'seamless stupa' (wuseng ta) constructed. The Emperor said, "I request that the Master [explain this]."
Regarding the style of the stupa: Zhongliang remained silent for a long time and then asked, "Do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand.

Zhongliang said, "I have an attendant named Yingzhen (who later resided at Danyuan) who indeed knows this matter. On the ninth day of the twelfth month, he passed away lying on his right side. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa.

He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dazheng. Shortly thereafter, the Emperor summoned Yingzhen to the inner palace and asked him about the previous conversation. After a long silence, Yingzhen asked, "Does Your Majesty understand?
The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. Yingzhen answered with a verse: To the south of Xiang and north of Tan, Within lies gold filling the entire land.
Beneath the shadowless tree, the boat of unity; In the crystal palace, there is no one who knows.

(Fushan’s Nine Bands states: "The ox-head faces south, the horse-head faces north; between them, gold fills the entire land," and so forth. Fifth, the Band of the Vertical and Horizontal Interpenetration of Principle and Phenomena [from the *Sengshi*]).
The fourteenth year of the Dali era, the Jiwu (Jiwei) year; in the fifth month, Emperor Daizong passed away. On the day of Gengshen, Dezong ascended the throne.

In the first year of Jianzhong, an imperial decree was issued prohibiting various military commands from petitioning for the establishment of temples and monasteries, as well as the ordination of commoners into the ranks of monks and nuns, and the abolition of the *ulambana* festival held within the palace.
Between Ze and Lu there was a monk named Puman, who would sometimes sing and sometimes laugh; his predictions were often proven accurate.

At the beginning of the Jianzhong era, he wrote a poem on the wall of a Buddhist temple in Luzhou that said: "This water connects with the Jing River; the two vermilion [streams] fill the valley with blood. The blue ox leads the red tiger."
It was then styled the Year of Great Peace (*Taiping*). These characters for the water, *cǐ* (泚), and the *Jīng* River originate from the military chaos at Jīngchuān.
The "Twin Zhuos" refers to Zhu Tāo and Zhu Cǐ. Regarding the "Blue Ox": the second year of Xuányuán was the *Yǐchǒu* year; *yǐ* is wood and *chǒu* is the ox.

This was the year the reign title was changed to Zhēnyuán. *Bǐng* is fire and *yǐn* is the tiger. That year, the rebels were suppressed. [In] the tenth month of the fourth year of Jiànzhōng, Zhu Cǐ...
The troops rebelled, and he usurped the national title of Qin. The Emperor visited Fengtian (as noted in the *Shihua*).

Chengguan, the commentator on the Avatamsaka Sutra, whose courtesy name was Daxiu, was first summoned to the palace in the third year of the Dali era to assist Amoghavajra in translating the scriptures.

While serving as the Grand Virtuous One (Dade) for the translation bureau, he declined the honor and retired to the Great Avatamsaka Monastery on Mount Wutai, where he engaged in profound reflection and extensive study.

He surveyed the various heterodox teachings and composed a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* according to the stages of faith, understanding, practice, and realization (*śraddhā-adhimukti-caryā-sākṣātkriyā*).
He divided the *Avataṃsaka* into four major sections, completing the work after four years, reaching the year of Guihai (1083), at which point the text was finished.
Jiazi: The first year of Xingyuan (764). In the fifth month, the capital was recovered. In the seventh month, the Emperor returned to the capital.
Chan Master Mingzan of Nanyue had previously resided at Shangfeng. During the Qianyuan era, Li Bi entered Mount Heng to pay his respects to him.
Zan was reciting a sutra when Bi said, "Are you not one who has retreated into seclusion? Do you not have aspirations for the clouds and the sky?
Zan spat at him, saying, "Do not try to provoke me. Bi’s expression did not waver. After a long while, seeing that Bi stood waiting without ceasing, Zan said, "Has your meal not yet arrived?
Bi replied, "It has not. Zan poked at the fire, pulled out a taro, and ate it. They conversed until they reached the point where Zan was about to depart; Zan then patted him on the back.
It was said: "He would have made a good Chancellor for ten years. When Li Mi came to power, he memorialized the Emperor regarding [Wang Wei's] noble conduct.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree to summon him. When the envoy reached his dwelling and delivered the message, saying, "The Son of Heaven has issued a decree;

Your Honor should please rise to express your gratitude," Wang Wei sat for a long time with tears streaming down his chin, remaining seated and paying no heed at all. The envoy returned and reported these matters to the Emperor, who praised him incessantly. Once...
He composed a song, saying: I have a single word: sever all thoughts and forget all conditions. It cannot be skillfully explained; it is transmitted only through the mind.
Furthermore, there is one more phrase: nothing surpasses direct giving. Subtle as a fine hair, yet vast beyond any location.

It is primordially perfected, requiring no labor of the loom. Worldly affairs are wearying; they are not as good as the mountain peaks. Green pines obscure the sun; emerald waters flow on long. The mountains—

Let the clouds serve as my curtain; let the night moon be my fishing line. Reclining beneath the wisteria vines with a block of stone for a pillow, I shall not court the Son of Heaven—how could I envy kings and lords?
With no anxiety regarding life or death, what more need I worry about? Water-moons have no fixed form;
I am always at ease. All phenomena are thus; they are fundamentally unborn. Sitting upright and free from affairs, when spring comes, the grass turns green of its own accord. —Sōtō (Sūnghoe) again.
The commentary on the poem states: Li Mi once studied at Hengyue Temple and associated with Chan Master Mingzan. Observing his conduct, he perceived that he was no ordinary man.
At midnight, he heard the sound of Mingzan’s chanting of the *buddha-śabda*, which resonated throughout the mountains and forests. Li Mi was quite knowledgeable in the art of music.
He was able to discern joy and sorrow through the resonance of the Sanskrit scriptures; first feeling melancholy and later filled with joy, he must have been one destined for demotion.
His time was drawing to a close. One night, [Liu] Zhong went secretly to visit him. Zàn invited him to sit, poked at the fire, pulled out some taro, and fed it to him, saying:
"I share half of my fortune with you; may your descendants enjoy its blessings. Be careful not to speak too much; you shall receive the office of Chancellor for ten years."
Bi bowed twice and withdrew.
On the day of Yichou, the first year of the Zhenyuan era was inaugurated.
On the day of Bingyin, it was the second year. Lectures were proclaimed at all the monasteries, and the Ullambana Assembly was held once again.
Wuchen (the fourth year): An earthquake occurred in the capital. An imperial edict was issued to welcome the finger-bone śarīra of the Buddha from Wuyouwang Temple in Qizhou;
it was brought into the inner court for veneration. In the tenth month of the following year, Dharma Master Chengguan was appointed as Professor Monk (Jiaoshou Heshang).

Xinwei (the 10th day of the fifth month). In the sixth month of the seventh year, the Emperor visited Changjing Temple to observe the translation of Buddhist scriptures. The Emperor composed a poem, and Taizu and his court officials all joined in with compositions.
Liu Zhitou composed the Stele Inscription for Master Mituo of Mount Nanyue, which states in brief: "During the reign of Emperor Daizong, there was National Preceptor Fazhao..."
It is said that his teacher, the Elder of Nanyue, possessed extraordinary virtue; the Son of Heaven faced south to pay him homage.
Because his Way could not be fully encompassed by official titles, the Emperor issued a formal decree naming his residence the "Bānrě Dàochǎng" (Prajñā Practice Hall) to honor his station.

During the reign of Emperor Dēngzōng, an imperial edict was further issued to praise him, and the site became known as Mítuó Sè (Amitābha Monastery). Those who followed his transformation numbered in the tens of thousands.

Guiyou (the tenth year of the cycle), the fourth month of the ninth year. On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, the relevant authorities prepared ceremonial carriages and the Buddhist section provided drummers and musicians to escort the Professor Monk into the palace to expound upon the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
He was granted the title National Teacher Qingliang (*Tongjian*).
Jiaxu, the ninth month of the tenth year. The Emperor wished to repair Shenglong Temple and required pine trees fifty *chi* in height, but none could be found.
Pei Yanling said, "I recently saw several thousand timber trees in a valley near Tongzhou, all of which are eighty *chi* long.
The Emperor replied, "During the Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras, we sought fine timber within the capital region and still could not obtain it; how could there be such things now?"
He replied: "When Heaven produces rare talent, it surely finds a sage ruler; thus the Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras emerged.
From where else could they have come? (Same source).
Shi Jiaoran possessed extraordinary talent and was revered by Yan Lugu, Yu Di, and other eminent gentlemen. When Lu Yu arrived...
Thus, they would engage in pure conversation all day long; the scholar-officials admired their refined bearing and felt ashamed to seek fame through literary works. They sighed, saying:

"If one possessed the broad learning of Confucius or the vast erudition of Xu Chen, yet merely flaunted the Way and boasted of righteousness before one's eyes, it would only serve to disturb the true nature.
How could this compare to the silent harmony with the Way found when meditative concentration is paired with mountain pines, clouds, and the moon—a state of ultimate stillness?"
"Yet our natures are the same. I shall now dismantle my mountain [hermitage] and gather my writings to burn them.

Later, when Li Hong, the Governor-General of Zhongcheng, visited him while serving as the Prefect of Huzhou, he requested his poems and essays. [Huijiao] replied, "I have set aside my brush and inkstone for twenty-four years."
Having attained nothing, he searched in darkness for the burdens of worldly things, which merely gave rise to the notions of self and person; these he had long since abandoned.

After his death, the Chancellor Yu Di sought them extensively among the common people and managed to obtain only ten fascicles. He then composed a preface and presented them to the court, where Emperor Dezong issued an edict to enshrine them in the Secret Library (Bige).
Yihai (the 10th day of the 11th month): The Vinaya Master Lingche, whose courtesy name was Yuancheng, resided at Yunmen Temple in Yuezhou.
At that time, high officials of great talent and reputation, such as Liu Changqing, Yan Wei, and Huangfu Zeng, all sent their calling cards to establish a friendship with him.
Lingche’s poetry was ranked alongside that of Jiaoran and Sengbiao. He authored the twenty-one fascicles of the *Lüzong xingyuan* (The Source of Practice in the Vinaya School). Initially, Lingche...

He traveled to the capital, where his reputation resounded throughout the imperial precincts. The monastic community, envious of his prominence, circulated malicious rumors and slandered him, leading to his punishment by exile to Tingzhou.
He entered Huicheng (Shaoxing) and remained there until the end of his life. The Chancellor Quan De’yu once composed a preface for his departure, stating:

"By observing his countenance, examining his words, and knowing his heart, one realizes he has attained stillness not by waiting for external circumstances to become quiet, but by being still within himself. — Lu De.
Yù was also on friendly terms with Dhyāna Master Xuán. When Xuán returned to India, Yù composed a preface to see him off, which read in brief:
"The śramaṇa suffers from being entangled by external views; once he has attained [realization], he suffers from being bound by internal views.

Now Master Xuán is carefree amidst these two views—neither external nor internal—darkly attuned to the ultimate subtlety. Furthermore, as for the peerless landscapes of the mountains and waters of Gōngū..."
Furthermore, in India, there is a pure realm for walking meditation (caṅkrama). One proceeds there shaking the mendicant’s staff (khakkhara), the mind vast and expansive.
This is because one arises in accord with conditions and brings about transformation through contact with things, rather than being led away by external defilements.
Bingzi, the twelfth year. Following the established custom for the Emperor’s birthday, monks and Daoists were ordered to engage in debate at Linqide Hall.
On this occasion, Confucian scholars were included in the discussion; the Emperor was greatly pleased (*Tongjian*).

The Emperor then commanded Dharma Master Chengguan, together with the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra, to translate the Sanskrit manuscripts of the latter portion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* presented by the Kingdom of Oḍra.

The Emperor personally attended the translation assembly. On one occasion, when he did not arrive, he immediately dispatched a monk with these instructions: "Due to the affairs of state, the Emperor is unable to attend.
He hereby grants his consent (*yuyu*) for the Dharma and the purity of the monastic proceedings. Once the translation is completed, it shall be presented to him.

When the ministers assembled in great numbers to observe the Emperor’s ascent to the throne, he expounded upon the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, saying: "That which reaches the furthest reaches of space is the 'Great' (*Mahā*), for its substance is boundless. It exhausts the vast ocean..."

It is vast like the ocean, yet its waters can be drunk; this is its profundity. The Dharma-gate is inexhaustible; this is its squareness. One may count the dust-motes of all lands, yet its function remains unfathomable; this is its breadth.

It transcends both the perceiving subject and the perceived object, illuminating the dark recesses of the ten directions; this is the Buddha. It spreads the fragrance of the myriad practices and causes the various virtues to blossom in glory;

this is the Flower. It perfects the myriad practices and virtues to adorn the Ten Bodies; this is the Ornament. It penetrates and gathers the profound and subtle to bring [the teaching] to completion.

The radiance of True Light is the Sūtra. These seven characters in total constitute the grand framework of this entire work. To realize one's original nature, there is nothing other than practice by which to be guided.

Therefore, it speaks of the boundless, supreme practices of Samantabhadra; as these practices arise, conceptual understanding ceases, wisdom is realized with perfect clarity, and unimpeded, harmonious penetration manifests for immediate enjoyment.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the purple robe and the title of Professor (Jiaoshou) Upādhyāya.

Ji-mao, the fourth month of the fifteenth year. On the anniversary of the Emperor’s birth, he issued an edict to the relevant authorities to provide ceremonial carriages to welcome Professor-Heshang Chengguan into the inner palace to expound the fundamental principles of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. As Chengguan ascended the seat, he said: "How great is the true realm!"

The myriad dharmas find their origin therein; it encompasses all while transcending all marks. It enters the realm of words and images yet remains boundless. Its wondrous existence is not existence, and its true emptiness is not emptiness.

Our Buddha attained this, wondrously practicing true awakening. He purified the dust of habitual tendencies until they were utterly cleansed, remaining tranquil within the domain of the ten thousand transformations, yet exerting his activity within the single void.
He merged his body with benefit so that they mutually contain one another, and his fame and radiance spread afar.
Our Sovereign has illuminated this through his sagacity; his spiritual discernment reaches the ultimate void, and his inner chamber is in harmony with the Great Accord (*mahā-saṃhita*).

His sacred writings eclipse those of a hundred kings, and his pure influence fans out across the ten thousand nations. He spreads the profound transformation to awaken the dreaming world and bestows the Heavenly Truth (*t’ien chen*) upon human nature and emotion.

Thus, the purport of the *Avataṃsaka* teachings is vast, expansive, profound, and subtle—it cannot be grasped through mere thought or ritual form. To lose its essential meaning is to practice in vain.
"Through kalpas of causes and conditions, he has attained the gateway [to the Dharma]. He equalizes all Buddhas in a single morning... (and so forth). The Emperor looked at his ministers and said:
"The Teacher of this realm speaks with elegance and brevity; his words are classical and appropriate. He is able to use the Holy Dharma to cool my mind.

I shall therefore bestow upon him the title of National Teacher, 'Qingliang' (Cooling). The Emperor further reflected: "Hitherto, I have clung to body and mind, and to the notions of self and others..."

Furthermore, to regard the fixed characteristics of all dharmas as such is a perversion. The ministers bowed twice with their heads to the ground and received the enlightened command upon the crowns of their heads.
Consequently, the high officials and ministers of both the inner and outer courts all honored him with the eight precepts and took him as their teacher (*Sengshi*).
○ Yu Chengxuan composed the inscription for the Wugou Jingguang Pagoda in Fuzhou, which states in brief: "The Censor-in-Chief, Lord Liu; the Military Supervisor, Lord Yu..."
They spoke to one another: "In repaying our sovereign, nothing is greater than promoting his welfare. In promoting welfare, nothing is greater than planting roots of goodness.

In planting roots of goodness, nothing is greater than the Buddha-dharma. Is not the foundation of the Buddha-dharma found in the *stūpa*? As for the *stūpa*, above it reaches the various heavens, and below it stabilizes the three realms.
The shade of its shadow is like the illumination of the sun and moon; it breaks through darkness to bring forth light. As for the bells..."
The resonance was like the playing of metal and stone instruments; hearing the sound, people gave rise to wholesome thoughts. Thus, all such merits returned to the King of Men.

Once his plans were concealed, he looked upon them with joy. Those who partook of the royal stipend delighted in giving alms; those who bore the Emperor’s favor took pleasure in offering their labor. No complaints were heard regarding the toil.
When the work was completed, the Emperor praised it highly and bestowed an imperial edict to inscribe the title. He granted—
It is named the Stūpa of Undefiled Pure Light of the Zhenyuan Era.
The *Book of Tang* records that Jia Dao, whose courtesy name was Langxian, was originally a monk named Wuben.

While traveling in the Eastern Capital, he encountered a decree by the Magistrate of Luoyang prohibiting monks from leaving the streets after midday. Jia Dao composed a poem lamenting this restriction, and Han Yu took pity on his verse.
He was a man of talent who taught others to abandon the teachings of the Buddha (Futu). He passed the jinshi examination and served as the District Magistrate of Puzhou before passing away.
When the Venerable Jun returned to Huainan, Liu Zongyuan composed a preface to see him off, stating:

"The Way of the Golden Immortal (Buddhism) is fundamentally rooted in filial piety and reverence; subsequently, it accumulates manifold virtues until it returns to emptiness and non-existence. Its teachings are termed Chan and Dharma."

He said: "The Vinaya is used to guide and support those who are deluded and turbid, yet it has long been neglected by the world. This Master [Daoyou] exhaustively investigated its esoteric meanings and elucidated the Supreme Vehicle, revering the three thousand rules of dignified conduct (*viniyaka*).
Although these must be maintained even in moments of haste, he once propagated this Way throughout the regions of the Yangtze and the Huai."
All people delighted in his character and received his grace; those who boarded the compassionate vessel and gazed toward the other shore numbered in the hundreds and thousands.

When the Son of Heaven heard of this, he summoned him to the palace to question him. He expounded and propagated the fundamental teachings, which greatly pleased the Emperor’s mind. The scholars and masses of the capital—
He was then uplifted, looking up to the moisture of the great clouds to plant the roots of virtue;

yet the Venerable One could not bear to fail in the debt of gratitude for his upbringing, and withdrawing with thoughts of the propriety of attending upon him, he made a fervent and urgent request that could not be denied.

Thus, staff in hand, he turned eastward and set out at dawn, shaking out his robes. Liu Gong, the Vice Director of the Right Bureau, who was thoroughly versed in the Buddhist teachings, [joined] the Venerable One...

To wander beyond the mundane world—this is how we first honored his arrival, and now we grieve his departure. Thus, the friends of the official residence have joined together to present him with poems as a gift.
I, [the author], have had a youth hold the bamboo slips to compose this preface, and I append these words to it: "The Venerable One is devoted to the practice of the Vinaya;
constant and enduring, it becomes ever more firm. Shall he not serve as a model for later students? He instructs all living beings, reaching out to every category of being."

How fortunate! Is this not one who has accumulated manifold virtues? To behold the high hall and perceive the distant as if it were near—is this not one whose foundation is filial piety and reverence?

If this is so, then his mind must have returned to emptiness and non-existence; having cast aside worldly attachments, he has ascended to the stages of realization. How, then, could one possibly know him?
The year of the Guiwei cycle, the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era.
In the first month of the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era, Emperor Dezong passed away.
On the day of Yibyou, Emperor Shunzong ascended the throne and changed the era name to Yongzhen. When the Emperor was still in the Eastern Palace, he once asked Chan Master Foguang Rimang in verse:
"From what direction does the Buddha come? To what direction does he go when extinguished? Since you say he is eternal..."
[The questioner asked: "He dwells in the world. Where is the Buddha now? [The answer was: "The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and returns to the unconditioned.
The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it eternally abides in the state of no-mind. Where there is thought, one returns to non-thought; where there is dwelling, one returns to non-dwelling.
He comes for the sake of sentient beings, and he goes for the sake of sentient beings. In the ocean of pure *tathatā*, the essence is serene and eternally abiding. Wisdom..."
This is excellent contemplation; do not give rise to further doubt. The Emperor asked again: "The Buddha was born in the royal palace and passed away beneath the twin śāla trees.
He dwelt in the world for forty-nine years, yet he also said that there is no dharma to be taught. Mountains, rivers, and the great ocean;

heaven, earth, and the sun and moon—all return to extinction when their time comes. Who can say they are without birth and death? My doubts remain as they were before. O Wise One, please explain this well."

[Question: "Discrimination. [Answer: The Buddha-body is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is through deluded sentiment that false discrimination arises. The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it has never known arising or ceasing.
When conditions exist, the Buddha appears in the world; when conditions are absent, the Buddha enters extinction.

He transforms sentient beings everywhere, like the moon reflected in water. It is neither permanent nor annihilated; neither born nor extinguished. To clearly perceive the state of no-mind is [the realization]. Self-...
However, there is no way to describe it in words. The Emperor was greatly pleased (according to the *Monastic History*).
The Emperor asked the National Teacher Qingliang for the essential point of the mind. He replied: "The ultimate Way is rooted in the mind; the dharma of the mind is rooted in non-abiding.
The essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous awareness that is never obscured. Its nature and characteristics are quiescent, yet it encompasses all virtuous functions. Through delusion..."

As for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it may appear chaotic; yet when one awakens to the true nature, the mind becomes empty, vast, and transparent. Although it is said that "mind itself is Buddha," this is known only by those who have realized it.
However, if there is realization or knowing, the sun of wisdom sinks into the realm of existence (*bhava*).

If there is neither illumination nor awakening, the clouds of darkness shroud the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If not a single thought arises, then the limits of the past and future [are transcended].
Severance. When the essence of illumination stands alone, both object and self are as they truly are; one directly reaches the source of the mind, where there is neither wisdom nor attainment.

Yet, delusion and awakening depend upon each other, and truth and falsehood stand in mutual relation. If one seeks truth by abandoning delusion, it is like discarding one’s shadow while toiling to tire the body.

If one realizes that delusion is itself truth, it is like being within a dark chamber when shadows vanish. If one remains without artifice yet illuminates with clarity, then all myriad concerns are simultaneously extinguished. If one allows things to proceed spontaneously in stillness—
Once this is known, all practices are thereby initiated. One may roam freely, allowing things to go as they will; yet dwelling in stillness, one reflects upon their source and flow.

Whether speaking or remaining silent, one does not lose the profound mystery; whether moving or still, one never departs from the *dharmadhātu*. When speech ceases, both knowing and silence are simultaneously forgotten;

when discussing contemplation, both silence and knowing are simultaneously illuminated. To speak of realization, it cannot be shown to others; to explain the principle, it cannot be understood without realization. Thus we know that awakening is silence.

In non-quiescence, true knowledge is non-knowing; by knowing that quiescence and knowledge are non-dual within the single mind, one accords with the Middle Way where both emptiness and existence are forgotten (from the *Sengshi*).

When Wei Gao, the Grand Secretary, passed away, his father had previously offered a meal to the Sangha for the sake of blessings when Gao was first born, at which time a strange monk appeared in response.
When the meal offering was completed, the wet nurse took the child to seek a blessing. The monk said to the assembly, "This child is Zhuge Wuhou.
In days to come, he shall administer a noble government in Shu; you should name him 'Wu' (Martial). Having spoken, he suddenly vanished.
Later, when Zhou Gao traveled for official service, his conduct in public life and his integrity were generally similar to those of Wuhou. He governed Shu for twenty-one years.
In his later years, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nankang. To this day, he is venerated with offerings in Sichuan. He had a profound affinity for the teachings of Śākyamuni.

When the stone statue at Jia Prefecture was first completed, Yao Gao composed a record for it, stating: "The circumference of its head is one thousand feet, the breadth of its eyes is twenty feet, and all its other marks of excellence are likewise proportionate.
Furthermore, he once instructed a male and female myna bird to recite the Buddha’s name; when the birds died, he performed the funeral rites according to the customs of the *śramaṇas*.
Upon his cremation, śarīras were obtained. Gao composed a record of them, which states in brief: "The primal essence bestows the five pneumas upon the myriad species;

though they be of scales, shells, feathers, or fur, there must inevitably be those who are clear, brilliant, and pure. Some blaze forth with the fire of *li*, while others receive the wondrous essence of *cang*;
all observe the patterns of human culture to serve it. Yet when the administration of the state undergoes change, even those bird-like creatures follow their innate capacities."

It is said: "The mark of emptiness is realized through non-recollection; the true bones are left behind once life has ceased. It was likely the manifestation of the Original Sage that moved the hearts of men;
though the conditions were diverse, they were united by means of the One True Transformation... (and so forth).
Bingxu (762): The first year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xuanzong. The Uyghurs presented tribute and brought a Manichean monk with them to China.
A temple was established to house him. As for his doctrine: they eat only after the sun has set; they do not consume meat, but do eat milk and curd.
The Uyghurs believed in and followed this faith, and the Khan would sometimes consult with him on state affairs. In the twelfth year, he dispatched the Manichean monks and others back home.
[The History of the Tang (as in the preceding *Tongjian*).

Dinghai, the second year [of the Yonghui era]. An edict was issued for the Chan Master of Ehu in Xinzhou to enter the Linqide Hall and be granted a seat to debate the meaning of the Dharma with the Dharma Master Dayi.
The Emperor attended to listen. A Dharma Master asked, "What are the Four Noble Truths? He replied, "O Holy Sovereign—"
The Emperor asked, "Where are the three emperors? He asked again, "The realm of desire has no dhyāna, and dhyāna abides in the realm of form. Upon what does this land rely for its establishment?
The Dharma Master replied, "I only know that the realm of desire has no dhyāna; I do not know that the realm of dhyāna has no desire. The Emperor asked, "What is dhyāna that is free from desire?
Huhū pointed his hand toward the air, made a single dot, and said, "Do you understand? The Dharma Master was at a loss.
The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master lectures on the sutras and śāstras endlessly, yet he cannot even manage this single point. Hu replied to the Emperor with a verse:
"To recognize the profound principle directly, The interlaced patterns and the corners are it. Those who do not recognize the profound principle Vainly labor as they point with their hands.
The [gǎn-āo] bird guards the void; The pond fish pass beneath its feet. The [gǎn-āo] bird knows nothing at all. The Emperor was moved.
He was greatly pleased and bestowed upon the Master the title of "Dà-yì" (Great Meaning). The Master then asked the assembly of teachers, "Ultimately, what constitutes the Way?
One replied, "Knowledge is the Way. Dà-yì said, "That cannot be. Knowledge is known by wisdom (*jñāna*); it cannot be known by consciousness (*vijñāna*).

How could consciousness be wisdom? That which is wisdom is the Way. Another replied, "Non-discrimination is the Way. Dà-yì said, "One must be able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)."
It does not move from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). How could there be non-discriminative wisdom?

Some oppose this, saying that the four dhyānas and eight samādhis constitute the Way. The Master says: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into numerical categories. How could the four dhyānas and eight samādhis be the Way?
Furthermore, those who oppose him are all met with refutations according to their capacities. Thus, he cites the question posed by Emperor Shunzong to Śīlabhadra regarding the Buddha-nature.
“Can it be seen? The Master replied, “The Buddha-nature is like the moon in the water; it can be seen, but it cannot be grasped.
Yinyi then asked the Emperor, “Since Śrī has already seen the moon in the water, why does he not catch it? The Emperor then asked, “What is this Buddha-nature? He answered:
