This did not deviate from what Your Majesty had asked; the Emperor understood this intuitively. Consequently, he came to esteem the Chan school all the more (from the *Sengshi*).

In the second month, an edict was issued appointing Dharma Master Duānfǔ to preside over the ritual ceremonies of the inner palace and to record the affairs of the monks of the Left and Right Quarters.
It was from Duānfǔ that the office of Senglù (Registrar of Monks) first began (from the *Tangshì*).

Jichou (18th year of the Zhenyuan era), the fifth month of the fourth year of the Yuanhe era: An imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities to cast a special golden seal to confer upon the National Teacher Chengguan the title of “National Teacher of Qingliang.
The National Teacher was appointed to preside over the affairs of the Imperial Preceptor’s Office (*Jiushi*).

The following year, the Emperor asked the National Teacher, “Regarding that which is expounded in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, what is meant by the ‘Dharmadhātu’? He replied, “The Dharmadhātu is the fundamental substance of the bodies and minds of all sentient beings.”
From the very beginning, it has been empty yet luminous and vast—nothing but the single realm of ultimate truth.
It possesses no form or appearance, yet it manifests the myriad phenomena throughout the great chiliocosm; it has no boundaries, yet it encompasses all that exists.

It shines brightly within the mind and eyes, yet its form cannot be seen; it radiates brilliantly amidst the objects of sensory perception, yet its principle cannot be divided. This is not for those who have not thoroughly penetrated the Dharma...
The Eye of Wisdom—the brilliant intelligence that is free from discursive thought—cannot perceive its own mind, despite such spiritual penetration.
Therefore, when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he sighed, "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;
yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they do not realize it. Thereupon, in accordance with the nature of the Dharma-realm, he preached the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

The sutra uses ultimate emptiness to eliminate emotional attachments; it harmonizes phenomena and principle, pervading all while remaining still and serene. When the Emperor listened to this profound discourse, he attained a vast and spontaneous realization.
Meng Jian, whose courtesy name was Jidao, served as the Regional Inspector of Changzhou. He later was promoted to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince.

He was highly skilled in poetry and deeply devoted to Buddhist studies; he frequently collaborated with Liu Bochu to translate Sanskrit texts. According to the *Jiushi* (Old History), Bochu served as Censor-in-Chief during the Baoli era.
Gimao (19th year). Liu Zhitou composed the Stele for Vinaya Master Daming of Mount Nanyue. It states in brief: "The Confucianist establishes benevolence and righteousness through ritual;
without it, they are ruined. The Buddhist maintains meditative concentration and wisdom through the Vinaya; without it, they are lost.

Therefore, one who departs from ritual regarding benevolence and righteousness cannot be spoken of as a Confucianist. One who deviates from the Vinaya regarding meditative concentration and wisdom cannot [be spoken of as a Buddhist]."

Regarding the term "Buddha": one who has attained this Way is truly a Great Enlightened Master. Whenever the teachings of the Buddha decline, his disciples inevitably diminish their observance of the precepts and depart from the sutras;

the Great Enlightened One fears this. Thereupon, he investigated the Vinaya so that the Great Dharma might be established, and mastered the scriptural teachings so that the profound meanings might be cultivated.
In all matters of clothing and utensils, every movement followed the master’s method; in speech and conduct, everything was [in accordance with the Way].
The Era of Wugu.
The 11th year, the Bingshen year. When Deng Yinfeng was traveling to Mount Wutai, his path led through Huaiyou.

At that time, Wu Yuanji was obstructing the way with his troops at Caizhou and was engaged in battle with government forces. The Master said, "I shall briefly alleviate their suffering. He then shook his mendicant’s staff into the air.
He flew through the midst of them. Both armies looked up in awe and marveled at the wonder; their hearts to fight were instantly stilled.
It was because of this that the government army was able to achieve its victory (according to the *Monastic Biographies*).
The Vice Minister Bai Juyi composed the "Epitaph for Master Shanghong of Jingyun Monastery in Fuzhou. It states in brief:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the *campaka* fragrance has faded, who shall turn back this decline? Master Jingyun—when Jingyun was born, he revived the Vinaya;
when Jingyun passes away, upon whom shall the Dharma generals rely? Formerly, when Jingyun came, those who entered his room returned [to the path]; now..."
The auspicious clouds have departed; those who entered the room were filled with grief (as recorded on the stele inscription).
Chan Master Guizong Zhichang had double pupils (*dvitīya-tāraka*). When he applied medicinal pressure to them, the corners of both eyes turned entirely red;
thus, he was known in the world as "Wiping Eyes. Li Bo, the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou, asked him: "I have heard that a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru; is this not false?"
Tánfǒ asked, "People say that you, Lord Shì, have read ten thousand scrolls of books—is this true? He replied, "It is.

The Master said, "From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet, you are no larger than a coconut; where, then, do those ten thousand scrolls reside? Bó bowed his head and attained realization.
Chan Master Foxincai’s verse says: "A mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru—this is a groundless doubt. Casting aside lute and books, I knock upon the gate of Chan.
Suddenly hearing where ten thousand scrolls cannot conceal, A flash of Chan mechanism is known only by oneself.
Known only by oneself, the red cassia tree is uprooted with its very roots and brought home."

*Dingyou* (the 12th year). The Horse-Lang Wife, wishing to convert those in the region of Shanxi, went to their location. People, seeing her womanly appearance and elegant demeanor, desired to take her as a wife.
She said, "I also wish to have a home, but only one who can recite the *Buménpǐn* (Universal Gate Chapter) in a single night shall serve me.
By dawn, more than twenty people had completed the recitation. The woman said, "A woman has but one body..."
"How could you possibly be matched with people like you? You should recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. By dawn, ten or so had mastered it;

the wife further taught her seven fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, stipulating that they should master them within three days. When the time arrived, only Lady Ma had mastered it. The wife ordered them all to pay their respects to formalize the marriage alliance.

Lady Ma prepared the wedding rites to go and fetch her, but the wife said, 'I am currently feeling unwell; wait until I have recovered a little before we meet. After the guests had dispersed, the wife—"

He had already died and, having subsequently decayed, was buried on the Sands of Golden Sand (*Jinsha Tan*). A few days later, an old monk arrived at the Ma family’s residence carrying his staff (*khakkhara*).
When asked how he had come there, the Ma family led him to the burial site. The monk probed the ground with his staff and saw that the corpse had already transformed;
only the skeletal remains of a golden chain were left. The monk pried up the bones with his staff and said to the assembly, "This is a Bodhisattva."

"Out of compassion for your heavy karmic obstructions, I have manifested these expedient means to transform you. You should contemplate the causes of goodness so as to avoid falling into the ocean of suffering.
Having said this, he flew through the air and departed. From that time on, those who venerated the Buddha became numerous throughout the region of Shanyou.

Wu-xu (the year 818 CE): In the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era, the Commissioner for Meritorious Works submitted a memorial stating that the stupa at Famen Temple in Fengxiang contained a finger bone of the Buddha.
According to tradition, it was opened once every thirty years; when opened, there would be abundant harvests and peace among the people. It was due to be opened the following year.

"Please welcome him. In the first month of the following year, the Emperor dispatched the Palace Messenger Du Yingqi, leading thirty palace women carrying incense and flowers, and headed a multitude of monks with musical offerings to welcome [the image] to the capital.
The Emperor ascended the Anfu Gate to receive and prostrate before it.

He kept it within the Forbidden City for three days of worship, during which five-colored lights appeared. All the officials offered their congratulations, and the Emperor was greatly pleased; he then sent it on its tour.

In all the monasteries, the ritual protocols of the Vinaya were fully observed, while the Grand Court Music Bureau, along with those from Chang’an and Wan’nan, provided music, banners, and blowing instruments that resounded and filled the roads.
Princes, dukes, officials, and commoners rushed to prostrate themselves in worship; they venerated and made offerings, fearing only that they might not arrive in time.
Some burned incense on their arms and heads as an act of devotion; others exhausted their entire fortunes to provide for the offerings. The crowds streamed forth without ceasing (Old History).
Han Yu, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Punishments, submitted a memorial offering earnest remonstrance, stating: "Buddhism is merely one teaching of the barbarians.
It entered China from the Later Han dynasty; it did not exist in antiquity. Formerly, the Yellow Emperor reigned for one hundred years and lived to the age of one hundred and ten.
Shaohao reigned for eighty-four years and lived to the age of one hundred. Zhuanxu reigned for eighty..."
[The reign of] Emperor Ku was four years; he lived to the age of ninety-eight. Emperor Xuaku reigned for seventy years and lived to the age of one hundred five.
Emperor Yao reigned for ninety-eight years and lived to the age of one hundred eighteen. Emperors Shun and Yu both reached the age of one hundred.
At this time, the world was at peace, the common people were secure and happy, and their lifespans were long and extended. And during this period...
In that land, there had not yet been a Buddha. Later, Tang of the Yin dynasty also lived to the age of one hundred. Tang’s grandson, Taiwu, reigned for seventy-five years;
Wuding reigned for fifty-nine years. Although the historical records do not state their specific ages at death, it is evident that they both likely reached an age of no less than one hundred years.
King Wen of Zhou was ninety-seven years old; King Wu was ninety.
[King Mu] was three years old. King Mu reigned for one hundred years; at that time, the Buddha-dharma had not yet entered China. It was not because of serving the Buddha that such things occurred.
It was during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty that the Buddha-dharma first appeared. Emperor Ming reigned for eighteen years.

Thereafter, periods of chaos and collapse succeeded one another, and their dynastic fortunes were not long-lasting. This was the case with the Song, Qi, Liang, Chen, and the Northern Wei dynasties and those that followed. Regarding the practice [of Buddhism]:
The Buddhas gradually became more cautious, yet the duration of their reigns was even shorter. Only Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty reigned for forty-eight years;

on three separate occasions, he surrendered his person to be offered as a gift to the Buddha. He ceased using sacrificial animals in the ancestral temple rites and limited himself to a single meal a day, consisting of vegetables and fruit.

Later, however, he was ultimately forced by Hou Jing and starved to death in Taicheng; the state also soon perished. Thus, it appears that while one may seek blessings by serving the Buddha, [the results are not always as expected].
On the contrary, they instead incurred calamity. Judging from this, it can be seen that the Buddha is not worthy of trust.
When Emperor Gaozu first received the abdication from the Sui, he first proposed to abolish [Buddhism]. At that time, the ministers lacked sufficient talent and insight;

they were unable to deeply understand the Way of the former kings, the proprieties of antiquity and the present, or how to propagate and clarify the sagely teachings to remedy these evils. Consequently, the matter was halted. I have often...
I harbor this regret. I humbly beseech Your Majesty, the Emperor, Sage, Holy, Martial, and Wise: Your divine sagacity and heroic valor have been unequaled for thousands of years.
At the beginning of Your reign, You did not permit the ordination of monks, nuns, or Daoist priests, nor did You allow the construction of temples or monasteries.
I have always believed that the will of the High Ancestor would surely be fulfilled by Your hand; yet now—
Even if you are unable to act immediately, how could you allow the situation to worsen further?

Now we hear that Your Majesty has ordered your ministers to welcome the Buddha’s relics from Fengxiang, that You have ascended the palace tower to observe them, and that they have been carried into the inner palace; furthermore, You have ordered various monasteries to take turns in making offerings to them.
Though I am extremely dull-witted, I know for certain that Your Majesty is not deluded by Buddhism, nor would You perform such acts of veneration merely for its sake.

This is merely for the sake of auspicious fortune. It is simply because the harvests are bountiful and the people are joyful that one accords with their hearts by providing strange spectacles and amusements for the officials and commoners of the capital.
How could a ruler as sagacious and enlightened as this ever be willing to believe in such matters?

Nevertheless, the common people are ignorant and deluded; they are easily misled and difficult to enlighten. If they were to see Your Majesty act in this way, they would surely believe it to be your sincere intention.

They serve the Buddha, all saying: "The Son of Heaven is a Great Sage, yet he still reveres and believes with a single mind; what are the common people compared to him? Why should we spare our own lives for the sake of the Buddha?
For this reason, they burn their heads and scorch their fingers in groups of hundreds and tens.

They strip off their clothes and scatter their coins from morning until evening, imitating one another, fearing only that they might be late. Whether old or young, they rush about, abandoning their worldly occupations and livelihoods. If they do not act immediately—

Furthermore, you have imposed prohibitions and restrictions; yet as they travel from one monastery to another, there are inevitably those who sever their arms or cut off pieces of their flesh as offerings.
This harms the social wind and ruins the customs, becoming a laughingstock throughout the four quarters—a matter no small one. Now, the Buddha was originally a man of the barbarian tribes;

his language was not mutually intelligible with that of the Middle Kingdom, and his clothing was of a different style. His mouth did not speak the Dharma-words of the former kings, nor did his body wear [their] garments.
The ceremonial robes of the former kings did not convey the righteousness between ruler and subject nor the affection between father and son.

Even had his person still been alive and he come to the capital to pay court at the imperial command, Your Majesty would have received him with no more than a single audience in the Xuanzheng Hall, a single reception in the Court of State Ceremonial, and the bestowal of a single set of robes, before escorting him out of the borders lest he delude the masses. How much less so in this case?
The body has long since perished; these are but withered and decaying bones, the dregs of the foul and impure. How could they be allowed to enter the palace precincts directly?

Confucius said, "Revere the spirits and ghosts, yet keep them at a distance. When the feudal lords of antiquity went to offer condolences in another state, they still required the presence of shamans and invocators.

"Originally, peach branches and bundles of reeds were first used to sweep away inauspiciousness before proceeding to offer condolences. Now, you have taken this filthy and decayed object without cause and personally inspected it;
yet the shamans and invocators did not precede you, the peach branches and reeds were not employed, and neither the ministers spoke of its impropriety nor the Censor raised the matter of its error.
I am truly ashamed of this. I beg that these bones be entrusted to the proper authorities to be cast into water or fire."
The root has been forever severed. The doubts of the world are eliminated, and the delusions of future generations are extinguished.
It causes all people in the world to know that the deeds of the Great Sage transcend the ordinary by tens of thousands of times. Is this not magnificent? Is this not a source of joy?
If the Buddha possesses spiritual power and can bestow calamity or fortune, then whatever misfortunes or transgressions there may be, they should fall upon my own person. O Supreme Heaven!

Encountering Snow at Lan Pass. My nephew Han Xiang suddenly appeared before me. Yu composed a poem for him, saying: A letter submitted this morning to the Ninefold Heavens; By evening, banished to Chaoyang—a road of eight thousand li. Yu’s younger brother was named Mian. His courtesy name was Zhongshi. He was a man of great talent and virtue. During the reign of Emperor Dezong, he served as the Minister of Justice. At that time, the Emperor’s younger sister, Princess Yongfu, was married to the Prince of Linwu. The Prince was arrogant and licentious, and he frequently committed offenses. Mian remonstrated with the Emperor on his behalf, and consequently, the Prince was executed. The Emperor, however, harbored resentment toward Mian. Later, when Mian was appointed Governor of Yangzhou, he was summoned back to court. Upon arriving at the capital, he was immediately imprisoned. After several months, he was released and permitted to leave. As he was departing, the Emperor ordered that he be executed upon reaching the border. As the early summer gradually grows hot, I hope your spiritual body remains peaceful and harmonious. I, Yu, am in poor health and find no meaning in my circumstances; having been demoted for certain matters, I have arrived here.

[Daowu] said, "One who does not come when invited three times is a *shilang* (senior official); one who comes of his own accord without being invited is Buddha-light. The Governor asked, "What is Buddha-light?

The Master said, "Look behind you at the constellation *Ji* (the Pleiades). One day, while the Governor was performing a sacrifice to the spirits by the sea, he visited Dadian and said, "I beg you to show me a single word regarding the essential point of the Buddha-dharma.
The Master remained silent for a long time. The Governor was at a loss. Sanping was serving as his attendant; thereupon...
He struck the meditation seat three times. The Master said, "What is this? Ping replied, "First move with concentration, then extract with wisdom.
The Master then prostrated. Sanping said, "The style of the Chan Master’s school is lofty and steep; you have found a point of entry through the attendant" (from *Sengshi*).

When Han Yu was serving as the Prefect of Chaozhou, he went to the sea to sacrifice to the gods and encountered the Buddhist master Da Dian.
Da Dian said, "As for your coming to serve as an official in the south, I have heard that it was because your words were so straightforward. Yet now, your countenance appears deeply troubled."
"However, it seems you are dissatisfied; why is that? Han Yu replied, "My own misfortune in Chao has been such that my blessings have been all the more profound.
One day, because my loyal words were not adopted, I was stripped of my post as Vice Minister of the History Bureau and banished to the sea eight thousand li away.
Wandering and fleeing, crossing over mountain ranges and the ocean, I lost my daughters and family. Upon reaching Chaoyang, a typhoon..."
Crocodiles! Calamities are unpredictable. Poisonous mists and pestilential vapors break out day and night; recoveries are rare while ailments abound.
Hair turns white and teeth fall out; now I am further tormented by anxiety. Exiled to a desolate land, how can my life be preserved?
When I came here, my path passed by the temple of Guangling. I prayed there, and fortunately, through its power, I ultimately escaped harm. Mù.
Since our Sovereign has achieved the merit of a restoration, I have composed this memorial to set forth the Way. I have had musical pieces established to inform the divine spirits.
When the eastern tour of Mount Tai was undertaken to report these achievements, if Heaven has indeed such an intention regarding this matter, then perhaps it will respond.

I, Yu, have described his meritorious deeds and composed songs and poems to offer as sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples. Day and night I have waited for the response, yet it has not arrived; I still hope—
"If you were to return quickly, would you not find it more peaceful and could you not truly rejoice?

Dian replied, "When you speak straightforwardly at court, do you do so out of loyalty to your sovereign while disregarding your own person, or do you still regard your own person and speak forcefully only to conform to others' wills?
To be loyal to one's sovereign while disregarding one's own person—if one's words are adopted, it is the glory of the sovereign; if they are not adopted, one simply departs."
There is exile; this is your duty. Why do you harbor such resentment in your breast?
If you still cling to your person and insist on speaking, it may be that your words are adopted and you gain the reputation of a loyal counselor while enjoying the benefits of being rewarded;
yet if they are not adopted, to be exiled is also an inevitable consequence of affairs. If you truly fear exile, then why not simply refrain from speaking? Furthermore, I—
I have heard it said that one who serves as a minister does not seek comfort regardless of the place, nor act without weighing the circumstances.
That you, having now encountered banishment, remain unsettled and instead hasten toward the times to pursue fame—this is likely not the excellence expected of a minister.

Furthermore, regarding the life and death, fortune and misfortune of men, how could their destiny not depend upon Heaven? You should simply cultivate yourself within and entrust your external fate to Heaven; this is sufficient.
Furthermore, how could that Guangling possibly bring calamity upon you? His Majesty succeeded to the treasures of Heaven;

yet when a treacherous minister held out in defiance, he had to campaign against him with provisions arriving like clouds, resulting in people filling the city as they were slain. Only after barely achieving a pacification have the wounds of war still not healed.
At this juncture, you further desire to perform the Feng and Shan sacrifices to announce your achievements, thereby agitating the world; yet your intent rests solely upon your own desires.
How can you, my son, bear to act thus? Moreover, to bring disorder upon yourself through exhaustion and to sacrifice to what is not a spirit is to be ignorant of destiny (ming).
To stir up that which the world does not desire, while seeking to achieve it for oneself—[how can you endure this?]
This is not knowing benevolence (*ren*). To speak forcefully in the name of loyalty, yet to become despondent when encountering adversity, is not knowing righteousness (*yi*).
To claim that disorder is order and report this to the August Heaven is not knowing propriety (*li*). And what do you take yourself to be doing by acting thus?
"Furthermore, regarding your dismissal, on what grounds was it based? Han Yu replied, "The Sovereign looked up to the Buddha-bone at Fengxiang and subsequently had it carried into the Great Palace.
I, Yu, maintain that Buddhism is merely one teaching of the barbarians;
it flowed into China since the time of the Later Han, having never existed in antiquity. In the past, [even] the Yellow Emperor, Yu, Tang..."
"During the transition between the Wén and Wǔ emperors, there were no Buddhas in the world, yet their reigns were long-lasting.

In the Han, Sòng, Chén, and Wèi dynasties, service to the Buddha was increasingly meticulous, yet there was no generation that did not suffer premature death and disorder. I fear Your Majesty may be deluded by this.

Is it not the case that one should not dismiss [the truth] merely because it does not apply to one's own person? Dàdiān said: "If this is so, then your words are erroneous. Furthermore, as for the Buddha, he is one who covers..."
He is a vessel for both humans and devas. His Way describes the mysteries of the myriad things; his words exhaust the principles of the hidden and the manifest, of nature and destiny.
His teaching is to abandon evil and pursue good, to discard the false and return to the true. As he views the world...
It is like a father’s relationship toward his son; if the son were to harm him, it would be as if the son were using a blade against his own father.
I have heard that those who observe people well look at where their Way resides, rather than comparing the status of the positions they occupy.
Kings such as Jie and Zhou, and ministers such as Zhi and Qiao, were all people of the Central Kingdom; yet they are not to be emulated because they lacked the Way.
Furthermore, Shun was born in the land of the Eastern Yi, King Wen was born in the land of the Western Yi, Youyu emerged from among the Rong, and Ji Zha emerged from among the Man.
Could these two sages and two worthies be called barbarians and thus considered unfathomable?
Now, you do not examine the Way of the Buddha, yet you merely dismiss it as that of a barbarian; how trivial your words are! You must surely consider—

If you argue that because something did not exist in antiquity it cannot be taken as a model, then Confucius and Mencius appeared during the decline of the Zhou dynasty, whereas Chiyou and Gusou lived in antiquity;
how could one discard the sages and worthies of the declining Zhou to take as a model the cruelty and obstinacy of antiquity?
Furthermore, do you claim that the Yellow Emperor and the Three Dynasties lived long lives because they had not yet encountered the Buddha? If so, [then...]

Wai-bing reigned for two years; Zhong-ren for four years. How premature their deaths were! You base your argument on the interval between the Han and Chen dynasties, claiming that because there were Buddhists, the rulers met with premature death and disorder.
Yet Emperor Ming of the Later Han was a preeminent sovereign of his age, and Emperor Wu of Liang lived to the age of eighty-three.
Why must it necessarily be the case that [the presence of Buddhism] leads to premature death and chaos? Han Yu, with a fierce and indignant expression—
He said: "That which you call 'Buddhism' does not, in its speech, discuss the Dharma-words of the former kings, but instead recklessly propounds theories of samsara and birth-and-death.
In its practice, it does not tread upon the path of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness, but falsely constructs doctrines of retribution, calamity, and fortune.
It lacks the righteousness between ruler and subject and the affection between father and son; it causes its followers not to spin silk..."
Wearing robes and eating without plowing, you are thereby destroying and violating the Way of the former kings; how could I remain silent and fail to refute you?
Dadian said, "How extreme is your lack of understanding! Suppose there were a person here who, throughout the entire day, could count to several tens, yet did not know that two times five equals ten;
everyone would surely laugh at him as a madman. You, however, spend your whole day speaking of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and good faith."
Yet you do not realize that the Buddha’s words regarding permanence, bliss, self, and purity are no different [from those of the sages].
Is this not like calculating ten and two, yet failing to know that five times two is ten? Furthermore, you claim to have frequently read the Buddhist scriptures;
can you explain how your doubts differ from those of the former kings? Han Yu said, "How could I possibly read those books? Da Dian said, "As for you..."
Since you have never read their books, how can you know that they do not discuss the "Dharma-words" of the former kings?

Furthermore, you ought not to say of yourself that you constantly read the books of Confucius while doubting those others to be wrong; this makes you a "dog of Shun," who hears someone else call something wrong and immediately deems it wrong himself.
This is the behavior of a "wife and concubine. Long ago, when Yao was staying at his lodgings, he kept his lodging animals...

It is like the dog. That which it saw was only Shun. One day, when Yao passed by his residence, the dog barked at him. This was not because it loved Shun and hated Yao; it was simply that it had never seen anyone other than Shun. Now, you take your constant sight of Confucius as being for the sake of learning, yet you have never read the Buddhist scriptures and thus find them strange. This is the logic of Shun’s dog. Furthermore, I have heard that when a woman marries, she leaves her father’s house for her husband’s. If she were to remain in her father’s house, she would be called unfilial. Now, you have left your own home to study under me; if you do not accept my teachings, you will be called unfilial. How much more so if you reject the Way of the Buddha! You must not harbor such doubts. If you do not believe, you may leave; I shall not detain you. If you do believe, you must practice it. Do not let your mind be unsettled. If you do not practice it, you will be called unfilial. If you practice it, you will surely attain the Way. Therefore, I urge you to practice it with all your heart.
