(From the *Ji Gujin Youxian Tongjian*). Year Yisi:
The first year of the Baoli era of Emperor Jingzong. Li Ao, courtesy name Xizhi, served as the Prefect of Langzhou.
Admiring the Way of Chan Master Weiyen of Yaoshan, he went to pay his respects. The Master was reciting a scripture and did not look up. Li said, "To see a person's face and not..."
Just as he heard the name, the mountain called out, "Governor! Li responded, "Yes. The mountain said, "How can you hold my ears in high esteem while treating my eyes with contempt?
Li thanked him and asked, "What is the Way? The mountain pointed upward with his hand, then pointed downward and asked, "Do you understand?
Li replied, "I do not understand. The mountain said, "Clouds in the blue sky; water in the pitcher. Li joyfully answered with a verse: *Refined is this physical form,* *And so forth.*
He resembled a crane in form. Beneath a pine tree stood two cases of scriptures. I came to inquire about them, but there was no other matter;
the clouds were in the blue sky, and the water was in the pitcher. He asked again, "What are precepts, concentration, and wisdom?

The Master said, "There are no such idle furnishings here. Yun said, "I cannot fathom this profound principle. The Master said, "If you wish to maintain this matter, you must truly head toward the highest heights."
"Standing atop the peak; walking on the bottom of the deep sea. If one cannot let go of things within the chamber of Min, they immediately become a leakage.

When Li took his leave, one night on Mount Yaoshan, he ascended the peak and saw the clouds parting to reveal the bright moon. He let out a great laugh, the sound of which traveled eighty or ninety *li* to Fengyang.
Hearing of this, Li Ao sent him a verse, saying: "I have chosen a secluded dwelling that accords with my rustic sentiments."

Throughout his entire life, he neither saw anyone off nor welcomed anyone. At times, he would ascend directly to the summit of a solitary peak; beneath the moon, he would part the clouds and let out a laugh.
Li Ao composed three treatises on the Restoration of Nature (*Fuxing shu*). The first states: "When the emotions are clouded, nature becomes obscured; by forgetting the emotions, one restores nature.
Through sincerity comes clarity, and through clarity, one exhausts the Way of nature and destiny. The second states: "Without thought, there is tranquil illumination. To bring this about—
"Know that it lies in the investigation of things. Third, it is said: "If one is muddled and does not reflect, one will ultimately not understand the Way.
Prime Minister Yu Gongdi remarked that Master Tong of Ziyu Mountain had grasped the ultimate principle of the Buddha-dharma and requested a word from the Master.

The Master said, "The ultimate principle of the Buddha-dharma requires that one set aside both emotion and intellect. The Prime Minister said, "I request it now. The Master said, "Ask me what you wish. The Prime Minister asked, "What is [the ultimate principle]?"
The Buddha. The Master called out, "Yu Di! Yu Di responded. The Master said, "Do not seek anything else. Yu Di did not yet understand.
When Chan Master Yaoshan heard of this, he remarked, "What a pity! This man of the Yu family was born amidst the Purple Jade Mountains, yet he has been buried there."
When Lord Yu heard these words, he went in person to visit Yaoshan. Upon meeting him, Yaoshan asked, "I have heard that you, Excellency, are at Ziyu performing great Buddhist services;
is this true? Yu replied, "I dare not claim such things. Hearing that the Great Master is compassionate and has words to save me, I have come here specifically today.
Yaoshan said, "If you have any doubts, ask freely. Yu asked, "What is the Buddha? Yaoshan called out to him, "Excellency!"
The Duke responded with an "Amen. The Master asked, "What is this? At these words, the Duke attained realization and prostrated himself in gratitude.
When Minister Xu arrived at Shanglan Monastery, he went into the Sangha Hall and asked the Head Seat, "How old are you? The Seat replied, "Sixty-eight."
Xu asked, "How many years of monastic seniority do you have? He replied, "Forty-seven. Xu said, "And how many summer retreats has the Holy Monk spent?

The Head Seat replied, "He received the precepts simultaneously with empty space. Xu then struck the meditation bench and said, "The subordinate official does not eat as much rice; it is the Head Seat who eats too much salt."
Bingwu, the second year. The śramaṇa Tanyan of Yuezhou, together with Xu Xun (style name Yuandu), constructed a stūpa.
Before the stūpa was completed, Xu Xun passed away. Tanyan lived to the age of one hundred and twenty, still awaiting the next incarnation of Xu Xun.
When Yueyang Prince Suocha came to govern Yue, he entered the temple and saw Tanyan. Tanyan said: "Xu Yuandu, why have you come so late? In the past..."
The stupa remains as it was before. The King suddenly realized that the construction of the stupa in his previous life was as if it had happened yesterday;

he then completed the stupa (this is the present-day Yingtian Stupa; according to a stone inscription). ○ Tanyan resided at Longxing Temple. When the main hall fell into ruin, the community requested that he repair it.
Tanyan said, "This is not within the karmic power of an old monk like me. Three hundred years hence, a patron wearing red robes will come."
This hall was originally built, and the monastic community carved an inscription in stone to record it. When Lord Pei Su served as the Governor of Yue, he donated his stipend to repair it.
This fulfilled the prophetic prediction of Master Yan, which had foretold a "red-robed man with the surname Pei. This refers to Xiao, the father of the Chancellor Xiu.
In the second year of the Baoli era, the year Bingwu, twelve emperors had passed away. Wenzong ascended the throne;
in the year Dingwei, he changed the era name to Tahe.
In the third year, the year Jiyou, the stone-carved Sūtra on the Wall at Chongxuan Monastery in Suzhou was completed, and Bai Juyi composed its inscription.

Briefly stated: Regarding the revelation, instruction, awakening, and entry into the wisdom and vision of all Buddhas—transcending the infinite through definitive meaning and extending endlessly through the Perfect Teaching—nothing is more venerable than the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Containing sixty-nine thousand five hundred and five words, it is unsurpassed for realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), for constructing the Gate of Non-duality, and for abiding in inconceivable liberation; nothing exceeds the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. It contains two... [words].
It contains seventeen thousand nine hundred and ninety-two words. It encompasses the four modes of birth and the nine classes of beings, leading them into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Yet, in truth, there is no one who has been delivered; in this regard, nothing surpasses the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. It contains five thousand eighty-seven words.

To destroy transgressions and accumulate merit, and to purify all evil realms of existence, nothing is more urgent than the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Sūtra*. It contains three thousand twenty words. It corresponds to...
Mindfully aspire to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; do not be hasty with the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, which consists of one thousand eight hundred words.
Use right view to contemplate the true nature; do not depart from the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra*, which consists of six thousand nine hundred and ninety words.
To explain self-nature and recognize primordial awareness (*mūla-bodhi*), nothing surpasses the *Dharmatā-guhyaka-sūtra*, which consists of three thousand one hundred and five words.
To realize that all phenomena are empty and rely upon Buddha-wisdom, nothing surpasses the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, which consists of two hundred and fifty-eight words.
These eight sūtras encompass the essential tenets of the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the three vehicles; they exhaust the secret treasury of the myriad Buddhas.
[From the *Wenji*] ○ Ryōkan converted his residence into a Buddhist temple and painted an image of Amitābha Buddha, to which he paid homage and performed services.
He himself composed a record stating: "My original teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, spoke thus: 'In the west, there is a world.'"

It is called "Ultimate Bliss" because it is free from the eight sufferings and the four evil realms. Its land is called "Pure Land" because it is devoid of the three poisons and the karma of the five turbidities.
Its Buddha is named Amitābha, for his lifespan is immeasurable and his merit, physical marks, and radiance are infinite.
I, your disciple Bai Juyi, in my declining old age, am afflicted by the ailment of wind-paralysis.
A depiction of the Western World (Sukhāvatī) was painted. Bowing his head and kneeling before the Buddha, he praised it, saying:
"In the Pure Lands of the World of Ultimate Bliss, there are no evil realms nor any sufferings. May those such as myself—old and sick—be reborn together with the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.
(Longshu Jingtuwen). ○ The poet Bai Juyi was favored by Emperor Xianzong and served in high office.

He was [the subject of] what was feared. During the reign of Emperor Wenzong, he served as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince and was posthumously honored with the title of Left Vice President of the Secretariat.
He subsequently withdrew from public life. Since his ambitions could not be realized, he gave himself over to literature and wine, able to follow his own inclinations and find contentment.

He took refuge in Buddhist teachings on birth and death, appearing as if he had forgotten his physical form; for months at a time, he would abstain from meat. Later, he shared a bond of affection with his younger brothers, Xingjian and Minzhong. His residence was in Lidaoli.
He dredged ponds, planted trees, and set up stone platforms; he built a tower on Fragrant Mountain (*Xiangshan*) and carved the Eight-Section Rapids.

He styled himself the "Madman Who Recites" (*Zuoyin xiansheng*) and formed a "Sacrificial Society" with the monk Rumang of Fragrant Mountain, calling himself the Layman of Fragrant Mountain (*Xiangshan jushi*). He lived to the age of seventy-five and was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Left (*Shangshu zuopusha*).
Gengxu (the 27th day of the fifth month), the fourth year of the Dàhé era. Liu Ke, Attendant-in-Ordinary, composed the "Record of the Fǎhuá Monastery at Shèngquán on Mount Dōng in Fúzhōu.
It states briefly: "Among the exquisite monasteries throughout the realm, those of Míng Prefecture are often praised as being exceptionally sublime.

Among them is the Fǎhuá Monastery on Mount Dōng, which serves as one of the primary 'Dharma caves' of the southeastern region. At the beginning of the Jǐnglóng era, the divine monk Huáidào first selected this site."
To the west of Aitong, a spring gushed forth and surged upward, dividing into two streams. One stream flowed to the kitchen for washing;
the other became a pond. Thereupon, a prophecy was recorded: "The contraction shall end the chaos; the surging shall bring peace. A spring also exists at a neighboring temple.
This spring was not efficacious. Subsequently, Huaiyi resided there; after Huaiyi, Zhichang resided there.

Zhichang was constantly attended by a celestial youth who served him in secret, and śarīras descended in concealment. The mountain deity listened to his sermons. The Buddhist Dharma in Min truly began with these three great masters.
This monastery does not harbor women, nor does it admit meat or alcohol; it is truly extraordinary.
Xin Hai, the fifth year. The Emperor was fond of eating clams. One day, there was one among the imperial kitchen staff that could not be opened.
The Emperor found this strange and burned incense while praying in silence. Suddenly, it opened, revealing an image of a Bodhisattva.

The Emperor was struck with wonder and issued an edict to send it to Xingshan Temple for veneration. He then asked his attendants, "What auspicious omen is this? One replied, "On Mount Zhongnan, there is..."

Master Weizheng was profoundly learned in the Buddha-dharma. [The Emperor] requested an imperial audience to question him. Chang then summoned him and questioned him. He replied to the inquiry, saying:
"Your servant has heard that nothing occurs without a corresponding cause; this is precisely to inspire Your Majesty’s faith. The Sūtra says:
'Those who should be saved by the form of a Bodhisattva, to them he manifests in the body of a Bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma for them. The Emperor said: 'The form of a Bodhisattva now...'"
"I have seen it. But I have not heard him preach the Dharma. The Emperor asked, "Upon seeing this, do you consider it permanent or impermanent?
Do you believe it or not? The Emperor replied, "This is a rare and marvelous thing; I believe it deeply. The Master said, "Your Majesty has already heard the preaching of the Dharma.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict to all monasteries throughout the realm, commanding that images of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva be established and venerated.
[Chuan-deng] (Yang):

Year of the Rabbit (Yi-mao), the seventh month of the ninth year. Li Xun memorialized that monks and nuns were excessively numerous, consuming and wasting both public and private resources. An imperial edict was issued for all local jurisdictions to test the monks and nuns;

those who failed to recite the scriptures according to the prescribed standard were all compelled to return to lay life as men or women, and the establishment of temples or the private ordination of monks was strictly prohibited.

(*Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government*) ○ In the tenth month, Zheng Zhu, wishing to garner the reputation of the monastic community, earnestly petitioned to rescind the purge of monks and nuns; the Emperor granted his request (*same as above*).
○ At the end of the Taihe era, Du Zong served as the Military Governor of Fengxiang. When an imperial edict was issued to purge the monks and nuns, five-colored clouds appeared over Qishan.
Since the mountain is near Famen Temple, the common people all claimed that the Buddha’s relics had manifested an auspicious omen.
Because the monks and nuns were uneasy, the Military Inspector wished to memorialize the Emperor about it. Zong said, "The clouds and mists have changed color; this is a matter for Ānanda.
If the Buddha truly loves the monks and nuns, he should manifest himself in the capital. Before long, a white rabbit was captured.
The Military Inspector again wished to memorialize, saying, "This is an auspicious omen from the West. Zong said, "Wild beasts are not yet tamed; for now, it would be best to keep it. Ten days later—
He died that very day. The military inspector was also pleased and believed it was a manifestation of divine response; he alone painted a picture of it and presented it to the Emperor.
When Zheng Zhu succeeded Li Cong as the governor of Fengxiang, he reported that purple clouds had appeared and presented a white pheasant.

In the eighth month of that year, sweet dew descended upon the cherry branches in front of the Zichen Hall. The Emperor personally went there to taste it, and the hundred officials offered their praises.
[Postscript] As recorded in the *Jiu Tang Shu*: Li Xun, courtesy name Zichi, rose from the status of a banished person during the reign of Emperor Wenzong and became Chancellor within a single year.

He once proposed that the Buddhist monks throughout the realm, who evade corvée labor and taxes while consuming the state’s resources for food and clothing, should be returned to the common people if their conduct was not pure.
Having assumed office, he personally petitioned to abolish this practice, thereby seeking to win popular favor. Later, because of his involvement in the [suppression of the]... [text ends]
The eunuch’s plot was leaked. Over a thousand members of Xun’s faction were beheaded.

Xun fled into the Zhongnan Mountains and sought refuge with the Buddhist master Zongmi, intending to shave his head and hide there. His disciples would not allow it, so he fled to Fengxiang, where he was captured by the military commander Minwu Jiang.
He was shackled and bound. Fearing that he would be subjected to cruel torture by the eunuchs, Xun said to the guards: "If you..."
"It would be better to reward them than to take their heads away," he said, and so he beheaded him. Zongmi, because of his secret instruction, was captured by eunuchs who intended to kill him.
Zongmi said with a serene expression, "I have been close with Xun for a long time. When a Buddhist is in distress, they are killed; death is indeed my allotted lot."
He was then released upon reaching adulthood.
In the *bingchen* year, the era name was changed to *Kaicheng*.

On the *wuwu* day of the third month in the third year, the Monk Superintendent Chengguan passed away. Throughout his life, this master served across nine successive reigns and held seven [official positions].
The Imperial Preceptor was one hundred and two years of age and had been a monk for eighty-three years. He stood nine chi and four cun tall;
his hands reached below his knees. His eyes emitted light at night, and by day they remained unblinking. He could hold two brushes simultaneously, and his voice resonated like a bell.
Emperor Wenzong, revering him as a sage-ancestor, suspended court affairs for three days and enshrined his entire body in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan.
Not long after, a Buddhist monk from India arrived at the imperial court and reported that he had seen a messenger passing through the air over the Pamir Mountains.
When questioned, the messenger replied, "I am the deity of the Mañjuśrī Hall in Northern India; I have come to take the great tooth of the Bodhisattva Avataṃsaka to my own country for veneration.
An imperial decree was issued to open the stūpa, and indeed one tooth was missing; only thirty-nine teeth remained. Thereupon, [the Emperor] passed away.
The śarīra were radiant and lustrous; his tongue was the color of a red lotus. His stupa was named Miaojue (Wondrous Enlightenment). The stele was composed by Pei Xiu (as recorded in the *Benzhuan*).
On the gengshen day of the first month in the fifth year of Kaicheng (840 CE), Emperor Wenzong passed away and Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne. The monk Weizhen [was present].
The Emperor was devoted to simple and orthodox teachings. Previously, he had sought blessings through sacrifices and prayers; now, the Daoist Zhao Guizhen spoke to him of the Way of the Immortals.
Both had entered the imperial palace, and the Emperor placed full trust in their words. In the ninth month, he summoned the Daoist Zhao Guizhen and others into the inner quarters.
He established a Jīnlù (Golden Register) ritual site. In the tenth month, the Emperor ascended the Mystic Altar (*xuántán*) and personally received the dharma registers (*fǎlù*).

Wáng Zhé, the Right Reminder (*yòu shíyí*), remonstrated, saying: "At the commencement of your royal enterprise, it is not appropriate to place excessive reliance on such superstitious practices. The Emperor would not accept his advice (*Tōngjiàn*). ○ Wǔzōng (name:
Yán)—this was the third Wǔ emperor to suppress the monastic community.

Xin-you (the 10th year of the Tianbao era): The reign title was changed to Huichang. In the sixth month, the Daoist Liu Xuanjing was appointed Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Guanglu Daifu).
Jia-zi (the fourth year of Huichang): The Daoist Zhao Guizhen was appointed Professor of the Left and Right Street Offices (Zuoyou Shendao Jiaoshou Xiansheng).

At that time, the Emperor was intent upon seeking immortality; Zhao Guizhen, taking advantage of his favor, invariably disparaged the Buddhists whenever he had an audience, asserting that they should be completely eliminated.

"Go. The Emperor deeply agreed with this. When Guizhen requested to debate with the followers of Śākyamuni once more, an imperial decree was issued to summon the monks and Daoists to the Linqide Hall for discussion.
Dharma Master Zhixuan ascended the seat of debate; his arguments were swift, precise, and powerful, such that the Daoist practitioners could not defeat him.

Zhixuan then memorialized the throne: "The King’s fundamental path is that of ritual and music. As for the Daoists’ practices of *du* (breathing exercises) and *tunna* (ingestion of qi), they are merely fit for those who dwell among the mountains and forests."
"Regarding such matters of exclusive privilege, I hope Your Majesty will not deign to take further interest. The Emperor’s expression was displeased.

The attendant officials suggested that Xuan compose a poem to explain himself. Xuan immediately presented five stanzas, which included the lines: "The crane's back is precarious, the dragon's back is slippery; O Sovereign, please stay for another thousand years.
The Emperor understood this as a subtle reproach and specifically granted him leave to return to his native place (from *Chuanteng lu*).
Yichou (the second year of the fifth cycle), the fifth year [of the reign]. The Emperor detested how monks and nuns were wasting and corrupting the empire and wished to eliminate them.

The Daoist Zhao Guizhen served as a censor and recommended Deng Yuanchao and Liu Xuanjing to further suppress the followers of Śākyamuni. First, they destroyed the monasteries in the mountains and wilds.

In the fifth month, an imperial edict was issued to consolidate and reduce the Buddhist temples throughout the empire; only four temples were to be retained in each of the two streets of the capital. Each...

Thirty monks were stationed at each monastery. At the seats of governance for the regional military commissioners (jiedushi) and the observation commissioners (canshishi), as well as at Chang'an, Hua, Shang, and Ru Prefectures, one monastery was established in each location.
These were divided into three grades: the superior grade stationed twenty monks, the middle grade ten, and the lower grade five.
All other monks and nuns, as well as Da Qin (Persian) muhu (magicians) and yao-seng (Zoroastrian priests—*yao* pronounced *xīngyān*; a term for foreign monks), were excluded.

All were diligently urged to return to secular life; temples were deemed unfit to remain, and a deadline was set for their demolition. Censors were dispatched to various circuits to supervise the process.

All assets, including property and fields, were confiscated by the government. Temple timber was used to repair official offices and post stations, while bronze statues, bells, and chimes were melted down to cast coins (*Tongjian*).
In the eighth month, an edict was issued to admonish the abuses of Buddhism, which was proclaimed throughout the realm.
In total, more than four thousand six hundred monasteries throughout the realm were destroyed.
Twenty-six thousand five hundred monks and nuns were returned to lay life, along with more than two thousand *mu-hu* (Muslims) and *xian-seng* (Zoroastrian priests) from Da Qin.

Over forty thousand *zhao-ti* (monasteries) and *lan-ruo* (hermitages) were demolished, yielding several million *qǐng* of fertile fields and one hundred fifty thousand male and female slaves. All the remaining monks were registered [under state control].

The Master and his disciples were no longer registered with the Ministry of Sacrifices (*Cibu*). The various officials presented a memorial to offer their congratulations. Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued stating: "In the Eastern Capital, only twenty monks shall remain.
In the various provinces, those who have twenty shall be reduced by half; those who have ten shall be reduced by three; and those who have five shall not be retained at all.
Consequently, many monks from Mount Wutai fled to Youzhou. Li Deyu summoned the official in charge of communications and said to him:

He said: "You go and tell the original commander that if Wutai serves as a general, why must he be inferior to those of Youzhou? If he serves as a soldier, he will certainly not be inferior to the soldiers of Youzhou.
Why do you vainly take the name of 'providing shelter' for him? His reputation has already stained the mouths of the people; have you not seen this?"
Lately, Liu Congjian has gathered countless idlers; what benefit is there in this? Zhang Zhongwu then sealed two swords and gave them to Juyong Pass, decreeing:
"Any wandering monk who enters the territory shall be executed. Wei Bo, the Director of the Court of State Ceremonies, considered that such matters should not exceed proper bounds.
Li Deyu disliked him and demoted him to the position of Vice Commander of the Lingwu Military Prefecture.
In the tenth month of this year, the Emperor received the ritual cap of the Three Caverns (*Sāndòng*) from the Daoist Liu Xuánjìng at Mount Héng (Tōngjiàn).
On the Bingyǐ day, in the third month of the sixth year, Wǔzōng fell ill due to his consumption of golden elixirs; carbuncles broke out on his back and malignant sores covered his entire body.
Consequently, he became restless and lost his composure, his mind falling into a state of derangement. He was unable to speak for ten days before passing away (at the age of thirty-three).
Emperor Wuzong resolutely sought to eliminate the teachings of the Buddha, yet he could not avoid falling under the influence of the Daoists.

From this we see that his judgment was mistaken; his intelligence was not free from delusion—it was merely a matter of differing preferences (from the *Tongjian*). The *Jiushi* (Old History) praises him, saying:
"Zhaosong [Wuzong] abolished the laws of the Buddhists and punished the ranks of the śramaṇas. His ambition was to take steps upon the vermilion ladder and seek the pearl in the crimson sea."
Master Shui, you merely observe the peripheral studies of Xiao Yan and Yao Xing, yet fail to realize the futile pursuits of Qin Shi Huang and Emperor Wu of Han.
It is because you have been deluded by the words of heterodox paths that you have one-sidedly disparaged the teachings of foreign lands.

Furthermore, since the teaching that came from the West has approached its millennium, the common people have grown accustomed to it as a custom; they fear its precepts more than the laws of the state and take pleasure in its followers.
This was no different from ascending to immortality. Yet, in a single day, he allowed a golden image to be defaced and discarded, and foreign books to be burned;
thus he harbored resentment toward those who prostrate themselves and provoked the anger of commoners. Although the Emperor praised his clear judgment, he listened to such biased views.
Xuanzong ascended the throne in the third month of this year. In the fifth month, Chancellor Li Deyu was dismissed for usurping authority.
An imperial edict stated that twelve individuals, including the Daoist masters Zhao Guizhen, Liu Xuanjing, and Deng Yuanchao, had deluded and misled the previous reign.

He slandered and destroyed the followers of Śākyamuni. The Emperor bestowed upon him a flogging in the imperial court; the remaining followers were executed, while others were banished to the southern frontiers and exiled to Mount Luofu.

An edict was issued to the two monastic districts (liangjie) of the capital throughout the empire, stating that in addition to the two existing temples already permitted to remain, eight more temples were to be established in each.

Monks and nuns were to continue being registered under the Gongde Office as before, rather than under the Ministry of State Affairs (Zhuguke). Those ordained as monks and nuns were still required to receive ordination certificates from the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu). Thus, the Buddhist teachings were abolished.
The Restoration of the August [Buddhism] (Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government): The three emperors of the Wu period followed depravity and evil.
At the request of their subordinates, they were persuaded to carry out a suppression. Yet after they were abolished, they flourished all the more;

it was like the frosty wind that withers things—it is but temporary. It is comparable to the spring following winter: one who wishes to utterly exterminate plants and trees would have to ensure there is no spring after winter.
That is acceptable. If Xunzi knew that spring follows winter, why would he have taken such trouble to personally assume the blame for his own faults and obstructed others from doing good?
What benefit would that have brought him? (From the *Fahufa lun*)
Su Che’s commentary states: The *I Ching* says, "That which transcends form is called the Way (*Dao*); that which is below form is called the vessel (*qi*).
Since the Five Emperors and the Three Kings, the world has been governed through vessels and forms, guiding the people with ritual and music and regulating them with government and law.
While the Way operated within these means, the people were unaware of it. Laozi embodied the Way, yet he did not involve himself in...
As for things, Confucius went so far as to compare them to dragons. Since the Eastern Han dynasty, the Buddha-dharma first entered China;
its Way corresponds with that of Laozi, both being what the *I Ching* calls "that which transcends form. Thus, the scholar-officials of the Han...
They could not clarify it. From the Wei and Jin dynasties onward, they understood it roughly. Those who loved it deeply desired to implement it in the world;
those who hated it deeply desired to eradicate it from the world. Both of these positions are incorrect.
The Way of Buddha and Laozi is the same as our Way, yet they desire to eradicate it. The teaching of Buddha and Laozi differs from our teaching, yet they desire to practice it.
They have all erred in this regard. Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty ruled over a mere corner of the land, yet he summoned both monastics and laypeople to translate scriptures and discuss the sublime;

those who gathered there numbered in the thousands. Nevertheless, the fall of the Yao clan occurred before his feet had even turned to walk away. As for Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty in the south of the Yangtze, his devotion to Buddhism was such as never before seen in previous generations;
yet he went so far as to offer himself as a slave, and both father and son fell into the hands of Hou Jing.

Those who deliberate on the matter observe the defeats of the Qin and Liang dynasties and conclude that the Buddha-dharma is not to be relied upon. During the reign of Emperor Taiwu of the Later Wei, he placed deep trust in Cui Hao;
Hao did not believe in Buddhism and urged the Emperor to expel the monastic community, destroy the scriptures, and demolish the temples. Thus, once the Buddha-dharma was extinguished...
Yet Hao was likewise exterminated for no crime. Emperor Wuzong sought longevity by following the private whims of Daoist practitioners;

he proscribed Buddhism and destroyed the monastic order, yet before a year had passed, he suddenly collapsed from a toxic fever. Those who observe the calamities of the Wei and Tang dynasties conclude that the Buddha-dharma must not be provoked.
Both views, however, see but one side of the matter. The Way of the Buddha and Laozi is not...
This is my personal teaching. This Way has existed since the beginning of heaven and earth. The gentlemen of antiquity used it to regulate their vital energy and nourish their minds;
its loftiness could not be compromised, and its purity could not be defiled.
Heaven, earth, the spirits, and all people would look upon them with reverence. It is by means of this Way that the Sage achieves speed without haste and arrives without traveling.
Thus it is. As for the Dao, there is nowhere it does not pervade among things; how, then, could it be subject to criticism?

Indeed, when one governs the world through physical forms and implements—guiding with ritual and music and regulating with government and law—the Dao operates within these means, yet the people do not perceive it.
"Ten thousand things grow together without harming one another; the Way proceeds in parallel without contradicting itself.

They merge so completely that their boundaries are no longer seen, and thus all under heaven undergo transformation. Is this not indeed identical to the underlying intent left behind by Confucius? (The Three Su Writings)
Xuanzong (reigned 846–859): In the *dingmao* year, he changed the era name to Dazhong. He was the third son of Emperor Xianzong and the uncle of Emperor Wuzong.
During his youth, Wuzong envied his talent and repeatedly sought to assassinate him. The eunuch Qiu Gongwu secretly protected him;
when the situation became critical, Gongwu shaved his hair for him, made him a *bhikṣu*, and sent him away on a long journey. Consequently, he visited many famous mountains throughout the realm.
Lan traveled to the abode of Chan Master An in Yanguan, Hangzhou. Master An was a high-ranking disciple of Mazu Daoshi.

One day, he gave instructions in advance to the administrative officers, saying, "A person of extraordinary character will arrive here tomorrow; several wandering monks (*xingjue seng*) will come to pay their respects."

When Dao’an first saw him, he found him extraordinary. He treated him with exceptional kindness, and every time they conversed, his sense of noble dignity increased further. Dao’an then said, “The monks of the monastery suffer from a lack of offerings for their meals;

I beg you to provide a memorial for a single offering. The Emperor immediately composed it for him. Upon reading it, Dao’an was struck with awe and realized that the offerings obtained by the monks through their proselytizing would be abundant.

He then said to the Emperor, “The time has come; do not let it stagnate. [I] entrust this to the Buddha. (Note: "Ni pan" refers to the dragon coiled in the mud, implying a period of waiting; "zhu yi fo" means to entrust the matter to the Buddha.)
Regarding matters after the Dharma’s passing: the Salt Official (Yanguan), who had remained for the longest time, left Hangzhou and traveled to Bai Zhang Mountain.

There he inscribed a poem which said: “The true traces of the Great Hero rest upon perilous peaks; The tiered pavilions of Sanskrit characters soar ten thousand spans high. Sun and moon pass daily across his shoulders;”
Mountains and rivers are long within the left palm; immortal flowers do not cease their splendor through the three springs. This sacred realm never knows the cold of the sixth month;
even more so, it is a place where few people of the upper reaches have traveled. Morning bells and evening chimes ring atop the emerald clouds.
One day, the Emperor went with Chan Master Xiangyan to Qixian Temple, where they ascended together to view the waterfall and composed a verse in linked lines. Xiangyan said: "Piercing the clouds..."
Penetrating through rocks without wearying; only from afar does one know the loftiness of his origins and destination. The Emperor continued: "How could the moisture of a brook remain forever?
It ultimately returns to the great ocean to become waves and surges. (This was inscribed on a stone at the mountain temple. When the Emperor arrived at Huangbo, he met Master Yun.

One day, while Baizhang was performing prostrations, the Emperor asked him, "If you do not seek the Buddha, do not seek the Dharma, and do not seek the Sangha, for what purpose do you perform these prostrations?
Baizhang replied, "I constantly prostrate to such matters. The Emperor asked again, "For what purpose do you prostrate? Baizhang then gave him a slap.
The Emperor said, "That was too coarse. Huangbo then struck him again, saying, "What are you talking about here, coarse or fine?

He struck him once more. Later, Chan Master Xuedou Xian composed a verse on this: "His majestic wind is formidable, yet he does not boast; Sitting upright within the world, he brings dragons and snakes to order.
The Great Zhong Emperor once lightly provoked him, And three times personally encountered his bared claws and fangs. The Emperor’s monastic name was Qiong.
(Jun’s Biographies of Eminent Monks) When the Emperor was still in his princely residence, he once had a miraculous dream, similar to the accounts of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.

From the very year of his "dragon-leap" ascension, the ministers and officials of the court welcomed him and established him upon the imperial throne. As he received his subordinates and settled the affairs of state, both the inner and outer courts were filled with harmony;
only then did they come to recognize his hidden virtues. At the beginning of his reign, he longed to see Master An of Yanguan. The Master...
He has already passed away long ago. The Emperor, in mourning, composed a poem which says: "In this age of the Dharma’s semblance, what calamity has befallen the teachings!

The splendor of the Śākya gate has lost its 'black dragon' pearl. I am too weary to tread the fragrant steps where fresh grass first grows; With a sorrowful clapping of hands, I gaze upon his countenance from another day.

The jade-handled staff forever leaves the seat of the Three Teachings; The golden sound shall eternally guard his tracks for ten thousand years. I know that for you, Master, the karmic conditions in this world have come to an end."
To which tier among the various heavens above should he belong? True Eulogy for Master An (anonymous): He has already equated the world to a mote of dust;
His body is but a floating blossom in space, a dream within a dream. Do not say that the dragon-like countenance can be distinguished by ordinary means;
Thus, it is through the divine eye that one recognizes a celestial being. (A verse by Su Shi)
Emperor Wuzong believed in the delusions of non-Buddhist paths and, harboring resentment toward his uncle’s virtue, submerged him in the palace latrines.

When Qiu Gongwu learned of Emperor Xuanzong’s sagacity and wisdom, he secretly protected him by becoming a monk and traveled with him throughout the empire. He remained for the longest time within the assembly of Master An at Yanguan.

Because Emperor Wuzong was enticed by the heresies of non-Buddhist paths, he utterly destroyed our Teaching; yet before long, it recoiled upon him like poison. When Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne, [he restored it] in its entirety.
He restored it. Although the flourishing or decline of the Buddha-dharma depends upon such factors, how can we know that this effort was not brought about by Master Dao’an?
Master Chou Wu’s virtue was no less than that of the Han dynasty’s Bing Ji, yet the New History omits him;
he appears only fragmentarily in the biography of Master Dao’an. This is truly lamentable (from the *Linjian Lu*).

Imperial Decree of the intercalary month in the first year of the Dazhong era: "Regarding the monasteries abolished in the fifth year of the Huichang era, if there are monks capable of restoring and maintaining them, they shall be permitted to reside therein;

the relevant authorities must not prohibit this. Since such residence runs contrary to the policies of the Huichang era, the abuses concerning monks and nuns shall all be restored to their former state.
(Tongjian) In the third month, an edict was issued stating: "The teaching of Śākyamuni provides spiritual sustenance..."
As for the source of principle, China has long practiced this Way. However, the previous dynasty’s reforms were excessive, resulting in practices that were erroneous and contrary to the truth.

Therefore, the sacred mountains and sublime landscapes throughout the empire—the monasteries abolished in the fifth year of Huichang—should be restored to their former state and maintained as before (Old History).
Wuchen (768), the second year [of the reign]. Pei Xiu, the Regional Inspector, was governing Xuancheng.

He frequently discussed the Way with eminent monks. A disciple said to the Duke, "I venture to ask: before the teachings of the Three Realms were established, people did not know how to practice cultivation, nor did they perceive cause and effect;
those who possessed great fortune were not few. Yet since these teachings have been practiced throughout China, the foolish have become fearful."
Sinners discard their evils; sages look toward blessings and increase their goodness. If one increases [goodness] without ceasing, then by now it ought to have reached the height of perfection.

If one discards [evil] without ceasing, then by now it ought to be entirely free of wickedness. Yet why is it that confusion, delusion, violence, and tyranny have not diminished since the time of the Qin and Han dynasties?
Why is it that blessings, wisdom, and sagacity have not increased since the time of the Wei and Jin dynasties? The reasons for this are manifold.
The paths converge here. To establish [this teaching], the myriad dharmas have flourished like falling snow. It is fitting that we, as human beings, should all ascend the path to enlightenment;
it is not fitting for the common masses to remain ignorant. From antiquity to the present, if people have been so deluded, and because of such stubbornness, is this not drowning?
The Master smiled and said to him: "When the Great Light first dawned, the Dharma was not yet complete. The Sages appeared in succession to act on behalf of Heaven."
They became craftsmen. By tying knots and drawing trigrams, the patterns of the refined and the simple underwent further transformation. With each sage established, a corresponding law arose;
thus the Way of Heaven and the affairs of humanity corresponded as clearly as matching seals.

Indeed, before the Lord of Suiren had fire, there would surely have been no stellar fire in the heavens, no fire for human food, no fire-omen signs on tortoise shells, and no fire-related disasters among things. Before the Lord of Shaohao had regulated metal...
Then there would surely have been no Venus in the heavens, no use for metal among humans, no auspicious signs of metal in the tortoise shell, and no calamities involving metal among things.
Yet, when the Sage carved wood to produce fire and forged stone to extract metal, the essential radiance took its sovereign place and manifested transformations above and below.
Thus we know that worldly phenomena and human affairs follow the Sage; by examining the source of spirit and investigating the limits of nature and destiny, [we find them rooted therein].
The memorial states: "He employs great skillful means to protect all living beings; yet the beings receive his benefits without knowing it.

It is as when the heavens revolve and things flourish and grow, yet everyone claims it is their own doing—who knows that it is so? Thereupon, the questioner attained a vast and clear realization of the flavor of the Buddha’s teaching.
When the imperial decree permitted the establishment of monasteries to propagate [the Dharma], the officials and commoners encouraged one another, and ten thousand people submitted a petition.

First, he established it at the outer walls of Xuan; subsequently, he restored Xinxing Temple. During the first year of the Renxu year of the Kaiyuan era, the Prime Minister Lord Pei was serving as the Prefect of Junzhou.
He entered Dajian Temple and asked the abbot, "What is depicted on the wall? The abbot replied, "It is the portraits of eminent monks.
The Lord said, "The portraits may be viewed, but where are the eminent monks? The assembly had no answer. The Lord remarked, "Is there perhaps no one here [who truly embodies them]?"
"Zen monk? [The Master] said, "Recently there was a monk who came to this temple to serve; he bears a strong resemblance to a Zen monk. Let us invite him here.

The Master then asked him about what had just transpired: "When I questioned the various Zen masters, each declined, and they requested that you, Venerable One, provide a turning word. The Master replied:
He then made an inquiry, recounting the previous conversation. The Master called out loudly, "Pai Xiu! The official responded, "Yes. The Master asked, "Where are you?
At that moment, the official realized his true home, as if he had recovered the jewel from within his topknot. This was Master Xiyun. The official then welcomed him to the prefecture.
He visited Longxing Temple to inquire about the Way and presented a verse of his understanding to the Master.

Upon receiving it, the Master sat down immediately and said, "Even if you understand it this way, you are still somewhat off the mark. To express it through paper and brush—how can that belong to our school?
After a short while, the official again composed a poem, saying: "Ever since the Great Being transmitted the Mind-Seal, A seven-foot body with a pearl upon the brow. Hanging the monk’s staff..."
Ten years I dwelt by the waters of Shu; today, the floating bowl crosses the banks of the Zhang. A thousand nāgas and elephants follow your lofty footsteps;
ten thousand li of incense and flowers form a sublime cause. I wish to serve you as your disciple, yet I do not know to whom you will entrust the Dharma.
The Master replied: "My mind is like the great ocean, boundless; my mouth spits forth red lotuses to nourish this sickly body.
I have only these two hands of non-action, which have never bowed in greeting to ordinary people.

The official then built a temple to invite him, but the Master would not accept, saying, "On Mount Huangbo in Min there are twelve peaks, yet one peak is missing. The official then constructed that peak, and the Master immediately took up residence there.
One day, the Duke held up a Buddha statue before the Master and said, "I request the Master to bestow a name upon it. The Master replied, "Pei Xiu. The Duke responded with an affirmative "Yes.
The Master said, "I have finished bestowing the name upon you. The Duke bowed in thanks. On another day, the Duke entered the monastery and saw a monk reading a scripture.
He asked, "What scripture are you reading? The monk replied, "The Scripture of the Silent Youth (*Mūkaputraka-sūtra*). The Duke asked, "How many fascicles does it have?"

[The Master] said, "Two fascicles. The Official said, "Since there are no words, why are there indeed two fascicles? The monk had no reply. (From *Sengshi*) One day the Official visited Master Shishuang.
Shishuang said, "I have a question to ask the Official. If our words do not accord, [I shall know you are not a true man]."
He left behind his ceremonial tablet (huk). The Duke said, "I request it. Shuang then snatched the tablet away and said, "In the hand of the Son of Heaven, it is called the 'Lord';
in the hand of an official, it is called the 'tablet. In the hand of this mountain monk, what do you call it? The Duke had no reply.

He then left behind his ceremonial tablet (*hù*). Later, he investigated the essential tenets of the *Enlightenment of Perfect Wisdom* (*Yuánjué*) with Chan Master Mì of Guīfēng (according to the *Sēngshǐ*).
The Chancellor was a native of Méngzhōu; his courtesy name was Gōngměi. Emperor Xuānzōng praised his talent, and during the Dàzhōng era, he served as a high official for six years.

Subsequently, he held various regional commands as a military governor (*jiédù*). By nature, he was refined and composed, and his integrity and conduct were strict and upright. The Emperor remarked, "He is truly a Confucian scholar," yet he was fond of frivolous pursuits.

Regarding his life as a butcher: although he lived by this trade, he generally abstained from wine and meat. He would often wear a coarse woolen robe while staying in the quarters of singing girls, carrying an alms bowl to beg for food.
He considered himself untainted by worldly passions and thus fit to preach the Dharma; he would seek out and explain the teachings for others.

He was particularly skilled at composing literary works, producing several tens of thousands of words in his writings, including the *Preface to the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng xù*) and the *Exhortation to Generate the Resolve for the Avataṃsaka Dharmadhātu* (*Huáyán fǎjiè xù quàn fā*).
The *Bodhicitta-vyākhyāna*, the *Cittotpāda-gāthā*, and Master Guifeng’s *Preface to the Various Explanations* are particularly refined and exquisite.
Although they were ridiculed and disparaged by those of his own time, his devotion to them did not wane. Even if there were authors in later generations, none would be able to surpass them.
He passed away in the first year of the Xiántóng era of Emperor Yìzōng, the Gēngyín year (880 CE), at the age of seventy-four (*Tángshū*).
Xinwei (the 5th year), the first month of the fifth year. An imperial edict summoned Chan Master Hongbian of Jingzhao to the inner palace.
The Emperor asked, "Why does the Chan school have the designations 'Northern' and 'Southern'? He replied, "The Chan gate originally has no north or south.

From the various patriarchs down to Master Hongren, there were two disciples: one was Huineng, who received the robe and dharma and resided in Lingnan; the other was Shenxiu, who remained in the north."
"Spreading the Transformation. Although the Dharma attained is one, there are differences between sudden and gradual in terms of guidance and the triggering of awakening;

hence it is said, "Sudden in the South, Gradual in the North. This does not mean that the Chan School possesses the designations of "North" and "South. The Emperor asked, "What are the names for precept, concentration, and wisdom? He replied, "Preventing wrongdoing and ceasing evil is called Precept (śīla).
When the six sense organs encounter objects and the mind does not follow after conditions, it is called Concentration (samādhi). When both mind and objects are empty, this is called Wisdom (prajñā)."
To survey all things without delusion is called wisdom (*prajñā*). The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'expedient means' (*upāya*)? He replied, "It is the gateway of skillful artifice.

To accommodate those of middling and inferior capacities by employing indirect methods to guide and instruct them is called expedient means. Even when teaching those of superior faculties, one may set aside expedient means and speak only of the Unsurpassed Way;
this too is a discourse of expedient means. This extends even to the profound words of the Patriarchs, which forget function and sever all designations—these likewise do not exist [independently]."
He manifested the traces of skillful means. The Emperor asked, "What constitutes the Buddha-mind? He replied, "Buddha means awakening.

To possess wisdom that awakens and illuminates is what is called the Buddha-mind. The Emperor asked, "If someone recollects the Buddha, how is it? He replied, "The Tathāgata has appeared in the world."
He taught according to their capacities. For those of superior faculties, he opened the gate of the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*), whereby they suddenly awaken to the ultimate principle.

Those of middling and inferior faculties were unable to understand it all at once; therefore, he opened the gate of contemplation, causing them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha so as to be born in Sukhāvatī.

The Emperor asked: "If one upholds sūtras and mantras while seeking the Buddha, what of that? He replied: "The Tathāgata’s various teachings of the Dharma are all for the sake of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*)."
"Of the hundreds of thousands of streams, there are none that do not flow toward the sea as their source. Likewise, all these diverse conditions return to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
The Emperor asked: "Since the Patriarch transmitted the seal of the mind, how is it that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of 'the dharma of non-attainment'?"
He replied: "In the Buddha’s single transformation, there is truly not a single dharma given to others; he merely reveals that each person's own nature is identical to the Dharma-treasury.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara merely certified Śākyamuni’s original dharma, and it was through having nothing to attain that he finally accorded with Dīpaṃkara’s original intent.
As the sutra says: 'No self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span possessor—this is the Dharma.'"

"Equanimity. Cultivate all wholesome dharmas without dwelling on appearances. The Emperor asked, "Since you, Chan Master, have realized the intent of the Patriarchs, do you still prostrate to the Buddha and read the sutras?
He replied, "For a śramaṇa to prostrate to the Buddha and read the sutras is the constant dharma of maintaining the tradition.

There are four types of retribution. One relies on the Buddha’s precepts to cultivate the body, seeks out spiritual friends, gradually cultivates pure conduct, and follows in the footsteps of the Tathāgata."

Regarding the traces of his practice, the Emperor asked: "What is sudden enlightenment? What is gradual cultivation? He replied: "To suddenly clarify one's own nature is to be no different from a Buddha.
Nevertheless, because there are defiled habits from beginningless time, one must rely on gradual cultivation as an antidote to cause the functioning of that nature to arise accordingly.

It is like a person eating rice; they are not satiated by a single mouthful. On this day, the debate lasted for seven *ke* (seven-fifths of an hour) before concluding. The Emperor was greatly [impressed].
[The Emperor] was pleased and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Yuanzhi. On this day, an imperial decree was issued to renovate the ancestral pagodas throughout the empire;

it was ordered that those who had not yet been granted posthumous titles be reported by their respective localities, and the Ministry of Rites (Taichang) was to examine their conduct and bestow eulogies thereupon (*Wudeng Huiyuan*). In the tenth month, the Secretariat and Chancellery memorialized:
"Now that the affairs on the borders have subsided, yet the construction at various monasteries in the prefectures and counties remains unfinished. We hope that for the time being..."
Regarding those prefectures whose territories were larger and more distant than those of the provinces and commanderies, it was permitted to establish one temple each;
however, no further Buddhist establishments were to be built in the rural villages. This was accordingly granted (Tongjian).
Ren-shen, the twelfth month of the sixth year. The Chancellery and Secretariat submitted a memorial: "The ordination of monks is not rigorous; some have fallen away from the Dharma.

The construction of temples lacks moderation, resulting in excessive waste and destruction. We request that from now on, in all prefectures, temples may be established only in accordance with the original imperial decree."

It was permitted to restore sacred sites and traces of excellence in the provinces; in counties with dense populations, it was permitted to establish one temple. A prohibition was enacted against the private ordination of monks and nuns throughout the year;
in the event of vacancies, qualified persons were to be selected to fill them, and they were to apply to the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu) for official certificates.
Those wishing to travel afar to seek teachers and examine the teachings were required to possess a public attestation from their respective prefectures. This was accordingly adopted (*Tongjian*).
Qiao Shang submitted a memorial stating: "The common people, with men plowing and women weaving, cannot even provide for their own warmth and full stomachs;
yet the monks sit at ease in magnificent dwellings, wearing fine clothes and eating sumptuous meals. On average, ten households cannot support a single monk.

Emperor Wuzong was indignant at this state of affairs and shaved the heads of one hundred seventy thousand monks; it was only then that the one million seven hundred thousand households of the empire were able to find relief."
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne, you have restored ruined temples; the sound of axes and adzes throughout the realm has not ceased until this day.

The number of ordained monks has nearly reached its former level. Even if Your Majesty does not accept my words, consider how Emperor Wuzong eliminated long-standing abuses—how could one possibly revive what had already been abolished?
Recently, when Your Majesty wished to repair and expand the East Gate, the Censors submitted a remonstrance, and [the project] was abruptly...

This was done to suspend labor services. Are the temples now being restored any more urgent than the matters at the East Gate? Is the labor required for these works any more arduous than the toil at the East Gate?
I pray that you will soon issue a clear edict: let those monks and nuns who have not yet been reinstated not be reinstated, and let those temples that have not yet been repaired not be repaired.
Only in this way may the common people find respite from their burdens. [The request] was not accepted (Tongjian).
The seventh month. The Secretariat and the Chancellery memorialized: "Your Majesty honors the teachings of Śākyamuni, and among the officials there are none who do not hasten to comply.
We fear that financial resources may prove insufficient, leading to the creation of unnecessary projects and the disturbance of public expectations.

We therefore request that local officials be authorized to exercise moderation in their expenditures and that those who ordain monks and nuns be entrusted with the task of selecting only those who possess virtuous conduct. If those of coarse character are permitted to enter the order, it will only further [disturb the people]."
This was not out of reverence for the Way, but rather because he had ceased his restorations at the Buddhist shrines in the countryside and was following [the practice] (as before).
Jiaxu, the eighth year. There was a monk on Mount Zhongnan who dwelt in a hermitage practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One day, the monk lost his *saṃghāṭī* robe.
He searched everywhere until he saw it being worn by a macaque sitting in solemn meditation among the cliffs. He also saw a troop of monkeys all...

He practiced meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and there were occasionally those who passed away while seated in meditation. Today, there is the Five Monkey Stūpa. When Emperor Xuanzong heard of these matters, he offered a verse of praise which said:
"Alas, you monkeys, able to enter meditative absorption; The heart-monkey remains unmoving for thousands of springs. Cease grasping at the red tree’s winter fruits;
Desist from playing with the solitary moon-disc in the azure pool. Your two eyes have already closed along with the green peaks; Your two eyebrows still face [the sky]..."
The Hundred Flowers Furrow Their Brows. Since his "sitting-transcendence" at Zhongnan, how many have awakened to the vanity of this floating life? (From *Shihua*).
In the tenth year of the Bingzi year, an imperial decree was issued for the two temples of Linggan and Huishan to establish ordination platforms (*jietan*).

It was ordered that qualified monks and nuns be invited to fill vacancies, with elders commissioned to select them and provide official warrants (*gongju*) for them to attend the two platforms and receive the precepts. [Two gold coins.]
Ten virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) were selected for each [province] to preside over these matters. Those who were deemed incapable were dismissed, while those who were capable were honored.

Upon returning to the province, no one was permitted to see the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*). Regarding official documents, no private accommodations were allowed. Furthermore, former monks and nuns were first selected;
only if there were none among the former monks and nuns deemed capable were outsiders selected (from the *Tongjian*).
The Hanlin Academician Pi Rixiu sent a letter to the *boshi* of the Imperial Academy, stating: "The teachings of the Western Regions are practiced by their followers day after day;
they take the selection and refinement of their methods as their primary task. When we look upon them, it is enough to bring shame upon the Western Regions."
Ji-mao (the year 859 CE): In the thirteenth year of the Dazhong era, Emperor Xuanzong passed away. He had occupied the throne for fourteen years;
he was intelligent, benevolent, respectful, and frugal, and the world hailed him as the "Lesser Taizong."

In the Gengchen year, Emperor Yizong changed the era name to Xiantong. In the fifth month, Cai Jing, the Grand Governor of Fuzhou, composed the "Record of the Sūtra Repository at East Forest Monastery on Mount Lu," which states:
"Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou, because the three teachings were not in accord, issued an edict to Lord Xiaoyao."

I have determined their relative merits. When contrasted, although the three teachings differ, they all ultimately converge upon goodness. While their manifestations vary in depth, their underlying principle is without gradation.

The capital has always held that those who adhere to the Eastern Teaching (Confucianism) merely see its differences because they cling to its outward traces; yet those with profound understanding and far-reaching insight must realize their essential unity.
The loyalty and reciprocity of Confucius, the gentleness and humility of Laozi, and the compassion of the Buddha—if one treads this path, there is blessing; if one deviates from it...

To do otherwise brings calamity. Regarding the three teachings of the gentleman, one should neither drown oneself in them nor destroy them; rather, one should explore their profound essence to assist in the cultivation of true purity.
If they are employed for the purpose of governance, order will surely flourish.

Renwu, the third year, summer, the fourth month. An imperial decree was issued for the two streets and four monasteries to each establish a *śīla-maṇḍala* (ordination platform) for twenty-one days to ordain people.
The Emperor’s devotion to the Buddha was most sincere; he constructed a platform within the Xantai Hall to serve as an inner monastery for nuns to receive the precepts.

Monks and nuns from both streets were all invited to participate. Furthermore, a lecture hall was established within the palace, where the Emperor himself announced the titles of the sutras and personally transcribed them by hand.
The Buddhist scriptures (*bānjiá*) were still frequently visited by the Emperor at various monasteries, where he bestowed gifts upon them without restraint (according to the *Tongjiàn*).
Li Qīnmíng, the Vice Director of the Office of Merit (*Sīxūn Yuànwài Láng*), submitted a memorial stating: "An ancient proverb says:

'If one man does not plow and one woman does not weave, there will surely be those who suffer from hunger and cold. Within the realm of Your Majesty’s sacred transformation, there are already approximately one hundred thousand monks and nuns; every day, each person..."
They consume two *sheng* per meal. For one hundred thousand people, the daily expenditure is two thousand *shi*. Calculating month by month from day to day, the total can be known.
Every monk is granted five bolts of silk and five *liang* of cotton wool annually. For one hundred thousand people, this amounts to five million bolts of silk and five million *liang* of cotton wool.
These people neither plow nor sericulture; they truly violate the great social order. I, your servant, believe that the assembly of monks is not [beneficial].

It is like a gathering of troops. The wealth of the Sangha is not equal to the wealth of the common people. As the Sūtra says: "When a sage is at the head of the state, there are no 'fortunate' subjects among the people.
That the people have much fortune is the misfortune of the state" (same as above).
Gengyin, the eleventh year, the eleventh month. On the Emperor’s birthday, he summoned the monks of the two monastic streets to enter the palace to lecture on the Way.
The Emperor was pleased and bestowed purple robes upon ten individuals, including Tanxian (Tongji).

Xinmao, the twelfth year. The Emperor visited An Guo Temple and bestowed upon the National Preceptor Zhi Xuan a precious throne made of *chendan* sandalwood, over twenty feet high, of such exquisite beauty as to be unsurpassed.
Zhi Xuan’s secular surname was Chen; he was popularly known as "Chan Pusa. He had mastered all three branches of Buddhist study with profound penetration.
His fame eclipsed that of his contemporaries, and his extraordinary deeds were numerous; these are recorded in the *Jiù Táng Shǐ* (Old History of the Tang).

At that time, ten thousand monks were provided with daily meals at the palace, and the Emperor himself performed hymns and chants (*zàn-bài*). Jì Wèizōng, courtesy name Màolín, was appointed as an Inspector (*jiānchá shì*) and subsequently promoted to Right Vice-Minister (*yòuchéng*). He submitted a petition offering earnest remonstrance.

[The Emperor] did not grant permission. Xiao Fang, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, submitted a memorial stating: "The Way of our Primordial Ancestor takes compassion and humility as its priority;
the style of the 'Unadorned King' (Confucius) takes benevolence and righteousness as its foremost principles. These have served as models for a hundred generations and must never be superseded.

As for the Buddha, he abandoned his station to leave the household life, taking up the ultimate in renouncing worldly attachments and seeking the extraordinary excellence of extinction after death. This is not something a sovereign should emulate."

"I pray that Your Majesty will occasionally open the Yan-ying Hall to receive the four high ministers, diligently seeking out the sufferings of the people, and reverently serving the ancestral shrines.
Beware of erroneous rewards and excessive punishments; their calamities will surely follow. Know that overcoming cruelty through non-killing brings forth immense blessings.

Abandon the lecture halls and personally apply yourself to the affairs of government. Although the Emperor offered him wine as a gesture of favor, he ultimately could not follow this advice. Furthermore, the *Jiu Tang Shu* records that [the Emperor] followed...
His courtesy name was Sidao. Later, he was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Lingnan. Emperor Yizong neglected state affairs and took pleasure in Buddhism and Daoism;

he summoned monastics into the inner palace to perform rites of prayer and sacrifice. He frequently visited Buddhist temples and bestowed extensive alms. [The Emperor] followed this [practice], yet [the official] remonstrated, saying:

"The Dharma of India involves severing attachments to attain extinction; it is not something a sovereign should emulate or admire. Now you are writing Indian scripts with your pen and reciting Buddhist scriptures with your mouth. It did not...
If one seeks to rectify errors in reward and punishment or to avert calamities by seeking blessings through excessive penalization, how much more so should this apply to the Buddha,
who is to be apprehended through awakening rather than sought through physical marks (from the *Tongjian*).
Guisi (the fourteenth year of the Xiandong era), the third month. The Emperor dispatched an envoy to Fengxiang Famen Temple to welcome the Buddha’s relics.
Among the many ministers who offered remonstrances, some even remarked that Emperor Xianzong had passed away while welcoming the Buddha’s relics.

The Emperor replied, "If I see them in my lifetime, I shall have no regrets even if I die. He then extensively constructed pagodas, jeweled canopies, incense-laden carriages, banners, flowers, and streamers.
They were covered with canopies and all adorned with gold, jade, brocade, embroidery, pearls, and jade-green feathers.

From the capital to the temple, for a distance of three hundred *li*, the roads were never free of carriages and horses, day or night. On the *renyin* day of the fourth month of summer, the Buddha’s relics arrived at the capital.
The procession was led by the imperial guard bearing weapons, while public and private musical performances resounded as if boiling over heaven and earth, stretching for thousands of li.
The magnificence of the ceremonial escort surpassed even that of the suburban sacrifices; it was far beyond what had been seen in the era of Yuanhe.

Wealthy households lined the roads with colorful banners, and at the *amogha-pūjā* assemblies, they vied with one another in displays of luxury and splendor. The Emperor ascended the Anfu Gate and descended from the tower to prostrate himself in worship. The [crowds] flowed...
Tears moistened his breast. He bestowed gold and silk upon the monks and the elders of the capital who had witnessed the events of the Yuanhe era.
He welcomed the Buddha’s relics into the imperial palace for three days, after which they were taken out and placed in the An-guo and Chong-hua monasteries.

From the Chancellor downward, all vied to offer gold and silk in such numbers that they could not be recorded. Consequently, an edict was issued to reduce the sentences of prisoners throughout the realm (from the *History of Tang*). The edict stated: "I, the Emperor..."
Possessing but meager virtue, I have succeeded to this great enterprise for fourteen years. With anxiety and diligence, I have occupied the throne, cherishing and nurturing all living beings.

Consequently, I have honored the teachings of Śākyamuni and held the profound gate of Emptiness in the highest esteem. I have invited the True Body [of the Buddha] to pray for blessings upon the common people, constantly mindful of the imperial ancestors.

Whether resting or rising, these matters occupied my thoughts: "Alas for my common people, who have fallen into the snares of legal punishment. How much more so when they are subjected to the heat and toxins of summer while bound in fetters.
For all prisoners currently incarcerated within the capital and throughout the various provinces of the empire, their sentences shall be commuted by one degree from death. —The Twelfth Month.
An imperial edict was issued to send back the Buddha’s bone relics to Famen Temple; as the people of the capital bid them farewell, they all wept with choked voices.
In the seventh month, the Emperor passed away (according to the *Jiu Tang Shu*).
Emperor Xizong: in the year Jia-wu, he changed the era name to Qiánfú. In the fourth year, Huang Chao plundered Henan and Jiangzhe.
In the fifth year, he captured Fujian; in the sixth year, he captured Guangnan, Jinghu, and Jianghuai.
In the gengzi year, the first year of Guangming, Huang Chao captured the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) and Tongguan Pass.
The Emperor fled the capital, and in the twelfth month, Chao seized the imperial city, declaring the state name Da Qi and establishing the era name Jintong.
Xin-chou, the first year of Zhonghe (881). Emperor Xizong fled to Shu, and the princes and members of the imperial clan all went into hiding.

The third son of the Emperor shaved his head to become a monk, named Pumen. While traveling and visiting Shi-shuang Zhu Chan, the Master [Zhu] spoke with him and marveled at his extraordinary nature, saying:
"You have come to life in a family of imperial nobility by virtue of your power of past vows; that you now follow my teaching is truly remarkable."
It was like a lotus flower blooming amidst fire. Hearing that [Zhaozhou] had entered the room at night, he asked about the matter of the Patriarch’s special transmission.

Zhaozhou said, "Wait until the mountain on which my desk stands nods its head, and I shall tell you the reason. Thereupon, [Xuefeng] attained awakening and took his leave. He traveled extensively through famous mountains.
Zhaozhou said, "When you meet 'Gan,' stop; when you encounter 'Chen,' dwell. Upon reaching Daqian in Shaowu, Xuefeng gazed upon it and cast down his iron staff; it settled wherever it fell.
He remained at the place where he had stopped. An old man there said, "There is a descendant of the Chen family who has long been hidden within these mountains.

Upon hearing the Master’s words, he cleared the weeds and climbed the mountain. As soon as the descendant of the Chen family saw him, he shared his seat with him and lived together. He then asked the Chen family for vegetable seeds, requesting a measure of them.
The Chen family gave him one *he* (a small measure). He entered the mountains to plow and sow; after several days, the vegetables were already green. Thereupon—
The mountain deity and the fierce tiger served him as his attendants. Chen, recognizing that the Master’s Way was superior, took his leave and departed.

One day, while the Master sat in meditative repose, an old man came to pay his respects and said, "I am not a human being; I am a dragon. Because I failed in my duty to send down rain, I have incurred the wrath of the High Heaven.
I venture to rely upon the power of your Way to save me from this calamity. The Master replied, "As for you having incurred the wrath of the High Heaven, what can I possibly do?"
Although he could easily change his form, after a short while a small snake about a foot long crawled into his sleeve. In an instant, wind and thunder shook the seat;

when the sky cleared, the snake departed. The old man returned and, weeping, apologized, saying, "Were it not for your Great Being’s blood defiling this mountain, I would have no way to repay your kindness.
He then hollowed out a rock below to create a spring. On other days when many people were there and there was no water, this spring [flowed].

The Master was also a temple administrator (*sīshī*). Fifteen *li* to the right of the monastery was the shrine where the Governor of Ōyō, Fǔshàn, had been enshrined during the Yíníng era of the Sui dynasty;

more than two hundred and seventy years had passed until this point, yet there was not a single day that offerings were not made. When the Master arrived at the shrine, he recited a verse to exhort them, saying:
"In awakening to the Way, life and death are one; though one dies, one does not forget within the midst of birth. The tiger submits through mindlessness; when people come..."

"Accompanied by wisdom, one subdues [afflictions]. Killing for the sake of sacrifice brings calamity through ten thousand kalpas of saṃsāra. To repay the kindness of gods and humans, the merit of an unobstructed feast (amogha-pūjā) is most powerful.
If you wish to plant seeds that shall bear fruit, this present life is the necessary provision. Everywhere people are struck with awe; I urge the Great King to practice the fast (upoṣadha).
In years past, within the hells, today it has become a heavenly realm. He further made an agreement, saying: "Can you eat only plain food?"

Only after he had killed [the beast] could he be considered a neighbor. That evening, the village elders dreamed that a deity said: "I have now received the precepts from the Chan Master and shall no longer partake of offerings of blood.
It will suffice to sacrifice according to the ritual for a bhikṣu. The deity further stated: "The Master and I shall compete in strength.

Beside the temple there is a giant pine tree that nearly reaches the heavens. The Master bends it down and sweeps it across the ground three times; I shall sweep it twice, and then I will submit. Thus it was recorded.
Cheng Huang Li composed a poem sent to a monk, saying: "At Dragon Lake, I once conversed with Youmin; With hands turning the pine branches, he swept the ground thrice.
Moved by this, his vegetarian practice remains as such even now; Hearing of your solitary purity, Master, I know you may be followed for study.
Furthermore, the newly ordained monk Shao wrote a poem, saying: "An ancient tree, cold crows, and smoke locked in by day; The numinous wind persists as kalpas repeatedly pass. Suddenly I think..."
Regarding the events of Yuanjue’s life, he spoke only of causes and did not discuss Chan. Examining this, it is not necessarily so that you [should] posthumously title him Chan Master Yuanjue.
On the day of his birth, which was the first day of the New Year (Shangyuan), dragons surely came to court, accompanied by auspicious vapors and auspicious clouds (as recorded in his biography).

Ren-yin, the second year. The Emperor fled from the Nao rebels and took refuge in Chengdu. He dispatched the Censor Guo Zun with an imperial edict to summon National Teacher Zhi-huan to the temporary capital for an audience.
The Emperor bestowed upon him purple robes and the title of National Teacher Wuda, entrusting him with the affairs of the Buddhist teachings (Tang History).

Gui-mao (the tenth day of the second month), the third year [of the Dazhong period]. National Teacher Zhixuan returned from Chengdu to Jiulong. Suddenly, while in meditative absorption, he saw a Bodhisattva stroke his head and comfort him.
Shortly thereafter, a pearl entered Zhixuan’s left thigh; it swelled up and caused intense pain. Upon it were the two characters "Chao Cuo.
Realizing this was a karmic debt from a previous life, he immediately passed away lying on his right side. The world says that Zhixuan was a descendant of Yuan Ang of the Han dynasty.
Shen’ang had a feud with Chao Cuo. It is also said that Xuan was a monk of eminent virtue who was difficult to approach;
because he accepted a sandalwood bed from him, Cuo immediately took revenge. In this year, Li Kelyong defeated Huang Chao and restored the capital.
In the fourth year, Kelyong pursued Chao and executed him.
Yisi (12 March): The first year of the Guangqi era, the third month. The Emperor returned to the capital. In the twelfth month, there was military turmoil, and the Emperor fled to Fengxiang.
The monk Huisheng of Fakong Temple in Wenzhou constructed a hut on the northern cliff and transcribed the Lotus Sūtra; when he reached the section on the Exhortation of Samantabhadra...

In the "Chapter on the Vow" (Pphal-p'um), two śarīra relics rained down from heaven. The commandery reported this, and the temple was granted the name Pŏnghyon Sŏnwon (Changdok-sa) by imperial decree (*Yongdŏng pyŏnnyeon*).
In the first year of Mundeok, the *wuśin* year, the Emperor returned to the capital in the second month; the Emperor passed away in the third month.
Wang Kon plundered the Western River region (West Chuan).
The sixteenth year of Emperor Zhaozong’s reign was the Jiyou year; he changed the era name to Longji.
The following year was Gengxu, the first year of Dashun. In the next year, Xinhai, Yang Xingmi seized Yangzhou and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wu.
Jiayin (18th year of the sexagenary cycle), the first year of Qianning. Chan Master Guanhui was a native of Lanxi in Wuzhou.

He first met the Chan Master Shishuang Qingzhu and requested to serve as his head seat (*dìyīzuò*). Having realized the principle of the single transmission, he became renowned in his time for his poetry.
The high officials, ministers, and great officers all followed him in his travels at the mere sight of his reputation. Upon arriving there, he went to pay his respects to the King of Wuyue, Qian Liu.
He had a verse that read: "A sword as cold as frost over fourteen prefectures. Qian Liu ordered it to be changed to "forty prefectures. Xiu replied, "A poem cannot be altered.
A solitary cloud and a wild crane—what heaven would they not fly to? Thereupon, he entered the Western Mountains of Yuzhang and later went to Shu.
He had an audience with the Ruler of Shu, King Wang Da. Presenting his circumstances, he offered this poem: "In Hebei and Hedong, every place is ravaged by calamity;
