Shi Qiji was a native of Yiyang in Tan; the son of the Hu family, he entered the monastic order as a novice under Chan Master Daopei of Dayue in his youth.
Yangshan Ji was a fellow student of the same school. While residing at Guanyin Monastery in Yuzhang, Ji took charge of the monastic affairs and composed a preface for the morning gruel, stating:
"The gruel is called a 'virtuous medicine' (liang-yao), praised by the Buddha. Its meaning surpasses the three types of giving, and its merit is marked throughout the ten directions.
May the aspirations of all noble and wise ones be fulfilled; having prepared this, may it forever support pure karma from this early hour. Later, he resided at Jingu Peak on Mount Xi.
The stone basin: this was his hermitage. During the Yuanyou era, Ma Chun, the Regional Transport Commissioner, inscribed these words upon the wall of the monastery:

“Zhi Dun’s carefree wanderer I did not meet; Casually dismounting my horse, I rested at the Lotus Palace. Wishing to inquire about the secluded life of Qi Ji, I find the seventy-year-old mountain monk’s ears are deaf.”
Wang Changshi annotated the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) and presented it to Yangshan. Upon receiving it, Yangshan threw it to the ground. Changshi turned pale with alarm.
Yangshan said, "As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes confused and loses the mind; why do you bother to annotate it? Changshi was speechless. Prime Minister Lu Xisheng visited Yangshan.
As he was leaving the main gate, Yangshan met him outside. The Prime Minister asked, "The three gates are all open; which disciple [should I enter]?"

"Through which gate do you enter? Shanshan said, "I enter through the gate of faith. The official then entered. He then asked, "What is it like when one leaves the realm of demons and enters the realm of Buddhas?
Shanshan struck him three times with the handle of his whisk. The official bowed. He asked again, "Does the Master observe the precepts? The Master said, "I do not observe the precepts.
"Do you practice seated meditation? He said, "I do not practice seated meditation. As the official was about to deliberate on this, Shanshan said, "Understood? The official understood.
Mogong said, "I do not understand. Baoshan then said, "Flowing along, he does not maintain the precepts; sitting upright, he does not practice meditation.
With three or five bowls of strong tea, his intent lies at the edge of the mattock. Mogong then returned to the guest quarters.
The next day, Baoshan went to see him and asked, "Did you realize the meaning of yesterday's encounter? Mogong replied, "Even the word 'realization' is unnecessary. Baoshan—
[The Master] said, "The single word 'awakening' is not for you, Excellency. At this, the Excellency attained realization.
Grand Marshal Wang Bin entered a temple and, upon reaching the Buddha hall, pointed to an alms bowl and asked the hall attendant, "What is this bowl?
The attendant replied, "It is a Bhaisajyaguru bowl. Wang said, "I have only heard of the Dragon-subduing bowl. The attendant said, "Wait until there is a dragon, and then..."

[The Master] descended. The King asked, "If one suddenly encounters the arrival of clouds grasping the sky and mist swirling about, what then? The Master said, "He does not even look back. The King said, "The talk has fallen away.
There was an official who entered the Tianwang Temple in Zhenzhou. Upon seeing the divine image, he asked the temple master, "What kind of merit-donor is this?
The master replied, "It is the Guardian King of the Nation. The official said, "Does it protect only this country?"
[The Master] was protecting other countries on all sides. The Governor said, "In Qin he is of Qin; in Chu he is of Chu.
The Official said, "On the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month, the city of Caizhou was broken. Where has the Heavenly King gone? The Master remained silent.
There was a scholar who visited Master Muzhou. The Master asked, "What studies have you pursued, sir? The scholar replied, "I am proficient in the twenty-four schools of thought."
The Master [Zhaozhou] took up his staff, pointed with it once, and asked, "Do you understand? Cui said, "I do not.

Zhaozhou said, "Then you say you understand the twenty-four styles of calligraphy, yet you do not even recognize the eight strokes of the character 'eternity' (永). On another occasion, a scholar came to visit the Master. The Master... [text ends].
The Master asked, "Which scripture do you specialize in? Zhai said, "I study the *Yi*. The Master said, "'The *Yi* says: 'The common people use it daily but do not know it.
What is it that they do not know? Zhai said, "They do not know the Dao. The Master said, "What is this Dao? Zhai was speechless. The Master said, "As expected, they do not know it.
Zhang Baohui went to visit Nan'uan. Nan'uan asked, "Are you not Zhang Baohui?"
"Do you understand? Zhang replied, "I dare not say I do. The Master drew a line in the air with his hand and said, "Do you understand? Zhang replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "If you do not even understand one, from where could you possibly get a hundred?"
Lü Dongbin visited Chan Master Huanglong. Lü Dongbin, also known as Lü Yan, was an immortal of the divine realm.
One day, as he was passing beneath Mount Huanglong, he encountered an old man coming from the south. He greeted him, asking, "Where is the drum sounding?
The old man replied, "Chan Master Huanglong is preaching the Dharma to the assembly, expounding upon Prajñā. Dongbin asked, "What does this mean?"

"Prajñā," [the Master] said. "One who has thoroughly penetrated this attains complete and clear realization; they suddenly transcend the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and forever abide in the Buddha-way, never falling back into *saṃsāra*.
The guest asked, "What is meant by 'thoroughly penetrating'? The Master replied, "To penetrate in one place is to penetrate in a hundred places and a thousand places.
This is called the wisdom-torch that shatters the darkness, the precious sword that slays the multitude of evils, and the ferry..."
It is the vessel for crossing the sea of suffering and extinguishes the evil realms of the three paths. The six sense-faculties do not exist; the four great elements are fundamentally empty.
One does not feel anger at slander, nor joy at praise. One neither cultivates good nor commits evil. The Way has no inherent substance;
it is named because of the Way. The Way has no inherent name; it is established because of the name. Contemplating all phenomena, one realizes the clarity of the true spirit.

Awakening—this is what is called "penetrating through inquiry. The guest said: "Have you not heard how the Lord of the Mysterious Origin (Laojun) nourishes his manifested body with the profound and subtle spirit?
He cultivates truth and refines his nature to preserve life and perfect the physical frame. Before the mountain forests, he swallows the sun and moon;
beneath the verdant cliffs, he subdues dragons and tigers. Transcending the mundane and entering the sacred, he transforms the yang into the yin, attaining longevity and eternal vision."
This is the Gate of the Method of Feathered Transformation and Ascension. Since the time of Zhongli [Quan], more than a hundred years have passed.

I have nurtured my spirit and sustained my life, so that my longevity is equal to the Root of Heaven. Qingcheng and Zifu are originally my own home; though the mulberry fields change, I remain forever present.
"The sun and moon pass away, yet I live on forever. How wondrous is the Way of the Old Lord! The elder said, "The explanations of you gentlemen each establish their own distinct traditions.
From my humble perspective, however, they do not yet constitute the ultimate perfection. Furthermore, the Great Way has various names;
in the teachings of Śākyamuni it is called Prajñā (Wisdom), and in common parlance it is called the Great Way. Yet it possesses nature while lacking form, and it is transmitted."
Yet it is not bestowed. It possesses form but lacks shape; it cannot be attained and yet can be seen. It is fundamentally rootless, eternally firm and eternally solid.
While heaven and earth have times of formation and destruction, True Awakening has no principle of saṃsāra. It neither increases nor decreases; it is without beginning and without end.
It is not constrained by the three realms, nor is it stained by attachment to the six sense objects. Thus was it first produced.
The Way [of the world] is like a mound or a wasteland; the Way of Prajñā is like Mount Tai. Heaven and earth wind around each other, separated by vast distances.

You, Master, have long practiced the arts of longevity. I have heard that where there is formation, there must be decay; where there is a beginning, there must be an end; where there is pleasure, there must be suffering.
To put it briefly, this is the natural principle of heaven and earth. As for your methods, even if they were to endure—
"Even after ten million kalpas, one will ultimately fall into emptiness and oblivion. The guest said, "If even a disciple is like this, how much more so his teacher?

The old man said, "As for what I have seen, regarding the place of profound mystery, my transformative understanding is not yet complete. I request that you see Huanglong, and only then shall its subtlety be resolved.
The guest asked, "I do not know how it would be. The guest laughed and said, "I fear that Huanglong will not recognize me. The old man said, "It should be so."

To lead one another, they eventually went together to the temple. They arrived just as the Master had ascended the hall to exalt the Dharma for the assembly. The Master already knew that the guest was among those seated below;
he took up the essential theme and said: "The Way has no separate Way; it is only the deluded who establish their own sects. The Gate has no separate Gate..."
Those who are deluded give rise to notions of "self" and "other. Qingsheng Peak and Zifu Palace are the portals through which the Mysterious Origin penetrates and transforms;
Penglai and Niwan are the places where he responds to changes according to circumstances. I fear that the common folk, drifting aimlessly, do not know the fundamental source of the Great Way.
To attempt to use this physical body, subject to the five desires, to falsely claim the arts of the immortals of the Nine Heavens is in vain;

for the dragon is but a beast of the herd, and the crane is but a bird that bears its form. To practice the inhalation of vital energy and swallowing of rosy clouds is ultimately but a heterodox method of this world;
to ingest fire and refine the body are all merely demonic arts for entering the marketplace. Vague and fleeting—how can these be true arts? Deep and obscure...
Alas! What, then, is the true Way? I fear that by seeking the Way through the Way, one may err by even a hair’s breadth and lose it for ten thousand kalpas.
Within the dusty world, the voice of the Tamer (the Buddha) is rarely heard; atop the flowering pillar, do not listen to the words of Lingwei.

He settled the profound mystery beyond the Way; he understood delusive thoughts within the field of the mind. At this moment, when the time for merely controlling cranes had passed, he listened attentively to the teaching of True Emptiness.
When the Master’s discourse reached this point, Lü Dongbin stepped forth from among the assembly and said, "A single grain of millet conceals a world;
within a half-measure of a cauldron, mountains and rivers are boiled. "What is the meaning of this? the Master asked. Dongbin replied, "Within a single grain of millet..."
"Let us set aside the world for a moment. What is it to boil mountains and rivers within a half-measure cooking pot?
The guest withdrew without speaking. The Master said, "You can only boil what is inside the pot; you cannot yet boil what is outside the pot.

He then descended from his meditation seat, clenched his fist firmly, and said, "I will strike you whether you can speak or not. The guest departed in anger. The Master addressed the assembly: [This concludes the entry.]

He returned to the hall for meditative stillness, saying, "Tonight, the flying sword will surely come to take the old monk’s head. When the assembly heard this, they were struck with amazement. The Master sat cross-legged and entered samādhi.
At the third watch, the flying sword indeed arrived, circling about searching for the Master. When the sword reached the front of his seat, the Master let out a single shout;
the sword immediately plunged into the earth. The next day, when Bin came to see the Master, the Master seized him firmly and said, "Within a single grain of millet..."

"The world is hidden within a half-sheng cauldron; mountains and rivers are boiled therein. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! At that moment, Bin broke into a cold sweat and prostrated at the Master’s feet, offering this verse:
"I have trampled the gourd to pieces and broken the zither; The edge of the sword has fallen to the ground—difficult indeed to find."
Now that I have seen Huanglong for the first time, I realize for the first time that all my efforts until now were in vain. Furthermore: An iron ox plows the earth to plant golden coins;
children carve stone figures and string them on threads. Within a single grain of millet lies a world; within a half-measure of a cauldron, mountains and rivers are boiled.
An old man with white whiskers has eyebrows hanging to the ground; a blue-eyed barbarian monk points his finger at heaven. If one wishes to head toward this—
[The Master] said, "He will understand it within. [The Guest] said, "The realm of profound mystery upon profound mystery must itself be even more mysterious.

The Master said, "This is a fine verse, yet there is one character that is not settled. The Guest asked, "I do not know which character. The Master said, "The character 'inner' (內) should be changed to the character 'outer' (外). The Guest then prostrated himself and departed.
When the Imperial Consultant, Duke Wang, was traveling by boat upon the Han River, a violent storm arose. Some suggested it was caused by his carrying rare and precious objects;

he emptied everything in his possession and cast it into the river, yet the wind grew even more fierce. He then cast into the water the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that he had recited throughout his life, whereupon the wind subsided as they reached Zhenjiang.
Behind the boat, an object appeared and disappeared at irregular intervals; when someone was sent to retrieve it, they saw—
Countless snail shells were formed into a single ball. Upon cutting it open for inspection, they were found to be [the remains of] those who had passed away; not even a single hair was damaged.
At that time, this [text] was sought out by the Elder of Mount Jinshan, Chan Master Zhenxie Liao, who carved the woodblocks to print and distribute them.
The Master’s preface states: "The Han River meets the Nine Rivers; reaching Nanxu, the distance spans several thousand *li*. Those who travel back and forth by boat are beyond counting. Unfinished.
Hearing that there was one who held this sutra and had come here from afar, Śaṅkhaśiras saw him and would not let him go.
Was it for fame and profit? Or for wealth and beauty? No; it must have been because he sought to escape saṃsāra and avoid birth and death by means of this [teaching].
Alas! Among all things, only humans are most sentient. Yet among them, there are those who do not hear this sutra throughout their entire lives; or who hear it but do not see it; or who see it but...
They lack faith; though they have faith, they are submerged by fame, profit, wealth, and sensual desire, and thus cannot uphold [the teachings].

Such people are not even equal to the conch-blower (Śaṅkha). Who could be called the most spiritually gifted? Dongbin is the most spiritually gifted among men; he does not merely rank alongside the conch-blower.
Having attained the secret instructions of the divine immortals, he considered himself to have transcended the mundane world and risen above the profane, believing none could surpass him.
Yet, upon first hearing Huanglong expound upon Prajñāpāramitā, he beheld in the Master the majestic bearing of Xiang Wang; subsequently, having come to believe, he submitted in humility.
Did he not offer that which was in perfect accord with Prajñāpāramitā, thereby knowing where to find refuge? Did he not escape saṃsāra and transcend birth and death? Alas!
"Profound, yet even more profound. This is like adding a point to an arrow already fixed in its notch. Nevertheless, even atop a hundred-foot pole, one must continue to advance.

From the end of the Tang dynasty through the Five Dynasties, in the year Bingshen—the third year of Qianning (896)—Ma Yin occupied Hunan, and Qian Liu concurrently governed both Zhejiang and Jiangzhe.
Li Maozhen set fire to the palaces of Chang’an.

Ding-si (the 4th day of the intercalary month), the fourth year [of the Later Liang]: Wang Chao, the leader of the Min army, passed away; his younger brother Wang Shenzhi seized Min and declared himself king.

Wu-wu (1898): The first and second years of the Guanghua era. During these years, Chan Master Xuānwěi of Mount Huá compiled the *Xuánmén Shèngzhòu Jí* (Collection of the Holy Lineage of the Mysterious Gate), arranging the机缘 (karmic conditions and dialogues) of the patriarchs from the Zhenyuan era onward. Xin-you (901): The first year of the Tianfu era.
Jiazi (1st day of the month): In the eighth month of the first year of the Tiānfú era, Emperor Zhāozōng passed away and Emperor Āi ascended the throne.
He reigned for three years, during which time Zhū Wēn was enfeoffed as the Prince of Liáng.
Dingmao (10th day of the month): In the third month of the fourth year of the Tiānfú era, the Emperor abdicated the throne to Zhū Wēn, the Prince of Liáng.
The Ten States of the Five Dynasties and the Usurpers: from the year Dingmao to Jiwu.
Under the Later Liang of the Zhu clan, the capital was first at Bian and later moved to Luo. There were two rulers for a total of seventeen years.
Dingmao: The first year of the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty. Taizu’s original name was Wen; Emperor Xizong of the Tang had bestowed upon him the name Quanzhong.
Upon receiving the abdication from the Tang and ascending the throne, he changed his name to Huang.
Wuchen (568), the second year. He raised an army and once again defeated Zhang Renbao at Yudang; during the battle, his boat was wrecked, and he barely managed to escape by floating on a spear.
His family members offered a meal for a thousand monks as an act of expiation (*Tongjian*).
The King of Min, Wang Shenzhi, previously during the third year of the Tianfu era of the Tang dynasty, invited Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun and Chan Master Xuansha Shibei to enter the inner palace.
The King asked, "What ultimate cause and effect do the Buddhas and Patriarchs cultivate so as to attain Buddhahood?
Xuefeng replied, "One must see one's nature (*xing*) before one can attain Buddhahood. The King asked, "How does one come to see one's nature? Xuefeng said, "Through awakening."
"In an instant, one fails to realize aeons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This matter cannot be pointed out in haste.
Among the hundreds and thousands of people in the mountains who have used this matter in secret for twenty or thirty years, not even one or two has been able to take it up.
How much less could you, Great King, as a secular sovereign with the myriad affairs of state so complex and urgent, ever manage to construct this true Dharma-gate? I pray that you, Great..."
"Your Majesty shall become a sovereign of the Buddha-dharma; with the tip of your brush, you will protect and deliver living beings—is this not a most auspicious thing?
The King was greatly delighted.
At the beginning of the Kaiping era, the King again invited Xuefeng and Xuansha into the palace to seek instruction on the Dharma of the Mind. Xuefeng called out to him:
"Great King, listen with a sincere heart. This illusory, empty body is the Great King’s Dharma-body.
All knowledge and vision are entirely the Great King’s own original nature, the true and heavenly Buddha. Great King, let your mind become like wood or stone; let it become like empty space."
Contemplate that the mind is no-mind; it arises from forgetfulness. When one’s own mind is naturally empty, one immediately awakens to the true mark (*dharmatā*).
The hundreds of thousands of samādhis and wisdoms are all contained within the Great King’s own mind. Now that you, Great King, already know your original nature, let go of everything at once;
do not allow even a hair’s breadth of further conceptualization to arise. This is called the "effortless effort. Such effort is never in vain; this is the path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The Profound Meaning: I pray that Your Majesty shall give rise to a great, expansive vow to maintain this [teaching] and proceed toward Buddhahood.

Suffering within saṃsāra is not easily overcome. The King paid homage to the Master, saying: "Throughout a hundred lifetimes, I have been fortunate enough to encounter such instruction. The Master said to the King: "Simply maintain constant emptiness and stillness in every thought;
this is the great cause for the fruit of daily life. Simply practice giving and extensively perform acts of benefit, making them all aids to the Path."
This is the gateway that does not restrict views of existence or non-existence; all things are sovereign therein, and one cultivates effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).
The King bowed in gratitude and offered twenty bars of gold, but both masters declined to accept it. The King then asked Xuansha, "This single true mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
from where, then, does this present body come? Xuansha replied, "This original source of true nature pervades throughout the sands of the Ganges."
The realms exist because of deluded conceptualization. There is a single point of the nature of consciousness that arises from the false conditions of father and mother;

it then transmits life and undergoes a thousand kinds of suffering. The body undergoes saṃsāra. "Buddha" means awakening. Great King, since you have already known and awakened to this, you will not fall into the evil destinies.
I pray that Your Majesty frequently examine your deluded thoughts, return to the truth, and harmonize with the Way. Thereupon, the Great King prostrated himself and believed.
Having received and practiced [the teaching], King Min entered Wansui Temple. Seeing a Buddha image, he asked National Teacher Yan, "What Buddha is this?
The Master said, "I ask Your Majesty to discern it. The King said, "Discerning is not the Buddha. The Master said, "Then what is it? The King was speechless.
The King of Min invited Chan Master Xian of Luoshan to ascend the seat for the opening of the hall. As soon as he adjusted his robes and looked out, he said, "Take care."
He then descended from his seat. The King took the Master’s hand and said, "How is this assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa any different from today?
The Master replied, "I took it for granted that Your Majesty was but a worldly man."
The King of Min invited Zen Master Mengbi of Jianzhou for a meal. The King asked, "Has the Master brought his brush with him?
The Master replied, "It is not a needle-case from Mount Xi; it is no more than the rabbit-hair pen from within the moon. "Since Your Majesty has deigned to ask," [the Master continued].
The mountain monk dares not fail to present this to you. He asked again, "What is the Dharma King? The Master said, "It is not the style of Mengbi.
The King understood the meaning.
Jisi (1029), the third year of Kaiping. Ma Yin, the Prince of Chu of Hunan, received a memorial from the Daoist Master of Mount Heng requesting a debate on doctrine with the Buddhist monks.
The Prince invited Chan Master Zhian of Yun’gai. When the tea had been finished, the Master borrowed a sword from the Prince;
grasping the sword, he addressed the Daoist Master, saying: "Your own scriptures state: 'Vaguely and indistinctly, within it...'"

"There is a thing. What thing is it? It is profound and obscure; within it there is an essence. What essence is it? If you can speak of it, I shall not strike you; if you cannot speak of it, I shall strike you. Daozheng remained speechless. He bowed and begged for forgiveness. Master An asked the King, "Do you recognize this man? The King said, "I do. An asked, "Who is he? The King said, "Daozheng. An said, "It is not he. His [pupil] struck him. The Master said, "The King has recognized the man. The King was greatly pleased. He bestowed upon Master An the title of *Dachang Daoshi* (Great Chang Dharma Master) and granted him a purple robe. He also conferred upon Daozheng the title of *Changdao Daoshi* (Dharma Master Who Propagates the Way). Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he said to his disciples, "I have lived with you for many years. You must practice the Way diligently and do not forget my instructions. Having spoken thus, he passed away. At that time, the Master was seventy-nine years old. His remains were enshrined at Mount Zhongnan. The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title of *Dajue Daoshi* (Great Awakening Dharma Master). His stupa was named *Jingzhi* (Pure Wisdom). His disciple Huiren succeeded him as the abbot. During the Kaiyuan era, the Emperor changed the name of the monastery to *Zhongnan Shanzhu Si*. In the second year of the Tianbao era, the Emperor further changed its name to *Zhongnan Changuan Si*. This is the origin of the name *Changuan*. The Master’s lineage flourished, and his influence spread throughout the world. His teachings were recorded by his disciple Huiren. They comprise three fascicles. This is the end. There is a thing. What thing is it? It is profound and obscure; within it there is an essence. What essence is it? If you can speak of it, I shall not strike you; if you cannot speak of it, I shall strike you. Daozheng remained speechless. He bowed and begged for forgiveness. Master An asked the King, "Do you recognize this man? The King said, "I do. An asked, "Who is he? The King said, "Daozheng. An said, "It is not he. His [pupil] struck him. The Master said, "The King has recognized the man. The King was greatly pleased. He bestowed upon Master An the title of *Dachang Daoshi* and granted him a purple robe. He also conferred upon Daozheng the title of *Changdao Daoshi*. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he said to his disciples, "I have lived with you for many years. You must practice the Way diligently and do not forget my instructions. Having spoken thus, he passed away. At that time, the Master was seventy-nine years old. His remains were enshrined at Mount Zhongnan. The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title of *Dajue Daoshi*. His stupa was named *Jingzhi*. His disciple Huiren succeeded him as the abbot. During the Kaiyuan era, the Emperor changed the name of the monastery to *Zhongnan Shanzhu Si*. In the second year of the Tianbao era, the Emperor further changed its name to *Zhongnan Changuan Si*. This is the origin of the name *Changuan*. The Master’s lineage flourished, and his influence spread throughout the world. His teachings were recorded by his disciple Huiren. They comprise three fascicles. This is the end.
When the Way is correct and harmonious, even one who has attained the status of a monk is merely a masterless, solitary soul. The King was greatly pleased;
because of this, the practitioners of the Way no longer caused such disturbances. The King frequently summoned Chan Master Qinshan Wensui to the inner palace to inquire about the Dharma.
At the age of twenty-six, while residing in the mountains, he once engaged in a debate on doctrine with a Daoist. The Daoist established his thesis, saying:
"Coarse words and subtle speech alike all return to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). The Master said: "The Daoist is a slave to the Buddha's house.
The Daoist said: "That is too coarse, sir. The Master asked: "Where, then, is the primary meaning? The Daoist was speechless. The King was greatly pleased.
The two kings of Yan and Zhao went to pay their respects to Chan Master Ren of Zhaozhou. The Master sat upright upon his seat and did not rise.
King Yan asked, "Which is more venerable: the King of Men or the Dharma King? Zhaozhou replied, "If he is among men, he is the most venerable among men;
if he is among dharmas, he is the most venerable among dharmas. The king merely acknowledged this with "So be it," and after a long silence, said, "Who is that Great [Person] of Zhenzhou?"

The King said, "Vassal King Zhao, you have consented, saying, 'I am but a disciple. The Master said, 'This old monk has lived in vain within these mountains and rivers, and thus failed to come before your face in person.
The attendants then requested that he preach the Dharma for the King. The Master thereupon expounded the essentials of the Dharma; the two kings praised him and showed even greater reverence."

Gengwu, the fourth year. The dhūta practitioner Weiqin of Mount Nanyue compiled the机缘 (jiyuan—circumstantial dialogues) of the patriarchs from the Guanghua era onward, producing four fascicles titled the *Continuation of the Baolin Tradition* (*Xu Baolin zhuan*).

Ren-shen: The first year of the Qianhua era was established. In the second year, the King of Wuyue, Qian Liu, invited Chan Master Youzhang of Ruiying Temple in Hangzhou to Mount Tiantai to establish a *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) Dharma assembly.
A great gathering of the ordained and laity took place across all the prefectures.
It was not until over a month later that the assembly dispersed.
On the day of Yihai, the first year of the Zhengming era, Chan Master Yun of Shimen (Venerable Sengdaqiqi) was residing at Huangyue when he moved to Jiaoshan;
on his way through Tanzhou, the Prince of Chu, the Ma family, came out of the city to welcome him and immediately asked: "What is the Patriarch?"
The Master [arrived from] the West; this is the Great Way. The Master said, "Good brother! The imperial carriage with its six dragons is a marvel of a thousand ages;
the ceremonial procession lines the jade streets as it emerges from the Golden Gate. The King was greatly delighted and invited him into the Tiance Palace to provide offerings.
Xinsi (the year of Xin-si), the first year of Longde. The Ruler of Shu and the Prince of Wu repeatedly sent letters urging the Prince of Jin to assume the title of Emperor.
Thereupon, he ordered the relevant authorities to purchase jade and manufacture ritual implements. During the destruction of Chang’an by Huang Chao, there was the Great Master Fanzhen of Weizhou.
He obtained the Imperial Heirloom Seal and concealed it for forty years. Upon reaching this point, he transmitted it to Zhen, treating it as his personal jade seal.

Intending to sell it, someone said, "It is the law of the transmission of the state. Zhen went to the Provincial Administration Commission (Xingtai) and presented it; his generals and aides offered their congratulations (*Tongjian*).
Later Tang, the Li clan [ruling under] Xunxu. Capital at Ye, later moved to Luo. Four sovereigns for fourteen years.
Guiwei year, second month of spring: Zhuangzong ascended the throne at Jinyang and changed the era name to Tongguang—this was the third year of Longde.
In the tenth month, he extinguished the Liang dynasty.
Jia-shen (the second year of the Tongguang era). At Mount Wutai, Chenghui claimed he could subjugate the celestial dragons and command them to summon wind and rain.
The Emperor placed his trust in him; the Empress, the imperial consorts, the imperial brothers, and the Crown Prince all paid him homage.

Chenghui sat peacefully in his seat without rising, so that none of the ministers dared not prostrate themselves. During a great drought, the Emperor traveled from the capital of Ye to welcome him there.
In Luoyang, prayers were offered for rain; it fell according to the appointed time, and the officials and commoners gazed upon it morning and evening.
In the third year, on the day of Yiyou, the Emperor visited Huayan Temple and asked Zen Master Hyujeong, "What deity is this?
The Master replied, "A Dharma-protecting deity. The Emperor asked, "Where did you go during the period of the suppression [of Buddhism]? The Master replied, "The heavens sent down rain."
The dew does not distinguish between flourishing and withering. The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon Master Baozhi the title of "National Teacher.
In the year Bingxu, Mingzong ascended the throne and changed the era name to Tiancheng. In the fourth month, Zhuangzong passed away; this was the fourth year of Tongguang.

Gengyin (17th day of the 4th month): The first year of Changxing. In the eleventh month of the fourth year, Emperor Ming passed away. Emperor Min, whose personal name was Conghou, ascended the throne.
Jiawu (2nd day of the 4th month): In the fourth month of that year, Zhuangzong’s adopted son, Prince Lu Congke, arrived with his troops, and Emperor Min fled into exile.
The fifth month. The Prince of Lu ascended the throne and changed the era name to Qingtai (Clear Peace).
On the day of Yiwu, in the second year, the Ruler of Jinling welcomed Chan Master Wenyi of Fayan to inquire about the Dharma.

He resided at Ba'en Temple and was granted the title Chan Master Jinghui (Pure Wisdom). Subsequently, he moved to Qingliang Temple and established the Fayan school. [The Emperor] invited the Master to enter the palace.
In the inner courtyard, [the Emperor] saw peony flowers and requested a poem. The Master said: "Clad in fur robes facing the fragrant clusters, From of old, it has been utterly different."
My hair has turned white from this day; the flowers were red last year. Their brilliance follows the morning dew; their fragrance pursues the evening breeze.
Why wait for them to wither and fall before realizing they are empty? Thereupon, he suddenly awakened to its meaning.
In the tenth month of the third year of the Qingtai era, Shi Jingtang’s troops arrived; the Emperor set himself on fire and died.
In the eleventh month, Jingtang was enthroned, and the state of Tang was extinguished.
Later, the Shi clan of Jin [ruled] with Jingtang as their capital at Bian. Two sovereigns reigned for eleven years.
In the year Bingshen, on the eleventh month, the High Ancestor ascended the throne and changed the era name to Tianfu.

Jihai (1059): The monk Daoduan of Shangzhu Temple saw a brilliant light among the mountains one night. Going to investigate it, he found fragrant wood and commissioned a craftsman to carve an image of Avalokiteśvara.
A white radiance blazed forth, such that at night it eclipsed the light of rows of candles, and by day it obscured the splendor of the great sun.
Once the image was completed, its spiritual efficacy became especially profound. In the year Gengshen of Qianyou (1020), a monk named Congxun beheld it and said: "I..."

While traveling to Luoyang, he obtained a relic of an ancient Buddha. He had treasured it for a long time and now wished to place it within the hair-tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) of the Bodhisattva to assist its divine protection.
The Master complied with his request; thus, the relic remains visible today between the crown and the fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa). (The character "huái" is pronounced "wén.")
Gengzi (the fifth year). King Xi of Min ordained eleven thousand commoners as monks.
In the following year, he constructed a seven-story stone pagoda at Xibu to the south of the city. Before the work was half-finished, a light like a canopy radiated forth for three nights.

Once it was completed, the brilliance shone up to the heavens for another three nights. The King was comforted and delighted; he subsequently issued an imperial edict bestowing the name "Jingguang" (Pure Light) upon it.
Below that, a monastery was established (Changle ji).
In the year Xinchou, Liu Zhiyuan, while still of humble station, was a son-in-law in the household of the Li family in Jinyang. He once tended horses and encroached upon monastic land;

the monk seized him and flogged him. When Zhiyuan arrived in Jinyang, he summoned the monk first, ordered him to sit, and comforted him with kind words before presenting him with gifts and seeing him off.
Especially generous. The hearts of the multitude were greatly delighted (*Tongjian*).
Later, Liu Shi Zhiyuan of the Later Han dynasty ruled from Taiyuan at the beginning of his reign, and subsequently established his capital at Daliang (Kaifeng).
The two rulers together held power for four years.
In the third month of the Dingwei year, Gaozu ascended the throne; he changed his name to Gao and, not forgetting the Jin dynasty, styled it the twelfth year of the Tianfu era.
Wu-shen (17th day): In the first month of the thirteenth year, Emperor Gaozu of the Han dynasty passed away. Emperor Yin was enthroned and changed the era name to Qianguo.
Geng-xu (29th day): In the third year of Qianguo, an envoy was dispatched to Hezhong and Fengxiang to collect the remains of those who had died in battle or perished from starvation and bury them.
At that time, there were twenty thousand monks and nuns gathered there.
The Later Zhou Guo clan; capital at Bian. Three rulers for a total of ten years. [Imperial decree:
On the occasion of the Sacred Festival (Śāstī-pūjā), monasteries were to establish *dharmaparyāya* assemblies (*dharmakṣetra*). (See the preceding "Record of Origins").
Emperor Taizu of the Zhou dynasty ascended the throne in the first month of the *xinhai* year and changed the era name to Guangshun.
The King of Wuyue commanded Chan Master Daoyan of Yongming to enter his palace to receive the Bodhisattva precepts; the master was subsequently bestowed the title Chan Master Dinghui Cihua.
One day, Daoyan wished to request the bronze statues of the Arhats from beneath the pagoda to bring to the new temple for veneration.
The King said, "Excellent. Last night, I dreamed of the sixteen *arhats* requesting to enter the temple with me. How marvelous that the response was so manifest!
He added the two characters "Yingzhen" (Arhat) to the Master’s title. After staying in seclusion for two months, he returned to the mountains.
Gui-chou, the third year [of the Tianfu era]. National Teacher Shao said to the monk Yiji of Wuyue: "The teachings of the Great Master Zhiyi have been distant for many years;
surely they have become widely scattered. Only the Kingdom of Silla possesses excellent original texts. I pray that you, Zen Master, will lend the power of your compassion."

He caused the "Human and Heavenly Eye" (Ren Tian Mu) to be opened once again in the eastern lands. The Master heard of this, and the King dispatched an envoy across the sea to transcribe and bring it back.
That the complete texts are now available throughout Tiantai is due to the efforts of both King Zhongyi and National Teacher Shao.
Furthermore, as Shao happened to share the same surname as Zhiyi, he was suspected of being his later incarnation (from the *Sengshi*).
Jiayin (4th year). Emperor Taizu passed away. Emperor Zizong ascended the throne and changed the era name to Xuande.

The following year, an imperial decree was issued that all monasteries throughout the empire not holding an official imperial plaque (*chier*) were to be merged; in total, more than three thousand such establishments were abolished.

Furthermore, it was decreed that anyone wishing to leave secular life as a monk or nun must obtain the consent of their grandparents, parents, or paternal uncles. This rule applied everywhere except for the two capitals and the region of Damingfu.

The Zhaofu (Bureau of Auspicious Omens) of Qingzhou issued a decree permitting the establishment of ordination platforms (*śīlā-sthāpana*). It prohibited both monastics and laypeople from practicing self-immolation, severing hands or feet, burning fingers as incense wicks, or wearing objects such as tongs;
these were deemed deceptive practices that delude the common people (*Tongjian*).
Yimao (the second year). An imperial edict was issued to the commanderies and kingdoms: "Each year, registers of the *saṃgha* shall be compiled.
Those who die or return to lay life shall be removed from the rolls as they occur. In this year, there were 2,700 temples remaining; 30,300 had been abolished (*Tongjian*).

The *Shiwu ji yuan* records that on the tenth day of the eighth month in the seventeenth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Minghuang, an edict was issued stating that monks and nuns should follow the ten [precepts].
The six-year-old register (*liùnián jiùjí*)—the system for providing official accounts for monks and nuns—originated from this. Furthermore, the *Sēngshǐ lüè* (Abridged History of the Sangha) states:

In the first month of the fourth year of the Tàihé era of Emperor Wénzōng of the Táng dynasty, the Cíbù (Ministry of Sacrifices) requested that the names of all monks and nuns throughout the empire be submitted to the provincial government so as to rely upon them for enrollment.
The creation of these registers began with the Tàihé era.

Bingchen (the third year of the Tianfu era): There was a monk named Ren. When [Zhou] Xingfeng became the Military Commissioner (Jiedushi), he trusted him and entrusted him with all matters of the military administration;
Ren was also granted the title of *jianjiao Sikong*. He maintained a household and his retinue followed him in and out as if he were a sovereign (*Tongjian*).

In the seventh month of autumn, the Emperor [considered that] because the government had not minted coinage for a long time, people in the private sector were melting down currency to make vessels and utensils.
Buddha images were [to be] increasingly reduced in number. In the ninth month, a supervising office was established to collect copper and cast coins.

With the exception of official items belonging to state and county officials, ritual objects for military use, and bells, stone chimes, cymbals, and gongs used in temples and monasteries—which were permitted to be retained—all other copper vessels and Buddha images held by the private sector were ordered to be surrendered to the government within fifty days;
their value was to be paid back. After this period, those who concealed them or failed to surrender them [were subject to punishment].
For those weighing five jin or more, the punishment is death; for those falling short of that, the sentencing shall vary accordingly. The Emperor said to his attendants:
"You ministers should not harbor doubts regarding the disparagement of the Buddha. Furthermore, the Buddha regarded the physical body as illusory and prioritized benefiting sentient beings.
Had his true body still been present, if it were to benefit the world, he would have wished to cut it into pieces to give as alms—how much more so in this case?"
Bronze statue. "If my own person could save the people, it would not be a matter of regret. Thereupon, the ministers did not dare to speak further.
The Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Image in Zhenzhou was extremely efficacious; the scholars and citizens of the prefecture wished to replace it with money.
The Emperor forbade it; as he was about to cut open [the statue’s] chest, the efforts of the multitude all failed at the wrists, and thus the work was halted halfway.
At that time, the śramaṇa Famin, whose earnest remonstrances were not accepted, composed the *Xianyan lun* (Treatise on Manifested Evidences) [recorded in the *Beishan lu*].

Jiwei (16 July 649), the sixth year. Emperor Shizu launched a northern expedition. A carbuncle broke out on his chest, and in the sixth month of summer, he passed away en route at the age of thirty-nine.
At that time, Emperor Gong, Zongxun, ascended the throne; he was only seven years old.
Gengshen: The first month of the seventh year of Xiande. Emperor Gong abdicated the throne to Zhao Kuangyin, the Commander-in-Chief;
he was the Taizu of the Song dynasty.
According to Yang Wengong’s *Tanyuan*, in the third year of Xiande, all bronze statues were destroyed to cast coins. Emperor Shizong addressed the Chancellor:
It was said: "In Buddhism, one sacrifices even one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain for the benefit of sentient beings without any sense of regret;
how much less would one cherish a bronze image? Song Taizu and Taizong witnessed this matter with their own eyes, and through it, they gained further faith in the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, at the beginning of their reigns, they restored Buddhist temples throughout the empire" (from the *Wai Zhuan* of Ou-yang Gong).
Yan Bing’s poem says: "The teachings first arrived during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han; In the Yongping era, the *utpala* flower blossomed from within the flames.

The frost-bell gradually reached through the three realms; The Brahma-temples slowly spread across the nine heavens. Though the Three Wu emperors suppressed the monks, the Sangha was not extinguished;

Though one Han dynasty sought to destroy the Buddha, the Buddha was not destroyed. If the Dharma-gate possessed no spiritual efficacy, It would surely have been reduced to a single heap of ashes in the Middle Kingdom."

Liu Xu, who served as Minister of Works (Sikong) and Chief Councilor (Pingchangshi), compiled the *Jiushi Tangshu* (Old History of the Tang), in which he recorded various extraordinary accounts of the Buddhas and patriarchs.

When Ouyang Xiu compiled the *Tangshu* (New History of the Tang) during the Song dynasty, he deleted them all. Subsequently, when Sima Guang compiled the *Zizhi Tongjian* (Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government), the accounts of the Buddhas and patriarchs were likewise omitted.
That which would have assisted in the transformation of the state was entirely excised and not preserved; this too is a one-sided view.
Yet it alone stands out prominently within the classics, illuminating and being transmitted to the world—how can this be considered insufficient? (General Discussion)
The Śramaṇa Dàolín of Tánzhōu submitted this commentary upon his journey to Dàyuán Prefecture to seek out the Tripitaka. The eminent scholar Lǐ Jié presented him with a preface in which he said:
"Those who practice the Confucian Way take pleasure in disparaging the followers of Śākyamuni. Their arguments invariably state:
'In the eras of Yù, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Kǒngfǔ, there were no followers of Śākyamuni. Since the followers of Śākyamuni arose during periods of decline and chaos, they ought to be abolished.'"
To prevent it from flourishing—such is the argument of the critics, which is superficial. They may know that it is so, but they do not yet know why it is so. Let me explain.
Once there was a man whose skin was plump and his complexion radiant; his vital energy was vigorous and his spirit clear.
He never sought out physicians nor ever prayed to spirits; he maintained a state of tranquil harmony and was free from any affliction of disease or calamity.
This is certainly good. Suppose a man is unfortunate enough to suffer from ailments caused by cold, heat, wind, or dampness;
then the techniques of acupuncture and moxibustion are employed, and the rituals of exorcism and propitiation proliferate. Are these two cases merely opposites?
It is simply that the conditions of being ill and not being ill differ in their circumstances. Alas! Before the Three Dynasties, the world was peaceful. The virtues of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu—
The Duke of Zhou and Confucius propagated its principles and maintained its teachings through the classics. Although the influence of the Way has declined, its gradual purification still persists.
Deceit does not overcome sincerity; the wicked know to avoid the good. During the final ages of the Three Dynasties, the world was afflicted by illness:

the influence of the Way declined greatly, deceit overturned sincerity, the good withdrew in mildness, and the evil employed force. Superiors and subordinates became mutual enemies, inciting a climate of resentment. Thus it was with the followers of Śākyamuni.
Their teaching takes purity and emptiness as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and gentleness and humility as forbearance (*kṣānti*); thus, resentment can be brought to rest.
It takes frugality and diligent toil as spiritual practice (*pratipatti*) and poverty or prosperity, longevity or early death, as cause and effect (*hetu-phala*);
thus, the lowly and the humble can find peace. Therefore, it is said: "Only through afflictions does one perceive the Buddha-nature. This is fundamentally the custom of a declining age.
This is to stimulate [the reader]. Now, as for the customs of a degenerate age, there is nothing at all that brings joy.
If it were not for the followers of Śākyamuni to rescue them from this, where else could one entrust one’s heart?

To argue that one does not blame the customs of a degenerate age, yet singles out the rise of Śākyamuni’s followers for criticism, is like a man suffering from illness who blames his physician for administering acupuncture, moxibustion, and medicinal treatment; he knows only of the Śākyamuni followers...
They arise because of the decline of an era, yet they do not realize that such decline requires the salvation of the Śākya school. Why is this so?

For when the world is already afflicted and its people are already distressed, were it not for the Śākya school to allow them to find peace in their own lot, the brave would stir up their spirits and think of fighting, while the wise would settle their minds and think of plotting;
thus, the commoners of the roads and fields would become a chaotic and swarming multitude.
It has arisen! Now, as for this single thread of the Śākya clan, no burden is imposed upon others; therefore, men of worth, wisdom, and brilliant clarity all direct their hearts toward it.
Those who cannot reach this understanding are fools; they are merely those who serve at the behest of others and thus remain subject to the customs of turmoil.
It is by relying on this that one may attain peace. As for the minor expenses of carving, engraving, and colorful painting—my [attitude toward them is such].

Therefore it is said: "One can know that such is the case, yet not know why it is so. During the final years of the Huichang era, Emperor Wuzong carried out a great suppression of the Śākyamuni [Buddhist] teachings;

the monasteries throughout the empire were demolished as if swept away. At the beginning of the new reign, the Son of Heaven established his title and proclaimed that the Śākyamuni teachings must not be abolished, issuing an edict to restore them.
Alas! I have already spoken of how the Śākyamuni teachings assist the world; had it not been for this...
"Your Majesty has clearly discerned the source of principle; how could you possibly re-establish it?
The Layman Huang Tingjian of the Mountain Valley said: "The dharma of the śramaṇa does not concern itself with the means of livelihood.

He begs for food until satisfied, accepts offerings at midday, and does not lodge overnight in forests. Thus, Zhaozhou used broken firewood to mend his meditation seat and sat in tranquil contemplation."
Thirty years ago, when I was at Yaoshan, he would wrap his belly with bamboo strips and follow the rule: "If one does not work for a day, one shall not eat.
Now, you destroy the property of a hundred commoner households to build a single dwelling, and provide the food of ten farming families to feed a single monk—is this not excessive?
Those who do not plow dwell in leisure while consuming jade-like delicacies; such people now constantly number in the thousands wherever they go. This is...

Because of the confiscations during the Huichang era, the imperial passion for architecture and engineering reached its limit; areas once home to dragons, elephants, tigers, and leopards were transformed into gilded and vermilion structures.
Consequently, there was the total destruction during the Guangming era—how can this not be forgotten? The presiding monk Xingying said:
"Indeed, the decrees of the Huichang and Guangming eras did nothing more than to depopulate the monasteries, burn their scriptures, and demolish their dwellings."
The palaces and towers of Vairocana fill the ten directions; they make no distinctions among any realms.
How could they ever occupy my dwelling? There is a great scripture, as vast as a trichiliocosm, hidden within a single mote of dust.
How could they ever burn my book? Herein there is no self and no person; there is no Buddha and no sentient beings.

"How could he possibly be among us? Tingjian said, "This superior man is a visiting guest within the Tathāgatagarbha and a wandering knight-errant within the ranks of the Bodhisattvas" (Record of the Kaiyuan Repairs).
The Mirror for Buddhist Benefactors Through Successive Dynasties, Volume Eight:

From the Great Tang through the Five Dynasties. Fierce sages and virtuous ministers, men of the age who exercised broad influence, cultivated their hearts of giving and diligently practiced the pure karma.

The texts of the Śrīvijaya (Baiye) tradition were fully and perfectly expounded and compiled into the Great Canon; the intent of the "Plucking of the Flower" was transmitted secretly and directly, establishing the Five Schools.
Lecture halls were spread out like chess pieces, and meditation seats were arrayed like stars—how could one have expected the upheaval of the Huichang era?
Suddenly, the campaigns against the Wei and Song were undertaken. Relying on the return of spring to the Buddhist gardens, the halls were filled with the fragrance of famous incense;

the teachings of the Elephant Vehicle flourished, and the sacred rites were compiled and established. Lands as vast as the瀚海 (Hanshai) and Tian-shan mountains all came under imperial jurisdiction, while the regions of the Dragon Court and Phoenix Nest were brought into submission.

All have been moistened by the sound of his teachings. The high officials and monastics who protect the Dharma and support the school are all like the dragon and the qilin of the Nala Garden, or the cypress and the elm of Jeta’s Grove.
I have mistakenly recorded them here following the movement of my brush; how could such a narrow view through a tube ever encompass them all?
There must surely be men of heroic spirit and outstanding character whose style transcends their peers; may they expand upon this account to illuminate future generations.
*Zhishi zajian* (A Mirror for Buddhist Aid through Successive Dynasties), Scroll Nine,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Xizhong of Yifeng, Min, during the Song Dynasty.
Part One.
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty was surnamed Zhao and named Kuangyin. He was the second son of Emperor Xuanzu.

In the second year of the Tiānchéng era of Emperor Mingzong of the Later Táng, the year of Dīnghài, he was born in the Jiámǎ Camp at Luóyáng. A divine light filled the room, and an extraordinary fragrance did not dissipate for an entire night.
Upon reaching adulthood, he entered Luóyáng and went to the southwest corner of the Great Buddha Hall at Yánshòu Monastery, where he rested his head upon a pillar base during the day.
While he was sleeping, a monk saw a red snake enter his nostril. Upon waking, the monk asked where [the snake] had gone.
It replied, "I wished to go to Shanzhou to see Minister Chai, but lacked the means. The monk said, "I have a donkey you may ride, and I shall also offer you money and silk.
Thereupon, they set out. As soon as Minister Chai saw him, he regarded him as extraordinary. Before long, Minister Chai became the Son of Heaven; this was the founding of the Zhou dynasty.
Regarding King Sejong: both he and King Sunjo served him. When Sejong took command of the imperial guards, he performed many great deeds.
One day, Sejong found a slip of paper among some documents that was over three feet long, upon which was inscribed: "The Commander-in-Chief shall become the Son of Heaven.
At that time, Zhang Yongde was serving as the Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Guards; Sejong consequently ordered Taizu to replace him. Taizu—
The Patriarch studied under Xin Wenyue. Wenyue also had a dream in which he invited the Emperor’s carriage.
When Shizu passed away and the young heir was still an infant, Taizu secretly harbored intentions of being enthroned.

On the first day of the first month of the seventh year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, the garrisons of Zhending reported that Liu Jun of Hedong had allied with barbarian tribes to launch an invasion. Emperor Gong then commanded Taizu—
The Northern Expedition. That very day, they departed from Aijing Gate and arrived at Chenqiao Station in the evening. Among the troops was Miao Xun, who was knowledgeable in astrology;
he brought Chu Zhao Fu to gaze upward at the sun’s color and point it out. They saw that beneath the sun there appeared another sun, with black light swirling and clashing for a long time.
Miao Xun said, "This is the mandate of Heaven. At the fifth watch that night, all the armies had assembled and said, "We..."

Having endured the frost and dew, he has exerted his strength for the sake of the state; yet, with no sovereign above him, who will reward his merit when his task is accomplished? It would be better to appoint me as Emperor.
At dawn, blades crossed in a chaotic melee as they gradually pressed toward the imperial quarters. Taizong entered and reported the matter; Taizu started up in alarm.
The military officers stood in the courtyard with blades bared, saying, "The various armies have no lord; we pray that you will appoint [the Prince of Jin] as Emperor."
The Grand Marshal was made Emperor by the Son of Heaven. Before Taizu had even had time to respond, the yellow robe was suddenly placed upon his person.

The various generals bowed in a circle and repeatedly cried out "Ten Thousand Years! They then escorted him onto a horse and forced him southward back to the capital. Entering through the Renhe Gate, he returned to the official residence.
Prime Minister Fan Zhi and others proceeded to Chongyuan Hall and summoned the civil and military officials; by the hour of Bu (the late afternoon), the ranks were settled. Respectfully...
The Emperor personally issued an edict from within the palace. The Director of the Xuanhui Bureau escorted Taizu to the Dragon Steps to receive his instructions.

Once the audience was concluded, the Chancellor assisted him in ascending the hall. He donned the imperial robes and performed the rites of abdication and succession. The assembled ministers offered their congratulations.

An edict was issued changing the seventh year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty to the first year of Jianlong. The state name was changed to Song. This was on the fifth day of the first month of the Gengshen year, a Yisi day. The Emperor—

He reigned for sixteen years before passing the throne to his younger brother, Emperor Taizong, who outshone the achievements of his predecessors. As sage after sage succeeded one another, they maintained and fortified the Buddha-Dharma;

thus the Five Lamps (Wǔdēng) became linked in their fragrant renown, and the monasteries consequently gained increased prestige. Alas, after seven successions, the reign reached that of Emperor Huí of the Miào Dynasty.
Although he was a most sagacious and supreme sovereign, he became deluded by the heterodox doctrines of the Left Way, leading to the events of the Jìngkāng era’s Bǐng year.
The calamity of the Wuhuan rebellion brought misfortune upon the common people. The Jurchen swept through the capital, and the two imperial palaces and their consorts were taken north on a hunt.

Emperor Kang, solitary as a single shadow, crossed the Yangtze River. Four generals secretly provided support and guarded him closely. On the day Dingwei, he changed the era name to Jianyan and established his capital at Wulin; this was the reign of Gaozong.
His wish for the restoration of the realm had not yet been fulfilled, and the life-vein of the state hung by a thread, though the steps of Heaven—though perilous—[remained].

Amidst the extreme hardships of military campaigns, and while kings and ministers galloped between the clash of blades and arrows, they were still able to turn their attention to the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), engaging in discourse and debate.
The famous monasteries of the Two Zhe regions stand as the crowning glory of the rivers and lakes;

the heavenly rains have nourished the grasses and trees, and their lingering influence persists even to this day. Prior to the founding of the Song dynasty, there were nine successive rulers, followed by seven more.
In total, there were sixteen sovereigns who reigned for three hundred and seventeen years; these are recorded as the history of the Southern and Northern Dynasties.
When Emperor Yihuang first visited Xiangguo Temple, he went to the Buddha hall and, after burning incense before the image, asked the Chief Monk (Senglù) Zanning whether one should prostrate or not.
The Chief Monk replied that one should not prostrate. When asked the reason, he said: "One does not prostrate before a present Buddha; one prostrates before the Buddhas of the past."
The Buddha smiled and nodded his head. Wen Zhonggong Ou Yangxiu said: "The monk-recorder Zanning was quite well-versed in books;
however, it happened that he coincided with the Emperor's inclinations, which is why he was treated with such courtesy" (*Gui Tian Lu*).
When the Song was about to rise, Li Houzhu of Jiangnan suddenly saw a deity appear atop the city wall.

Its head was as large as a chariot wheel, its forehead bore a divine pearl, and it held a golden stupa in its hands. Soldiers and civilians all witnessed this, and after several days, the deity vanished.
Subsequently, an imperial edict was issued for all prefectures and counties to establish Tianwang Temples (Nanshi).

In the Kingdom of Jiangnan, it was the custom for monks to undergo examinations on their mastery of the scriptures. The disciples of Chan Master Guizong Quan were all practicing meditation and contemplation;
the Master then composed a verse and presented it to the Prefect, saying: "To compare [the mind] with forgetting the self is to merge with the Great Void;

It spares us from having intimacy or estrangement within the harmonious breath. Who would have known that virtue has no use at all? Today, being a monk, one values the ability to read and write. At that time, the Prefect reviewed [the verse].

He deliberated with his subordinates and said: "In a sandalwood forest, there must be no other kinds of wood. Only the Master’s single cloister shall be exempt from the scriptural examination on the Nine Banners."
Wuchen (the first year of the Kaibao era): The Kingdom of Koryŏ submitted a memorial, having heard of the fame of Chan Master Yanshou of Mingzhao Monastery.
They dispatched monks to inquire after the Way and paid him the respects due to a disciple. They presented gifts including a golden-threaded *kāṣāya*, crystal prayer beads, and a golden water flask.
Furthermore, they commissioned thirty monks to paint a map of China and sent them back in succession to receive the Dharma.
Each country transforms its own region. Its ruler, Yu Hui, regularly read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and vowed to be reborn in the Central Kingdom.
One night, he dreamed that he arrived in China; the territories he traversed were exactly as depicted in maps. Upon waking, he composed a verse, saying:
"Due to the causes and conditions of evil karma, I am now near the Khitans. For one year, how many varieties of tribute have been offered? In a dream, I suddenly reached the land of China."
Borrowing from the lines "Midnight, as the water-drops of the watch leak away" (from the *Biannian*).
In the year Yihai, Emperor Taizong ascended the throne.
In the first year of Taiping Xingguo, the year Bingzi, he visited Kai bao Temple to burn incense. There he saw a monk reading a scripture. The Emperor...
The Emperor asked, "What sutra are you reading? The monk replied, "The *Benevolent Kings Sutra for Protecting the State*. The Emperor said, "Since this is my own sutra, why is it in your hands?
The monk was speechless. Xuedou Xian provided this substitute response: "The August Heaven has no partiality; it assists only virtue.
When the Emperor saw the monk coming to court, he asked, "Where have you come from? The monk reported, "I have been parted from Vulture Peak ever since that day until now."
The Emperor asked, "What proof do you have? The monk remained silent. Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "This poor monk has come specifically for this purpose.
Because Master Ji had presented a diagram of the three realms to the Emperor, the Emperor asked, "In which realm do I reside? Master Ji had no reply. Baoning Yong spoke on his behalf:
"Your Majesty, where would you not be honored as Sovereign? One day, the Emperor held up his alms bowl and asked Prime Minister Wang:
Suizhi: "Since this is that which cannot be lifted at the head of Mount Dayu, why is it in your hands, O寡人 (Oligarch)?
Suizhi was speechless. Shishuang spoke on his behalf: "Your Majesty possesses power. The Emperor once dreamed of a divine being who requested that Your Majesty give rise to the *bodhicitta*.
At court the following morning, he questioned his attendants: "How does one give rise to the *bodhicitta*? Xuedou spoke on his behalf: [silence].
Truly, this is something rarely heard of in antiquity or the present.

In the fifth year of the Jihao cycle, the Monastic Registrar Zanning compiled the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) in ten fascicles and presented it to the throne; by imperial decree, it was included in the Buddhist canon.
Zan Ning continued to serve as a compiler in the Historiography Bureau. He reached the age of eighty-four. At that time, Wang Chune was also in the bureau;

he was well-versed in astrology and calendrical science. When Wang calculated Zan Ning’s destiny, he found that according to the Sanming, Qinlüe, Liuren, and Dunjia systems, none of them indicated longevity or nobility.
Wang Chune said to Ning, "When you were born, the Tiangui star was precisely positioned at your gate; you must surely be a man of heroic integrity."
When Marquis Wang was at the tomb, Ning said: "Do not speak of the time he was alive.
When King Wenmu Yuan Gan went to Lin’an County to pay respects at the grave, it began to rain upon reaching the gate.
He took shelter under the eaves for a very long time before bathing the infant swaddled in silk embroidery and departing (*Wanhuagu*).
Qian Liu once memorialized that the true-body relic stupa of Śākyamuni was located in Mingzhou;
it was constructed by King Aśoka, and of the eighty-four thousand stupas [he built], this was one-nineteenth of them. Emperor Taizong then ordered that the relics be taken [to the capital].
Offered within the Imperial Palace, the Emperor composed this hymn of praise for the Buddha’s tooth relic: Accomplished through myriad kalpas, the seal-patterns are exquisite;

had it not been from the Southern Mountain, it would likely have been difficult to find. Beholding it with my own eyes, its multiple layers glisten with golden luster; held in my hands, a single fragment radiates a jade-like cold brilliance.

Refined through a hundred fires, its spiritual essence penetrates through; concealed for a thousand years, its radiant color remains perfect. It must surely be the fruit of cultivation through the profound secrets of the True Path. The Righteous... [text ends]
"Do not regard this with indifference. He then vacated the grounds of Kaibō-ji Temple to construct an eleven-story pagoda to enshrine it (from the *Yang Wengong Tanyuan*).
The Emperor once said to his attendants, "In my previous lives, I have personally attended upon the Buddha’s seat;
it is only because I do not possess the knowledge of past lives that I am unable to see this clearly. (Same as above) One day, the Emperor visited the pagoda at Kai Bao Si to burn incense.
Seeing a monk there, he asked, "Who are you? The monk replied, "I am the keeper of the pagoda. The Emperor said, "Why do you act as the keeper of my pagoda?"
The Master remained silent. Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "The entire nation knows.
In the year *xinsi* (1041), there were three foreign monks—Faxian, Fatian, and Shihu—who arrived from the Western Regions.

Emperor Taizong, having received a Buddhist prophecy, subsequently established the Translation Institute (*Yijingyuan*). He recruited fifty youths and ordered them to study and learn [the scriptures]. From Jiangnan...
Li Wang’s son, Weijing, possessed such profound insight that he was able to master the texts of India.
From the Jin through the Tang dynasties, whenever Indian monks arrived from the Five Indies, they would collaborate with Chinese scholars proficient in Indic phonology to produce translations.

By the Kaiyuan era, the total number of translated scriptures, vinayas, śāstras, and collections amounted to five thousand forty-eight fascicles. The *Guochao Huiyao* (Imperial Court Compendium) records that during the Taiping Xingguo era:
In the sixth month of the seventh year, the Xin-si year, the Translation Institute was completed. In the seventh month of autumn, the Imperial Carriage visited the Translation Institute.

An edict was issued for the monks specializing in Sanskrit studies to receive the oral translations and compose the written text, while the monks of the Left and Right Quarters of the Monastic Order were charged with detailed revision.

In the twelfth month, one śramaṇa specializing in Sanskrit studies was selected to serve as the *bishou* (scribe/recipient), and ten śramaṇas specializing in doctrinal studies (*yixue*) were appointed as *zhengyi* (proofreaders of the meaning). Thereafter, by...
Weijing served as the scribe for the *Fanxue* (Brahmanic Studies). During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, the śramaṇa Yanzong was appointed as a scholar of the Translation Institute;
it was from this point onward that monks were first granted official titles.

In the Tang dynasty, Amoghavajra was appointed as a Minister of the Household with the same rank as a Grand Master of Ceremonies, acting as the Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, and was also conferred the title of Chao-san Dafu; the scribes for these works were drawn from among the court officials. Buddhatāra...
Luo translated the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), with Fang Rong serving as the scribe. For the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fang Rong likewise served in that capacity.

In the fourth year of the Yongxi era of Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty, Faxian was promoted by examination to the rank of Palace Steward (*Guānglù qīng*) and the title of Court Dispersing Grandee (*Cháosàn dàfū*).

Fatian was repeatedly appointed to the rank of Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (*Hónglù qīng*) and was additionally granted the title of Court Dispersing Grandee. Weijing was the son of Congjian, the younger brother of the former ruler of Wu, Li Yu.

He served as the scribe for the translation of the *Brahma-śikṣā*. During the Xiangfu era of the Dazhong period, he participated in the translation of scriptures and was appointed as a Provisional Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Shiguanglu Qing*).
(Note: During the reign of Taizu, the monk Yuandai was also granted the rank of Chao Sandafu; *Shiwu Jiyuan*.)

The Emperor composed a preface to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which states in brief: "I lament that the karma of non-cultivation is so vast; I grieve over the foolishness of those who cling stubbornly to their views.
This is not something for inferior men to perform, nor can it be fathomed by those of shallow understanding. How great are the words of the Sage!
They are profoundly worthy of trust and submission... (and so forth).

Prime Minister Lü Gongzheng was a native of Luoyang. During his humble years, his circumstances were precarious and desolate. For a full month, heavy snow fell incessantly, and he visited every prominent and wealthy family, yet few showed him any compassion for his urgent need.
He composed a poem, saying: "Ten times I knock at vermilion gates, nine times they remain closed;

Covered in wind and snow, I return once more. Entering the door, I am too weary to look upon my wife and children’s faces; I stir the cold hearth, but find only ashes throughout the night. On his way...

On the way, he encountered a monk who took pity on his distress and invited him back to the monastery. The monk provided him with food and clothing, and gave him some coinage. Within a single month, it was all exhausted.
When Lü visited him again, the monk said, "This is not a long-term plan. You should move your household to the corridors of the temple and receive food from the community;
this can serve as a long-term plan. Lü followed these words. No longer constrained by the lack of food and clothing, he subsequently became resolute.
Zhixing submitted his name to the official register. That year, he passed the provincial examination. The monk provided funds for travel and clothing, escorting him to the capital.
During the metropolitan examination, he was selected for the palace examination and announced as the grand champion (*da kuai*). He was initially appointed as the Vice Prefect of the Western Capital.

When he met with the monk, it was as if nothing had changed. Ten years later, he was appointed to the executive branch; whenever he encountered imperial sacrifices, his stipends were all sent to the monk’s quarters. One day, the Emperor asked: [text fragment]
The Emperor asked, "Your Excellency has participated in numerous suburban sacrifices; why have you not requested your salary? He replied, "I have private debts of gratitude that I have yet to repay.

The Emperor pressed him for the truth, and he answered accordingly. The Emperor said, "Is there such a person among the monks? He then bestowed upon him the purple robe and the title of *Shi* (Master) to honor his extraordinary merit.
Every morning at dawn, Lord Lü would rise and pay homage to the Buddha, praying to Heaven: "Those who do not believe in the Triple Gem..."
"May you be born into my family. May your descendants, generation after generation, receive stipends at court.
In the year Wuxu, Emperor Zhenzong ascended the throne and changed the reign title to Xianping. The Palace Secretary Wang Yuni submitted a memorial outlining five matters.
First: To purge and refine the monks and nuns might cause alarm; therefore, let us temporarily suspend the ordination of people and the construction of temples for one or two decades.
This will allow their numbers to naturally diminish over time, which is also one way to remedy existing abuses (*Yanxinglu*).
In the second year [of the Tianxi era], State Councilor Chen Shu, Duke Jin, had long been a non-believer in Buddhism and held its followers in low esteem.
He frequently urged the abolition of the Translation Institute with words of great vehemence. Zhenzong replied, "The flourishing of the Three Teachings has occurred for a very long time;
there have been many instances of their destruction in previous dynasties. We shall simply preserve them and refrain from further discussion."
Jiǎchén (the year 1004), the first year of the Jīngdé era:

The monk Dàoyuán of Eastern Wú compiled the records of the karmic conditions of the patriarchs from the Kaipíng era onward, together with the *Bǎolín zhì* and the *Shèngzhòu zhì*, into thirty fascicles titled the *Chuándēng lù*. He presented it to the imperial court.
The Emperor reviewed this and praised it highly, ordering Yang Yi and others of the Hanlin Academy to edit and correct it for inclusion in the canon and distribution throughout the realm.
In the second year, Princess of Chenguó was enfeoffed as the Princess of Wú in the eighth month; she entered Zíshèng Temple to become a nun.
He was titled the Great Master of Compassionate Wisdom and Enlightenment (Cien Zhengjue Dashi) and granted the name Qingyu. A separate Chongzhen Monastery was constructed for him to reside in.

On the day he received full ordination, an imperial edict was issued to all monasteries throughout the realm, ordering each to grant one person the privilege of entering the monastic order (*Shiwu Jiyuan*, as previously cited).
Wu-shen (the 9th year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era), autumn, the seventh month. Flying locusts covered the sky. The Emperor visited the Pagoda of Kaiyuan Temple to offer prayers for its removal;
his petition was efficacious. He composed an imperial eulogy, which reads: "In the West dwells a Sage, Śākyamuni, Who bestows compassion upon all beings and is honored by the world.
I constantly vow to advance in cultivation and increase wondrous fruits, Hoping thereby to bring abundant benefit to the common people."
The above is the Preface to the *Śālistambha-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teachings). Now, the Way is not remote; the human teachings fundamentally have no fixed categories.
Although the forms of wriggling creatures differ from one another, their nature of eternal bliss is the same. It is due to the entanglement of craving and desire that the cycle of rebirth increases.
For this reason, the Sage of Kapilavastu appeared in the world and extended his compassion to the region of Śrāvastī, expounding the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.
The Dharma enables all sentient beings to be fully delivered; it follows worldly ways to lead them back to the Truth.

Thus, between the twin trees, he universally addressed the assembly of the Mahāyāna, demonstrating what the five faculties should be cautioned against and resolving doubts concerning the Four Noble Truths.

He sought to proclaim the profound mysteries of the Dharma so that the minds of the multitude might become firm and steadfast. Such is the ultimate expression of Great Compassion. I, the Emperor, reverently succeed [to his legacy].

Qingji, with a sense of shame regarding my meager virtue, have always followed the instructions of my predecessors, hoping thereby to guide others toward the secret exegesis. Having read this sutra, I have constantly cherished it with reverence;
desiring that it be circulated for the benefit of others, I have thus composed these annotations. Although my ignorance makes it difficult to achieve perfection, I have endeavored to do so.
By fortunate grace, I have been able to complete this through diligent study; it is now further ordered to be engraved upon wooden printing blocks.
My hope is that it may be transmitted to all states, so that all within the human community may strive to turn toward it in unison. (Based on the preceding chronological compilation.)

The Emperor wished to establish Lady Zhangxian as Empress but had not yet reached a decision. He summoned the ascetic Lou Daozhe of Lianshui to enter the inner palace and ordered the consorts and ladies-in-waiting to come forth to see him.
The Master examined them, numbering about two hundred in total, yet none spoke a word. When he came to Lady Zhangxian, he suddenly said, "Your Majesty should treat this person well.
The Emperor marveled at this, and his intention was finally settled. [Lady] Zhangxian Ming-su Liu became Empress Dowager. Completed.
Du Ren followed his father down the Gorges as a youth and arrived at Yuquan Temple. There was an elder there skilled in physiognomy who said to his father, "You are a man of noble destiny.
