Upon seeing Du Ren, he was greatly astonished and said, "Your nobility lies in this very person. Why do you not proceed to the capital?
He presented him with one hundred taels of white silver. When they reached the capital, the Emperor was presiding over the Southern Capital and had recently taken a consort into the palace.

Upon her accession to the throne, she was first made a *cairen* (talented lady), then promoted to *Chenfei* (Imperial Consort), and finally attained the rank of Empress (*Zhengwei*). Her reputation throughout the palace filled the world.
When Renzong ascended the throne, the Empress Dowager presided from behind the curtained screen. The former Elder of Yüquan had already been residing at Changlu in Yizhen;

she summoned him to the capital, and upon his arrival, he remarked that Changlu lacked a triple-gate entrance (*sammén*). The Empress Dowager then commissioned the construction of it using the vessels and furnishings from her own palace.

Meeting him at such a time, his nobility may well be known. While the Empress Dowager presided from behind the curtain, she bestowed upon him immeasurable gifts (as recorded in the *Mianxiu Wanhuagu*).
In the *Renxu* year, Renzong ascended the throne.

Guihai (the tenth day of the tenth month): The first year of the Tiānshèng era was inaugurated. Early in the summer, Yang Ji, the Governor of Ningzhou, presented embroidered Buddha images for the Emperor’s longevity on the occasion of the Qiányuán Festival.
The Emperor praised the *Lotus Sūtra*, saying: "Boundless wondrous meanings are extensively contained within it;
Sixty thousand words or more, bound in seven scrolls. From between his white jade teeth flow śarīras; Upon his red lotus tongue, rays of light are emitted. His throat..."

The sweet nectar within flows gently, moistening all; the *amṛta* within the mouth cools drop by drop. Even if the sins one has committed were as heavy as mountains, they can be extinguished by just two or three lines of the wondrous Dharma.
In the twelfth month of the first year of the Tiānshèng era, the regions of Dìngxíng, Dài, Bìng, and Xīn in the capital experienced earthquakes.

The Emperor proceeded to the Dàqìng Hall to assemble monks and Daoist priests for vegetarian feasts and incantations to pray for divine protection. Mán Qí, the Right Attendant Censor, submitted a memorial stating:

"The Dàqìng Hall is the principal residence of the state and the ceremonial palace of the court. It is not appropriate for Your Majesty to enter it except when performing major rites or wearing the ritual robes."
Consequently, [the Emperor] has never presided over the court, and the ministers have been unable to appear before the courtyard except during major imperial audiences.

How can it be permitted for ordinary monks and Daoists to disturb the space above him day after day and month after month? This is not what is meant by the "correct Dharma" or the "dignity and majesty of the sovereign.
Furthermore, it was said: "Previously, when the twin pavilions of Xingguo Monastery were destroyed by fire, the flames extended to the ancestral halls."

In less than a few moments, nothing remained but lingering embers. Your Majesty ought to straighten your robes to seek forthright counsel and adjust your posture to seek the rectification of state affairs.

To instead initiate internal sacrifices and incantations within the palace quarters and monasteries is like walking backward while seeking to move forward, or trying to stop a boiling cauldron by removing the hot water from beneath it;
the futility of such actions is clearly evident. [The Emperor] did not accept [the advice]. — From the *Zhishi Guan* (Office of the Rectifier of History).
Ye Qingchen submitted a memorial, stating in brief: "Now that calamitous portents have arisen repeatedly, Your Majesty remains complacent and does not regard them as extraordinary.
You merely employ eunuchs to travel throughout the four quarters to perform Buddhist rites and Daoist rituals; this is not what is meant by the actual practice of averting disaster.
(From the *Song Biannian*).
In the sixth month of summer, the sixth year of the Tiānshèng era, a star fell in the southwest, as large as a bushel and sounding like thunder.
At that time, the subordinate prefectures were also suffering from drought, and prayers for rain were being held at Wéndé Palace. Censor Lǐ Zuò submitted a memorial stating:
"Wéndé Palace is the hall where the Son of Heaven proclaims his governance. Whenever unusual portents occur, it is customary to command the monastics to chant hymns within its precincts."
"It was not for the purpose of decorating the outer court" (same source).
Jisi, the seventh year [of the Tianxi era]: Li Zunxue, the Commandant, compiled the *Tiansheng Guangdeng Lu* in thirty fascicles and presented it for imperial inspection.
The Emperor personally composed a preface and issued an edict for its inclusion in the Imperial Canon (same source).

Wu-yin (the year 1038): The first year of the Baoyuan era. In the sixth month of the second year, Zong Qi, who concurrently served as Record Keeper of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, submitted a memorial, which stated in brief:
"At present, there are three redundancies and three wasteful expenditures. The number of monks and Daoists increases daily without any fixed limit;

furthermore, they separately construct shrines for deities and vie with one another in repairing temples and pagodas—these are the redundancies. To provide tents and canopies is called 'making offerings,' and to hold land and property is called..."

The constant holding of *daochang* (sites of enlightenment) vegetarian feasts and incantation rituals occurs almost every day; this is a source of expenditure. Yet, they neither levy corvée labor nor draft forced service, sitting idly while enjoying the reputation of hosting these feasts, all claiming:
"This does not cost the state treasury; it uses only the people's own wealth. This is truly the height of insolence and subversion of authority.
Now, the people are the foundation of the state, and the state is the foundation of the people. Wealth does not come from Heaven, but emerges from the Earth. As for labor, it is not...
To employ ghosts while using humans for labor, and to abandon the state to seize the people—this is a single great injury [to the Way]. (From the *Dongdu Shilüe*).

In the first and second years of the Qingli era, the year of Xinsi, locusts and floods occurred in succession. The Emperor took responsibility for these misfortunes by blaming himself and prayed to the Buddha for blessings and protection.

Tian Kuang, the Director of the Bureau of Imperial Edicts, submitted a memorial, the gist of which stated: "The cause of the disasters lies in the heavy burden of corvée labor and taxation, and the suffering of the people..."

I am filled with sorrow and resentment that Your Majesty has not yet consulted with the high ministers of the two councils on how to remedy this situation, but instead intends to appease the divine retribution by offering a single incense burner and a few prayers at the spirit tablets. This is why I cannot help but speak.

In the ninth month of the autumn of that year, Zhang Dexiang was appointed to oversee the compilation of the National History (*Guoshi*), concurrently serving as the Director for Polishing Texts at the Translation Institute (*Yijingyuan*). (Mao)

Qī was appointed as an official for refining the language of translated scriptures. From then on, the refinement of translated scriptures became included in the titles of officials from the provincial governments downward.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Qǐnglì era (4701), the Śarīra stupa at Kāibō Monastery was destroyed by fire.

The Emperor dispatched a high-ranking eunuch to retrieve the Śarīra relics and bring them into the inner court for veneration. There were many wondrous and supernatural manifestations; the princes and dukes of the entire capital [gathered to witness this].

Noble persons came to pay their respects and vied with one another to offer gold and silk, restoring it once again. The Emperor composed a hymn of praise, saying: "The Three Sovereigns concealed their substance and all returned to the earth;
The Five Emperors hid their forms and likewise became dust. The Master [Confucius] was revered as a sage within the realm;

The Lord Lao [Laozi] was also spoken of as true upon this world. When the body is buried, one sees only an empty tomb left behind; Where can one manifest the person to show it to future generations? Only..."
"The bone-relics of our Master remain; having undergone a hundred refinements, their color remains ever new. Yu Jing, the sole起居注 (Director of the Court Annals), submitted a memorial stating:
"The divination of the Five Elements is fundamentally concerned with calamities and transformations; one ought to respond to the will of Heaven with caution and fear.

Yet I have heard that an imperial decree has been issued to retrieve the previously interred *śarīra* relics and bring them into the inner palace. Rumors are circulating along the roads that these *śarīra* are now within the inner court."
This is a strange anomaly. I fear that those who are artful and sycophantic will promote this as a supernatural marvel and seek to rebuild it once again.

Your servant has heard that the way of emperors and kings is such that if they can be diligent and frugal, their virtue will win the hearts of the people; thus, even in the face of peril and difficulty, they will surely find peace and salvation in the end.

Since military operations were launched on the western frontier, the state treasury has been exhausted and the accumulated wealth of the officers and commoners has vanished in nine out of ten households.

If Your Majesty does not take pity on the suffering of the people but instead extensively pursues frivolous expenditures to serve the Buddha in pursuit of blessings, this is not what the world expects.
As for the claim that the śarīra was not destroyed when subjected to fire, it must have originally been within the earth, such that the fire could not reach it. If one says of the śarīra...
To claim that it can emit strange lights and that there must surely be a divine spirit inhabiting it is a false statement.

Furthermore, if a single stupa cannot even protect itself and was destroyed by fire, how much less could it rely on its own merit to provide protection for the people? In the past, when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty built the Changgan Stupa, the śarīra relics within it also frequently emitted light;
yet when Taicheng fell, how could it have brought about any blessing? This is especially true in the case of a foreigner.
The military academies all called for Śāri to enter the palace; such inauspicious words were particularly loathsome (the above is from the *Biannian*).
The Emperor bestowed the *mornie* robe offered by Goryeo upon Chan Master Yuan of Yunju. Su Shi of the Hanlin Academy composed a eulogy for it, the gist of which states:
"If it is kept in its case, one sees the robe but not the Master; if it is worn and not in the case..."
One sees the Master but does not see the patch-robed monk; yet the patch-robed monk and the Master are neither one nor two.
To gaze at them with profound vision, they are like lice and nits, or dragons and elephants [as inscribed on the stone at Jinshan].
Jichou (1049), the first year of the Huangyou era. When the Emperor heard the name of Chan Master Nan, he issued an edict for him to reside at Jingyin Monastery.
Nan pleaded illness and did not dare accept the summons. An imperial decree was issued ordering him to recommend someone to take his place; he consequently recommended Huailian.

Some said, "The Sage Emperor honors and exalts virtue and morality, sending an envoy with a letter so that the grace extends even to the springs and rocks. Why does the Master so firmly decline? The Master replied, "I have occupied this position unworthily."
As for the monastic community, my hearing and sight are not acute; I am fortunate to dwell in peace beneath the forest trees, eating vegetables and drinking water.
Even Buddhas and patriarchs have things they would not do, let alone others. As the sages of old said, "It is difficult to dwell long under a great name.

Throughout my life, I have practiced the principle of contentment and have not burdened myself with fame or reputation. If the heart feels weary [of worldly affairs], when will it ever be satisfied? (The Right Dharma)
*Yanzang* (The Eye Treasury). Dongpo said: "To know contentment is honor; to know sufficiency is wealth. To avoid fame is to preserve one's integrity;
to begin well and end well—this was attained by Master Ne. (The master’s name was Ju-ne, courtesy name Zhong-min; son of the Qian family of Zhongjiang, Zizhou. *Baojun*.)
On the nineteenth day of the second month of the second year, Chan Master Huailian arrived at the capital.

After the midday meal was concluded in the Huacheng Hall, an imperial edict was proclaimed, ordering him to expound the Dharma according to the ritual protocols of the South. Qingman, the Great Master Ciyun and Director of the Left Street of Monks, was commissioned to offer the formal invocation and express gratitude.
Having finished his speech, he recited this verse: "The spring returns to the Imperial Garden; The Royal Assembly is convened. Since the Ten-Thousand-Wagon Sovereign has arrived, like Shun..."

Your Majesty, the two monastic communities have had the honor of serving at Your Majesty’s brow. Now that this is a day of gentle warmth, it is precisely the occasion for the proclamation [of the Dharma].

It is fitting to discuss the ancestral path so as to accord with Your Majesty’s sincere intent. I respectfully submit this. Lian then ascended the seat. After the exchange of questions and answers was concluded, he said:

"Before the hall of the ancient Buddhas, there has never been any divergent teaching; yet within the circulating phrases, there are indeed many discourses. Those who attain them possess wondrous function."
There is no deficiency. Those who lose this find themselves obstructed at every turn. Thus, by streams and mountains, clouds and moon, the same breeze blows everywhere;

by waterfowl and forest trees, the Way is manifested at every point. If one enters the gate of Kāśyapa, it is as if the wind of Yao sweeps vast and clear, and the sun of Shun shines with lofty brilliance.
The village elders sing their praises and the fishermen dance for joy. At such a time, there is pure delight in non-action.

Huìzhào replied, "How could I have known such a thing would happen? The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict appointing him as the abbot of Jingyin Chan Temple in Shifang, granting him the title Chan Master Dàjué.
The compiled manuscript of Master Sun Juehua’s letter to his late teacher states: "From the Three Dynasties onwards, successive sages have inherited one another;

government has been effective and people harmonious, and the lineage of the Way has continued without interruption. It was not because Buddhism had not yet arrived that [the era] was deemed deficient.

From the end of the Zhou and the rise of the Ji through the changes from Qin to Han, the legal nets and penal systems covered the skies and spread across the wilds; it was not because Buddhism had already arrived that these were abolished. 4.
The "Sea-claw Division" (Hǎizhuǎofēn) produced heterodox doctrines with rapid emergence; this was most extreme from the Tang dynasty through the Five Dynasties period.

Amidst myriad affairs and the ten thousand mechanisms of governance, where order and chaos were never constant, what benefit could the Buddhist teachings possibly provide? Occasionally there were those who wore grass garments, ate only wood-fruits, dwelt in crags, and drank from mountain streams, yet these did no more than pursue their own solitary perfection.

Furthermore, there were those with reputations but deviant conduct, whose pretenses were false and not genuine; thus, the transformative influence of the teachings had not yet been realized, and the decline continued.
"Has it not arisen? The Master must surely have a way to distinguish this; we await his explanation. The Master replied:

"The meaning of the wondrous Way was entrusted by the Sages to the *Yi* (Book of Changes). During the decline of the Zhou, the laws of the former kings were destroyed and rites and righteousness daily perished.

Thereupon, eccentric words and heterodox arts emerged sporadically to confound the common people. When our Śākyamuni’s teaching entered the Middle Kingdom, it was purely based on the primary truth (*paramārtha*)."
To manifest this to people, one establishes compassion from beginning to end for the sake of transforming sentient beings; this is also a means of responding to the times.
Since the birth of the human race, when the primal simplicity had not yet dispersed, the teachings of the Three Sovereigns were concise and plain—this was the Spring.

As the apertures of emotion were daily excavated, the teachings of the Five Emperors became detailed and ornate—this was the Summer. As times and the world changed, emotions shifted accordingly, and the teachings of the Three Kings became more intricate.
And yet it is solemn. In antiquity, when the Shang and Zhou dynasties issued their proclamations and oaths, later scholars found them difficult to understand;

yet the people of those times listened to them without dissent—how did their customs differ from those of today? When these traditions fell into decay, reaching the Qin and Han eras, there was no depravity to which they did not descend;
there were things in the world that one could hardly bear to hear. Our Buddha, however, unified all by means of the nature of life and death.

The principle is this: they teach through the practice of compassion. Just as Heaven has four seasons revolving in succession to generate and sustain all things, so too the teachings of the sages support one another to transform the world.
Yet when these reach their ultimate limit, none can avoid falling into decline;
such is the inevitable trace of decay. The Way, however, is but one. It is essential that sages and worthies arise from time to time to rescue it.
...and so forth. From the Han dynasty until the present, more than a thousand years have passed.

Social customs have become increasingly decadent, and those who follow the ranks of the Sages have split into three schools, each contending with the others and denigrating one another, not knowing which path to follow. The Great Way lies desolate, and none know how to return to the truth.
This is truly lamentable.
The Third Year of the Huangyou Era of the Great Song, the year of Xinmao. It has been one thousand years since Śākyamuni Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa.
On the ninth day of the twelfth month of the fourth year, an imperial messenger was dispatched to deliver a message from the Emperor to Chan Master Liàn of Jingyin, saying: "Cái..."

Qu Jian brushed aside the people who had raised objections and stood firm. Just as Liai was about to join the assembly for the morning gruel, Qu rose to express his gratitude and presented a verse, saying:
"Not bamboo, yet possessing joints; Three stars encircle the lunar palace. One person dwells beneath the sun;
He does not share the lot of the common folk. The Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased. He engaged in a dialogue with Master Liai, and the verses were transcribed and bestowed upon him. All...
Seventeen Chapters. ○ Master Hualiang of Huayan remarked: "The verse 'The mind itself is Buddha' is like driving a wedge into empty space.
Nevertheless, when Master Liaoyuan responded to the Imperial inquiry, he did so in accordance with the occasion;
likewise, when responding in the Forbidden Grove and discussing Chan in the Secret Palace, Master Liaoyuan’s words were also profoundly significant (Linjian Lu).
Lian submitted a memorial offering a verse, requesting to retire to the mountain forests. The Emperor said, "The mountains are the very substance of *tathatā* (suchness);

where would you go? He did not grant the request, saying: "The green mountains are the substance of *prajñā* and *tathatā*; where would the Imperial Verses be taken?"; he then bestowed upon him a camphor bowl.
Lian took it to the envoy and burned it, saying: "Our Dharma uses dyed robes and earthenware [bowls]."
He ate from his bowl. This bowl was not in accordance with the Dharma. When the messenger returned and reported this, the Emperor praised him highly.
Emperor Renzong and Chan Master Lian shared in the joy of the Dharma through many exchanges of poetic verses. However, they all followed the Emperor’s own words;
he did not dare to venture forth any novel or profound expressions. Yet, when one examines what he composed in his daily life, it is as follows:
There are many startling phrases [in his work]. The world’s suspicion that he was gambling with "pottery as stakes" (va-zhu) is incorrect.

Formerly, during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, Bao Mingyuan served as a Secretariat Drafter (Zhongshu Sheren). Emperor Wen was fond of literature and considered himself beyond compare.

Mingyuan perceived this intent; therefore, he frequently employed vulgar expressions in his writings. The world’s claim that his talent was exhausted is indeed true. He greatly realized the duality of body and world.
Wang Fei remarked, "Mingyuan served his sovereign with profound devotion; yet Renzong realized the subtleties of the Way and treated literary compositions as so much spit and saliva.
This [work] by no means resembles the prose of the Song dynasty. However, I know that Lia’s wisdom was deep, and such was the method he had to employ to respond to the world.
(From *Línjiān Lù*; the Master was a son of the Chen family of Qīngwéi.)
Jia-wu, the first year of the Zhihe era. The Emperor dreamed that he had arrived at the gate of Jingde Temple and saw a dragon coiled upon the ground.

He immediately dispatched someone to investigate it, only to find it was merely a monk sleeping soundly. When asked the monk’s name, the messenger returned to report it. The Emperor reviewed the report and found the name was Daolong.

King Hui remarked, “This is an auspicious omen. The following day, he summoned him to the inner palace (beonjeom) and inquired about the essential tenets of his school. The monk’s responses were as swift and clear as echoes following sounds, which greatly pleased the King.
He was lodged at Daesangguk-sa Temple. The King exchanged verses with him, and such communications flowed incessantly along the roads.

On some occasions, he entered the royal presence and stayed overnight within the imperial precincts; the honors accorded to him were exceptionally generous. The King bestowed upon him the title of State-Commissioned Master Mingwu (Ŭngje Myeong-o Daesi). The King summoned Yong...

He engaged in dialogue with Yuanlin, whose sharpness of wit was swift and incisive. The Emperor was delighted. Daoleng immediately submitted a memorial, saying: "I am originally a commoner, mingling my tracks among the marketplace.
Through the influence of the Buddha-dharma, I have had the fortune to draw near to Your Majesty’s countenance. Entering and leaving the imperial court, I have received most profound grace."

As the years have passed in succession, my ailments and infirmities have persisted. My body has not yet retired to the mountain forests, as I remain here greedily basking in the imperial grace like a dewdrop or rain.

Having allowed matters to drift to this point, shame and guilt fill my face. I reverently consider that Your Majesty, endowed by Heaven with sagely divinity, possesses innate knowledge of the wondrous Way.

Dyeing my brush with elegant phrasing, I shall let it shine like the sun, illuminating and adorning the myriad things below. That I, your humble servant, have been granted the honor of composing a response in rhyme is a privilege I have barely begun to grasp, like mist upon the peaks;
I have only caught a glimpse of its full scope. Though others may remain silent, how could I, your servant, fail to reflect upon this?

I have recently observed the monk Huailian, who has recently been summoned from the mountain retreats to the capital; his discourse captures the very source of the tradition, and his phrasing stands preeminent among his peers. The Imperial Prohibition... [text ends]
Attendant Lin asked, "In discussing Chan within the secret palace, Your Majesty is beyond my capability. I venture to recommend myself as Your Majesty's successor.
I humbly beseech Your Sacred Compassion to permit me to recuperate from my illness and await my end at a small monastery on Mount Lu; I am overwhelmed by my deep affection for the imperial carriage.

When this memorial was submitted, it was not granted. An imperial decree was issued stating that a vihāra should be constructed north of the Cao Gate for him to reside in, and it was bestowed with the name "Huayan" (Flower Adornment).

At Yanchansi, once the Master had retired from his duties, he was joyful to behold their countenances. Among those who frequented him in his secluded dwelling were particularly extraordinary monastics and renowned scholars.
Monk Long would sleep outside the temple gate at night and ascend the heights of the secret palace by dawn;

there he would pay his respects to the sovereign and discourse on the supramundane Dharma, providing benefit to both the teachings and the state. He was truly one of those possessed of extraordinary abilities who could transform the world.
What an extraordinary patch-robed monk! Even after his passing, his name was heard throughout the monastic communities, let alone his karmic encounters and recorded sayings.
One cannot help but sigh deeply at this (from the *Sengbao zhuan*).
Bingshen (the third year of the Jiayou era). In the third year, as the succession to the throne had not yet been established, the Emperor burned incense and prayed in silence at night.
The following day, he prepared a vegetarian feast in Huacheng Hall and reverently invited the divine monk, the Great Being Fahua, to descend from the heavens; however, the Master declined.

At dawn, the Emperor donned his ceremonial robes and stood solemnly waiting. Suddenly, a messenger arrived with a report stating that Fahua was proceeding directly toward the palace from the Right Aisle Gate, accompanied by attendants.
Weihézhì replied, "It cannot be. The Emperor smiled and said, "I have invited him here for this very purpose. After a short while, he arrived.
The Emperor said, "Because the succession has not yet been established, the high ministers all speak of it. Fahua must decide this matter once and for all. The Master requested paper and a brush.
He wrote thirteen or fourteen lines in succession and then threw down his brush without further words; none could fathom his intent.
Later, when Emperor Yingzong ascended the throne, it was revealed that he was the thirteenth son of Prince An-yi of Pu, thereby verifying the former prediction (from the *Monk Biographies*).
Shen Guogong Yijian asked Master Lü, "Today we offer prayers for the Emperor; what should we discuss?

The Master bowed deeply with palms joined and said, "Ten thousand years! Ten thousand years! Ten thousand ten thousand years! The Duke had previously participated in the drafting of the fundraising petitions, and this was after the vegetarian feast had concluded.
The Duke asked about the future fortunes of his officials. [The Master] took up his brush and wrote the two characters "Bozhou" (Maozhou) in large script.

Later, when the Duke was dismissed from office and learned that he himself would govern Bozhou, he searched through his travel bags and suddenly found those two characters before him; only then did he realize it was a prior sign of recognition.
Shi Qisong, styled Qianzi, was of the Li clan of Tanjin in Tengzhou. He was a devoted friend of Ou Yanggu (later known as Wenzhong Gong) of Yuzhang.

At a time when Wenzhong Gong had authored the *Benlun* (Discourse on the Origin) and Li Taibo had written the *Qianshu* (Book of Qian) to refute Buddhism, the Master composed the *Yuanjiao lun* (Treatise on the Source of the Teachings) in one hundred thousand words to clarify the single thread that unifies Confucianism and Buddhism.

He also annotated the *Chanzong dingxiang tu* (Illustrations of the Fixed Phases of the Chan School) and wrote the *Chuandfa zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage of the Transmission of the Dharma).

In the "Chapter on Protecting the Teachings," he cites the Buddha’s five precepts and correlates them with the Confucian Five Constants, explaining away their criticisms as follows: not killing is benevolence; not stealing is righteousness;
not committing sexual misconduct is propriety; not drinking intoxicants is wisdom; and not engaging in false speech is faith. He further explains the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) as follows:

Regarding "not killing": it means not to violently harm even a single thing for no reason; it does not mean merely abstaining from eating its meat. Regarding "not stealing": it means not to take what is not rightfully one's own;
it does not mean merely abstaining from pilfering a single object. Regarding "not engaging in sexual misconduct": it means not to disrupt the union of a couple.
One who refrains from false speech does not deceive others with words. One who refrains from intoxicants does not allow drunkenness to disturb their cultivation of the mind.

One who refrains from frivolous speech does not embellish erroneous words to delude the multitude. One who refrains from divisive speech does not engage in contentious talk with others behind their backs.
One who refrains from harsh speech does not revile others nor speak of unrighteous matters. One who refrains from envy is without...
Envy and jealousy originate in one's thoughts. To be "without anger" means not harboring resentment or hatred in the heart.
To be "without delusion" means not being ignorant of the causes of good and evil. By cultivating the first five [precepts], one is endowed with the capacity to become a human being;
by cultivating all ten together, the reward is rebirth in heaven. If the people of the world were each to cultivate these accordingly, every person would achieve perfection.
"Good! If every person were good, yet the world were not well-governed, such a thing has never occurred. Someone said: 'The Buddha speaks only of "nature" (xing).

Since nature is easily understood, it is the same as what is spoken of in the *Zhongyong*. What need is there for the Buddha? The Master replied: 'The Buddha’s discourse on nature is identical to that in the secular books;
this shows that the Sage shares the same nature as the world. When people widely attain this commonality, they will broaden their practice of the Way.'"

In virtue, we share a sincere heart; in discipline, we share the observance of fasting and purification; in merit, we share the dedication of our goodness to others, so as to bring blessings upon our parents and support our sovereign in bringing peace to the world.

Could it be deemed a cause for concern for the Middle Kingdom? Once the work was completed, he traveled to the capital, where he presented it to Lord Wang Su, the Dragon Diagram (Longtu) official serving as Governor of Kaifeng.
Upon reading it, Emperor Renzong sighed with admiration and entrusted it to the Translation Court (Chuanyufa).

The collection was compiled and entered into the Imperial Canon. Prime Minister Han Qi and State Councilor Ou Xiu read his writings and praised them effusively, saying, "Is there such a youth among the monks?
They issued an imperial edict to honor him, granting him a purple robe and bestowing upon him the title of Great Master Mingjiao.
Later, Wang Su of the Hanlin Academy composed the *Fujiao pian* (Treatise on Assisting the Teachings) for Shi Qisong and submitted it to Emperor Renzong as a memorial.

In brief: Your servant has personally devoted himself to the teachings of Śākyamuni. Having examined their deletions, additions, commentaries, and sub-commentaries, this is not mere speculative discourse;

rather, the treatises are both profound and subtle. May Your Majesty, in the leisure between the myriad affairs of state, find deep delight in the Dharma. I humbly request that you deign to examine them;

if there is anything worthy of adoption, I pray that an order be issued for the Secretariat to scrutinize them in detail and that they be specially included in the Tripitaka. (From the *Sengbao zhuan*).
Gui-mao (the tenth day of the twelfth lunar month): On the *xinhai* day of the ninth month of the seventh year, a great sacrifice was held in the Mingtang. The imperial amnesty decree stated:

"To all temples and monasteries throughout the empire that have not yet been granted official names, special titles shall be bestowed. The censor Sima Guang submitted a memorial, stating: "I humbly submit that the teachings of Buddhism and Daoism offer no benefit to the governance of the world;
rather, they gather and harbor the idle and the indolent, thereby wasting and harming the virtuous people. For this reason, the State has made its regulations explicit..."
The Imperial Decree states: "If anyone constructs even a single chamber of a temple or nunnery, they shall be permitted to report it;

they shall be penalized according to the 'Leftover Edict' (Yizhi) and the structure shall be demolished. Your servant has heard that those who occupy the position of sovereign wash their hearts clean and attend to the people with singleness of purpose;

thus, when commands are issued, prohibitions are enforced, and none dare not to comply. Yet now, you establish laws to forbid such acts beforehand, while subsequently issuing amnesties to encourage them. This is contradictory.
Regarding all the commands of the state, how shall the people know where to follow them? As for the single provision concerning pardons, I beg that it be no longer implemented.
This will ensure that edicts are trusted by the people, so that the idle and lazy cannot engage in misconduct. (From the *Song Bianian*).

Jiachen (the year 1064): Emperor Yingzong ascended the throne and changed the era name to Zhìpíng. Three years later, Chan Master Huailian submitted a memorial requesting to return to the mountain forests, stating:
"Your servant has heard that the Great Way is non-action, yet within it all things find their response;

when the Sage rules with leniency, the common people attain the fulfillment of their lives. How much more so now, at this dawn of prosperity and harmony, may one enjoy the principle of ease and security. Looking up..."

Jin Yu-yun has humbly assembled with trepidation. Your servant Huai-lian reflects that since the years past, by the mistaken favor of the late Emperor, he was granted the honor of succeeding to the ancestral seat;
he has been especially bathed in the imperial grace. Though many seasons have passed, he has not forgotten his humble origins in the mountains and marshes.

I have repeatedly requested to retire from office, yet I have not received a reply. Now that Your Majesty has ascended the throne and the whole world turns toward your virtuous influence, I wish to propagate the Buddha’s teachings to repay the benevolence of a Yao-like sovereign.
Alas, in my declining years I am increasingly frail, and my long-standing ailments have grown more severe.
Yesterday, I relinquished my various duties and retired to reside at the temple. I have humbly received Your Majesty’s gracious decree, dispatching an envoy to escort me back to the temple;

yet, by imperial command, I am further instructed to remain in the Divine Capital for the time being. Reflecting upon this, I consider myself a body of no utility, yet I have truly been granted an extraordinary encounter.

This is the virtue of Heaven and Earth granting me a second life, while I, a mere weed of the fields, offer my heart in gratitude for such profound flourishing. I pray that Your Sacred Compassion will descend like rain upon me.
The grace of Your Majesty is as impartial as the illumination of the sun and moon. You have humbly conformed to human desires and graciously acceded to my humble wishes.

It is my hope that this decrepit and dull form may finally fulfill its aspiration for the forest and the springs. Yet, though this lowly insect has achieved its purpose, it truly lacks the spirit of Yi Shui.

The emaciated horse increases its neighing, giving rise only to thoughts of longing for the imperial carriage. I vow to diligently engage in incense-burning and recitation to repay the grace of my birth and upbringing.

As I am about to depart for the Imperial Court, I cannot bear the intensity of my gaze toward Heaven and my longing for the Sage; my agitation and trepidation reach their utmost limit. I respectfully submit this memorial to take my leave, along with the previously requested eulogy on returning home:

"A thousand clusters of cloud-mountains, ten thousand valleys of flowing streams" (Imperial Note: "The Dharma is widely practiced; it does not merely consist of channels and valleys"). My idle body desires—

I grow old upon this peak (one must examine this with great care; it is not merely a matter of this peak). I pray for boundless longevity in my remaining lives (may all the stars share the same lifespan as Heaven).

A single incense stick of pure fragrance fills the stone pavilion (pervading the entire Dharma-realm, where all is at ease and extinguished). After the Emperor finished reading the petition, he bestowed upon him a written edict, saying:

Chan Master Huailian of Dajue Temple has enjoyed the sacred favor of the late Emperor, to whom he was repeatedly granted divine edicts and who frequently received his expressions of reverent sincerity.

He has now requested to retire to the forest hermitages; we grant his petition so that he may fulfill his desire for leisure. Whenever he passes through minor monasteries, he may reside there according to his inclination;
however, he must not be compelled to stay at major Chan monasteries. Once Master Lian has crossed the river, he shall remain briefly at Mount Jinshan.
Hu went to Siming and composed a memorial for Jiufeng Qian. He was then appointed to reside at Yuwang Monastery.

The people of Siming collectively contributed funds to construct a pavilion to house the imperial poems and verses he had been granted; it was titled "Chen Kui" (Imperial Calligraphy). They commissioned Su Shi, the Hanlin Academician, to write a record for it.
At that time, the Baowen Pavilion was being constructed in the capital, and by imperial decree, a copy was taken to be stored there. [At that time,] Yuan Tong of Mount Lu...
Upon first meeting Lia, Master Nü expected him to be a vessel of great capacity. Someone asked, "How did you know this? He replied, "This man is central and upright, leaning toward neither extreme;
his demeanor is dignified whether in motion or stillness. Furthermore, he possesses the virtues of a scholar and a man of integrity, and his speech is concise yet exhaustive in its principle."
Ordinary people endowed with such natural capacities rarely fail to become accomplished vessels (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
In the first month of the fourth year of Dingwei, he granted names for temples and observatories built privately. The imperial edict stated:

"As for the temples and observatories previously built privately by the common people, those numbering more than thirty rooms shall all be preserved; I grant them the name 'Shengshou' as their official title" (Bian nian).
When Zhang Yongde lived in Suizhou, there was a scholar living next door who was bedridden with illness. Zhang treated him and restored his health.

[The scholar] possessed a method for placing mercury together with medicinal herbs inside a crucible, whereby it would immediately turn into gold. As they were about to part, Yongde requested the secret technique, but [the scholar] said, "It must not be."
"I am not stingy," [the monk] said. "I fear it might shorten your lifespan. Yongde, keep this. Yongde took his leave, saying, "I shall see you again on the banks of the Huai River.
Later, when Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty was campaigning at Shouchun, Yongde followed him there. While out hunting, he encountered a monk who was the same scholar he had met before.
The monk said to Yongde, "If you see two people whose birth sign is the Pig, serve them well; they shall ensure your prosperity for fifty years."
Noble. Later, he encountered Taizu and Taizong, both of whom were born in the year of the Pig (*hai*).

(*Dongdu shilüe*) Qian Ruoshui said of himself: "When I first went to take the imperial examinations, I paid my respects to Master Chen Bo. As I was about to leave, he invited me to return ten days later.

When the appointed time arrived, I went there respectfully; he welcomed me into his mountain study. A brazier had already been prepared, and he was sitting with a monk, both wrapped in coarse woolen cloaks."

As he sat, I greeted him with the customary rites of inquiry regarding his health and well-being; yet he was exceedingly haughty and aloof. I was young and full of vigor, feeling quite indignant at this treatment.
The monk stared intently at Ruoshui for a long while without speaking, then used his fire-tongs to write three characters—“cannot be done” (zuò bù dé)—into the ashes, yet he did not explain them.
The following day, I visited Chen again and asked the monk’s name as well as what he had said. Chen replied, “Ma.”

The Daoist was one who embodied the Way. His practice of the Way was lofty and pure, and his learning reached both heaven and man. In particular, regarding the discernment of people, he possessed a profound insight characteristic of a divine immortal.
You wished to remain and study the Way, yet your mind remained undecided; you therefore requested the Daoist to resolve your doubts.

He replied, "You lack the skeletal constitution for a divine immortal, but you shall obtain a high office. It is simply that you must courageously withdraw from the midst of the turbulent current. (From the *Yanshi Jiaxun*)
When Prime Minister Wang Wenzheng Gong Dan was young, he served in the History Library together with Qian Ruoshui.
There was a monk skilled in physiognomy who said to Ruoshui, "The Gentleman Wang will one day reach the pinnacle of officialdom; his nobility shall be beyond compare.
Ruoshui asked, "The Gentleman Wang’s face is asymmetrical and his throat-bone is prominent; how can he be so noble? The monk replied, "After he becomes a Chancellor, his face—"

He should have rectified himself. His jawbone was prominent, his ears were thin, and his physical appearance was austere. On the day he attained the rank of *xiang* (high official), his character became full and tranquil, and his desires few;
he maintained an extremely frugal lifestyle. He passed away in the ninth month of the first year of the Tianxi era. The Emperor attended his funeral.
While ill in bed, the Duke had people shave his head and don monastic robes, likely out of remorse for his former conduct as a layman (*bian nian*).

Duke Zhanghui Wang Sui was a native of Heyang. Outwardly he appeared stern and formal, yet his governance was often characterized by excessive leniency. By nature, he admired the character of Pei Xiu of the Tang dynasty.
Serving as the Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Yushi Zhongcheng), he was dispatched to govern Qiantang. There, he visited Chan Master Xiaoshou at Xingjiao Temple;
their words and insights were in perfect accord, and they became friends beyond the secular world. Upon reaching the rank of Chancellor (Xiangwei), he acted as a bulwark for the Dharma gate.

Dichi, at the end of his life, wrote a verse which said: "The lamp in the painted hall has already been extinguished; pointing my finger, to whom shall I speak? Departing and staying are fundamentally ordinary;
the spring breeze sweeps away the lingering snow. He passed away in profound stillness, which was likely due to the spiritual power of his vast compassion and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

(From the *Tongdushi lüe*) Lord Li Wenjing, whose courtesy name was Hang, enjoyed a reputation for being a man of great virtue. He was well-versed in the Buddhist scriptures and held a particular distaste for worldly glory and profit. While serving as Chancellor...
His dwelling was cramped and narrow, yet he lived there with complete ease. When his family members urged him to renovate a residence, he replied:

"I receive a generous salary and occasionally receive unexpected gifts; by calculation, it would indeed be possible to build a house. However, reflecting upon the Inner Canon, I consider this world to be defective."
"How could one obtain perfect fulfillment? How could one seek personal satisfaction? Human life lasts from morning until evening; how can one dwell long?
To rest upon a single branch in the forest is merely to find contentment for oneself. Later, when the Master fell ill, he passed away while reclining on his right side.
Although it was midsummer, his body remained for seven days without any foul odor emanating from the chamber. People said this was proof of his spiritual practice (*Yánxíng lù*).
The Gong of Wenzhong, Ouyang Xiu, was from the outset a non-believer in the teachings of Śākyamuni. As he wrote in a poem repaying Chan Master Jingzhao: "I do not study what the Buddha taught;
why trouble the Master to suddenly knock at my gate? I am currently preoccupied with benevolence and righteousness, while you, sir, are idly enjoying the waters and clouds.
Furthermore, in his reply to Chan Master Weiwu, he said: "Why do you alone admire me? You have forgotten to distinguish yourself from others. How could this be [the case]?

[This is] knowledge. Once, when the Duke was serving in Luoyang, he traveled to Mount Song. He dismissed his attendants and went forth with unrestrained ease. Upon reaching a mountain temple, he entered;
tall bamboos filled the courtyard, the frost was clear, birds were singing, and the scenery was vivid.

The Duke rested upon the steps of the hall. Beside him sat an elderly monk reading a scripture with composure. When the Duke spoke to him, the monk did not respond with much regard. The Duke marveled at this and said, "You [must be a great man]."
"Master Shan, how long has it been? He replied, "A very long time. The official asked again, "What sutra do you recite? "The Lotus Sutra," he said.

The official asked, "Among the eminent monks of antiquity, most were able to cast off their bodies with laughter and ease at the moment of death. What path leads to such a state? He replied, "It is the power of meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*) alone.
The official asked further, "Why is it that nowadays there is such silence and nothingness? The old monk smiled and said, "People of old..."
If one’s mindfulness is fixed upon meditative concentration and wisdom, how could one be distracted at the moment of death? People today, however, dwell in distraction at every thought;
how then could they attain concentration at the end? When Public Official Wen Zhong heard this, he was so greatly startled that he did not even realize his knees had bent in reverence.

Xie Hishen often composed essays to record these matters; thereafter, he came to deeply believe them. Although he still delighted in the refined and elegant style of the *Sao*, he associated with all the eminent and virtuous monks.
In his travels, he was renowned for his talent and wisdom; how could one not be intoxicated by his heart? As in the verse he presented to Master Tanyi:

"Once gone to the mountain forests, there is no returning; among the ancients, there were likewise our Confucian scholars. I envy you, who know where to rest; you have returned to the Double Grove to build your hermitage.

When the monk Wenying of Luoyang came to pay his respects, he said: "If one has not entered the sphere of Master Ou, how can there be poetry in this world? I did not expect to steal your style and meter, yet—"

I value your dignified bearing; in establishing your affairs, you distinguish neither between inner and outer realms. Relying on your mind alone, you remain equanimous in both adversity and prosperity.

I beg that you take up a position of administrative authority, where you may exhaustively offer counsel and deliberation to assist in governance. In his poem of parting, the Duke wrote: Your flying staff knocks at my study door, And we are able to enjoy another meeting.

A solitary guest from the dry lands of India, With the simple and profound talent of Shao Ling. How sincere is your pursuit of the Way! All thoughts of vying for fame have long since turned to ash. The mountain forests...
The composition of this poem is complete; it should be sent from the side of the sun. The Wu monk Huìqín paid his respects and took his leave, saying:

"I recall your words were solemn and prudent, like those of Níqiú; your editorial work on the *Tángshū* was thorough in its power. To bring peace to the age and transform sentient beings, you must rise to serve as the boat that ferries across the river.
The Master continued the rhyme, saying: "I rejoice in returning to my old home for one hill; I am ashamed that I cannot supplement the robes of Shùn, yet I do not regret being like Yī."
Zhou said, "Your Lordship now seeks the Way and will return to the south by boat; we shall no longer travel together on the same vessel down the Bian Canal.

Upon hearing of the extraordinary and transcendent reputation of Chan Master Yuan of Fushan, the Duke went to his quarters. However, the Master showed no sign of being different from others; he was sitting beside some guests playing chess.
The Duke took the opportunity to request that the Master expound the Dharma based on the game of chess. The Master then had the drums beaten and ascended the seat, saying: "If one were to discuss..."
This matter is like two families playing Go. What does this mean? It means that as adversaries who understand one another, they do not yield when the opportunity arises.

If one is trailing by five points or leading by three, it is only by opening a new path that one may succeed. There is a certain class of people who only know how to make a living move by retreating to the sidelines;

they do not understand how to seize the corners or break through the passes. When their hard positions and tiger-mouths are displayed simultaneously, once the board is broken, their efforts are in vain.

How vast and profound! This is what is called the Way. Fat edges are easy to find; lean corners are difficult to seek. When thought and action arise, one often loses the connection; when the mind is coarse, one frequently strikes one's head.
Do not boast of being a master of the state; do not vainly speak of being an immortal. Let us not ask about winning the board or losing the counters;
tell me, when black and white have not yet been distinguished, where does that first move fall? After a long silence, he said: "Even if..."

Nineteen horizontal lines—how many people are lost in delusion and awakened? Master Wen sighed deeply at this. Once the Master had ascended to the two government offices, one day he was stricken by illness.
Suddenly in the middle of the night, he dreamed that he arrived at a certain place resembling an official residence. There he saw ten men wearing ceremonial caps and robes sitting in a circle.
One man said, "How have you, Minister, come to this place? You ought to return to your quarters immediately. Following these words, the Master departed.
After walking ten paces from the gate, he went again to question them, saying, "Are you not perhaps those known as the Ten Kings spoken of by the followers of Śākyamuni?

They replied, "Indeed. He asked further, "When worldly people provide meals for the monastic community, recite scriptures, and perform meritorious deeds, is it for the sake of accumulating blessings for the deceased?"
"Is there not benefit in this? He replied, "How could there not be benefit? Once he awoke from his illness, it was completely cured. From that time on, he placed firm faith in the Buddha-dharma.
In his later years, the Duke’s friendship with those beyond the secular world became profound; his feelings were expressed through his words (from the *Danyang Ji*).

The monk Zuxiu of Shu, whose courtesy name was Zizhi, authored the *External Biography of Lord Ouyang*. Su Yangzhi Xiang wrote its preface, which states in brief: "The gentleman [regards] the Buddha's..."
Regarding this teaching: it was not witnessed during the eras of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, or the likes;

yet after Confucius and Mencius, successive generations of former scholars, though they were within the state and not few in number who sought to prohibit it, nevertheless allowed its currents to flow unchecked within the realm.

Throughout antiquity and the present, there have been those who maintained this view. Master Dushou, however, held that because Danzhu was insufficient to receive the mandate of governance, Yao abdicated in favor of Shun.
Shun was likewise concerned about Shangjun and abdicated the throne to Yu; it was with the "revolution" of Tang and Wu that this teaching first began.
Had Confucius been in charge of affairs, how would he have differed from this? From the time of Yao until King Wu, no Buddha had yet been born; there was a reason for this.
After Cheng and Kang had passed away, the Buddha then manifested his traces;

yet he did not fully establish himself in the Middle Kingdom, waiting instead for a sage to be born in Lu to synthesize the great achievement within the teachings of the ancient emperors. How profound this was!

When the Sage was beset by difficulties in Lu, Wei, Chen, and Song—desiring to dwell among the nine tribes of the Yi and riding on a raft to float across the sea—at that time, [he considered] the teachings from tens of thousands of li abroad.
If this were applied to the Middle Kingdom, who among the Son of Heaven or the feudal lords would listen to it? The Buddha’s Dharma is not transmitted lightly;
unless one awakens the sentiments of others by manifesting its principles, seeking it from afar will likely fail to produce a swift response.

These were all the writings of Master Xiu from the capital, containing tens of thousands of words of arguments that startle the ancients and shake the present, yet they have not been transmitted to the world.
Du Qigong (Du Kezhi) and Zhang Wending (Zhang Zideng) both retired from office and resided in Suizhou. They frequented one another’s quarters in the village lanes.
There was a man named Zhu Chengshi who practiced medicine and moved among these two elders. Whenever Lord Qi laughed at An Dao’s devotion to Buddhism, Zhu took an opportunity to say to Wending:
"Lord Du is a great man of this world; it is a pity that he does not yet know this matter. Lord Du...
"His strength is failing; why not encourage him to exert himself? Wen-ding said, "Your connection with this old man is mature, while I can only assist you.
Zhu then took his leave. One day, Lord Qi summoned Zhu and felt his pulse with great urgency.
Zhu said to the messenger, "Go first and inform the Lord, saying simply that he has not yet finished reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The messenger did as instructed. Lord Qi—

The Duke remained silent. After a long while, Zhu arrived. He invited him to sit and said, "I had considered you a man of broad learning and capable understanding, yet I did not expect that recently you have become so dull-witted.
What kind of talk is this so-called *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*? Why are you so addicted to it?
The subtle words of the sages do not go beyond Confucius and Mencius. To abandon these and take up those [foreign texts] is a great delusion. Zhu replied, "The Excellency has not yet—"
"Reading this scripture, how can one know it does not surpass Confucius and Mencius? Upon examining it, it seems to exceed them.

He produced the first fascicle from his sleeve and said, "Minister, please examine it. Qi then took it up and read it with careful attention; before he knew it, he had finished the entire scroll. Suddenly, struck with great astonishment, he exclaimed, "How could such a book exist in this world?
He dispatched messengers to bring all the volumes so that he might read them through completely. He marked the text with red ink in his own hand.
He said, "You are truly my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). You have known the Way for a long time; why did you not tell me?
I shall immediately order my carriage to visit Master Wending and relate these matters. An Dao said, "It is like a person who has lost an object and suddenly finds it again;
one should rejoice at having found it, rather than regretting whether it was found early or late. It was not that I did not wish to inform you, but because of you..."
"Master Zhu’s karmic conditions were ripe; therefore, I sent him away. Even when Buddhas and Patriarchs transform others, they must rely on those who share their same purpose.
Lord Qi was greatly pleased; thereupon, he devoted himself inwardly (as recorded in the *Linjian Lu*).

Duke Zhang Wending was serving as the Governor of Chuzhou when he once visited Mount Langya. He paced back and forth along the corridors, unable to bear leaving. Upon reaching the library, he was moved to tears.

Pointing to a scripture case between the beams, he said, "This is the work of my previous incarnation. He ordered it to be brought out for inspection; it was two fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* that he had written himself.
Having purified himself through fasting and bathing, he continued writing from where he had left off; the new script did not differ in the slightest from the previous one.
It appears that a monk from the Jizang Monastery in his previous life had passed away before completing the transcription of a sutra.
Later, while serving as the official Zhu Yan, he read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and attained a realization regarding the luminous subtlety of the true mind.
He then asked the lecture-monk Yijiang, "After this body dies, where does this mind reside? Jiang replied, "Before this body has died."
"Where is this mind? After a long silence, Zhu presented a verse, saying: "The four elements need not be awakened to sequentially; The six sense faculties are empty when they function.
It is difficult to present it to the Master through speech or silence; It resides only within ordinary speech and silence."
When Wenzhong Gong Yang Yi received a letter from Tang Ming Song, he replied: "We face each other yet do not know one another; though a thousand li apart, we share the same wind.

The Śākya [Buddhists] claim that all things in the world are illusory, urging people to go against the natural order and contravene the Way. Their fundamental intent differs and their applications diverge; how can their words enter the ears and their meanings penetrate the heart?

In the seventh month of the third year of Gengxu (1070), Lord Wang Anshi of Jing requested that the garden where he resided in Shangyuan County be converted into a Buddhist temple;
by imperial decree, it was granted the name Bao Ning Chan Temple (*Bian nian*). During the Xining era, when the Lord held the office of Chancellor, he was resolute in his intent.

He implemented the Green Sprouts Law. His son, Pang, who served as a Lecturer on the Classics at Chongzheng Hall, presented thirty memorials and acted as a secret assistant to his father, striving to ensure the new laws were carried out without regard for the people's resentment.

Not long after, Pang died. While the Duke was in retirement following his resignation from the相位 (Prime Minister), he saw, as if in a dream, an official leading a man with an iron cangue upon his shoulders.
The man wailed before him, saying that his punishment resulted from [the Duke’s] conduct.

Regarding the Green Sprouts Law (*qingmiao fa*), he asked the imperial envoy for release from it. The envoy replied, "The construction of a temple and the offering of a vegetarian feast for the monks may exempt you.
Consequently, he donated his residence to build a temple and performed memorial rites for the posthumous merit of his beloved son (from the *Yansheng lu*).

In the eighth year, Anshi was appointed Chancellor once again. One day, after the audience for state affairs had concluded, the Emperor asked, "Does the Buddha-dharma provide any benefit to our Central Kingdom?
Anshi replied, "It cannot be said that it provides no benefit. Both the noble and the petty alike know to revere and follow its teachings;
how could this not be a great benefit? (Biannian)
Emperor Shenzong divided the sixty-four cloisters of the State Preceptor into eight: two for Chan and six for Vinaya. He appointed the high-ranking eunuch Liang Congzheng to oversee the project.
An imperial decree was dispatched via express courier summoning Chan Master Zongben to preside over Hui-lin Monastery in the capital.

After three days of inquiries and greetings from the imperial envoys, the Emperor issued an edict for the Master to expound the Dharma at the monastery gate. A multitude of ten thousand people paid their respects and gazed upon him; the Dharma assembly was truly magnificent.
It was believed that Maitreya had descended from heaven to the human realm. The following day, he was summoned for an audience at the Yanhe Hall.

The officials had him practice the ceremonial protocols before leading him in. Once the audience was concluded and the "Shanhu" (Mountain-Cry) salutation finished, he ascended the hall and was granted a seat.

The Emperor asked, "In which monastery did you receive your training? He replied, "Chengtian Yong'an. The Emperor rejoiced in his sincerity and instructed him that, as the Chan school was flourishing, he should skillfully propagate it.
When Daozhi withdrew, the Emperor watched him depart with his eyes and said to those around him, "He is truly a monk of merit and wisdom.

On the first day of the New Year, the Emperor visited the State Preceptor’s residence; he commanded that the assembly of Chan practitioners not come out to welcome him. The Master respectfully received this imperial decree and propagated the Buddhist teachings.

The capital was situated in the four directions; all turned toward him in reverence and were moved to faith and submission. When the Shenzong Emperor passed away, he summoned Zhenjue Ben to preach the Dharma at Funing Palace.
Seeing that Ben had once been honored by the late Emperor, the attendants wept uncontrollably upon beholding him.

Emperor Zhezong bestowed upon him the honorary title of Chan Master Yuanzhao. His Imperial Uncle, Prince Jing, personally delivered the imperial edict to confer it upon him. This occurred during the Zhizheng era.
In the first year of the Yuanshou era, [Zhaozhou] announced his intention to retire due to old age. The court granted his request, issuing an edict that stated: "He may wander freely as he pleases;

wherever he arrives, no one shall compel him to serve as an abbot. The Master joyfully ascended the seat and took leave of the assembly, saying: "I am originally a guest with no home; how could I not wander as I please?
With a favorable wind, I add oars and sweeps; the boatman heads for Yangzhou. Once the Master had departed the capital, the King...
The Duke was a man of noble rank; the carriages accompanying him to see him off were linked in continuous succession. Master [Xing] was the son of the Guan family of Wuxi, Changzhou.
Wang Xianmu, during the early Han dynasty, saw the Master ascend the seat and, looking around with his eyes, realized his own fundamental mind. I have heard Master Aśvaghoṣa say:

"When the Tathāgata was in the world, the physical forms and minds of sentient beings were exceptionally diverse; yet when he uttered his single, perfect sound, each received understanding according to their kind."
(Sengbaozhuan). The Attendant Official, Mr.
Wu Fu, said to Chan Master Jiantang Ji: "The ancients extinguished their hearts and stilled their ambitions amidst a thousand crags and ten thousand gullies;
drinking from mountain streams and eating from the trees, they seemed to have severed all intent for fame and office, yet one day they were presented with purple robes."
The Emperor’s edict commanded that he conceal his brilliance and hide his traces beneath the humble labor of a miller, having originally no intention of seeking honor or advancement;
yet he now stands in the ranks of those who transmit the Lamp. Thus, because he attained it through a mind free of desire, his Way is great and his virtue vast.

Had he calculated it with a sense of seeking, his reputation would have been base and his ambition narrow. Only the Master’s capacity for judgment was profound and far-reaching, allowing him to follow in the footsteps of the ancients.
Only then can one dwell in seclusion among the crags and valleys and ultimately become a vessel of excellence for the monastic community.
The patch-robed monks of today lack internal self-mastery and pursue external splendor; they have little foresight and no grasp of the great principles.
Consequently, they are unable to support the religious teachings, and thus fall far short of the ancients (from the *Baoguang*).
The Emperor summoned Gongzhu, who was serving at the Shen-guan Yuan (Office for Examining Officials) under the Ministry of Personnel, and they discussed the principles of governance at great length.

The conversation eventually reached the doctrines of emptiness and non-being held by the followers of Śākyamuni and Laozi. Gongzhu asked, "Did Yao and Shun understand this Way? The Emperor replied, "How could Yao and Shun have not known it?"
Gong Zhi said: "Although Yao and Shun knew this, they nevertheless considered 'knowing men' and 'settling the people' to be difficult;
this is precisely what made them Yao and Shun" (Dongdu shilüe).

Yitian, the State Preceptor of Goryeo, renounced his royal status to enter the monastic life. He traveled by sea to Mingzhou and submitted a memorial requesting to tour various monasteries to seek instruction and receive the Dharma.
An imperial edict appointed Yang Jie, a Court Attendant of the Fourth Rank, to serve as his host.

At every monastery he visited throughout the Wu region, he was welcomed and escorted with the same protocol accorded to a prince or high minister. Upon reaching Jinshan, the Elder Liaoyuan received him upon his own couch.
When they were about to unfold the large sitting mat, Cigong asked in surprise for the reason. Yuan said, "Yitian is also a monk from a foreign land;
yet such are the regulations of the monastic community (*conglin*), and they cannot be altered. Cigong said, "It would be better to follow the current customs a little;
to seek something different from other regions is surely the mind of an old man. Yuan said, "Not so. To bend the Way to conform to worldly custom means that other regions have already lost it first."
"One-Eyed. How could this demonstrate the teacher-disciple lineage to the scholars of China? When the court heard of this, they regarded Yuan as one who understood the great principles.
The Prince of Cao submitted his name, and the Divine Emperor (Shenkao) bestowed upon him the purple robe and the title of "Teacher" (shihao) to honor him (*Sengbaozhuan*).
Wu-wu: The first year of Yuánfēng. Heaven had suffered from a prolonged drought. Within the inner palace, the Emperor performed prayers with great intensity.
One night he dreamed of a monk riding a horse through the air, exhaling clouds and mist from his mouth. Upon waking, it rained heavily.

The following day, he dispatched a high-ranking eunuch to seek out the appearance of the object seen in his dream at the Three Gates of the Xiāngguó Temple. Among the five hundred Arhats [there], he found one who matched the description.
Upon reaching the thirteenth statue, it was roughly similar; he immediately invited it inside to examine it, and it was exactly as the Emperor had dreamed.
Prime Minister Wang Yuyu composed a poem on the joy of rain, saying: "The worthy minister brings the rain to fulfill all hopes;

the divine monk exhales mist in response to earnest prayer. Yuan Canhou said: "The immortal steed pierces the clouds beneath the ceremonial ranks; the Buddha’s flowers blow rain that flows around the heavens."
This is a record of events from a particular time (*Shihua*).
Chan Master Jingzhi Daozhen, courtesy name Boxiang, was the son of the Dai family of Gutian in Fuzhou.

While traveling to Danyang, he boarded a boat that traveled to the capital, where he went to visit Chan Master Jingyin Dajue Liaan. Liaan appointed Daozhen to lead the assembly. When Liaan returned to Wu, [Daozhen followed him].
The multitude requested that he produce a successor. On the day he opened the hall, Emperor Ying sent an envoy to bestow incense, a purple robe, and a formal title.

Nobles and high officials flocked to his gate daily, yet he regarded them all with a single glance. During the reign of Emperor Shenzong, when Empress Dowager Cisheng passed away, an imperial decree arrived for him to preach at the Qingshou Palace.
A monk asked, "When the Empress Dowager has ascended to the immortal realm, where will she return? He replied, "The water flows."
"Originally in the sea, yet when the moon sets, it does not leave the sky. The Emperor was greatly pleased and treated him with increased respect. He granted him very generous audiences.
The Emperor lamented the decline of the Buddha-dharma and took pity on the defects of the scholastic traditions (nāma-rūpa).

He first appointed two monasteries, Huilin and Zhikai, as State Preceptors (Sang-kuo) and commanded that the abbots be chosen from among the most eminent monks. ○ Three monks from Goryeo arrived to study; Zhen [was selected].
He attained awakening according to his faculties and took his leave to return to his kingdom. Zhen was a man of profound dignity and quiet withdrawal; he seemed as if unable to speak.
He resided in the western corner of the capital city, never leaving his door for over thirty years, remaining as if it were but a single day. He maintained the utmost simplicity in his personal life.
Having no personal preferences, he was able to have Wen Yuke paint ink bamboo upon the walls of his quarters.

He said to others, "If travelers see this, their minds will naturally feel refreshed and cool; this gentleman truly preaches the Dharma on my behalf. Huang鲁直 (Huang Tingjian) inscribed his portrait, saying:
"The tiger has no teeth; the dragon lies coiled and does not roar. Under the black moon of a thousand forests, the six realms [of existence]..."
Cloud-shaded, with distant mountains for eyebrows and red apricots for cheeks; Married to the East Wind without a matchmaker.
Even a housewife in her thirties and fifties Once knew how to apply rouge and powder. (From *Sengbaodian*)

Daxiangguo Temple. Its founder was Chan Master Yi, a native of the Peng clan of Fuzhou. He first resided at Jianfu Temple in Raozhou, and Emperor Shen宗 summoned him to reside at Zhihai, bestowing upon him the title Zhengjue (Right Awakening).
On the day he opened the hall for his formal sermon, the Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to present incense. After the Master had finished expressing his gratitude, he said:
"O sons of the Bodhisattvas, if you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of time and season. Why is this so?"
The gentle breeze blows softly, unveiling the brows of the slender willows. The spring days linger long, warming the tongues of the yellow orioles.
The flowers in the courtyard are like brocade; the grasses on the marshes are like carpets. Butterflies dance and bees hum; fishermen sing and woodsmen chant.

The sounds of bells and sutras mingle with pipes and strings; the followers of Confucius and the sons of Śākyamuni intermingle. Ancient and modern are of one accord; left and right, one encounters the source. Thus it is.
Thus, by observing a single speck of dust, the ten directions appear simultaneously; by listening to a single sound, all lands are heard at once.

Though they discuss the profound and expound the subtle, they do not differ from ordinary beings; though they undergo a thousand transformations and myriad changes, they do not depart from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Every instance has its basis, and every thing is without partiality. Without needing to hesitate, it is brilliantly manifest of itself. Even if one perceives this, one must possess a spirit of bold independence.

Clear! It is like seeing the sun by day. If one approaches the gate of the patch-robed monk, heaven and earth are vastly different. Therefore it is said: "Do not seek the Three Vehicles; seek the ancestral source.
The Three Vehicles do not suffice to serve as a conduit for the Lord. You now wish to transcend the study of the Three Vehicles:
"At the end of the night, the monkey cries on a distant peak. I have stood long; take care. Farewell.

Fayun Temple in Tokyo. Chan Master Fashou was the son of the Xin family of Longcheng in Qinzhou. Wang Anshi invited him to reside at Zhongshan. In the Jiazi year of the Yuanfeng era, the Princess of Yue and Marshal Zhang petitioned for him to reside at Fayun as its first patriarch. On the day he opened the hall, Emperor Shen宗 dispatched an imperial messenger to present incense and bestowed upon him a *moluona* (monastic robe). *Fazhuan* (Biographies of the Dharma) states: "The Master’s dharma name was Fashou; his secular surname was Xin. He was born in Longcheng, Qinzhou. From childhood, he possessed an extraordinary nature. At age twenty-one, he received the full precepts from Master Shouyuan of Xiangguo Temple in Chang'an. He traveled extensively through various regions, visiting eminent masters to resolve his doubts. Later, he resided at Huayan Temple in Jingzhou, where he encountered the Chan Master Daowu of Mount Huangbo. Hearing the Master’s discourse, he attained great awakening. Subsequently, he visited the Chan Master Wuxue at Mount Tiantong in Mingzhou, where he further resolved his remaining doubts. He then returned to Jingzhou and dwelt at Huayan Temple. During the reign of Emperor Yingzong, he was summoned to the capital and appointed as the Abbot of the Great Xiangguo Chan Monastery. When Emperor Shenzong ascended the throne, he was invited to reside at the newly established Fayun Chan Monastery in Dongjing. On the day he opened the hall, the Emperor sent an imperial messenger to present incense and bestowed upon him a *moluona*. He subsequently retired to Mount Yunju in Hongzhou."*1* *1. *Fozu tongji*, fascicle 42.* The Master was deeply versed in both the exoteric and esoteric teachings. His disciples numbered over three thousand, including the National Teacher Miaodao, the State Preceptor Zhiyan, and others. He passed away on the eighth day of the second month in the third year of the Yuanyou era at the age of seventy-nine. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Fajie. His remains were enshrined at Fayun Temple. The Emperor granted him the posthumous title Chan Master Fajue. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Master’s writings include the *Xinxiu xu chanyuan qinggui* (Newly Revised Rules of Purity for Chan Monasteries), the *Changuan ce* (Cessation and Contemplation Notes), the *Jingde chuan deng lu xuji* (Continued Records of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era), and other works totaling over one hundred fascicles.
