The Record states: "Although the object is small, it represents the gravity of the Dharma. After the Master has finished expressing his gratitude and ascended the seat to offer incense, he raises his whisk and says:
"I deeply rely upon the holy sovereign and worthy ministers for appointing this mountain monk as the presiding master of Fayun. Now tell me, by what does this mountain monk preside?
He suddenly brandishes the master’s staff and asks: "Do you understand? And tell me, what does the Fayun master’s staff possess?"

[He] struck the meditation seat once and said: "This very act proclaims [the truth]. May it support the imperial succession from above, looking up with hope that the sagacious sovereign may bring the spring of fragrance to the myriad nations.
May the loyal and virtuous ministers assist in the destiny of a thousand years. I humbly pray that you will cherish yourself.
He was subsequently granted the title Chan Master Yuantong.

In the third month of the eighth year of the Yuanfeng era, Emperor Shenzong was unwell, and the succession had not yet been determined. Prime Minister Wang Gui presented the name of Zhezong for consideration;

the Emperor nodded his approval. The Empress Dowager instructed Gui, saying, "The Emperor has been taking medicine, and the Crown Prince has transcribed Buddhist scriptures by hand to pray for his recovery.
She then showed them to Gui and the others; the characters he had written were extremely upright. Gui and the others bowed and offered their congratulations. On that day...
He was established as the Crown Prince. At that time he was seven years old (Chronological Record).
Bingyin year: Emperor Zhezong changed the era name to Yuanyou. First Year: [The Emperor] summoned Jingyin Zhen, Huelin Ben, and Fayun Xiu.
The three elders expounded the Dharma at Funing Palace to offer posthumous rites for the late Emperor, who had ascended to the realm of the immortals.

As the masters had previously preached before the imperial presence during the former reign, their teachings were all most excellent; consequently, each was bestowed with purple robes and a title of honor to commemorate their excellence (Linjian Lu).
The State Preceptor of Goryeo submitted a memorial requesting that the teachings of Xianshou be transmitted back to his native country for circulation.

By imperial decree, the two monastic districts were ordered to nominate a suitable candidate to receive the dharma. The relevant authorities deemed Master Rishi of Jueyan Temple in Dongjing to be the most appropriate choice;
however, he sincerely submitted a memorial declining the honor and nominated the monk Daoyuan of Huinyin Monastery in Hangzhou as his substitute, which was fully in accord with public consensus.

The Emperor issued an edict appointing Yao Fei Lang Yang Jie as the ceremonial host. Upon arriving at Qiantang, he received the Dharma from the monk Daoyuan, who dwelt by the seashore and was renowned for his spiritual practice.
Toward the end of the Yuanfeng era, Prince Uicheon of Goryeo came to court and went to pay his respects to him.

Later, his disciples came to court again and reported that the Queen Mother had sent two golden stupas to offer prayers for the Emperor’s longevity. At that time, Su Shi was serving as the Governor of Hangzhou.
He did not accept it but memorialized the throne, saying: "If I were to receive it but fail to respond, the distant barbarians would harbor resentment.
To grant them a generous reward on that account would be to fall directly into their trap" (Dongdu shilüe).
Chan Master Juehai Ruichong of HuiLin Chan Monastery in Tokyo was the son of the Zhong family of Jiangning Prefecture.

Prime Minister Han Gong Jiang and Grand Preceptor Wen Gong Yanbo both held him in high esteem. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at HuiLin Monastery. On the day he ascended the Dharma hall, [he spoke as follows].
Emperor Chejong dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense. After the Master had finished expressing his gratitude, he said:

"By imperial decree, this humble monk is to open the hall for the sake of the nation, to circulate the Ultimate Way, and to enlighten humans and devas," and so forth. After a long silence, he said: "The intent of the Three Vehicles is difficult to manifest;
thus, with one impartial phrase, we celebrate the Great Peace. On this day, we circulate the *Prajñāpāramitā* and gather all wondrous goodness to offer our supreme prayers."

To Your Sacred Person: We humbly pray that the precious throne may remain forever firm and the phoenix calendar ever renewed. May you shine like the sun and moon and encompass all like heaven and earth;
may your station be as exalted as the North Star and your longevity equal that of the Southern Mountain. We most reverently entreat you to cherish yourself.
Hangzhou. Chan Master Dàtōng Shànběn of Jìngcí was the son of the Xūn family of Yíngzhōu. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Fáyún Monastery.

On the day he ascended the hall for his inaugural sermon, Emperor Zhézhōng dispatched an envoy to bestow incense and a *mòná* (patchwork robe). After the ceremony of expressing gratitude was concluded, a monk asked:

"Your name has been transmitted to the inner palace, and imperial favor has descended from the Nine Layers [of Heaven]. Now that you have donned this *mòná*, how will you repay this kindness? The Master said: "The heavens are so high they cannot be measured."
The monk said: "The net of Indra is layered upon layer without interruption; the intersecting stages fully unfold before the eyes. The Master said:
"The earth is vast, supporting all things without end. Then he continued: "I respectfully consider that our nation has long enjoyed peace, and its refined culture is now flourishing.
It universally guides all sentient beings and greatly promotes the Three Teachings. Thus, the profound Prajñāpāramitā abides here for a long time; these are the sincere words of the Golden Mouth."
This is not a falsehood.

Chan Master Desun of Fotuo was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Hui-lin Monastery. Emperor Zhezong dispatched an envoy to present incense, to which the Master replied, "I shall open the hall on this very day.
He then composed a brief prayer for the Emperor, saying: "I reverently pray that the Sun of Shun and the Sun of the Buddha may shine ever higher together."

It is clear that the wind of Yao and the ancestral wind blow together; the myriad regions are free from affairs. This is a time of flourishing prosperity, when the four seas are peaceful and serene, and the people delight in the transformation of ascendant peace.
Having long established [this tradition], I offer my respects. (The Master was summoned three times by imperial decree to enter the inner hall and ascend the seat.)
Quanzhou. Kaiyuan Temple. Great Master Zhizhen (Zhitian). Originally from the Lu clan of this province, he traveled to the capital.
Hearing of the Master’s reputation for the Way, King Xuoguo summoned him into the palace to expound the Dharma. The King asked, "What is the fundamental matter of the Buddha-dharma?"
The Master said, "Seeing one's nature is precisely this. The King asked, "How can one come to see one's nature? The Master replied, "It is not apart from the twelve periods of the day;

walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—all are the sites of enlightenment for the ancient Buddhas. Thereupon, the King awakened to the profound principle and secretly harmonized with the spirit of the school.

He immediately ordered the monks of the Four Dhyānas to enter the palace to seek further certification of his realization. He then provided a meal for a thousand monks and read the entire Tripitaka as a celebration.
The Emperor presented him with a *monā* robe. The Imperial Seal of Emperor Huizong was inscribed upon a golden ring, which read: "Bestowed upon the Dharma Master Zhenjue;
may we together attain the fruit of Buddhahood in the future.
This was in the fourth month of the first year of the Jianzhong Jingguo era (1101), concerning Chan Master Jinshan Fojian Weizhong, a native of Tingzhou.
The Empress sent an envoy to present incense in honor of the birthday of the Crown Prince, Duke of Goryeo, requesting that the Master take his seat.

A monk asked, "The celestial fragrance has descended from afar to celebrate the auspicious occasion of the Prince's birth; now that the imperial messenger has graced this assembly, we pray to hear the essential points of the Dharma.

The Master said, "A favorable breeze comes without end; the red sun shines boundlessly. The entire assembly rejoiced. On the fifth and seventh days of the mourning period for Emperor Zhezong, he entered the palace.
He ascended the throne and bestowed upon him ceremonial robes and a title as a Master to honor his virtue.

In the year Xinsi, Emperor Huizong changed the reign era to Jianzhong Jinggu. Chan Master Weibai of Foguo Temple compiled the *Xudeng Lu* (Continued Record of the Lamp), collecting the recorded sayings and karmic conditions of the patriarchs from the Tiānshèng era onward.
Upon its completion, he presented it for imperial review; the Emperor read it and personally composed a preface.

It was issued for inclusion in the Tripitaka. On the sixteenth day of the third year of Yuánfú, during the fifty-seventh day of Emperor Zhézhōng’s mourning period, he ascended the seat at Fúníng Hall in accordance with an imperial decree. After the incense had been offered, a monk asked:
"The Great Sovereign has passed away; in what realm of retribution does he now reside? Does he not dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven? [The Master replied: "He is already in the Lotus..."
In the Flower World, a monk said, "If it is so, then a single phrase that is spiritually resonant transcends all multitudes; it stands far beyond the Three Vehicles and requires no cultivation.
The Master said, "One must indeed be such a person to be able to proceed in such a manner. The monk asked, "Is it permitted to reveal even a hint of this message?
The Master said, "On the borders of a sagely and enlightened sovereign, you may freely display your family style. The monk said, "Nine..."
"Amidst the lotus blossoms, one personally beholds the Buddha; hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas roam together. The Master said, "It is not improper to speak thus.

The Master then said: "I, the monk Weibai, prostrate myself before the imperial decree to perform the recitation of the Prajñāpāramitā before the sacred remains of the Great Emperor, thereby providing spiritual sustenance for the celestial carriage.
I humbly pray that the Emperor’s sagely nature may be perfectly luminous, that his thousand rays of light may shine forth brilliantly, and that his holy body..."
He is sovereign, adorned with myriad virtues. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, lotus flowers support his feet; in the Tuṣita Heaven, exquisite robes encircle his body.
Furthermore, manifesting divine majesty, he protects and blesses the state. We humbly pray that you will cherish yourself. The Master thrice received imperial edicts.
While preaching the Dharma in the inner court, he was granted purple robes and the honorary title of Foguo Chan Master.
On the second month of the first year, the Empress Dowager passed away. On the fifth week [after her death], an imperial decree summoned Chan Master Jingyin Weiyue to ascend the seat at Cide Hall.
Holding up the incense, he said: "Of all the soil under heaven, there is none that is not the King’s soil. Now tell me, from where does this incense for discernment originate?"
"What soil is appropriate? If you can say it, then white stones will have days of dissolution, and the swirling vapors will endure for endless years.

Pervading all of empty space and the entire Dharma realm, they become clouds and canopies, manifesting endlessly. Thus, one may offer these to those who have ascended to the immortal journey, being born directly in the Buddha-land.

[The summary of the essential principles follows... If we rely on the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings—whether partial or complete, sudden or gradual, half or full, the single voice—[the principle remains the same].
This cannot avoid being like grasping at the finger as the moon, or entering the sea to count its sands;

it is exactly like the reflection of the moon in a clear pool or the sound of a bell in the late night—emitting sound according to the strike and dispersing not with the waves. Yet these are still matters belonging to the shore of birth and death (and so forth).
Thus did the Emperor Zhenzong of our Great Song dynasty say in his verse: "The First Patriarch sat in meditation at Shaolin."

The teachings were not transmitted; only the mind was transmitted. Later generations have failed to awaken to the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The Seal of Secrecy has always possessed a profound and wondrous principle.
How great is this wondrous principle of True Suchness! It is most subtle and most deep; without those of great capacity and great vessels, one cannot comprehend it.
Why is this? Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are themselves a mass of fire. The Iron Mountain stands naturally at every fork in the road;

It pervades the entire realm of *sāhasra-lokadhātu*; truly, this is a rare encounter once in a thousand years! (And so forth).

It is just like when the King of Śrāvastī wished to go to Vulture Peak to see the Buddha; he commanded his ministers and officials that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests must all go together to see the Buddha.
He declared, "If even a single blade of grass or a single tree does not go, I shall not see the Buddha. Great assembly, right now—

Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests—neither departing nor arriving, neither coming nor going;
profoundly still and impartial, towering and immovable; manifesting as both civil and martial, and as both Chan and Vinaya.
Together in the Ninth Heaven, before the Hall of Compassionate Virtue, we behold the Buddha at the same time.
O virtuous ones, it is not that you do not see him; but tell me, how do you see him? (After a long pause, he says: His double pupils shine with the inexhaustible light of sun and moon;

his prominent nose is as magnificent as the beauty of mountains and rivers. This monk, Weiyue, having humbly received the Imperial decree, is commanded to ascend this seat to proclaim Prajñā. I respectfully accept.
For the sake of the Great Empress Dowager, whose karmic conditions in this realm have come to an end and whose earthly retribution has been fully exhausted;
as the forty-nine days have concluded, she has ascended to the immortal journey. We reverently contemplate the Empress Dowager: her pure wisdom is primordial, and her supreme spirit moves alone.

She came to manifest the traces of maternal virtue, her merit supporting the Three Courts; she departed to repay the causes of the Dharma-realm, her fruition perfected in the Ten Stages. We humbly pray that in the Tuṣita Heaven...

In the palace, he accompanied the Buddha-mother Māyā, strolling at leisure in one place. In the stainless world, together with the Naga-daughter Sāgara, they shall equally attain perfect enlightenment.

He turned his radiant physical light back upon the imperial house, causing the ancestral altars to flourish and shine brightly. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed the title of Chan Master Fayu upon him.

Renwu, the first month of the first year of the Ningchong era. On the occasion of Emperor Zhezong’s one-year mourning period (daixiang), an imperial edict was issued for the elders of the Six Schools to enter the palace to discourse on Chan.
After Chan Master Yue ascended the seat, the Imperial Pharmacist attended the proclamation of Elder Weiyue of Jingyin Monastery to expound upon Prajñā.

Profoundly reviving the tradition of his school, he was specially granted the title of Chan Master Furi (Sun of the Buddha) along with ten official certificates from the Ministry of Sacrifices and gifts of gold and silk.

Lord Li Duan, a Palace Guardian, wished to recommend him for ceremonial robes. The Great King of Jingzhou submitted a memorial requesting the bestowal of the honorary title Chan Master Huijue (Wisdom Enlightenment), and the Imperial Ancestral Temple personally inscribed the two characters "Fayu" (Dharma Rain) to grant to him.
The Master’s name was Weiyue; he was the son of the Chen family of Changxi in Fuzhou, and at the age of seven...
He entered Xilin Tianfu Chan Monastery to leave the household life, where he received the tonsure under Master Che. Traveling to study, he visited Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben;
when Emperor Shen宗 summoned Ben to reside at Hui-lin Monastery, the Master followed him into the capital and served as the head of the assembly at Hui-lin.
Yuanzhao returned to his native place. The Master resided at Huayan and later moved to Jingyin. Subsequently, he requested leave to return to his home country, and Yuanzhao complied with this wish.
He passed away while seated at Gushan. Upon cremation, countless śarīras were found, which were divided and interred; stupas were erected at Xilin.
In the second month, Chen Ju, the Commissioner for Transport in Hebei, submitted a memorial stating that Huang Tingjian had composed the inscription for the Chengtian Monastery in Jingnan.

Its summary reads: "When Confucian scholars discuss the expenses of a single Buddhist temple, they say it is equivalent to the assets of a hundred middle-class families and is truly a parasite upon the grain and silk of the common people;
even I would say this is so. However, the good people in the world are few, while the evil are many..."
The punishments and rewards of kings govern the external; the calamities and blessings of the Buddha govern the internal.
Thus, for the teachings of the world, what small contribution could there not be? Yet Confucianists constantly seek to conjoin them while suppressing one—what kind of logic is this?
Because of this, Tingjian incurred slander and defamation, which ultimately led to his journey to Yizhou (according to the *Biannian*).

In the ninth month of the third year, Chongning Temple was established; this was because Cai Jing, noting that the Imperial Birthday was drawing near, requested that temples be established in all prefectures and regional capitals, and the request was granted.
The imperial decree sent to Cai Jing and Qin Yu stated: "Now that the Tianjing Festival is imminent..."
The whole world inclines its heart [toward you]. We look up with reverence as the Buddha’s vehicle transforms and guides all classes of beings.
If you would permit me to present this humble memorial, it would surely increase the auspicious blessings of my sincere aspirations (and so forth).

On the occasion of the Heavenly Peace Festival (Tiānníngjié), the Emperor summoned various eminent masters of the Chan and doctrinal schools into the inner palace and bestowed upon them Dharma robes and the honorary title of "Master of Precious Enlightenment" (Bǎojiào Shīhào).
The nun Hui-guang, Master of Pure Wisdom (Jìngzhì Dàshī) at Miaohui Temple in the Eastern Capital, was the daughter of the Fan family of Chengdu.
He was also included among them. Consequently, the assembly was ordered to preach the Dharma according to their seniority. When it was Guang’s turn at the end of the sequence, he ascended the seat;

after the question-and-answer session was concluded, he looked out over the great assembly and said: "If we speak of Chan or discuss the Way, then the great Chan masters have already finished speaking on those matters.
When it comes to me, a mountain monk, what could I possibly say here? Have you not seen the former sages say: 'A thousand kinds of words, ten thousand varieties...'"
[The Master] said, "I understand. I only wish to instruct you that your mind must not be obscured. Since it is thus, how is it ultimately? He then covered his head with his dharma robe.
After a long silence, he said, "With the patched robe covering the head, all matters cease. At this moment, even this mountain monk understands nothing at all.
Thereupon he descended from the seat. Among the tens of thousands of monastics and laypeople who heard him, there was none who did not sigh in admiration (from the *Sengzhuan*).
Chan Master Wugai of Suzhou Yong’an Temple was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Huilin Chan Temple in the Great State Preceptor’s Monastery.
Empress Dowager Huigong once saw him from beneath the palace curtains; after his audience with the Emperor concluded, he ascended into the air and departed.

From that time on, she had the imperial cuisine prepared by the Grand Kitchen offered as sustenance for the Master, and ordered that the remains of what the Master had eaten be returned to the palace. Furthermore, because of the [Master’s] spiritual power over the earth...
Brocade. He had a dharma robe manufactured and personally attached a meditation plaque to it before bestowing it upon him, to manifest his sincerity in serving the Dharma.
During the winter months, he bestowed upon him a red brocade canopy, as well as various items such as clothing and utensils, all of which were illuminated by the dharma robes granted from the palace.
[Fayan] returned these gifts to Fayun and Fozhao. Fozhao, in turn, sent them to Bao Feng’s Zantang, saying: "This brocade dharma robe is for you, my dharma brother."
He practiced the Way of his former masters. When Zhantang entered nirvana, he remained to preside over the mountain gate (same source).
The Grand Marshal Chen Liangbi invited Chan Master Cheng of Jingyin, along with Fazen, Yuanwu, Cishou, and the Great Dharma Master, to a vegetarian feast at his residence.
At that time, Emperor Huizong went there in private to observe the dharma assembly; he was well-versed in the Avatamsaka Sutra.
He questioned the various Chan masters before the assembly, saying: "The Buddha established his teachings, ranging from the Small Vehicle to the Perfect and Sudden.
One must first sweep away emptiness and quiescence to personally realize true permanence; only then, adorned by the myriad dharmas, can one be called a Buddha.

Yet a Chan master’s single shout transforms an ordinary person into a sage. This seems to contradict the various sutras and treatises. Now, if this single shout can penetrate the five teachings, it is [acceptable]."
"To speak correctly: if one cannot enter [this], it is called false speech. The various Chan masters were sincere.

Cheng said, "Regarding what the Dharma Master has asked, it is insufficient for the three great Chan masters to provide a response. The junior Elder of Jingyin can cause the Dharma Master to be free from delusion.
Cheng then summoned Shanshan. Shanshan responded with an assent. Cheng said, "What the Dharma Master calls 'Buddha-dharma' is the Hinayana."
The Teaching has its meanings. The Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna is the meaning of being neither existent nor empty. The Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna is the meaning of being both existent and empty simultaneously.
The Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle is the meaning of being non-empty yet not existent, and not existent yet non-empty—just like my single shout.
It is not only that he can enter the five teachings; even as for the hundred crafts, the various arts, and the hundred schools of thought, he can enter them all.
Truly, when Cheng gave a shout, he asked Shan, "Did you hear it? Shan replied, "I heard it. Cheng said, "Since you heard it, then this shout exists;
thus you have succeeded in entering the Hinayana teaching. A moment later, he called Shan again and asked, "Did you hear it?"
[The Master] said, "I did not hear it. Cheng said, "Since you did not hear it, then this one shout is non-existent;

thus, you can enter the Initial Teaching (Shijiao). Again, he looked at Shan and said, 'When I first gave the shout, you said it existed. Now that the sound has long since faded, you say it does not exist.

To say it does not exist implies that what was initially real is now gone; to say it exists implies that what currently is real was previously absent. Being neither existent nor non-existent, one can enter the Final [Teaching]. "
Jiao Cheng also said: "When I have one shout, that 'having' is not merely having; it is having because of non-having.
When I do not have one shout, that 'non-having' is not merely non-having; it is non-having because of having. Thus, being and non-being are simultaneous, enabling one to enter the Sudden Teaching."
Cheng also said: "This one shout of mine does not function as a single shout; it transcends existence and non-existence, and both intellectual understanding and conceptualization are forgotten.
When the Way is present, not even a speck of dust stands; when the Way is absent, it stretches across the void. It is precisely this one shout."
One hundred thousand million *he*-cries enter into this one *he*-cry; this is what it means to enter the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
When Shan suddenly rose from his seat, he bowed twice before Cheng. Cheng spoke again to Shan, saying: "It is not only the case that a single *he*-cry is thus;
even down to speech and silence, movement and stillness—at all times, in all places, regarding all things and all affairs—it is the same."

It accords with both principle and capacity, being comprehensive and leaving nothing out. Thereupon, the fourfold assembly rejoiced at hearing what they had never heard before, and the Emperor’s countenance was filled with great delight (from the *Monastic Biographies*).
Jia-shen (May 16), the third year of Chongning. An imperial decree was issued to bring the Buddha’s tooth relic into the palace.
As the *śarīra* fell through a crystal casket, they descended like raindrops. The Emperor praised it, saying: “The Great Being Śākyamuni Is equal to a single speck of dust in the void.
To all who seek him he responds; In every land he manifests his body. As pure as jade, his thousand-spoked wheel is bright; Refined a hundred times, his diamond remains new. I...”
Now I pay respectful homage. May his universal vows deliver all classes of beings. Prime Minister Zhang Gong Shangying said:
"The Emperor Huizong knew that I was fond of Buddhism, and he once spoke of this matter to me in person."
The Imperial Praise of the Lotus Sutra says: "The sacred texts of all Buddhas are truly worthy of praise; The seven fascicles of the Lotus Sutra are as flawless as jade.
Generations of princes have offered worship to it, And successive emperors have presented incense and flowers. To uphold it upon one’s head exhausts the sins of kalpas of poverty;
To take refuge in it surely evokes blessings as vast as the sands of the Ganges. A single phrase brings immediate transcendence beyond Buddha-nature; Why need one speak further outside the gate?"
The Three Vehicles (along with the preceding "Peaceful and Great Prosperity Seal").
Summer of the second year of Zhenghe. On the sixteenth day of the fourth month, the Right Street Monk Registrar, Great Master Ciyun Shanyin, presented a petition at the Imperial Court, stating:

"I humbly submit that for the sake of the Buddhist teachings, on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, by imperial decree, [the office] was established as the Bureau of Daoist Records (Daolu). Dong...

I, Nan Yun, submit this petition. Regarding all matters concerning the destruction of the Han Celestial Master and others by the Buddhist clergy, I have had the relevant authorities consult the currently circulating Tripitaka to identify and destroy such texts.
Furthermore, I now venture to address Your Majesty’s court, despite the risk of being intrusive, to present these observations.

It is essential that the Great Canon of the monasteries throughout the empire—which was originally commissioned for carving, printing, and distribution by the imperial decrees of the Great Ancestor and the Second Ancestor—be preserved.
It has circulated through the capital’s monasteries and the residences of the empresses and consorts; the scriptures in the Gongdeyuan Library were likewise bestowed by our present dynasty.
Furthermore, the *Bianzheng lun* was once included in the *Chongwen zonglu* by Emperor Renzong, as if it were a book from the Imperial Archives.
To suddenly incinerate such works would be something that the heart of a gentleman could not bear. We reverently reflect upon the State:

When the task was accomplished and order established, and when government and instruction flourished, the ancestral lineages were revered; as for all existing books, there is no precedent for their destruction.
Take for instance Yangzi, whose words "beating down benevolence and righteousness" and "extinguishing ritual and music" are yet called by the world an indictment of Laozi.
Furthermore, Zhuangzi composed chapters such as "The Robber Zhi" and "The Fisherman," yet the world says these are slanders against Confucius. Nevertheless...
Yet the Way of Laozi flourished ever more, and the Way of Confucius became increasingly prominent.
This is why Mencius had the cautionary words regarding the total reliance on books. It is clear that those who disparage [a teaching] are in fact honoring it.

Today, within the Daoist tradition, there are treatises such as the *Huzheng lun* (Treatise on Protecting the Correct) and the *Chuxie lun* (Treatise on Eliminating the Heterodox), which revile and reject the followers of Śākyamuni; their harmfulness is great. Yet the Buddhist school has never...

We beg for the removal of these slanders. We humbly entreat Your Excellency’s compassionate favor to examine this matter in detail, so that the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism shall not be permitted to mutually disparage one another, but instead take gentleness and non-contention as their primary concern.
May each maintain its own Way, thereby contributing even in a small measure to the Great Qing’s efforts to promote civilization.
We pray that a specific imperial edict be issued to prohibit the citation of words that revile the Daoist teachings, and to exempt them from searches and confiscations.

"The inclusion of the Tripiṭaka in the imperial canon would be a great blessing for the world. Thereupon, the matter was reported to the imperial court. On the eleventh day of the sixth month, a sacred edict was issued in accordance with the petition.
Three years later, a large tree by the roadside in Jiazhou was broken by the wind. An official investigating bandits saw within the trunk of the tree...

There was a monk whose beard and hair covered his body and whose fingernails and toenails reached his waist. He subsequently reported this to the court, and by imperial decree, he was ordered to be carried on a sedan chair to the palace.
At that time, the Dharma Master Sūtradhara from India brought him out of his samādhi with a golden gong and asked, "In what era’s lineage does this monk belong?"
It is said that the Eastern Jin monk Huichi, while traveling to Mount Emei at an unspecified time, asked whether his elder brother Master Huiyuan was still alive.
Zongchi replied, "Dharma Master Huiyuan passed away seven hundred years ago. Thereupon, Huichi ceased speaking. He then asked, "Now that I have arrived here, to which direction do you wish to return?
[Huichi] replied, "To the marketplace of Chenliu. The Emperor then ordered an artist to paint a portrait of the Master and distribute it throughout the realm.
He traveled on. He was further granted three verses which said: "The ancient adept of seven hundred years— Who can know the news from within his samādhi?

How could he compare to one who returned to the West with a single shoe? Birth and death are but vain labor; wood has no skin. "One mountain is hidden in the marsh, and thus the body is hidden as well.
In all under heaven there is no place to hide; the Way may be approached directly. I send word to Zhuang Zhou: do not attempt to deliberate upon it. It is not found within the trees..."

This is a man carrying a burden and hurrying along. The bodies of these two sentient beings are not insentient matter; they are the very bodies of each person within the state of meditative absorption.
If you can realize that Bodhi has never had a tree, there is no need for arduous toil—this is Lu Neng (from the *Wuku*).
Dingyou (the seventh year), the fourth month of summer. The assembled ministers presented a memorial enthroning him as the Emperor Daojun, the Master of the Way.
The edict issued from the Daoist Academy stated in brief: "I am the eldest son of the Supreme God, serving as the Celestial Lord of the Great Void.

Moved by compassion for the land of China being subjected to the teachings of the golden barbarians, I have entreated the Supreme God to become a sovereign of men, so that the world may return to the True Way. You, my ministers..."
A memorial was submitted proposing that I be enthroned as the "Lord of the Way, the Preceptor of the Teaching" (Daojun), with this title to be used exclusively within the religious community.
Shortly thereafter, an edict was issued for Wang Fu, Grand Master for Literary Composition and Director of the Academy; Cai You, Academician of the Xuanhe Hall;

and others to attend the Xuanhe Hall to witness the descent of Shenxiao. Wang Fu composed a record of the event and presented it to me. From then on, matters involving supernatural anomalies were not recorded in full.

Lin Lingsu was enfeoffed as a "Golden Gate Feathered Guest" (*jīnmén yùkè*). He submitted a memorial requesting that all Buddhist temples and Daoist monasteries throughout the empire be renamed Shengxiao Palaces (*shénxiāo gōng*).
The Emperor granted his request. While Lingsu lectured on the scriptures within the palace, the Emperor set up a curtained screen beside him. Lingsu would have someone from below pose questions;
however, what he said contained nothing extraordinary or sublime, being instead interspersed with vulgar and humorous chatter. The Emperor and those above and below [the screen] were [amused].

He laughed heartily. There was no longer any ritual of sovereign and subject. Could he be called an enlightened ruler? An imperial decree was issued to all temples throughout the realm, ordering them to be renamed Tianning Wanshou Guan (Temple of Ten Thousand Years of Peace and Longevity).
Shortly thereafter, they were further renamed Shenxiao Yuqing Wanshou Gong (Palace of the Jade Purity and Ten Thousand Years of Longevity of the Divine Empyrean) (both from the preceding *Biannian*).

Jihai (the first year of the Xuanhua era), the first month of the first year of Xuanhua: An imperial edict was issued to change the title of the Buddha to "Great Awakened Golden Immortal" (*Dajue Jinxian*);

all others were to be called "Immortals" (*xianren*) or "Great Beings" (*dashen*). Monks were to be addressed as "Virtuous Persons" (*deshi*), and those under the age of twenty were to be called "Virtuous Boys" (*detong*), wearing the attire of the Way (*dao*). However, their way-caps (*daoguan*) were to bear insignia.
His virtue was preeminent beyond all praise; furthermore, he took monasteries as palaces and cloisters as observatories. He designated nuns as "women of virtue" and monks as "sages.

The Buddha was granted the robes of the Celestial Honored One, while the Sangha followed the Daoist tradition by wearing crowns. They prohibited bronze gongs and the casting of stupas and images. Alas, how strange! (As before).

Chan Master Dao of Wenshu Monastery in Changde Prefecture ascended the hall to address the assembly after changing his monastic robes, saying: "The matter of the Patriarch’s coming from the West is, this morning, exceptionally new.
Formerly I bore the appearance of a bhikṣu; now I wear the form of the Lord Lao. I don a silver-brown robe over a crane-feather cloak and wrap my head in a *bāoyè* (banana-leaf) turban.
A guest of the forest and springs with nothing to do, I have received the sovereign's grace twice over. Thus it is said: 'If you wish to know the Buddha..."*
Regarding the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*), one should contemplate the seasonal causes and conditions. Let us say: what is the season right now?

Vairocana wears a jeweled crown to manifest that within the ultimate there is the conventional; Mañjuśrī, appearing as an old man, dons a crane-feather cloak to conform to the exigencies of the times.
If it is so for this one person, it is so for all others. Everyone should firmly establish the monastic groves; this is a source of joy.
They gathered with the assembly of immortals to drink together the *míxiān* wine, chanting the *bùxū* verses in unison.

Some read the *Língbǎo dùrén jīng*, while others discussed the elixirs of longevity and immortality. Beneath the moon, they played the zither, their fingertips emitting the sounds of primordial antiquity.
Spread out like a chessboard before the hall, a sublime move emerges beyond the realm of divine mechanisms. To take one step forward is to reach the heavens of the Great Brahma;
to retreat one step is to remain within the city of the Nine Darknesses. But what if one neither advances nor retreats?

Even if you were to transcend and transform upon the path of the Three Purities, it would still ultimately be but a single illusory body caught in saṃsāra. (Stone Inscription from the Original Temple)
The *Zhaosong Gong Chen Guanjianzhai Zouyi* states: "Confucianism and Buddhism differ in their outward manifestations (*ji*) but are identical in their Way (*dao*).

Those who do not know how to employ them properly rely on their manifestations; the fasting and purification rites of the Liang dynasty and the quest for immortals under the Han dynasty are examples of this.
Those who skillfully employ their own minds are like our imperial ancestors. To rely on the manifestations leads to stagnation, and once one is stagnant, [the Way] becomes susceptible to being lost."

To attack: if one employs their mind, there will be penetration; once penetrated, nothing can be further debated. The traces of Han Liang may be subjected to attack, but who can debate the mind of the Founding Ancestors?
By employing the "non-action" (*wuwei*) of Laozi, these people were allowed to rest;
by employing the "beneficiality" of the Śākya (Buddhism), none in the world could contend with them. These are the proven effects already realized by the Ancestors.
Laozi said, "The wise do not speak. The Śākya [Buddha] said, "Cease, cease! Do not speak. Confucius said, "Be silent and take note of it.
These were the practices personally enacted by our ancestors; how could they be conjectured or discussed by those who merely rely on words?
(From the *Song Bianian*).

In the ninth month of the second year, an imperial decree was issued to reinstate the teachings. Monks of the Śākya and Bodhisattva orders throughout the empire were permitted to retain their traditional titles.
After Master Wenshu resumed his teaching, he ascended the hall and said: "I do not don the robes of a monk, but wear the feathered garments; I have taken on the form of the Old Lord."
These signs seem quite appropriate. For over a year and a half, I have reflected quietly upon them: in general, both prosperity and decline each have their own appointed time.

Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, repeatedly prophesied that the Dharma would face difficulties; this is clearly recorded within the teachings, and there is no one who does not know it in detail. When comparing these with the current era...

At this very time, Māra seized the opportunity to confuse the orthodox tradition: monks altered their monastic forms, the Buddha’s name was changed, false interpretations were fabricated, and the scriptural texts were edited and excised.
The sound of the gongs and cymbals ceased, while the begging bowls were made to appear full. Through various kinds of deceitful frauds, they sought to mislead the Sagely Sovereign.
Fortunately, our Emperor, by virtue of his sagely character and sagely brilliance, did not forget the sacred entrustment and did not allow the Teaching to fall into ruin.
A special imperial edict was bestowed and promulgated throughout the realm, permitting monks and nuns to once again don their robes and shave their heads.

This is truly like cold ashes catching fire again or withered wood flourishing anew. Without abandoning their worldly forms, they have assumed the form of monastics; without departing from the realm of Māra, they have entered the realm of the Buddha.

The Dharma drum resounds once more, and the collapsing order is restored. Those who were lost in the wine of immortals are transformed into those partaking of the ambrosial jade nectar. They walk forth...
Empty words are transformed into songs for returning home. Setting down the silver and wooden tablets, one picks up the *niṣīdana* mat.
Yesterday, one bowed with hands clasped; today, one greets with "I bow" and "How do you do? It is only the old manner that has changed, not the old person.
"I venture to ask: were there one or two people here in the assembly in the past? After a long silence, he said: "Even the autumn wind knows how to loathe disorder;
it has blown away the ashes of the Way from those years. (From a stone inscription at this temple.)
Jiachen (the 6th year of the Xuanhua era), during the Shangyuan Festival. The Emperor was observing the lanterns from atop the palace tower.

The curtains and screens were so thick and dense that those below had no way of knowing what transpired above. Suddenly, a man leaped out from among the crowd; he wore black cloth garments and pointed his finger at the curtain, saying to the Emperor:
"What deity do you possess that you dare to destroy my teaching? Now I tell you: retribution is imminent. The Emperor—
He was extremely enraged. He dispatched an imperial messenger to issue an edict for his execution. The Emperor was deeply displeased and, as a result, abandoned his evening revelry for one night.
The man was handed over to the prison to be dealt with, yet in the end, it remained unknown who he was (from the *Yeshi*).

In the year Bingwu, the Qinzhong Emperor ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jingkang. In the first month, the Jin generals Wao-li-pu (Wanyan Li-nu) and Nian-han (Wanyan Shuo) attacked the capital.
They requested an audience with the Emperor, who went to Qingcheng. After two nights, he returned to the palace.

Ziyou composed a record for the monks' hall at Qixian. Upon reading it, one feels a chilling awe; it is as if a cliff were collapsing and flying down, and the Wei River were rushing by, its cold piercing to the bone.
When Liu Yiweng met with Master Foyin, the latter was quite self-important. When Chan Master Zhenjing Wen came to visit, he went to Guizong.
In the Dharma Hall, he saw Liu. Liu immediately asked, "Venerable sir, how many years have you been performing this play? Jing said, "I am here specifically to listen for the musicians.
Liu said, "I do not enter this association. Jing said, "What can be done? You are currently right in the midst of the performance.
As Liu hesitated, Jing clapped his hands and said, "Frog Zen—only a single leap! Later, while sitting together, Liu pointed to his patched robe and said:
"What do you call this? Jing said, "A Zen robe. Liu asked, "What is Zen? Jing then shook out his sleeves and said, "I cannot shake it out.
Liu remained silent. Jing then gave him a blow and said, "Your skill is such as this;
did you think you could test the old monk? Liu merely bowed his head.
The Prefect, Duke Wenkang Wang Shu, upon meeting Chan Master Cizhao, presented this verse to Chan Master Daguan:

"Government is simple, cutting off the clamor of the dust; Because of you, the Master, I have opened the northern window. The essence is subtle, barely manifesting stillness; My ears are heavy, wishing to forget all words."

The Buddhas and Patriarchs have two layers of faults; mountains and rivers are swallowed in a single gulp. You, Master, are now one who knows this; setting this aside, with whom else could one discuss it?
The Master approved of this. Li Duanyuan asked Chan Master Daguan Ying: "When a person dies, where do they go? He replied: "If you do not yet know life, how can you know death?"
“[I] know death. Li said. “As for birth, I already know it. The Master asked, “From where does birth come? Li hesitated.
The Master gripped his chest and said, “Right here, what are you thinking about? Li said, “I understand. I only knew the journey was long; I did not realize I had lost my way.
The Master pushed him away and said, “A hundred-year dream—only today have I finally awakened. He then asked, “Heaven...”

"Regarding the hells of the hall: are they ultimately existent or non-existent? The Master said: "Even the Buddhas have no words to speak of them. It is like having eyes yet seeing flowers in the sky;
it is like seeking the moon in water that is not there. It is truly laughable to see a prison before one's very eyes and yet fail to seek heaven beyond the mind.
One simply does not realize that joy and fear reside in the mind, and that good and evil constitute the objective realm. Great Minister, you need only understand this."
"Your own mind is naturally free from delusion. Li asked, "How does one bring the mind to clarity? The Master replied, "Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all.
Li further asked, "Where does the mind return? The Master said, "I ask the Grand Marshal to return to your residence. Li then drank his wine in silence and departed.
Li Duanyi observed this and asked Chan Master Daguan, "How can one reach the Western Pure Land?
The Master said, "Right now you are sitting amidst carved beams and painted rafters, yet you still wish to be born in the Western Pure Land. You prefer the artificial over the real.
Li asked, "Is it that the Buddha is not truthful? The Master replied, "The Buddha is not false; it is simply that you, Great Minister, are deluded. How could I [be at fault]?"
[The Master] said, "You have fallen into delusion. The Master continued, "If it were not delusory, why would one seek the Pure Land of the West?
Generally speaking, 'Pure Land' refers to the nature of purity. The 'West' is the place where the sun sets; it is intended to serve as a place for people to turn toward and take refuge in.
To know this place of refuge is itself the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī). Li then expressed his gratitude and departed.
The scholar Dao Jingchun asked Daguan, "What use does Buddhism have for the world? The Master said, "It is indispensable in our daily lives. Dao Jingchun asked, "How is it used?
The Master said, "When it is in the eye, it is called seeing; when it is in the ear, it is called hearing. Dao Jingchun asked, "What does that have to do with the Buddha?
The Master said, "If it did not concern the affairs of the Buddha, what would constitute seeing and hearing? Dao Jingchun said, "One naturally possesses eyes and ears."
The Master said: "All people, Buddhas, and even non-Buddhas have ears and eyes; it is only because they lack Buddhahood that they are unable to see and hear.
'Buddha' has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*); because one possesses right awakening, one is called a Buddha. If one lacks right vision, all is but false understanding.
One need not wear flames upon one's head or tread upon lotus flowers; the yellow scrolls and red volumes constitute the Buddha-dharma. (Jing)
He attained realization through pure silence (as recorded in the *Sengbaozhuan*).
Duan Shizi was a native of Wuxing. Upon first witnessing the performance of the lion dance, he awakened to the essential point of the mind. He resided on Mount Xi Yu.

He was able to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. When people of Hu-lake vied with one another to invite him, he received a hundred coins; he then opened his case, recited a few lines, and departed with the money.
He was fond of singing the lyrics of the "Fisherman. When Chancellor Zhang Zhitou invited him to ascend the seat, he ordered Yu Xiulao to compose a preface, which said:
"Before the seven cases of the Lotus Sūtra have been recited, the single note of the Fisherman is heard first. At the end...
When he reached this point, he gestured with his hand in a dismissive manner and said, "Stop, stop! He then sat down and chanted in a drawn-out tone:
"Originally a fisherman of Xiao and Xiang, wandering east, west, south, and north. The assembly responded with a chorus of acclaim. Wudeng looked at them with a smile and said:
"I contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. [The Master] descended from his seat. Hearing of his reputation, Qin Shaoyou one day traveled to Gaoyou.
Qin invited him to ascend the seat at Guanghui Temple, whereupon the Master pointed with his hand and said: "In the heavens there is no peerless moon;
in the human world there is but this single monk. In this hall, the wind is cool and still; through the ages, the meaning is clear. Shaoyou was moved to tears.
During the Xining era, when the Duke of Zheng, Fu, was stationed at Bozhou, he invited Chan Master Yong of Huayan in Yingchuan to ascend the seat.
Upon seeing the Master’s gaze and movements, which were like those of an elephant king turning in circles, the Duke felt a subtle realization; he then hurried to the abbot’s quarters.
He ordered an attendant monk to enter the room. Upon seeing him, the Master said, "The Excellency has already entered; Fu Bi is still outside.

When Gong heard this, sweat poured down his back, and he immediately attained great awakening to the essence of the mind. Later, while living in Luoyang after his retirement from office, he sent a verse to Dharma Master Yongde and Chan Master Yuanzhao, which read:
"Because I saw Master Yongde, my realization and entry became profound; Through successive conditions, I received the transmission of the Elder Master."

My heart. To the southeast, I speak in vain of the distance between mountains and rivers; yet my eyes now face the Lingguang and Miaoyin [Pagodas]. Your letter says: "I, Bi, have devoted myself to the ancestral Way for many days.
I have always regretted not meeting a person of clear vision who could open up my ignorance and coarseness. Although I have long heard of your eminent virtue, I had no means to pay you a visit.
Yesterday, by good fortune, I was appointed to govern Haozhou; as the districts of Hao and Yingchuan share a common border, I have therefore..."

Mr. Zhang Bishu Jingshan invited Master Yong to visit him. They stayed together for nearly a month, during which time the Master, through the power of his compassion and skillful means, enabled me to attain a realization.
However, as the summer retreat was approaching, I had to return abruptly to Yingzhou in the fourth month.

Regarding the process of polishing and refining my practice, I have not yet achieved any significant merit; old age and illness persist, and my dull faculties find it difficult to enter the path. As the ancients said...
As the Master of Spirits has said: "I did not expect that, approaching old age, I would hear of the ultimate matter.
Today, I have seen it in you, Bi. What a blessing! What a blessing! Although I received the Dharma from Master Yong, its original source comes from you, the Old Monk.
Your lineage is most authentic and must be upheld; I wish to maintain it as well. I pray further that you will bestow your compassion upon me, accepting me and granting me your distant grace.
To guide and lead others: to cause those who have not yet arrived to arrive. This is precisely what Nan-yueh did for Pang Yun, and what Pai-chang did for Pei Hsiu.
How could they be any different? (From the *Yan-xing-lu*)
One evening at dusk, Sima Wen Gong saw Kangjie and said, "Tomorrow the monk Xiuyong will open the hall to preach the Dharma.
Lord Zheng wishes to go with you to listen. Although Lord Zheng was poor and could not be persuaded regarding the Buddha, he nevertheless went.
This was not convenient from a logical standpoint. Later, when Guang (Zhang Shangying) advanced [to speak] without dispersing his words, he said, "Master, why do you not stop him?

Kangjie replied, "I regret that I heard of this too late. The next day, Duke Zheng indeed went forward. Later, when Kangjie saw Duke Zheng, he said to him, "When you were at the third command, Your Honor did not rise;
when a monk opened the hall, Your Honor then came out. Duke Zheng was startled and said, "Bi did not yet know of your thoughts" (as before).

Former Clerk Lü Dàlín submitted this memorial to you, Your Honor, on behalf of [his] elder brother: "I, Dàlín, shall explain it. In antiquity, the Three Ducal Ministers had no official duties; only those possessing virtue occupied these positions.
When the Great Way was not yet clearly understood, people gravitated toward heterodox studies. Failing to enter the teachings of Śākyamuni, they then entered the systems of Zhuangzi and Laozi.
They harbored doubts that the Sages had not exhausted all truths, and they held the rites and righteousness in low esteem, deeming them unworthy of study. Thus it was.
This has led to the obscurity of human relations and the withering of all things.
Now that you, a great man of mature virtue, possess a heart of compassion, it would be no difficulty for you to take the Way upon yourself and restore fallen customs through your public efforts.

As for the refinement of the spirit and transformation of the breath, seeking only longevity—this is the preference of those who dwell in mountain valleys and withdraw from the world to cultivate themselves alone; how could it be otherwise?

"This is what the world expects of you, sir. The Master smiled but did not answer. Consequently, when Zhang Biyu Yin used his power and status to overawe the monk, the Master wrote him a letter, saying:
"Among those of the Chan school, when they encounter matters that are overly elaborate and lack directness, they call them 'entanglements' (geteng).
They often treat such things with contempt and ridicule; thus, I have composed a 'Song of Entanglements,' which is included in my collected works."
I, Bi Gu, have previously witnessed the reasons for this; thus, I shall now attempt to deliberate with you upon the matter. I do not know what you think.
Generally speaking, there is a fundamental distinction between the nature and understanding of worldly people and that of monastics; their life stories differ significantly in many respects.
Furthermore, monks have been ordained since childhood and have long spent their days reading the sutras; thus, all that they hear and see consists of Buddhist affairs.
After shaving their heads, they travel in groups, going wherever they wish to go.

Beyond practicing Zen and seeking the Way, they have extensively gathered what they have seen and heard among the assembly, and their speech has been further refined and tempered by the eyes of their teachers. Suddenly, upon encountering a person of clear vision, as soon as—
Once you have set it aside and established yourself, you will possess a point of view; you can then take all that you have previously seen and heard as evidence for your own practice.
How clear and unimpeded this is! As for people like us, worldly folk, we have been steeped in the affairs of the world since our youth.
Upon reaching adulthood, one marries, raises children, labors for food and clothing, and runs about in pursuit of official service.

As for the yellow scrolls and red axes [of the scriptures], they often never even enter one's hands. Even when one seizes leisure to read and contemplate them, it serves merely as material for conversation;

how could one ever have penetrated their underlying principle? Furthermore, the scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants are each bound by their respective vocations; how could they know of the Dharma of the monastic groves?
As for the matter of "seeking instruction": by what means could one possibly go about it?
Where is there anyone traveling the mountains in a group to practice Zen and inquire after the Way, or to form such extensive covenants?

Even if a person of clear vision were to happen upon such an opportunity by chance, and lacked even a single flavor of diligent practice, how much could they possibly ask, and how much could they possibly attain? Furthermore, there would be nothing to ask.
Having seen this, they take their own experience as evidence and no longer engage in extensive investigation. Their depth is like that of one drilling for water;

having obtained but a single word or half-phrase, and being by no means yet clear, they immediately gaze at the clouds in the sky and point their nostrils toward heaven. They claim, "I have already surpassed the Buddhas and transcended the patriarchs;
all the sages stand beneath my shadow. Thus, they do not deign to look upon the Buddhist sutras or Chan records, using them as a pretext to avoid entanglement.
Regarding the "Lament of the Wisteria," my humble view is that I am deeply apprehensive. As for me, Bi, if I were not to study Chan, I would let it be;

but since I have already prepared my body and mind to study it, I must proceed with meticulous care and circumspection. I must probe deeply and search far, penetrating to the very summit and the very bottom, reaching through to the bone and the marrow.
Only when everything is spontaneously manifest, luminous and pure, and free from even a speck of dust or a trace of obscuration, will I dare to cast down the hook.

This book [of mine]—this matter is no small one. You must directly cast off the root of birth and death from beginningless kalpas, as well as that which governs birth and death, and only then will you be able to contend with Old Man Yama.

Do not allow yourself to be misled by the idle talk of common people, taking it as your study; do not let yourself be deceived by such things. My sincere wish. (The above is from the *Yōngōroku* and *Kidan*).
When the Duke served as Chancellor, he was enfeoffed as the Duke Wenzhong of Han. Upon retiring from office and returning home, he devoted himself daily to the profound study of Buddhist learning.
He once studied under the masters Wuben and Huayan Yong, and his state of thorough realization and awakening was always evident in his speech and demeanor. Ah!

To reach such a sudden and clear understanding of this matter while at the pinnacle of human status—truly, he may be called a man of immeasurable capacity. Yin-zhi’s writings are profoundly penetrating.

He was profoundly enlightened and could also expound the meaning of the Dharma to Master Yuanzhao. He recounted the history of the lineage, citing how Master Guling, in his final years, had the opportunity to hear the ultimate teaching;
he considered this for himself, saying, "How could I be deceiving others?"
When Minister Zhang Shangying was serving as the grain transport commissioner for Jiangxi, he visited Chan Master Zhaojue of Donglin and interrogated him regarding his realization.
Finding that their views were in perfect accord, Zhang certified him, saying: "My Dharma heir Cigu Jing resides at Yuxi;
he is also one with whom you may converse. Furthermore, Gong Dezhuang spoke of Doushui Yue, noting that he was a person of keen intelligence. Consequently, Zhang proceeded to [investigate] him.

When Fubogufenning arrived, the various Chan masters came out to welcome him. First he paid his respects to Yuxi Ci, then to the other mountain masters, and finally he asked Yue about the Master, saying, "I have heard that you are skilled in literary composition.
Yue laughed heartily and said, "The Commissioner has lost one of his eyes!
Since I am a ninth-generation descendant of Linji, for me to discuss literary composition with the Commissioner is just like the Commissioner discussing Chan with me."
Wujin did not agree with this explanation. He then forcefully counted on his fingers and said, "This is nine generations. One day prior, Doushuai had dreamed that the sun was rising in the sky;
he reached out with his hand to seize it and spun it around. This signifies the principle of "turning and circulating.

Wujin heard that the Commissioner would soon pass through there and thought, "I must prick him deeply and strike him painfully. If he is willing to turn his head, it will be a fortunate event for our school. First...
Zuo said, "In these times, gentlemen and officials are accustomed to receiving offerings and service; I fear that if you provoke them, they may act perversely and cause trouble.
Yue said, "Even if it causes my afflictions to regress, there is nothing else to worry about at my monastery. Wujin asked how far it was to Yuxi, and he replied, "Fifteen li.
Dou-shuai said, "At five li, it will already be late; we shall stay overnight at Dou-shuai. Thus, Wujin stayed with him.
Following the pleasant conversation, [Wu-jin] praised Donglin. Yue was unwilling to accept his assessment, so Wu-jin then inscribed a brief verse for the "Waterfall Pavilion" (Pùbù xuān), which said:
"Not seeking its place of descent on Mount Lu; the elephant king’s nostrils needlessly reach the heavens. This was intended as a satire of Yue’s refusal to acknowledge Donglin.
When Gong gradually turned the conversation toward matters of the Chan school, Yue said, "Today, I am discussing the affairs of the Commissioner."
"I am weary. Take care and go to sleep. Later, when the night was deep, Yuan Yue arose and discussed this matter with Wujin.

He burned incense and requested the Buddhas of the ten directions to bear witness, asking, "Since Donglin has already certified you, Administrator, do you have even the slightest doubt regarding the words and teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
The Administrator replied, "I do. Yuan Yue asked, "What words do you doubt? He said, "I doubt the 'Single-Legged' [verse] of Xianglin."
The Verse: Regarding the occasion of Deshan’s alms-bowl, Yue said, "Since you have doubts about this, how can you possibly be without doubt regarding the rest?
As for that final phrase—does it exist or not? Gong replied, "It exists. Yue burst into loud laughter and returned to his quarters.
He closed the door and slept soundly all night without closing his eyes even once. At the fifth watch, he got out of bed and accidentally knocked over the footstool;
suddenly he attained realization, and uttered this verse: "The drum falls silent and the bell has ceased; returning with the alms bowl, a single thrust from Yantou was like a clap of thunder."
"Indeed, you shall live for only three years. [The official] thought, "Could it be that I have encountered his prediction?
He then knocked on the gate of the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have already caught the thief. Zhiyue asked, "Where are the stolen goods? The official was speechless.
Zhiyue said, "Commissioner, please depart; let us meet tomorrow. The following day, the official brought up the previous conversation. Zhiyue then said to him, "To study Chan..."

It is simply that the life-root (*jīvitendriya*) has not yet been severed; one relies on words to produce understanding, and because the vital energy is exhausted and strength is faint, one unconsciously falls into the realm of sound and form.
You have already attained awakening regarding such teachings as these. However, when it comes to the most subtle point, it causes people to be neither aware nor cognizant of it.
It must be that all sentiments of right and wrong are exhausted and both the ordinary and the sage are eliminated, so that one turns a step out of the path of error. Thus, he composed a verse:
As for the realization: in the midst of ordinary activity, every step is as it should be. When the mind dwells within sounds and forms, how could it be obstructed by existence or non-existence?

With the one mind there is no duality; the myriad dharmas are not distinct. Cease distinguishing between essence and function; do not select between the refined and the coarse. Unimpeded when facing critical moments, responding to things without restriction.
When sentiments of right and wrong are exhausted, both the mundane and the sacred are eliminated. Who gains and who loses? What is near and what is distant? Grasp the head...

He makes a tail where there is no tail; he points to reality as being empty. He turns his body toward the realm of demons and shifts his feet onto the path of the heterodox. Realizing that these are neither contrary nor conforming, one does not violate the essential practice.
The Master said: "One move that hits the mark is the ultimate state of effortless spontaneity. Yet, you must know that beyond east, west, south, and north, there is something else."
Facing the great furnace, he turns it over and hurls it back; appearing and disappearing, moving freely in all directions, he never departs from the conditions of adversity or favor.

As for these present shadows and reflections, if one were to call them "the Lord," they would surely fail to recognize the "Empress. He invited the Master to Jianchang, observing him step by step along the way.
There were ten verses describing these events, to which the Master replied with ten verses of his own. The eighth year of the Yuanyou era.

The eighth month. Master [Xuedou] had three "gates" (kuan), which Master [Yunmen] eulogized as follows: The first says: "Tearing through the weeds to investigate the profound is sought only for the sake of seeing one's nature.
Where, right now, does this person’s nature reside? Master [Yunmen] said: "The summer trees are lush and green, the cuckoo calls; The sun pierces the floating clouds, the universe is clear.
Do not ask Zeng Xi about his father while facing Zeng Shen; I know well that a filial son avoids pronouncing his father’s name."
The second [verse] says: "Only by realizing one's own nature can one be liberated from birth and death. When the light of the eyes falls away, how does one achieve liberation? The Master said:
"When the ghost-messenger arrives with his talisman to fetch him from the human realm, the jeweled crown in heaven is already fading in color. This is the opportune moment for a skillful turn;
do not let Old Yama know of it too easily. The third [verse] says: "Once one has been liberated from birth and death, one knows the place of departure. The four great elements..."
"Where does one part of time go? The Master said: "The drum calls for the wife of Li of East Village; the west wind in the vast wilderness drenches her robes in tears.
By the green reeds and red smartweed on the banks of the Jiangnan, she sits instead as Zhang San upon the fishing pier.
When the Master first led the assembly at Mount Lu, Xie Huisi (Hongshuai) Xiong Botong invited him to reside at Doushuai for five years. One.
One day he spoke a verse, saying: "Forty-eight [years], saints and ordinary people alike have been slain; not a hero indeed. The road at Long'an is slippery.
Then, suddenly, he passed away.
Master Wu-jin and Master Da-hong-en discussed the essentials of Chan and the teachings, exchanging inquiries (as detailed below). In response, [Wu-jin] wrote:

"I have humbly received your profound instructions regarding the *qing-liang* (cooling) and *lin-ji* (Linji) public cases (as detailed below). How can one be 'just so' by departing from these two paths?
That superior man is difficult to confront; one can only retreat three thousand li. As for the separate letter..."

[The Master] wrote a preface to exhaust his feelings. [Dongshan] then sent a separate note to show his gratitude. On the blank paper enclosed within the seal, he wrote a verse to send to Dongshan, saying:
"There is no need to travel three thousand li back; Why must you again inflict thirty strokes of the cane?
All is a true treasure-trove as vast as the sands of the Ganges; At night’s chill, I have burned through every lamp for reading. Dongshan composed four verses in response.
There is no need to run three thousand li backward; vast, clear waves arise from level ground. At the top of the hundred-foot pole, one laughs without ceasing;
Linji and Deshan merely lean their ears toward it. (1) Why must one again inflict thirty blows of the rattan?
Letting go or holding fast—this is the reliance. The Layman’s transmission must surely still exist; the Three Peaks stand like tripods, their blue layers tiered upon tier. (2) All of these are...
The true treasure-trove of the Ganges sands serves, for a time, as a point of refuge for those in the human realm. When arriving, there is no mouth with which to question Lu Neng;
one is startled by the clay ox swallowing the Great Image (3). On a cold night, he picks up the lamp for reading; an old monk with a tattered robe covering his head.
How shameful that Vimalakīrti possessed such great spirit, while I pity myself—sickly and utterly incapable (4). One day, the Master said:
While visiting Cuiyan, Chan Master Ji came out to welcome him. Upon seeing him, the official asked, "What is the scenery of Cuiyan?
Ji replied, "The gate faces the thousand-fathom well of Hongya; the stone bridge divides the waters as they wind around the pines and cypresses. The official took Ji’s hand and said:
"I have long heard of the Master's reputation; why is it that you are like this? Guizong replied, "It was merely by chance. The official then continued:
"A wild monk welcomes guests down from the misty peaks. I ask: what is the meaning of Cuiyan? The gate faces Hongya’s thousand-fathom well;

the stone bridge divides the waters as they wind around pines and cypresses. Joyfully, he returned to the abbot’s quarters. Later, the official visited Shangfeng Temple on Mount Nanyue and saw [the following].
An old monk sat upright. The Master asked, "How many years of age are you? He replied, "Ninety-six. The Master asked, "Are your eyes clear?

He replied, "They are still able to thread a needle. The Master asked, "Are your teeth firm? He replied, "They are still capable of chewing stone lotuses. The Master asked, "Have you ever traveled as a pilgrim (xingjiao)?
He replied, "In my youth, I studied the Way of the Patriarchs. The Master asked, "Whom did you see [as a teacher]? He replied, "Finally, I saw Tong’an. Do you remember?"
"Is there a phrase of the same meaning? [The Master] said: "When facing guests, I never speak of worldly talk; when the water is clear, the fish appears, yet it does not swallow the hook. He asked:
"If one suddenly encounters someone who seizes the clouds and grasps the mist, what then? [The Master] said: "Remember that which is three inches away from the hook;
do not follow the common crowd in looking at things haphazardly. The official immediately lit incense, prostrated himself, and left a verse, saying: "A hundred years of light..."
Lacking four years of my full term, I sit precariously in this aged forest and spring. My eyes are still clear enough to pierce needle and thread;
my teeth remain firm enough to chew stone lotuses. Having traveled extensively to visit the various patriarchs in my youth, I have attained a distinct branch of Chan in my later years.
Had you not come to visit me after passing by, how could I have produced this small volume from within my bag?
Wen Lugu and Lü Shengong were serving as Supervisors of Jingnan when they saw Hao wearing a cloth loincloth.
They wrote letters recommending Hao to the Prefect of the province; by chance, the seat of Dayang was vacant, so they brought him there.

Not long after, Wujin sent a letter saying, "I have long thirsted for your instruction, yet I regret that I am constrained by my official duties and cannot personally attend upon you. Upon seeing the letter, Hao said, "I am no dead man."

He then took up his staff and went to Jingzhu to see Wujin. Later, the Duke invited him to reside at Yuyuan. When he ascended the hall to open the dharma assembly, all the officials were gathered together.
Daoshao ascended the seat, looked out at the great assembly, and said, "Do you not see? After a long silence, he spoke again: "Do you not see?"
Wujin Cao, speaking with a Shu accent, said, "The Master sees you. Hao responded at once, "I only need for the Official to see me," and immediately descended from his seat.

While the Official was at the Jie Tan Yuan (Precept Platform Monastery) in Jiangning Prefecture, he was reading Xuedou’s *Nian Gu* (Capping Phrases on Ancient Cases), reaching the story of Baizhang’s visit to Mazu.
The record states: "Gold from a great forge should not change its color. Suddenly, [Yunmen] threw down the scroll and said, "If this is truly so, how could Linji have his day today?
He then offered this verse: "The Master of Ma’s single shout at Daxiong Peak Caused the skull to go deaf for three days.
When Huangbo heard it, he was startled and stuck out his tongue; From this, the House Style was established in Jiangxi. He then presented this to Master Ping.

After the war had ended, he sent a letter to the Master, saying: "Last summer, while studying the lineage of Linji, I realized deeply that you, Layman, have attained great capacity and great function.
I therefore requested a copy of your previous verse draft. The Master wrote the verse again and sent it to him: "The tongue protruding and the ears deaf—Master, you already know.
Beating one’s chest, one can only cry out to the blue heavens. Performing somersaults within the assembly at Panshan— Only upon reaching this point does one truly understand."
Regarding the eccentric monk Puhua (during the third year of the Daguan era), Master Gongzhuo’s *Record of Zhaohua Monastery* states:

"As for the teaching of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, its Buddhas and the matters of the One Vehicle Bodhisattvas are such that beginning and end are a single thought-moment; past and present are a single instant; cause and effect are a single Buddha. All...
The Sage is of one nature; the ten directions are one land; the three realms are one body; the True, Semblance, and Final Dharma Ages are one teaching;

and the beginning, middle, and end are one limit. Taking the Ten Faiths as the commencement of entering the Buddha-way and the Ten Grounds as the culmination of attaining Buddhahood—the Ten Abidings, Ten Practices, Ten Transferences, Ten Grounds, and the Eleventh Ground—are termed the five stages. Each stage...
"Endowed with ten" means that the *pāramitās* are the primary focus. In the causes and effects of the five stages, there are fifty in each;
adding the five causes and five effects of the fundamental stage itself makes one hundred and ten.
This constitutes the Buddha-field of the Avataṃsaka world and the Dharma-gate of the youth Sudhana. While the Avataṃsaka world consists of one hundred and ten, one is added to it.
Why is this? First, the stage of the Buddha is the cause of all dharmas. The five stages are the dharmas that are indicated.
Sudhana is the person who inquires into the Dharma and puts it into practice.

The temple was granted the name Longxiang Xingqing Chan Temple, and Ruian County was ordered to provide one estate of farmland.

Incense and lamps were provided for these purposes. One hundred and twenty small boats were allocated to serve as official transport. Every year, two novice monks were ordained to repay the Sage’s unfailing grace.
The Emperor bestowed the four characters "Qinghui Yuguang" (Clear Radiance and Bathed Light), which were displayed in the abbot's quarters of the dormitory hall;
the imperial calligraphy remains resplendent upon the rocks and waters to this day.
Xin Hai, the first year of the Shaoxing era (1131), the third month of the first year. An imperial edict was issued summoning Master Ziyuan from Jiangzhou:
“朕 (Zhen) have heard that Master Ziyuan is exclusively devoted to the practice of the Pure Land and possesses profound spiritual conduct.

It is hereby decreed that the local governor be instructed to grant him leave so that he may return to the Imperial Garden to deliver lectures. This edict is issued as a mark of encouragement; it is hoped you will take full cognizance of this. Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued to the Eight [Bureaus].”
Master Zi. Wherever you go, act as my personal representative. I am fully aware that the Sage of Sukhāvatī possesses profound and vast compassionate vows, vowing to receive all sentient beings.
Those who take refuge with faith and joy should constantly maintain visualization and contemplation.
Clarifying the spirit and abiding in tranquil meditation, there was no outward display or ostentation. As for one who could fully expound [the Dharma]:

I have previously examined the memorial from the Nine Rivers. There was a monk named Ziyuan, who practiced and emulated the Pure Society of the White Lotus and gathered together the great conditions of Mount Lu.
He transformed seventy thousand monastics and cultivated the sixteen sublime contemplations without interruption for a long time; there was nothing that did not accord with his aspirations.
Thus you have attained rebirth there. You are now summoned to attend the Dēshou Hall to lecture on the great meaning of Pure Land practice.
We hereby grant you one golden-embroidered *śāla* robe with celestial-flower patterns and a set of gold *vajra* rings and hooks.
Let the Master proceed to the palace in accordance with this edict to receive these items and report his arrival. This decree is issued for your information; you should take full cognizance of it.
Warm greetings in spring. I hope you have been well lately. I send this letter with few words.

On the twenty-first day of the second month in the twelfth year, the issuance of *duodì* (ordination certificates) was suspended; even though it was by special imperial decree, the officials were ordered to submit a memorial on the matter.
Previously, when the Lin’an Prefecture requested *duodì* for the repair of the Guanyin Hall, the Emperor specially granted five thousand strings of cash. The Emperor said: "I observe that..."
If the ruler wishes to eliminate the two teachings of Śākya and Laozi, or to disparage their followers, it will be inappropriate in every respect and will only cause them to flourish all the more.
By now not issuing *fangdu* certificates (monastic licenses), the situation can gradually be cleared, and our Way will prevail.
In the fifth month of the thirteenth year [of the Shaoxing era], Zhang Jiu-cheng incurred the calumny of being a member of a faction.

Subsequently, Zhan Da-fang, the Right Censor-in-Chief, stated: "Recently, there were those who incited groundless rumors; Zhang Jiu-cheng was truly the leader of this, while the presiding monk of Mount Jing-shan, Zong-gao, followed suit by joining in.
Consequently, Zhang Jiu-cheng was sent for administrative placement in Nan-an Commandery, and Zong-gao was exiled to Heng-zhou. (Furthermore, according to the *Shaoxing Zheng-lun*, Qin...)

When Qin Hui was in power, Zonggao did not join his faction. Because he was accused of slandering the government along with Zhang Jiu Cheng, he was forced to return to secular life and was sentenced to administrative detention in Hengzhou, followed by transfer to Meizhou. After Qin Hui’s death, he returned to the monastic order and resided at Mount Jing.
In the eighth month of the twenty-seventh year, the remaining monastic and Daoist ordination certificates (*duòdì*) held by various circuits were collected at the request of the Three Departments.
The Emperor said: "Yesterday, I promoted He Yunchong, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, to have an audience with me.
