I asked him about the current number of monks and Daoists. Yunchong replied that there were two hundred thousand monks and barely ten thousand Daoists. I have observed many officials who revere the Buddha."

Among the discussions held during that interval, many touched upon the matter of ordination certificates (*duodie*). I remarked: "From now on, arable lands will increasingly fall into neglect, and those who consume food without tilling the soil will become numerous.
Yet there still remain two hundred and ten thousand people [eligible for ordination]. If we were to issue further ordination certificates, it would be to drive cultivators into the monastic order.
Furthermore, each laborer is allotted one hundred *mu* of land; if one man becomes a monk, one hundred *mu* of land will go uncultivated."
Since the Buddha’s teachings first entered China during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dynasty, they have ultimately been impossible to abolish.
It is not that I myself intend to sever them; however, as the number of monastics increases, those who do not engage in agriculture will become numerous. (The above is arranged chronologically.)
Chan Master Jia Tangjun was a native of Ning County in Fuzhou.

Having read the *Zhengmeng* by Zhang Zai of Hengqiu, which set forth eight arguments to refute the Buddha’s teachings as heterodox, the Master feared that in the future these would obscure the orthodox doctrine.

He therefore composed the *Jue qi xin lun* (Treatise on Resolving the Awakening of Faith) and presented a memorial to the imperial court, stating: "Within a fertile field there are weeds; if they are not cleared away early, there will be nothing left to nourish [the grain]."
"Jiahe: Within a great forest there are thorns and brambles; if they are not cut down and cleared away, there will be no way to nurture rare timber.

Your 'Rectifying the Enlightenment' (Zhengmeng), which propounds the doctrine of destroying the Buddha, is truly the weeds and tares of the field of merit—it is the thornbush of Daolin. It must be weeded out and cut down."
How could this be neglected? Buddhism has flowed eastward to Zhendan for twelve hundred years. Its manifest traces and clear verifications are recorded in the various canons;

they may be called detailed indeed. As for its transformation, it uses compassion to transform the violent and evil, joy and equanimity to transform stinginess and greed, impartiality to transform resentment and hatred, and forbearance to transform anger and malice. This tradition of transformative influence has been transmitted... and harmonized.
"It illuminates the four seas and truly provides assistance to the imperial administration. Is it not a grave error to characterize this as heterodox, as the *Zhengmeng* does?
(etc. After Emperor Gaozong finished reading it, he sealed it with his imperial seal and issued a notification to the court gates, decreeing that no further dissenting opinions were to be permitted.
Praise for the Lotus Sūtra: To enter the grove of the Tathāgata’s merits, one must apply oneself diligently to the Lotus Sūtra.
The "Parable of the Three Chariots" is vast in its great compassion; the words of these seven fascicles bring profound benefit.

It could once churn the long river into cream and curd, and transform the great earth into pure gold. Such a sūtra, such a scripture, is difficult to encounter; it may not be met again for ten thousand kalpas or a thousand lifetimes.
A Contemplation on Upādhyāya Pūrnaghata (Baguī Wángshī). A single cloud in the azure sky; a solitary moon in the vast firmament. Able to dwell beyond all things—how profound and remote!
Yet accustomed to hiding within the bustling markets—how truly extraordinary! As for his belongings, he carries nothing but a staff and a cloth bag. How vast his capacity!
How can the pivot of opportunity be hindered by the stench of wine, meat, and blood? Adieu! In the jade halls and crystal towers, there falls yet more snow.
When Emperor Xiaozong was still in the state of concealment, Pan wrote in response: The bag contains heaven and earth; the staff carries the sun and moon. Rough and rugged indeed!
The peerless among saints; simple and innocent. The hero among monks. When his command is issued: one blow, one trace of a welt.
When he provokes the spark: to kill, one must see blood. Distinct, distinct! Clearly, it is but a single snowflake in the furnace.
Hōtō Shindō’s *Eulogy on the Cloth Bag*: Its capacity encompasses the great void; its eyes suspend the sun and moon.

Dwelling in the celestial palace, it is the peerless one among the heavens; Abiding in the human realm, it is the preeminent hero among men. When he lets down his cloth bag, he sits and cuts off the four continents;
When he lifts up his staff, the entire earth breaks into a flow of blood. Distinct and distinct! Clear and clear!

The principles involved were so profound that they could not be easily resolved. Li Gong submitted a memorial on their behalf, and the two Emperors were greatly pleased (the third praise for a great event in the monastic community).
In the twenty-ninth year, Chan Master Zonggao of Mount Jing was transferred to Meizhou; he received imperial permission to act according to his own convenience.

In the third month of the following year, he was granted a certificate to once again become a monk. The year after that, he resided at Yuyang Monastery; the year after that, he returned to reside at Mount Jing (as noted previously).

When Emperor Xiaozong was still in the rank of crown prince, he personally inscribed the three characters "Miaoxi An" (Wondrous Joy Hermitage) and bestowed them upon Master Gaofeng. Upon his accession to the throne, the Emperor first inquired after the Master’s well-being and issued an edict to him;
however, as the Master happened to be bedridden with illness at the time, the Emperor instead conferred upon him the title "Chan Master Dahui."

Guiwei (the 26th day of the tenth month): Emperor Xiaozong changed the reign title to Longxing. The following year, ten thousand *sengdie* (monastic certificates) were issued and entrusted to the Metropolitan Commandery to be distributed among the various provinces.

Furthermore, twenty thousand more were issued and entrusted to the various provinces for sale. Chen Lianghan submitted a memorial, stating: [...text omitted... Chen Lianghan submitted a memorial, stating: [The text continues with his critique of the policy].
The sale of ordination certificates (*du-du*) had been practiced for over twenty years; while the population increased, it did not result in any lack of benefit.

However, in the spring of the *Xinsi* year, as the border affairs began and expenditures grew extensive, the practice was finally permitted. At the outset of the decree, people vied with one another to sell them.
As the people of Tang once said, "Ten households cannot support a single monk. Those now permitted to be ordained already number more than ten [thousand].
Together with those previously converted, there are likely three or four hundred thousand households that cannot find rest.
One does not know how much benefit this brings to the state; yet now, three or four hundred thousand households are unable to set down their shoulders from toil.
Furthermore, the population is secretly diminished and the common people are harassed and disturbed—not merely by one hundred thousand, but surely the harm caused is no small matter.
(Chronicle). The year of Yiyou:

the reign title was changed to Qiandao. At that time, while visiting Lower Zhushan Temple on the upper reaches, he saw three things—a mountain resembling the Land of Buddha, a water-strainer in the kitchen, and an Avalokiteśvara statue in the hall of walking meditation.
When he questioned the monks about them, none were able to provide further answers. He then summoned Lingyin.
Master Seshu Huo asked Master Tangyuan: "Since the mountain flew here from the Buddha-land, why does it not fly away?
Tangyuan said: "Motion is not as good as stillness. He asked again: "Sentient beings in the water can be filtered with a bag;

but for sentient beings within fire, what will you use to filter them? Tangyuan said: "That family has a path of their own that reaches through the heavens. He asked again: "When sentient beings encounter difficulties..."
"Recite the name of Avalokiteśvara to save from suffering. Avalokiteśvara’s hand holds a rosary; what is he reciting? Yuan said, "Seeking others is not as good as seeking oneself.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict ordering the master to convert the lecture hall into a Chan monastery. The Master submitted a memorial, saying:
"The Teachings clarify the Buddha’s words; Chan awakens to the Buddha’s mind. Because one perceives the Buddha’s mind through the Buddha’s words, their underlying principle is one and the same."

Thereupon he retired for the night. He descended to Zhushan and enshrined the Master’s portrait before Foguoshan. From that time forward, whenever the Imperial Majesty encountered the anniversary of the Master’s passing, he would prepare vegetarian feasts (*zhai*).
His spiritual radiance attained the Way, and with a mind of emptiness, he responded to all things. The Emperor repeatedly summoned Chan Master Huotang into the inner palace;

his responses to the imperial inquiries pleased the Sovereign, who bestowed upon him the honorary title "Foyan. By imperial decree, Chan Master Deguang of Yuyangshan was ordered to cross the river on the second month. The Emperor—

Question: I have heard that in antiquity there was one who crossed a river by means of a bamboo hat. It is recorded that once, while traveling on the road, Huangbo encountered a strange monk walking with him;
this was an arhat. Upon reaching Tiantai, they encountered a swollen river that could not be forded. Huangbo planted his staff there and waited for a long time.
The strange monk took his bamboo hat as a boat, climbed upon it, and floated away across the river. Huangbo pointed at him and scolded, saying, "This self-satisfied fellow! I—"
"I have known you for a long time. He then struck and broke the monk's leg. A strange monk bowed his head and said, "The practitioner’s fierce intensity is beyond my reach.
The Emperor said, "This may indeed be called supernatural power. The monk submitted, saying, "In our school, we do not value supernatural powers; we value only the clarity of the eye."
The Emperor said, "It must be so," and bestowed upon him the honorary title of Master Fozhao, issuing an imperial decree for him to reside at Lingyin. One day, he was summoned for an audience.
The Emperor asked, "Are my mind and the Buddha-mind the same or different? The Master replied, "Directly beneath, there is no second person."
The Emperor said, "In that case, the Buddha is the mind, and the mind is the Buddha. The Master replied, "To manifest all forms is the mind; to be free from all forms is the Buddha.
The Emperor asked, "Since ancient times, there have been many emperors and heroes, yet few have been able to believe in this Way.
The Master said, "It is not that Your Majesty does not understand. I only pray that Your Majesty will carry this Way through to its end. The Emperor said, "I shall strive [to do so]."
"Competing in diligence, one should act as the Zen Master has said. One day he summoned the Master and asked, "What was accomplished by Śākyamuni during his six years in the Snow Mountains?
Please explain this clearly. The Master replied, "I thought Your Majesty had forgotten. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
An imperial decree accompanying a verse by Zen Master Fozhao states: "When one wishes to speak of mind and Buddha, it is difficult..."
Clarifying the distinction: both are subtle and unimpeded penetrations. Leaping out, one is not bound by a thousand layers of fetters;

at the ends of the earth and the corners of the sea, one goes as one pleases, west or east. Again, a verse says: "A single whisk on the head of the bed—raising it or setting it down, neither is correct.
Baizhang was still dull-witted; one shout entered the subtle essence. (Presented to Chan Master Fozhao; carved in stone at Lingyin.)

Jia-wu (1174): The reign title was changed to Chunxi. In the seventh year, the Emperor summoned Chan Master Fozhao to inquire about the gradual stages of cultivation for a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).
The Master set forth these matters in detail for his report. The Emperor further bestowed an imperial edict stating:

"The Ten Grounds presented by the Chan Master are indeed the gradual stages of a Bodhisattva’s cultivation, proceeding from the mundane to the sacred. What room is there for further doubt? Only now do I realize the [true] feet [of the Way]."
Tread firmly upon the ground of reality. Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, let there be no interruption until [the practice] reaches full maturity.
Whether it be defilement or purity, both become obstacles. To escape these maladies of dhyāna—namely, activity, cessation, maintenance, and extinction—one should follow the words of the Chan masters:

constantly brandish the blade, straighten the backbone, and arouse a mind of diligence, fearing even the slightest lapse into indolence. Whenever one reflects upon this, one must remain ever vigilant and earnest.
I have never dared to treat this matter lightly. Yet nowadays, worldly people regard Chan as empty rhetoric and its discourse as mere frivolous debate;
such is their ignorance of the Way. This matter is of the utmost importance—how could it ever be exhausted by the brush? I have merely recorded what I have attained here.
Chan Master Fozhao shared a karmic affinity with Imperial Preceptor Shangshen. He frequently received imperial edicts and repeatedly stayed at the monastery.
During the Qianchun era, an imperial edict was issued to inquire about the subtle cultivation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the exaltation of Prajñā.
It is truly said that one must be ever-vigilant and diligent, never daring to be negligent; how could this be mere empty words? This was a rare opportunity encountered at such a time.
In the third month of that year, the Emperor summoned Chan Master Sisi Qing of Jingci Temple to enter the Wenyoudian Hall for an audience.

Before the formal meeting had concluded, the Emperor asked, "How would you praise the place where you have gained mastery throughout your life? He replied, "This precisely expresses the intimacy of Your Majesty’s encounter with this humble monk.
The Emperor praised him, saying, "Advancing steadily from the top of the hundred-foot pole; to kill a man, one must be fierce and resolute."
Han: Wearing tattered clothes and eating coarse food is not considered poverty; within it lies a bright pearl worth hundreds of millions. The Master said:

"Today Your Majesty has granted me a vegetarian feast and tea, and I have further been honored with this encomium. I shall compose a verse on the spot to express my gratitude for even a fraction of Your Majesty’s kindness.

The Emperor specially bestowed this encomium upon this poor monk. This encomium is like extracting jewels from a mountain in infinite measure. If a patch-robed monk wishes to continue the lamp of the Patriarchs, he must rely on this.
"Directly before the pivot, keep your eyes raised high. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the honorary title of Master Fohui (Buddha-Wisdom).
At that time, Gaozong was relaxing at Deyou Palace; he took the painting to view it and presented it in a scroll made of jade-patterned brocade as a return gift.

From then on, the jar emitted the scent of musk and the needle’s point emerged from its sheath. The Emperor visited Dayuanjue Jiao Temple and inscribed a poem, which begins: "The ancient temple in spring..."
The mountains are green and even more beautiful; tall pines and long bamboos hold emerald mist. Drawing water, I intend to heighten my passion for tea;

for a while, I shall seek a bed to sleep in a monk’s quarters. (Furthermore: Only after sitting for a long time do I realize that spring days are long; within stillness, the mind-ground is naturally cool and clear.
"Every person possesses perfect enlightenment, yet how often do they truly awaken? One sees only the dust of worldly toil, vast and boundless day after day.

He also wrote the two characters "Returning Clouds" (Guīyún) and bestowed them upon the head monk Dèxìn. From then on, he repeatedly summoned the Chan Master Yī of Jìngcí and the Dharma Master Nè, lecturer at Shàngzhú, to enter the palace, granting both the title "Discerning Talent" (Biàncái).
[The Emperor] also composed a eulogy for the *Lotus Sūtra*, which begins: "The Sublime Dharma..."
The *Lotus Sūtra* in seven fascicles can cause wisdom to realize true illumination; it cuts through nails and cleaves iron to eliminate doubt.
To cast off armor and lay down weapons requires sincere resolve. Śrāvakas and those of Perfect Enlightenment gather in this assembly; kings and princes all have their names inscribed therein.
If one does not contemplate the words of the Tathāgata while alive, what will one do after death to break through the iron city?

Gui-mao, the second day of the second month in the tenth year of the Chunxi era (1178 CE). The Emperor bestowed the *Imperial Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* upon Master Bie-feng Baoyin of Mount Jing, ordering its publication.
Baoyin submitted a memorial of thanks and further presented this verse: "The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present..."
With this same broad and long tongue, amidst where there is no path, he opens a way for all beings.

He parts the clouds over a thousand peaks and releases a single orb of the moon, causing all people upon the great earth to be fully illuminated beneath his words; yet even this awakening is nothing to be perfected.
"Even illusion has nothing that can be extinguished; even this 'nothing' is itself non-existent. A single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace—homage to Buddha after Buddha!
Each word contains no separate teaching. Having read this during the second watch of the night, the Emperor was greatly pleased.
Subsequently, he summoned him for an audience and asked, "What kind of person were Zhuangzi and Laozi? Yan replied, "They could only be considered small-vehicle śrāvakas within the Buddha-dharma."

This person was one of the Hinayana school. Loathing the body as if it were shackles and discarding wisdom as if it were mixed poison, he used the fire of transformation to cremate his body and entered the realm of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).
This is precisely what Zhuangzi meant when he said: "The form can indeed be made like withered wood; the mind can indeed be made like extinguished ashes.
His wishes were thus fulfilled, and he was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Huibian. [The Emperor] was residing at the Chonghua Palace.
Having examined Han Yu’s “Discourse on the Origin of the Way,” I have composed this "Refutation of the Origin of the Way," saying:

I observe that in Han Yu’s “Discourse on the Origin of the Way,” he speaks of the mutual confusion of Buddhism and Daoism, and the mutual sublation of the Three Teachings; yet no one has been able to refute this.

Furthermore, his writing is prolix and his reasoning circuitous; when measured against the intent of the Sage, it is not yet clearly evident. Why is this? Because the Śākya school specializes in investigating...
Regarding life and nature, one discards the physical form and does not cling to names or appearances; thus, one naturally has no concern with worldly affairs.

How much less, then, would one be involved with ritual, music, benevolence, or righteousness? Nevertheless, precepts are still established: namely, not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not drinking intoxicants, and not speaking falsely.
Now, not killing is benevolence (*ren*); not stealing is righteousness (*yi*); not committing sexual misconduct is ritual propriety (*li*); and not drinking is wisdom (*zhi*).
Do not believe this recklessly. Such is the case with Zhongni (Confucius). How could he be far from [the Way]? The Master moved with ease within the Middle Way;
he was a sage. What he did was not non-ritual and non-music? Was there anything that was not benevolence and righteousness? How, then, could one give him a name?
He was like the movement of Heaven and Earth, the circulation of Yin and Yang without beginning or end—how could there be a distinction between spring, summer, autumn, and winter?
These are merely provisional names given by the sages. It is just like the distinctions between ritual, music, benevolence, and righteousness;
it was inevitable that the sages had to establish these teachings to govern the world. If one investigates and seeks the truth behind these provisional names, they reveal the Dao.
The Dao is the source of benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music; benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music are indeed the functions of the Dao. Thus said Yang Xiong...
It is said that Laozi struck down benevolence and righteousness and abolished ritual and music. Now, if we examine the traces of Laozi’s writings, there are three things he treasures:

namely, compassion (*ci*), frugality (*jian*), and not daring to take precedence over the world. Confucius said, "Gentleness, kindness, respectfulness, frugality, and yielding," and he also said, "Only benevolence (*ren*) is great.
Is what Laozi calls compassion not perhaps the greatest form of benevolence? [The interlocutor] says: No.
"To dare to be the first in the world"—is this not the greatest form of humility? Yet, when it comes to their convergence with the Way, each school emphasizes its own particular aspect.
What they value is purity, stillness, and unity; however, in relation to the Sage Confucius, they appear to run in opposite directions.

This is merely because those who follow the later currents of the three teachings and lack discernment cling to these differences as being inherently distinct. Now, as for Buddhists and Daoists, they sever discursive thought and practice non-action to cultivate the body and mind.
And that is all. Confucius’s teaching for governing the world differs only in its application. It is like using a plow to weave or a loom to plow;
those of later generations merely became confused and perplexed, surely losing the underlying principle. Someone asks: "How should one eliminate this confusion? I reply:
"Use Buddhism to cultivate the mind, Daoism to regulate the body, and Confucianism to govern the world."
This is appropriate. Only a sage is able to bring about such harmony; it must not fail to be discussed.
Since ascending the throne, [the Emperor] has desired to exhaust his own realization and cultivation in order to clarify the words of the Buddha-Dharma and rescue the multitude of deluded beings.

Gengxu: Emperor Gaozong reigned for five years, adopting the era name Shaoxi. He maintained the fullness of his reign and preserved the achievements of his predecessors, while reverently honoring the holy teachings.
However, Empress Dowager Li was fierce and jealous; she repeatedly established Prince Jia as the heir apparent.

Yimao: Emperor Ningzong reigned; he changed the era name to Qingyuan. In the first year, there was a drought. The imperial carriage visited the Guanyin Hall of Mingqing Temple, where prayers were answered with efficacy.
Both those within and without the court were filled with joy.
Wuchen (戊辰): the first year of Jiading (嘉定). The fourth year. The year Xinwei (辛未):
Emperor Taizu of the Great Yuan succeeded Heaven and established the Ultimate.
The thirteenth year of Jiading: the year Gengchen (庚辰).
In the fourteenth year of the Jiading era, on the Mid-Autumn Festival, when Emperor Taizhu of the Taiyuan reign ascended the throne,
Ningzong personally inscribed the two characters "Gufeng" (Lonely Peak) and bestowed them upon the abbot of Xindong Chan Temple in Fuzhou,
the monk Deshou. The Chan Master submitted a memorial, citing the dialogue between a monk and Caoshan regarding the cause of the snow covering the thousand mountains.
"Extremely solitary, the peak is not white. The Subject [Dahui] wrote these words, saying: "Heaven and Earth are revealed alone.

By this, he seeks to repay the Imperial Grace with even a ten-thousandth part of its merit. Furthermore, he offered two verses of thanks to the Empress, the Queen, who constantly paid homage to Avalokiteśvara:

"In the Hall of Manifest Origin, the family style is revealed; His strategic methods are naturally and utterly distinct. Throughout the entire world, not even a speck of dust stands; Truly excellent!"
How wondrous! Where is there that is not perfectly penetrating? Having been graced by the extraordinary favor of rain and dew, the iron tree blooms with flowers of even more brilliant color.
The myriad phenomena and the entire cosmos perform a dance together, all crying out "Ten Thousand Years! before the Sage (from the *Benlu*).
In the year Yiyou (1235), Emperor Lizong ascended the throne and changed the era name to Baoping. In the fourth year, a drought occurred.

An imperial edict summoned Chan Master Huikai, the abbot of Baoning Temple, to enter Wende Hall, where he ascended the seat to pray for rain; his prayers were answered. The Emperor bestowed upon him the honorary title "Foyan" (Buddha-Eye).
Dingyou (the year 1257), the first year of the Jiaxi era. Empress Dowager Tu passed away. An imperial edict summoned Chan Master Shifan, the abbot of Mount Jing, to an audience at the Xiuzheng Hall;
the Emperor bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered robe and further commanded him to ascend the seat at Ciming Hall, conferring upon him the title of Chan Master Fojian.
Following the passing of Emperor Gongseng Renshuo, an edict was again issued for him to ascend the seat, whereupon he declined the request.
He retired to the mountain forests. Emperor Ningzong bestowed upon him the honorary title of Master Yuanzhao.

During the Jiaxi era, an imperial decree ordered that monks and Daoists throughout the empire must purchase gold rings, purple robes, and ivory tablets to qualify for positions as abbots at various monasteries.
A monk from Lingyin Monastery named Zhongyuan submitted a memorial stating: "The teachings of Buddhism and Daoism are intended as means to save the world."
The reason why it [Buddhism] coexists with Confucianism and Daoism within the realm of heaven and earth is that it enables one to awaken to the true nature and not fall into false views;
its merit is not easily measured. Our Great Emperor Taizu said, "The Way of the Śākya clan supplements the teachings of transformation.
The Imperial Ancestral Temple also stated: "Use Buddhism to govern the mind, use Daoism to govern the body, and use Confucianism to govern..."
In this world, Zhang Wending Gong remarked that the austerity of Confucianism and Daoism both converge upon the teachings of the Śākya clan;

likewise, the masters of the Guanzhong and Luoyang traditions necessarily studied and relished the scriptures of the Śākya clan before they were able to continue the transmission of the Zhusi (Confucius) lineage.

That these [teachings] assist the worldly instruction is by no means a minor contribution. Now, regarding the decree concerning the observance of mourning attire, there are inevitably benefits and harms within it; for the sake of purity and clarity...

"To reside here would make it a place where profit and desire contend with one another; this seems not to be for the welfare of the state" (and so forth). Upon the submission of this memorial, the matter was consequently shelved. Yuan’s courtesy name was Shuangshan;

he was a native of Fucheng in Min and the third-generation descendant of Miam. The Emperor approved his petition, and he was immediately appointed to the position of *zhuxing* (Administrator of the Monastery), with Prime Minister Chen acting as his supporter.

Yuan then offered this verse: *Jingzuan* (The Succession of Scenery) [Note: The term *zhuxing* refers to the administrative head of a monastery, while *shuoxiang* (樞相) refers to a high-ranking official, likely the Chancellor or a member of the Council of State.]
Xing Shu assisted in the esoteric mechanisms of statecraft; he forgot his own person to submit a memorial, thereby offending the imperial majesty.

What he feared was that the ancestral Way would be treated as lightly as a leaf, rather than that the court would begrudge him its purple robes. All the elders were intimidated by him, yet we rely on the fact that His Majesty does not forget the sacred entrustment.
Xinchou (the first year of Chunyou). The Emperor dreamed that Guanyin was born amidst bamboo and rock. He had an image carved upon stone and composed a eulogy for it, saying:
"Your supernatural powers are most wondrous; Whether hidden or manifest, they cannot be fathomed. Your merit and virtue are boundless; How swift is your response to invocation!
May there be harmony in the seasons and abundance in the years, To bless our living people. May the weapons be laid aside and punishments cease, To bring peace to this royal kingdom."

He further inscribed the four large characters "Guangda Linggan" (Vast and Great Spiritual Response) above the sacred name of Avalokiteśvara, and additionally wrote out one scroll of the *Heart Sūtra*.
He composed a record of these miraculous responses and personally inscribed them all to be bestowed upon Upper Zhi Mountain, where they were carved into stone.

Furthermore, he offered a verse in praise of the Thousand Buddhas, which says: "One Buddha is not two; how could there be any distinction among the thousand Buddhas? They are like the waters everywhere, reflecting the moon wherever it appears."
Gone without coming; neither born nor extinguished. After the plum blossoms have opened, deep snow covers the village ahead.
Gengxu—The tenth year of Chunyou. The Jin people submitted.
The Great Yuan Emperor Xiaozong ascended the throne at the Great Golden City, which is the old city of the present-day capital.

Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty dreamed of traveling to a mountain temple and issued an edict to all famous mountains and monasteries throughout the realm, ordering each to submit a painting of its site.

Upon viewing them, [the Emperor] recognized it as Xuedou Temple in Mingzhou; he then inscribed the four characters "Famous Mountain that Responded to a Dream" (Yingmeng Mingshan) and bestowed them upon it.
At that time, Chan Master Guangwen of Yǎnxī presided over this seat by special imperial decree as its abbot.
Previously, while the Master was residing at Xiaojingci in Mingzhou, Chancellor Zheng Qingzhi intended to prepare a burial site for himself behind the temple.
The Master thereupon offered this verse: "Speaking of Minister Pei amidst Mount Huangbo, I recall Prince Shu by the side of Dulong Hill. May the Chancellor [live long]..."

He obtained Xiqian Temple, where the illustrious name of the Duke of Zheng has endured for a thousand ages. The Duke subsequently commissioned a separate residence for him, and the Master resided at Xuedou.
Later, he moved to Yuwang, Jingci, Lingyin, and Jingshan—five times receiving imperial edicts and yellow documents, repeatedly receiving summons from the Emperor.

He stayed three nights in the Guantang Hall and engaged in debate before the Secret Palace. He was granted the title Chan Master Fozhi. During the Jingding era, he submitted a memorial to the Throne. [End of Document]△ Onward.
In mourning, [the Emperor] granted money to assist with the funeral and specially inscribed the two characters "Daming" (Great Brightness) to name his hermitage.

He was granted fields for the sustenance of its guardians, and the remaining benefits extended to his kin. By imperial decree, the tomb of Lady Lin, the Buddha-Mother, was granted at the western side of Fushi.
The Master was a native of Sanshan and was the third-generation descendant of Zeweng Dahui.

Chan Master Chijue Daochong of Lingyin Monastery was issued an imperial edict to confiscate his vegetable plots for the construction of a tomb for a favorite. The Master beat the drum and ascended the hall, saying:
"Wishing to leave but not leaving, one is hindered by leaving; wishing to stay but not staying, one is hindered by staying. Fundamentally, there is no hindrance.
The ten continents and three islands are the realm of cranes; the four seas and five lakes are the world of dragons. Having descended from the seat, he wrapped his waist-cloth and departed.
He set out on his travels. When the court deliberated and sought to appoint him as abbot, he remained steadfast and could not be swayed from his resolve.

Later, Prime Minister Zhao Jiezhai Ruoyu built Fahua Temple at Lake Tai and invited him to serve as its founding patriarch. Subsequently, he was presented with an imperial edict to reside at Mount Shuangjing.
The Gengshen year, the first year of Jingding of Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty. The Jiazi year, the first year of Zhongtong of Emperor Shizu of the Great Yuan.
The first year of Zhiyuan of Emperor Shizu of the Great Yuan.
Yichou (the second year of the sexagenary cycle). Emperor Duozong of the Song dynasty. The first year of Xianchun.
Emperor Duozong was born in the eighth prince’s residence during the Gengzi year of Jiaxi. After three days, he wailed and cried incessantly day and night.

His wet nurse carried him to a nearby academy and saw the shadow of a pagoda pasted there from his former life as a practitioner of asceticism and a solicitor for alms at Mount Yuwang. He broke into a silent laugh. His mother—
He was exceedingly joyful; when separated from him, he would cry again. Upon seeing him once more, he smiled, and taking hold of his hand, he ceased crying altogether.
The Great King joyfully inquired as to the reason for this. The wet nurse answered with the facts.

Only then did the Father King realize that his former ascetic practices were the cause for the construction of the Śarīra stūpa. He then descended to the temple and questioned the presiding monk about the matter.

The monk related in detail how, since returning from the provincial capital with his arm severed, the blood had not ceased and he had passed away. When the date was calculated, it was the very day of the Emperor’s birth.

The Father King then pointed to the treasury and renovated the stupa. Later, when Emperor Lizong was established as the Crown Prince, while he was in the Eastern Palace, he dreamed one night that a divine being told him:
"The Jade Emperor, moved by your merit of severing your arm to repair the Śarīra stupa, rewards you by making you a Great Peace Emperor for ten years" (from *Yeshi*).
Yihai (the second day of the intercalary month): The infant ruler Xian of the Song dynasty, a son of Emperor Duozong, ascended the throne and changed the era name to the first year of Deyou.
In the following year, Cizi, in the first month, the great army arrived at Lin’an. Empress Dowager Xie took up residence behind the curtain, and the entire nation surrendered.
The Great Yuan enfeoffed him as Duke of Yingguo. His younger brothers, Guang and Yi, fled to Min.
In the winter of the Bingzi year, the great army attacked Fujian. Duke Guang reached Dianchuan and passed away. Duke Yi remained at Yashan. In the Jimao year, the great army attacked Yashan;
Lu Xiufu cradled the prince and threw himself into the sea, dying there.
The Song dynasty: from its founding in Gengshen until the fall of Bianjing in Bingwu of the Jingkang era, there were nine sovereigns.
When the two emperors were taken north as captives, the Jurchens seized their territory, comprising one hundred and thirty-two prefectures across the north of the Yangtze River.

Emperor Gaozong moved the capital south to Hangzhou. From the year Dingwei until Bingzi, the state was lost; there were seven sovereigns, totaling three hundred and seventeen years, including the preceding period.
Now, the founding ancestor of the Song dynasty bore a majesty that rivaled his sovereign and possessed merits that went unrewarded;
having no place to set foot, he seized the moment of peril to strike, and by traversing all under heaven, he established his household.

Yet how could he have expected that midway, amidst a moment of jesting, he would lose his way, allowing the Jin people to employ their long-standing tactics of capture and seizure? Thus, Gaozong’s crossing to the south was but a stroke of luck.
As for the achievements of [Emperor] Xing, although he occupied but one corner of the realm, he still relied upon the splendor of more than a hundred years of imperial rule.
Now that the destiny of the state has reached its end—alas! It seems Heaven is about to inaugurate an era of Great Peace.
That a sage bestowed it is beyond the reach of human deliberation.
Since the Great Yuan first arose and the six realms were unified, the empire has been governed with great peace; how magnificent and flourishing this is! Such a thing has never occurred before.
Dharma Master Yongdao of Xiangji Monastery was of the Mao clan from Dongying. He specialized in the two treatises of *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and *Śata-dharmaka*.

By imperial precedent at Tianning Monastery, he received the title Baojue. In the second year of the Xuanhua era, an edict was issued to change the designation of monks to "virtuous practitioners" (*deshi*).

Accompanied by Vinaya Master Mingwu and Huayan Lecturer Huirui, he engaged in a debate with the Daoist Lin Lingsu regarding the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, appealing his case to [the throne].

In the morning, he offended the imperial will and was exiled to Daozhou. In the sixth month of the second year, by virtue of a general amnesty, his sentence was commuted and he was transferred from Changsha, where he met the Venerable Jiyin.
He presented him with a poem which said: "Master Dao’s courage is greater than his own body; He dared to defy the dragon’s scales and submit a memorial of remonstrance."
Desiring only to shoulder the Buddha-dharma upon his own back, he willingly extended his neck to receive the axe and hoe. For three years in exile, his heart remained free of shame;

returning ten thousand *li* away, his countenance was not withered. It is recently heard that those who maintain the discipline of the Teaching’s gate now follow the court in their official boots and tablets.
Having sought permission for this, on the fifth day of the fifth month of the seventh year, I respectfully received the imperial decree to proceed as the former Master Baojue, Mao Qiudao.
Having repeatedly received amnesties, he was specially granted permission to resume his monastic tonsure as before. Since then, he has frequently enjoyed the fullness of imperial grace.

Not long after, at the beginning of the Jianyan era, the Lord Marshal who served as the Imperial Resident in the capital—Master Zong, who had mastered the Way and its Virtue—ordered that he be provisionally appointed as a *Xuanchiao Lang* (Imperial Instructor) to serve as a Commissioner for the Imperial Resident’s Office to issue proclamations of amnesty.
He concurrently held the office of Chief Counselor to the Military Commandant’s Office, participating in military deliberations and assisting the troops. Thus...
He traveled to the regions of Huai and Ying, where he exhorted the local gentry and nobility to contribute tens of thousands of coins to assist the state and support the army.
He was repeatedly summoned to attend the Council of State at the imperial encampment to deliberate on affairs of state; however, the high ministers and officials earnestly urged him to return home.

Initially, he had been appointed as a civil official with concurrent military rank and financial authority, assigned to lead military forces to aid the royal house. He declined the appointment with a verse, saying: "In years past, for the sake of the Dharma, I suffered the punishment of branding."
The heavenly messengers acted as guards for the generals; they were imprisoned and sent southward for half a cycle. Traveling ten thousand *li* back and forth, the journey was long.
Yet, amidst frost and ice, their integrity remained as firm as pine and bamboo; even before the furnace and coals, their resolve stayed as unshakable as iron and stone.

They vowed to become disciples of the Buddha, rather than plotting to serve as high ministers or officials. [This was] sought from the Three Departments and the Secretariat; the Office for Rewarding Merit was established.
The Son [of Heaven] received the imperial decree: "I hereby specially bestow upon you the title of Dharma Master Baojue Yuantong Fazhi. The official document from the Ministry of Rites states:

"According to the ancestral laws regarding the aforementioned dharma-title, it corresponds to the rank of Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu Qing*). Following the Chongguan era, six-character dharma-titles were established;

in comparison with your rank and merit, and further acknowledging the commendation by the Central Secretariat for your protection of the Dharma, you are granted the name Fazhi (Dharma-Way). Furthermore...

An imperial edict was issued in the second month of the third year of the Xiangxing era [1135 CE], directing that [the monks] attend the court to rectify the order of the prayer halls alongside the Daoists Liu Ruqian and others. The relevant decree stated in brief:

"During the Chongning and Daguan eras, Daoists such as Wang Zisi and Lin Lingsu improperly usurped official ranks and threw the state administration into disorder; consequently, a precedent was established whereby the Daoist ranks were placed above those of the clergy."
I have observed that since the Jingkang and Jianyan periods, the official ranks of all Daoists have already been revoked.

Those without official hereditary status ought to follow the long-standing precedents of our imperial ancestors. I humbly beseech Your Majesty’s Court to issue a clear decree to grant a special correction of this matter.
It was promulgated throughout the realm to rectify customs. At that time, however, it had not yet been put into practice.

It was not until the tenth month of the thirteenth year of the Shaoxing era that the order was once again reorganized; the seating positions for monks and Daoists were established such that the monks always sat to the east, which became a permanent regulation. Master Fashi...
On the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month in the seventeenth year, Daoist Lin Lingsu passed away.
Having gained favor through heterodox arts (*zuo-dao*), his influence had overwhelmed the age at that time. Yet the Dharma Master [Fahai] confronted him in debate without yielding a single word;
in thus upholding the gates of the Teaching and benefiting sentient beings, he truly did not fail his original vow. (Dongdu Shilue)

Chan Master Foguo Qin was summoned for an audience at the beginning of the Jianyan era. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Yunju. Later, he returned to Sichuan to reside at Zhaojue and Ziyuan.
When Lord Zhang Xu asked him about the Way, the Master said: "Those of superior wisdom and sharp faculties must focus solely on authentic investigation.
At the time of such investigation, one acts prior to the stimulus and turns away from external objects. Yantou said: "To turn away from objects is..."
To be above is to transcend things; to follow after things is to be below. If one can turn back from things, one swiftly places all things beneath one’s influence.

Whether seizing or releasing, contracting or expanding, everything is brought under one's command. He expressed this in verse: "Receiving the light and gathering the radiance, trust in the true nature.
Every matter is perfectly accomplished; every thing is new. If there is still a mind within, there will still be objects. How could one move a step beyond the thoroughfare? The Master.

Prostrating himself in devotion, he offered this verse: "Outside the teachings, the single transmission is the pivot of Buddhas and Patriarchs; Originally there is neither awakening nor delusion. When drifting clouds disperse, the primordial sky remains;
The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. The Master approved, saying: "In days to come, you shall serve as a high minister;
do not forget your heart’s resolve to protect the Dharma."
Chan Master Daguang Miaogao appeared in the world and resided at Mount Jing. When the Prefect invited him to Lingyin Monastery, he ascended the hall;
upon descending from the seat, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Feng Ji asked, "Master, you once said, 'I will not act like this little insect. Why then have you failed?"
The Master said, "The entire earth is Upāsaka Gao; how can you grope for it? As Feng hesitated, the Master struck him with his palm.
At that moment, the assembly turned pale with alarm, but Feng laughed loudly and said, "I have met the Elder in the Buddha-dharma.
Previously, Gong had visited Chan Master Yuan of Longmen, and upon meeting Master Gao, he attained a profound and subtle realization. He then provided the funds to print and distribute the Tripitaka.
In the one hundred and eighteen scriptural collections (*piṭaka*), there is a verse that says: "I am addicted to the malady of delusion; though possessing wealth, I store it in vain.
I make no provision for my descendants, nor do I provide for carriages and horses. It is not for the sake of articles of play, nor to purchase the pleasures of sound and form."
With no southern fields where a single awl could be stuck, and not even a solitary tile for a humble hut, all that his monthly stipend provided was enough to redeem Buddhist scriptures.
He dispatched Jie across ten thousand *li* to welcome them back, traversing rugged and distant roads; he enshrined them within a great monastery to reveal the path to all who wander in delusion.
I hope that all who peruse this shall enter the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa*. For the sake of a half-gāthā, ancient Buddhas even sacrificed their entire bodies;
yet I now give with material wealth, and not even a trace of pain has pierced my skin. When comparing myself to the Buddha, our experiences of suffering and joy differ ten-thousandfold.
The reason he did not begrudge his wealth was not that his nature was inherently foolish. I ask those who cling to their money: from beginning to end, you calculate every fraction of a grain.
When impermanence suddenly arrives, can you truly avoid birth and death? His courtesy title was Budong Jushi (Immovable Layman). He was a native of Shu.
Minister Zhang Jiucheng went to Shanquan Temple to receive instructions and visited Master Hu Wuding to inquire about the method for governing the mind.
Master Hu said, "Simply read the *Mencius* and categorize the passages concerning benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*) together.

One day, while on the toilet, he was reflecting on Mencius’s words, "The heart of commiseration is the sprout of benevolence," when he suddenly heard the croaking of frogs and attained a realization. He then recounted this as follows:
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? he asked. "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Suddenly, his sweat broke out and soaked his back. He composed a verse, saying:
"Under the moon in the blue sky, a single croak of a frog; It shatters heaven and earth, making all one family. At such a moment as this, who can understand?
Only Xuan Sha knows the ache in his feet on the mountain pass. Later, because he went to visit Master Shang, he saw the true eulogy for Miaoxi, which said:
With a coarse bamboo staff of black lacquer, he struck even when the Buddha arrived, saying: "If there were someone who possessed the Buddha-dharma...

He then proceeded to Mount Jing, where upon meeting Miaoxi, they discussed the principle of *gewu* (investigating things). [Miaoxi] said, "In learning, nothing precedes the extension of knowledge (*zhizhi*); only after one can extend knowledge can one investigate things.
The Master said, "You know only of investigating things (*gewu*), but you do not know that there is also 'things being investigated' (*wuge*). [Miaoxi] asked, "How could this be?"
[The monk] said, "There is no expedient means. The Master said, "A minor history records that during the Tang dynasty, there was one who conspired with An Lushan to rebel;

he had once served as the Governor of Langzhou and possessed a portrait of himself. When Emperor Minghuang visited Shu, he saw it and became enraged, ordering an attendant official to draw his sword and behead him."
That man was in Shaanxi when his head suddenly fell to the ground. Upon hearing this, Master Gong attained enlightenment and said: "Zi Shao [said] 'the mind exhausts things' (ge wu);
Tan Hui [said] 'things exhaust the mind' (wu ge). If you wish to know the 'One Thread,' it is simply two times five hundred."
Wang Shiqing of Meian visited Chan Master Yun’an Qing; their conversation was harmonious, and he offered this verse:
"Listening to the Dharma-King’s teaching, Everywhere else is as dense as reeds and hemp. Only at Zhongfu Temple remains The *tánhuā* flower blooming through vast eons. The Master approved of it.
When the Master was fourteen or fifteen years old, he knew how to practice meditation at the foot of a pine tree. Suddenly, he had a realization and said: "The entire great earth..."

He manifested the gates of liberation; where in the ten directions was his honor not proclaimed? This morning, joyfully beholding his natural likeness, his entire being is utterly free from the marks of the chisel or hammer.
He then took leave of his kin to practice the dhūta austerities, ascended Mount Shuangjing to behold Wondrous Joy (Sukhāvatī), and later resided at Jiangshan to proclaim the Way.
His support for the declining dharma and his benevolent reputation were so pervasive that all considered him to be the reincarnation of Master Bao.

When Chancellor Zhengxian Gong Chen Junqing was serving as the Prefect of Jiankang, he convened a great assembly of Zen monks to interrogate them on the dialogue concerning "having a phrase" and "not having a phrase.
When the abbots of various mountains responded simultaneously, they could not avoid being too caught up in the conceptual path.
Finally, the Daoist Zhen of Baoning said: "Zhang beats oil, Li beats oil; they do not beat the whole body, but only the head. The Chancellor greatly [appreciated this].
Yue. When Master Qian resided at Jiangshan, Zhen was from Anxi; he met Miaoxi on Huoyan Peak.
Subsequently, Assistant Minister You Gongxiang heard that the followers of Śākyamuni possessed a "Dharma for transcending the world" and his heart turned toward it with admiration.
He visited Chan Master Chiyuan of Guizong, intending to devise a plan for seclusion. Zhu Wen Gong sent him a poem which included the lines: "You who have fled to Chan, do not be in such haste."

To conclude the section on the circumstances within this district: during my tenure as Governor of Danchou, the Emperor summoned me to the palace balcony and personally asked, "What magnificent sights are there in the geographical maps of the Southern Terrace?
I replied, "The Great Peace and Abundant Blessings Temple, and the Ten-Thousand-Year Flourishing of Guoqing.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said, "I have heard that the Stone Bridge is the site where the five hundred arhats appeared suddenly during the Han dynasty. You..."
"What dharma do you dwell in? The Master raised his fist and said, "I have the Vajra-King Jewel Sword.

The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him the four characters "Sui-chu Lao-ren" (The Elder Who Accomplishes His Initial Purpose). Upon arriving at the prefecture, the Master governed the people with benevolence and compassion;

however, the southern region was frequently plagued by droughts and floods. The Master wrote a poem which says: "Before the rain falls, a single day becomes a vast deluge; once it clears, three days pass and..."
*Youqian*. Everyone says that Heaven is difficult to serve. When it comes to Heaven, even beyond Mount Tiantai, it is difficult.
The *Zhuangyuan* (Metropolitan Graduate), Duke Wang Shiming, while traveling to Wannian Temple on Mount Tiantai, had a dream one night involving the abbot Guang.
A divine being spoke to him, saying: "Tomorrow, the Head Seat Yan will arrive at the mountain. Early the next morning, when he was announced for reception, it was indeed the Duke.
The presiding monk called out, "Head Seat Yan, you have come! At that moment, the Duke was still ignorant of his true nature.

He asked the reason for this, and subsequently arrived at Stone Bridge. Upon reading the inscription on its stele, he realized the events of his previous life; he then composed a verse, which begins with the word "Stone."
Before reaching the bridge, he already knew it; entering the realm was like returning from a dream. The monk called me "Yan, the Head Seat.
In a previous life, I once wrote the inscription for the Stone Bridge at Mount Tiantai—the land where Buddhas and immortals dwell.

Through the power of my former efforts, I received a karmic response in this life, becoming the foremost in the world. Yet, even so, I had long since participated in the early teachings of the Vice Minister Suichu.

Master Zhishi later resided at Danqiu. He governed the people with compassion and protected the Teaching with reverence. That he obtained retribution after his passing—how can this be easily measured?
It is truly as the saying goes: "He possesses the precious sword of the Vajra King. How could this be mere empty talk?
The Court Gentleman Han Zicang sought the Way from Chan Master Qing of Caotang and sent him a letter, saying: "Recently, I have been reading the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp).
My understanding has surpassed my expectations, and it resonates deeply with my own mind. However, worldly entanglements are manifold and habitual tendencies are diverse;

it is not easy to dissolve them. There must be a vital point for focused application of the mind. I pray that you will not withhold your instruction. He replied: "If you wish to investigate this matter, you must first cultivate goodness..."
Do not allow either of these two paths of evil to sprout in your mind; they can obstruct the eye of human wisdom. You need not read many texts;

the gate of awakening is right before your eyes (and so forth). Having received this guidance, Zicang expressed his intent, saying: "The bells and tripods [of the court] and the mountain forests [of the hermit] are of one essence.
Amidst leisure is the aesthetic interest, and within stillness is the person. Bring all that is heard and seen back to empty illumination, nourishing one's nature and preserving the mind."
He did not answer. The Master was greatly pleased and addressed the assembly, saying: "Birds sing in the secluded trees, heralding mid-spring;
Though they have eyes, they are as if blind; their ears are deaf to sound. Outside the gate, the peach blossoms are nearly spent; I know not who can succeed to the spirit of Yun."
Pang Gong Lianggui of the Zhongshu Secretariat went to visit Chan Master Hongluo of Huqiu and asked, "How does one attain realization of the Way?

The Master said, "The Way belongs neither to knowledge nor to ignorance; simply investigate in this manner, and you will naturally attain realization. [Li]anggui said, "I do not yet understand these profound words;
I beg the Master to point it out once more. The Master said, "To know is deluded cognition; not to know is indeterminate consciousness (*avyākṛta*). See into this!"
He attained it. Duke Xu possessed a single eye. He pointed this out with a verse, saying: "Before the staff is raised, one already knows where it will fall—two or three steps ahead.
How could one possibly explain it through words? One must seek it for oneself. This old monk’s tongue is already too short; let us instead listen as empty space engages in dialogue."
Minister Li Gongchunian visited Mount Kuangshan (where Zhang Chan established his foundation) and invited Master Hua of Ying’an to say:

"Upon the summit of the high peak is a small Tiantai; the Dharma assembly is now being unfolded. Two hundred years ago there was a Zen practitioner who previously galloped forth and came within these very walls.
The Master replied: "This mountain is already superior to Tiantai; the summit is vast and silent."
The True Eye is opened; infinite waters and clouds are difficult to approach. Yet, it allows the Lord who Sweeps the Ground to come. The Lord responds with another verse:
"I beg leave to retire in leisurely ease, freed from the Three Dignities. I pray that the Mysterious Barrier of the Buddhas and Patriarchs be struck open.
The Fist of Killing and Giving must be displayed, lest people say I have deceived them into coming."

Zhang Gongyang, the Director of the Imperial Guard and a practitioner of the Yuezhai school, once visited Chan Master Mianjie. Later, he informed him in a letter of the manner in which he had attained realization, stating:

"In the past, when I first entered the meditation hall, I was graced by his oral instructions. Since returning home, amidst my various engagements, I have constantly used this matter to spur myself on."
One day, while sitting in meditation, he brought up the "dog" kōan. Suddenly, his chest opened wide like the vast void, entirely free of obstruction.
He realized that the words and phrases of the patriarchs are merely gateways for people to enter the Way; to cling to them and fail to let them go is a great illness.
From then on, worldly conditions and mundane thoughts did not require conscious effort to dispel; they were naturally purified and exhausted. Regarding the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients:
"What I was once bewildered by, I now have no doubt regarding (and so forth). The Master assembled the community and ascended the hall, saying:
'Dwelling amidst wealth and nobility, one is not misled by that wealth and nobility. With bare hands, one pushes open the gate of liberation;

in all four directions and eight points, one strides alone. Ha! Ha! Ha! How rare and precious! May those who hear, see, perceive, and know all join their palms together. An iron ox gives birth to a phoenix.'"
"Huáng'ér, Prime Minister Qian Xiàngxián has invited Chan Master Yuàn of this hermitage to the Huguo Temple to inquire about the Way. The Master said:

'If one wishes to investigate this matter, one must forget the dharma when the mind is attained, and forget the mind when the dharma is forgotten; only then can it be realized. If attachment to the dharma is not yet forgotten, even if one accords with the principle, [it is still insufficient]. "
"It is not a matter of awakening. The Duke said, "As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into the realm of conceptual thought.
How can one avoid falling into conceptual thought? The Master said, "It is fundamentally without sores; do not wound it. The Duke said, "To call this the 'Seal of the Mind' is but empty talk.

The Master said, "As soon as it touches the lips, it falls into conceptual thought. At these words, the Duke attained a sudden and profound realization. The Master then showed him a verse, which began: "The eyebrows..."
The eyelashes are most intimately joined; the nostrils and the lips are likewise neighbors. Why do these closest parts not see one another?
It is entirely because they are of one body, constituting the whole person.
The Inner Secretary (Zeng Gong) once went in person to see Chan Master Fohai Yuan, presenting him with a verse that said: "Alas! This blind donkey, a pestilence to the monastic groves!
With one roar that shakes the earth, the celestial mechanism is leaked. If someone further asks, 'What about this?
he picks up his whisk and suddenly cuts them across the mouth. Yuan said, "That too is a fine piece of wood."
Prime Minister Li Gong saw Chan Master Fuyan Cheng and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

He asked Cheng this three times, and each time Cheng pointed to the cypress tree in the courtyard in response. Li was joyfully enlightened and presented a verse, saying: "Appearing and disappearing amidst the clouds, filling the great void;
It turns out there is not a single speck of dust within the perfect circle. Again and again I asked about the meaning of the coming from the West; He only pointed [to the tree]."

Before the cypress tree in the courtyard, Zhao Gong Shanguan, the Vice Prefect, visited Chan Master Luyuan of Ruyuan in Shaoyou. Upon hearing the Master’s instruction to the monks regarding the "direct meaning from the West," he attained realization.
His verse says: "What is the direct meaning from the West? I have been singing for long, yet remain halfway there. The Hook.
The bandits reached home and were still defeated by the bandits. I now know for certain that I am wearing the broken military talisman upon my person.

When Minister Chen Gong Qufei visited Chan Master Dayuan Zhi, they discussed the Way together. Suddenly he attained realization and presented this verse, saying: "I have spontaneously attained the Dharma for settling the mind."
Leisurely, he did not compose poetry. Suddenly, on the Double Ninth, he could not help but gaze upon the chrysanthemum branches.
Zhang Gongshe of the Southern Studio visited Chan Master Wanan Yan and said: "Wherever the Way resides, it can be manifested through the mind."
"It cannot be sought through effort. The Master asked, "What do you mean? The Master said, "One who understands medicine has few illnesses. The Official said, "When I see it, I see it;
when I try to think about it, I am already at fault. What then? The Master said, "To know it is the same as not knowing it. The Official said, "..."

"How should one know when the time is right? The Master said, "Hearing sounds and seeing forms are exactly as they always have been. The official was suddenly enlightened. He remained there and composed a verse, saying:
"Hearing sounds and seeing forms are exactly as they always have been; Whoever examines them closely, the principle of the refined and the coarse naturally manifests.
It is like the void containing the azure sky; There has never been even a hair’s breadth of excess."
Dai-zhi Lu You, known as Gōngyǒu, asked Chan Master Sōnyuán Yuè of Línghyìn, "May I hear about the study of mind-to-mind transmission?

The Master said, "Since it is a transmission of the mind, how could it be obtained through hearing? Gōngyǒu attained understanding and offered this verse: The Way is not something that can be heard; How could it be grasped by means of words? If you wish to know the Buddha’s intent, Look directly at your own face before birth.
How many times have I driven my carriage into the imperial city? Whenever I encountered a monk, my eyes would turn green in unison. Only today do I realize the distinctiveness of the Chan school:
they speak of existence and discourse on emptiness, yet one must listen with the eye.
Chen Gong Guiqian, the State Counselor, inquired about the Dharma of the mind with Chan Master Yuelin Guan. The Master said, "The Buddha can be realized through awakening;
he cannot be sought through forms. To drown oneself in names and appearances while seeking him is like boiling sand in search of a meal. Gong drank this in silence and departed;
having reached the source through deep study, his mind regarding birth and death was shattered.
Furthermore, Master Zheng of Xishan twice sent letters inquiring about the essential points not yet transmitted. The Master replied: "I have long been asked about matters within the Chan school.
Looking up at your open-mindedness and delight in the good, I see that you ask whether or not one should contemplate a *hwadu*.
As I observe it, there is originally no fixed meaning to this. If not a single thought arises, the whole body is the Buddha; how then could there be a *hwadu*? And again:
Your instruction states: "To recite the words of the Buddha and practice the deeds of the Buddha, one will surely attain realization after a long time.

By practicing in this manner, one does not fail to become a virtuous person of this world. However, regarding the Zen school, one must see through to the fundamental radiance of one's own original ground before it can be considered ultimate. (And so forth.)
The layman Ti-chang Chen Yi was a scholar of Buddhism who attained profound clarity. He visited Chan Master Xuefeng Xu and presented this verse:
"In the secret seat, one investigates until the subtlest details are reached; In the end, one must spontaneously forget all artifice. There are no Buddhas or patriarchs who can transcend it."
How could body and mind still be subject to compliance or resistance? Though the solitary luminosity is vividly clear, one still recognizes it as a shadow;

though the towering presence is uniquely revealed, one still wears clothes over it. One laments those who claim to have attained realization and manifest spiritual power, yet even they say they sought a teacher and obtained something to return home with.
(Furthermore: Who knows the ultimate point within this? Those who know return, but those who arrive are rare. To see or hear is already a mistaken understanding; to depart from sound and...
The physical world turns contrary; the green mountains and blue waters clarify the profound principle. The cry of cranes and the song of orioles reveal the wondrous mechanism.
If you seek him with intention, you will never meet him; if you are without mind, you encounter him everywhere.

When Master Shui-xin Ye, the Minister of the Board of Rites, visited Chan Master Jian of Bei-jian while the latter was residing at Guangxiao Temple in Tai-zhou, the Minister addressed the Master with this verse:
"Master Jian’s poetic lines are truly startling; Six times you leap and soar, yet your body remains unmoving. Tell the fine sons and daughters of the eastern house:
Though they smear themselves with red and green, spring cannot be restrained. When the Master moved to Jingci Temple, eminent scholars and officials flocked to the capital.
There was not one who did not pass through his gate to pay their respects. Zhang Chengzi of Xujiang inscribed the Master’s collection, saying:

"Regarding his prose, Zongmi does not know whether he is senior or junior; as for his poetry, if one were to combine Chanliao and Juefan, they would together be but a single person, none of whom could equal him.
Although he established a name through his poetry and prose, his mastery of the Buddha-dharma was even more remarkable. When Mr. Shuixin retired to live among the fields, at that time—

Chan Master Zhao of Huaihai traveled to Dongjia and inscribed a poem at Jiangxin Temple. When the Duke heard that it contained verses of extraordinary elegance, he dispatched a messenger to invite him.
The Master presented three regulated verses; one of them reads: "Words flow like the Yangtze and Han rivers to the east, Long ago established the orthodox tradition from Yi and Luo.
Among the few figures since the Restoration, To the south of the Big Dipper, there is only you, O Duke. Upon hearing this, [the Duke]...

The Way governs with peace, as if drafting a petition on grass; my former arguments were never at odds with those of the Rong. Were it not for this, I would have long since departed through the imperial gates;
there remains only my solitary loyalty, the same as of old. In a poem for the Master’s farewell journey to Yandang:

The sea is vast and the Huai River deep, reaching ten thousand li. My poetic passion surges like the spring wind. Seeking further, I shall dwell by the precipitous Dragon Pool, Cutting and shaping mist and clouds into characters.
He was skilled in calligraphy. Later, the Master resided at Jiangxin. Through his stays at Yuyang, Jingci, Lingyin, and Shuangjing, his reputation resounded throughout the age.
The layman Xinzhai Ge Tan visited Chan Master Wuan Jin and later met Chan Master Fohai Yue.
He cited the words previously shown; Yue then composed a verse to expound upon them separately. One day, he cited the phrase "It is not mind.
[The master] attained sudden clarity and wide-open realization. The verse says: Neither mind, nor Buddha, nor yet any object— Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, the mountain looms abrupt.
Within the shadows of the slanting sun, he turns his body upside down; A solitary wild fox leaps into the den of the golden-haired lion.
The Grand Tutor Lü Gong Huìqīn cultivated the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* for thirty years. While reading Master Li’s *Avataṃsaka-śāstra*, he suddenly attained awakening to suchness (*tathatā*).
He composed this verse: "I have long desired to see Mañjuśrī, directing my mind toward Mount Wutai.
Who would have known that upon these yellow leaves, you pointed out the arrival of wondrous radiance?"
When the layman Zhigan Qian Chenggong Xiangzu was governing Jinling, he invited Chan Master Wuyong Quan to reside at Baoning.
[Qian] went there to inquire about the Way. He composed a verse for the occasion of Elder Ruiyan’s inauguration at a monastery, which says: "In years past, I too dwelt upon Mount Man;
From before the Hall of Empty Illumination, our messages passed. Since I have not changed my former way of walking, Why need one call out for the master again?"

The Elder: Zhi-xin, Layman Ji Si-lang Hao, frequently studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and visited the Patriarch Ying-’an Hua. Within less than ten days, he had ascended to the inner sanctum of the Dharma hall.
He sent a verse to his colleague, Professor Kang, which said: "At my gate is the shop of Sun Bin; at my home..."
Cun Gan-zhi’s wife: sleeping at night yet waking early. Who awakens and who is deluded?
County Magistrate Shi Qiao Tong asked Master Wei Hongzhi Jue, who sent this verse to Master Shi Chuang Gong:
"The mechanism is like wind and clouds, with release and gathering; The mind is like the bright moon, polished as an autumn mirror. In those years, he personally received from Heaven..."
Record of Tongji. The waters of the mountain stream are waveless as they flow upstream. Gong succeeded Hongzhi.
The State Councilor, Duke Fugong Zhirou, was a spiritual friend to Chan Master Lan’an Xu of Yishan.
As they parted, the Duke said: "I recall in years past we often met; your responsive discourse and eloquence were truly spirited. Now you are old."
I am returning home; I vow to bind our mutual longing into a future cause.
Minister Ceng Jifu once associated with Chan Master Kong of Dongshan and sent him a poem, which said: "The poetic style of Jiangxi was inherited by Master Kong;
he has long since turned away from worldly affairs to practice Chan, and no one can pull him back. His profound and secret gāthās are marvelous under heaven. No one [could match him].
As it appears in the *Dowip* (Record of the Way School):
When Grand Councilor Zheng Gong Qingxi sent Chan Master Gufeng Xiu to accept the invitation of Vice Minister Xiang of Fuyang to Mount Nang, he wrote:
"Recently I met Nan-shan at West Temple; we intended to accompany each other like solitary clouds in our leisure. This...
Having left Nangshan, it has been but two nights; solitary clouds come and go between the two mountains. (Furthermore: The name of this solitary peak has moved the Imperial Court;
the ink of the imperial inscription in the temple remains fresh. Ascending once more to the highest point of the solitary peak, one’s spirit pervades the great chiliocosm of dust-motes.
Master Hong of Pingzhai in the Zhongshu Secretariat was a relative of Master Li of Tianmu in their home village. He sent a verse to the Master which said:
"An inverted staff of withered vines stands in the evening breeze; The mountain’s glow does not flow eastward with the waters. The duckweed has fallen away and the reeds grow old;
Earth is vast and heaven is high—a single wild goose."
When Minister of State Cheng Gongxu was serving in the Ministry of Rites, he engaged in discussion with the Chan Master Shitian Xun.

They shared many profound insights regarding the hidden mysteries of the Dharma. The Minister once remarked: "The troubles of worldly involvement merely serve to accumulate the burdens of the mundane dust;

transformation through non-action is truly the essential path for transcending the world. He expressed this in a verse: "With you, I am of the same Mount Mei; You dwell [in the realm of the absolute]."
"The mountain forests are my capital and court; night is dark and day is bright—there is no duality in this view. How would it be to dwell together in the seclusion of the woods? The Master replied:
"Your Excellency’s deeds are sung in the folk songs of the people; I beg only that you preserve your integrity throughout your life under the Sage Court.

If you are willing to set your heart upon this Way, though we are in different circumstances, we are nonetheless of the same root. He further presented a verse to the Master: "Two feet accustomed to traveling the world..."
On the road, may you lend me one night’s rest; the moon falls through the pine-window, cold as if splashed upon me. In my paper tent, I dream deeply of Wei the Immortal;

accustomed to chewing wax, I have long grown weary of worldly flavors. Yet fearing that my study of the sutras might fall into mere verbal interpretation, the Master still harbors a touch of hometown sentiment—grant me this single blow directly to the chest.
Senior Minister Dan Shan, Mr. Weng He, returned from Guangdong. On the way, he encountered Mei Pass, where he saw the Covered Bowl Rock and the Chisel-Staff Spring.
He composed fifty-six characters and waited for the Elder Min of Nanhua to return so that he might present them to the Sixth Patriarch, while also sending them to the Elder Jianfeng, saying:
"The Buddha departed from this empty mountain six hundred years ago; The talk of Mei Pass remains as it was before. Free from dust..."
From where could anything be summoned? There is a Dharma difficult to transmit that resides within you. Within the seas, two schools divided into Northern and Southern;
atop the peaks, a single staff reached to the Western Heaven. If you can inquire of the Patriarch regarding the True Mind Seal, look at what is upon the Paṇḍaka Rock.
The Inner Secretary Su Yangzhi was visited by a monk who recited three poems by fellow monks. The first of them recognized the man as a madman; the second praised his skill.
When he recited the verse of Chan Master Cihang Puxian: "The mountains and rivers of the great earth are all but waves, Surging and surging, flowing day and night.
I look upon my own body like a small skiff; Only the old Yantou understands my song. Su realized that the man was a true kinsman.
The Duke said, "He is truly a Chan monk. Everyone agreed that he possessed the discerning eye of both the monastic and the lay.

Vice Minister Yegong Shuixin once sent a letter to Chan Master Lian of Shiyuan, in which he wrote: "I have often maintained that when the Buddha entered China, his teachings were initially regarded as a heterodox sect;
subsequently, they became entangled with the Way of the Sages. Those who possess resolve must apply their refinement to investigate this thoroughly."
Subtly, he sought to surpass [the Confucian tradition], yet in the end, he was unable to distinguish it from it; instead, his intent merely converged with theirs.

Since their aims were insufficient to illuminate both paths clearly, have scholars perhaps neglected this point? Recently, I have examined his writings and synthesized his doctrines; truly, there are points that accord with the discourse on *xingming* (nature and destiny).
However, the categories and items he discusses are extremely numerous, and the instances of internal contradiction are not few. Thus, one cannot simply say: "It is not so."
If one seeks with a mind that exists, it is as you say: "It cannot be attained by means of a non-existent mind. Which is right? Which is wrong? Which is contradictory? Which is to be followed?

Because of this, I have come to seek your earnest admonition and inspiration. He replied: "I have received your analogy; though the categories in the Buddhist scriptures are numerous, there are not few instances where they contradict one another.

How could I dare not set forth my own limited views? The Buddha takes precept, concentration, and wisdom as his fundamental principles. As for the objects of perception, they encompass the six sense faculties, yet [the mind] remains unmoving."
The mirror of the mind is unconfused by any conditions. The sun and moon shine brightly; rain and dew moisten all things; waters flow and flowers bloom;
hawks soar and fish leap—all these are fully possessed within my own nature. Beyond direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the essential point lies in illuminating the myriad differences as one.

When principle and phenomena merge in harmony, after long days and deep months, the wondrous wisdom of true emptiness will spontaneously seal the original mind. Your Eminence, you gallop like a thoroughbred horse, following in the footsteps of Shengyan and Xuanzang.
From Confucius’s hurried errands to Mencius, Xunzi, Dong Zhongshu, and Jia Yi—who among them could claim that it is difficult to discern what accords with nature?

This is simply because delusive wisdom has not yet been dispelled, false sentiments have not yet been eliminated, and floating thoughts entangled with external conditions have congested the source of the mind.

The ancient masters employed manifold methods of guidance and instruction, not limited to a single path. If one can withdraw the gaze and turn the hearing inward, there is fundamentally no Buddha apart from the mind. Not...

"Whenever questions are asked, the categories are numerous; this is because their words are contradictory. From this, Master Gong came to understand where [Buddhism] leads. In a letter to Zhu Wen-gong, he wrote:

"While I was in Jingzhou, I had nothing else to do but read Buddhist scriptures. Thereupon I realized that these marvelous and extraordinary doctrines from beyond the world are fundamentally incapable of being confused with the Way of Governance (political philosophy).
The reason why they have become intermingled and the subject of dispute is simply that readers have not investigated them deeply."
Master Zhu Wenong once spoke to his students, saying: "The Chan Master Qing of Caotang once told beginners:
'Do you not see how a cat catches a mouse? Its four paws are planted firmly on the ground; its head and tail are aligned in a straight line; its eyes do not blink; its mind has no other thought.
Because it remains motionless, when it finally moves, the mouse has nowhere to escape. I urge you to apply these words, and you will surely attain something."
They enter [the Way]. Although their practice differs from the Way, that which they attain is without distinction between self and other.
For this reason, Wu Gong Wenzhao, the Governor of Huizhou, when the monk Chong brought with him the Chief Seat Ben of Mount Jing, composed a verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
A venomous snake and a fierce tiger stand blocking the road; an iron wall and silver mountains lie across behind. There is no door to exit and no path to retreat.
How can one express this in ordinary terms? Master He replied: "A venomous snake and fierce tiger face each other in vain;
