An iron wall and silver mountains needlessly stretch across. It is best to return upon the sound of a single long flute; Where else would you seek the source of doubt?"
At Shijia Temple in Liuhe County, Zhenzhou, there was Master Miaoying, whose secular name was Bo Hua.
He traveled among the scholar-officials with his art of physiognomy, and his predictions regarding misfortune or fortune, longevity or early death, were frequently and remarkably accurate.

In a letter from the Minister of Revenue Sun Zhongyi to his elder brother, the Palace Secretary Shu Ni, it is briefly stated: "When I visited Quanzhou, I went to see Master Miaoying; I took my bedding with me and followed him through."
In his evening discourse, [Dahui] remarked that for Duan [Shicheng], death was still far off. His faith and compliance can be seen from this.

As for Master Sun’s actual lifespan, it reached the age of *qiyi* (one hundred and ten). Although Hua possessed extraordinary abilities and understanding, he remained steadfastly committed to the practice of *dhūta*.

Zhang [Zongyan] held Master Sun in particularly deep esteem and profound regard; he inscribed a verse upon his portrait, saying: "The ground of his mind is vast and tranquil, originally devoid of things; his countenance is carefree and elegant."
Yi had naturally transcended the mundane world. Daily he recited one *zàng* of the Avalokiteśvara Dharani; his spiritual practice was such that it could ferry those lost at the ford.
When Jiaorun’s seat at Mount Xiao was vacant, he invited Hua to preside over it. Hua declined with vigor, saying, "I am but a fool who has never studied Chan.
How would I dare to rashly undertake such a matter? Those who heard this praised his words as virtuous. Administrative Commissioner Li Taifa often sent him poems, one of which said: "I wish..."

He knows that ears and eyes are the true ladder. His life-force bones are lofty and arched, piercing the *fuxi* mark. In his later years, he no longer sent news from the Plum Ridge; throughout his life, his companions were equal to Zhaozhou.
The *sūtras* and *śāstras* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges constantly turned within his mind; the tongs and hammer of the ancient Buddhas he carried in his own hands.
Having surely traversed the mountains and rivers of the two Guang provinces, he packed his bag and traveled together through the east and west. Alas! Those in this world who harbor their arts—
Those who steal fame and presumptuously occupy great monasteries are merely acting out of vanity; you ought to diminish such pretensions somewhat.

The Record-keeper Ji of Huye was a distant descendant of the Imperial Guard Commandant Li Wenhe of Tiantai. Having received the position of Record-keeper at Lingyin and served as the secretary for literary correspondence at Jingci, he was admired by his contemporaries for his refined elegance.
Yet when he became reckless and wild, he would entrust his writings to taverns, and there were instances where his conduct sullied his reputation.
The Master was sent to the Heavenly Treasury (the capital). Lord Zhao, the Governor of the Prefecture, ordered him to submit a written statement. In his petition, the Master wrote a single verse:
"Lax and indolent, I have donned the black robes for forty years; My affinity has mostly been with poetry and wine. I idly watch the play within Maitreya’s radiance."

"Intoxicated, he sleeps atop the crown of Vairocana; casting off his hands, he can outwit the Ten Sages. Bowing his head, he pays no heed to the Three Worthies. Throughout the vast universe, no one recognizes him;
they merely say this mad monk disturbs the marketplace. After Yin finished reading it, he immediately released him.

He further composed a parting poem for the Magistrate of Tiantai, saying: "In youth, you have mastered the arts of governance, filling your noble aspirations; you shall surely stride boldly upward to Mount Penglai."
Leai [the blade] has made a small trial with the ox-knife in a town of a thousand households; the steed’s hooves were originally not for the talent of a mere hundred-li journey.

Though the farewell banquet sang of being urged to depart at dawn, the harmonious atmosphere brought down from his carriage surpassed the return of spring. Do not worry that there will be no one to recommend you on the road ahead; there is surely a connoisseur waiting outside the provincial office.
After death, he paid his respects, saying: "The leg-wrap strikes high, the inspiration is inexhaustible; leaning on his staff, he enters the clouds."
Amidst the chaotic peaks, someone asked the mountain monk where he was going. He replied, "The ancient tradition of Tiantai and Nanyue.
Although men of high station repeatedly invited him to famous monasteries, he did not accept.
Chan Master Fushu was a native of Yutian in Fuzhou. He shared the teaching seat at Kaiyuan Temple in Fusha.

When Provincial Governor Cheng Gongbi vacated a monastery to select someone to fill the position, he invited the Master for an audience. Upon seeing that the Master’s appearance was unrefined, the Governor ultimately said nothing and withdrew.
He further ordered his attendants to carry a reed boat and a copy of the *Dharmapada* to request the Master’s praise. They caught up with him on the bank of a stream south of the water.

The Master took a brush and wrote: "Vast and empty, there is no sage; the tip of the tongue is bald. A single reed spans the waves as my clumsy stratagem fails. Advancing, there is no gate; retreating, there is no path.
The cries of the shorebirds cut short the wind across the river. When he commanded them again to welcome the Master, the Master then vanished.
The Senior Seat Huaiwang Shan Xuanshou first heard Master Xiang’s night discourse at Huangbo in Junyang, where he was moved by the words:
“A single leaf drifting through the void reveals autumn; the Dharma-body must penetrate the clamor. He attained realization. Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Jing to see Dahui.
When Zen Master Rimen Wen received the summons from Mount Huaiyu, Xuanshou went with him, and together they established a dharma community.
Wang Shengxi was serving as the Magistrate of Yichun and requested that Foyan Xuan reside at Nanyuan. Xuan rebuffed him, saying, "I am but a monk who lives on alms;
I truly have no desire to appear in the world. When Wang She-ren Yang climbed the mountain to visit him, he presented him with a poem which said:

"A master of robes and alms, ever content with his bowl of rice— No one has ever seen him descend the mountain. When we meet, he says only that he has no skill to offer; How could he possibly act as..."
*Honglou Yingzhi Shi* (Poems Composed for the Imperial Court Regarding Honglou).
The head seat Deguan of Tian’ai Jingsingyan had lived in seclusion for thirty years, never venturing beyond the mountains.

When Provincial Governor Geng of Longxue took office in the region, he specifically sent an invitation from Ruiyan to welcome him. Deguan declined with a verse, which said: "For over thirty years, I have alone kept my door closed..."
How could an official pass from the customs office ever reach the green mountains? Cease using the trivial affairs of the human world to trade for my lifelong leisure beneath the forest trees.
When the imperial messenger arrived again, he firmly declined the appointment. Master Geng laughed and said, "Today, you are of the lineage of Yishan."
The Head Seat Juefeng Qiong wore a single robe through both cold and heat for over forty years, never setting foot among the laity.

When Prime Minister Zhao Ruyu, Prince of Fu, governed Fujian, he heard of his reputation and repeatedly offered him the leadership of great monasteries, yet Qiong consistently declined. He sent a verse to him which said:
"Upon the ten-thousand-fathom peak, snow forms a mound; A single withered tree leans against the crag’s edge. Its green remains unchanged through the passing seasons."
Han Cao: "I shall wait for the spring breeze to blow; it will not turn me back. At that time, all those in the military command tent harmonized with him.

The head seat Baiyun Jizhao had kept his door closed for forty years. When Zhao Gong Xijing, the Military Commissioner of Fu, sent emissaries three times with an invitation from Xuefeng, he declined with a verse, saying:
"By nature, I am a monk of the Imperial Court who has nothing to do; I discuss the profound and speak of the Way."
Lacking all capacity, he languidly lets the days pass, still finding them burdensome. How could he dare to soil the ancestral lamp with empty fame? He holds his ground and will not yield;
let no one wrest from him his resolve.
Nanchang Xin was beyond doubt a man of talent; he had already achieved renown for his poetry. Xu Shichuan and Hong Yupu ranked his verses as lofty and ancient.
Later, he followed Dahui to Hengyang, where he lived in seclusion. At Daowu, he stripped wood to build a leaf-hut for his own cultivation.

When Zhang Gong, the Layman of Yuhu, governed Tanzhou, he heard of his reputation and exerted great effort to invite him to emerge from reclusion at Luyuan in Xiangxi, presenting him with [a letter of recommendation].
The poem says: "A scroll of poetry has accompanied me for forty years; In the midst of busyness, I have realized the Zen of the bamboo whisk.

Now, in my old age, I dwell in a temple west of the Xiang River; Lying down, I watch the waters of the Xiang strike the heavens. (And: "Within these lines there is an eye; only through awakening does one know it.
At the place of awakening, one must surely apply the awl with force. Body and mind are one, not two separate functions— When Niaoke picked up the cloth hair and blew upon it, faith was born."
The Harmony says: The story of the bamboo whisk was selected for that year. Directly beneath it, no self-interest—this is not Chan.
Having encountered the true eye of the Champion, I dare to take up the agalloch incense before the assembly of humans and devas.
Shitan Jieshouzuo was invited by Wang Gong Dachang, the Transport Commissioner of Huaidong, to [join him at] Tianning Monastery in Yizhen.
He declined with a verse, saying: "A single awakening brings the mind empty and the myriad realms at rest; Who would be willing to let their name fall among men?
How is it that only Master Wang Insists on binding this mountain with official documents? Wang Gong Bo-da, the Grand Councilor, then invited him to [join him at] Chi[shan].

Yang Meishan. Yan Gong Yizhong, the Vice Minister, invited him to Tianning Monastery in Yan, but he declined both times. He subsequently built a thatched hut on Mount Tianmu. Master Hong Tiao of Pingzhai said to him: "Two points of eye-light upon the bull’s back; a nest of spring colors by the falling flowers. Worldly ties do not reach such a deep mountain place, yet I fear that the very depth of the mountains will give rise to worldly ties. The Master replied: [The Master’s verse: "The moon is high, the clouds are thin; The mountain road is long, the valley deep. A single staff leans against the wall; The cold window receives the morning light. The world has no news of me; I have no news of the world. Master Hong Tiao said: "How can you say there is no news? The sound of the wind in the pines and the cry of the night bird—these are all news. The Master replied: "If one hears it, it is news; if one does not hear it, it is not news. Master Hong Tiao said: "If you do not hear it, how do you know it is not news? The Master replied: "If I knew it was not news, I would be hearing it. During the Great Yuan’s auspicious era, our dynasty was founded and established across the realm, encompassing all four quarters.
Emperor Taizu, the Holy Martial Sovereign, grasped the Mandate of Heaven and rose from the northern lands; through his divine prowess, he assumed the destiny of an emperor.

Emperor Taizong, following the succession of the various sagely ancestors, brought his great enterprise to fruition. He utterly destroyed the remnants of the Jin and pacified Bian and Cai, bringing stability to Central China.

However, hearing that his realm was once again disturbed by the conscription of troops, the common people were struck with alarm; he then dispatched couriers on horseback to return home, while his kinsmen and allies escorted him back in their carriages.
Emperor Shizu was the foremost among the legitimate grandsons of Emperor Taizu and stood among the ranks of the late Emperor’s maternal brothers;
he was the eldest by virtue of his excellence, being the sole individual in that position. Even amidst the intervals of military campaigns, [he remained steadfast].

Furthermore, he possessed benevolence and compassion, generously bestowing gifts to relieve the masses; he was truly fit to be the sovereign of the world. In the fourth month of the gengshen year, he ascended the imperial throne.
